# Apache Airflow

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Airflow

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2015 (open sourced by Airbnb)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">3.4.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-11-06</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Python</Field>
  <Field name="type">Workflow orchestration platform</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[airflow.apache.org](https://airflow.apache.org)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/airflow](https://github.com/apache/airflow)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Airflow 3.4.0 release notes and documentation, PyPI (apache-airflow 3.4.0, apache-airflow-providers-apache-spark 6.3.4) and the provider source at tag providers-apache-spark/6.3.4</Verified>

**Apache Airflow** is an open source platform for developing, scheduling and monitoring workflows, such as batch data pipelines and machine learning jobs, in which each workflow is defined as Python code.[^index] Airflow does not process data itself; it decides when tasks run, in what order, and what happens when they fail. In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Airflow commonly starts the [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) jobs and other steps that load and transform tables.

## Concepts

An Airflow workflow is a **Dag** (directed acyclic graph): a model that holds everything needed to run a workflow, including its schedule, its tasks and the dependencies between them, and callbacks for when it completes.[^index] Because Dags are Python code, they can be generated dynamically and parameterized.[^index]

Each step in a Dag is a **task**, usually created from an **operator**, a reusable template for one kind of work such as running a shell command or submitting a Spark job. Operators for external systems are shipped in separately versioned **provider** packages.[^spark-ops]

## Architecture

In Airflow 3.4, a minimal installation has the following required components:[^arch]

- a **scheduler**, which triggers scheduled workflows and submits tasks to the **executor** (a configuration of the scheduler that runs inside the scheduler process, not a separate component);
- a **Dag processor**, which parses Dag files from a **Dag bundle** and stores them in serialized form in the metadata database;
- an **API server**, which serves the REST API and the user interface, and through which tasks report their state back to Airflow without direct database access;
- a **metadata database**, usually PostgreSQL or MySQL, which stores the state of tasks, Dags and variables.

Optional components include **workers** (for example long-running processes with the CeleryExecutor, or pods with the KubernetesExecutor), a **triggerer** that runs deferred tasks in an asyncio event loop, and a plugins folder.[^arch]

## History

Maxime Beauchemin started Airflow at Airbnb in October 2014. It was open sourced on Airbnb's GitHub and announced in June 2015. The project entered the Apache Incubator in March 2016, and the ASF announced Apache Airflow as a top-level project in January 2019.[^n1]

Airflow 2.0.0 was published on 17 December 2020 and Airflow 3.0.0 on 22 April 2025.[^pypi] Airflow 3 introduced the Task Execution Interface (AIP-72), which moves Airflow toward a client-server architecture with an API server and a Python Task SDK, along with Dag versioning, a new React-based user interface and event-driven scheduling on data assets.[^n2] The latest release on 22 November 2026 is Airflow 3.4.0, released on 6 November 2026.[^n3]

## Orchestrating Apache Spark

Airflow runs Spark through the `apache-airflow-providers-apache-spark` provider package. Its latest version on 22 November 2026 is 6.3.4, published on 24 October 2026; it requires Airflow 2.11.0 or later and Python 3.11 or later.[^n4][^pyproject] Version 6.3.4 contains these operators:[^spark-ops][^src]

| Operator | Module | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SparkSubmitOperator` | `operators.spark_submit` | Wraps the `spark-submit` binary to launch an application; the default connection is `spark_default`. |
| `SparkSqlOperator` | `operators.spark_sql` | Runs a Spark SQL query through the `spark-sql` binary. |
| `SparkJDBCOperator` | `operators.spark_jdbc` | Extends `SparkSubmitOperator` to move data between Spark and JDBC databases. |
| `PySparkOperator` | `operators.spark_pyspark` | Runs a Python function that receives a Spark session, locally or against a [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) server; also available as the `@task.pyspark` decorator. |
| `SparkPipelinesOperator` | `operators.spark_pipelines` | Wraps the `spark-pipelines` CLI to run or dry-run a [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines) project. |

`PySparkOperator` became available as an operator in provider 5.5.0, and `SparkPipelinesOperator` was added in 5.6.0.[^changelog] `SparkPipelinesOperator` takes a `pipeline_spec` path and a `pipeline_command` of `run` (the default) or `dry-run`.[^n5]

The following Dag, for Airflow 3.4 with provider 6.3.4, checks a declarative pipeline with a dry run, runs it, and then submits a Spark application:

```python
from datetime import datetime

from airflow.sdk import DAG
from airflow.providers.apache.spark.operators.spark_pipelines import SparkPipelinesOperator
from airflow.providers.apache.spark.operators.spark_submit import SparkSubmitOperator

with DAG(
    dag_id="lakehouse_daily",
    schedule="@daily",
    start_date=datetime(2026, 11, 1),
    catchup=False,
):
    check = SparkPipelinesOperator(
        task_id="pipeline_dry_run",
        pipeline_spec="/opt/pipelines/sales/spark-pipeline.yml",
        pipeline_command="dry-run",
    )
    run = SparkPipelinesOperator(
        task_id="pipeline_run",
        pipeline_spec="/opt/pipelines/sales/spark-pipeline.yml",
    )
    report = SparkSubmitOperator(
        task_id="build_report",
        application="/opt/jobs/build_report.py",
    )

    check >> run >> report
```

## Use in an open lakehouse

Airflow sits above the engines in an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse). It can order ingestion, transformation and maintenance jobs that run on Spark, [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) or other engines against tables in [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) or [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) format. With [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines), the division of work is that SDP orders the datasets inside one pipeline, while Airflow schedules the pipeline as a whole and connects it to work outside Spark.

# Apache Celeborn

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Celeborn

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) (originally Alibaba)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">0.7.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-08-16</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Java, Scala</Field>
  <Field name="type">[Remote shuffle service](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Remote_shuffle_service)</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[celeborn.apache.org](https://celeborn.apache.org)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/celeborn](https://github.com/apache/celeborn)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink), [Apache Uniffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Uniffle), [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v0.7.0 tag of apache/celeborn (README.md, docs/README.md, docs/deploy.md, docs/deploy_on_k8s.md, docs/configuration/client.md, docs/decommissioning.md), the Celeborn download page, the Celeborn incubation status page and proposal, and the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark</Verified>

**Apache Celeborn** is an open source [remote shuffle service](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Remote_shuffle_service): a cluster of master and worker servers that stores and serves the intermediate [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle) data of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) and Hadoop MapReduce jobs, so that the data does not live on the compute nodes' local disks. The project describes itself as an intermediate data service whose current focus is shuffle data.[^readme] Celeborn is a top-level project of the Apache Software Foundation.

## History

Celeborn was started at Alibaba in 2020 under the name "RemoteShuffleService" and open sourced in 2021.[^proposal] It entered the Apache Incubator on 2022-10-18, made its first Apache release (0.2.0-incubating) on 2023-03-01, and graduated to a top-level project on 2024-03-21.[^incubator]

The latest release is 0.7.0, published on 2026-08-16.[^download] In 0.3.0 the Spark shuffle manager class was renamed from `org.apache.spark.shuffle.celeborn.RssShuffleManager` to `org.apache.spark.shuffle.celeborn.SparkShuffleManager`.[^readme]

## Architecture

A Celeborn cluster has three components:[^readme]
- **Master** manages resources and keeps shared state consistent across master nodes with the Raft protocol.
- **Worker** handles read and write requests and merges the data for each reducer.
- **Client**, including the **LifecycleManager**, which keeps the metadata of each shuffle and runs inside the Spark driver.

Celeborn balances load with **slots**, a logical count of how many partitions a worker can hold. A worker's slot count is its total usable disk size divided by the average shuffle file size, and the master spreads partitions across workers by tracking slot usage.[^readme]

## How does a shuffle work with Celeborn?

In a Celeborn shuffle, map tasks push their data to workers instead of writing it to local disk. The README describes the steps: mappers register the shuffle with the LifecycleManager, which requests slots from the master; workers reserve the slots and create files; mappers push data to the assigned workers, which merge it, replicate it to a peer and flush it to disk; once all mappers finish, the workers commit the files, and reducers ask for file locations and read the merged data.[^readme]

Server-side replication is controlled by `celeborn.client.push.replicate.enabled` (default false). The deployment guide recommends turning it on, except when there is only one worker or when HDFS is the storage.[^readme][^clientconf]

## Which engines does Celeborn support?

The 0.7.0 release supports:[^readme][^quickstart]
- **[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)** 3.0 through 4.2. Spark 4.x clients need Java 17 and Scala 2.13.
- **[Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink)** 1.18 through 2.3, for batch jobs only. Flink loads Celeborn through its `shuffle-service-factory.class` setting.
- **Hadoop MapReduce** 3.
- **Apache Tez**, with a client the README marks as experimental.

## How do you use Celeborn with Apache Spark?

A Spark application uses Celeborn by putting the Celeborn client jar on the classpath and replacing the shuffle manager. The deployment guide's settings include:[^readme]

```properties
spark.shuffle.manager               org.apache.spark.shuffle.celeborn.SparkShuffleManager
spark.serializer                    org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer
spark.celeborn.master.endpoints     clb-1:9097,clb-2:9097,clb-3:9097
spark.shuffle.service.enabled       false
# Dynamic allocation without the external shuffle service (Spark 3.5.0 or later)
spark.shuffle.sort.io.plugin.class  org.apache.spark.shuffle.celeborn.CelebornShuffleDataIO
spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled false
```

Spark selects the shuffle implementation with `spark.shuffle.manager` and the shuffle storage implementation with `spark.shuffle.sort.io.plugin.class`; Celeborn plugs into both.[^sparkconf] A Kryo serializer is required because the Java serializer does not support relocation of serialized objects. The guide also recommends keeping [AQE](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_query_execution) and skew-join handling on, and setting `spark.sql.adaptive.localShuffleReader.enabled` to false.[^readme]

## How is Celeborn deployed?

Celeborn runs as its own cluster, separate from the compute engine. On hosts, operators start masters and workers with `sbin/start-master.sh` and `sbin/start-worker.sh`; for high availability, several masters form a Raft group.[^deploy] On [Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Kubernetes), the project provides a Helm chart.[^k8s]

Workers store shuffle data on local disks or remote storage. `celeborn.storage.availableTypes` accepts `MEMORY`, `HDD`, `SSD`, `HDFS`, `S3` and `OSS`, with `HDD` as the default.[^clientconf] Workers can be decommissioned through a REST API, which lets an operator drain a worker before removing it.[^n1]

## Celeborn compared with Apache Uniffle

<Hatnote>Main article: [Remote shuffle service](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Remote_shuffle_service)</Hatnote>

[Apache Uniffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Uniffle) is the other remote shuffle service at the ASF. Both push map output to dedicated servers and plug into Spark through `spark.shuffle.manager`. Celeborn's 0.7.0 release covers Spark up to 4.2 and Flink batch jobs, while Uniffle 0.10.0 lists Spark 2.3 to 3.5, MapReduce and Tez.[^readme][^n2] The [Remote shuffle service](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Remote_shuffle_service) article has a full comparison table.

- [Apache Uniffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Uniffle)
- [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle)
- [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor)

# Apache DataFusion Comet

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_DataFusion_Comet

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Comet</Field>
  <Field name="developer">Apache Software Foundation (sub-project of Apache DataFusion); originally developed at Apple</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">0.1.0 (July 2024); 1.0.0 on 2026-08-07</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">1.2.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-11-03</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Rust, Scala, Java</Field>
  <Field name="type">Native execution plugin for Apache Spark</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[datafusion.apache.org/comet](https://datafusion.apache.org/comet)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/datafusion-comet](https://github.com/apache/datafusion-comet)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Apache Gluten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Gluten), [Native execution engine (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Native_execution_engine_(Spark)), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Project Tungsten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Tungsten)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the GitHub releases and tags of apache/datafusion-comet (1.0.0, 1.1.0, 1.2.0), README.md and the user guide at the 1.2.0 tag (installation, Spark version compatibility, configs, operators, Iceberg, Delta Lake, memory tuning), the Comet versus Gluten comparison page, the top-level project proposal page and issue #6793, and the Apache Arrow blog post of 2024-03-06 announcing the donation</Verified>

**Apache DataFusion Comet** (usually just **Comet**) is an open source plugin for [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) that replaces supported Spark SQL operators and expressions with implementations that process Apache Arrow columnar data, most of them native Rust code built on the Apache DataFusion query engine.[^readme] Spark still parses, optimizes and schedules the query, and existing Spark SQL, DataFrame and PySpark code runs without changes.[^readme] Comet is a sub-project of Apache DataFusion and one of the [native execution engines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Native_execution_engine_(Spark)) available for Spark.[^tlp]

## What is Apache DataFusion Comet?

Apache DataFusion Comet is a Spark plugin that translates a Spark physical plan into a serialized form and passes it to native code for execution. Comet uses its own Protocol Buffers format for the plan, and execution is delegated to Apache DataFusion, a query engine written in Rust.[^cmp] Unlike [Apache Gluten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Gluten), which supports several native backends, Comet is built for one engine and does not plan to support others.[^cmp]

Apache DataFusion Comet keeps data in Arrow columnar format through operators, expressions, shuffle and broadcast. Inside that pipeline, operators and expressions run either as Rust code through DataFusion or as JVM code that works directly on Arrow batches.[^readme]

## History and status

Apache DataFusion Comet was originally implemented at Apple. The Apache Arrow project management committee announced the donation of Comet to Apache Arrow on 2024-03-06; at that time DataFusion was itself part of Arrow.[^donation] When DataFusion became a top-level ASF project in April 2024, Comet became a sub-project of Apache DataFusion.[^tlp]

Apache DataFusion Comet published its first release, 0.1.0, in July 2024. Version 1.0.0 followed on 2026-08-07 and 1.1.0 on 2026-10-06.[^tlp] The latest release is 1.2.0, published on GitHub on 2026-11-03.[^rel120]

The Comet community is preparing to make Comet a separate top-level ASF project named "Apache Comet". As of 2026-11-23 this is a proposal: the tracking issue is open, the board resolution has not been adopted, and the plan lists the 2026-12-16 ASF board meeting as the target.[^tlp][^epic]

## Which Spark versions does Comet support?

Apache DataFusion Comet 1.2.0 supports Apache Spark 3.4, 3.5, 4.0, 4.1 and 4.2. The installation guide lists the tested patch versions 3.4.3, 3.5.9, 4.0.4, 4.1.3 and 4.2.0.[^install] Spark 4.3 is not on the list. Comet requires JDK 17 or later; JDK 11 support ended with the 1.1.0 release. Spark 3.4 support has been deprecated since 1.0.0 and is planned for removal.[^install]

The installation guide also notes that Comet may not fully work with proprietary forks of Apache Spark, such as the Spark versions offered by cloud service providers.[^install]

## How does Comet work with Apache Spark?

Apache DataFusion Comet is added to the Spark class path as a JAR built for a given Spark and Scala version, and enabled through Spark's plugin interface. A typical configuration from the project README:[^readme]

```bash
$SPARK_HOME/bin/spark-shell \
    --jars $COMET_JAR \
    --conf spark.driver.extraClassPath=$COMET_JAR \
    --conf spark.executor.extraClassPath=$COMET_JAR \
    --conf spark.plugins=org.apache.spark.CometPlugin \
    --conf spark.shuffle.manager=org.apache.spark.sql.comet.execution.shuffle.CometShuffleManager \
    --conf spark.comet.explain.fallback.enabled=true \
    --conf spark.memory.offHeap.enabled=true \
    --conf spark.memory.offHeap.size=4g \
    --conf spark.executor.memoryOverhead=2g
```

Apache DataFusion Comet has two main switches. `spark.comet.enabled` (default true) turns the extension on, and `spark.comet.exec.enabled` (default true) turns on native execution; both must be on for operators to run natively.[^configs]

Comet shuffle is controlled by `spark.comet.shuffle.enabled`, which requires `spark.shuffle.manager` to be set to `CometShuffleManager` or, for Apache Celeborn, `CometCelebornShuffleManager`. Shuffle data is written as Arrow IPC and compressed with lz4 by default (`spark.comet.shuffle.compression.codec`, which also accepts zstd and snappy).[^configs] The native shuffle supports hash and range partitioning, with a JVM path for partition key types that the native code does not handle.[^readme]

Apache DataFusion Comet shares Spark's off-heap memory pool, sized by `spark.memory.offHeap.size`, as a budget for its reservations. Native memory that the pools do not track has to fit in `spark.executor.memoryOverhead`.[^memory] The default pool type, set by `spark.comet.exec.memoryPool`, is `fair_unified`.[^configs]

## What runs natively and what falls back?

Apache DataFusion Comet runs whole subtrees of native operators together. If a query stage contains an operator that Comet does not support, that stage falls back to regular Spark execution, and the operator reference states that results are unaffected.[^ops] Each supported operator can be turned off with `spark.comet.exec.OPERATOR.enabled=false`, for example `spark.comet.exec.sort.enabled=false`.[^ops]

Natively supported work in Comet 1.2.0 includes Parquet scans, projections and filters, hash aggregates, hash, sort-merge and broadcast joins, and shuffle, plus hundreds of Spark expressions in the math, string, date and time, array, map, JSON, hash and predicate categories.[^readme] Structured Streaming operators, Cartesian joins, pickled (non-Arrow) Python UDFs and typed Dataset operators such as `map` and `groupByKey` fall back to Spark and are not on the roadmap.[^ops]

Apache DataFusion Comet can report why a stage did not run natively. `spark.comet.explain.fallback.enabled` (default false) logs the reasons, and the extended explain format `spark.comet.explain.format` (default `verbose`) annotates the plan with fallback reasons and a summary of how much of it was accelerated.[^configs]

## Does Comet support Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake?

Apache DataFusion Comet has a native [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) reader that scans data and delete files in Rust and is enabled by default; `spark.comet.scan.icebergNative.enabled=false` turns it off. The guide says it was tested with Iceberg 1.5, 1.8, 1.9, 1.10 and 1.11 and with Hadoop, Hive and REST catalogs ([Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog)). Native Iceberg writes are off by default and enabled with `spark.comet.write.iceberg.enabled=true`. HDFS-backed tables fall back to Spark.[^iceberg]

Support for [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) in Comet is experimental. It covers DSv1 Delta table scans through Comet's native Parquet scan, needs a separate `comet-contrib-delta-spark` JAR next to `delta-spark`, and is off by default (`spark.comet.scan.delta.enabled`).[^delta]

## Comet vs Gluten

Apache DataFusion Comet and [Apache Gluten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Gluten) have similar architectures: both are Spark plugins that serialize the physical plan and execute it natively. Gluten serializes plans as Substrait and supports several engines ([Velox](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Velox) and ClickHouse in Gluten 1.7.0), while Comet uses its own Protocol Buffers format and only DataFusion. The comparison page, maintained by the Comet community and described there as likely biased, names the implementation language (Rust for DataFusion, C++ for Velox) as the main practical difference, for example for teams that write native UDFs.[^cmp] See [Native execution engine (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Native_execution_engine_(Spark)) for a wider comparison.

# Apache Gluten

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Gluten

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">Apache Software Foundation; initiated by Intel and Kyligence</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2022 (project start); entered the Apache Incubator on 2023-12-15</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">1.7.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-08-26</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala, C++, Java</Field>
  <Field name="type">Native execution plugin for Apache Spark SQL</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[gluten.apache.org](https://gluten.apache.org)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/gluten](https://github.com/apache/gluten)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Velox](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Velox), [Apache DataFusion Comet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_DataFusion_Comet), [Native execution engine (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Native_execution_engine_(Spark)), [Project Tungsten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Tungsten)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Apache Incubator status page for Gluten, the ASF graduation announcement of 2026-03-05, the ASF board history page for Gluten, the GitHub releases of apache/gluten (v1.7.0 and v1.8.0-rc0), the Gluten downloads page, and README.md, docs/Configuration.md and docs/backends/velox/get-started/Velox.md on the main branch and the v1.7.0 tag</Verified>

**Apache Gluten** is an open source plugin for [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) that converts Spark SQL physical plans into plans for a native engine, such as [Velox](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Velox) or ClickHouse, and runs the supported parts of a query in native code instead of in the Java virtual machine (JVM).[^readme] Gluten keeps Spark's scheduling, fault tolerance and APIs, so DataFrame code and SQL queries do not change; only the cluster configuration does.[^readme] Gluten is a top-level project of the Apache Software Foundation (ASF) since 2026, and it is one of the [native execution engines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Native_execution_engine_(Spark)) available for Spark.[^incubator]

## What is Apache Gluten?

Apache Gluten is a middle layer between Spark and a native SQL engine. Its README describes the design principle as reusing Spark's control flow while offloading compute-intensive data processing to the native side. The name is Latin for "glue".[^readme]

Apache Gluten converts the Spark physical plan into a [Substrait](https://substrait.io) plan, passes it to the native side through the Java Native Interface (JNI), and builds a chain of native operators from it. Results come back as Spark `ColumnarBatch` objects through Spark's columnar API, and Gluten uses the Apache Arrow data format as its in-memory representation.[^readme]

Apache Gluten supports two backends. The Velox backend uses [Velox](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Velox), a C++ library of data processing components. The ClickHouse backend uses a ClickHouse fork maintained by Kyligence. The design allows more backends to be added.[^readme] The ASF graduation announcement also mentions future integration with Apache DataFusion as a goal of the extensible design.[^asfnews]

## History and status

Apache Gluten was initiated by Intel and Kyligence in 2022; its README lists BIGO, Meituan, Alibaba Cloud, NetEase, Baidu, Microsoft, IBM and Google among other contributing companies.[^readme] Releases up to 1.1.1 were made before the project joined the ASF and are marked "non-Apache release" on the downloads page.[^downloads]

Apache Gluten entered the Apache Incubator on 2023-12-15. Its first Apache release in the incubator was 1.2.0 on 2024-09-03, followed by 1.3.0, 1.4.0 and 1.5.0 (2025-10-29).[^incubator] The project graduated on 2026-02-18, the date the ASF board established it as a top-level project, and the ASF announced the graduation on 2026-03-05.[^incubator][^asfnews][^board] Gluten is therefore no longer incubating.

The latest Apache Gluten release is 1.7.0, published on GitHub on 2026-08-26.[^rel170] A release candidate for 1.8.0 (v1.8.0-rc0) was tagged on 2026-11-17 but is not a release.[^releases]

## Which Spark versions does Gluten support?

Apache Gluten uses a shim layer to support several Spark versions at once, and its README says it supports the latest three to four Spark releases during a development cycle.[^readme] The Gluten 1.7.0 binary release is built for Spark 3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 4.0 and 4.1.[^downloads][^readme170] On the main branch the list is Spark 3.4, 3.5, 4.0 and 4.1.[^readme] No Gluten release lists Spark 4.2 or 4.3. The Spark 4.0 and 4.1 builds of the Velox backend need JDK 17 or later and Scala 2.13.[^velox]

## How does Gluten work with Apache Spark?

Apache Gluten is enabled through Spark's plugin interface. A basic configuration from the project README sets the plugin class, turns on Spark off-heap memory, puts the Gluten JAR on the driver and executor class paths, and switches to Gluten's columnar shuffle manager:[^readme]

```bash
spark-shell \
  --conf spark.plugins=org.apache.gluten.GlutenPlugin \
  --conf spark.memory.offHeap.enabled=true \
  --conf spark.memory.offHeap.size=20g \
  --conf spark.driver.extraClassPath=${GLUTEN_JAR} \
  --conf spark.executor.extraClassPath=${GLUTEN_JAR} \
  --conf spark.shuffle.manager=org.apache.spark.shuffle.sort.ColumnarShuffleManager
```

Apache Gluten needs off-heap memory because native operators allocate memory outside the JVM heap. The configuration guide says Gluten uses `spark.memory.offHeap.size` to size native memory even when off-heap is disabled, and recommends a larger value if the plugin runs out of memory.[^config] Spark's own default for `spark.memory.offHeap.enabled` is false.[^sparkconf]

Apache Gluten's columnar shuffle reuses the shuffle service of Spark core but adds a columnar exchange operator, so that data stays in columnar form between stages.[^readme] The Velox backend also works with the remote shuffle services Apache Celeborn and Apache Uniffle.[^velox]

Apache Gluten has a `spark.gluten.enabled` setting (default true), but the configuration guide calls it experimental and recommends enabling or disabling Gluten through `spark.plugins`. With `spark.gluten.ui.enabled` (default true), Gluten adds its own page to the Spark web UI.[^config]

## What runs natively and what falls back?

Apache Gluten offloads only the operators and expressions that the chosen backend supports. For anything else it falls back to vanilla Spark, and it inserts ColumnarToRow and RowToColumnar conversions where the plan moves between Gluten's columnar data and Spark's internal row format.[^readme] Because each conversion has a cost, Gluten has settings that send larger parts of a plan back to Spark, for example `spark.gluten.sql.columnar.wholeStage.fallback.threshold` and `spark.gluten.sql.columnar.query.fallback.threshold`, which count ColumnarToRow transitions and vanilla leaf nodes (both default -1, off).[^config]

Some fallbacks are on by default for correctness. `spark.gluten.sql.ansiFallback.enabled` (default true) makes Gluten fall back to Spark when ANSI mode is on, and `spark.gluten.sql.fallbackRegexpExpressions` can send all regular expressions to Spark because the native engine uses RE2, which differs from `java.util.regex` in a few cases.[^config] In Spark 4.3.0, `spark.sql.ansi.enabled` defaults to true, so this setting applies to queries that run with Spark's default configuration.[^sparkconf]

## Which table formats does the Velox backend read?

The Velox backend of Apache Gluten can scan [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) tables (including column mapping), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) tables in both copy-on-write and merge-on-read form, [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) copy-on-write tables and Apache Paimon tables without a primary key. Each format needs a build profile (for example `-Pdelta` or `-Piceberg`) that adds it to the Velox bundle JAR.[^velox] The 1.7.0 release notes include a native statistics tracker for Delta writes.[^rel170]

# Apache Hive

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation); created at Facebook</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">Apache top-level project since September 2010</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">4.2.1</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-08-24</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Java</Field>
  <Field name="type">SQL data warehouse system and metastore</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[hive.apache.org](https://hive.apache.org/)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/hive](https://github.com/apache/hive)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Hive Metastore](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_Metastore), [Hive on Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_on_Spark), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Hive home and downloads pages (releases and end-of-life notices to 4.2.1), HiveConf.java and the top-level modules at the rel/release-3.1.3, rel/release-4.0.0-alpha-1, rel/release-4.0.0-alpha-2, rel/release-4.0.0, rel/release-4.0.1, rel/release-4.1.0 and rel/release-4.2.1 tags, HIVE-12300, HIVE-26134, HIVE-27972, the ASF committee information and the 2009 VLDB paper on Hive</Verified>

<Status level="active">The Hive 1.x, 2.x and 3.x release lines are end of life (declared in 2024); the 4.x line is maintained. Hive 4 removed the Spark execution engine, and the MapReduce engine has been deprecated since Hive 2.[^downloads]</Status>

**Apache Hive** is a distributed SQL data warehouse system that runs queries over files in distributed storage, together with the [Hive Metastore](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_Metastore), a service that stores table metadata for Hive and for other engines.[^home] Hive was built at Facebook to give Hadoop users a SQL-like language instead of hand-written MapReduce programs.[^paper] Today the two halves of the project have different roles in an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse): the metastore is still a widely used [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog), while the query engine competes with engines such as [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) and [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino).

## Query engine and metastore

The name "Hive" covers two things that are often confused.

|  | Hive query engine (HiveServer2) | Hive Metastore (HMS) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it does | Compiles HiveQL into jobs and runs them; HiveServer2 serves JDBC and ODBC clients[^home] | Stores databases, tables, partitions and their locations, and serves them over a Thrift API[^home] |
| Who uses it | Hive users and BI tools that connect to HiveServer2 | Hive, Impala, Spark and other engines[^home] |
| Runs on | Apache Tez (default in Hive 4.1 and later) or the deprecated MapReduce engine[^conf421] | A standalone service backed by a relational database |
| Lakehouse role | One SQL engine among several | A shared catalog, and since 4.1.0 also an Iceberg REST catalog endpoint[^downloads] |

A system that "uses Hive" may use only the metastore. [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) and [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) read and write tables registered in the Hive Metastore without running any Hive queries; see [Hive Metastore](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_Metastore) for how each engine connects.

## Execution engines

Hive compiles queries for one of several execution engines, selected with `hive.execution.engine`. The available engines and the default have changed across releases, as the configuration source at each release tag shows:

| Release | Engines | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 3.1.3 | `mr`, `tez`, `spark` | `mr`[^n1] |
| 4.0.0-alpha-1 | `mr`, `tez`, `spark` | `mr` |
| 4.0.0-alpha-2 to 4.0.1 | `mr`, `tez` | `mr`[^conf400] |
| 4.1.0 to 4.2.1 | `tez`, `mr` | `tez`[^conf421] |

- **MapReduce** was deprecated in Hive 2.0.0 (HIVE-12300).[^n2] It is still selectable in Hive 4.2.1, where the configuration describes it as a historical engine that "may be removed without further warning".[^conf421]
- **Spark** (Hive on Spark) was removed from the main branch by HIVE-26134 in 2022; the `spark-client` module is present at the 4.0.0-alpha-1 tag and absent from 4.0.0-alpha-2 onward.[^n3] See [Hive on Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_on_Spark).
- **Tez** became the default in Hive 4.1.0 (HIVE-27972).[^n4] LLAP (Low Latency Analytical Processing) adds persistent daemons and caching on top of Tez for interactive queries.[^home]

## Features

The Hive project lists, among its main features, full ACID transactions for ORC tables and insert-only transactions for other formats, built-in compaction, a cost-based optimizer based on Apache Calcite, replication, and Kerberos authentication with Apache Ranger for authorization.[^home] Hive reads and writes [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) tables through a storage handler; the `iceberg` module is part of the source tree from the 4.0.0-alpha-1 tag onward.[^home][^n5]

## Releases and end of life

The Hive 4 line is the only maintained line. The project's news page records these milestones:[^downloads]

- 4.0.0, the first final Hive 4 release, on 29 March 2024.
- End of life of the 1.x line (April 2024), the 2.x line (May 2024) and the 3.x line (October 2024). The 3.x notice says no further updates or releases are planned.
- 4.1.0 on 31 July 2025, which added JDK 17 support, the standalone metastore packages and a REST catalog server.
- 4.2.0 on 23 November 2025, which made JDK 21 the minimum Java version.
- 4.2.1 on 24 August 2026, a bug-fix release with security fixes in the metastore, HiveServer2 and the Avro SerDe.

## History

A Facebook team described Hive in a 2009 VLDB paper as an open source data warehouse on Hadoop whose SQL-like language, HiveQL, was compiled into MapReduce jobs.[^paper] Hive became a top-level Apache project in September 2010.[^n6] HCatalog, a table and storage management layer for Hadoop, merged into Hive in March 2013.[^downloads]

- [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino)

# Apache Hudi

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) (originally Uber)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">1.2.1</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-09-24</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Java (main project); Rust (hudi-rs)</Field>
  <Field name="type">[Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format)</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[hudi.apache.org](https://hudi.apache.org)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/hudi](https://github.com/apache/hudi)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Hudi download page and GitHub release release-1.2.1, the Hudi docs and the ASF incubator record</Verified>

**Apache Hudi** (pronounced "hoodie") is an [open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) and data lake platform that adds tables, transactions, record-level upserts and deletes, indexes and table services to data stored in open file formats on a data lake.[^overview] Hudi is designed for incremental pipelines that apply streams of changes to tables, as well as for batch workloads. It is one of the table formats used in an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), and engines such as [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), Apache Flink and [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) can query Hudi tables.[^overview]

## How it works

### Timeline

Every change to an Apache Hudi table, including writes, table services and schema changes, is recorded as an action on the Hudi timeline. The timeline is a log of actions at points in time (instants) and is the source of truth for the state of the table. Each action has a requested instant, which acts as the transaction ID, a completed instant, a state (requested, inflight or completed) and a type.[^timeline]

Action types on the Hudi timeline include commit, delta commit (for merge-on-read tables), replace commit, clean, compaction, log compaction, clustering, indexing and rollback.[^timeline]

### File groups and file slices

Apache Hudi organises data into file groups. An update to an existing file group produces a new file slice tied to the commit that wrote it, and an insert can start a new file group. A query checks the timeline for completed writes and reads only the latest committed file slices, so it does not see files from writes still in flight.[^tabletypes]

## Features

### Table types

Apache Hudi has two table types, which define how writes are stored.[^tabletypes]

| Table type | How updates and deletes are written | Trade-off stated in the Hudi docs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Copy on write (CoW) | A new base file is written in the file group; no log files are used. | Queries read only base files; writes can be slower because base files are rewritten. |
| Merge on read (MoR) | Changes go to log files, which are merged with base files at query time and folded in by periodic compaction. | Lower write latency; query performance depends on whether log files have been compacted. |

### Query types

Hudi supports snapshot queries, incremental queries and read-optimized queries.[^overview] Incremental queries return only data written since a given instant on the timeline, with the latest value for each record key. A change data capture (CDC) form of incremental query returns inserted, updated and deleted records with before and after images and the operation that caused each change.[^tabletypes]

### Indexes

Apache Hudi maintains indexes that map each record key, optionally with its partition path, to the file group that holds it. For copy-on-write tables the index avoids joining incoming records against the whole table to decide which files to rewrite. For merge-on-read tables it bounds the change records each base file must be merged with. Secondary indexes build on the same mapping.[^indexes]

### Table services

Hudi runs table services that are recorded on the timeline like any other action. Cleaning removes file slices that are no longer needed, compaction merges log files into base files, and clustering rewrites file groups with a new sort order or layout.[^timeline]

## History

Hudi was originally developed at Uber, under the name "Hoodie", to support upsert and incremental consumption in Uber's ingestion, ETL and machine learning pipelines.[^proposal] The project entered the Apache Incubator on 17 January 2019 and graduated to a top-level Apache project on 20 May 2020.[^incubator]

The Apache Hudi download page lists release 1.2.1 as the newest version.[^download] Its GitHub release was published on 24 September 2026.[^release] The project also publishes patch releases on older lines; for example, 1.1.2 was published on GitHub after 1.2.1.[^n1]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Apache Hudi tables hold data in open file formats on cloud or object storage, with the timeline and metadata stored alongside.[^overview] Hudi's record-level upserts, indexes and incremental queries are aimed at pipelines that apply streams of changes and pass only changed records to downstream tables, for example between layers of a [Medallion architecture](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Medallion_architecture).[^tabletypes] [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)'s UniForm feature can also expose Delta tables to Hudi readers (in preview).[^n2]

## Engine support

The Hudi documentation names [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), Apache Flink, Presto, [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) and Apache Hive as query engines for Hudi tables, with quick start guides for Spark and Flink.[^overview] Trino's Hudi connector requires Hudi 0.12.3 or later.[^n3] Hudi-rs is a native Rust implementation with Python bindings, for use outside the Java virtual machine.[^overview][^n4]

## Limitations

Each Apache Hudi table type has a cost. Copy-on-write writes can be slow because a whole base file is rewritten even when only a few of its records change. Merge-on-read query performance varies with how far compaction has caught up with the log files.[^tabletypes] Both table types rely on table services such as cleaning, compaction and clustering being scheduled and run.[^timeline]

Engine support for Hudi features varies, and some connectors set a minimum Hudi version.[^n5]

- [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)
- [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)
- [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet)

# Apache Iceberg

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">1.12.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-09-29</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Java (reference implementation)</Field>
  <Field name="type">[Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format)</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[iceberg.apache.org](https://iceberg.apache.org)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/iceberg](https://github.com/apache/iceberg)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Iceberg releases page (1.12.0), the Iceberg table spec and the ASF incubator record</Verified>

**Apache Iceberg** is an [open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) for large analytic tables stored as files in a distributed file system or object store. The Iceberg specification describes how a table's schema, partitioning and data files are tracked in metadata files, so that several engines can read and write the same table with transactional guarantees.[^spec] Iceberg is a common table layer in an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), where data stays in open file formats such as [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) and is shared between engines such as [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) and [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB).

## How it works

Apache Iceberg tracks individual data files instead of directories. Table state is held in a metadata file that records the schema, partition configuration, properties and snapshots. Each snapshot points to manifest files, and each manifest lists data files together with their partition values and column statistics.[^spec]

Every change to an Iceberg table writes a new metadata file and replaces the old one with an atomic swap. Writers work optimistically: a writer prepares its change, then commits by swapping the table's metadata pointer from the version it started from to the new version. If another commit happened first, the writer must retry against the new current version. Readers use the snapshot that was current when they loaded the table and do not take locks.[^spec]

The atomic swap of the metadata pointer is performed by a catalog. Catalog types supported by the Iceberg Spark integration include a REST catalog, the Hive Metastore and a directory-based Hadoop catalog,[^sparkconf] and Iceberg also provides a JDBC catalog.[^n1] The REST catalog is an HTTP protocol defined by the Iceberg project,[^rest] described further in [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog). Catalog services such as [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris) and [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog) are covered in their own articles.

## Features

### Snapshots and time travel

Each write to an Apache Iceberg table creates a new snapshot. Snapshots are the basis for reader isolation, time travel queries and rollback. Branches and tags are named references to snapshots, each with its own retention policy.[^branching]

In Spark SQL, Iceberg supports time travel with the `TIMESTAMP AS OF` and `VERSION AS OF` clauses. `VERSION AS OF` accepts a snapshot ID or a branch or tag name.[^sparkq]

```sql
-- Iceberg 1.12.0 with Spark SQL
SELECT * FROM prod.db.events TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-11-01 00:00:00';
SELECT * FROM prod.db.events VERSION AS OF 10963874102873;
SELECT * FROM prod.db.events VERSION AS OF 'audit-branch';
```

### Hidden partitioning

Apache Iceberg produces partition values from column values, for example the day of a timestamp column, and records the relationship in table metadata. Queries filter on the source column and Iceberg skips files that cannot match. Users do not need to know how the table is partitioned or add a separate partition filter, as they would with a Hive-style partition column.[^partitioning]

### Schema and partition evolution

Apache Iceberg supports adding, dropping, renaming, reordering and widening columns, including fields in nested structures. Schema changes are metadata changes and do not rewrite data files. Columns are tracked by unique IDs, so a change to one column does not change the values read from another.[^evolution] The partition layout of a table can also change in place, for example from daily to hourly partitions, without creating a new table.[^evolution]

### Format versions

The Iceberg specification is versioned. The format version increases when a feature breaks forward compatibility, meaning older readers would not read the newer table correctly. Versions 1, 2 and 3 are complete and adopted; version 4 is under development and not formally adopted.[^spec]

| Format version | Main additions (per the spec) |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Analytic tables built on immutable Parquet, Avro and ORC files |
| 2 | Row-level deletes through delete files; stricter writer requirements |
| 3 | New types (nanosecond timestamps, variant, geometry, geography, unknown), column default values, multi-argument transforms, row lineage, binary deletion vectors, table encryption keys |
| 4 (in development) | Restructured metadata tree, combined data file and deletion vector entries, relative locations, table constraints; new equality deletes no longer allowed |

## History

Iceberg was developed at Netflix. The proposal to the Apache Incubator described it as a table format designed to improve on the Hive table layout, and stated that it was under active development at Netflix.[^proposal] The project entered the Apache Incubator on 16 November 2018 and graduated to a top-level Apache project on 20 May 2020.[^incubator]

Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 was released on 29 September 2026. That release removed Spark 3.4 support.[^releases]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Apache Iceberg tables sit on object storage, and a [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog) holds the pointer to each table's current metadata file. Because the table state is defined by the specification and not by one engine, a table written by one engine can be read by another that implements the same format version. Pipelines that move data through layers, such as the [Medallion architecture](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Medallion_architecture), can use Iceberg tables at each layer.

## Engine support

Connectors for [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), Apache Flink and Apache Hive are maintained in the main Iceberg repository, with a separate runtime artifact for each supported engine version.[^multiengine] [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) reads and writes Iceberg tables through its Iceberg connector,[^n2] and [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB) reads them through its iceberg extension.[^n3] The Iceberg project also maintains implementations in Python (PyIceberg), Rust and Go in separate repositories.[^n4][^n5][^n6]

## Limitations

Apache Iceberg tables need regular maintenance. Snapshots accumulate until they are expired, and data files are not deleted while any retained snapshot still references them. Each commit also writes a new metadata file, so tables with frequent commits, such as streaming tables, may need old metadata files cleaned up.[^maintenance]

Support for newer features depends on the engine. A table can be kept on an older format version so that engines without support for newer features can still use it.[^spec]

# Apache Mesos support in Spark

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Mesos_support_in_Spark

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Spark on Mesos, Mesos cluster manager</Field>
  <Field name="field">Cluster resource management</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Before Spark 1.0; Spark was first built on Mesos</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`mesos://` master URLs, coarse-grained and fine-grained modes, `MesosClusterDispatcher`</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) 3.5 and earlier</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Spark on Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_Kubernetes), [Spark on YARN](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_YARN), [Spark 3 to Spark 4 migration](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_3_to_Spark_4_migration)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v3.1.1, v3.2.0, v3.5.0 and v4.0.0 tags of apache/spark (docs/running-on-mesos.md, docs/core-migration-guide.md, resource-managers/), SPARK-35050, SPARK-44442, the Spark 4.0.0 release notes, the Apache Attic page for Mesos and the ASF board minutes</Verified>

<Status level="removed" since="Apache Spark 3.2.0">Removed in Apache Spark 4.0.0. Use [Spark on Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_Kubernetes), [Spark on YARN](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_YARN) or the standalone cluster manager instead. Deprecated by SPARK-35050 and removed by SPARK-44442.[^jira44442]</Status>

**Apache Mesos support in Spark** was the integration that let [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) use Apache Mesos as its cluster manager: a Spark application pointed at a `mesos://` master URL received resources from Mesos and ran its [executors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor) as Mesos tasks.[^mesos35] Spark itself was first written as a Mesos framework. Spark deprecated Mesos support in 3.2.0 and removed it in 4.0.0, so Spark 3.5 is the last release line that can run on Mesos.[^mig400][^jira44442]

## Status

Mesos support was deprecated in one minor release and removed in the next major release.

- **Deprecated in Spark 3.2.0.** SPARK-35050, "Deprecate Apache Mesos as resource manager", has fix version 3.2.0. Its description gives the reason: a thread on the Mesos dev list said that Mesos was moving to the Apache Attic and ceasing development.[^jira35050] From 3.2.0 the Mesos page of the Spark documentation opens with the note that Mesos support "is deprecated as of Apache Spark 3.2.0" and "will be removed in a future version", and the core migration guide says the same.[^mesos35][^mig400]
- **Removed in Spark 4.0.0.** SPARK-44442, "Drop mesos support", has fix version 4.0.0. The `resource-managers/mesos` module is present at the v3.5.0 tag and absent at the v4.0.0 tag. The Spark 4.0.0 core migration guide states: "In Spark 4.0, support for Apache Mesos as a resource manager was removed."[^jira44442][^mig400] The 4.0.0 release notes list SPARK-44442 and show the `mesos` library dependency (1.4.3) as removed.[^r400]
- **Fine-grained mode** was deprecated earlier, in Spark 2.0.0, as the Mesos documentation noted until support ended.[^mesos311]

The Mesos project itself is also gone. The ASF board approved a resolution to terminate the Apache Mesos project on 20 August 2025, and the Apache Attic records that Mesos retired in August 2025 and that its move to the Attic was completed in October 2025.[^board][^attic]

## History

Spark began at UC Berkeley as an application of Mesos. The 2010 HotCloud paper that introduced Spark says that "Spark is built on top of Mesos", a "cluster operating system" that lets several parallel applications share a cluster, and that building on Mesos reduced the programming effort Spark needed.[^paper] Spark later supported other cluster managers as well (its own standalone manager, Hadoop YARN and Kubernetes), and Mesos became one option among several.

When the Mesos community discussed moving the project to the Attic, Spark deprecated its integration (SPARK-35050, April 2021).[^jira35050] The Mesos board reports record attic discussions again in 2023 and a request in February 2024 to hold off, before the board terminated the project in 2025.[^board] By then Spark had already removed the integration from its main branch in September 2023, in the work that became Spark 4.0.0.[^jira44442]

## How it worked

A Spark application used Mesos by setting its master URL to `mesos://host:5050`, or to `mesos://zk://host1:2181,host2:2181/mesos` for a Mesos cluster with several masters coordinated through ZooKeeper.[^mesos35] The Spark 3.5 documentation describes two scheduling modes, chosen with `spark.mesos.coarse`:[^mesos35]

- **Coarse-grained mode** (default, `spark.mesos.coarse=true`): Spark acquired one long-lived Mesos task per machine and ran an executor in it, much like executors on other cluster managers.
- **Fine-grained mode** (`spark.mesos.coarse=false`, deprecated since 2.0.0): Spark created one Mesos task for each Spark task, so cores moved between applications as tasks finished, at the cost of higher task launch overhead.

For cluster deploy mode, operators ran the `MesosClusterDispatcher` (started with `sbin/start-mesos-dispatcher.sh`) and submitted applications to its URL. The documentation warned that the dispatcher had no authentication.[^mesos35]

```bash
# Spark 3.5 and earlier only; in Spark 4.0 spark-submit accepts only yarn, spark://, k8s:// and local masters
./bin/spark-shell --master mesos://host:5050
```

## Migrating off Mesos

Applications that ran on Mesos need another cluster manager to move to Spark 4. Spark 4.0 documents three: the standalone cluster manager, Hadoop YARN and Kubernetes.[^n1] Kubernetes is the closest match for a shared, multi-tenant cluster: each executor runs in its own pod, as each coarse-grained executor ran in its own Mesos task. All `spark.mesos.*` settings stop having any effect and should be removed from configuration files. See [Spark 3 to Spark 4 migration](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_3_to_Spark_4_migration) for the other changes in the same release.

# Apache Parquet

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) (originally Twitter and Cloudera)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">parquet-format 2.14.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-09-11</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Thrift (format definition); Java (parquet-java)</Field>
  <Field name="type">Columnar data file format</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[parquet.apache.org](https://parquet.apache.org)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/parquet-format](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi), [Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the parquet-format 2.14.0 release announcement, the Parquet file format documentation and the ASF incubator record</Verified>

**Apache Parquet** is an open source, column-oriented data file format for efficient storage and retrieval of analytic data. Parquet stores the values of each column together and supports per-column compression and encoding, and it is implemented in many programming languages and analytics tools.[^overview] In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Parquet files commonly hold the table data, and [open table formats](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) such as [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) and [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) add table metadata and transactions on top of Parquet files.

## Specification and implementations

The Apache Parquet project separates the format from its libraries. The parquet-format repository holds the official specification and the Thrift definitions of the file metadata (`parquet.thrift`); it contains no code for reading or writing files. The parquet-java repository, formerly named parquet-mr, holds the Java libraries and tools.[^overview] Other implementations include Apache Arrow (C++, Go and Rust), [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB), ClickHouse, cuDF and Polars, and the project publishes a table of which format features each one supports.[^impl]

## How it works

### File layout

An Apache Parquet file begins and ends with the 4-byte magic number `PAR1`. Between them come the column chunks, then the file metadata, then a 4-byte little-endian length of the metadata. The metadata records where every column chunk starts. Because it is written after the data, a writer can produce a file in a single pass; a reader first reads the footer, then reads only the column chunks it needs.[^fileformat]

### Row groups, column chunks and pages

A Parquet file contains one or more row groups, each a horizontal slice of the rows. A row group holds exactly one column chunk per column, and each column chunk is stored contiguously in the file. Column chunks are divided into pages, the smallest unit of encoding and compression.[^concepts]

| Level | Contains | Unit of |
| --- | --- | --- |
| File | One or more row groups and the footer metadata | Whole-file reads |
| Row group | One column chunk per column | Parallel processing of a file |
| Column chunk | One or more pages for one column | Column input and output |
| Page | Encoded, optionally compressed values | Encoding and compression |

### Nested data

Apache Parquet was designed for nested data from the start. It uses the record shredding and assembly algorithm from Google's Dremel paper, encoding nested structure with definition and repetition levels instead of flattening nested names.[^motivation][^readme] Null values are not stored in the data; nullness is recorded in the run-length encoded definition levels.[^n1]

## Features

### Types

Apache Parquet keeps a small set of physical types (such as INT32, INT64, DOUBLE and BYTE_ARRAY) and uses logical type annotations to say how to interpret them. For example, a string is a BYTE_ARRAY with a STRING annotation.[^logical] The specification also defines a Variant type for semi-structured data such as JSON, encoded as a value and a metadata binary so that nested fields can be read by path.[^n2]

### Encodings and compression

Parquet defines encodings including plain, dictionary, run-length/bit-packing hybrid, several delta encodings, byte stream split and ALP (adaptive lossless floating-point).[^encodings] Data and dictionary pages can be compressed with one of several codecs, and the codec can be chosen per column.[^n3][^motivation]

### Statistics, page index and Bloom filters

Readers can skip data using metadata stored in the file. Column statistics hold minimum and maximum values, and dictionaries let readers rule out values inside that range. An optional Bloom filter answers "definitely not present" or "probably present" for a value, which helps on high-cardinality columns.[^n4] The optional page index stores per-page statistics so that a reader can skip individual pages without reading every page header.[^n5]

## History

Parquet originated as a joint effort of Twitter and Cloudera; the parquet-format README carries the notice "Copyright 2013 Twitter, Cloudera and other contributors".[^readme] The project's stated aim was to make compressed, efficient columnar storage available to any project in the Apache Hadoop ecosystem without favouring one processing framework.[^motivation]

Parquet entered the Apache Incubator on 20 May 2014 and graduated on 22 April 2015.[^incubator] The Apache Software Foundation announced Parquet as a top-level project on 27 April 2015.[^n6]

parquet-format 2.14.0 was released on 11 September 2026. It added chronological ordering of INT96 timestamps, a FILE logical type and the ALP encoding.[^release]

## Use in an open lakehouse

Apache Parquet defines single files, organised internally into row groups, column chunks and pages.[^concepts] Grouping many files into one table, with commits and snapshots, is the job of an [open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format). The [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) specification lists Parquet as one of its data file formats, alongside Avro and ORC.[^n7] [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), Iceberg and [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) all store Parquet data files, which is what allows Delta Lake's UniForm feature to expose one copy of the data through several table formats.[^n8]

## Engine support

[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) reads and writes Parquet through a built-in data source.[^n9] [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB) reads and writes Parquet files directly.[^n10] The Parquet implementation status page lists feature support for Arrow C++, parquet-java, Arrow Go, Arrow Rust, ClickHouse, cuDF, hyparquet, DuckDB, Polars and DataHaskell.[^impl]

## Limitations

Apache Parquet implementations do not all support the same features of the format, so a file that uses a newer encoding or logical type may not be readable by every tool.[^overview][^impl] The specification keeps older representations for compatibility: the ConvertedType annotation is deprecated, but writers must still write it next to LogicalType so that old readers work.[^logical] The INT96 timestamp type is deprecated, yet the project notes it was still common in files produced as of 2024.[^impl]

[^n9]: [Parquet Files](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-data-sources-parquet.html). *Apache Software Foundation*. Retrieved 2026-11-22.
[^n10]: [Reading and Writing Parquet Files](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/data/parquet/overview). *DuckDB*. Retrieved 2026-11-22.

# Apache Polaris

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2025 (0.9.0-incubating)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">1.9.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-11-14</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Java</Field>
  <Field name="type">[Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog), [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) server</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[polaris.apache.org](https://polaris.apache.org)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/polaris](https://github.com/apache/polaris)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog), [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Polaris download page, the 1.9.0 documentation and the Apache Incubator status page</Verified>

**Apache Polaris** is an open source catalog for [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) tables that implements the [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) API, so that several query engines can read and write the same tables through one catalog.[^incubator][^docs] Polaris adds role-based access control and credential vending on top of the REST protocol.[^docs] It is a top-level project of the Apache Software Foundation (ASF).[^grad]

## History

The Polaris incubation proposal states that the project was first developed from ideas of many employees within Snowflake, that most core developers came from Snowflake and Dremio, and that the code was licensed under the Apache License 2.0.[^proposal]

Polaris entered the Apache Incubator on 9 August 2024.[^incubator] The first release listed on the project's download page is 0.9.0, dated 11 March 2025, and version 1.0.0 followed on 9 July 2025.[^downloads]

Polaris graduated from the Incubator to become an ASF top-level project in February 2026. The project announced the graduation on 19 February 2026, and the ASF announced it publicly on 5 March 2026.[^grad][^n1]

## How it works

Polaris exposes the Iceberg REST API, so any engine with an Iceberg REST client can connect to it. The project site lists engines such as [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), Apache Flink, Apache Doris, Dremio OSS, StarRocks and [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino).[^home]

A Polaris server holds one or more catalogs. An internal catalog is managed by Polaris and supports reads and writes. An external catalog is managed by another provider, is synced into Polaris, and is read-only. Each catalog has a storage configuration for Amazon S3, Azure or Google Cloud Storage. Inside a catalog, namespaces group tables and can be nested.[^docs]

## Access control

Polaris uses role-based access control (RBAC) in three layers. Privileges are granted to catalog roles, catalog roles are granted to principal roles, and principal roles are assigned to principals. A catalog role belongs to one catalog, and the relationship between principals and principal roles is many-to-many.[^rbac]

Privileges in Polaris are grouped by securable object: catalog, namespace, table, view, policy and semantic model. Examples are `TABLE_READ_DATA` and `NAMESPACE_LIST`.[^rbac]

## Credential vending

Polaris vends temporary storage credentials to query engines during query execution, so the engines do not need their own long-lived access to cloud storage.[^docs] The [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) specification defines this mechanism, under the name vended credentials, as a way for a catalog to return storage credentials together with a loaded table.[^n2]

## Other features

**Generic tables** let Polaris register tables that are not Iceberg tables, defined by a name, a format (for example `delta` or `csv`) and an optional base location. They share namespaces with Iceberg tables. The documentation marks generic tables as beta.[^n3]

**Catalog federation** connects Polaris to existing metadata services. The namespaces, tables and views of a federated catalog stay in the remote system. The 1.9.0 documentation has integration guides for Iceberg REST, Hive Metastore, Hadoop catalog and BigQuery Metastore, and federation is disabled by default.[^n4]

**Policies** are catalog entities that define rules for actions on catalogs, namespaces, tables or views. The predefined types cover data compaction, metadata compaction, orphan file removal and snapshot expiry. Polaris stores and resolves policies but does not run the maintenance work itself; external engines do that.[^n5]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Apache Polaris serves as the shared catalog for Iceberg tables. Because Polaris speaks the standard Iceberg REST protocol, engines connect with their existing Iceberg REST clients instead of a Polaris-specific connector, and access rules defined once in Polaris apply to every engine that uses it.[^home][^rbac]

## See also

- [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog)
- [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)
- [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog)
- [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog)
- [Open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse)
