# Apache Spark

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2010 (open sourced)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala, Java, Python</Field>
  <Field name="type">Distributed data processing engine</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[spark.apache.org](https://spark.apache.org)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark](https://github.com/apache/spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines), [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the spark.apache.org news page and release notes (latest release 4.3.0), the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark and its documentation</Verified>

**Apache Spark** is an open source, distributed engine for large-scale data processing, with high-level APIs in Java, Scala, Python and R and an optimized engine that runs general execution graphs.[^docs-index] Spark runs batch queries, SQL, stream processing and machine learning on one engine, on a single machine or on a cluster. In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Spark is one of the engines that reads and writes [open table formats](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) such as [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) and [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) through a shared [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog).

## Architecture

A Spark application runs as a set of independent processes on a cluster. The **driver** program holds the `SparkContext` (wrapped by `SparkSession` in the DataFrame API) and plans the work. The driver connects to a **cluster manager**, which allocates resources, and then obtains **executors**: processes on worker nodes that run computations and store data for the application. The driver sends application code and then **tasks** to the executors.[^cluster]

Each Spark application gets its own executor processes, which stay up for the whole application. This isolates applications from one another, but it also means two Spark applications cannot share in-memory data without writing it to external storage.[^cluster]

### Execution model

Spark evaluates transformations lazily. A transformation such as a filter or a join only records how a dataset is derived; Spark computes it when an **action**, such as `collect` or a write, needs a result. The Spark documentation explains that this lets Spark run more efficiently, for example by returning only the result of a final aggregation to the driver instead of a large intermediate dataset.[^n1]

A Spark **job** is a parallel computation that Spark starts in response to an action. Spark divides each job into **stages**, sets of tasks that depend on one another in a similar way to the map and reduce stages of MapReduce, and sends each **task** to one executor.[^cluster]

The **deploy mode** sets where the driver runs. In cluster mode, the driver is launched inside the cluster; in client mode, the process that submits the application runs the driver outside the cluster.[^cluster]

### Cluster managers

Spark 4.3 supports three cluster managers: Spark's own **standalone** manager, **Hadoop YARN** and **Kubernetes**. Applications are submitted to any of them with the `spark-submit` script. Each driver also serves a web UI, by default on port 4040.[^cluster] The project also maintains a separate Spark Kubernetes Operator for running Spark applications and clusters through Kubernetes custom resources.[^docs-index]

## APIs and libraries

Spark exposes several libraries on top of its core engine:[^docs-index]

- **Spark SQL and DataFrames**: structured data processing through SQL or the DataFrame and Dataset APIs, optimized by the Catalyst query optimizer.[^r200][^n2]
- **[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming)**: stream processing built on the Spark SQL engine, using the same DataFrame operations as batch queries.
- **MLlib**: a library of machine learning algorithms and pipelines.[^n3]
- **pandas API on Spark**: a pandas-compatible API that runs on Spark. It was added in Spark 3.2.0.[^r320]
- **GraphX**: graph processing.[^docs-index]

The R API (SparkR) is marked as deprecated in the Spark 4.3 documentation. Spark 4.3 runs on Java 17, 21 or 25, Scala 2.13 and Python 3.11 or later.[^docs-index]

A short PySpark example that reads a table and aggregates it:

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("example").getOrCreate()

orders = spark.read.table("sales.orders")
daily = orders.groupBy("order_date").agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue"))
daily.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("sales.daily_revenue")
```

## Spark Connect

<Hatnote>Main article: [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect)</Hatnote>

Spark Connect is a client-server protocol, introduced in Spark 3.4, in which a thin client sends unresolved logical plans to a Spark server over gRPC and receives results as Apache Arrow batches.[^connect] The client does not run inside the driver process, so applications can run in IDEs, notebooks and services away from the cluster. Besides the Python and Scala clients in the main repository, the Spark project maintains separate Spark Connect clients for Go, Rust and Swift.[^n4][^n5][^n6] Spark 4.0 added a lightweight Python client package (`pyspark-client`) and the `spark.api.mode` setting, which lets a classic application switch to Spark Connect.[^r400]

## Spark Declarative Pipelines

<Hatnote>Main article: [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines)</Hatnote>

Spark Declarative Pipelines (SDP), added in Spark 4.1.0, is a framework in which a user declares datasets (streaming tables, materialized views and temporary views) and the flows that fill them, and Spark works out the dependency order, parallelism, checkpoints and retries.[^r410] Pipelines are run with the `spark-pipelines` command line tool.[^n7]

## History

Spark started in 2009 as a research project at the AMPLab of the University of California, Berkeley, and was open sourced in early 2010. The project moved to the Apache Software Foundation in 2013.[^history] The ASF announced on 27 February 2014 that Spark had graduated from the Apache Incubator to become a top-level project.[^n8]

| Version | Announced | Selected changes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1.0.0 | 2014-05-30 | First release of the 1.x line[^news] |
| 2.0.0 | 2016-07-26 | First, experimental release of Structured Streaming[^news][^r200] |
| 3.0.0 | 2020-06-18 | First release of the 3.x line; adaptive query execution, dynamic partition pruning[^news][^n9] |
| 3.4.0 | 2023-04-13 | Python client for Spark Connect[^news][^n10] |
| 4.0.0 | 2025-05-23 | First release of the 4.x line; VARIANT type, SQL user-defined functions, pipe syntax, Arbitrary State API v2 (`transformWithState`)[^news][^r400] |
| 4.1.0 | 2025-12-16 | Spark Declarative Pipelines; Real-time Mode in Structured Streaming; SQL scripting and VARIANT enabled by default[^news][^r410] |
| 4.2.0 | 2026-07-14 | SQL `CHANGES` clause for change data capture; Auto CDC in Declarative Pipelines[^news][^r420] |
| 4.3.0 | 2026-10-30 | Stateful queries in Real-time Mode; SCD Type 2 Auto CDC; start of a quarterly feature-release cadence[^news][^r430] |

Older release lines continue to receive maintenance releases; Spark 4.2.1, 4.1.4 and 4.0.5 were announced on 27 October 2026, three days before 4.3.0.[^n11]

## Use in an open lakehouse

Spark reads and writes lakehouse tables through table format connectors and its catalog plugin API. A catalog is registered by setting Spark properties under `spark.sql.catalog.<name>`; the [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) documentation, for example, shows a catalog of type `rest` that talks to an [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog).[^n12] [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) is enabled with the `io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension` SQL extension and the `DeltaCatalog` session catalog.[^n13]

Because the table data sits in open formats such as [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) and the metadata sits in a catalog such as [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog) or [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), the same tables Spark writes can be queried by other engines, for example [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) or [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB). Spark is commonly used for the ingestion and transformation layers of a [medallion architecture](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Medallion_architecture), with [Apache Airflow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Airflow) or Spark Declarative Pipelines deciding when each step runs.

# Apache Uniffle

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Uniffle

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) (originally Tencent)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">0.10.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2025-09-25</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Java (server and clients), Go (Kubernetes operator)</Field>
  <Field name="type">[Remote shuffle service](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Remote_shuffle_service)</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[uniffle.apache.org](https://uniffle.apache.org)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/uniffle](https://github.com/apache/uniffle)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Apache Celeborn](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Celeborn), [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v0.10.0 tag of apache/uniffle (README.md, pom.xml, docs/server_guide.md, docs/operator/README.md, patch/spark), the Uniffle download page, the Uniffle incubation status page and proposal, and the v0.7.0 tag of apache/celeborn</Verified>

**Apache Uniffle** is an open source [remote shuffle service](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Remote_shuffle_service) for distributed computing engines: a cluster of coordinators and shuffle servers that receives the [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle) data of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), Hadoop MapReduce and Apache Tez jobs, stores it in memory, on local disk or in remote storage such as HDFS, and serves it to the tasks that read it.[^readme] The project describes the change as moving shuffle from a "local file pull-like style" to a "remote block push-like style". Uniffle is a top-level project of the Apache Software Foundation.

## History

Uniffle was started at Tencent in 2020 under the name "Firestorm" and open sourced on GitHub in 2021.[^proposal] It entered the Apache Incubator on 2022-06-06, released 0.6.0 as its first incubating release in October 2022, and graduated to a top-level project on 2025-02-19.[^incubator]

The latest release is 0.10.0, published on 2025-09-25.[^download]

## Architecture

A Uniffle cluster has three parts:[^readme]
- A **coordinator** cluster, which collects the status of shuffle servers and assigns them to jobs.
- A **shuffle server** cluster, which receives shuffle data, merges it and writes it to storage.
- Optional **remote storage**, such as HDFS.

Shuffle servers can store data as memory plus local files, memory plus remote storage, or memory plus local files plus remote storage. The server setting `rss.storage.type` takes the values `MEMORY_LOCALFILE`, `MEMORY_HDFS` and `MEMORY_LOCALFILE_HDFS`, and the README recommends the last one for production.[^readme][^server]

Stored shuffle data uses two files per partition: a data file that holds all the blocks for the partition, and an index file with metadata for each block.[^readme]

## How does a shuffle work with Uniffle?

With Uniffle, the Spark driver asks a coordinator which shuffle servers to use. Each map task buffers its records, requests memory from a shuffle server, and sends the data; the server caches it in memory and flushes it to storage. After writing, the task reports all its block IDs to the shuffle server so that readers can check that they received every block, and it records its task attempt ID in the map status so that speculative execution works. Reduce tasks then read from shuffle servers, remote storage or both, depending on the storage type.[^readme]

## Which engines does Uniffle support?

The 0.10.0 README lists:[^readme]
- **[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)** 2.3, 2.4 and 3.0 through 3.5. The release's Maven build profiles go up to Spark 3.5.[^pom]
- **Hadoop MapReduce**, built against Hadoop 2.8.5 and 3.2.1.
- **Apache Tez**.

## How do you use Uniffle with Apache Spark?

A Spark application uses Uniffle by adding the client jar and replacing the shuffle manager:[^readme]

```properties
spark.serializer             org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer
spark.shuffle.manager        org.apache.spark.shuffle.RssShuffleManager
spark.rss.coordinator.quorum <coordinatorIp1>:19999,<coordinatorIp2>:19999
```

Dynamic allocation needs extra setup. For Spark 3.5 and later, setting `spark.shuffle.sort.io.plugin.class=org.apache.spark.shuffle.RssShuffleDataIo` lets Spark release executors without the external shuffle service. For older versions, Uniffle ships patches for Spark 2.3.4, 2.4.6, 3.0.1, 3.1.2, 3.2.1, 3.3.1 and 3.4.1 that must be applied before rebuilding Spark.[^readme] The `spark.shuffle.sort.io.plugin.class` hook is Spark's shuffle storage API, available since Spark 3.0.0.[^n1]

## How is Uniffle deployed?

Uniffle is deployed as its own cluster, separate from the compute engine. Coordinators and shuffle servers are configured through `conf/rss-env.sh`, `coordinator.conf` and `server.conf`, and a coordinator can hand default client settings to jobs through a dynamic client configuration file.[^readme] On [Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Kubernetes), the Uniffle operator manages Uniffle clusters; its API is in beta (`v1alpha1`) at 0.10.0.[^operator] The project also ships a web dashboard.[^n2]

## Uniffle compared with Apache Celeborn

<Hatnote>Main article: [Remote shuffle service](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Remote_shuffle_service)</Hatnote>

[Apache Celeborn](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Celeborn) is the other remote shuffle service at the ASF. The two share the same basic design: map output is pushed to dedicated servers, and the engine connects through `spark.shuffle.manager`. The table shows where they differ in their latest releases.

|  | Apache Celeborn 0.7.0 | Apache Uniffle 0.10.0 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Control plane | Masters, with state replicated through Raft[^celebornreadme] | Coordinator cluster[^readme] |
| Spark versions | 3.0 to 4.2[^celebornreadme] | 2.3 to 3.5[^readme] |
| Other engines | Flink 1.18 to 2.3 (batch), MapReduce 3, Tez (experimental)[^celebornreadme] | MapReduce, Tez[^readme] |
| Kubernetes | Helm chart[^n3] | Operator (beta)[^operator] |
| Origin | Alibaba, 2020[^n4] | Tencent, 2020[^proposal] |
| Top-level project since | 2024-03-21[^n5] | 2025-02-19[^incubator] |

# Arrow-optimized Python UDF

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Arrow-optimized_Python_UDF

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Arrow Python UDF, `useArrow=True` UDF</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 3.5.0 (SPARK-40307); default since Spark 4.2.0</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`udf(useArrow=...)`, `spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled`, Arrow record batches, Python worker</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (PySpark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[User-defined function (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/User-defined_function_(Spark)), [Pandas UDF](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Pandas_UDF), [Apache Arrow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Arrow)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (SQLConf.scala, python/pyspark/sql/functions/builtin.py, the "Apache Arrow in PySpark" tutorial, the PySpark UDF user guide, the PySpark migration guide), the Spark 3.5.0, 4.0.0 and 4.2.0 release notes and the 2023 Databricks blog post on the feature</Verified>

In PySpark, an **Arrow-optimized Python UDF** is a regular row-at-a-time Python [user-defined function](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/User-defined_function_(Spark)) whose input and output move between the JVM and the Python worker as [Apache Arrow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Arrow) batches instead of pickled Python objects.[^arrow] The function code is the same as for a pickled UDF; only the transfer and the type coercion rules change.[^arrow] [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) introduced Arrow-optimized Python UDFs in version 3.5.0 and made them the default for `pyspark.sql.functions.udf` in version 4.2.0.[^r350][^upgrade]

## What changed compared with pickled Python UDFs?

A pickled Python UDF serializes every row with cloudpickle on its way to and from the Python worker, and the PySpark user guide says this causes performance bottlenecks with large inputs and outputs.[^guide] An Arrow-optimized Python UDF still calls the function once per row, but Spark ships the rows in Arrow batches, a columnar format shared by the JVM and Python.[^arrow][^guide]

|  | Arrow-optimized Python UDF | Pickled Python UDF |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Serialization between JVM and Python | Apache Arrow batches | Pickle (cloudpickle) |
| Function receives | Python objects, one row per call | Python objects, one row per call |
| Type coercion of results | Arrow type system; errors on unsafe conversions since Spark 4.1 | Falls back to `None` on many type mismatches |
| Default in Spark 4.3.0 | Yes (since 4.2.0) | No; set `useArrow=False` or the configuration to `false` |

Sources for the table: the PySpark Arrow guide and the migration guide.[^arrow][^upgrade]

In a Databricks benchmark for Spark 3.5, an Arrow-optimized Python UDF ran about 1.6 times faster than a pickled Python UDF for a single transformation, and about 1.9 times faster when UDFs were chained on a 32 GB dataset, on a cluster of three workers with 16 vCPUs and 122 GiB each.[^blog]

## How is Arrow optimization turned on or off?

The `useArrow` argument of `pyspark.sql.functions.udf` controls a single UDF. When `useArrow` is not set (`None`), the session configuration `spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled` decides.[^arrow][^builtin]

In Spark 4.3.0, `spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled` defaults to `true`, and the optimization applies only when the function takes at least one argument.[^sqlconf] The default changed to `true` in Spark 4.2.0 (SPARK-54555); before that, Arrow optimization had to be requested explicitly.[^upgrade][^r420]

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import udf

@udf(returnType="int")                  # Arrow-optimized by default in Spark 4.2+
def slen(s: str) -> int:
    return len(s)

@udf(returnType="int", useArrow=False)  # pickled Python UDF
def slen_pickled(s: str) -> int:
    return len(s)

# Restore pickled UDFs for every UDF in the session that does not set useArrow:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled", "false")
```

## How does type coercion differ?

Type coercion matters when the Python value a UDF returns does not match its declared return type. The PySpark guide says pickled UDFs often fall back to `None` on a mismatch, which can lose data silently, and that converting dates, datetimes and tuples to strings can give ambiguous results; Arrow-optimized UDFs use Arrow's type system to make the coercion consistent.[^arrow] The full coercion tables are in the pull request that the guide links (apache/spark#41706).[^arrow]

Several behaviour changes in Spark 4.x affect Arrow-optimized UDFs:[^upgrade]
- **Spark 4.1** removed an unnecessary conversion to pandas objects in the serializer, which changes coercion when the output type differs from the declared schema. `spark.sql.legacy.execution.pythonUDF.pandas.conversion.enabled=true` restores the old behaviour.
- **Spark 4.1** supports user-defined types (UDTs) as input and output instead of falling back to a pickled UDF; `spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.legacy.fallbackOnUDT=true` restores the fallback.
- **Spark 4.1** turned on `spark.sql.execution.pandas.convertToArrowArraySafely` by default, so integer overflow, floating point truncation and loss of precision in returned data raise errors.
- **Spark 4.2** made Arrow optimization the default, as described above.

## Other settings

`spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.concurrency.level`, added in Spark 4.0.0 (SPARK-50446), runs an Arrow-optimized Python UDF with more than one level of concurrency, which the configuration description says can help UDFs that do a lot of I/O. It has no default and must be greater than 1 when set.[^sqlconf][^n1]

The Arrow batch size is set by `spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch`, default 10,000 rows.[^arrow]

## Arrow-optimized Python UDF vs pandas UDF and Arrow UDF

An Arrow-optimized Python UDF changes only the transfer; the function still handles one row at a time. A [Pandas UDF](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Pandas_UDF) or an Arrow UDF (`arrow_udf`, Spark 4.1.0 and later) is vectorized: the function receives a whole batch as pandas or PyArrow objects.[^guide] Python UDTFs have the same switch, `spark.sql.execution.pythonUDTF.arrow.enabled`, which also defaults to `true` since Spark 4.2; see [Python UDTF](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Python_UDTF).[^upgrade]

# Bloom filter (data files)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Bloom_filter_(data_files)

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Parquet bloom filter, ORC bloom filter, split block bloom filter (SBBF)</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data layout; query optimization</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Per-column filter stored in the file, expected number of distinct values, false positive probability, reader-side check</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), Apache ORC, [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) (write properties), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (reader and writer options)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Runtime filter](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Runtime_filter), [Predicate pushdown](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">BloomFilter.md at apache-parquet-format-2.12.0, the parquet-hadoop README at apache-parquet-1.17.0 (the parquet-java version in the Spark 4.3.0 pom.xml), the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/sql-data-sources-load-save-functions.md, docs/sql-data-sources-orc.md, pom.xml, SQLConf.scala), the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 configuration docs, and the Delta Lake protocol at v4.4.1</Verified>

A **bloom filter in a data file** is a compact, per-column structure that a writer stores inside a columnar file, such as an [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) or ORC file, so that a reader can tell that a value is definitely not in a row group without reading its data. It answers membership questions with "definitely no" or "probably yes" and never gives false negatives.[^spec] It is not the same thing as the bloom filter that [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) builds during a join, which is a [runtime filter](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Runtime_filter). This page compares the two and links to the detailed articles.

## Which bloom filter is meant?

|  | Bloom filter in a data file | Runtime bloom filter (Spark) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Built when | Once, when the file is written | For each query, from the filtered side of a join[^rule] |
| Stored | In the file, one filter per column chunk | In memory, discarded after the query |
| Keys come from | The column values in that file | The join keys of the creation side |
| Helps with | Equality and `IN` filters with literal values, on columns where min/max statistics do not separate files | Joins where one side is small and filtered and the other is large |
| Skips | Row groups that cannot contain the value | Rows of the large side before the shuffle |
| Turned on by | Writer properties per column (off by default) | `spark.sql.optimizer.runtime.bloomFilter.enabled` (default true)[^sqlconf] |
| Main article | This page, [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Predicate pushdown](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown) | [Runtime filter](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Runtime_filter) |

## Parquet bloom filters

Parquet's bloom filter is the **split block bloom filter** (SBBF), which hashes values with xxHash (XXH64). The specification states its goal as predicate pushdown for high-cardinality columns using less space than dictionaries: minimum and maximum statistics cannot rule out a value that falls inside a column chunk's range, and a bloom filter can.[^spec]

In parquet-java 1.17.0, the version bundled with Spark 4.3.0, the writer and reader properties are:[^pom][^pj]
- `parquet.bloom.filter.enabled` (default false) turns on writing, for all columns or for one column with `#column.path`.
- `parquet.bloom.filter.expected.ndv#column.path` sets the expected number of distinct values; without it the filter uses the maximum size.
- `parquet.bloom.filter.fpp` sets the false positive probability (default 0.01).
- `parquet.bloom.filter.max.bytes` caps the filter size (default 1048576 bytes).
- `parquet.filter.bloom.enabled` (default true) lets the reader use bloom filters to skip row groups.

Spark passes these as table or writer options. The Spark documentation shows a table created with `parquet.bloom.filter.enabled#favorite_color` set to true and `parquet.bloom.filter.expected.ndv#favorite_color` set to 1000000:[^loadsave]

```python
(users.write
    .option("parquet.bloom.filter.enabled#user_email", "true")
    .option("parquet.bloom.filter.expected.ndv#user_email", "1000000")
    .parquet("/data/users"))
```

## Bloom filters in table formats and ORC

- **[Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)** does not define a table-level bloom filter in its open protocol: the Delta transaction log protocol at v4.4.1 has no bloom filter feature, and Delta's data files are Parquet files, so bloom filters in a Delta table are the Parquet column filters inside those files.[^deltaprotocol]
- **[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)** sets Parquet bloom filters with the table property `write.parquet.bloom-filter-enabled.column.<col>` (not set by default), together with `write.parquet.bloom-filter-fpp.column.<col>` (default 0.01) and `write.parquet.bloom-filter-max-bytes` (default 1 MB). For ORC files it uses `write.orc.bloom.filter.columns` and `write.orc.bloom.filter.fpp` (default 0.05).[^icebergconf]
- **Apache ORC** files written by Spark get bloom filters through the `orc.bloom.filter.columns` option.[^n1]

## When do bloom filters in data files help?

A bloom filter helps when a query filters a column for equality (or `IN`) and the minimum and maximum statistics do not exclude files, which is typical for high-cardinality, unsorted columns such as IDs, emails or UUIDs.[^spec] It adds little for range filters, which min/max statistics already handle, or for columns whose chunks are dictionary encoded, because a reader can already rule out values that are not in the dictionary.[^spec] A filter that is too small for the column's real number of distinct values has a high false positive rate, so setting the expected number of distinct values matters.[^pj]

- [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)

# Broadcast join

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Broadcast_join

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Broadcast hash join, map-side join, `BroadcastHashJoin`</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed query processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Build side (small table), stream side (large table), `BroadcastExchange`, `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`, `BROADCAST` hint</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Sort-merge join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Sort-merge_join), [Shuffle hash join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle_hash_join), [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution), [Driver (Apache Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Driver_(Apache_Spark))</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/sql-performance-tuning.md, docs/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-hints.md, SQLConf.scala, SparkStrategies.scala, joins.scala, BroadcastExchangeExec.scala, QueryExecutionErrors.scala) and EXPLAIN output and configuration defaults from a PySpark 4.3.0 run</Verified>

A **broadcast join** is a join strategy in which the smaller table is copied in full to every [executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), so that each task can join its part of the larger table locally, without a [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle) of the larger table.[^perf] In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) it appears in plans as `BroadcastHashJoin` (for equality joins) or `BroadcastNestedLoopJoin` (for other conditions), fed by a `BroadcastExchange`. Spark picks it automatically when one side is estimated below `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` (default 10 MB). It is usually the fastest join when one side is small, and the most common cause of driver memory errors when that side is larger than expected.

## How does a broadcast join work in Spark?

A broadcast hash join in Spark SQL has three steps, all visible in the Spark 4.3.0 source:[^bex]

1. **Collect.** Spark runs the small side (the **build side**) and collects its rows to the [driver](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Driver_(Apache_Spark)).
1. **Build.** The driver builds a hash table (a `HashedRelation`) keyed on the join columns.
1. **Broadcast.** The driver broadcasts the hash table to the executors. Each task of the large side (the **stream side**) probes the table for each of its rows.

In a physical plan from PySpark 4.3.0, a join of a 1,000,000-row range with a 100-row range looks like this:

```
*(2) BroadcastHashJoin [k#9L], [k#11L], Inner, BuildRight, false, false
:- *(2) Project [id#8L AS k#9L]
:  +- *(2) Range (0, 1000000, step=1, splits=2)
+- BroadcastExchange HashedRelationBroadcastMode(List(input[0, bigint, false]),false)
   +- *(1) Project [id#10L AS k#11L]
      +- *(1) Range (0, 100, step=1, splits=2)
```

`BuildRight` means the right input is the broadcast side. There is no `Exchange` on the large side, so the scan, the join and any later narrow operators run in one stage (codegen stage 2 above).

## When does Spark choose a broadcast join?

For an equality join with no hint, Spark's join selection picks a broadcast hash join first, if one side is small enough to broadcast and the join type allows that side to be the build side. If both sides are small, Spark broadcasts the smaller one.[^strategies] "Small enough" means an estimated size in bytes at or below the threshold.[^joins]

| Setting | Default (4.3.0) | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` | 10 MB (10485760 bytes) | Maximum estimated size of a table to broadcast automatically; -1 disables automatic broadcast[^perf] |
| `spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` | (none; same as the above) | The threshold used by [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution) with runtime sizes[^perf] |
| `spark.sql.broadcastTimeout` | 300 seconds | How long to wait for the broadcast to complete[^perf] |
| `spark.sql.maxBroadcastTableSize` | 8 GiB | Hard limit on the built table size; above it the query fails (since 4.1.0)[^sqlconf] |

The decision uses estimated sizes. For a table without statistics, Spark assumes `Long.MaxValue` bytes and does not broadcast it unless it knows the table is small.[^sqlconf] `ANALYZE TABLE` and the [cost-based optimizer](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Cost-based_optimizer_(Spark)) improve these estimates. If the planner did not choose a broadcast join, [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution) can still switch a sort-merge join to a broadcast join once a side's runtime size is below the adaptive threshold, although the Spark documentation notes this is less efficient than planning it from the start.[^perf]

The build side must be the side whose unmatched rows do not need to be returned. For a left outer join, Spark can broadcast only the right side; for a right outer join, only the left side.[^joins] A full outer join cannot use a broadcast hash join.[^joins]

## Broadcast hints

A hint asks Spark to broadcast a relation even when its estimated size is above the threshold. In SQL, `BROADCAST`, `BROADCASTJOIN` and `MAPJOIN` are accepted; in the DataFrame API, `hint("broadcast")` or the `broadcast()` function.[^perf][^hints]

```sql
SELECT /*+ BROADCAST(r) */ *
FROM sales s JOIN regions r ON s.region_id = r.id;
```

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

sales.join(broadcast(regions), sales.region_id == regions.id)
```

When both sides of a join carry hints, `BROADCAST` takes priority over `MERGE`, `SHUFFLE_HASH` and `SHUFFLE_REPLICATE_NL`. Spark does not guarantee that the hinted strategy is used, because a strategy may not support the join type.[^perf] A hint also overrides `autoBroadcastJoinThreshold=-1`: in PySpark 4.3.0, a join with `hint("broadcast")` was planned as `BroadcastHashJoin` with automatic broadcast disabled.

## When does broadcasting backfire?

A broadcast join moves the whole build side through the driver and into every executor, so its cost grows with the build side and with the cluster size. The problems this causes are documented in Spark's source and settings:

- **Driver out of memory.** The build side is collected and the hash table is built on the driver.[^bex] If that runs out of memory, Spark fails the query with an error that it does not have enough memory to build and broadcast the table, and suggests disabling broadcast by setting `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` to -1 or increasing `spark.driver.memory`; for file tables it also suggests running `ANALYZE TABLE`.[^qee]
- **Hard limits.** A broadcast fails if the built table reaches `spark.sql.maxBroadcastTableSize` (8 GiB), or if the collected side has too many rows: 512,000,000 in general, and a lower limit derived from the hash map's maximum capacity when the join key is not a single `long` column.[^bex][^sqlconf]
- **Timeouts.** If building and sending the table takes longer than `spark.sql.broadcastTimeout` (300 seconds), the query fails.[^perf]
- **Wrong estimates.** A table that looks small to the planner, for example after a filter whose selectivity is overestimated, or a forced `BROADCAST` hint on a table that has grown, can be far larger at run time.
- **Executor memory.** Every executor holds a copy of the table for the duration of the join, in addition to its own work.

The usual fixes are to remove the hint, lower `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` or set it to -1, filter the build side before the join, or give the driver more memory.[^qee]

## Broadcast join compared with the other join strategies

|  | Broadcast hash join | [Sort-merge join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Sort-merge_join) | [Shuffle hash join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle_hash_join) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Shuffles | None on the large side; the small side goes through the driver | Both sides | Both sides |
| Memory need | Whole build side in the driver and in every executor | Low; sorts spill to disk | Build side of one partition in one task's memory |
| Chosen by default when | One side is below `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` | No side is small enough to broadcast and the join keys are sortable | Only when `spark.sql.join.preferSortMergeJoin` is false, or by hint or AQE |
| Full outer join | Not supported | Supported | Supported |

Sources: SparkStrategies.scala and joins.scala at v4.3.0.[^strategies][^joins]

# Broadcast variable

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Broadcast_variable

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">`SparkContext.broadcast`, shared read-only variable</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Driver-side value, chunked BitTorrent-like distribution, per-executor cached copy, `unpersist()` and `destroy()`</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Accumulator](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Accumulator), [Broadcast join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Broadcast_join), [Join strategy hints](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Join_strategy_hints), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/rdd-programming-guide.md, docs/tuning.md, docs/configuration.md, docs/spark-connect-overview.md, docs/sql-performance-tuning.md, core broadcast/TorrentBroadcast.scala, core unsafe/map/BytesToBytesMap.java, sql BroadcastExchangeExec.scala, SQLConf.scala, python/pyspark/sql/connect/session.py) and the PySpark 4.3.0 Broadcast.destroy API reference</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a **broadcast variable** is a read-only value that the driver sends once to every [executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), where it is cached and shared by all tasks, instead of being shipped again with every task. It is one of Spark's two kinds of shared variable; the other is the [accumulator](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Accumulator).[^rddguide] Broadcast variables are part of the `SparkContext` API and are not available to [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) clients; DataFrame code uses a [broadcast join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Broadcast_join) instead.[^connect]

## What is a broadcast variable used for?

A function passed to a Spark operation such as `map` normally gets its own copy of every variable it uses, shipped with each task. When tasks use a large object from the driver, such as a lookup table, a broadcast variable sends it to each executor once.[^rddguide] The Spark tuning guide says that tasks larger than about 20 KiB are probably worth optimizing, and that turning a large driver-side object into a broadcast variable reduces the size of each serialized task and the cost of launching a job.[^tuning]

Spark already broadcasts the common data that tasks within one stage need. An explicit broadcast variable is therefore useful mainly when tasks in several stages need the same data, or when keeping the data in deserialized form matters.[^rddguide]

## Example

```python
rates = {"EUR": 1.08, "GBP": 1.27, "JPY": 0.0067}
b_rates = spark.sparkContext.broadcast(rates)

usd = orders_rdd.map(lambda o: (o.id, o.amount * b_rates.value[o.currency]))
total = usd.map(lambda kv: kv[1]).sum()   # action: the map runs now and reads b_rates

b_rates.unpersist()   # free executor copies; b_rates is re-sent if used again
refunds_usd = refunds_rdd.map(lambda r: r.amount * b_rates.value[r.currency]).collect()

b_rates.destroy()     # last step: free everything; b_rates can no longer be used
```

The value is read with `.value`. It should not be changed after it is broadcast, so that every node sees the same value.[^rddguide] Because transformations such as `map` are lazy and run only when an action needs a result, the broadcast value is read when the action runs, not when `map` is called.[^rddops] `unpersist()` releases the copies on executors, and a later use broadcasts the value again. `destroy()` releases all resources, after which the variable cannot be used. Neither blocks by default.[^rddguide] The PySpark API reference says to use `destroy()` with caution, because a destroyed broadcast variable cannot be used again; it therefore belongs after the last action that reads the variable, including actions on RDDs built earlier.[^destroy]

## How is a broadcast variable distributed?

Spark's default implementation, `TorrentBroadcast`, is BitTorrent-like. The driver splits the serialized value into chunks and stores them in its block manager. Each executor fetches the chunks it lacks from the driver or from other executors that already have them, then stores them so that more executors can fetch from it. This stops the driver from being the bottleneck when every executor needs a copy.[^torrent]

Two settings control the transfer: `spark.broadcast.blockSize` (default `4m`) is the chunk size, and `spark.broadcast.compress` (default true) compresses broadcast data with `spark.io.compression.codec`.[^config]

## How large can a broadcast be?

The Spark docs set no specific maximum for `SparkContext.broadcast`. The practical limit is memory: the value is created on the driver, and each machine keeps a cached copy.[^rddguide] `SizeEstimator.estimate` can show how much heap a broadcast value will take on each executor.[^tuning]

Broadcast joins in Spark SQL have explicit limits. Spark plans one automatically when a table is under `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` (default 10 MB), waits up to `spark.sql.broadcastTimeout` (default 300 seconds) for the broadcast, and fails a broadcast table of 8 GiB or more (`spark.sql.maxBroadcastTableSize`, added in 4.1.0) or with too many rows: 2<sup>29</sup> / 1.5 (357,913,941) rows for a hash join whose key is not a single `LongType` column, and 512,000,000 rows otherwise.[^btbm][^perf][^sqlconf][^bee]

## Are broadcast variables supported in Spark Connect?

No. A Spark Connect client talks to the server through logical plans and has no access to the `SparkContext`; the Spark docs list `SparkContext` and RDDs among the APIs that Spark Connect does not support.[^connect] In the PySpark Connect client, reading `spark.sparkContext` raises `JVM_ATTRIBUTE_NOT_SUPPORTED`.[^csession]

The DataFrame equivalent works in both classic Spark and Spark Connect: put the lookup data in a small DataFrame and join with a `BROADCAST` [hint](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Join_strategy_hints) or `pyspark.sql.functions.broadcast()`.[^perf]

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

rates_df = spark.createDataFrame(list(rates.items()), ["currency", "rate"])
usd = orders.join(broadcast(rates_df), "currency")
```

## Broadcast variable compared with broadcast join

|  | Broadcast variable | Broadcast join |
| --- | --- | --- |
| API | `SparkContext.broadcast` (RDD and UDF code)[^rddguide] | DataFrame / SQL join with a broadcast hint or automatic planning[^perf] |
| Spark Connect | Not available[^connect] | Available |
| Size limits | None documented; bounded by driver and executor memory | 10 MB automatic threshold; hard limits of 8 GiB and a row limit of 357,913,941 or 512,000,000 rows, depending on the join key[^perf][^bee] |
| Typical use | Lookup tables or models inside RDD functions or UDFs | Joining a large table with a small one without shuffling the large one |

# Bucketing

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Bucketing

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Bucketed tables, CLUSTERED BY ... INTO n BUCKETS, bucket join</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data layout; query optimization</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Bucket columns, number of buckets, hash function, optional sort columns, catalog metadata</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) (bucket partition transform)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Partition](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), [Storage partitioned join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Storage_partitioned_join), [Liquid clustering](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Liquid_clustering), [Sort-merge join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Sort-merge_join)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (SQLConf.scala, DataFrameWriter.scala, V1Writes.scala, partitioning.scala, DataSourceScanExec.scala, docs/sql-data-sources-load-save-functions.md, docs/sql-performance-tuning.md), Spark JIRA, the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 spec and Spark configuration docs, and AbstractDeltaCatalog.scala at Delta Lake v4.4.1</Verified>

**Bucketing** is a table layout in which rows are assigned to a fixed number of logical buckets by hashing the values of one or more bucket columns, so that all rows with the same key land in the same bucket; each bucket is stored as one or more files, whose names carry the bucket ID.[^fdw] In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a bucketed table lets a join or aggregation on the bucket columns skip the [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), because the data is already grouped the way the operator needs it. Spark's file layout for buckets follows the bucketing scheme of [Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive);[^writer] in [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) the same idea is the `bucket[N]` partition transform, and [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) does not support bucketed tables.

## How does bucketing work in Apache Spark?

Spark writes a bucketed table with `DataFrameWriter.bucketBy` (optionally with `sortBy`), available since Spark 2.0, or with `CLUSTERED BY ... INTO n BUCKETS` in SQL. Bucketing and sorting apply only to persistent tables written with `saveAsTable`, because the bucket specification is stored in the catalog.[^loadsave][^writer]

```python
(orders.write
    .bucketBy(64, "customer_id")
    .sortBy("customer_id")
    .format("parquet")
    .saveAsTable("sales.orders_bucketed"))
```

```sql
CREATE TABLE sales.customers_bucketed
USING parquet
CLUSTERED BY (customer_id) INTO 64 BUCKETS
AS SELECT * FROM sales.customers;
```

A bucket is not a single file. Every write task that holds rows for a bucket writes its own file for that bucket, and a task starts a new file when it reaches `maxRecordsPerFile`; Spark appends the bucket ID and a file counter to each file name.[^fdw]

For Spark's own bucketed tables, the bucket ID is the same expression Spark uses for hash partitioning during a shuffle: a Murmur3 hash of the bucket columns, modulo the number of buckets. The source code comment explains why: matching the shuffle's distribution lets Spark shuffle only one side when it joins a bucketed table with a table that is not bucketed.[^v1writes][^partitioning]

## When does bucketing remove a shuffle?

Spark can skip the shuffle when the plan needs data clustered on the bucket columns and the scan already provides it:
- **Joins.** A [sort-merge join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Sort-merge_join) or shuffled hash join of two tables bucketed on the join keys, with the same number of buckets, needs no `Exchange`. If the bucket counts differ and the larger is a multiple of the smaller, `spark.sql.bucketing.coalesceBucketsInJoin.enabled` (default false, since 3.1.0) can merge buckets on the larger side, as long as the ratio is at most `spark.sql.bucketing.coalesceBucketsInJoin.maxBucketRatio` (default 4). The setting's documentation warns that coalescing reduces parallelism.[^sqlconf]
- **Aggregations and windows** grouped or partitioned by the bucket columns.
- **One-sided joins.** When only one table is bucketed, Spark shuffles only the other side, because the bucket hash matches the shuffle hash.[^v1writes]

By default `spark.sql.requireAllClusterKeysForCoPartition` (true, since 3.3.0) requires the join keys to cover all the clustering keys before Spark removes the shuffle. This avoids skew that can come from eliminating shuffles.[^sqlconf]

Bucketing also helps filters. A filter on a bucket column with an equality, `IN` or `IS NULL` condition (and `AND` or `OR` combinations of them) lets Spark read only the matching bucket files, which is called **bucket pruning**.[^fss]

## Settings that control bucketing

| Setting | Default | Since | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `spark.sql.sources.bucketing.enabled` | true | 2.0.0 | When false, Spark treats bucketed tables as ordinary tables. |
| `spark.sql.sources.bucketing.autoBucketedScan.enabled` | true | 3.1.0 | Spark skips the bucketed scan when the query has no operator that uses bucketing, or when an exchange sits between the scan and that operator. |
| `spark.sql.sources.bucketing.maxBuckets` | 100000 | 2.4.0 | Largest bucket count allowed. |
| `spark.sql.bucketing.coalesceBucketsInJoin.enabled` | false | 3.1.0 | Merges buckets on the larger side of a join when one count divides the other. |

All values are from `SQLConf.scala` at Spark 4.3.0.[^sqlconf] The automatic choice of bucketed scan was added in SPARK-32859, and bucket coalescing in SPARK-31350 and SPARK-32286, all fixed in 3.1.0.[^n1][^n2]

## How can you tell if bucketing was used?

In `EXPLAIN` output, a file scan that reads buckets lists `Bucketed: true` and `SelectedBucketsCount` (for example "8 out of 64") in its metadata, and there is no `Exchange` between the scan and the join or aggregate.[^scanexec] If the scan does not read buckets, the value gives the reason: `false (disabled by configuration)`, `false (disabled by query planner)` or `false (bucket column(s) not read)`.[^scanexec]

## Spark bucketing vs Hive bucketing

Spark's bucket layout looks like Hive's but uses a different hash function, so Spark-native bucketed tables are not compatible with Hive's bucketing.[^writer] When Spark writes into a Hive-format bucketed table, it uses Hive's hash and Hive's bucket file naming instead, so that Hive and other engines can read the result; SPARK-32709 and SPARK-32712 added this in Spark 3.3.0.[^v1writes][^n3][^n4]

## How does bucketing interact with table formats?

**[Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)** rejects bucketed tables: at Delta Lake 4.4.1, creating a Delta table with a bucket specification raises an "operation not supported" error, and combining `CLUSTER BY` with `CLUSTERED BY ... INTO BUCKETS` is rejected with a message to remove the bucketing.[^delta][^n5] Delta tables use partitioning or [liquid clustering](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Liquid_clustering) for data layout instead.

**[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)** has bucketing as a partition transform. `bucket[N]` hashes a value with the 32-bit Murmur3 hash (x86 variant, seed 0), drops the sign bit and takes the result modulo N.[^icebergspec] Because it is a partition, a bucket partition gets [partition pruning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition_pruning) from the table metadata, not from file names. An Iceberg bucket hash does not match Spark's shuffle hash, so Spark removes the shuffle through a [storage partitioned join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Storage_partitioned_join) instead, using the partitioning that a Data Source V2 table reports. This needs `spark.sql.sources.v2.bucketing.enabled` (default true, since 3.3.0) on the Spark side and `spark.sql.iceberg.planning.preserve-data-grouping` (default false) on the Iceberg side.[^sqlconf][^perf][^n6]

```sql
-- Iceberg: bucketing as a partition transform
CREATE TABLE prod.db.orders (id BIGINT, customer_id BIGINT, amount DECIMAL(10,2))
USING iceberg
PARTITIONED BY (bucket(16, customer_id));
```

## Limitations

- Bucketing is fixed at write time. Changing the number of buckets or the bucket columns means rewriting the table.
- Spark-native buckets are readable as buckets only by Spark, because of the hash function.[^writer]

[^perf]: [Performance Tuning (Spark 4.3.0)](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/sql-performance-tuning.html). *Apache Software Foundation*. Retrieved 2026-11-23.

# Business Source License

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Business_Source_License

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">BSL, BUSL, BSL 1.1</Field>
  <Field name="field">Software licensing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Licensor, Licensed Work, Additional Use Grant, Change Date, Change License</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">Terraform (1.6.0 and later), Materialize, CockroachDB (19.2 to 24.2)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[MinIO](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MinIO), [Open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the BSL 1.1 text published by MariaDB, the LICENSE files of hashicorp/terraform, MaterializeInc/materialize and cockroachdb/cockroach (v19.1.0, v19.2.0 and current), the HashiCorp and Cockroach Labs announcements and the Linux Foundation OpenTofu announcement</Verified>

The **Business Source License** (BSL, also written BUSL) is a source-available software license, published by MariaDB, under which the source code can be read, changed and redistributed, but production use is allowed only as far as the licensor's **Additional Use Grant** permits, until each version converts to an open source license on its **Change Date**.[^bsl] The license text itself says it "is not an Open Source license".[^bsl] In data infrastructure the BSL is best known from vendors that moved projects off open source licenses to stop competitors from selling hosted versions; the move of HashiCorp's Terraform in 2023 led to the OpenTofu fork.

## How it works

The BSL is a template. A licensor fills in a short parameter block at the top, and the fixed license text below it applies to those values:[^bsl]

| Parameter | What it sets |
| --- | --- |
| Licensor | Who grants the license. |
| Licensed Work | The software and version covered. |
| Additional Use Grant | Which production use is allowed before the Change Date. Without a grant, only non-production use is allowed. |
| Change Date | When the version converts. The conversion happens on the Change Date or on the fourth anniversary of the version's first public release, whichever comes first. |
| Change License | The license the version converts to. It must be GPL version 2.0 or later, or a license compatible with it. |

Without an Additional Use Grant, the BSL lets anyone copy, modify, create derivative works of and redistribute the code, and make non-production use of it.[^bsl] Each version has its own clock: a newer release starts a new period, so the latest code is always under the restrictive terms while versions older than the change period become open source.[^bsl]

## Is the BSL open source?

No. The BSL text states that it is not an Open Source license, and that the Licensed Work will eventually be made available under one, namely the Change License.[^bsl] Code under the BSL is often called *source available*: anyone can read it, but the restriction on production use conflicts with the Open Source Definition's rule that a license must not restrict anyone from using the program in a specific field of endeavor.[^n1] A version becomes open source only when it reaches its Change Date.

## Use in data tools

The parameters vary a great deal between projects, so "under the BSL" says little until the parameter block is read.

| Project | Previous license | First BSL version | Additional Use Grant (summary) | Change period | Change License |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Terraform (HashiCorp, now IBM) | Mozilla Public License 2.0[^hashi] | 1.6.0[^tf] | Production use allowed, except offering it to third parties on a hosted or embedded basis to compete with the licensor's paid versions[^tf] | Four years from publication[^tf] | MPL 2.0[^tf] |
| Materialize | Not covered here | Each release; the current LICENSE names a dated version[^mz] | Production use within memory and disk limits per installation, and no commercial database service that lets third parties define views[^mz] | Four years (the current LICENSE has a Change Date of 23 November 2030)[^mz] | Apache License 2.0[^mz] |
| CockroachDB (Cockroach Labs) | Apache License 2.0 (core, up to 19.1)[^crdb191] | 19.2[^crdb192] | Use allowed, except a commercial database service that lets third parties create tables[^crdb192] | Change Date 1 October 2022 for 19.2[^crdb192] | Apache License 2.0[^crdb192] |

HashiCorp announced on 10 August 2023 that future releases of its products would move from the MPL 2.0 to the BSL 1.1, while its APIs, SDKs and almost all other libraries would stay under the MPL 2.0.[^hashi] On 20 September 2023 the Linux Foundation announced OpenTofu, which it described as an open source successor to the MPLv2-licensed Terraform.[^n2]

The BSL is not always the last step. Cockroach Labs used it for the CockroachDB core from 19.2, then announced in August 2024 that from version 24.3 it would retire its Core offering and consolidate on a single enterprise license, with free tiers for individuals and smaller companies; the code remains source available.[^n3] The repository's current `LICENSE` file is the CockroachDB Software License, not the BSL.[^n4]

## What the BSL is not

- **Not a single set of terms.** Two BSL projects can have opposite production rules, because the Additional Use Grant is written by each licensor.
- **Not the same as the AGPL.** The GNU AGPLv3 is an open source license that allows any use but requires source code for network-served modifications; [MinIO](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MinIO) used it for its community edition and never moved to the BSL.[^n5]
- **Not retroactive.** A license change applies to new versions. Releases published under an earlier open source license stay available under it, which is what makes forks such as OpenTofu possible.[^hashi]

## Use in an open lakehouse

The core open lakehouse projects (for example [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) and [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)) are under the Apache License 2.0. The BSL matters at the edges of a stack: infrastructure as code, databases and streaming tools that a team runs next to the lakehouse. For each such tool the questions are the same: what the Additional Use Grant forbids, whether the planned use is production use, and which version converts to which license on which date.

- [MinIO](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MinIO)
- [Open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse)
- [Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation)
- [Linux Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Linux_Foundation)

# Caching and persistence

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Caching_and_persistence

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">`cache()`, `persist()`, `CACHE TABLE`, storage levels</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Storage levels, storage memory, in-memory columnar cache, LRU eviction, `unpersist()`</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark memory management](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_memory_management), [Checkpointing (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Checkpointing_(Spark)), [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD), [Garbage collection in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Garbage_collection_in_Spark)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/rdd-programming-guide.md, docs/sql-performance-tuning.md, docs/sql-ref-syntax-aux-cache-cache-table.md, docs/tuning.md, docs/job-scheduling.md, sql/api Dataset.scala, python/pyspark/sql/dataframe.py)</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), **caching** or **persistence** keeps the computed partitions of a DataFrame, table or [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD) in executor memory or on local disk, so that later actions reuse them instead of recomputing them from the source. `persist()` takes a storage level that says where and how the data is kept; `cache()` is `persist()` with the default level.[^rddguide] A cache is fault tolerant: a lost partition is recomputed from its lineage.[^rddguide]

## Cache vs persist

`cache()` and `persist()` differ only in the storage level. The default is different for DataFrames and RDDs:

| API | `cache()` uses | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DataFrame / Dataset (Scala, Java) | `MEMORY_AND_DISK` | [^dataset] |
| DataFrame (PySpark) | `MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER`, changed to match Scala in 3.0 | [^pydf] |
| SQL `CACHE TABLE` | `MEMORY_AND_DISK`, unless set with `OPTIONS ('storageLevel' ...)` | [^cachetable] |
| RDD | `MEMORY_ONLY` | [^rddguide] |

Caching is lazy. `cache()` only marks the DataFrame; the data is stored the first time an action computes it.[^rddguide] `CACHE TABLE` is the exception: it caches immediately unless written as `CACHE LAZY TABLE`.[^cachetable]

DataFrames and tables are cached in Spark SQL's in-memory columnar format. Spark then scans only the needed columns and picks a compression codec per column (`spark.sql.inMemoryColumnarStorage.compressed`, default true).[^perf] Spark 4.3.0 also documents an Apache Arrow based cache format as an alternative.[^perf] Cached data is shared by all Spark sessions on the cluster.[^cachetable]

## Storage levels

| Level | Where | If it does not fit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MEMORY_ONLY` | Memory, deserialized | Partitions that do not fit are not cached and are recomputed when needed |
| `MEMORY_AND_DISK` | Memory, deserialized | Partitions that do not fit go to disk |
| `MEMORY_ONLY_SER`, `MEMORY_AND_DISK_SER` (Java and Scala) | Memory, serialized (one byte array per partition) | As above; smaller in memory but more CPU to read |
| `DISK_ONLY` | Local disk only | n/a |
| `..._2` variants, for example `MEMORY_AND_DISK_2` | As above, replicated on two nodes | As above |
| `OFF_HEAP` (experimental) | Off-heap memory, serialized; requires off-heap memory to be enabled | n/a |

<small>Source: RDD Programming Guide, Spark 4.3.0.[^rddguide]</small>

In Python, stored objects are always serialized with Pickle, so the serialized and deserialized levels behave the same for RDDs.[^rddguide]

## How to cache in PySpark and SQL

```python
from pyspark import StorageLevel

dim = spark.read.table("main.sales.dim_customer").filter("active")
dim.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)
dim.count()          # action that fills the cache

# ... several queries that reuse dim ...

dim.unpersist()
```

```sql
CACHE TABLE active_customers AS SELECT * FROM main.sales.dim_customer WHERE active;
UNCACHE TABLE active_customers;
```

The Storage tab of the Spark UI lists everything cached in the application with its size in memory and on disk.[^perf]

## Where cached data lives

Cached blocks use **storage memory** in the executor's unified memory region. Storage and execution borrow from each other, and execution can evict cached blocks down to `spark.memory.storageFraction` (default 0.5) of the region.[^tuning] When memory is short, Spark drops old partitions in least-recently-used order. `unpersist()` removes data at once; it does not block unless called with `blocking=True`.[^rddguide] See [Spark memory management](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_memory_management).

## When does caching hurt?

- **The data is used once.** The RDD guide describes the gain from persisting as reuse: each node keeps the partitions it computes and reuses them in other actions on that dataset or datasets derived from it.[^rddguide] If no later action reads the cached data, nothing is reused, and storing the partitions is extra work and memory with no gain.
- **It takes memory from execution.** Cached data competes with the working memory of tasks; more cache can mean more [spill](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spill_(memory)) for joins and aggregations.[^tuning]
- **It adds GC pressure.** The Spark docs name interference between tasks' working memory and cached data as one cause of garbage collection problems, and recommend caching less when the old generation is nearly full: "it is better to cache fewer objects than to slow down task execution".[^tuning] See [Garbage collection in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Garbage_collection_in_Spark).
- **It blocks executor scale-down.** With [dynamic allocation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dynamic_allocation), executors that hold cached data are not removed by default (`spark.dynamicAllocation.cachedExecutorIdleTimeout` is infinite).[^jobsched]
- **Recomputing is cheap.** The RDD guide advises not to spill to disk unless the functions that computed the data are expensive or filter a lot of it; otherwise recomputing a partition may be as fast as reading it from disk.[^rddguide]

## Caching compared with checkpointing

|  | Caching / persistence | [Checkpointing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Checkpointing_(Spark)) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Keeps lineage? | Yes; lost partitions are recomputed from the source[^rddguide] | No; the plan is cut and the data is read back from the checkpoint[^dataset] |
| Where | Executor memory or local disk | Reliable storage set with `setCheckpointDir` (or executor storage for local checkpoints)[^dataset] |
| Survives executor loss? | Recomputed (or read from a replica with `_2` levels) | Yes for reliable checkpoints |

## See also

- [Spark memory management](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_memory_management)
- [Checkpointing (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Checkpointing_(Spark))
- [Garbage collection in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Garbage_collection_in_Spark)
- [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD)

# Catalog plugin API (Spark)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Catalog_plugin_API_(Spark)

<Infobox type="concept" name="Catalog plugin API">
  <Field name="also_known_as">CatalogPlugin, Spark multi-catalog API, DSV2 catalog API</Field>
  <Field name="field">Metadata management in query engines</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">CatalogPlugin, TableCatalog, SupportsNamespaces, StagingTableCatalog, FunctionCatalog, ViewCatalog, ProcedureCatalog, CatalogExtension</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark); catalogs from [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Data Source V2](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_Source_V2), [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog), [Hive Metastore](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_Metastore), [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (CatalogPlugin.java, TableCatalog.java, CatalogExtension.java, DelegatingCatalogExtension.java, SQLConf.scala, docs/sql-v2-data-sources.md), the Spark 3.0.0 release notes, Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 Spark docs and source, Delta Lake v4.4.1 source and docs, the Unity Catalog 0.7.0 Spark connector docs and source, and the Spark versions supported by Delta Lake 4.4.1 and Unity Catalog 0.7.0 (release notes) and Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 (Maven Central runtime artifacts)</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), the **catalog plugin API** is the part of [Data Source V2](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_Source_V2) that lets an external catalog register under a name and serve namespaces, tables, views, functions and procedures to Spark SQL; its root interface is `org.apache.spark.sql.connector.catalog.CatalogPlugin`.[^plugin] It is how [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) and [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog) plug into Spark,[^icecfg][^deltabatch][^ucspark] and it allows one Spark session to query tables from several catalogs with three-part names such as `catalog.schema.table`.

## What is CatalogPlugin?

`CatalogPlugin` is a marker interface with three methods: `initialize(name, options)`, `name()` and a default `defaultNamespace()`. Spark loads the class through a required public no-argument constructor and then calls `initialize` once.[^plugin] The interface has been part of Spark since 3.0.0 and is annotated `@Evolving`.[^plugin] The Spark 3.0.0 release notes list it as "Catalog plugin API" (SPARK-31121).[^r300]

## How is a catalog registered?

A catalog is registered with the configuration key `spark.sql.catalog.<name>`, whose value is the implementing class. Every key of the form `spark.sql.catalog.<name>.<key>` is passed to `initialize` in a case-insensitive map with the prefix removed.[^plugin] For example, `spark.sql.catalog.lake.type=rest` reaches the catalog named `lake` as the option `type=rest`.

Two settings control defaults. `spark.sql.defaultCatalog` names the current catalog when none has been set, and defaults to `spark_catalog`.[^sqlconf] `spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog` sets the implementation of the built-in session catalog; its default, `builtin`, is Spark's own `V2SessionCatalog`, and a replacement must stay consistent with the built-in catalog, typically by extending `CatalogExtension`.[^sqlconf]

## What does TableCatalog add?

A plugin gains abilities by implementing more interfaces. `TableCatalog` extends `CatalogPlugin` with `listTables`, `loadTable`, `createTable`, `alterTable`, `dropTable` and related methods, and returns `Table` objects that Spark reads and writes through Data Source V2.[^dsv2doc]

`TableCatalog` also carries [time travel](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Time_travel_(SQL)). Overloads `loadTable(ident, String version)` and `loadTable(ident, long timestamp)`, with the timestamp in microseconds since the Unix epoch, return a table at a past state; the default implementations throw a "no such table" error, so a catalog supports time travel only if it overrides them.[^tablecatalog] An overload that receives the write privileges a statement needs was added in 3.5.3.[^tablecatalog]

| Interface | Adds | Since |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TableCatalog` | Table lifecycle: list, load, create, alter, drop | 3.0.0[^tablecatalog] |
| `SupportsNamespaces` | Namespace (database or schema) DDL | 3.0.0[^ns] |
| `StagingTableCatalog` | Atomic `CREATE TABLE AS SELECT` and `REPLACE TABLE AS SELECT` through staged tables | 3.0.0[^staging] |
| `CatalogExtension`, `DelegatingCatalogExtension` | Wrap the built-in session catalog and delegate to it | 3.0.0[^ext] |
| `FunctionCatalog` | List and load user-defined functions | 3.2.0[^func] |
| `ProcedureCatalog` | Stored procedures called with `CALL` | 4.0.0[^proc] |
| `ViewCatalog` | View DDL and view reads | 4.2.0[^view] |

The built-in session catalog is not a `ViewCatalog`; views in `spark_catalog` still use the V1, Hive-compatible code path, and V2 view support applies to catalogs registered under their own names.[^dsv2doc]

## How do Iceberg, Delta Lake and Unity Catalog register catalogs?

**Apache Iceberg** provides two classes. `org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog` is a standalone catalog backed by a Hive, Hadoop, REST, Glue, JDBC or Nessie catalog, selected with an option such as `type=rest`. `org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkSessionCatalog` replaces `spark_catalog`, serves Iceberg tables itself and delegates other tables to Spark's built-in catalog.[^icecfg] In the Iceberg 1.12.0 source, `SparkSessionCatalog` implements `CatalogExtension`, and the shared base class of both implements `StagingTableCatalog`, `ProcedureCatalog` and `SupportsNamespaces`.[^icessc][^icebase]

**Delta Lake** replaces the session catalog. Its documentation sets `spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog` to `org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog`, together with `spark.sql.extensions=io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension`.[^deltabatch] In the Delta Lake v4.4.1 source, `DeltaCatalog` derives from `AbstractDeltaCatalog`, which extends Spark's `DelegatingCatalogExtension`, so non-Delta tables fall through to the built-in catalog.[^deltasrc]

**Unity Catalog** OSS registers a named catalog with `io.unitycatalog.spark.UCSingleCatalog`, plus `uri` and authentication options under the same prefix, and its guide makes that catalog the default with `spark.sql.defaultCatalog`. The same guide also configures Delta Lake's extension and `DeltaCatalog`.[^ucspark] In the 0.7.0 source, `UCSingleCatalog` implements `StagingTableCatalog` and `SupportsNamespaces`.[^ucsrc]

## Example

The connector releases cited on this page do not all support Spark 4.3. Delta Lake 4.4.1 is built for Spark 4.0.1, 4.1.0 and 4.2.0,[^delta441] Unity Catalog 0.7.0 publishes Spark connectors for Spark 4.0.x, 4.1.x and 4.2.x,[^uc070] and Iceberg 1.12.0 publishes Spark runtimes for Spark 3.5, 4.0 and 4.1.[^icemvn] The newest Spark line that all three support is therefore 4.1.

The following PySpark session targets Spark 4.1 with Scala 2.13. It puts Delta Lake in the session catalog and adds an Iceberg REST catalog named `lake` and a Unity Catalog catalog named `unity`. Class names and option keys follow the cited project docs.[^icecfg][^deltabatch][^ucspark]

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = (
    SparkSession.builder
    # Spark 4.1, Scala 2.13
    .config("spark.jars.packages", ",".join([
        "io.delta:delta-spark_4.1_2.13:4.4.1",
        "org.apache.iceberg:iceberg-spark-runtime-4.1_2.13:1.12.0",
        "io.unitycatalog:unitycatalog-spark_4.1_2.13:0.7.0",
    ]))
    .config("spark.sql.extensions", "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog",
            "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.lake", "org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.lake.type", "rest")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.lake.uri", "http://localhost:8181")  # Iceberg REST server
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.unity", "io.unitycatalog.spark.UCSingleCatalog")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.unity.uri", "http://localhost:8080")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.unity.auth.type", "static")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.unity.auth.token", "<token>")
    .getOrCreate()
)

spark.sql("SELECT * FROM lake.sales.orders LIMIT 10").show()
spark.sql("SHOW NAMESPACES IN unity").show()
```

## Catalog plugin vs. Hive Metastore

The catalog plugin API is an interface inside Spark; a [Hive Metastore](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_Metastore) is a metadata service. Spark's built-in `spark_catalog` can be backed by a Hive Metastore, and plugins such as Iceberg's `SparkCatalog` with `type=hive` can use one as their store, but the plugin decides how names map to tables.[^icecfg] See [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog) for the broader term.
