# Catalyst optimizer

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Catalyst_optimizer

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Catalyst, Spark SQL optimizer</Field>
  <Field name="field">Query optimization</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">2014, with Spark SQL (described in a SIGMOD 2015 paper)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Trees and rules, analyzer, logical optimizer (rule batches), physical planner (strategies), code generation</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Logical plan and physical plan](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Logical_plan_and_physical_plan), [Whole-stage code generation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Whole-stage_code_generation), [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution), [Cost-based optimizer (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Cost-based_optimizer_(Spark)), [Predicate pushdown](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown), [Project Tungsten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Tungsten)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the SIGMOD 2015 paper "Spark SQL: Relational Data Processing in Spark", the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (Optimizer.scala, SparkStrategies.scala, SQLConf.scala, StaticSQLConf.scala, docs/sql-ref-syntax-qry-explain.md, docs/sql-performance-tuning.md), the Spark 3.0.0 release notes, the Delta Lake quickstart, the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 Spark configuration page and plan change logs and EXPLAIN output from a PySpark 4.3.0 run</Verified>

The **Catalyst optimizer** is the extensible query optimizer of Spark SQL in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark); it turns every SQL query and DataFrame or Dataset program into an optimized physical plan by applying rules to trees in four phases: analysis, logical optimization, physical planning and code generation.[^paper] SQL queries and DataFrame operations, including those written in Python and R, all go through Catalyst.[^paper] The paper that introduced Catalyst, "Spark SQL: Relational Data Processing in Spark", was written by Michael Armbrust, Reynold Xin, Matei Zaharia and others at Databricks, MIT CSAIL and the AMPLab at UC Berkeley, and presented at SIGMOD in 2015; it gives May 2014 as the first release of Spark SQL.[^paper]

## How does Catalyst work?

Catalyst represents a query as a **tree** of immutable nodes, such as expressions (`Add`, `Literal`) and operators (`Filter`, `Join`). A **rule** is a function from one tree to another, usually written with Scala pattern matching; for example, a rule can fold `Add(Literal(1), Literal(2))` into `Literal(3)`. Rules are grouped into **batches**, and each batch runs until the tree stops changing (a fixed point) or a set number of times.[^paper]

The paper describes four phases. In the physical planning phase Catalyst may generate several plans and compare them by cost; the other phases are purely rule-based.[^paper]

| Phase | Input | Output | Examples of what happens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Analysis | Unresolved logical plan from the SQL parser or the DataFrame API | Resolved (analyzed) logical plan | Look up tables in the catalog, resolve column names, assign unique attribute IDs, apply type coercion[^paper] |
| 2. Logical optimization | Analyzed logical plan | Optimized logical plan | Constant folding, predicate pushdown, column pruning, boolean simplification[^paper][^opt] |
| 3. Physical planning | Optimized logical plan | Physical plan (`SparkPlan`) | Pick join strategies, pick hash or sort aggregation, push filters into data source scans[^paper][^strategies] |
| 4. Code generation | Physical plan | Java bytecode for parts of the query | [Whole-stage code generation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Whole-stage_code_generation) compiles chains of operators into one function[^paper] |

In Spark 4.3.0 the logical optimizer is a long list of named batches, for example "Operator Optimization before Inferring Filters", "Infer Filters", "Join Reorder" (used by the [cost-based optimizer](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Cost-based_optimizer_(Spark))) and "RewriteSubquery".[^opt] Since Spark 3.0.0, [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution) adds a further round of optimization at run time, using runtime statistics.[^r300][^perf]

## Which Catalyst rules can be seen in EXPLAIN?

Rules do not appear by name in `EXPLAIN` output, but their effects do. `EXPLAIN EXTENDED` (or `df.explain(mode="extended")`) prints the parsed, analyzed and optimized logical plans and the physical plan, so a rule's work shows as a difference between two of them.[^explain] The examples below are from PySpark 4.3.0.

| Rule (Spark 4.3.0 class name) | What it does | How it shows in EXPLAIN |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ConstantFolding` | Evaluates constant expressions at planning time | `(id % cast(2 as bigint))` in the analyzed plan becomes `(id % 2)` in the optimized plan |
| `PushDownPredicates` | Moves filters below projections and joins, toward the data | A `Filter` written after a join appears under the join, on each input |
| `InferFiltersFromConstraints` | Derives new filters from join conditions and existing filters | A join on `id` with `id > 10` on one side gets `id > 10 AND isnotnull(id)` on both sides |
| `ColumnPruning` | Removes columns that no later operator needs | A Parquet scan lists only the needed columns, for example `FileScan parquet [id#42L]` |
| `BooleanSimplification` | Simplifies boolean expressions | `y > 3 AND true` becomes `y > 3` |
| Data source pushdown (physical planning) | Hands filters to the data source | `PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(id), GreaterThan(id,10)]` on a `FileScan parquet` node; see [Predicate pushdown](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown) |

To see the rules by name, set `spark.sql.planChangeLog.level` to `WARN`. Spark then logs each rule that changes the plan, with the plan before and after. For the query `spark.range(10).selectExpr("id + (1 + 2) as y").filter("y > 3 and true")`, PySpark 4.3.0 logged `ConstantFolding`, `BooleanSimplification` and `PushDownPredicates` among the optimizer rules, along with analyzer rules such as `ResolveReferences`.[^sqlconf]

```python
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.planChangeLog.level", "WARN")
df = spark.range(10).selectExpr("id + (1 + 2) AS y").filter("y > 3 AND true")
df.explain(mode="extended")
```

Individual rules can be turned off with `spark.sql.optimizer.excludedRules`, a comma-separated list of rule names (since 2.4.0). Spark does not guarantee that every listed rule is excluded, because some rules are needed for correctness.[^sqlconf]

## Extending Catalyst

Catalyst was built to be extended. The paper names new data sources, including ones that accept pushed-down filters, user-defined types and new optimization rules as extension points.[^paper] In Spark 4.3.0, the static setting `spark.sql.extensions` takes a list of classes that add rules, planner strategies, parsers and functions to every session.[^static] Table formats use this hook: [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) is enabled with `spark.sql.extensions=io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension`,[^delta] and [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)'s SQL extensions with `org.apache.iceberg.spark.extensions.IcebergSparkSessionExtensions`.[^icecfg]

## What Catalyst is not

- **Not the execution engine.** Catalyst decides what plan to run. How the chosen operators use memory and CPU is the work of [Project Tungsten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Tungsten) and the executors.
- **Not used by the RDD API.** Programs written with RDDs and arbitrary functions are run as written. Only DataFrame, Dataset and SQL operations, whose structure Spark understands, are optimized by Catalyst.[^paper]

# Checkpointing (Spark)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Checkpointing_(Spark)

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Lineage checkpoint, streaming checkpoint</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">RDD and DataFrame checkpoints, local checkpoints, checkpoint directory, Structured Streaming `checkpointLocation`</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Caching and persistence](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Caching_and_persistence), [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics), [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (core RDD.scala, sql/api Dataset.scala, python/pyspark/sql/dataframe.py, docs/configuration.md, docs/streaming/apis-on-dataframes-and-datasets.md) and the Delta Lake protocol at tag v4.4.1</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), **checkpointing** is saving data or query progress to storage so that later work can start from the saved copy instead of recomputing it, and the word names two different features. **Lineage checkpointing** saves the data of an [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD) or DataFrame to storage and cuts its lineage or query plan, so that later work starts from the saved data instead of recomputing everything. **Streaming checkpoints** are the progress and state that a [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) query writes to its `checkpointLocation` so it can restart where it stopped.[^rdd][^ss] The two share a name but not a purpose, a format, or an API. This page is a short guide to which is which.

## Kinds of checkpoint

| Kind | API | What it saves | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RDD checkpoint | `sc.setCheckpointDir(dir)`, then `rdd.checkpoint()` | The RDD's partitions, in the checkpoint directory; references to parent RDDs are removed[^rdd] | Cut long lineage, for example in iterative algorithms |
| RDD local checkpoint | `rdd.localCheckpoint()` | The RDD's partitions in executor storage, through the caching layer[^rdd] | Cut lineage without the cost of a reliable file system; not fault tolerant |
| DataFrame checkpoint | `df.checkpoint(eager=True)` | The DataFrame's data in the checkpoint directory; the logical plan is truncated[^dataset] | Stop a query plan from growing in loops |
| DataFrame local checkpoint | `df.localCheckpoint(eager=True)` | The data in executor storage[^dataset] | Faster, but executor loss can fail the job |
| Structured Streaming checkpoint | `.option("checkpointLocation", path)` on `writeStream` | Offsets processed in each trigger, and running state such as aggregates[^ss] | Restart a query after failure or shutdown |
| [DStreams](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Streaming_(DStreams)) checkpoint | `StreamingContext.checkpoint(dir)` | Metadata defining the computation, and generated RDDs saved to reliable storage[^dstreams] | Recovery for the DStreams API, deprecated since Spark 3.4.0[^spark42075] |

## Lineage checkpointing (RDD and DataFrame)

An RDD checkpoint is lazy. `rdd.checkpoint()` only marks the RDD, and the data is written at the end of the first action on it. The Spark source recommends persisting the RDD first, because writing the checkpoint otherwise recomputes it.[^rdd]

A DataFrame checkpoint is eager by default: `df.checkpoint()` runs a job right away and returns a new DataFrame whose plan starts from the saved data.[^dataset] With `eager=False`, the saved data may differ from what the job used if the plan is non-deterministic and tasks are retried, so the Spark docs recommend `eager=True` for a deterministic snapshot.[^dataset] DataFrame checkpointing has been in the Dataset API since Spark 2.1.0 and works with [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) since Spark 4.0.0.[^pydf]

The checkpoint directory comes from `SparkContext.setCheckpointDir` or, since Spark 4.0.0, the `spark.checkpoint.dir` configuration. Spark does not delete checkpoint files when the checkpointed data goes out of scope unless `spark.cleaner.referenceTracking.cleanCheckpoints` (default false) is set.[^config]

```python
# spark.checkpoint.dir is set when the session starts, for example
#   --conf spark.checkpoint.dir=s3a://bucket/checkpoints

df = spark.read.table("main.ml.features")
for i in range(20):
    df = update_step(df)          # user function; each step adds to the plan
    if i % 5 == 4:
        df = df.checkpoint()      # cut the plan every five iterations
```

Local checkpoints are faster because they skip the reliable file system, but executor loss makes the data unreachable and can fail the job. The Spark source warns that local checkpointing is not safe with [dynamic allocation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dynamic_allocation), which removes executors together with their cached blocks.[^rdd] Lineage checkpointing is also different from [caching](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Caching_and_persistence), which keeps lineage and recomputes lost partitions.

## Streaming checkpoints

A Structured Streaming query with a `checkpointLocation` saves its progress (the range of offsets processed in each trigger) and its running state to that path, using checkpoints and write-ahead logs. On restart with the same location, the query continues where it left off. The location has to be a path in an HDFS-compatible file system.[^ss] Streaming checkpoints are needed for the end-to-end guarantees described in [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics).

A streaming checkpoint is tied to one query. Deleting it, or pointing a changed query at it, changes what the query reprocesses; the Structured Streaming guide's section "Recovery Semantics after Changes in a Streaming Query" lists which changes are allowed between restarts.[^ss]

## Delta Lake checkpoints

[Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) uses the word for a third thing: a **checkpoint** in the Delta transaction log is a Parquet file that summarizes the table's state at a version, so readers can rebuild a snapshot without replaying every JSON commit, and old log entries can be cleaned up.[^delta] Delta checkpoints are written by the table format, not by Spark's checkpoint APIs.

- [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming)
- [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics)
- [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD)
- [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)

# Collation (Spark SQL)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Collation_(Spark_SQL)

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">String collation, collated string type</Field>
  <Field name="field">SQL query engines</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`COLLATE` clause, `UTF8_BINARY`, `UTF8_LCASE`, ICU-based `UNICODE` and locale collations, `_CI`, `_AI` and `_RTRIM` modifiers, `DEFAULT COLLATION`</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark error classes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_error_classes), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/sql-ref-syntax-aux-show-collations.md, SqlBaseParser.g4, CollationFactory.java, collationExpressions.scala, RewriteCollationJoin.scala, SQLConf.scala, error-conditions.json, sql-tests collations-basic results), the Spark 4.0.0, 4.1.0, 4.2.0 and 4.3.0 release notes and the PostgreSQL collation documentation</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a **collation** is a property of the `STRING` type that sets how Spark SQL compares, sorts, groups and joins string values, for example whether `'a'` equals `'A'`. Spark SQL added string collation support in Spark 4.0.0 (SPARK-46830).[^r400] The default collation, `UTF8_BINARY`, compares the raw UTF-8 bytes; other collations make comparisons case-insensitive, accent-insensitive, trailing-space-insensitive or locale-aware.[^show]

## What collations does Spark SQL support?

Spark SQL has two kinds of collation. Two, with their `_RTRIM` variants, are built into Spark and do not depend on a locale: `UTF8_BINARY` (case- and accent-sensitive byte comparison) and `UTF8_LCASE` (case-insensitive). The others come from the International Components for Unicode (ICU) library: `UNICODE`, which uses the locale-independent Unicode rules, and locale collations such as `en_USA`.[^show] The Spark 4.3.0 build uses ICU4J 78.3.[^pom]

A collation name can carry modifiers. `_CI` makes it case-insensitive, `_AI` accent-insensitive and `_RTRIM` ignores trailing spaces, giving names such as `UNICODE_CI_AI`, `en_USA_CI` or `UTF8_BINARY_RTRIM`.[^show][^factory] The `SHOW COLLATIONS [LIKE pattern]` command, added in Spark 4.2.0 (SPARK-49543), lists every collation with its language, country, case and accent sensitivity, pad attribute and ICU version.[^r420][^show]

## How to set a collation in Spark SQL

A collation can be attached at several levels, according to the Spark 4.3.0 grammar:[^grammar]
- on a column type: `STRING COLLATE UTF8_LCASE`, and also on `CHAR` and `VARCHAR`;
- on an expression: `name COLLATE UNICODE_CI`, or the function `collate(expr, 'UTF8_LCASE')`;
- as a default for new objects: a `DEFAULT COLLATION` clause on `CREATE TABLE`, `CREATE SCHEMA`, `ALTER TABLE`, `ALTER SCHEMA` and SQL functions.

Schema-level default collation for tables arrived in Spark 4.1.0 (SPARK-52219), and Spark 4.2.0 extended collation support to `CHAR`/`VARCHAR`, `CREATE TABLE AS SELECT` and SQL user-defined functions.[^r410][^r420] The function `collation(expr)` returns the fully qualified collation of a value; for a plain string literal it returns `SYSTEM.BUILTIN.UTF8_BINARY`.[^expr]

## How does collation affect comparison, grouping and joins?

Collation changes the result of every operation that compares strings. In Spark's own test suite, a table with the values `aaa`, `AAA`, `bbb` and `BBB` produces four groups when grouped by a `UTF8_BINARY` column and two groups when grouped by a `UTF8_LCASE` column. A filter `= 'aaa'` on the `UTF8_LCASE` column returns both `aaa` and `AAA`, and a self-join on that column matches each value with both spellings.[^tests]

Spark's hash joins compare keys by their bytes, which is wrong for a collation in which different bytes can be equal. The analyzer rule `RewriteCollationJoin` therefore wraps equality join keys of non-binary collations, including those nested in structs and arrays, in a `CollationKey` expression, so that equal values under the collation produce equal keys and hash joins still work.[^join]

Both sides of a comparison must agree on one collation. Spark picks it by strength: a `COLLATE` clause is explicit and wins; a column, variable or subquery result carries an implicit collation; a literal carries the default collation and loses to either. A literal compared with a `UTF8_LCASE` column is therefore compared case-insensitively.[^coercion]

If two explicit collations conflict, or two columns with different implicit collations meet, the query fails with `COLLATION_MISMATCH` (SQLSTATE `42P21`); its `IMPLICIT` sub-condition suggests adding a `COLLATE` clause.[^errjson] See [Spark error classes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_error_classes) for how such conditions are structured.

## Limitations

- Non-`UTF8_BINARY` strings are not allowed in map keys unless `spark.sql.collation.allowInMapKeys` is set; it defaults to false.[^sqlconf]
- Some functions do not support every collation and fail with `UNSUPPORTED_COLLATION.FOR_FUNCTION`.[^errjson]
- Since Spark 4.1.0 the user-facing hash functions ignore collation (SPARK-52828); `spark.sql.legacy.collationAwareHashFunctions` restores the earlier behaviour.[^r410][^sqlconf]
- Since Spark 4.3, a streaming file sink rejects a partition column that is a string with a non-default collation such as `UTF8_LCASE`.[^n1]
- Several correctness bugs involving non-binary collations have been fixed in recent releases, for example in `NOT IN` subqueries and constraint inference (SPARK-54852 and SPARK-55647 in 4.2.0, SPARK-57727 in 4.3.0).[^r420][^r430]

## Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (name STRING COLLATE UTF8_LCASE) USING parquet;
INSERT INTO users VALUES ('Alice'), ('ALICE'), ('bob');

SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE name = 'alice';   -- 2
SELECT name, count(*) FROM users GROUP BY name;    -- 2 groups: alice/ALICE and bob

SELECT 'a' = 'A';                                  -- false (UTF8_BINARY)
SELECT 'a' COLLATE UTF8_LCASE = 'A';               -- true
SELECT collation('a' COLLATE UNICODE_CI);          -- SYSTEM.BUILTIN.UNICODE_CI
```

## Collation in other SQL engines

Collation is a general SQL concept, and engines implement it differently. PostgreSQL offers a `libc` provider based on the operating system locales and an `icu` provider, and it supports case-insensitive and accent-insensitive comparison through user-defined "nondeterministic" collations; its documentation notes that these carry a performance cost and do not support some pattern-matching operations.[^pg] In Spark, the built-in `UTF8_LCASE` collation gives case-insensitive comparison without ICU.[^show]

# Column pruning

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Column_pruning

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Projection pushdown, projection pruning, schema pruning (for nested fields)</Field>
  <Field name="field">Query optimization</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Optimizer rule that removes unused columns, a connector that accepts a required schema, a columnar file format</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Predicate pushdown](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown), [Partition pruning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition_pruning), [Aggregate pushdown](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Aggregate_pushdown), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (Optimizer.scala, SchemaPruning.scala, SupportsPushDownRequiredColumns.java, DataSourceScanExec.scala, FileScan.scala, SQLConf.scala), Spark JIRA SPARK-4502, the Apache Parquet file format docs, and the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 spec and Spark source</Verified>

**Column pruning** is a query optimization in which an engine reads only the columns that a query uses, and drops every other column as early as possible in the plan, ideally before the data leaves storage. When the pruning reaches the data source, it is also called **projection pushdown**. In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), column pruning combines an optimizer rule, a connector interface and the columnar layout of formats such as [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet); **nested column pruning** extends it to individual fields inside struct columns.

## Why does column pruning matter?

In a columnar file format, each column is stored separately, so a reader can skip the bytes of the columns it does not need. Apache Parquet stores the values of each column of a row group together in a column chunk, so a query that selects a few columns of a wide table reads only the chunks of those columns in each row group.[^parquet] Column pruning is the step that tells the reader which columns those are.

Column pruning also reduces the work after the scan. Fewer columns mean smaller rows in memory, in [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle) files and in broadcasts.

## How does column pruning work in Apache Spark?

Column pruning in Spark happens in two places.

The optimizer rule `ColumnPruning` "attempts to eliminate the reading of unneeded columns from the query plan." It walks the logical plan and inserts or narrows projections, so each operator receives only the columns that operators above it need.[^optimizer]

The pruned column list then reaches the data source. A Data Source V2 connector accepts it by implementing `SupportsPushDownRequiredColumns` (since Spark 3.0.0), whose `pruneColumns(StructType requiredSchema)` method receives the schema the query needs. The interface allows partial pruning: a source may prune top-level columns but not nested fields.[^sprc] Built-in file sources receive the required schema directly and pass it to the Parquet or ORC reader.

```python
df = spark.read.parquet("/data/events")          # a wide table
(df.filter("event_type = 'click'")
   .select("user_id", "event_ts")
   .explain("formatted"))
# The scan's ReadSchema lists only user_id, event_ts and event_type.
```

## What is nested column pruning?

Nested column pruning (also called schema pruning) reads only the struct fields a query uses, instead of the whole struct column. For a column `customer struct<id: bigint, name: string, address: struct<...>>`, the query `SELECT customer.id FROM orders` reads only `customer.id` from the file.

In Spark, nested pruning for file scans is done by the `SchemaPruning` rule, which applies to Parquet and ORC and is controlled by `spark.sql.optimizer.nestedSchemaPruning.enabled` (default true, since 2.4.1).[^schemapruning][^sqlconf] The feature was introduced through SPARK-4502, "Spark SQL reads unneccesary nested fields from Parquet", fixed in Spark 2.4.0.[^n1]

Two related settings prune nested fields in other parts of the plan; neither prunes the physical scan:[^sqlconf]
- `spark.sql.optimizer.expression.nestedPruning.enabled` (default true, since 3.0.0) prunes nested fields from expressions inside operators.
- `spark.sql.optimizer.serializer.nestedSchemaPruning.enabled` (default true, since 3.0.0) prunes nested fields from object serializers.

## How can you check that columns were pruned?

Each scan in `EXPLAIN FORMATTED` output shows a `ReadSchema` entry with the schema the scan actually reads, including the pruned nested fields.[^scanexec][^n2] For `SELECT customer.id FROM orders`, a pruned scan shows `ReadSchema: struct<customer:struct<id:bigint>>`, and an unpruned scan shows the full struct. After the query runs, the scan's `size of files read` metric in the Spark UI reports the bytes read.[^scanexec]

## What stops column pruning?

- **Row-oriented formats.** CSV and JSON files store whole rows, so the reader must still parse every row even when it returns fewer columns.
- **Operators that need all columns**, such as `SELECT *`, `df.collect()` on the full DataFrame, or a UDF that takes the whole row as input.
- **Nested pruning limits.** Nested pruning is limited to Parquet and ORC file scans, and to Data Source V2 sources that prune nested fields in `pruneColumns`.[^schemapruning][^sprc]

## Column pruning in table formats

**[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)** projects columns by field ID, not by name: "Columns in Iceberg data files are selected by field id", so pruning stays correct after columns are renamed or reordered.[^icebergspec] Iceberg's Spark scan builder implements `SupportsPushDownRequiredColumns`.[^n3]

**[Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)** data files are Parquet files, and the Delta protocol defines how Delta data types map to Parquet types, so a Delta scan in Spark reads through the Parquet reader and benefits from the same column pruning.[^n4]

# Copy-on-write and merge-on-read

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Copy-on-write_and_merge-on-read

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">CoW and MoR; write modes for row-level operations</Field>
  <Field name="field">Table formats</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Rewritten data files (copy-on-write); delete files, deletion vectors or log files merged at read time (merge-on-read)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Deletion vector](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Deletion_vector), [Small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem), [Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Iceberg table spec and configuration documentation (1.12.0), the Delta Lake deletion vectors documentation and PROTOCOL.md at v4.4.1, and the Apache Hudi table types documentation (version 1.2.1)</Verified>

**Copy-on-write** and **merge-on-read** are the two strategies an [open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) can use to apply row-level updates and deletes to data stored in immutable files. With copy-on-write, the writer rewrites every data file that contains a changed row, so readers only read data files. With merge-on-read, the writer records the change separately (as delete files, [deletion vectors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Deletion_vector) or log files) and readers combine those records with the original data files at query time.[^hudi-types] The choice moves cost between writes and reads. [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) and [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) all support both approaches, with different names and defaults.

## Why the choice exists

Lakehouse data files, usually [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), are written once and never changed in place. The Iceberg specification requires that files are not moved or altered once they are written, and states that data and metadata files are immutable until they are deleted.[^icespec] A `DELETE`, `UPDATE` or `MERGE` that touches one row must therefore either produce a new copy of the file without that row, or leave the file alone and write a note saying the row is gone.

The Delta Lake documentation states the copy-on-write cost directly: by default, deleting a single row means rewriting the entire Parquet file that contains it.[^delta-dv]

## Copy-on-write

In copy-on-write, a row-level operation reads each affected data file, writes a new file with the changes applied, and commits a snapshot that replaces the old file with the new one. Readers see only complete data files and do no merging. The cost is write amplification: the whole file is rewritten even when a small fraction of its rows changed.[^hudi-types]

Iceberg's Spark integration reports this cost as a metric: `spark.delete.num-copied-rows` counts unmodified rows that were rewritten in copy-on-write mode and is zero in merge-on-read.[^ice-writes]

## Merge-on-read

In merge-on-read, the writer adds a small record of the change and leaves existing data files untouched. Each project encodes the record differently:

- **Apache Iceberg** (format version 2 and later) writes delete files. Position deletes mark a row by data file and row position; equality deletes mark rows by column values, such as `id = 5`. In format version 3, position deletes are stored as deletion vectors in Puffin files, and position delete files are deprecated.[^icespec]
- **Delta Lake** attaches a deletion vector to the data file's entry in the transaction log, marking rows as logically deleted while they stay physically in the file. Readers must skip those rows.[^delta-proto]
- **Apache Hudi** merge-on-read tables write updates and deletes to log files next to a columnar base file, and a periodic compaction merges the log files into a new base file. Queries on such tables can be snapshot queries, which merge the logs for the freshest data, or read-optimized queries, which read only the compacted base files.[^hudi-types]

Merge-on-read makes writes cheaper but adds work to every read until the changes are compacted into rewritten data files. Hudi's documentation notes that merge-on-read query performance depends on whether the log files have been compacted.[^hudi-types]

## Comparison

|  | [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) | [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) | [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| How the strategy is chosen | Per operation, with table properties `write.delete.mode`, `write.update.mode` and `write.merge.mode`[^ice-conf] | Table property `delta.enableDeletionVectors`[^delta-dv] | Table type, fixed when the table is created: `hoodie.datasource.write.table.type` or `hoodie.table.type`, values `COPY_ON_WRITE` or `MERGE_ON_READ`[^hudi-conf] |
| Default | `copy-on-write` for all three properties[^ice-conf] | Files are rewritten unless deletion vectors are enabled on the table[^delta-dv] | `COPY_ON_WRITE`[^hudi-conf] |
| Merge-on-read record | Position delete files (v2), equality delete files, deletion vectors (v3)[^icespec] | Deletion vectors stored in files or inline in the log[^delta-proto] | Log files attached to a base file[^hudi-types] |
| Requirements | Merge-on-read requires format version 2 or later[^ice-conf] | Reader version 3 and writer version 7 with the `deletionVectors` table feature[^delta-proto] | The table type cannot change between writes[^hudi-conf] |
| Folding changes back into data files | Data file compaction with `rewrite_data_files`, which can select files by delete count or delete ratio[^ice-proc] | `OPTIMIZE`, DML with deletion vectors disabled, or `REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE)`[^delta-dv] | Compaction of merge-on-read file groups[^hudi-types] |

## Example

In Iceberg the mode is a table property, so one table can use merge-on-read for deletes and copy-on-write for merges.[^ice-conf]

```sql
-- Apache Iceberg (Spark SQL): merge-on-read for DELETE and UPDATE, copy-on-write for MERGE
ALTER TABLE db.events SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'write.delete.mode' = 'merge-on-read',
  'write.update.mode' = 'merge-on-read',
  'write.merge.mode'  = 'copy-on-write'
);
```

The Delta Lake equivalent enables deletion vectors on the table: `ALTER TABLE t SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.enableDeletionVectors' = true)`. Doing so upgrades the table protocol, and clients that do not support deletion vectors can no longer read the table.[^delta-dv]

## Choosing a strategy

The projects document the tradeoff in general terms rather than with a fixed rule.

Apache Hudi gives the most explicit guidance. Its documentation describes copy-on-write as suited to read-heavy workloads, batch ETL, data warehousing on data lakes and slowly changing reference data, and merge-on-read as suited to change data capture pipelines, streaming ingestion, hybrid batch and streaming workloads, and tables with frequent updates and deletes. Its comparison lists copy-on-write as having higher write latency and update cost and lower query latency, and merge-on-read the reverse.[^hudi-types]

Delta Lake describes deletion vectors as a storage optimization that avoids rewriting Parquet files for some operations, with reads applying the recorded deletions. Its documentation adds that `UPDATE`, `MERGE` and `OPTIMIZE` do not guarantee that all recorded deletions get applied, so `REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE)` is the command that rewrites every affected file.[^delta-dv]

Apache Iceberg documents the properties and their defaults, and documents compaction as the way to rewrite files with many deletes, but its configuration page does not recommend one mode over the other.[^ice-conf][^ice-proc]

# Cost-based optimizer (Spark)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Cost-based_optimizer_(Spark)

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">CBO, Spark SQL cost-based optimization</Field>
  <Field name="field">Query optimization</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 2.2.0</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Table and column statistics, `ANALYZE TABLE`, cardinality estimation, join reordering, histograms</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Catalyst optimizer](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Catalyst_optimizer), [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution), [Broadcast join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Broadcast_join), [Logical plan and physical plan](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Logical_plan_and_physical_plan), [Hive Metastore](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_Metastore)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Spark 2.2.0 release notes, SPARK-16026, the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (SQLConf.scala, docs/sql-performance-tuning.md, docs/sql-ref-syntax-aux-analyze-table.md, docs/sql-ref-syntax-qry-explain.md) and ANALYZE TABLE, DESCRIBE and EXPLAIN COST output from a PySpark 4.3.0 run</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), the **cost-based optimizer** (**CBO**) is the part of the [Catalyst optimizer](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Catalyst_optimizer) that uses table and column statistics, such as row counts, distinct values and minimum and maximum values, to estimate how many rows each step of a query produces, and uses those estimates to choose join orders and join strategies.[^sqlconf][^perf] Spark 2.2.0 introduced cardinality estimation for filter, join, aggregate, project and limit operators and cost-based join reordering.[^r220] The umbrella issue for the framework, SPARK-16026, was closed with fix version 2.3.0.[^jira16026] In Spark 4.3.0 the CBO is still off by default (`spark.sql.cbo.enabled=false`), and most queries rely instead on size estimates and on [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution) at run time.

## What statistics does Spark use?

The Spark tuning guide lists three sources of statistics:[^perf]

- **Data source**: statistics that Spark reads from the data itself, such as the counts and minimum and maximum values in [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) file metadata.
- **Catalog**: statistics stored in the catalog, such as the [Hive Metastore](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_Metastore), and collected or updated by `ANALYZE TABLE`.
- **Runtime**: statistics that Spark measures while a query runs, used by [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution).

Without the CBO, Catalyst still uses one statistic everywhere: the estimated size in bytes of each plan node. That size decides, for example, whether a table is small enough for a [broadcast join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Broadcast_join).[^perf] When the size of a table is unknown, the internal default `spark.sql.defaultSizeInBytes` is `Long.MaxValue`, so the optimizer does not broadcast a table unless it knows the table is small.[^sqlconf]

## How do you collect statistics with ANALYZE TABLE?

`ANALYZE TABLE` collects statistics for one table, or for all tables in a database, and stores them in the catalog for the optimizer.[^analyze]

| Statement | What it collects |
| --- | --- |
| `ANALYZE TABLE t COMPUTE STATISTICS NOSCAN` | Table size in bytes only, without scanning the data |
| `ANALYZE TABLE t COMPUTE STATISTICS` | Row count and size in bytes |
| `ANALYZE TABLE t COMPUTE STATISTICS FOR COLUMNS a, b` | Table statistics plus column statistics for the listed columns |
| `ANALYZE TABLE t COMPUTE STATISTICS FOR ALL COLUMNS` | Table statistics plus column statistics for every column |
| `ANALYZE TABLES IN db COMPUTE STATISTICS` | Table statistics for every table in the database |

Source: Spark 4.3.0 SQL reference.[^analyze] A `PARTITION (...)` clause limits the statement to some partitions.

`DESCRIBE EXTENDED` shows what was collected.[^perf] After `ANALYZE TABLE t1 COMPUTE STATISTICS FOR ALL COLUMNS` on a 1,000-row Parquet table in PySpark 4.3.0, `DESCRIBE EXTENDED t1` reported `Statistics: 5665 bytes, 1000 rows`, and `DESCRIBE EXTENDED t1 id` reported `min 0`, `max 999`, `num_nulls 0`, `distinct_count 1000`, `avg_col_len 8`, `max_col_len 8` and `histogram NULL`.

Histograms are not collected by default. With `spark.sql.statistics.histogram.enabled=true` (default false, since 2.3.0), `ANALYZE TABLE ... FOR COLUMNS` also builds equi-height histograms, which improve estimates but cost an extra table scan.[^sqlconf] Statistics are not refreshed automatically when data changes, unless `spark.sql.statistics.size.autoUpdate.enabled` is set (default false), and even then only the table size is updated.[^sqlconf]

## When is the CBO used?

The CBO is used only when it is turned on, and its parts have separate switches. All of them are off by default in Spark 4.3.0:[^sqlconf]

| Setting | Default | Since | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `spark.sql.cbo.enabled` | false | 2.2.0 | Estimate plan statistics (row counts, column statistics) from the collected statistics |
| `spark.sql.cbo.joinReorder.enabled` | false | 2.2.0 | Reorder joins by estimated cost (join reordering in the CBO) |
| `spark.sql.cbo.joinReorder.dp.threshold` | 12 | 2.2.0 | The maximum number of joined nodes for the dynamic programming algorithm |
| `spark.sql.cbo.starSchemaDetection` | false | 2.2.0 | Reorder joins with a star schema heuristic |
| `spark.sql.cbo.planStats.enabled` | false | 3.0.0 | Fetch row counts and column statistics from the catalog into the logical plan |

The effect is visible with `EXPLAIN COST`, which prints the optimized logical plan with statistics.[^explain] In this PySpark 4.3.0 run, table `t1` has 1,000 rows and `t2` has 10, both analyzed for all columns, and the query is `SELECT * FROM t1 JOIN t2 ON t1.k = t2.k WHERE t1.id < 100`. With the CBO off, the filter does not change the size estimate, and the join is estimated at 7.8 MiB:

```
Join Inner, (k#5104L = k#5105L), Statistics(sizeInBytes=7.8 MiB)
:- Filter ((isnotnull(id#5103L) AND (id#5103L < 100)) AND isnotnull(k#5104L)), Statistics(sizeInBytes=5.5 KiB)
:  +- Relation spark_catalog.default.t1[id#5103L,k#5104L] parquet, Statistics(sizeInBytes=5.5 KiB)
+- Filter isnotnull(k#5105L), Statistics(sizeInBytes=1438.0 B)
   +- Relation spark_catalog.default.t2[k#5105L,name#5106] parquet, Statistics(sizeInBytes=1438.0 B)
```

With `spark.sql.cbo.enabled=true`, the same plan carries row counts. The filter `id < 100` is estimated at 101 rows (the true count is 100), and the join estimate falls to 4.4 KiB:

```
Join Inner, (k#5104L = k#5105L), Statistics(sizeInBytes=4.4 KiB, rowCount=101)
:- Filter ((isnotnull(id#5103L) AND (id#5103L < 100)) AND isnotnull(k#5104L)), Statistics(sizeInBytes=2.4 KiB, rowCount=101)
:  +- Relation spark_catalog.default.t1[id#5103L,k#5104L] parquet, Statistics(sizeInBytes=23.4 KiB, rowCount=1.00E+3)
+- Filter isnotnull(k#5105L), Statistics(sizeInBytes=290.0 B, rowCount=10)
   +- Relation spark_catalog.default.t2[k#5105L,name#5106] parquet, Statistics(sizeInBytes=290.0 B, rowCount=10)
```

## CBO and Adaptive Query Execution

The CBO and [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution) solve the same problem at different times. The CBO works before the query runs, from statistics that must be collected in advance and can be stale. AQE works during the query, from exact sizes of completed shuffle stages, but can only change the parts of the plan that have not run yet.[^perf]

# Data catalog

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Lakehouse catalog, metastore</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data management, data governance</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Namespaces, table metadata pointers, commit coordination, access control, credential vending</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog), [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), Lakekeeper, any [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), [Open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Iceberg REST catalog specification and OpenAPI file, the Apache Polaris documentation, the Unity Catalog OSS documentation, the Delta transaction log protocol and the Lakekeeper site</Verified>

A **data catalog**, in a lakehouse, is the service that names tables and other data assets, records where each table's current metadata lives, coordinates commits, and decides who may read or write each asset. Engines ask the catalog which files make up a table and whether the current user may access them before they read any data. In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), the catalog is reached through an open API, so that several engines share one view of the same tables. Open source examples include [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog), [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris) and other implementations of the [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) specification.

## Role in a lakehouse

An [open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) describes how one table is stored, but it does not say how a table is found by name or how concurrent writers agree on its current version. The catalog fills both gaps.

The Unity Catalog OSS documentation summarizes the catalog's job as answering three questions for an engine before it reads data: which files hold the table's data, whether the user may read them, and what the table's schema is.[^ucwhat]

For [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) tables, the Apache Polaris documentation states that a catalog must store the current metadata pointer for each table (a mapping from table name to the location of its current metadata file) and must update that pointer atomically when a new table version is committed.[^polaris-docs] This atomic swap is the basis of Iceberg's serializable isolation.[^icespec]

For [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) tables, the transaction log is stored alongside the data, so a table can be read without a separate metastore.[^deltaproto] The Delta protocol also defines catalog-managed tables, in which the managing catalog becomes the source of truth for whether a commit succeeded.[^deltaproto]

## Functions

A lakehouse catalog typically provides the following functions.

- **Namespace.** Assets are organized in a hierarchy. Unity Catalog uses a three-level namespace, `catalog.schema.asset`.[^ucwhat] The Iceberg REST catalog API organizes tables into namespaces.[^restyaml]
- **Metadata pointer and commits.** The catalog records each table's current version and accepts or rejects commits from writers.[^polaris-docs]
- **Access control.** With authentication and authorization enabled, Unity Catalog OSS checks ownership and privileges such as `USE_CATALOG`, `SELECT` and `MODIFY` on every request.[^ucwhat]
- **Credential vending.** The catalog issues short-lived storage credentials scoped to one table or volume, so that an engine can read or write only the data the user is allowed to access.[^ucwhat]
- **Discovery.** Because namespaces, tables and schemas are available over an API, engines and AI agents can list what exists instead of inferring it from storage paths.[^olio-agentic]

## The Iceberg REST catalog specification

<Hatnote>Main article: [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog)</Hatnote>

The Iceberg REST catalog specification is an OpenAPI definition of a catalog API for Iceberg tables. The Iceberg project created it because pluggable catalogs had to be implemented separately in every language, which made it hard for engines and commercial offerings to support many catalogs. With the REST protocol, a new language or engine needs only one client implementation to work with any compliant catalog.[^icerest]

The Iceberg documentation lists further benefits of the REST protocol: change-based commits that let the server resolve conflicts and retry, root metadata written by the catalog service, multi-table commits, lazy snapshot loading, and secure table sharing through credential vending or remote signing.[^icerest] The Iceberg documentation compares the role of the REST protocol to that of Hive's Thrift protocol for the Hive Metastore.[^icerest]

A client signals delegated storage access with the `X-Iceberg-Access-Delegation` request header. The defined values are `vended-credentials`, `remote-signing` and `none`, and the server may honor any or none of the requested mechanisms.[^restyaml]

## Open source catalogs

| Catalog | Description | Table formats and APIs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog) | A catalog for tables, volumes, functions and models; an LF AI & Data project. Databricks created it and open sourced it in 2024.[^ucwhat][^uc-home] | Delta Lake and Iceberg; Unity Catalog REST API, UC Delta API and Iceberg REST catalog API[^uc-home] |
| [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris) | An Apache Software Foundation catalog for Apache Iceberg[^polaris] | Iceberg; implements the Iceberg REST API[^polaris] |
| Lakekeeper | An Iceberg REST catalog written in Rust, under the Apache License[^lakekeeper] | Iceberg; Iceberg REST catalog API[^lakekeeper] |

Apache Polaris lists Apache Spark, Apache Flink, Trino, Apache Doris, Dremio OSS and StarRocks among the engines that work with it through the Iceberg REST API.[^polaris] Unity Catalog lists Spark, DuckDB, PyIceberg and Daft among the clients with governed access.[^uc-home]

## Catalogs and AI agents

In an [agentic lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Agentic_lakehouse), the catalog is the main control point for AI agents. It tells an agent which tables exist and which it may touch, and it vends storage credentials scoped to the agent's identity, so that an agent can be limited to writing in its own sandbox namespace.[^olio-agentic]

## Limitations

A catalog governs only access that passes through it. The Unity Catalog OSS documentation warns that anyone holding direct storage credentials can bypass the catalog's checks, so the storage must also be locked down as part of a secure deployment.[^ucwhat]

# Data skew

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_skew

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Skew, hot keys, partition skew</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Uneven [partition](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition) sizes, straggler tasks, hot keys</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (AQE skew join), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) (adaptive skewed join, local-global aggregation), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Salting](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Salting), [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution), [Spill (memory)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spill_(memory))</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/sql-performance-tuning.md, docs/web-ui.md, docs/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-hints.md, adaptive/OptimizeSkewedJoin.scala), SPARK-29544, the Apache Flink 2.3 docs (Adaptive Batch, Performance Tuning) and the Trino 484 docs</Verified>

**Data skew** is an uneven distribution of data across the [partitions](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition) of a distributed computation, so that a few tasks process far more data than the rest and the whole stage waits for them. In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), skew usually appears after a [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), when many rows share the same join or grouping key and all land in one task. Spark's [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution) (AQE) splits skewed join partitions automatically; other cases need manual fixes such as [salting](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Salting).[^perf]

## How to recognize data skew in the Spark UI

Data skew shows up as a gap between the typical task and the slowest task in one stage. The Spark UI stage page shows summary metrics for all tasks of a stage, including task duration, GC time, shuffle read size and records, and shuffle spill.[^webui] A skewed stage has a maximum duration and shuffle read size many times the median. The REST API returns the same summary as quantiles, by default 0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0, and accepts other quantiles such as `?quantiles=0.01,0.5,0.99`.[^monitoring]

Other signs of skew in the Spark UI are spill or high GC time in only the largest tasks, which the per-task table on the same page shows, and a stage that sits at a few running tasks long after most have finished.[^webui] See [Spill (memory)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spill_(memory)) and [Garbage collection in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Garbage_collection_in_Spark).

## What causes data skew?

- **Hot keys.** A join or `GROUP BY` key with one very common value (a default customer ID, a popular product, `NULL`) sends all of its rows to one shuffle partition, because a shuffle brings all the values for a key together in one place (`hashpartitioning` in the plan).[^rddguide]
- **Skewed source files.** Uneven input files or table partitions give some scan tasks much more data than others. See [Small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem).
- **Partitioning that does not match the data.** Repartitioning by a low-cardinality column puts many rows in few partitions.

## How Spark handles skew: AQE skew join

Spark 3.0.0 added a skew join rule to the new AQE framework.[^spark29544] After the shuffle stages on both sides of a join have run, AQE checks partition sizes. A partition is skewed when it is larger than `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor` (default 5.0) times the median partition size and also larger than `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes` (default 256 MB). AQE splits such a partition into several tasks, replicating the matching partition of the other side.[^perf] The feature is on by default (`spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled`) whenever AQE is on, and AQE is on by default since Spark 3.2.0.[^perf]

AQE can split only the sides that the join type allows. In Spark 4.3.0 it can split the left side of inner, cross, left semi, left anti and left outer joins, and the right side of inner, cross and right outer joins; it applies to sort-merge and shuffled hash joins.[^skewrule] Full outer joins and skewed aggregations are not split by this rule; for those, [salting](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Salting) or a two-stage aggregation is still used.

For writes, the `REBALANCE` hint asks AQE to even out output partitions and to split skewed ones, which keeps very large files out of a [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) or [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) table.[^hints][^perf]

```
spark.sql.adaptive.enabled                                   true
spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled                          true
spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor            5.0
spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes  256MB
```

## Manual remedies

- **Broadcast the small side.** A [broadcast join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Broadcast_join) has no shuffle on the large side, so a hot key in the large table cannot pile up in one task. Use the `BROADCAST` [hint](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Join_strategy_hints) when the small side fits.[^perf]
- **Salting.** Add a random suffix to the hot key on one side and replicate the other side, so one key's rows spread over many tasks. See [Salting](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Salting).
- **Filter or handle hot values separately.** Rows with a `NULL` join key never match in an inner join, so filtering them out before the join removes a common hot key.
- **Pre-aggregate.** Aggregating before a join reduces the rows per key that the shuffle has to move.

## Data skew compared across engines

|  | Apache Spark | Apache Flink | Trino |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Automatic skewed join handling | AQE skew join splits skewed sort-merge and shuffled hash join partitions at runtime; on by default[^perf] | The Adaptive Batch Scheduler's skewed join optimization splits skewed partitions in batch jobs; on by default, controlled by `table.optimizer.skewed-join-optimization.strategy`[^flinkab] | No dedicated skew splitting is documented; the cost-based optimizer can choose a broadcast join instead of a partitioned join[^trinocbo] |
| Skewed aggregations | Partial aggregation before the shuffle (`partial_sum` in plans); salting by hand | Local-global (two-phase) aggregation, and split distinct aggregation (`table.optimizer.distinct-agg.split.enabled`)[^flinktuning] | Not documented as a separate feature |
| Skewed writes | `REBALANCE` hint with AQE splits skewed output partitions[^hints] | Automatic balancing of data distribution in the Adaptive Batch Scheduler[^flinkab] | `redistribute-writes` (default true) hashes data across nodes before writing, to limit the effect of skew[^trinogen] |

# Data Source V2

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_Source_V2

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">DSV2, DataSource V2 API, connector API</Field>
  <Field name="field">Query engine extensibility</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">CatalogPlugin and TableCatalog, Table, ScanBuilder and Scan, WriteBuilder and BatchWrite, pushdown mix-ins</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark); used by [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) and the Spark JDBC source</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Catalog plugin API (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Catalog_plugin_API_(Spark)), [Predicate pushdown](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown), [Time travel (SQL)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Time_travel_(SQL))</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/sql-v2-data-sources.md, the org.apache.spark.sql.connector Java interfaces and their @since tags, python/pyspark/sql/datasource.py), the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 and Delta Lake Spark configuration docs, the Unity Catalog Spark integration guide, and the Spark 2.3.0, 3.0.0, 3.3.0, 3.5.0, 4.0.0 and 4.3.0 release notes</Verified>

**Data Source V2** (**DSV2**) is the connector API of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark): a set of Java interfaces in the `org.apache.spark.sql.connector` package that lets an external system plug its catalogs, tables, reads and writes into Spark's query planning and execution.[^dsv2doc] A connector starts from a small core and opts in to features such as filter pushdown, columnar reads, row-level `DELETE`/`UPDATE`/`MERGE` and catalog support by implementing mix-in interfaces. The Spark documentation names the built-in JDBC source, [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) and Lance as users of the API.[^dsv2doc]

## What problem does Data Source V2 solve?

The earlier Data Source V1 API depended on Scala. Data Source V2 is a pure Java API, adds native catalog integration (namespaces, tables, views, functions and procedures), and lets a connector receive pushed-down filters, columns, aggregates, limits and offsets. A connector can also report its data layout so that Spark skips shuffles and sorts, or ask Spark to repartition and sort rows before a write.[^dsv2doc]

Data Source V2 also unifies batch and streaming. The same `Table` abstraction serves batch reads, micro-batch and continuous streaming reads, and streaming writes, chosen by the capabilities the table declares.[^dsv2doc][^cap]

## History

Spark 2.3.0 introduced "Data source API V2" (SPARK-15689) as an experimental API and warned that breaking changes should be expected.[^r230] Spark 3.0.0 refactored the API (SPARK-25390) and added the catalog plugin API (SPARK-31121); the core interfaces `Table`, `TableProvider` and `TableCatalog` carry `@since 3.0.0`.[^r300][^table]

Later releases extended the API rather than replacing it. Spark 3.3.0 added complete aggregate pushdown, top-N pushdown and the `AS OF` time travel syntax (SPARK-37219); Spark 3.5.0 added `MERGE` and `UPDATE` handling for delta-based and group-based sources.[^r330][^r350] Spark 4.0.0 added the Python Data Source API (SPARK-44076), a Python wrapper for lightweight connectors.[^r400] In 4.3.0 core interfaces such as `Table`, `TableCatalog` and `ScanBuilder` are annotated `@Evolving`, and some newer ones, such as `SupportsRowLevelOperations` and `SupportsRuntimeV2Filtering`, are `@Experimental`.[^tablejava][^tablecatalogjava][^scanbuilderjava][^rowlevel][^runtimefilter]

## What are the entry points?

A Data Source V2 connector enters Spark in one of two ways.[^dsv2doc]

- **`TableProvider`** returns a `Table` from a map of options, such as a path or a Kafka topic. It is used with `spark.read.format(...)`. Built-in file sources add `SupportsCatalogOptions` so that option-based tables can take part in DDL through the session catalog.
- **`CatalogPlugin`** is registered under a name with `spark.sql.catalog.<name>=<class>` and exposes a catalog of namespaces and tables (and optionally views, functions and procedures). Iceberg and Delta Lake use this route. See [Catalog plugin API (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Catalog_plugin_API_(Spark)).

## How does the read path work?

A table that implements `SupportsRead` returns a `ScanBuilder`. Spark negotiates pushdown with the builder, calls `build()` to get a logical `Scan`, and turns that into a physical `Batch`. The `Batch` returns an array of `InputPartition` objects, one per Spark task, and a serializable `PartitionReaderFactory` that creates a `PartitionReader` on each [executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor). Readers return rows or columnar batches.[^dsv2doc]

A `Scan` can add further mix-ins. `SupportsReportPartitioning` reports how output is partitioned, which enables storage-partitioned joins without a [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle); `SupportsReportOrdering` reports sort order; `SupportsReportStatistics` feeds the cost-based optimizer; and `SupportsRuntimeV2Filtering` accepts filters at execution time for dynamic partition pruning.[^dsv2doc]

## Which pushdown interfaces exist?

Pushdown in Data Source V2 is a negotiation: Spark calls a method on the `ScanBuilder` with the operators, the connector returns what it cannot handle, and Spark evaluates the rest itself.[^dsv2doc] The documented order is sample, filter, aggregate, limit or top-N, offset, then column pruning.[^dsv2doc] See [Predicate pushdown](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown) for the general idea.

| Mix-in on `ScanBuilder` | Pushes down | Since |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SupportsPushDownRequiredColumns` | Column pruning | 3.0.0[^src-req] |
| `SupportsPushDownFilters` | Filters as V1 `Filter` objects | 3.0.0[^src-f1] |
| `SupportsPushDownV2Filters` | Filters as V2 `Predicate` expressions; preferred over the V1 variant | 3.3.0[^src-f2] |
| `SupportsPushDownAggregates` | Aggregates and group-by | 3.2.0[^src-agg] |
| `SupportsPushDownLimit`, `SupportsPushDownTopN` | `LIMIT`, and `ORDER BY` with `LIMIT` | 3.3.0[^src-lim] |
| `SupportsPushDownTableSample` | `TABLESAMPLE` | 3.3.0[^src-sample] |
| `SupportsPushDownOffset` | `OFFSET` | 3.4.0[^src-off] |
| `SupportsPushDownJoin` | Joins whose two sides the same underlying source can process together (for example two JDBC scans on one server) | 4.1.0[^src-join] |

## How does the write path work?

A table that implements `SupportsWrite` returns a `WriteBuilder`. Mix-ins on the builder select the write mode: `SupportsTruncate`, `SupportsOverwriteV2` (overwrite rows matching a filter) and `SupportsDynamicOverwrite` (overwrite partitions). The builder produces a logical `Write`, which produces a `BatchWrite` or a `StreamingWrite`.[^dsv2doc]

`BatchWrite` uses a two-phase commit. Each task's `DataWriter` commits or aborts its own part and returns a message; after all tasks finish, the driver calls `commit(messages)` or `abort(messages)`. Data from individual tasks should not be visible to readers until the driver commit succeeds.[^dsv2doc] A `Write` that implements `RequiresDistributionAndOrdering` makes Spark insert a shuffle and sort before writing, which table formats use for clustering.[^dsv2doc]

For row-level DML, a table implements `SupportsRowLevelOperations`. Group-based sources (copy-on-write) rewrite whole files or partitions; delta-based sources (merge-on-read) accept a stream of row changes. Simpler deletes can go through `SupportsDeleteV2`, whose `canDeleteWhere` lets Spark fall back to a rewrite when the source cannot drop rows by predicate alone.[^dsv2doc] See [Copy-on-write and merge-on-read](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Copy-on-write_and_merge-on-read).

## Example

The Python Data Source API wraps Data Source V2 for connectors written in Python. This PySpark sketch defines a source with two input partitions, registers it and reads it:[^pyds]

```python
from pyspark.sql.datasource import DataSource, DataSourceReader, InputPartition

class EvenOddSource(DataSource):
    @classmethod
    def name(cls):
        return "even_odd"

    def schema(self):
        return "id INT"

    def reader(self, schema):
        return EvenOddReader(int(self.options.get("n", "10")))

class EvenOddReader(DataSourceReader):
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n

    def partitions(self):
        return [InputPartition(0), InputPartition(1)]   # one Spark task each

    def read(self, partition):
        for i in range(partition.value, self.n, 2):
            yield (i,)

spark.dataSource.register(EvenOddSource)
spark.read.format("even_odd").option("n", "6").load().show()
```

## Use in an open lakehouse

Open table formats reach Spark through Data Source V2. Iceberg registers `org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog` and Delta Lake registers `org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog` as Spark catalogs, and the Spark documentation lists both projects as users of the API.[^dsv2doc][^icecfg][^deltabatch] [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog) OSS connects to Spark through its own catalog class, `io.unitycatalog.spark.UCSingleCatalog`.[^ucspark]

# DataFrame

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DataFrame

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Data frame, Spark DataFrame</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data processing APIs</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Spark 1.3.0 (DataFrame API in Apache Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Named, typed columns (a schema); rows; a logical plan in Spark</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (PySpark, Scala, Java, R), pandas, Polars</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Dataset (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dataset_(Spark)), [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [Apache Arrow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Arrow), [User-defined function (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/User-defined_function_(Spark))</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/sql-programming-guide.md, docs/sql-migration-guide.md, Dataset.scala, python/docs/source/tutorial/sql/arrow_pandas.rst, the PySpark upgrade guide), the Spark 1.3.0, 2.0.0 and 3.2.0 release notes, the pandas 3.1.1 documentation, the Polars user guide and PyPI</Verified>

A **DataFrame** is a table-like data structure made of named columns, each with a data type, and rows. In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a DataFrame is a distributed collection of rows organized into named columns, conceptually equivalent to a table in a relational database, and it is the main API of Spark SQL in Python, Scala, Java and R.[^guide] The same word names the in-memory, single-process tables of pandas and Polars, which share the tabular shape but differ in where the data lives and when work is done. This page explains the Spark DataFrame and compares it with those two.

## What is a DataFrame in Apache Spark?

A Spark DataFrame is a [Dataset](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dataset_(Spark)) organized into named columns. In Scala, `DataFrame` is a type alias of `Dataset[Row]`; in Java it is written `Dataset<Row>`; Python and R have only the DataFrame.[^guide] DataFrames can be built from files, tables, external databases or existing [RDDs](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD).[^guide]

A Spark DataFrame does not hold its data in the driver. Internally it represents a logical plan that describes how to produce the data. Transformations such as `select`, `filter` and `groupBy` return new DataFrames, and nothing runs until an action such as `count`, `show` or a write is called. Then Spark's optimizer turns the logical plan into a physical plan that runs in parallel on [executors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor); `explain()` shows both plans.[^dataset]

With [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), a PySpark or Scala DataFrame lives in a thin client: the client sends unresolved logical plans to the Spark server over gRPC and receives results as Apache Arrow batches.[^connect]

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F

spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()

orders = spark.read.parquet("s3://bucket/orders/")      # no data is read yet
daily = (orders
         .filter(F.col("status") == "shipped")
         .groupBy("order_date")
         .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue")))         # still only a plan

daily.explain()   # prints the physical plan
daily.show(5)     # action: Spark runs the job on the executors
```

The same query in Spark SQL:

```sql
SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM parquet.`s3://bucket/orders/`
WHERE status = 'shipped'
GROUP BY order_date;
```

## How do Spark DataFrames work with table formats?

In an open lakehouse, Spark DataFrames are the usual way to read and write tables in [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) and [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) files. For example, the Delta Lake quick start writes a DataFrame with `data.write.format("delta").save(path)` and reads it back with `spark.read.format("delta").load(path)`.[^n1]

## Spark DataFrame vs pandas vs Polars

|  | Apache Spark DataFrame | pandas DataFrame | Polars DataFrame |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Where the data lives | Partitions spread across executors in a cluster; the DataFrame object is a plan[^dataset] | In memory; pandas is designed for in-memory analytics[^pdscale] | In memory on one machine[^plhome] |
| Evaluation | Lazy: transformations build a plan, actions run it[^dataset] | Eager[^plpandas] | Eager `DataFrame` and lazy `LazyFrame`; in many cases the eager API calls the lazy engine[^pllazy] |
| Query optimizer | Spark's query optimizer turns the logical plan into a physical plan[^dataset] | None (operations run as called)[^plpandas] | Query planner with predicate and projection pushdown in lazy mode[^pllazy] |
| Parallelism | Tasks across many executors and machines[^guide] | Not built in; the pandas docs point to other libraries for parallel and distributed work[^pdscale] | Multi-threaded across the CPU cores of one machine[^plhome] |
| Row index | No row labels | Labeled row and column axes[^pdapi] | None; rows are addressed by integer position[^plpandas] |
| Memory format | A binary internal format produced by encoders[^dataset]; Arrow for data exchange with Python[^arrow] | NumPy arrays by default; columns can be backed by PyArrow[^pdarrow][^plpandas] | Arrow memory specification, with its own compute implementation[^plhome][^plpandas] |
| Languages | Python, Scala, Java, R, SQL[^guide] | Python | Core in Rust; Python, R and NodeJS APIs[^plhome] |
| Latest version (checked 2026-11-23) | PySpark 4.3.0[^pypi] | pandas 3.1.1[^n2] | Polars 2.1.0[^n3] |

## How do you move data between Spark, pandas and Arrow?

`DataFrame.toPandas()` collects a Spark DataFrame to the driver as a pandas DataFrame, and `SparkSession.createDataFrame()` accepts a pandas DataFrame. Both use Apache Arrow when `spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled` is true, and since Spark 4.2 it is true by default.[^arrow][^n4] Since Spark 4.0, `DataFrame.toArrow()` returns a PyArrow Table and `createDataFrame()` accepts one; a Polars DataFrame can be exchanged through Arrow this way.[^arrow][^plhome]

Both `toPandas()` and `toArrow()` bring every row to the driver, so the Spark documentation advises using them only on a small subset of the data.[^arrow]

The pandas API on Spark (`pyspark.pandas`), added in Spark 3.2.0, offers a pandas-like API whose operations run on Spark DataFrames.[^n5]

## History

Spark 1.3.0 added the DataFrame API, described in the release notes as an evolution of the RDD API with named fields and schema information, for Python, Scala and Java.[^n6] It replaced `SchemaRDD`.[^migration] Spark 2.0.0 unified DataFrame and Dataset in Scala and Java, making DataFrame a type alias for `Dataset[Row]`.[^n7]
