# Dataset (Spark)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dataset_(Spark)

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Typed Dataset, `Dataset[T]`</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data processing APIs</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Spark 1.6.0</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">A JVM type `T`, an [encoder](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Encoder_(Spark)) for that type, a logical plan</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (Scala and Java APIs)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[DataFrame](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DataFrame), [Encoder (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Encoder_(Spark)), [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (Dataset.scala, package.scala, Encoder.scala, docs/sql-programming-guide.md, docs/sql-getting-started.md, docs/sql-migration-guide.md, docs/spark-connect-overview.md) and the Spark 1.6.0 and 2.0.0 release notes</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a **Dataset** is a strongly typed, distributed collection of objects of one JVM type `T` that can be transformed in parallel with functional operations such as `map` and `filter` or with relational operations such as `select` and `groupBy`.[^dataset] It combines the typed lambdas of the [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD) API with the optimized execution engine of Spark SQL.[^guide] The Dataset API exists only in Scala and Java; a [DataFrame](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DataFrame) is the untyped Dataset of `Row` objects, and it is the only form available in Python and R.[^guide]

## How is a Dataset different from a DataFrame?

A DataFrame is a Dataset whose element type is the generic `Row`. In Scala the alias is declared in the `org.apache.spark.sql` package object as `type DataFrame = Dataset[Row]`; in Java the type is written `Dataset<Row>`.[^n1][^guide]

Both forms share one class, so both kinds of operation are available on any Dataset. The Spark documentation calls column-based operations such as `select` and `groupBy` "untyped transformations", and operations that take a lambda over `T`, such as `map`, `filter` and `groupByKey`, "typed transformations".[^started][^migration] A DataFrame becomes a typed Dataset with `as[T]`, which maps columns to fields by name.[^dataset]

Like a DataFrame, a Dataset is lazy. It represents a logical plan, transformations return new Datasets, and an action such as `count`, `show` or a write runs the optimized physical plan on the [executors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor).[^dataset]

## What does a Dataset need an encoder for?

<Hatnote>Main article: [Encoder (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Encoder_(Spark))</Hatnote>

Every Dataset needs an [encoder](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Encoder_(Spark)) for its type. The encoder maps `T` to Spark's internal type system, and Spark uses it to generate code that serializes objects into a compact binary form.[^dataset] Spark can filter, sort and hash data in that form without turning the bytes back into objects, which is the difference from Java or Kryo serialization of RDD elements.[^started]

In Scala, `import spark.implicits._` supplies encoders for primitive types and case classes. In Java, encoders come from static methods on `Encoders`, such as `Encoders.bean(Person.class)`.[^encoder]

## Example

This Scala example is adapted from the Spark SQL examples at v4.3.0. It reads a JSON file into a DataFrame, converts it to a typed Dataset of a case class, and applies a typed and an untyped transformation.[^n2]

```scala
import org.apache.spark.sql.{Dataset, SparkSession}

case class Person(name: String, age: Option[Long])

val spark = SparkSession.builder().getOrCreate()
import spark.implicits._

val people: Dataset[Person] =
  spark.read.json("examples/src/main/resources/people.json").as[Person]

val adultNames: Dataset[String] =
  people.filter(p => p.age.exists(_ >= 21)).map(_.name)   // typed

val byAge = people.groupBy("age").count()                   // untyped, returns a DataFrame
byAge.show()
adultNames.show()
```

The same query in PySpark uses a DataFrame and column expressions, because Python has no typed Dataset:

```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

people = spark.read.json("examples/src/main/resources/people.json")
adult_names = people.filter(F.col("age") >= 21).select("name")
adult_names.show()
```

## Why does PySpark have no Dataset API?

The Dataset's value is compile-time type safety: the compiler checks that a lambda receives a `Person` and returns a `String`. When Spark 2.0 unified the two APIs, the migration guide noted that compile-time type safety is not a language feature of Python and R, so the Dataset concept does not apply to them and the DataFrame stays their main abstraction.[^migration] The programming guide adds that, because Python is dynamic, many of the Dataset's benefits are already available there; for example, a field of a `Row` can be read by name as `row.columnName`.[^guide]

PySpark code that needs per-row Python logic uses a [user-defined function](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/User-defined_function_(Spark)) or `mapInPandas`, which maps an iterator of pandas DataFrames to another, rather than a typed `map`.[^n3]

## Does Spark Connect support Datasets?

Yes. The Spark Connect Scala client supports most Scala APIs since Spark 3.5, including `Dataset` and `KeyValueGroupedDataset`. User-defined functions, which typed transformations rely on, work by default in the shell and need extra set-up in standalone applications.[^connect] See [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect).

## Is the Dataset API deprecated?

No. The `Dataset` class is annotated `@Stable` at the v4.3.0 tag, and the Spark 4.3.0 documentation presents it as a current API for Scala and Java.[^dataset][^guide]

## History

Spark 1.6.0 added the Dataset API (SPARK-9999) as a new API, similar to RDDs, for working with custom objects and lambda functions while using the Spark SQL execution engine.[^n4] Spark 2.0.0 unified DataFrame and Dataset in Scala and Java, so that DataFrame became a type alias for `Dataset[Row]`, and introduced a typed `Aggregator` API for Datasets.[^n5]

# Deletion vector

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Deletion_vector

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">DV</Field>
  <Field name="field">Table formats</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Delta Lake 2.3.0 (reads); Apache Iceberg format version 3</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Bitmap of deleted row positions (64-bit Roaring bitmap), reference to one data file, cardinality</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Copy-on-write and merge-on-read](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Copy-on-write_and_merge-on-read), [Small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">Delta Lake PROTOCOL.md at tag v4.4.1 and the Delta Lake deletion vectors documentation, the Apache Iceberg table spec and Puffin spec at tag apache-iceberg-1.12.0, and the Iceberg maintenance documentation</Verified>

A **deletion vector** (DV) is a compact bitmap, stored outside a data file, that marks which rows of that data file are deleted. Readers skip the marked rows, so a table can delete or update individual rows without rewriting the immutable data file that holds them.[^deltaproto][^icespec] Deletion vectors are one way of implementing the merge-on-read strategy for row-level changes. [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) and [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) (from format version 3) both define them, and the two encodings are closely related.

## How it works

A deletion vector is a set of row positions in one data file, counting from zero. In both formats the set is a 64-bit Roaring bitmap: each 64-bit position is split into a 32-bit key (the high bytes) and a 32-bit sub-position, and each key points to a 32-bit Roaring bitmap of sub-positions.[^deltaproto][^puffin] Roaring bitmaps switch between an integer array, a bitmap and run-length encoding per block of values, which keeps both sparse and dense deletes small.[^deltaproto]

A row is deleted if its position is set in the deletion vector that applies to its data file. The table metadata records which data file a deletion vector belongs to and how many rows it removes (its cardinality).[^deltaproto][^icespec]

| Approach | What is written for a one-row delete | What a reader does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Copy-on-write | A new copy of the whole data file without the row | Reads the new data file |
| Position delete file (Iceberg v2) | A file listing (data file path, row position) pairs | Treats a row as deleted if a delete file has an entry for its file and position |
| Deletion vector | A bitmap for that single data file | Skips the set positions while reading the data file |

The rows of this table are drawn from the Iceberg delete format definitions and the Delta Lake deletion vector documentation.[^icespec][^deltadoc]

## Delta Lake

In the Delta transaction log protocol, deletion vectors are a table feature. A table must use reader version 3 and writer version 7 and list `deletionVectors` in both its reader and writer features. Writers may only create new deletion vectors when the table property `delta.enableDeletionVectors` is true, but readers must honour existing deletion vectors whether or not the property is set.[^deltaproto]

A deletion vector is attached to a file's `add` or `remove` action through a descriptor with a `storageType`: `u` for a file whose path is derived from a UUID relative to the table, `p` for an absolute path, or `i` for a bitmap stored inline in the log, base85-encoded. The descriptor also holds the offset, size in bytes and cardinality. Deletion vector files live in the table root and can hold vectors for data files in several partitions.[^deltaproto]

The protocol's reader requirement is that rows invalidated by a deletion vector must not be returned. Its writer requirement is that a file added with a deletion vector must carry a correct `numRecords` statistic.[^deltaproto]

Support arrived across several releases. According to the Delta Lake documentation, scans with deletion vectors are available from 2.3.0, `DELETE` from 2.4.0, `UPDATE` from 3.0.0 and `MERGE` from 3.1.0. The same page marks the feature as being in experimental support mode.[^deltadoc]

```sql
-- Delta Lake: enable deletion vectors (upgrades the table protocol)
ALTER TABLE events SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.enableDeletionVectors' = true);

-- Later: rewrite every file that has soft-deleted rows
REORG TABLE events APPLY (PURGE);
```

Enabling deletion vectors upgrades the table protocol, after which clients without deletion vector support cannot read the table. From Delta Lake 3.0 the table feature can be dropped again to restore compatibility.[^deltadoc]

## Apache Iceberg

Format version 3 of the Iceberg spec adds binary deletion vectors. They are stored as the `deletion-vector-v1` blob type in Puffin files and tracked in delete manifests by file location, blob offset (`content_offset`) and length (`content_size_in_bytes`), together with the referenced data file.[^icespec] One Puffin file can hold deletion vectors for many data files.[^icespec]

Deletion vectors replace position delete files in version 3. Position delete files are deprecated, must not be added to v3 tables, and existing ones stay valid until the deletes for that data file are next updated, at which point they must be written into a deletion vector.[^icespec] Equality delete files are unaffected and remain the way to delete rows by column value.[^icespec]

The spec allows at most one deletion vector per data file in a snapshot. Writers must merge new deletes with the existing vector or position delete files, so when a deletion vector is present, readers can ignore matching position delete files.[^icespec] At read time, a deletion vector applies to a data file when the paths match, the data file's sequence number is less than or equal to the vector's, and the partitions are equal.[^icespec]

The Puffin blob wraps the bitmap with a length, the magic bytes `D1 D3 39 64` and a CRC-32 checksum. The Puffin spec says its big-endian length and checksum fields were chosen for compatibility with existing deletion vectors in Delta tables.[^puffin]

## Compaction and purge

A deletion vector hides rows but does not remove their bytes, so both projects provide ways to rewrite data files and drop the deleted rows physically.

In Delta Lake, changes recorded in deletion vectors are applied when files are rewritten: by DML run with deletion vectors disabled, by `OPTIMIZE`, or by `REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE)`. Only the last guarantees that every file with soft-deleted rows is rewritten. The old files remain until `VACUUM` removes them.[^deltadoc]

In Iceberg, the spec requires that when a data file is removed, any deletion vector for it is removed from the delete manifests, though the Puffin file holding it need not be rewritten.[^icespec] The `rewrite_data_files` procedure can select data files for rewriting by the number of deletes or the ratio of deleted rows, and the `removeDanglingDeleteFiles` action drops deletion vectors whose data file is no longer live.[^iceproc][^icemaint]

## Not to be confused with

- **Position delete files** in Iceberg v2 also mark rows by position, but as rows in a separate data file that can reference many data files, rather than one bitmap per data file.[^icespec]
- **Merge-on-read log files** in [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) record updates and deletes for a file group in log files that compaction merges into a new base file; Hudi's documentation describes them as log files, not deletion vectors.[^huditypes]

- [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)

# Delta Lake

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">Delta Lake project, a [Linux Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Linux_Foundation) project (created by [Databricks](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Databricks))</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2019 (open source)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">4.4.1</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-05</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala, Java (Delta Spark); Rust (delta-rs)</Field>
  <Field name="type">[Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format)</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[delta.io](https://delta.io)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/delta-io/delta](https://github.com/delta-io/delta)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Delta Lake 4.4.1 GitHub release and the Delta Transaction Log Protocol (PROTOCOL.md)</Verified>

**Delta Lake** is an [open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) and storage framework that adds ACID transactions to tables stored as [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) files in a distributed file system or object store. A Delta table records every change in a transaction log kept next to the data, and the Delta Transaction Log Protocol specifies how readers and writers use that log.[^protocol] Delta Lake is one of the table formats used in an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), with connectors for engines such as [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) and Apache Flink.[^readme]

## How it works

A Delta Lake table is a directory that holds data files and a `_delta_log` subdirectory. The log contains JSON files named by table version, zero-padded to 20 digits. Each JSON file holds an atomic set of actions, such as adding or removing a data file or changing table metadata, that turns the previous version of the table into the next one.[^protocol]

Delta Lake writers work in two phases. They first write new data files optimistically, then commit by adding the next numbered entry to the log. The table therefore has a single serial history of versions. Readers use the log to choose which data files make up a consistent snapshot, so they are isolated from concurrent writes.[^protocol] The project states that Delta Lake provides serializability for concurrent reads and writes.[^readme]

Checkpoints, also stored in `_delta_log`, contain the full replayed state of the table at one version. Readers start from the newest suitable checkpoint so that they do not need to replay every JSON entry.[^protocol]

Because all metadata is stored with the data, a Delta table does not need a separate metastore to be read, and a static table can be copied with ordinary file system tools.[^protocol] The protocol also defines catalog-managed tables, in which a catalog ratifies commits and clients must contact that catalog to find the latest ones.[^protocol]

## Features

### Time travel

The Delta Lake log keeps older table versions readable, so a reader can query the table as of an earlier version. For time travel, the checkpoint used to rebuild the state must not be newer than the requested version.[^protocol] Data files that are no longer in the latest version can be removed by the vacuum command after a retention period, which defaults to 7 days.[^protocol]

### Protocol versions and table features

Each Delta table declares a minimum reader version and a minimum writer version. The protocol version increases when a change to the specification is not forward compatible, so that older clients refuse tables they cannot interpret correctly. From reader version 3 and writer version 7, a table instead lists named table features, and a client must support every listed feature to read or write the table.[^protocol]

### Other features in the protocol

The Delta protocol specification defines, among others:[^protocol]
- **Deletion vectors**, which mark rows in a data file as deleted without rewriting the file.
- **Change data files**, which record row-level changes for readers of a change feed.
- **Column mapping**, which maps logical column names to physical names.
- **Row tracking**, **in-commit timestamps**, **type widening** and the **variant** data type.
- **Iceberg compatibility** table features, which constrain writers so that Iceberg metadata can be produced for the table.

### UniForm

Delta Universal Format (UniForm) lets Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi clients read Delta tables. UniForm generates Iceberg or Hudi metadata asynchronously after Delta commits, over the same Parquet data files. Iceberg and Hudi clients can only read such tables; Hudi support is in preview.[^uniform]

## History

Delta Lake was created by [Databricks](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Databricks). Databricks announced the open sourcing of the Delta Lake project under the Apache License 2.0 on 24 April 2019.[^opensource] On 16 October 2019 the Linux Foundation announced that it would host Delta Lake under an open governance model.[^lf]

Delta Lake 4.4.1, a patch release on top of 4.4.0, was published on 5 October 2026. Its Delta Spark artifacts are built for Apache Spark 4.2.0, 4.1.0 and 4.0.1, with Scala 2.13.[^release]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Delta Lake tables live on object storage in Parquet, and engines read the transaction log to find the current files. With catalog-managed tables, a [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog) takes part in each commit and is the source of truth for the latest versions.[^protocol] UniForm allows the same table to be read by Iceberg clients without copying the data.[^uniform]

## Engine support

The Delta Lake project lists connectors for Apache Spark (read and write), Trino (read and write), Apache Flink (write, preview), PrestoDB (read) and Apache Hive (read). The delta-rs library gives Rust code, with Python bindings, direct access to Delta tables.[^readme] [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB) reads Delta tables through its delta extension.[^n1] Delta Spark also ships [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) client and server artifacts.[^release]

## Limitations

Delta Lake's ACID guarantees depend on the storage system. The project requires atomic visibility of files, mutual exclusion so that only one writer can create a given log file, and consistent directory listing.[^readme] On Amazon S3, for example, writes from multiple clusters must be enabled explicitly by configuring a LogStore implementation (such as one backed by DynamoDB) that supplies the mutual exclusion S3 lacks.[^n2]

Delta Lake keeps backward compatibility, so newer versions read tables written by older versions, but forward compatibility can break: an older client may not read a table that uses newer protocol features.[^readme] UniForm has its own limits; for example, the documentation lists tables with deletion vectors as unsupported.[^uniform]

- [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet)

# Directed acyclic graph (Spark)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph_(Spark)

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">DAG, Spark DAG, RDD lineage graph</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">RDD lineage, narrow and shuffle dependencies, DAG scheduler, stages, task scheduler</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Job, stage and task](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Job,_stage_and_task), [Narrow and wide transformations](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Narrow_and_wide_transformations), [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD), [Lazy evaluation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Lazy_evaluation), [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (core DAGScheduler.scala, docs/rdd-programming-guide.md, docs/web-ui.md, python/pyspark/core/rdd.py, python/pyspark/sql/dataframe.py, WholeStageCodegenExec.scala), the SIGMOD 2015 Spark SQL paper, the Airflow 3.4.0 documentation and a PySpark 4.3.0 run</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), the **directed acyclic graph** (**DAG**) of a job is the graph of datasets and the operations that connect them; Spark's DAG scheduler cuts this graph into stages at [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle) boundaries and runs the stages in dependency order.[^dag] "Directed" means each edge points from an input dataset to the dataset computed from it, and "acyclic" means no dataset depends on itself. The same graph, read backwards from a result, is the **lineage** that Spark uses to recompute lost data.

## What does the DAG scheduler do?

The DAGScheduler is the high-level scheduling layer in the [driver](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Driver_(Apache_Spark)). For each job, the Spark 4.3.0 source describes it as computing a DAG of stages, tracking which RDDs and stage outputs are already materialized, finding a minimal schedule, and submitting each stage as a TaskSet to the lower-level task scheduler.[^dag]

The DAG scheduler has four further duties, all listed in its source:[^dag]

- **Stage boundaries.** It breaks the RDD graph at shuffle boundaries. Operations with narrow dependencies, like `map` and `filter`, are pipelined into one set of tasks in a stage; a shuffle dependency needs a map stage that writes output files and a later stage that reads them after a barrier.
- **Reuse.** It remembers which RDDs are cached and which shuffle map stages have already produced output, so it does not recompute them.
- **Placement.** It computes preferred locations for each task from cached data, shuffle data or the input's own locations, and passes them to the task scheduler.
- **Recovery.** When shuffle output files are lost, it resubmits the stages that produced them. Failures inside a stage that are not caused by lost shuffle files are retried by the task scheduler.

The result of these steps is visible in the Spark web UI. A job's detail page draws its DAG, with vertices for the RDDs or DataFrames and edges for the operations, and each stage detail page draws the stage's part of the graph.[^webui]

## Where are the stage boundaries?

A stage boundary is placed at every shuffle dependency, and nowhere else. Within one stage, every task applies the same chain of operations to a different partition. In the end, every stage has only shuffle dependencies on other stages.[^dag]

For DataFrame and SQL queries, the shuffle dependencies come from `Exchange` operators in the physical plan. The plan below (from a PySpark 4.3.0 run with [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution) and broadcast joins turned off; plan IDs removed) has two `Exchange` nodes feeding a sort-merge join, so the job has three stages: one for each input side and one for the join.

```
*(5) Project [k#9L]
+- *(5) SortMergeJoin [k#9L], [k#11L], Inner
   :- *(2) Sort [k#9L ASC NULLS FIRST], false, 0
   :  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(k#9L, 200), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS
   :     +- *(1) Project [id#8L AS k#9L]
   :        +- *(1) Range (0, 1000000, step=1, splits=2)
   +- *(4) Sort [k#11L ASC NULLS FIRST], false, 0
      +- Exchange hashpartitioning(k#11L, 200), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS
         +- *(3) Project [id#10L AS k#11L]
            +- *(3) Range (0, 100, step=1, splits=2)
```

Which operators create a shuffle is covered in [Narrow and wide transformations](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Narrow_and_wide_transformations).

## What is lineage?

Lineage is the record of the transformations that produced a dataset. Spark's cache is fault tolerant because of it: if a partition of a persisted RDD is lost, Spark recomputes it with the transformations that originally created it.[^rddguide] The 2015 Spark SQL paper describes RDDs the same way: the system recovers lost data using the lineage graph, by rerunning operations such as a filter to rebuild missing partitions.[^paper]

Shuffle files support the same recovery. Spark keeps them until the RDDs that use them are no longer referenced, so that the map side does not have to run again if the lineage is recomputed.[^rddguide]

Lineage can be printed. `RDD.toDebugString()` returns a description of an RDD and its recursive dependencies.[^rddpy] For DataFrames, `explain()` plays the same role (see [Logical plan and physical plan](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Logical_plan_and_physical_plan)).

A long lineage has a cost: the plan grows with each step, and recomputing it after a failure repeats every step. `DataFrame.checkpoint()` truncates the logical plan by saving the data to the checkpoint directory; the PySpark reference recommends it for iterative algorithms, where the plan may grow exponentially. It works with Spark Connect since 4.0.0.[^pydf]

## What the Spark DAG is not

- **Not an orchestration DAG.** In [Apache Airflow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Airflow), a Dag models a whole workflow: its schedule, its tasks (for example submitting a Spark job) and the dependencies between them.[^airflow] A Spark DAG lives inside one Spark job: the driver builds it for an action and schedules its stages.[^dag]
- **Not the query plan itself.** For DataFrame and SQL code, the [Catalyst optimizer](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Catalyst_optimizer) first produces logical and physical plans, which are trees of operators.[^paper] Each physical operator executes as an RDD of rows (in the Spark 4.3.0 source, `doExecute()` returns an `RDD[InternalRow]`), and the DAG scheduler works on that RDD graph.[^wscg]

# Driver (Apache Spark)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Driver_(Apache_Spark)

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Spark driver, driver program</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`SparkContext`, DAG scheduler, task scheduler, query planner, web UI (port 4040)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [SparkContext](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkContext), [SparkSession](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkSession), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [Job, stage and task](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Job,_stage_and_task)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/cluster-overview.md, docs/submitting-applications.md, docs/configuration.md, docs/rdd-programming-guide.md, docs/running-on-kubernetes.md, docs/spark-connect-overview.md, python/pyspark/sql/dataframe.py, BroadcastExchangeExec.scala, QueryExecutionErrors.scala), a PySpark 4.3.0 run, and the Trino 484 concepts page</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), the **driver** is the process that runs an application's `main()` function, creates the [SparkContext](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkContext), turns the program into tasks and schedules those tasks on [executors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor).[^cluster] Every Spark application has exactly one driver. The driver plans the work and coordinates the cluster; the executors read data, run the tasks and hold cached and shuffled data. Where the driver runs is set by the deploy mode, and its memory is a common cause of failures when results or broadcast tables are pulled back to it.

## What runs in the driver and what runs in executors?

The Spark driver holds the application's control flow. It connects to a cluster manager (standalone, YARN or Kubernetes), acquires executors, sends them the application code, and then sends them tasks to run.[^cluster] For DataFrame and SQL work, the driver also parses, analyzes and optimizes each query with the [Catalyst optimizer](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Catalyst_optimizer) and builds the physical plan. The DAG scheduler in the driver splits each job into stages and the task scheduler hands the tasks to executors.[^dag] Each driver serves a web UI, typically on port 4040, that shows its jobs, stages, tasks, executors and storage.[^cluster]

| Work | Runs in the driver | Runs in executors |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Program logic outside Spark operations (loops, Python variables, `print`) | Yes | No |
| Query parsing, analysis, optimization and physical planning | Yes | No |
| Job, stage and task scheduling; retry decisions | Yes | No |
| Functions passed to `map`, `filter` and UDFs | No | Yes, inside tasks |
| Reading files, shuffling, joining and aggregating rows | No | Yes |
| Results of `collect()`, `take()` or `toPandas()` | Received here | Computed and serialized here |

The split matters for side effects. Calling `rdd.foreach(println)` in cluster mode prints to each executor's standard output, not the driver's, because the function runs inside the executors.[^rddguide]

The driver must stay reachable by its executors for its whole lifetime, so it has to be network addressable from the worker nodes. The Spark documentation recommends running it close to the workers, preferably on the same local network.[^cluster]

## Client mode vs cluster mode

The deploy mode decides where the Spark driver process runs. In **client** mode the submitter launches the driver outside the cluster; in **cluster** mode the cluster framework launches the driver inside the cluster.[^cluster] `spark-submit --deploy-mode` (or `spark.submit.deployMode`) selects it, and the default is `client`.[^submit][^config]

|  | Client mode | Cluster mode |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where the driver runs | Inside the `spark-submit` process on the submitting machine[^submit] | On a node inside the cluster; on Kubernetes, in a driver pod[^submit][^k8s] |
| Console input and output | Attached to the submitting console; suited to the Spark shell and other REPLs[^submit] | Not attached; read the driver log from the cluster |
| Typical use | A gateway machine co-located with the workers[^submit] | Submitting from a machine far from the workers, such as a laptop, to reduce driver to executor latency[^submit] |
| Setting driver memory | Must be passed as `--driver-memory` or in the defaults file, because the driver JVM has already started when `SparkConf` is read[^config] | `spark.driver.memory` works as a normal setting; `spark.driver.cores` applies only in this mode[^config] |

Spark's standalone cluster manager does not support cluster mode for Python applications.[^submit] A PySpark 4.3.0 session started without options reports `spark.submit.deployMode` as `client`.

## Why does the driver run out of memory?

The Spark driver's JVM heap is set by `spark.driver.memory` (default `1g`). On YARN and Kubernetes in cluster mode, `spark.driver.memoryOverhead` adds non-heap memory, which also has to cover a Python process that goes with a PySpark driver.[^config] The common causes of a driver out-of-memory error all move data into this process:

- **Collecting large results.** `collect()` fetches the entire dataset to a single machine and can make the driver run out of memory; the Spark guide suggests `take(n)` when only some rows are needed.[^rddguide] The PySpark API reference gives the same warning for `DataFrame.collect()`, `toPandas()` and `toArrow()`: all the data is loaded into the driver's memory.[^pydf]
- **Large total result size.** `spark.driver.maxResultSize` (default `1g`) limits the total serialized results of all partitions for one action; a job above the limit is aborted. Setting it high, or to 0 for unlimited, can lead to driver out-of-memory errors instead.[^config]
- **Broadcast joins.** For a [broadcast join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Broadcast_join), Spark SQL collects the small side to the driver, builds the hash table there and then broadcasts it. If the driver runs out of memory while doing so, Spark reports that there is not enough memory to build and broadcast the table and suggests disabling broadcast with `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold=-1` or raising the driver memory.[^bex][^qee]

## Driver and Spark Connect

With [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), the client application no longer runs in the same process as the Spark driver. The client sends unresolved logical plans to a Spark Connect server, and that server runs the driver and its `SparkContext`. The client therefore cannot reach the driver JVM directly and has no access to the `SparkContext` or the static Spark configuration.[^connect] Several Connect sessions share one server's driver; state backed by the shared `SparkContext`, such as cached datasets and global temporary views, is shared across those sessions.[^connect]

## Spark driver compared with other uses of the word

The word "driver" means something different in [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), which causes confusion when reading Trino documentation next to Spark's.

|  | Spark driver | Trino driver |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | One process per Spark application that plans and schedules all work[^cluster] | A sequence of operator instances inside a Trino task[^trino] |
| Closest counterpart in the other engine | The Trino coordinator, which receives statements from clients and plans them[^trino] | A Spark task, which runs a pipelined chain of narrow operations inside an executor[^dag] |
| How many per query | One for the whole application, across all its queries | Many, running on the workers[^trino] |

# DuckDB

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">DuckDB Foundation and contributors; originally Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica (CWI)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2019-06-27 (v0.1.0)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">2.0.1 (LTS)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-11-20</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">C++</Field>
  <Field name="type">In-process analytical SQL database</Field>
  <Field name="license">MIT License</Field>
  <Field name="website">[duckdb.org](https://duckdb.org)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/duckdb/duckdb](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the DuckDB release calendar, the v2.0.1 GitHub release and the DuckDB 2.0 documentation</Verified>

**DuckDB** is an open source, in-process SQL database management system designed for analytical query workloads. It runs embedded inside a host application instead of as a separate server process, and it uses a columnar, vectorized query engine.[^why] Through extensions, DuckDB reads [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) files and [open table formats](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) such as [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) and [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), which makes it a single-node engine for an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse).[^ext]

## History

DuckDB was created by Mark Raasveldt and Hannes Mühleisen at the Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica (CWI) in Amsterdam, the Netherlands.[^faq]

The first tagged release, v0.1.0, was published on GitHub on 27 June 2019.[^n1] Version 1.0.0 was released on 3 June 2024.[^n2] Version 2.0.0 was released on 21 October 2026 as a long-term support (LTS) release, followed by 2.0.1 on 20 November 2026.[^calendar]

The DuckDB Foundation is a non-profit organization that holds the intellectual property of the project, and its statutes keep DuckDB open source under the MIT License. DuckLabs, a company based in Amsterdam co-founded by Raasveldt and Mühleisen, provides commercial support and employs the core contributors.[^faq]

DuckLabs joined Amazon Web Services (AWS) in September 2026. According to the project FAQ, the intellectual property of DuckDB remained with the DuckDB Foundation and the project continues as open source.[^faq]

## Design

DuckDB runs embedded in the process of the application that uses it, by default without a separate database server. It has no external dependencies at build time or at run time; building it needs only a C++17 compiler.[^why]

DuckDB targets online analytical processing (OLAP): long-running queries that read large parts of a dataset, such as aggregations and joins across several tables. Its execution engine is columnar and vectorized, so it processes batches of values instead of one row at a time, which lowers the overhead per value.[^why]

DuckDB compiles for Linux, macOS and Windows on x86 and ARM processors, and it can run in a web browser through DuckDB-Wasm.[^why]

## Releases and support

Starting with version 1.4.0, every other DuckDB release is an LTS release, which receives community support for about one year. Version 2.0.0 is an LTS release with an end-of-life date of 22 October 2027. The release calendar lists version 2.1.0 as planned for the first half of 2027, with tentative dates.[^calendar]

## Extensions

DuckDB adds features through extensions. The core extensions maintained by the DuckDB team include:[^ext]
- `parquet`, to read and write Parquet files.
- `httpfs`, to read and write files over HTTP(S) and Amazon S3.
- `iceberg`, for the Apache Iceberg table format.
- `delta`, for the Delta Lake format.
- `ducklake`, for the DuckLake format.
- `unity_catalog`, for [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog) connectivity.
- `glue`, for AWS Glue Data Catalog connectivity (marked experimental).

The DuckDB documentation classifies the `parquet` and `httpfs` extensions as primary, with community support, and the lakehouse format extensions as secondary, supported on a best-effort basis.[^ext]

## Use with Apache Iceberg

The DuckDB `iceberg` extension reads Iceberg tables in two ways. It can read a single table directly from storage by pointing at the table metadata, which needs no catalog and is read-only. It can also attach an [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog), which unlocks the full feature set, including writes.[^iceberg]

A REST catalog is attached with a secret that holds the OAuth client credentials and an `ATTACH` statement:[^iceberg]

```sql
CREATE SECRET iceberg_secret (
    TYPE iceberg,
    CLIENT_ID 'admin',
    CLIENT_SECRET 'password',
    OAUTH2_SERVER_URI 'https://catalog.example.com/v1/oauth/tokens'
);

ATTACH 'warehouse' AS my_catalog (
    TYPE iceberg,
    SECRET iceberg_secret,
    URI 'https://catalog.example.com'
);
```

The DuckDB documentation gives setup instructions for several catalogs, including Amazon S3 Tables, AWS Glue, Cloudflare R2 Data Catalog, [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), Lakekeeper, SeaweedFS and Google Cloud BigLake. The Polaris example sets `ACCESS_DELEGATION_MODE 'vended_credentials'`.[^n3]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), DuckDB is an engine that reads the same tables as distributed engines such as [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) and [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), through a shared catalog. The Unity Catalog documentation, for example, shows DuckDB attaching a Unity Catalog catalog with the `unity_catalog` and `delta` extensions, querying and appending to its Delta tables, and creating catalog-managed tables.[^n4]

- [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)
- [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog)

# Dynamic allocation

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dynamic_allocation

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Dynamic resource allocation, `spark.dynamicAllocation`</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 1.2.0; shuffle tracking (no external shuffle service needed) in 3.0.0</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Request policy (backlog timeouts, exponential ramp-up), remove policy (idle timeouts), shuffle data preservation</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) on standalone, YARN and Kubernetes</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [External shuffle service](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/External_shuffle_service), [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Caching and persistence](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Caching_and_persistence)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/job-scheduling.md, docs/configuration.md, docs/running-on-kubernetes.md) and SPARK-27963</Verified>

**Dynamic allocation** is an [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) feature that adds [executors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor) to an application when tasks are waiting and removes executors that sit idle, so that an application holds only the resources its current work needs. It is off by default (`spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=false`) and works on the standalone, YARN and Kubernetes cluster managers.[^jobsched] Because removing an executor would also remove the [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle) files it wrote, dynamic allocation needs a way to keep shuffle data available: an [external shuffle service](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/External_shuffle_service), shuffle tracking, shuffle block migration or a shuffle storage plugin.[^jobsched]

## How does dynamic allocation scale executors?

**Adding executors.** When tasks have been pending for `spark.dynamicAllocation.schedulerBacklogTimeout` (default 1s), Spark requests more executors, and it requests again every `spark.dynamicAllocation.sustainedSchedulerBacklogTimeout` (default: the same value) while the backlog lasts. Each round asks for twice as many as the last: 1, then 2, 4, 8 and so on. The Spark docs compare this to TCP slow start: cautious at first, but able to ramp up quickly.[^jobsched][^config]

**Removing executors.** An executor that has been idle for `spark.dynamicAllocation.executorIdleTimeout` (default 60s) is removed. Executors that hold cached data are kept by default, because `spark.dynamicAllocation.cachedExecutorIdleTimeout` is infinite.[^jobsched][^config]

| Setting | Default |
| --- | --- |
| `spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled` | false |
| `spark.dynamicAllocation.minExecutors` | 0 |
| `spark.dynamicAllocation.maxExecutors` | infinity |
| `spark.dynamicAllocation.initialExecutors` | `minExecutors` (or `spark.executor.instances` if larger) |
| `spark.dynamicAllocation.executorAllocationRatio` | 1 (request enough executors for full parallelism) |
| `spark.dynamicAllocation.schedulerBacklogTimeout` | 1s |
| `spark.dynamicAllocation.executorIdleTimeout` | 60s |
| `spark.dynamicAllocation.cachedExecutorIdleTimeout` | infinity |
| `spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled` | true |
| `spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.timeout` | infinity |

<small>Source: Spark 4.3.0 configuration reference.[^config]</small>

## How is shuffle data kept when executors are removed?

During a shuffle, each executor writes its map output to local disk and serves those files to other executors. If dynamic allocation removed that executor, the files would have to be recomputed.[^jobsched] Spark 4.3.0 accepts four ways to avoid this; one of them must be configured with dynamic allocation:[^jobsched][^config]

| Approach | Setting | How it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shuffle tracking | `spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled` (default true, since 3.0.0) | Spark keeps executors alive while they store shuffle data for active jobs, so no external service is needed[^config][^spark27963] |
| [External shuffle service](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/External_shuffle_service) | `spark.shuffle.service.enabled=true` | A long-running process on each node serves shuffle files after the executor that wrote them is gone[^jobsched] |
| Decommissioning with shuffle migration | `spark.decommission.enabled` and `spark.storage.decommission.shuffleBlocks.enabled` | Before an executor is removed, its shuffle blocks are copied to other executors[^config] |
| Shuffle storage plugin | `spark.shuffle.sort.io.plugin.class` (experimental) | A custom `ShuffleDataIO` stores shuffle data in reliable storage[^config] |

Shuffle tracking is the simplest because it needs no extra service. Its trade-off is that an executor holding shuffle data is not released until the shuffle is garbage collected, unless `spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.timeout` sets a limit.[^config]

## How does dynamic allocation behave on Kubernetes?

Spark on Kubernetes does not support the external shuffle service, so `spark.shuffle.service.enabled=true` cannot be used there.[^jobsched] Kubernetes deployments use shuffle tracking (on by default), decommissioning with shuffle block migration, or a shuffle storage plugin.[^jobsched] With `spark.decommission.enabled`, Spark decommissions an executor instead of killing it when dynamic allocation removes it; when block manager decommissioning (`spark.storage.decommission.enabled`) is also on, Spark tries to migrate the executor's RDD and shuffle blocks to other executors first.[^config] `spark.storage.decommission.fallbackStorage.path` can name a storage location, for example an S3 path, for blocks that cannot be moved to another executor; Spark does not clean it up.[^config]

On Kubernetes, `spark.kubernetes.dynamicAllocation.deleteGracePeriod` (default 5s) is how long Spark waits for an executor pod to shut down before a forceful kill.[^k8s] Shuffle and spill files go to `emptyDir` volumes by default, which do not outlive the pod; persistent volume claims created on demand per executor (`claimName=OnDemand`) are one way to give executors larger local storage when they are created dynamically.[^k8s]

## Caveats

- **Standalone mode cores.** Without `spark.executor.cores`, each standalone executor takes all cores of a worker, and dynamic allocation can acquire many more executors than expected. The docs recommend setting cores explicitly (see SPARK-30299).[^jobsched]
- **Cached data.** Executors with cached blocks are never removed by default. With `spark.shuffle.service.fetch.rdd.enabled`, executors that hold only disk-persisted RDD blocks can be released, and the blocks are served by the external shuffle service.[^jobsched]
- **Local checkpoints.** The Spark source warns that local checkpointing is not safe with dynamic allocation, which removes executors together with their cached blocks. See [Checkpointing (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Checkpointing_(Spark)).[^rdd]

## Example

```
spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled                  true
spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled  true
spark.dynamicAllocation.minExecutors             2
spark.dynamicAllocation.maxExecutors             50
spark.dynamicAllocation.executorIdleTimeout      120s
spark.executor.cores                             4
```

# Dynamic partition pruning

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dynamic_partition_pruning

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">DPP, runtime partition pruning</Field>
  <Field name="field">Query optimization</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Partitioned fact table, filtered dimension table, equi-join key on a partition column, broadcast reuse or a pruning subquery</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (since 3.0.0), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) and other Data Source V2 connectors through runtime filtering</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Partition pruning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition_pruning), [Runtime filter](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Runtime_filter), [Broadcast join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Broadcast_join), [Predicate pushdown](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown), [Star schema](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Star_schema)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (PartitionPruning.scala, PlanDynamicPruningFilters.scala, CleanupDynamicPruningFilters.scala, DynamicPruning.scala, joins.scala, predicates.scala, SQLConf.scala, SupportsRuntimeV2Filtering.java), Spark JIRA SPARK-11150, and the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 Spark source</Verified>

**Dynamic partition pruning** (DPP) is a query optimization in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) that skips partitions of a table using filter values that are only known while the query runs, typically the join keys that survive a filter on the other side of a join. It targets star-schema queries, where a large fact table partitioned by a key is joined to a small, filtered dimension table. DPP was added in Spark 3.0.0 (SPARK-11150) and is on by default.[^jira][^sqlconf]

## Why is dynamic partition pruning needed?

Static [partition pruning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition_pruning) needs the filter on the partitioned table itself. In a star-schema query the filter is on the dimension table, and the fact table is constrained only through the join:

```sql
-- sales is partitioned by date_key; dim_date is small
SELECT d.calendar_month, SUM(s.amount)
FROM sales s
JOIN dim_date d ON s.date_key = d.date_key
WHERE d.is_holiday = true
GROUP BY d.calendar_month;
```

Without DPP, Spark reads every partition of `sales` and discards non-holiday rows at the join. With DPP, Spark first evaluates the filtered `dim_date`, collects its `date_key` values, and scans only the `sales` partitions with those keys.

## How does dynamic partition pruning work in Apache Spark?

DPP is an optimizer rule, `PartitionPruning`. When a join has an equality condition between a partition column on one side and a column on the other side, the rule inserts a `DynamicPruningSubquery` filter on the partitioned side. The subquery holds the filtering side of the join, and Spark decides during physical planning how to run it.[^rule]
1. If the join is planned as a [broadcast hash join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Broadcast_join), Spark reuses the broadcast of the filtering side as the pruning filter, so the dimension table is read only once.
1. Otherwise, if the estimated benefit outweighs the cost of running the filtering side twice, Spark keeps a separate subquery.
1. Otherwise, Spark drops the pruning filter.[^rule][^n1]

With the defaults, step 2 does not happen. `spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.reuseBroadcastOnly` is true, so DPP applies only when a broadcast exchange can be reused.[^sqlconf] In practice DPP depends on the dimension side being small enough to broadcast.

The benefit estimate compares the size of the partitioned side after pruning with the size of the filtering side. It uses column statistics when they exist (`spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.useStats`, default true) and otherwise a fallback filter ratio (`spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.fallbackFilterRatio`, default 0.5).[^rule][^sqlconf]

## When does dynamic partition pruning apply?

The rule at Spark 4.3.0 inserts a pruning filter only when all of the following are true:[^rule]
- The join condition contains an equality (`=`) between the two sides.
- The key on the pruned side traces back to a partition column of a file source or Hive table, or to an attribute that a Data Source V2 scan accepts for runtime filtering.
- The join type allows pruning that side. Inner and left semi joins can prune either side; a left outer join can prune only its right side, and a right outer join only its left side.[^joins]
- The filtering side is not a streaming plan, and it contains a predicate that is likely to be selective (a comparison, `IN`, `LIKE`, a string predicate and similar) or a small input that is already materialized.[^rule][^n2]

## When does dynamic partition pruning not apply?

Common reasons a star join gets no DPP:
- **The fact table is not partitioned on the join key.** DPP prunes partitions, not files or row groups. Joins on non-partition columns can use a [runtime filter](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Runtime_filter) instead.
- **The dimension side has no selective filter.** Without a filter, every key survives, so there is nothing to prune.
- **The dimension side is not broadcast.** With `reuseBroadcastOnly` at its default (true), a sort-merge join gets no DPP.[^sqlconf]
- **The join type is wrong for the side.** For example, the preserved side of an outer join (the left side of a left outer join) cannot be pruned.[^joins]
- **The filtering side is non-deterministic.** If the filtering plan is non-deterministic, Spark replaces the dynamic predicate with `true` before physical planning.[^rule]
- **DPP is turned off** with `spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.enabled=false`.[^sqlconf]

## What does dynamic partition pruning look like in a plan?

In the physical plan, the scan of the partitioned table lists the dynamic filter in its `PartitionFilters`, wrapped in `dynamicpruningexpression(...)`. With broadcast reuse, the filter refers to a `SubqueryBroadcast` node that reads the broadcast built for the join, and the reuse rule turns the duplicate broadcast exchange into a `ReusedExchange` node.[^n3][^n4][^n5] After the query runs, the scan's `number of partitions read` metric in the Spark UI's SQL tab shows how many partitions were read.[^n6]

## Dynamic partition pruning with table formats

Data Source V2 tables take part in DPP through the `SupportsRuntimeV2Filtering` interface (since Spark 3.4.0), which lets a scan drop input partitions using the runtime predicate.[^n7] [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)'s Spark batch scan implements it, so DPP prunes Iceberg partitions, including hidden partitions derived from a source column.[^n8]

## Dynamic partition pruning vs runtime filter

DPP and the Spark [runtime filter](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Runtime_filter) both push information from one side of a join to the other at run time. DPP removes whole partitions at the scan and needs a partition column as the join key. The runtime filter, added in Spark 3.3.0, inserts a bloom filter on any join key to reduce the rows that go into a shuffle, and Spark does not add one where DPP already applies.[^sqlconf][^n9]

# Encoder (Spark)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Encoder_(Spark)

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">`Encoder[T]`, Dataset encoder</Field>
  <Field name="field">Serialization in distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Spark 1.6.0</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">A schema (`StructType`), a class tag, generated serializer and deserializer code</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (Scala and Java APIs)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Dataset (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dataset_(Spark)), [DataFrame](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DataFrame), [Project Tungsten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Tungsten), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [Apache Arrow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Arrow)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (Encoder.scala, Encoders.scala, AgnosticEncoder.scala, ExpressionEncoder.scala, Dataset.scala, sql/connect/common/.../client/arrow/ArrowSerializer.scala and ArrowDeserializer.scala, docs/sql-getting-started.md, docs/sql-programming-guide.md)</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), an **encoder** is the object that converts a JVM object of type `T` to and from Spark SQL's internal row representation; every typed [Dataset](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dataset_(Spark)) needs one for its element type.[^encoder] The encoder tells Spark the schema of `T` and lets it generate code at runtime that serializes objects into a compact binary format.[^dataset] Encoders are part of the Scala and Java APIs; PySpark has no Dataset API and so no encoders.[^guide]

## What does an encoder do?

An encoder maps the type `T` to Spark's internal type system. For a class `Person` with a string field `name` and an integer field `age`, the encoder tells Spark to generate code that writes each `Person` into a binary structure, which usually takes less memory than the objects and is laid out for efficient processing.[^dataset]

The public interface is small. `trait Encoder[T]`, available since Spark 1.6.0, has two members: `schema`, the `StructType` that a `T` becomes as a row, and `clsTag`, a `ClassTag` used to build arrays of `T`. Encoders must be thread-safe.[^encoder]

## How is an encoder different from Java or Kryo serialization?

[RDDs](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD) serialize their elements with Java serialization or Kryo. Both encoders and those serializers turn objects into bytes, but encoders are generated dynamically and use a format that lets Spark filter, sort and hash the data without deserializing it back into objects.[^started] Because the encoder also gives Spark a schema, a Dataset of case classes shows up with ordinary named columns that Spark SQL can query.[^encoder]

## How do you get an encoder?

In Scala, encoders are usually provided implicitly by `import spark.implicits._`, which covers primitive types such as `Int` and `String` and product types such as case classes. If no encoder is found, compilation fails with the message "Unable to find encoder for type T", which points to that import.[^encoder]

```scala
import org.apache.spark.sql.{Encoder, Encoders}

case class Order(id: Long, customer: String, amount: Double)

import spark.implicits._
val orders = Seq(Order(1L, "acme", 120.0), Order(2L, "globex", 75.5)).toDS()
orders.printSchema()     // id: long, customer: string, amount: double

val enc: Encoder[Order] = Encoders.product[Order]
println(enc.schema.simpleString)   // struct<id:bigint,customer:string,amount:double>
```

In Java, encoders are passed explicitly, taken from static methods on `Encoders`, for example `spark.createDataset(data, Encoders.STRING())`. Encoders can be combined into tuples with `Encoders.tuple` or derived from a Java Bean with `Encoders.bean(MyClass.class)`.[^encoder]

## Which encoders does the Encoders object provide?

| Method | Encodes | Since |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `BOOLEAN`, `INT`, `LONG`, `DOUBLE`, `STRING`, `DECIMAL`, `DATE`, `TIMESTAMP` and other primitives | Boxed Java types and `java.sql` date and time types, one column each | 1.6.0 |
| `BINARY` | `Array[Byte]` | 1.6.1 |
| `LOCALDATE`, `INSTANT` | `java.time.LocalDate`, `java.time.Instant` | 3.0.0 |
| `DURATION`, `PERIOD` | `java.time.Duration`, `java.time.Period` (interval types) | 3.2.0 |
| `LOCALDATETIME` | `java.time.LocalDateTime` | 3.4.0 |
| `row(schema)` | A generic `Row` with the given schema | 3.5.0 |
| `CHAR(n)`, `VARCHAR(n)` | Strings with a length limit | 4.0.0 |
| `LOCALTIME`, `GEOMETRY`, `GEOGRAPHY` | `java.time.LocalTime` and geospatial types | 4.1.0 |
| `bean(Class)` | A Java Bean, field by field | 1.6.0 |
| `kryo`, `javaSerialization` | Any public type, as a single binary column | 1.6.0 |

The methods and versions are taken from the `@since` tags in `Encoders.scala` at v4.3.0.[^encoders]

The `kryo` and `javaSerialization` encoders store the whole object as one binary field, so Spark cannot see or prune its fields. The source describes Java serialization as extremely inefficient and to be used only as a last resort.[^encoders]

## How do encoders work inside Spark?

At v4.3.0 the encoders returned by `Encoders`, such as `StringEncoder` behind `Encoders.STRING`, are `AgnosticEncoder` instances.[^encoders] An `AgnosticEncoder` holds all the information about a type, such as its fields, options, arrays and maps, without fixing how the conversion is done, so different implementations can be generated from it.[^agnostic]

In classic Spark, the engine builds an `ExpressionEncoder` from it: a serializer and a deserializer written as Catalyst expressions, which convert an object to an `InternalRow` and back and take part in code generation.[^expr] In the [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) Scala client, the same `AgnosticEncoder` drives an `ArrowSerializer` and `ArrowDeserializer` that convert user objects to and from [Apache Arrow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Arrow) batches.[^n1][^n2]

## Why does PySpark have no encoders?

PySpark has no typed Dataset, so it has nothing for an encoder to describe. Spark's documentation explains that compile-time type safety is not a feature of Python, and that the DataFrame, a Dataset of `Row`, is the main abstraction there.[^guide][^n3] A PySpark [DataFrame](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DataFrame) carries a schema of named, typed columns instead; Python logic over rows runs in [user-defined functions](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/User-defined_function_(Spark)).

# Event time and processing time

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Event_time_and_processing_time

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Event-time and processing-time semantics</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Event timestamp carried in the record, clock of the processing machine, skew between them, [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink), Kafka Streams</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), [Windowing (stream processing)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Windowing_(stream_processing)), [Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming programming guide and Kafka integration guide, `python/pyspark/sql/functions/builtin.py` at tag v4.3.0 of apache/spark, the Apache Flink 2.3 "Timely Stream Processing" page, the Kafka Streams 4.4 core concepts page and the Dataflow Model paper (VLDB 2015)</Verified>

In [stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing), **event time** is the time at which an event actually happened, recorded in the event itself, and **processing time** is the time on the clock of the machine that handles the event. The two differ because events are delayed by networks, queues, retries and outages, so a stream processor that groups by event time and one that groups by processing time can give different answers for the same data. In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), event time is an ordinary timestamp column of a DataFrame, and windows, [watermarks](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) and stateful operators use it to produce results that do not depend on arrival order.[^ss-start]

## What is event time?

Event time is the timestamp that describes when something happened: when a sensor took a reading, when a user clicked, when a payment was authorized. The Spark programming guide defines event time as the time embedded in the data itself, and uses the example of counting events generated by IoT devices per minute by the time the device produced them rather than the time Spark received them.[^ss-start]

In the Flink documentation, event time is the time each event occurred on its producing device; it is usually embedded in the record before it reaches the engine, and the progress of event time depends on the data, not on any wall clock.[^flink-time]

## What is processing time?

Processing time is the system time of the machine that runs an operator at the moment it handles a record. An hourly processing-time window contains whatever records reached the operator while its clock showed that hour.[^flink-time] Processing time needs no coordination between machines and gives the lowest latency, but its results depend on how fast records arrive and move through the system, and on outages, so they are not deterministic.[^flink-time]

Some sources add a third notion, **ingestion time**, the time at which a record entered the pipeline, for example when a Kafka broker appended it to a partition. The [Apache Kafka](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Kafka) source in Spark exposes this kind of timestamp as the `timestamp` column, together with a `timestampType` column, next to `key`, `value`, `topic`, `partition` and `offset`.[^ss-kafka]

## Why do event-time and processing-time results differ?

The Dataflow paper from Google describes the gap between the two clocks as **skew**: the event time of an event never changes, but the skew between event time and processing time changes constantly, so records arrive late and out of order.[^dataflow]

The Spark guide gives a concrete case. A word generated at 12:04 (event time) reaches the application at 12:11 (processing time). A count by event time adds the word to the window 12:00 to 12:10; a count by arrival time would put it in a later window. Structured Streaming keeps the partial aggregate for the older window so that the late record still updates it.[^ss-apis]

Reprocessing shows the same effect. Event-time results are the same whether a day of data is processed live or replayed a week later, because the timestamps come from the data. Processing-time results of a replay depend on when the replay ran. Flink's documentation states that event-time operations give consistent results for out-of-order or late events and when reprocessing historic data, provided all the data has arrived.[^flink-time]

Event time has a cost: the engine must wait for late records before it can call a result final. Because it can only wait for a finite time, event-time processing has a limit on how deterministic it can be.[^flink-time] A [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) expresses that waiting time.

## How does Structured Streaming use event time?

Structured Streaming treats each event as a row and event time as a column of that row, so a window over event time is a grouping key like any other. The same event-time window query can therefore run on a static DataFrame of historical logs and on a stream.[^ss-start] The `window`, `session_window` and `window_time` functions take this column as input, and `withWatermark` declares how late it may be.[^ss-apis]

Spark has no separate processing-time API for windows. The `session_window` documentation notes that a streaming query can use the `current_timestamp` function to generate windows on processing time.[^builtin] Processing time also governs when micro-batches run, through the [trigger](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trigger_(Structured_Streaming)), and the processing-time timers and TTL of [transformWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState).

## Example

This PySpark query counts clicks per 10-minute window by event time. The `event_time` column comes from the JSON payload; the Kafka `timestamp` column is kept only to show the difference. A click with an `event_time` of 12:04 that arrives at 12:11 is still counted in the window that starts at 12:00, as long as it is within the 15-minute watermark delay.

```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

raw = (spark.readStream.format("kafka")
       .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker:9092")
       .option("subscribe", "clicks")
       .load())

clicks = raw.select(
    F.from_json(F.col("value").cast("string"),
                "user STRING, page STRING, event_time TIMESTAMP").alias("c"),
    F.col("timestamp").alias("kafka_time"),      # set by Kafka
).select("c.*", "kafka_time")

per_window = (clicks
    .withWatermark("event_time", "15 minutes")
    .groupBy(F.window("event_time", "10 minutes"), "page")
    .count())
```

Grouping by `kafka_time` instead would count the same click in the window that starts at 12:10.

## Event time and processing time in other engines

|  | Spark Structured Streaming | Apache Flink | Kafka Streams |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| How event time is set | A timestamp column in the DataFrame, named in `window` and `withWatermark`[^ss-apis] | A `TimestampAssigner` in a `WatermarkStrategy`[^flink-time] | A `TimestampExtractor` that reads a timestamp from each record[^kstreams] |
| How event-time progress is tracked | Watermark: maximum event time seen minus the delay[^ss-apis] | Watermarks that flow through the stream[^flink-time] | **Stream time**, which advances only when new records arrive[^kstreams] |
| Processing-time windows | By windowing on `current_timestamp`[^builtin] | Built-in processing-time window assigners[^flink-time] | A `TimestampExtractor` that returns the current wall-clock time[^kstreams] |
