# Exactly-once semantics

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Exactly-once processing, exactly-once delivery, effectively-once</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing), distributed systems</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Replayable source, checkpointed progress and state, idempotent or transactional sink</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink), Kafka transactions and Kafka Streams ([Apache Kafka](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Kafka)), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing), [Watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), [Streaming lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_lakehouse)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming guides, the Apache Flink 2.3 documentation, the Apache Kafka 4.4 design and Streams documentation, the Delta Lake streaming documentation and the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 Flink documentation</Verified>

In [stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing), **exactly-once semantics** is the guarantee that each input record affects the result exactly once, with nothing lost and nothing duplicated, even when parts of the system fail and work is retried. Engines usually achieve it by replaying input after a failure and making sure the replay does not change the result twice, not by literally processing each record once. For this reason the guarantee is sometimes called **effectively-once**.

## Delivery guarantees

The Apache Kafka documentation defines three levels of guarantee:[^kafka-design]

| Guarantee | Definition | Typical cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| At-most-once | Messages may be lost but are never redelivered | No retry after a failure |
| At-least-once | Messages are never lost but may be redelivered | Retry or replay without deduplication |
| Exactly-once | Each message is processed once and only once | Replay combined with idempotent or transactional output |

Apache Flink describes the same three outcomes for recovery: no effort to recover (at most once), nothing lost but possible duplicates (at least once), and nothing lost or duplicated (exactly once).[^flink-ft]

## What it means and what it does not

Two guarantees are often confused, and the Spark Real-time Mode documentation separates them explicitly:[^ss-rtm]

- **Exactly-once processing** (or exactly-once state): each input record's effect on the state the engine manages, such as an aggregation count, is applied effectively once across failures and restarts. Flink states its guarantee in the same terms: every event affects the state managed by Flink exactly once.[^flink-ft]
- **End-to-end exactly-once** (or exactly-once delivery): each record affects the external system, such as a table or topic, exactly once. This is a property of the sink as well as the engine.[^ss-rtm]

Exactly-once does not mean that user code runs once per record. After a failure, an engine re-runs the work since the last checkpoint, so functions, API calls and log lines in that work can run again. Only effects that pass through a sink with the right guarantees are deduplicated.

## The end-to-end requirement

Engine documentation converges on three conditions:

1. **A replayable source.** After a failure the engine must be able to read the same data again from a recorded position, such as a Kafka offset. Spark assumes every source has offsets for this purpose; Flink requires that the source can rewind to the position stored in the checkpoint.[^ss-start][^flink-conn]
1. **Recorded progress and deterministic processing.** The engine records what it has read, and its state, in a checkpoint, so a replay starts from a consistent point. If processing is not deterministic, a replay can produce different output from the first attempt.
1. **An idempotent or transactional sink.** Writing the same output twice must have the same effect as writing it once (idempotent), or output must become visible atomically together with the recorded progress (transactional). Flink states that the sink must commit transactionally or write idempotently.[^flink-conn][^flink-ft]

## Implementations

### Spark Structured Streaming

<Hatnote>Main article: [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming)</Hatnote>

Structured Streaming uses checkpointing and write-ahead logs to record the offset range processed in each trigger, and its built-in sinks are designed to be idempotent so that reprocessing is safe. The Spark documentation states that replayable sources and idempotent sinks together give end-to-end exactly-once semantics under any failure.[^ss-start]

The guarantee depends on the sink. In the Spark 4.3 documentation the file sink is exactly-once, while the Kafka sink and `foreach` sink are at-least-once, and for `foreachBatch` it "depends on the implementation".[^ss-apis] Real-time Mode keeps exactly-once processing, but because it commits offsets at the end of each batch, after records have reached the sink, a failure can re-write records; it does not yet ship an exactly-once sink.[^ss-rtm]

`foreachBatch` gives only at-least-once writes by default. The Spark guide recommends using the `batchId` passed to the function to deduplicate output and get exactly-once.[^ss-apis] [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) supports this directly: with the `txnAppId` and `txnVersion` writer options, Delta identifies a repeated write of the same batch and ignores it.[^delta-stream]

```python
APP_ID = "orders-to-silver"   # unique per streaming query

def write_batch(batch_df, batch_id):
    (batch_df.write.format("delta")
        .option("txnAppId", APP_ID)
        .option("txnVersion", batch_id)   # a replayed batch is skipped
        .mode("append")
        .save("/data/silver/orders"))

(orders.writeStream
    .foreachBatch(write_batch)
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/data/_checkpoints/orders-to-silver")
    .start())
```

If the checkpoint is deleted and the query restarts with a new one, batch IDs start again from 0, so the application ID must change; otherwise Delta ignores the new writes as duplicates.[^delta-stream]

### Kafka transactions and Kafka Streams

Since Kafka 0.11.0.0, the producer supports an idempotent mode that prevents duplicate log entries when a send is retried, and transactions that write to several topic partitions atomically. Consumers with the `read_committed` isolation level only see messages from committed transactions.[^kafka-design] Kafka Streams uses these features: with `processing.guarantee` set to `exactly_once_v2` (the default is `at_least_once`), it commits input offsets, state store updates and output records atomically. Exactly-once v2 requires brokers at version 2.5.0 or newer.[^kstreams]

The Kafka documentation notes that exactly-once delivery to other destination systems generally requires the cooperation of those systems; one approach is to store the consumer's offset in the same place as its output.[^kafka-design]

### Flink two-phase commit sinks

Flink takes consistent snapshots of operator state with checkpoint barriers, a variant of the Chandy-Lamport algorithm.[^flink-ft] For external sinks, Flink 1.4.0 introduced `TwoPhaseCommitSinkFunction`: a sink pre-commits an external transaction when a checkpoint starts and commits it only after the checkpoint completes.[^flink-blog] Current sinks expose a `DeliveryGuarantee` of `NONE`, `AT_LEAST_ONCE` or `EXACTLY_ONCE`.[^flink-conn] With `EXACTLY_ONCE`, the Kafka sink writes records in a Kafka transaction committed on each checkpoint, so output becomes visible only after a checkpoint, and the Kafka transaction timeout must exceed the checkpoint and restart time to avoid data loss.[^flink-kafka]

## Why table formats make good sinks

[Open table formats](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) commit each write as a single atomic change to table metadata, which is the transactional sink the end-to-end requirement asks for. A streaming engine can tie each commit to its own checkpoint, so a replayed batch either is detected as already committed or replaces an uncommitted attempt. Delta Lake states that its transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch jobs write to the same table concurrently.[^delta-stream] The [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) Flink sink guarantees exactly-once semantics, committing to the Iceberg table after each successful Flink checkpoint.[^iceberg-flink] [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) lists exactly-once ingestion of new events from Kafka as a capability of its Hudi Streamer tool.[^hudi-streamer] This is one reason the [streaming lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_lakehouse) pattern writes streams directly into tables.

## Where it breaks

- **External side effects.** Calls to APIs, emails or writes to systems outside the sink run again on replay. Only the sink's effects are protected.
- **Non-idempotent `foreachBatch` code.** A function that appends to a table or calls a service without using `batchId` produces duplicates when a batch is retried.[^ss-apis]
- **At-least-once sinks.** The Spark Kafka sink and `foreach` sink are at-least-once, so downstream readers must tolerate or remove duplicates.[^ss-apis]
- **Non-replayable sources.** The Spark socket source, for example, does not provide end-to-end fault-tolerance guarantees and is meant only for testing.[^ss-apis]
- **Lost or reset checkpoints.** The checkpoint holds the recorded progress. Deleting it or reusing identifiers incorrectly breaks deduplication, as the Delta `txnAppId` rule shows.[^delta-stream]
- **Consumers outside the transaction.** Exactly-once through Kafka transactions holds for consumers that read only committed messages (the `read_committed` isolation level); the Flink Kafka sink documentation states the same condition.[^kafka-design][^flink-kafka]

# Executor

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Spark executor</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Task slots (cores), execution memory, storage memory, local disk for shuffle files</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Partition](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/cluster-overview.md, docs/configuration.md, docs/tuning.md, docs/job-scheduling.md, docs/running-on-kubernetes.md), the Trino 484 concepts page and the Apache Flink 2.3 architecture page</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), an **executor** is a process launched for one application on a worker node; it runs the application's tasks and keeps data in memory or on disk between them.[^cluster] The driver plans the work and the executors do it. The same word appears in other engines with a different meaning, so this page also compares the Spark executor with a [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) worker, an [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) TaskManager and a Kubernetes pod.

## What an executor runs

A Spark executor runs **tasks**. A task is the unit of work that the driver sends to one executor, and each task processes one [partition](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition) of a dataset.[^cluster][^rddguide] Spark divides each job into stages, and every task in a stage applies the same function to a different partition.[^dag]

An executor runs several tasks at the same time, each in its own thread inside the executor process.[^cluster] Besides running tasks, the executor stores cached data and writes the shuffle files that later stages read; it also serves those files to other executors unless an external shuffle service does that work.[^jobsched]

## Cores and task slots

The number of tasks an executor can run at once is set by its cores. `spark.executor.cores` sets the cores per executor; its default is 1 on YARN and all available cores of the worker in standalone mode. `spark.task.cpus` (default 1) sets the cores each task needs, and the number of concurrent tasks on an executor is `floor(executor cores / spark.task.cpus)`.[^config] These concurrent places for tasks are often called task slots.

A stage with more partitions than free slots runs in waves: when a task finishes, the slot takes the next pending task. If a task fails, Spark retries it; `spark.task.maxFailures` (default 4) is the number of consecutive failures of one task before the job fails.[^config]

## Memory

Each executor is a JVM process. `spark.executor.memory` (default `1g`) sets its heap. On YARN and Kubernetes, Spark also requests non-heap overhead memory, `spark.executor.memoryOverhead`, which by default is the executor memory multiplied by `spark.executor.memoryOverheadFactor` (0.10), with a minimum of 384 MiB. The container size is the sum of executor memory, overhead, off-heap memory and PySpark memory.[^config]

Inside the heap, Spark uses a unified memory region for two purposes. **Execution memory** holds data for shuffles, joins, sorts and aggregations; **storage memory** holds cached data. `spark.memory.fraction` (default 0.6) sets the size of this region as a fraction of the heap minus 300 MiB, and the rest is left for user data structures and Spark metadata. Execution can evict cached blocks, but only down to the share set by `spark.memory.storageFraction` (default 0.5).[^tuning] When execution data does not fit, Spark spills it to local disk.[^rddguide]

## Lifetime and relation to the driver

Each Spark application gets its own executors. Without dynamic allocation they stay up for the whole application, and tasks from different applications never share a JVM. Two applications therefore cannot share in-memory data except through external storage.[^cluster] The driver must stay reachable from the executors for its whole lifetime, and executors send heartbeats to it, by default every 10 seconds, so that it knows they are alive.[^cluster][^config]

## Dynamic allocation

With dynamic resource allocation, Spark adds executors when tasks are waiting and removes executors that are idle. It is off by default (`spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled`) and works on standalone, YARN and Kubernetes.[^jobsched] Spark requests executors in rounds that grow exponentially (1, 2, 4, 8 and so on), and removes an executor after it has been idle for `spark.dynamicAllocation.executorIdleTimeout` (default 60 seconds). Executors that hold cached data are kept by default, because `spark.dynamicAllocation.cachedExecutorIdleTimeout` defaults to infinity.[^jobsched][^config]

Removing an executor would lose the shuffle files it wrote. Dynamic allocation therefore needs one way to keep them: an external shuffle service, shuffle tracking (`spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled`, default true), shuffle block migration during decommissioning, or a shuffle storage plugin. Spark on Kubernetes does not support the external shuffle service.[^jobsched][^config]

## Spark executor compared with similar terms

|  | Spark executor | Trino worker | Flink TaskManager | Kubernetes pod running an executor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A process started for one Spark application[^cluster] | A server in a Trino cluster that runs tasks and processes data[^trino] | A JVM process that runs the subtasks of a dataflow and buffers and exchanges data streams[^flink] | A Kubernetes pod that contains one executor container[^k8s] |
| Coordinated by | The application's driver | The coordinator, which parses and plans queries[^trino] | The JobManager[^flink] | The Spark driver, through the Kubernetes API[^k8s] |
| Unit of concurrency | Task slots (executor cores divided by task CPUs) | Tasks, which run drivers over splits[^trino] | Task slots; each slot is a fixed share of managed memory, with no CPU isolation[^flink] | Same as the executor inside it; the pod CPU request does not change task concurrency[^k8s] |
| Shared between applications or queries? | No; only the jobs of one application use it | Yes; workers are servers of the cluster, and each query may use up to `query.max-memory-per-node` of user memory on a worker[^trino][^n1] | In a session cluster, jobs share the cluster; in an application cluster, only one application's jobs run[^flink] | No; the pod ends when the executor ends |
| Lifetime | The application, or shorter with dynamic allocation | The Trino cluster | The Flink cluster (session) or the application (application cluster)[^flink] | The executor; pods are cleaned up when the application completes[^k8s] |

A Flink task slot and a Spark task slot are close but not the same. A Flink slot reserves a fixed share of a TaskManager's managed memory, and by default subtasks of the same job can share a slot.[^flink] A Spark slot is a share of an executor's cores; all tasks on an executor draw on one unified memory pool.[^tuning]

On Kubernetes, the pod and the executor are two layers. The pod's memory request and limit are the sum of `spark.executor.memory` and `spark.executor.memoryOverhead`, and `spark.kubernetes.executor.request.cores` can set the pod's CPU request apart from `spark.executor.cores`.[^k8s] Shuffle and spill files go to `emptyDir` volumes by default, which do not outlive the pod.[^k8s]

## Example

A configuration for executors with four task slots each, scaled by dynamic allocation:

```
spark.executor.cores                             4
spark.executor.memory                            8g
spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled                  true
spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled  true
spark.dynamicAllocation.minExecutors             1
spark.dynamicAllocation.maxExecutors             20
```

# Executor decommissioning

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor_decommissioning

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Graceful decommission, node decommissioning, block manager decommissioning</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 3.1 (SPARK-20624)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`spark.decommission.enabled`, shuffle and RDD block migration, fallback storage, decommission signal</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Spark on Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_Kubernetes), [Spark Kubernetes shuffle storage](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Kubernetes_shuffle_storage), [Spark Kubernetes pod template](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Kubernetes_pod_template)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (core/.../internal/config/package.scala and Worker.scala, deploy/k8s/Config.scala, BasicExecutorFeatureStep.scala, decom.sh, YarnAllocator.scala, docs/configuration.md, docs/job-scheduling.md, docs/core-migration-guide.md, docs/spark-standalone.md), SPARK-20624 and its sub-tasks, and the Spark 3.1.1 and 3.4.0 release notes</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), **executor decommissioning** is the graceful shutdown of an [executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor): Spark stops sending it new tasks and, when storage decommissioning is on, copies its cached RDD blocks and [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle) files to other executors or to fallback storage before the executor exits.[^config][^jira20628] It lets an application lose executors, for example to dynamic allocation, spot or preemptible nodes or a node drain, without recomputing the data those executors held. Decommissioning is off by default and is controlled by `spark.decommission.enabled`.[^config]

## How does executor decommissioning work?

A decommission starts when the cluster manager or the driver tells an executor to leave. The scheduler then treats the executor as inactive and schedules no new tasks on it.[^jira20628] With `spark.storage.decommission.enabled` set, the executor's block manager migrates its blocks: shuffle files when `spark.storage.decommission.shuffleBlocks.enabled` is true and cached RDD blocks when `spark.storage.decommission.rddBlocks.enabled` is true.[^config]

Once its running tasks and all migrations are done, the executor exits on its own; this behaviour came from SPARK-31197 in Spark 3.1.0.[^n1] The driver updates the location of each migrated shuffle block, so reduce tasks fetch it from the new executor.[^pkg] Since Spark 3.4.0, a fetch failure caused by a decommissioned executor does not count toward `spark.stage.maxConsecutiveAttempts`, because `spark.stage.ignoreDecommissionFetchFailure` defaults to true.[^config]

With `spark.decommission.enabled` and dynamic allocation both on, Spark decommissions idle executors instead of killing them.[^config] Shuffle block migration through decommissioning is one of the documented ways to make dynamic allocation safe without an external shuffle service.[^jobsched]

## Which configuration keys control decommissioning?

The main keys are defined in Spark core. Versions are those listed in the Spark 4.3.0 configuration reference and source.[^config][^pkg]

| Key | Default | Since | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `spark.decommission.enabled` | false | 3.1.0 | Turns on graceful decommissioning |
| `spark.storage.decommission.enabled` | false | 3.1.0 | Decommissions the block manager, so blocks are migrated |
| `spark.storage.decommission.shuffleBlocks.enabled` | true | 3.1.0 | Migrates shuffle files; needs a migratable shuffle resolver such as sort-based shuffle |
| `spark.storage.decommission.shuffleBlocks.maxThreads` | 8 | 3.1.0 | Threads used to migrate shuffle files |
| `spark.storage.decommission.rddBlocks.enabled` | true | 3.1.0 | Migrates cached RDD blocks |
| `spark.storage.decommission.fallbackStorage.path` | none | 3.1.0 | Storage path, for example `s3a://spark-storage/`, used when no executor can take the blocks; must end with a path separator |
| `spark.storage.decommission.fallbackStorage.cleanUp` | false | 3.2.0 | Lets Spark delete its fallback storage data |
| `spark.storage.decommission.shuffleBlocks.maxDiskSize` | none | 3.2.0 | Disk space an executor uses for received shuffle blocks before it rejects more |
| `spark.executor.decommission.killInterval` | none | 3.1.0 | Expected time until an outside service kills a decommissioned executor; used to decide which of its tasks to speculate |
| `spark.executor.decommission.forceKillTimeout` | none | 3.2.0 | Time after which Spark forces a decommissioning executor to exit |
| `spark.executor.decommission.signal` | PWR | 3.2.0 | Signal that starts decommissioning in the executor |

The block-migration defaults changed in Spark 3.4. Since then, Spark migrates both cached RDD blocks and shuffle blocks once `spark.decommission.enabled` and `spark.storage.decommission.enabled` are true; setting the `rddBlocks` and `shuffleBlocks` keys to false restores the earlier behaviour.[^migration]

Fallback storage is not cleaned up unless `spark.storage.decommission.fallbackStorage.cleanUp` is true, and the Spark documentation recommends managing the path with a time-to-live policy.[^config][^pkg] A low `forceKillTimeout` can stop migrations before they finish, so the documentation advises a high value.[^config]

## Which cluster managers trigger executor decommissioning?

**Kubernetes.** When `spark.decommission.enabled` is true, Spark adds a `preStop` lifecycle hook to the executor container that runs `spark.kubernetes.decommission.script` (default `/opt/decom.sh`, since Spark 3.2.0).[^k8sfeature][^k8sconfig] The script in the Spark image sends `SIGPWR` to the executor JVM and waits for it to exit, so deleting or evicting the pod starts a graceful decommission.[^n2] Since Spark 3.3.0, `spark.kubernetes.executor.decommissionLabel` and `decommissionLabelValue` label pods that are being decommissioned, for use with pod disruption budgets and pod deletion cost.[^k8s] Shuffle storage options that complement decommissioning on Kubernetes are described in [Spark Kubernetes shuffle storage](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Kubernetes_shuffle_storage).

**Standalone.** With decommissioning enabled, a standalone worker registers a handler for `spark.worker.decommission.signal` (default `PWR`, since 3.2.0) and decommissions itself and its executors when it receives the signal.[^worker][^n3] The Master web UI also has a `/workers/kill` endpoint for decommissioning workers; `spark.master.ui.decommission.allow.mode` (default `LOCAL`, since 3.1.0) controls which hosts may call it.[^n4]

**YARN.** Since Spark 3.4.0, the YARN allocator watches for NodeManagers in the `DECOMMISSIONING` state and asks the driver to decommission the executors on those hosts.[^yarn][^rel340] This works only when the external shuffle service is disabled; with `spark.shuffle.service.enabled` true, Spark logs a warning and skips YARN executor decommissioning (SPARK-39018).[^yarn][^n5]

## Example

Decommissioning on Kubernetes with shuffle migration and an object-storage fallback:

```
spark.decommission.enabled                          true
spark.storage.decommission.enabled                  true
spark.storage.decommission.shuffleBlocks.enabled    true
spark.storage.decommission.rddBlocks.enabled        true
spark.storage.decommission.fallbackStorage.path     s3a://spark-storage/
spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled                     true
```

## What is the history of executor decommissioning?

Holden Karau opened SPARK-20624, "SPIP: Add better handling for node shutdown", in May 2017. It proposed handling preemption that Spark does not choose, such as YARN over-commit and cloud spot or preemptible instances, by moving data off the node or at least not scheduling new tasks there.[^jira20624] The umbrella ticket is still marked In Progress, with some sub-tasks open.[^jira20624]

The core sub-tasks shipped in the Spark 3.1 line: avoiding new tasks on decommissioning nodes (SPARK-20628), shuffle block migration (SPARK-20629), cached block migration (SPARK-20732), decommissioning as part of dynamic scaling (SPARK-31198) and fallback storage (SPARK-33545).[^jira20628][^rel311] The Spark 3.1.1 release notes, published on 2 March 2021, list it as experimental node decommissioning for Kubernetes and standalone.[^rel311][^n6]

Spark 3.4.0 added YARN support (SPARK-30835), stopped rerunning tasks whose shuffle data had already migrated (SPARK-41469) and ignored fetch failures caused by decommissioned executors (SPARK-40481).[^rel340] Spark 4.3.0 added `spark.storage.decommission.shuffleBlocks.bufferRacingMigrations` (default true), which keeps a migration report that reaches the driver before the map output is registered and applies it once registration happens.[^pkg]

# Executor memory overhead

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor_memory_overhead

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">`spark.executor.memoryOverhead`, memory overhead, non-heap memory</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">JVM native memory, Python workers, other processes in the container, container memory limit</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) on YARN and Kubernetes</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark memory management](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_memory_management), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Garbage collection in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Garbage_collection_in_Spark)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/configuration.md, docs/running-on-kubernetes.md, docs/running-on-yarn.md), Hadoop yarn-default.xml (stable docs) and the Kubernetes "Assign Memory Resources to Containers" task page</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), **executor memory overhead** is the memory that Spark requests for each [executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor) container on top of the JVM heap, to cover everything in the container that is not on the heap: JVM internals, native libraries, Python worker processes and other processes. It is set by `spark.executor.memoryOverhead` and applies on YARN and Kubernetes.[^config] When the executor process as a whole uses more memory than its container allows, the cluster manager kills the container, even if the JVM heap still has room.

## How is memory overhead sized?

By default, `spark.executor.memoryOverhead` is `spark.executor.memory` × `spark.executor.memoryOverheadFactor`, with a minimum of `spark.executor.minMemoryOverhead`.[^config]

| Setting | Default | Since |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spark.executor.memoryOverhead` | executor memory × factor, at least the minimum | 2.3.0 |
| `spark.executor.memoryOverheadFactor` | 0.10; 0.40 for non-JVM jobs on Kubernetes | 3.3.0 |
| `spark.executor.minMemoryOverhead` | 384 MiB | 4.0.0 |

<small>Source: Spark 4.3.0 configuration reference.[^config]</small>

The full container size is the sum of `spark.executor.memory`, `spark.executor.memoryOverhead`, `spark.memory.offHeap.size` and `spark.executor.pyspark.memory`.[^config] An executor with `spark.executor.memory=8g` and no other settings gets about 819 MiB of overhead, so a container of about 9 GiB. The higher factor for non-JVM jobs on Kubernetes exists because, in the words of the Spark docs, such tasks "commonly fail with 'Memory Overhead Exceeded' errors".[^config]

## What lives outside the JVM heap?

- **JVM and native overheads.** The Spark docs list VM overheads, interned strings and other native overheads.[^config]
- **Python workers.** In PySpark, Python worker processes run beside the executor JVM in the same container. Their memory is counted in the overhead unless `spark.executor.pyspark.memory` is set, in which case it is a separate, limited amount added to the container request.[^config] Python UDFs and pandas UDFs that load large objects use this memory.
- **Other processes in the container.** Anything else started in the executor's container counts against the overhead.[^config]
- **RAM-backed local directories on Kubernetes.** With `spark.kubernetes.local.dirs.tmpfs=true`, shuffle and spill files live in memory and count toward the pod's memory, so the overhead factor should be raised.[^k8s]

Off-heap memory set with `spark.memory.offHeap.size` is not part of the overhead; it is added to the container separately.[^config] See [Spark memory management](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_memory_management).

## Why do executor containers get killed?

YARN and Kubernetes both enforce the container's memory limit from outside the JVM. The JVM heap cannot grow beyond `spark.executor.memory`, but native and Python memory can, and when the process as a whole goes over the limit the container is terminated.

- **On YARN**, the NodeManager enforces physical memory limits for containers by default (`yarn.nodemanager.pmem-check-enabled`, default true).[^yarndefault]
- **On Kubernetes**, a container that allocates more memory than its limit becomes a candidate for termination; the pod status then shows `OOMKilled` and exit code 137.[^k8smem] The Spark Kubernetes docs also describe exit code 137 as a SIGKILL, possibly a container OOM, and exit code 52 as a JVM out-of-memory error.[^k8s]

A container kill and a JVM `OutOfMemoryError` are different failures. A JVM heap OOM means the heap was too small for the task; the fix is more `spark.executor.memory`, more partitions, or less data per task. A container kill with a healthy heap means the non-heap side was too small; the fix is more overhead, setting `spark.executor.pyspark.memory`, or reducing native or Python memory use. On YARN, Spark 4.3.0 adds `-XX:OnOutOfMemoryError='kill %p'` to executor JVM options by default (`spark.yarn.executor.oomKill.enabled`), so a heap OOM also ends the executor process.[^yarn]

Spark 4.3.0 on Kubernetes can also react to these failures with `org.apache.spark.scheduler.cluster.k8s.ExecutorResizePlugin`, which is enabled by registering it in `spark.plugins`. Every `spark.kubernetes.executor.resizeInterval`, the driver reads each executor container's memory usage, and when usage exceeds `spark.kubernetes.executor.resizeThreshold` of the current limit it raises the memory request and limit in place by `spark.kubernetes.executor.resizeFactor`, with no configured upper bound. It requires Kubernetes 1.33 or later (in-place pod resize through the `pods/resize` subresource), a metrics server or other provider of the `metrics.k8s.io` API, and a driver service account allowed to list pods, get pods in the `metrics.k8s.io` API group and patch `pods/resize`. The heap size does not change, so the extra memory goes to off-heap and native use, and Kubernetes may reject or defer a resize when the node lacks free memory.[^k8sresize]

```
spark.plugins                              org.apache.spark.scheduler.cluster.k8s.ExecutorResizePlugin
spark.kubernetes.executor.resizeInterval   1m
```

## Example

A PySpark job whose Python UDFs need about 2 GiB per executor:

```
spark.executor.memory            8g
spark.executor.memoryOverhead    1g
spark.executor.pyspark.memory    2g
```

Each executor container is then 11 GiB: 8 GiB heap, 1 GiB overhead and 2 GiB reserved for Python.[^config]

# External shuffle service

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/External_shuffle_service

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">ESS, Spark shuffle service, `spark_shuffle` (YARN auxiliary service name)</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 1.2</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Long-running per-node process, shuffle file server, state store (RocksDB by default)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) standalone workers and YARN NodeManagers; not supported on Kubernetes</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Dynamic allocation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dynamic_allocation), [Push-based shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Push-based_shuffle), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/job-scheduling.md, docs/configuration.md, docs/running-on-yarn.md, docs/spark-standalone.md), the Apache Celeborn and Apache Uniffle project sites</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), the **external shuffle service** (ESS) is a long-running process on each node of a cluster that serves the [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle) files written by [executors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), so those files stay available after the executor that wrote them has been removed or has failed. It runs independently of Spark applications and their executors, and was introduced in Spark 1.2.[^jobsched] It is enabled with `spark.shuffle.service.enabled` (default false) and listens on port 7337 by default (`spark.shuffle.service.port`).[^config]

## Why does the external shuffle service exist?

In a shuffle, each executor writes its map output to local disk and then acts as the server for those files when other executors fetch them. If the executor goes away before the next stage has read the files, the map tasks that produced them have to run again.[^jobsched]

This matters most with [dynamic allocation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dynamic_allocation), which removes idle executors while the application is still running; a straggler can keep a shuffle open after the executors that wrote it are idle.[^jobsched] With the ESS enabled, executors fetch shuffle files from the service instead of from each other, so shuffle output can still be served after the executor's lifetime. The service also lets shuffle fetches continue if an executor fails.[^jobsched][^config]

The ESS can also serve RDD blocks persisted on disk, when `spark.shuffle.service.fetch.rdd.enabled` is true (default false). With dynamic allocation, executors that hold only disk-persisted blocks are then treated as idle and can be released.[^config]

## Where does the external shuffle service run?

| Cluster manager | Where the ESS runs | How to enable it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Standalone | Inside each Spark worker | Start the workers with `spark.shuffle.service.enabled=true`[^jobsched] |
| YARN | As a YARN auxiliary service inside each NodeManager, class `org.apache.spark.network.yarn.YarnShuffleService` | Add `spark_shuffle` to `yarn.nodemanager.aux-services` in `yarn-site.xml`, put `spark-<version>-yarn-shuffle.jar` on the NodeManager classpath, raise the NodeManager heap (`YARN_HEAPSIZE`, 1000 by default) and restart the NodeManagers[^yarn] |
| Kubernetes | Not supported | Use an alternative (below)[^jobsched] |

On YARN, a cluster can run more than one version of the shuffle service at once in isolated classloaders, on YARN 2.9.0 or later, because the shuffle service is not always compatible with other Spark versions.[^yarn] On both standalone and YARN, the service can store its state on local disk so that it survives a restart of the service; the state store uses RocksDB by default, and LevelDB is deprecated.[^yarn][^standalone]

```xml
<!-- yarn-site.xml on every NodeManager -->
<property>
  <name>yarn.nodemanager.aux-services</name>
  <value>mapreduce_shuffle,spark_shuffle</value>
</property>
<property>
  <name>yarn.nodemanager.aux-services.spark_shuffle.class</name>
  <value>org.apache.spark.network.yarn.YarnShuffleService</value>
</property>
```

The application then sets `spark.shuffle.service.enabled=true`.[^config]

## What are the alternatives on Kubernetes?

Spark on Kubernetes does not support the external shuffle service.[^jobsched] Spark itself offers three other ways to keep shuffle data when executors are removed:[^jobsched][^config]

- **Shuffle tracking** (`spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled`, default true): Spark keeps alive the executors that store shuffle data for active jobs.
- **Decommissioning with shuffle block migration** (`spark.decommission.enabled` and `spark.storage.decommission.shuffleBlocks.enabled`): an executor copies its shuffle blocks to other executors before it is removed, optionally to a fallback storage path such as an S3 bucket.
- **A shuffle storage plugin** (`spark.shuffle.sort.io.plugin.class`, experimental): a custom `ShuffleDataIO` stores shuffle data in reliable storage.

Separate open source **remote shuffle services** take the shuffle data out of executors altogether. [Apache Celeborn](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Celeborn) describes itself as an intermediate data service for compute engines, for shuffle and spilled data, with Spark integration and a Kubernetes deployment guide.[^celeborn] Apache Uniffle is a remote shuffle service that lets Spark applications store shuffle data on remote shuffle servers, with a Kubernetes operator.[^uniffle]

|  | External shuffle service | Shuffle tracking | Decommission migration | Remote shuffle service |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Extra process | One per node | None | None | Separate cluster |
| Kubernetes | Not supported | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Executors can be released while their shuffle is in use | Yes | No (unless `shuffleTracking.timeout` is set)[^config] | Yes, after migration | Yes |

# foreachBatch

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/ForeachBatch

<Infobox type="concept" name="foreachBatch">
  <Field name="also_known_as">`DataStreamWriter.foreachBatch`</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 2.4.0</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">User function called once per micro-batch with the batch DataFrame and the batch id</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (Scala, Java, Python; Spark Connect since 3.5.0)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Output mode](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Output_mode), [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Streaming checkpoint](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_checkpoint)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming programming guide (Using Foreach and ForeachBatch) and Real-time Mode guide, `python/pyspark/sql/streaming/readwriter.py` at tag v4.3.0 of apache/spark, SPARK-24565, the Delta Lake table streaming and merge documentation, and the Databricks foreachBatch page</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), **foreachBatch** is a sink that calls a user function once for every micro-batch, passing the batch's output as an ordinary DataFrame together with a unique batch id, so that any batch API can be used to write it. It is the standard way to write a stream to a system that has a batch writer but no streaming sink, to write one batch to several places, and to apply row-level upserts, such as a [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) `MERGE`, from a streaming query. foreachBatch was added in Spark 2.4.0 and is available in Scala, Java and Python.[^ss-fb][^jira]

## How does foreachBatch work?

The function takes two arguments: a DataFrame with the micro-batch's output, and the batch id.[^ss-fb] Inside it, the DataFrame is a batch DataFrame, so every batch operation and writer works, including operations that streaming DataFrames do not support.[^ss-fb]

```python
def write_batch(batch_df, batch_id):
    batch_df.write.format("jdbc").options(**jdbc_options).mode("append").save()

(stream_df.writeStream
    .foreachBatch(write_batch)
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/checkpoints/to_jdbc")
    .start())
```

foreachBatch works only in micro-batch execution. It does not work with the continuous trigger, where `foreach` is the alternative, and it is not supported in Real-time Mode, which processes records one at a time.[^ss-fb][^rtm] The `foreach` sink, also available since Spark 2.4 in Python, calls user code per row through `open`, `process` and `close` methods.[^ss-fb]

foreachBatch has supported Spark Connect since Spark 3.5.0. In Spark Connect mode it behaves differently: the function does not have access to variables defined outside it.[^rw]

## Is foreachBatch exactly-once?

By default, foreachBatch gives only at-least-once write guarantees. If a query fails after the function has written a batch but before the batch is recorded in the commit log, the batch runs again after restart. The batch id makes exactly-once possible: the function can use it to detect and skip a batch that was already written.[^ss-fb] For the same batch id, the output DataFrame is guaranteed to be the same, provided every operation in the query is deterministic.[^rw] See [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics) and [Streaming checkpoint](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_checkpoint).

### Idempotent writes to Delta Lake

Delta Lake supports this directly. The writer options `txnAppId` (any unique string, such as the query id) and `txnVersion` (a monotonically increasing number, such as the batch id) identify a write, and Delta ignores a write whose combination it has already committed.[^delta-stream]

```python
app_id = "orders_to_two_tables"

def write_twice(batch_df, batch_id):
    batch_df.persist()
    (batch_df.write.format("delta").mode("append")
        .option("txnAppId", app_id).option("txnVersion", batch_id)
        .saveAsTable("main.sales.orders"))
    (batch_df.filter("amount > 1000").write.format("delta").mode("append")
        .option("txnAppId", app_id).option("txnVersion", batch_id)
        .saveAsTable("main.sales.large_orders"))
    batch_df.unpersist()
```

If the checkpoint is deleted and the query restarts with a new one, batch ids start again from 0, so the query must use a different `txnAppId`; otherwise Delta ignores its writes as duplicates.[^delta-stream]

## How are upserts written from a stream?

Streaming sinks for table formats append rows or replace the table; the Delta Lake and [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) Spark sinks support append and complete [output modes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Output_mode).[^delta-stream][^iceberg] To update existing rows, the query runs a `MERGE` inside foreachBatch. The Delta Lake documentation uses this pattern to write streaming aggregates in update mode, which it describes as much more efficient than complete mode, to apply a stream of change data, and to deduplicate with an insert-only merge.[^delta-merge]

```python
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

target = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "main.sales.customer_totals")

def upsert(batch_df, batch_id):
    (target.alias("t")
        .merge(batch_df.alias("s"), "s.customer_id = t.customer_id")
        .whenMatchedUpdateAll()
        .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
        .execute())

(totals_stream.writeStream
    .foreachBatch(upsert)
    .outputMode("update")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/checkpoints/customer_totals")
    .start())
```

The Delta documentation warns that the merge must be idempotent, because a restart can apply the same batch more than once. Because merge reads its input more than once, the reported input rate can be a multiple of the real one, and caching the batch before the merge avoids the extra reads.[^delta-merge] Databricks states that foreachBatch is required for Delta Lake merge operations in Structured Streaming.[^db-fb]

## Common pitfalls

- **Recomputation.** Each action on the batch DataFrame can recompute the batch, including re-reading the source. Writing to several places should be wrapped in `persist()` and `unpersist()`.[^ss-fb]
- **State reloads.** In a stateful query, several actions on the same batch DataFrame, such as `count()` then `collect()`, evaluate the query several times and reload state each time; the Spark guide recommends persisting the DataFrame inside the function.[^ss-fb]
- **Empty batches.** The function can receive an empty DataFrame, and code that assumes rows can fail. Databricks gives examples where a Delta source produces an empty micro-batch, such as an `OPTIMIZE` with no files to process.[^db-fb]
- **End-to-end semantics.** Operations applied inside foreachBatch are outside Spark's incremental planning, so the user has to reason about their correctness across batches and retries.[^ss-fb]

# Garbage collection in Spark

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Garbage_collection_in_Spark

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">JVM GC in Spark, GC pressure</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">JVM heap generations, GC time metric, G1GC (the JVM default on server configurations since JDK 9), GC tuning flags</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) on the Java Virtual Machine</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark memory management](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_memory_management), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Caching and persistence](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Caching_and_persistence), [Spill (memory)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spill_(memory)), [Executor memory overhead](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor_memory_overhead)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/tuning.md, docs/web-ui.md, docs/monitoring.md, docs/configuration.md, core/src/main/resources/org/apache/spark/ui/static/executorspage.js), the Spark 4.3.0 overview page and OpenJDK JEP 248</Verified>

**Garbage collection in Spark** is the work the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) does inside each [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) [executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor) and driver to find objects that are no longer used and free their memory. Spark runs on the JVM, so every task's objects live on the heap and are cleaned up by the JVM garbage collector (GC). When the heap is under pressure, the GC runs often or for long pauses, and tasks slow down even though they do no extra useful work.[^tuning]

## What does the GC time column in the Spark UI mean?

The Spark UI reports **GC time** in two places.

- **Stage page.** In the task summary and the task table, GC time is the total time the JVM spent in garbage collection while that task ran.[^webui] The REST API exposes it as `jvmGCTime`, in milliseconds.[^monitoring]
- **Executors tab.** The "Task Time (GC Time)" column shows total task time and GC time per executor.[^webui][^exectpl] The UI shades the cell red when GC time is more than 10% of total task time.[^execjs]

GC time is measured per JVM, and several tasks run in one executor JVM at once. A long collection pauses all of them, so tasks that ran at the same time on one executor often show similar GC time. Executor-level metrics also split GC into minor and major collections (`MinorGCCount`, `MinorGCTime`, `MajorGCCount`, `MajorGCTime`).[^monitoring]

## Symptoms of GC pressure

- GC time is a large share of task time, and the Executors tab shows red cells.[^execjs]
- The Spark docs single out full GCs: if a full GC runs several times before a task completes, there is not enough memory for executing tasks.[^tuning]
- Very long pauses can delay the heartbeats that tell the driver an executor is alive. Executors send one every `spark.executor.heartbeatInterval` (default 10s), and `spark.network.timeout` (default 120s) is the default for the block manager heartbeat timeout.[^config]
- The executor fails with `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded` or a heap OOM. This is different from a container kill; see [Executor memory overhead](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor_memory_overhead).

## What causes GC pressure?

The Spark docs give two main causes. First, the cost of garbage collection is proportional to the number of Java objects, so data structures with many small objects (a `LinkedList` instead of an array of primitives, boxed values, nested collections) cost more. Second, a task's working memory competes with the data cached on the same executor.[^tuning] Large deserialized caches, [skewed](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_skew) tasks that hold a lot of data at once, and user code that collects large collections in memory all add to the live heap.

DataFrame and SQL operations put less load on the GC than RDDs of Java or Python objects, because Spark SQL keeps rows in a compact binary format and allocates its own memory pages for sorting, hashing and shuffle. See [Project Tungsten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Tungsten).[^tmm]

## How to reduce GC time

The Spark tuning guide recommends these steps, in this order of effort:[^tuning]

1. **Use serialized caching.** Persisting in serialized form leaves one byte array per partition instead of many objects; the docs call this the first thing to try. (In PySpark, cached RDD data is always serialized.)[^rddguide]
1. **Cache less.** If the old generation is close to full, lower `spark.memory.fraction`; it is better to cache fewer objects than to slow down task execution.
1. **Size the young generation.** If there are many minor collections but few major ones, give Eden more memory.
1. **Use G1GC settings for large heaps.** The JVM that the deployment runs Spark on sets the default collector. Spark 4.3.0 runs on Java 17, 21 or 25,[^overview] and G1 has been the default collector on server configurations since JDK 9.[^jep248] With large executor heaps, raising `-XX:G1HeapRegionSize` can help.[^tuning]

GC flags for executors go in `spark.executor.defaultJavaOptions` or `spark.executor.extraJavaOptions`. The heap size itself cannot be set there; it comes from `spark.executor.memory`.[^tuning][^config]

```
spark.executor.memory              16g
spark.executor.extraJavaOptions    -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=32m -Xlog:gc*:file=/tmp/gc-{{EXECUTOR_ID}}.log
```

Spark replaces `{{APP_ID}}` and `{{EXECUTOR_ID}}` in `spark.executor.extraJavaOptions` with the application and executor IDs, which gives each executor its own GC log.[^config]

# GPU acceleration in Spark

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GPU_acceleration_in_Spark

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">GPU-accelerated Spark, Spark on GPUs</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 3.0 (accelerator-aware scheduling)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">GPU resource scheduling, SQL plugins, GPU machine learning libraries</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark (formerly RAPIDS Accelerator), [Apache Gluten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Gluten), cuML Spark</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark resource profiles](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_resource_profiles), [Native execution engine (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Native_execution_engine_(Spark)), [Velox](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Velox)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/configuration.md, python/pyspark/ml/torch/distributor.py), the NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark download, configuration, supported operators, FAQ and getting-started pages and its v26.10.0 GitHub release, the apache/gluten README and VeloxGPU.md on the main branch, and the NVIDIA/cuml-spark repository</Verified>

**GPU acceleration in Spark** is the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to run parts of an [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) application, either by scheduling GPUs to tasks that use them directly (for example deep learning training) or by replacing Spark SQL operators with GPU implementations. Apache Spark itself provides the first part: since Spark 3.0, its scheduler can request GPUs for executors and assign GPU addresses to tasks.[^r300][^conf] Running Spark SQL and DataFrame operators on a GPU needs a plugin such as the NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark, formerly called the RAPIDS Accelerator for Apache Spark.[^dl]

## Comparison of GPU options for Spark

|  | Apache Spark GPU scheduling | NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark | Apache Gluten with Velox cuDF | cuML Spark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What runs on the GPU | User code that reads the GPU addresses Spark assigns (RDD functions, pandas UDFs, ML training)[^conf] | Supported Spark SQL and DataFrame operators, file scans and writes[^overview] | Velox plan nodes converted to cuDF operators[^glutengpu] | PySpark ML algorithms backed by the cuML library[^cumlspark] |
| How it is enabled | `spark.executor.resource.gpu.amount`, `spark.task.resource.gpu.amount`, a discovery script, or a [resource profile](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_resource_profiles)[^conf] | `spark.plugins=com.nvidia.spark.SQLPlugin` plus the `rapids-4-spark` jar[^onprem][^dl] | `spark.gluten.sql.columnar.cudf=true` in a GPU build of Gluten[^glutengpu] | Change the import, for example `spark_rapids_ml.feature.PCA` in place of `pyspark.ml.feature.PCA`[^cumlspark] |
| Unsupported work | Not applicable; Spark does not use the GPU itself[^conf] | Falls back to the Spark CPU implementation; RDD operations are not accelerated[^overview] | Falls back to CPU operators, with row and columnar conversion[^glutengpu] | Algorithms not in its list are not provided[^cumlspark] |
| Status | Part of Apache Spark since 3.0.0[^r300] | Release v26.10.0, published 2026-11-05[^rel] | Experimental; documented on the main branch, not in the v1.7.0 release[^glutengpu] | Release v26.06.0, published 2026-07-22[^cumlrel] |
| Spark versions | 3.0.0 and later[^r300] | 3.3.0 to 4.2.0 in release v26.10.0; 4.3.0 is not listed[^dl] | Same as Gluten on CPU[^glutengpu] | Not stated in the README |
| License | Apache License 2.0[^sparklic] | Source code Apache 2.0; documentation CC BY 4.0[^lic] | Apache License 2.0[^glutenreadme] | Apache License 2.0[^cumlspark] |

## How does Apache Spark schedule GPUs?

Apache Spark schedules GPUs as a custom resource named `gpu`. An application sets `spark.executor.resource.gpu.amount` (default 0) for GPUs per executor and `spark.task.resource.gpu.amount` for GPUs per task; fractional task amounts let several tasks share one GPU. On YARN and Kubernetes, the executor also needs `spark.executor.resource.gpu.discoveryScript`, and Kubernetes needs `spark.executor.resource.gpu.vendor`, for example `nvidia.com`.[^conf] Spark then assigns GPU addresses to each task, which user code reads with `TaskContext.get().resources()`.[^conf] Since Spark 3.1, [Spark resource profiles](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_resource_profiles) let one stage request GPU executors while other stages use CPU-only executors.[^conf]

Spark's own GPU support is used by machine learning code inside Spark. `pyspark.ml.torch.distributor.TorchDistributor`, added in Spark 3.4.0, runs distributed PyTorch training on Spark; with `use_gpu=True` (the default) on a cluster it requires `spark.task.resource.gpu.amount` of at least 1.[^torch]

## What is the NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark?

The NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark is a set of Spark plugins, built on the cuDF library and UCX, that run DataFrame and SQL processing on NVIDIA GPUs. NVIDIA renamed it from the RAPIDS Accelerator for Apache Spark; the GitHub repository moved from `NVIDIA/spark-rapids` to `NVIDIA/cudf-spark`, and the artifact name `rapids-4-spark` stays the same for now.[^dl][^readme] The plugin hooks into Spark at the Catalyst level, after the language APIs have been converted to a DataFrame plan, so it applies to PySpark, Scala, Java and SQL alike.[^faq]

The cuDF plugin is turned on with `spark.plugins=com.nvidia.spark.SQLPlugin`. NVIDIA's on-premise example combines it with Spark's own GPU settings, `spark.executor.resource.gpu.amount=1` and `spark.task.resource.gpu.amount=0.25`.[^onprem] The getting-started guide asks for Apache Spark 3.3 or later and one GPU per executor.[^overview]

```bash
spark-submit \
  --jars rapids-4-spark_2.13-26.10.0.jar \
  --conf spark.plugins=com.nvidia.spark.SQLPlugin \
  --conf spark.executor.resource.gpu.amount=1 \
  --conf spark.task.resource.gpu.amount=0.25 \
  --conf spark.rapids.sql.explain=NOT_ON_GPU \
  app.py
```

### Which operators and formats run on the GPU?

The cuDF plugin replaces physical operators such as `FileSourceScanExec`, `FilterExec`, `ProjectExec`, `HashAggregateExec`, `SortExec`, `WindowExec`, `ShuffleExchangeExec`, `BroadcastHashJoinExec`, `ShuffledHashJoinExec` and `SortMergeJoinExec`, and pandas UDF operators such as `MapInPandasExec`.[^ops] Its supported-operators page lists GPU reads for Avro, CSV, [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), Hive text, [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), JSON, ORC and [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), and GPU writes for Delta Lake, Hive text, Iceberg, ORC and Parquet. Timestamps are supported only in the UTC time zone.[^ops]

The cuDF plugin's FAQ states that only a limited set of SQL and DataFrame operations is supported; some MLlib functions such as PCA are accelerated, while GraphX and RDD code are not. Dataset operations that take Scala or Java functions, such as `flatMap` or `foreachPartition`, still run correctly but mostly on the CPU.[^faq]

### What happens when an operator is not supported?

When the cuDF plugin cannot run an operation on the GPU, that part of the plan runs on the Spark CPU implementation, so the query still completes.[^overview] The plugin decides this with rules, not the Spark scheduler.[^faq] `spark.rapids.sql.enabled` (default true) turns GPU SQL on or off, and `spark.rapids.sql.explain` logs the parts of a plan that were not placed on the GPU, for example with the value `NOT_ON_GPU`.[^configs]

## What other GPU options exist for Spark?

[Apache Gluten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Gluten), a project that offloads Spark SQL execution to native engines such as [Velox](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Velox), documents an experimental GPU path on its main branch: with `spark.gluten.sql.columnar.cudf=true`, Velox plan nodes are converted to GPU operators built on cuDF, and unsupported operators fall back to the CPU.[^glutengpu] See [Native execution engine (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Native_execution_engine_(Spark)) for CPU-based native engines.

cuML Spark (repository `NVIDIA/cuml-spark`) provides PySpark ML compatible algorithms on GPUs, including KMeans, LinearRegression, LogisticRegression, PCA, RandomForestClassifier and UMAP.[^cumlspark]

# GraphFrames

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphFrames

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">GraphFrames community (originally UC Berkeley, MIT and Databricks)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2016</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">0.12.3</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-05</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala, Python</Field>
  <Field name="type">Graph processing library for Apache Spark (DataFrame-based)</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[graphframes.io](https://graphframes.io)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/graphframes/graphframes](https://github.com/graphframes/graphframes)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[GraphX](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphX), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the graphframes/graphframes repository at tag v0.12.3, the GitHub releases API (latest release v0.12.3) and graphframes.io</Verified>

<Status level="active">Latest release 0.12.3, published 5 October 2026.[^rel]</Status>

**GraphFrames** is an open source graph processing package for [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) that represents a graph as a pair of Spark DataFrames, one of vertices and one of edges, and provides graph algorithms, the Pregel and AggregateMessages APIs, and a motif-finding query language on top of them.[^readme] It has APIs in Scala, Java and Python, and it is developed outside the Apache Spark project. When the Spark community voted in 2024 to deprecate Spark's RDD-based [GraphX](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphX) library, the vote result named GraphFrames as a migration target.[^vote]

## Data model

A GraphFrame is built from two DataFrames. The vertex DataFrame must have a column named `id` with a unique ID for each vertex. The edge DataFrame must have columns named `src` and `dst` with the source and destination vertex IDs. Both can have any other columns, which act as vertex and edge attributes. A GraphFrame can also be built from an edge DataFrame alone, in which case the vertices are inferred from the edges.[^create]

Because a GraphFrame is made of DataFrames, graph queries are planned by Spark's Catalyst optimizer and Adaptive Query Execution, and graph results can be joined, filtered and written like any other DataFrame.[^about]

## Relation to GraphX

<Hatnote>Main article: [GraphX](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphX)</Hatnote>

The GraphFrames documentation describes the project as aiming to provide the functionality of GraphX plus features that take advantage of DataFrames, such as motif finding and DataFrame-based serialization.[^about] The two libraries differ in representation and optimization:[^about]

|  | GraphX | GraphFrames |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Graph representation | `VertexRDD` and `EdgeRDD` | `vertices` and `edges` DataFrames |
| Optimization | Its own partitioning strategy and partition index | Catalyst optimizer and Adaptive Query Execution |
| Languages | Scala (Spark guide) | Scala, Java, Python |
| Part of Apache Spark | Yes | No (separate project) |

GraphFrames provides most algorithms either as a native DataFrame implementation or as a wrapper over GraphX. Its own benchmarks show GraphX can still be the better choice for small and medium graphs, so the library keeps conversion methods between the two.[^about] Since release 0.10.0, GraphFrames ships its own internal fork of GraphX (package `org.apache.spark.graphframes.graphx`, Maven artifact `graphframes-graphx`) instead of using the GraphX in Spark. The project treats the fork as internal API.[^about][^install][^quick]

The GraphFrames documentation states that GraphX is deprecated upstream and no longer maintained. Apache Spark itself had not marked GraphX deprecated as of Spark 4.3.0; see [GraphX#Status](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphX#status).[^about]

## Motif finding

Motif finding searches a graph for structural patterns. GraphFrames expresses patterns in a small domain-specific language passed to `find`: `(a)-[e]->(b)` is an edge `e` from vertex `a` to vertex `b`, and patterns are joined with semicolons. The result is a DataFrame with one struct column per named vertex or edge.[^motif]

The language supports anonymous elements (`(a)-[]->(b)`), negated edges (`!(b)-[]->(a)`), undirected patterns (`(a)-[e]-(b)`), fixed-length paths (`(a)-[e*2]->(c)`) and bounded variable-length paths (`(a)-[e*1..3]->(c)`). Unbounded paths are not supported. Conditions on vertex or edge attributes are applied as DataFrame filters on the result. Motif finding is translated into a series of joins, and the documentation suggests enabling Spark's cost-based optimizer and join reordering to improve it.[^motif]

## Algorithms

The user guide covers centrality metrics, traversals and connectivity, community detection, subgraphs, message passing, Pregel, labeled property graphs and graph machine learning.[^readme] Algorithms listed in the documentation include:[^quick][^readme]
- Traversal and connectivity: breadth-first search, shortest paths, all simple paths, connected components and strongly connected components.
- Ranking and structure: PageRank, parallel personalized PageRank, triangle count, K-Core, cycle detection (Rocha-Thatte) and maximal independent set.
- Community detection: label propagation and power iteration clustering.
- Embeddings: random-walk embeddings with Word2Vec or Hash2Vec.

The quick start marks which algorithms have a native GraphFrames implementation. PageRank, parallel personalized PageRank, strongly connected components and SVD++ run through GraphX in that table.[^quick]

## Example

The following PySpark example builds a small graph, prints in-degrees and uses motif finding to find pairs where one vertex calls the other a friend and is called an enemy back. It follows the project README and runs on Spark 4.x after `pip install graphframes-py==0.12.3` and starting PySpark with `--packages io.graphframes:graphframes-spark4_2.13:0.12.3`.[^readme][^install]

```python
from graphframes import GraphFrame

v = spark.createDataFrame([(1, "Alice"), (2, "Bob"), (3, "Charlie")], ["id", "name"])
e = spark.createDataFrame(
    [(1, 2, "friend"), (2, 1, "friend"), (2, 3, "friend"), (3, 2, "enemy")],
    ["src", "dst", "relationship"],
)
g = GraphFrame(v, e)

g.inDegrees.show()

(g.find("(a)-[e]->(b); (b)-[e2]->(a)")
  .filter("e.relationship = 'friend' AND e2.relationship = 'enemy'")
  .show())
```

## Spark Connect

GraphFrames supports [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) through a server plugin. The Spark Connect server is started with the `graphframes-connect` package and the setting `spark.connect.extensions.relation.classes=org.apache.spark.sql.graphframes.GraphFramesConnect`. The only client bundled with the package is the PySpark client, which detects a Spark Connect session and uses the plugin automatically. The documentation warns that the plugin is not compatible with Databricks' managed Spark Connect without a vendor-specific build.[^install] Spark Connect and Spark 4.x support were first released in GraphFrames 0.9.0.[^n1]

## Releases and governance

GraphFrames is published to Maven Central under the `io.graphframes` namespace, with separate artifacts per Spark major version and Scala version (for example `graphframes-spark4_2.13`), and to PyPI as `graphframes-py`. The installation page lists support for Spark 3.x and 4.x.[^install] The latest release, v0.12.3 of 5 October 2026, fixes connected-components correctness issues.[^rel]

The project was created as a collaboration among UC Berkeley, MIT, Databricks and the open source community, and is now maintained by a group of individual contributors. It is licensed under the Apache License 2.0 and is not an Apache Software Foundation project.[^readme] The project's blog post for release 0.9.2 describes a revival in 2025, after a long gap in development, prompted by the GraphX deprecation discussion in Spark; the same post announced the new Maven group ID, the new PyPI name and the graphframes.io site.[^n2] The design is described in the 2016 paper "GraphFrames: An Integrated API for Mixing Graph and Relational Queries" by Dave et al.[^n3]

# GraphX

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphX

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) project)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">Spark 0.9.0 (alpha); stable API since Spark 1.2.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">Spark 4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala</Field>
  <Field name="type">Graph processing library (RDD-based)</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[GraphX Programming Guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/graphx-programming-guide.html)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark (graphx/)](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/v4.3.0/graphx)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[GraphFrames](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphFrames), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (GraphX source and programming guide), the Spark 0.9.0, 1.2.0 and 4.0.0 to 4.3.0 release notes, SPARK-50857 and the October 2024 dev-list vote</Verified>

<Status level="proposed">A dev-list vote to deprecate GraphX passed in October 2024, but the deprecation ticket (SPARK-50857) is still open and Spark 4.3.0 carries no deprecation annotation or notice for GraphX. The vote result described GraphX as not currently maintained and suggested [GraphFrames](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphFrames) as a migration target.[^jira50857]</Status>

**GraphX** is the graph processing library of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark): it extends Spark's resilient distributed dataset (RDD) with a property graph, a directed multigraph with user-defined properties on each vertex and edge, and provides graph operators, a Pregel API and a library of graph algorithms.[^guide] GraphX still ships with Spark 4.3.0, but a 2024 proposal on the Spark dev mailing list noted no meaningful active development in the preceding three years.[^discuss] The Spark community then voted to deprecate it, and as of Spark 4.3.0 that decision has not been applied to the code or documentation.[^vote][^jira50857]

## Status

Whether GraphX is deprecated depends on which source is read, and the sources do not agree.

- **Spark code and documentation (4.3.0):** The `graphx` module at the v4.3.0 tag has no `@deprecated` annotations on its public API, and the GraphX programming guide has no deprecation notice.[^guide] The Spark 4.0.0 to 4.3.0 release notes list no GraphX deprecation; the 4.0.0 notes deprecate SparkR and other APIs, but not GraphX.[^r400]
- **Spark dev mailing list:** In September 2024 a thread on the Spark dev mailing list proposed deprecating GraphX before the 4.0 branch was cut, noting no meaningful active development for over three years.[^discuss] The vote that followed closed on 7 October 2024 and was declared passed, with two -1 votes. The result email proposed a documentation note saying that GraphX "is not currently maintained and if maintainers are not found may be removed in future minor versions", and recommended GraphFrames or openCypher on Spark as migration targets.[^vote]
- **JIRA:** SPARK-50857, "Mark GraphX as deprecated", was opened in January 2025 with a link to the vote. It is unresolved and has no fix version.[^jira50857]
- **GraphFrames documentation:** The GraphFrames project states that GraphX "is deprecated in the upstream Apache Spark and is not maintained anymore", and its quick start says GraphX was deprecated in Spark 4.0.x.[^gfabout][^gfquick] The GraphFrames blog links its statement that GraphX was deprecated to the dev-list discussion thread.[^n1] No Spark 4.x release includes a GraphX deprecation.

In short: the Spark community voted to deprecate GraphX and the vote result described it as unmaintained, but no Spark release up to 4.3.0 marks it deprecated. The GraphX module and its API are still part of Spark 4.3.0. Both the vote result and the GraphFrames project point new graph work to [GraphFrames](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphFrames).

## History

GraphX first shipped as an alpha component in Spark 0.9.0, where the release notes recommended it over the older Bagel API.[^n2] In Spark 1.2.0 GraphX graduated from alpha and gained a stable API, with a guarantee that applications written against it would keep working in future Spark versions without code changes. The same release introduced the `aggregateMessages` API and deprecated `mapReduceTriplets`.[^n3]

## Programming model

A GraphX graph is a pair of distributed collections: a `VertexRDD` of vertex IDs and properties and an `EdgeRDD` of edges with properties. Like RDDs, graphs are immutable, distributed and fault tolerant; operators return new graphs.[^guide]

The guide groups the API into:[^guide]
- **Property and structural operators**, such as `mapVertices`, `reverse`, `subgraph` and `mask`.
- **Join operators**, such as `joinVertices` and `outerJoinVertices`, that bring RDD data into a graph.
- **Neighborhood aggregation** through `aggregateMessages`, which sends messages along edges and merges them at each vertex.
- **Pregel**, a bulk-synchronous, vertex-centric API for iterative algorithms. The guide recommends it for iterative computation because it unpersists intermediate results correctly.
- **Graph builders**, such as `GraphLoader.edgeListFile`, `Graph.apply` and `Graph.fromEdges`.

The algorithm library at the v4.3.0 tag contains PageRank, connected components, strongly connected components, label propagation, shortest paths, triangle count and SVD++.[^n4]

The following Scala example runs in the Spark 4.3 shell in classic mode, where `sc` is the `SparkContext`. It builds a three-vertex graph and runs dynamic PageRank until the ranks change by less than the tolerance.

```scala
import org.apache.spark.graphx.{Edge, Graph}

val users = sc.parallelize(Seq((1L, "alice"), (2L, "bob"), (3L, "carol")))
val follows = sc.parallelize(Seq(
  Edge(1L, 2L, "follows"), Edge(2L, 3L, "follows"), Edge(3L, 1L, "follows")))

val graph = Graph(users, follows)
val ranks = graph.pageRank(0.0001).vertices

ranks.join(users).collect().foreach { case (_, (rank, name)) =>
  println(f"$name%s: $rank%.3f")
}
```

## Limitations

GraphX is built on RDDs and the `SparkContext`.[^guide] The Spark Connect documentation lists `SparkContext` and RDD as unsupported in Spark Connect for both Python and Scala, so GraphX programs need a classic Spark application rather than a [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) client.[^n5] Because GraphX works on RDDs, it does not use the Catalyst optimizer that plans DataFrame queries; the GraphFrames project cites this, and the memory cost of serializing JVM objects in RDDs, as reasons for its DataFrame-based design.[^gfabout]

## Alternatives

<Hatnote>Main article: [GraphFrames](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphFrames)</Hatnote>

[GraphFrames](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphFrames) is a separate open source package that represents a graph as two Spark DataFrames (vertices and edges). It adds motif finding and runs through the DataFrame engine. It provides conversion to and from GraphX, and from version 0.10.0 it ships its own internal fork of GraphX for the algorithms that it does not yet implement natively.[^gfquick] The October 2024 vote result also named openCypher on Spark as a possible target.[^vote]
