# Higher-order functions (Spark SQL)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Higher-order_functions_(Spark_SQL)

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Lambda functions, HOFs</Field>
  <Field name="field">Query languages, nested data processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 2.4.0 (SQL); 3.1.0 (PySpark functions)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Lambda expressions (`x -> expr`), array functions (`transform`, `filter`, `aggregate`, `exists`, `forall`, `zip_with`), map functions (`transform_keys`, `transform_values`, `map_filter`, `map_zip_with`)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark SQL](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_SQL), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Parameterized queries (Spark SQL)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Parameterized_queries_(Spark_SQL))</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (higherOrderFunctions.scala, FunctionRegistry.scala, python/pyspark/sql/functions/builtin.py, error-conditions.json, the PySpark Arrow guide) and the Spark 2.4.0, 3.1.1, 4.0.0 and 4.3.0 release notes</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) SQL, a **higher-order function** is a built-in function that takes a lambda function as an argument and applies it to the elements of an array or the entries of a map, such as `transform`, `filter` and `aggregate`.[^hof] Higher-order functions let a query work on nested collections in place, without exploding them into rows and grouping them back, and without a user-defined function. Spark 2.4.0 introduced them in SQL, and Spark 3.1 added them to the PySpark functions API.[^r240][^r311]

## What is a lambda function in Spark SQL?

A Spark SQL lambda function is written as parameters, an arrow and a body: `x -> x + 1` for one parameter, or `(acc, x) -> acc + x` for several. Spark allows a lambda only as an argument of a higher-order function; using one elsewhere raises an error that says a lambda function should only be used in a higher order function.[^errors] In the Spark source, the built-in higher-order functions are documented in the function group `lambda_funcs`.[^hof]

Subqueries are not allowed inside higher-order functions. Spark 4.0.0 blocked them for correctness (SPARK-47509), and the error message asks the user to remove all subquery expressions from higher-order functions.[^r400][^errors]

## Which higher-order functions does Spark SQL have?

The following table lists the built-in higher-order functions registered in Spark 4.3, with the version given in each function's documentation:[^hof][^registry]

| Function | Works on | Lambda | What it returns | Since |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `transform(arr, f)` | Array | `x -> ...` or `(x, i) -> ...` (i is the index) | A new array with `f` applied to each element | 2.4.0 |
| `filter(arr, f)` | Array | `x -> bool` or `(x, i) -> bool` | The elements for which `f` is true; the index argument is available since 3.0.0 | 2.4.0 |
| `aggregate(arr, start, merge [, finish])` | Array | `(acc, x) -> ...`, optional `acc -> ...` | One value, folded from `start` over all elements | 2.4.0 |
| `reduce(arr, start, merge [, finish])` | Array | As `aggregate` | Alias of `aggregate`, registered since 3.4.0 | 3.4.0 |
| `exists(arr, f)` | Array | `x -> bool` | True if `f` holds for at least one element | 2.4.0 |
| `forall(arr, f)` | Array | `x -> bool` | True if `f` holds for every element | 3.0.0 |
| `zip_with(a, b, f)` | Two arrays | `(x, y) -> ...` | An element-wise merge; the shorter array is padded with nulls | 2.4.0 |
| `array_sort(arr, f)` | Array | `(left, right) -> int` | The array sorted with a comparator; the comparator form exists since 3.0.0 | 2.4.0 |
| `transform_keys(m, f)` | Map | `(k, v) -> newKey` | A map with new keys and unchanged values | 3.0.0 |
| `transform_values(m, f)` | Map | `(k, v) -> newValue` | A map with unchanged keys and new values | 3.0.0 |
| `map_filter(m, f)` | Map | `(k, v) -> bool` | The entries for which `f` is true | 3.0.0 |
| `map_zip_with(m1, m2, f)` | Two maps | `(k, v1, v2) -> ...` | A merged map; a value is NULL when its key is missing from one map | 3.0.0 |

Null handling follows three-valued logic. For example, `exists(array(1, null, 3), x -> x % 2 == 0)` returns NULL, while `forall(array(1, null, 3), x -> x % 2 == 0)` returns false, because the element 1 already fails the predicate.[^hof]

## How do transform, filter and aggregate work?

The following Spark SQL query applies three array functions and one map function to a single row:[^hof]

```sql
SELECT
  transform(amounts, x -> x * 2)             AS doubled,      -- [20,50,80]
  filter(amounts, x -> x > 15)               AS large,        -- [25,40]
  aggregate(amounts, 0, (acc, x) -> acc + x) AS total,        -- 75
  exists(amounts, x -> x > 30)               AS any_over_30,  -- true
  transform_values(tags, (k, v) -> v * 10)   AS tags_x10      -- {"a":10,"b":20}
FROM VALUES (array(10, 25, 40), map('a', 1, 'b', 2)) AS t(amounts, tags);
```

`aggregate` starts from the initial state, applies `merge` to the state and each element in order, and then applies `finish` to the final state; without `finish`, the identity function is used.[^hof] The result type of `merge` must match the type of the start value. If it does not, Spark fails the query with a `DATATYPE_MISMATCH.UNEXPECTED_INPUT_TYPE` error that names the type required by the start value.[^hof] This is a common mistake when the start value is the integer literal `0` and the elements are `BIGINT`, `DOUBLE` or `DECIMAL`; the fix is to cast the start value, for example `CAST(0 AS BIGINT)`.

## How are higher-order functions used from PySpark?

PySpark exposes the same functions in `pyspark.sql.functions`, where the lambda is a Python function that takes and returns `Column` objects. The functions were added in PySpark 3.1.0 and support [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) since 3.4.0.[^builtin] The Python function is not run per element. PySpark calls it once with placeholder columns to build a Spark expression, so the body may use `Column` methods, functions from `pyspark.sql.functions` and Scala user-defined functions, but not Python user-defined functions (SPARK-27052).[^builtin]

```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

df = spark.createDataFrame([(1, [10, 25, 40])], ["id", "amounts"])  # array<bigint>

df.select(
    F.transform("amounts", lambda x: x * 2).alias("doubled"),
    F.filter("amounts", lambda x, i: (x > 15) & (i > 0)).alias("large_after_first"),
    # The start value is cast to bigint to match the element type.
    F.aggregate("amounts", F.lit(0).cast("bigint"), lambda acc, x: acc + x).alias("total"),
).show()
```

PySpark also provides `reduce`, added in 3.5.0, with the same arguments as `aggregate`.[^builtin]

## Higher-order functions vs explode and user-defined functions

Before Spark 2.4.0, the usual ways to compute over an array column were to explode it into rows and aggregate them back, or to write a user-defined function (UDF). Spark 2.4.0 added higher-order functions to make complex data types easier to process (SPARK-23899).[^r240]

|  | Higher-order function | `explode` then `GROUP BY` | Python UDF |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stays within one row | Yes | No; one row per element, then a regrouping step | Yes |
| Runs in the JVM as a Catalyst expression | Yes[^hof] | Yes | No; data is transferred between the JVM and Python worker processes[^arrow][^config] |
| Element order and index | Available (`(x, i) -> ...` in `transform` and `filter`)[^hof] | `posexplode` returns the position with each element[^n1] | Available |

Spark 4.3.0 added code generation for array higher-order functions (SPARK-37019) and fixed wrong results from semantic equality checks of higher-order functions that capture lambda variables (SPARK-60508).[^r430]

## Use in an open lakehouse

Tables in [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) and [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) often store nested arrays, maps and structs, for example line items in an order or attributes in an event. Higher-order functions let Spark SQL clean, filter and summarize these nested values in a single `SELECT` or in a `MERGE` source query, without changing the table's row granularity.

# Hive Metastore

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_Metastore

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">HMS, Hive metastore service</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data management, table catalogs</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Thrift API service, relational database for metadata, warehouse directory, optional Iceberg REST catalog endpoint</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive) (standalone metastore); clients in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) and [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog), [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog), [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Hive downloads page (releases to 4.2.1), MetastoreConf.java and HiveConf.java at rel/release-4.2.1, the standalone-metastore module at that tag, HIVE-28059 and HIVE-29062, HiveUtils.scala and docs/sql-data-sources-hive-tables.md at the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark, CatalogUtil.java at apache-iceberg-1.12.0 and the Trino 484 metastore documentation</Verified>

<Status level="active">No Hive release deprecates the metastore. Hive 4.1.0 ships it as a standalone component and adds an Iceberg REST catalog endpoint to it; the older Hive 1.x, 2.x and 3.x release lines are end of life.[^downloads]</Status>

The **Hive Metastore** (HMS) is the metadata service of [Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive): it stores the names, schemas, partitions and storage locations of tables in a relational database and serves them to engines through a Thrift API.[^hivehome] Engines other than Hive, such as [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), Impala and [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), use the same service, which made it the shared table catalog of the Hadoop-era data lake. In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse) the Hive Metastore is one of several [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog) options, next to catalogs that implement the [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) API.

## What the Hive Metastore stores

The Hive Metastore keeps metadata, not data. For each table it records the database (namespace), columns and types, partition values, the storage location of each partition and the file format and SerDe used to read it. The Hive project describes it as the central store of metadata for tables and partitions, reached through the metastore service API by clients that include Hive, Impala and Spark.[^hivehome]

The metadata lives in a relational database accessed through JDO. In Hive 4.2.1 the default connection URL is an embedded Apache Derby database (`jdbc:derby:;databaseName=metastore_db;create=true`), which suits tests; production deployments point it at a server database. The default warehouse directory for managed tables is `/user/hive/warehouse`, and the Thrift service listens on port 9083 by default.[^mconf]

## How engines use it

Each engine connects to the Hive Metastore with its own client and its own idea of what a table is.

- **[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)** uses the Hive Metastore as its persistent catalog when Hive support is enabled. Spark 4.3.0 bundles a Hive 2.3.10 client and can talk to metastores of versions 2.0.0 to 2.3.10, 3.0.0 to 3.1.3 and 4.0.0 to 4.1.0, set with `spark.sql.hive.metastore.version` and `spark.sql.hive.metastore.jars`.[^sparkhive][^n1]
- **[Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino)** uses a Thrift metastore (`hive.metastore=thrift`, the default) for its Hive, Delta Lake and Hudi connectors, configured with `hive.metastore.uri`, and offers `hive_metastore` as one Iceberg catalog type.[^trino]
- **[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)** ships a `HiveCatalog` (catalog type `hive`). It stores a pointer to the table's current metadata file in the metastore and uses the metastore to make commits atomic.[^icebergcat]

## Hive Metastore and the Iceberg REST catalog

The Hive Metastore and REST catalogs are often presented as old and new, but since Hive 4.1.0 the metastore can be both. HIVE-28059 added an Iceberg REST catalog to the metastore in 4.1.0, and HIVE-28658 added a REST catalog client in 4.2.0.[^hive28059][^n2] In Hive 4.2.1 the endpoint is a servlet that is off by default (`metastore.catalog.servlet.port` is -1), serves the path `iceberg`, and uses JWT authentication unless `metastore.catalog.servlet.auth` selects none, simple or OAuth 2.[^mconf]

|  | Hive Metastore (Thrift API) | Iceberg REST catalog |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Protocol | Thrift RPC, port 9083 by default[^mconf] | HTTP and JSON, defined by an OpenAPI specification[^restspec] |
| Table formats | Hive tables in any supported file format; Iceberg tables through a metadata pointer | Iceberg tables and views |
| Commit model | Coordinated by each client; Iceberg's `HiveCatalog`, for example, takes a metastore lock around each commit[^n3] | The client sends updates with requirements; the server checks the requirements and applies the commit, or rejects it with a conflict[^restspec] |
| Client coupling | Clients must match a supported metastore version (for example Spark's version list)[^sparkhive] | Any client that speaks the REST specification |
| Example implementations | Hive standalone metastore | [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog), [Project Nessie](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Nessie), the Hive Metastore REST endpoint[^hive28059] |

## Standalone metastore

The metastore code was moved into its own `standalone-metastore` module during Hive 3.0 work, so that it can run without the rest of Hive.[^n4] At the rel/release-4.2.1 tag that module contains separate client, common, server, tools and REST catalog submodules.[^n5] Hive 4.1.0 was the first release to provide the metastore as a standalone component in binary and Docker image form (HIVE-29062).[^downloads][^n6]

## Status

The Hive Metastore is not deprecated in any Hive release, and Hive 4.2.1, released on 24 August 2026, fixed security issues in it.[^downloads] What has ended is support for old release lines: the Hive community declared the 1.x line end of life in April 2024, the 2.x line in May 2024 and the 3.x line in October 2024.[^downloads]

This matters for Spark users. The Hive client bundled with Spark 4.3.0 is version 2.3.10, from a line that is end of life; a Spark application that connects to a Hive 4 metastore must load matching client jars through `spark.sql.hive.metastore.jars`.[^sparkhive]

## Limitations

- **Hive-shaped model.** The metastore models tables as directories of files with partitions. Table formats such as Iceberg keep their real metadata in their own files and use the metastore only for a pointer.[^icebergcat]
- **Version coupling.** Thrift clients must be compatible with the server version, which is why Spark lists the metastore versions it supports.[^sparkhive]
- **Governance.** The metastore records metadata; authorization is left to other projects. The Hive project names Apache Ranger for authorization and Apache Atlas for lineage.[^hivehome]

# Hive on Spark

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_on_Spark

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Spark execution engine for Hive, `hive.execution.engine=spark`</Field>
  <Field name="field">SQL query execution</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Hive 1.1.0 (2015)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Hive compiler and metastore, Spark as the execution engine, the `spark-client` module</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive) 1.1 to 3.1</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive), [Hive Metastore](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_Metastore), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Spark Thrift Server](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Thrift_Server)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">HIVE-7292, HIVE-26134 and HIVE-23885, HiveConf.java, pom.xml and the ql and spark-client modules at the rel/release-3.1.3, 4.0.0-alpha-1, 4.0.0-alpha-2 and 4.0.0 tags of apache/hive, the Apache Hive downloads page, the Hive on Spark getting started page and the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (Hive tables and distributed SQL engine docs)</Verified>

<Status level="removed">Removed in Apache Hive 4.0.0 (first in 4.0.0-alpha-2). Use Apache Tez as the Hive engine, or Spark SQL with Hive support instead. Hive never marked the engine deprecated first; HIVE-26134 removed it from the main branch in April 2022. The last Hive line that had it, 3.x, was declared end of life in October 2024.[^hive26134]</Status>

**Hive on Spark** was an execution engine option in [Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive) that ran HiveQL queries as [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) jobs instead of MapReduce or Apache Tez jobs; users turned it on with `set hive.execution.engine=spark;`.[^gs] It was a Hive project feature: Hive kept its own parser, optimizer and [Hive Metastore](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_Metastore), and used Spark only to run the work. It first shipped in Hive 1.1.0 and was removed in Hive 4.0, so it is unavailable in every maintained Hive release.[^hive7292][^hive26134]

## Status

Hive on Spark was removed without a deprecation release in between.

- **Removed from Hive's main branch in April 2022.** HIVE-26134, "Remove Hive on Spark from the main branch", was resolved on 26 April 2022. Its description links a dev-list discussion and says there was no activity on keeping the feature up to date, and that removing it would help ongoing development and make testing cheaper.[^hive26134] In that thread, a reply from February 2022 says the last development was around October 2018 and calls the code dead weight.[^thread]
- **First releases without it.** The `spark-client` module and the Spark execution package (`ql/.../exec/spark`) are present at the Hive 4.0.0-alpha-1 tag, which was cut before the removal, and absent from 4.0.0-alpha-2 (released 16 November 2022) and 4.0.0 (released 29 March 2024).[^downloads][^tree400] In Hive 4.0.0, `hive.execution.engine` accepts only `mr` and `tez`; in Hive 3.1.3 it also accepted `spark`.[^conf400][^conf313]
- **No maintained release has it.** The Hive community declared the 2.x line end of life in May 2024 and the 3.x line end of life in October 2024, which leaves only the 4.x line, where the engine does not exist.[^downloads]

An earlier ticket, HIVE-23885 "Remove Hive on Spark", was opened in July 2020 and closed as a duplicate.[^n1]

## History

HIVE-7292, the umbrella ticket for Hive on Spark, was opened in June 2014. It gave three reasons: many Hive users already ran Spark and could drop MapReduce or Tez from their clusters; the option would bring Spark users to Hive; and queries with several reduce stages would run faster.[^hive7292] The feature shipped in Hive 1.1.0, released on 8 March 2015.[^hive7292][^downloads]

Each Hive line was tested against one Spark version. The getting started page lists Spark 1.2.0 for Hive 1.1.x, Spark 2.0.0 for Hive 2.3.x and Spark 2.3.0 for Hive 3.0.x, and the Hive 3.1.3 build file still sets `spark.version` to 2.3.0.[^gs][^n2] No Hive release lists support for Spark 3 or later.

## How it worked

Hive compiled a HiveQL query into a plan of map and reduce work, as it did for its other engines, and with the Spark engine submitted that plan to a Spark application through its `spark-client` module. The getting started page required a Spark build that does not include the Hive jars, and it recommends building Spark with the `parquet-provided` profile (and `orc-provided` for Spark 2.3.0 and later) to avoid dependency conflicts.[^gs]

```sql
-- Hive 3.1.x and earlier only; Hive 4 rejects this value
set hive.execution.engine=spark;
SELECT country, count(*) FROM page_views GROUP BY country;
```

## What Hive on Spark is not

Several Spark and Hive combinations have similar names. Only the first row below is Hive on Spark.

| Name | Which project runs the SQL | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Hive on Spark** (`hive.execution.engine=spark`) | Hive parses and plans; Spark executes | Removed in Hive 4.0[^hive26134] |
| **Shark** | A Spark-based project that replaced Hive's execution engine with Spark | Development ended in July 2014 in favor of Spark SQL[^shark] |
| **Spark SQL with Hive support** (`enableHiveSupport()`) | Spark parses, plans and executes; Hive supplies the metastore and SerDes | Active in Spark 4.3.0[^sparkhive] |
| **[Spark Thrift Server](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Thrift_Server)** | Spark SQL, behind a JDBC/ODBC server that corresponds to HiveServer2 | Active in Spark 4.3.0[^sts] |

The 2014 post that ended Shark described Hive on Spark as a separate Hive community effort, aimed at organizations with existing Hive investments that wanted to run them on Spark, while Spark SQL became the main path for SQL on Spark.[^shark] In Spark 4.3.0, Hive support means reading and writing Hive tables through a Hive metastore; Spark 4.3.0 bundles a Hive 2.3.10 client and can connect to metastores from 2.0.0 to 4.1.0.[^sparkhive]

## Replacements

A Hive deployment that used the Spark engine has two paths. It can stay on Hive and move to Hive 4 with Tez, the engine that Hive 4.1 and later use by default (see [Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive)). Or it can move the SQL to Spark itself: Spark SQL reads the same tables through the [Hive Metastore](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_Metastore), and the Spark Thrift Server gives JDBC and ODBC clients a HiveServer2-compatible endpoint.[^sparkhive][^sts] Queries need checking on either path, because HiveQL behavior and Spark SQL behavior differ.

# Iceberg File Format API

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_File_Format_API

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">FormatModel API; pluggable file formats in Iceberg</Field>
  <Field name="field">Table formats, data file input and output</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Iceberg 1.11.0 (May 2026)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`FormatModel`, `FormatModelRegistry`, read and write builders, compatibility test kit</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) Java library (Parquet, ORC, Avro; Spark, Flink, Arrow and generic object models)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Apache ORC](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_ORC), [Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), [Logical type](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Logical_type)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">Apache Iceberg source at tags apache-iceberg-1.10.0, 1.11.0 and 1.12.0, the 1.11.0 and 1.12.0 release notes, the File Format API announcement post, GitHub issue apache/iceberg#12225 and its pull requests, and the dev@iceberg.apache.org discussion and vote threads</Verified>

The **Iceberg File Format API** is a set of Java interfaces in [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) that puts every data file format behind one common reader and writer contract, so that engines read and write Iceberg data files through a registry instead of format-specific code. A format supplies a `FormatModel`, which pairs a file format with an in-memory object model (for example Spark rows or Flink rows) and builds readers and writers for it; the `FormatModelRegistry` stores the available models.[^blog] The API shipped in Iceberg 1.11.0 with implementations for Parquet, ORC and Avro.[^pr15254][^releases] Support for additional formats, such as Vortex and Lance, is discussed and prototyped but is not part of any release.

## Status

The File Format API is a released part of the Iceberg Java library, not a change to the Iceberg table specification.

- **Shipped.** The 1.11.0 release notes, for the release of 19 May 2026, list the File Format API interfaces and the Parquet, ORC and Arrow format model implementations.[^releases] The `org.apache.iceberg.formats` package is absent at tag apache-iceberg-1.10.0 and present at 1.11.0 and 1.12.0.[^javadoc111] Iceberg 1.12.0, released on 29 September 2026, carries the same package.[^releases][^javadoc112]
- **Not shipped.** No new data file format has been added through the API. At 1.12.0 the Java `FileFormat` enumeration lists Puffin, ORC, Parquet, Avro and the metadata JSON file, and Appendix A of the table spec defines type mappings only for Avro, Parquet and ORC.[^fileformat][^icespec] A proof-of-concept pull request for Lance through the API was opened in March 2026 as a draft not intended for merge, and was closed.[^lance]
- **Documentation.** As of November 2026 the versioned Iceberg documentation has no page for the API; a pull request proposing one is open.[^docspr]

## Motivation

Before the API, Iceberg's Java code supported Parquet, Avro and ORC through format-specific readers and writers in each engine integration. The proposal issue states that new version 3 features, such as new column types and default values, need changes at the file format level, and that because these changes were made separately per format, not every feature was available for every format. It also names emerging formats, Vortex and Lance, as candidates for use cases such as fast random access.[^issue]

The announcement post describes the old code as fragmented: Spark, Flink and the generic Java implementation each kept their own format-specific readers, writers and feature handling, with large branching code paths, so that projection, filtering and delete file handling needed separate work for each format and engine pair.[^blog]

## How it works

A `FormatModel<D, S>` names the `FileFormat` it handles, the Java class of the rows it produces and consumes (`D`), and the class of the engine schema (`S`). It returns a `ReadBuilder` for an input file and a `ModelWriteBuilder` for an output file.[^javadoc112] Engines can define their own object models and register them, which lets custom in-memory representations use Iceberg's file format handling.[^javadoc112]

Engines then ask the registry for a builder by file format and row class, instead of branching on the format themselves.[^blog]

```java
// Builders obtained from the registry (method names as given in the announcement post)
FormatModelRegistry.readBuilder(fileFormat, clazz, inputFile);
FormatModelRegistry.dataWriteBuilder(fileFormat, clazz, outputFile);
FormatModelRegistry.equalityDeleteWriteBuilder(fileFormat, clazz, outputFile);
FormatModelRegistry.positionDeleteWriteBuilder(fileFormat, clazz, outputFile);
```

At 1.12.0 the Iceberg source tree contains format models for Avro, Parquet and ORC, a generic model for Iceberg records, an Arrow model for vectorized reads, and Spark and Flink models.[^releases][^pr15254][^pr15329][^pr15328] The position delete writer builder is documented as applying to format version 2 tables only, since version 3 tables must not add position delete files and use [deletion vectors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Deletion_vector) instead.[^pr15980][^icespec]

### Compatibility test kit

The announcement post called a Technology Compatibility Kit (TCK) the most important next step, to validate correctness, type support and compatibility of new format implementations.[^blog] A first TCK was merged in March 2026 and is part of 1.11.0, and further TCK tests (for example for the writer builder) were added for 1.12.0.[^tck][^tck2]

## History

Péter Váry opened the proposal issue and a discussion thread on the Iceberg dev mailing list on 11 February 2025, with a linked design document.[^issue][^discuss] The first implementation was a single large pull request that changed the interfaces, the format implementations and the engines together; the interfaces were later split into a separate pull request.[^pr12298]

In May 2025 a vote on the proposal was called on the dev list; it listed the expected results as the same performance, a formal API, simpler engine and format code, better testability, and the ability to introduce or deprecate file formats with little disruption.[^vote] Review continued on the design document and pull requests.

On 6 February 2026 Ryan Blue wrote on the dev list that the API was ready to be committed, starting with the interfaces pull request, with the aim of including it in the next release to help unblock the DataFusion Comet integration.[^discuss] The interfaces were merged that day, and the Spark and Flink integrations followed on 17 and 18 February 2026.[^pr15329][^pr12774][^pr15328] The project announced the finalized API on 20 February 2026, and it shipped in 1.11.0.[^blog][^releases]

## Planned work

The announcement post lists next steps that were not part of the release: moving the Spark Comet reader to a format model so it can live in the Comet repository, a full Vortex integration, completing the TCK, and column families (vertically split files that allow partial updates without rewriting whole files).[^blog] These are plans, not shipped features.

# Iceberg position delete

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_position_delete

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Position delete file; positional delete</Field>
  <Field name="field">Table formats</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) format version 2</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Data file path, row position, optional deleted row values</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Deletion vector](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Deletion_vector), [Copy-on-write and merge-on-read](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Copy-on-write_and_merge-on-read), [Small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Iceberg table spec at tags apache-iceberg-1.8.0, apache-iceberg-1.11.0 and apache-iceberg-1.12.0, the Iceberg 1.8.0, 1.9.0, 1.11.0 and 1.12.0 release notes, TableMetadata.java and the configuration, Spark queries and Spark procedures documentation at apache-iceberg-1.12.0</Verified>

<Status level="deprecated" since="Iceberg format version 3">Use [deletion vectors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Deletion_vector) instead. Writers must not add position delete files to v3 tables; existing ones in tables upgraded from v2 stay valid. Position delete files remain the normal merge-on-read output for v2 tables, and v2 is still the default format version in Iceberg 1.12.0.[^spec]</Status>

In [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), a **position delete** marks one row as deleted by naming the data file that holds it and the row's position in that file, counting from zero. In format version 2, position deletes are stored in **position delete files**, which are separate data files of (file path, position) pairs that readers apply when they scan the table.[^spec] Format version 3 deprecates position delete files and stores position deletes as [deletion vectors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Deletion_vector) instead, one bitmap per data file.[^spec] Position delete files are one of the ways Iceberg implements [merge-on-read](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Copy-on-write_and_merge-on-read).

## Status

The Iceberg table spec marks position delete files as deprecated in format version 3. Its section on position delete files says that existing position deletes must be written to deletion vectors when the deletes for a data file are next updated, and the row-level delete section says that position delete files must not be added to v3 tables, but existing position delete files are valid.[^spec] The same rules are in the spec at the apache-iceberg-1.8.0 tag, the first release that could write deletion vectors.[^spec180][^releases]

The deprecation applies to the format version, not to the Iceberg library. Iceberg 1.12.0 still creates new tables with format version 2 unless `format-version` is set, and in a v2 table a merge-on-read `DELETE`, `UPDATE` or `MERGE` still writes position delete files.[^tablemeta][^config] Position delete files are deprecated only for tables that have moved to format version 3 or later.

One part of the v2 design has been deprecated and removed in the Java library. The v2 spec allows a position delete file to also store the deleted row's values, but the spec notes that no implementation writes them; the Java implementation deprecated reading and writing that column in 1.11.0, and the 1.12.0 release notes list the removal of position delete files with row data.[^spec][^releases]

## How it works

A position delete file stores rows of a struct called `file_position_delete`. Each row has a `file_path`, the full URI of the target data file, and a `pos`, the ordinal position of the deleted row in that file. A third, optional column, `row`, can hold the deleted row's values.[^spec] The rows must be sorted by `file_path` and then `pos`, so that a columnar reader can skip entries for other files and can apply deletes while it streams through a data file instead of holding them in memory.[^spec]

At read time, a position delete file applies to a data file in the same partition whose data sequence number is less than or equal to the delete file's, unless a deletion vector already covers that data file. Because the comparison includes equal sequence numbers, a delete can remove rows added in the same commit.[^spec] One position delete file can hold deletes for many data files. When all its deletes are for one data file, the manifest entry can record that file in `referenced_data_file`, which lets planners skip the delete file for every other data file.[^spec]

Each delete operation adds new delete files, so a table that takes many small row-level changes collects many small position delete files. Iceberg provides the `rewrite_position_delete_files` Spark procedure to compact them and to drop entries that point to data files that are no longer live.[^procs] This is one form of the [small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem).

## Position delete file compared with related mechanisms

|  | Position delete file | Deletion vector | Equality delete file |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Format versions | v2; deprecated in v3, not allowed for new writes[^spec] | v3 and later[^spec] | v2 and later[^spec] |
| Identifies rows by | Data file path and row position | Row position, as a bitmap tied to one data file | Values of one or more columns, such as `id = 5` |
| Files per data file | Many; any number of delete files can cover a data file | At most one per data file in a snapshot | Many |
| Stored as | A Parquet, Avro or ORC file; the spec recommends the table's default file format | A blob in a Puffin file | A Parquet, Avro or ORC file |

[^spec]

Equality deletes are not affected by the v3 change. They delete rows by value rather than by position, and v3 tables can still add them.[^spec]

## Upgrading to format version 3

When a v2 table is upgraded to v3, its existing position delete files stay in table metadata and still apply. The first time a writer adds a deletion vector for a data file, it must merge that file's existing position deletes into the vector, and from then on readers can ignore position delete files that match a data file with a vector.[^spec] A position delete file that covers several data files has to stay in metadata until every data file it covers has a deletion vector.[^spec] Iceberg 1.9.0 added a Spark action to rewrite v2 position deletes as v3 deletion vectors.[^releases]

## Example

In Spark with an Iceberg catalog, a merge-on-read `DELETE` on a v2 table writes a position delete file, which the `position_deletes` metadata table shows:[^queries][^config]

```sql
CREATE TABLE demo.db.orders (id BIGINT, status STRING)
USING iceberg
TBLPROPERTIES ('format-version' = '2', 'write.delete.mode' = 'merge-on-read');

INSERT INTO demo.db.orders VALUES (1, 'open'), (2, 'open'), (3, 'closed');
DELETE FROM demo.db.orders WHERE id = 2;

SELECT file_path, pos, delete_file_path FROM demo.db.orders.position_deletes;
```

With `'format-version' = '3'`, the same `DELETE` writes a deletion vector instead; Iceberg 1.8.0 added support for showing deletion vectors in the `position_deletes` table.[^releases]

# Iceberg REST catalog

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Iceberg REST Catalog API, IRC</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data engineering</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">2022 (client in Apache Iceberg 0.14.0)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">OpenAPI specification, configuration endpoint, namespace, table and view endpoints, access delegation</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog), Lakekeeper, Apache Gravitino, Project Nessie</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog), [Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">rest-catalog-open-api.yaml at tag apache-iceberg-1.12.0 and the documentation of each listed implementation</Verified>

The **Iceberg REST catalog** is an OpenAPI specification, maintained in the [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) project, that defines an HTTP interface between Iceberg clients and a catalog service. It standardizes how an engine lists namespaces, loads and commits tables and views, and obtains access to the underlying storage, so that any engine with an Iceberg REST client can use any catalog that implements the specification.[^spec] In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), it is the common protocol that separates the choice of [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog) from the choice of query engine.

## History

Apache Iceberg 0.14.0, released on 16 July 2022, added a common REST catalog client that uses change-based commits so that commit conflicts are resolved on the service side.[^releases]

The specification is a file named `rest-catalog-open-api.yaml` in the `open-api/` directory of the Iceberg repository. It is licensed under the Apache License 2.0, and its `info` block describes it as the specification for the first version of the REST Catalog API, with all routes under the `/v1/` path.[^spec]

## What the specification standardizes

The specification groups its routes into several areas:[^spec]
- **Configuration.** Clients call `GET /v1/config` first. The server returns default and override properties that configure the client, and an optional list of the endpoints it supports.
- **Namespaces.** Routes to list, create, load, check and drop namespaces and to update their properties.
- **Tables.** Routes to list, create, load, check, drop, rename, register and unregister tables, and to report metrics.
- **Commits.** A table commit has two parts: requirements, which the server checks before applying changes (for example `assert-ref-snapshot-id`), and updates to the table metadata. Servers must reject unknown requirements or updates with a 400 status code. A separate transactions route commits updates to several tables atomically.
- **Views.** Routes to list, create, load, replace, drop and rename views.
- **Server-side scan planning.** Routes through which a client can ask the catalog to plan a table scan.

Each route after `/v1/` takes an optional `{prefix}` path segment, which a server can use for its own hierarchy, such as one catalog per prefix.[^spec][^glue]

The `/v1/oauth/tokens` endpoint in the specification is deprecated. The specification says that it has been deprecated since Iceberg (Java) 1.6.0, that it will be removed in Iceberg (Java) 2.0, and that clients should set the `oauth2-server-uri` property to point at an OAuth server instead.[^spec]

## Credential vending and remote signing

The specification lets a catalog control access to the data files as well as the metadata. A client signals that it supports delegated access by sending the `X-Iceberg-Access-Delegation` header with one or both of the values `vended-credentials` and `remote-signing`. The server may supply access by any or none of the requested mechanisms.[^spec]

With **vended credentials**, the server returns storage credentials for Amazon S3, Azure Data Lake Storage, Google Cloud Storage or other stores in the `storage-credentials` field of the load-table response. Clients must check that field before looking for credentials in the table configuration. A separate route, `GET /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table}/credentials`, loads fresh vended credentials for a table.[^spec]

With **remote signing**, the client does not receive credentials. Instead, it sends each object storage request to the catalog's `sign` route, and the catalog returns a signed request.[^spec] Project Nessie's documentation describes the trade-off: vending needs a security token service but adds no round trip per request, while signing works without one but adds a REST call for every storage request.[^nessie]

## Implementations

The table lists catalogs whose own documentation states that they implement the Iceberg REST catalog API. It is not complete.

| Catalog | License or type | Endpoint path | Storage access documented |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris) | Apache License 2.0[^n1] | See project docs | Vended credentials[^polaris] |
| [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog) (open source) | Apache License 2.0[^n2] | `/api/2.1/unity-catalog/iceberg` | Vended credentials[^uc] |
| Lakekeeper | Apache License 2.0, written in Rust[^n3] | See project docs | Vended credentials for S3, ADLS and GCS; remote signing for S3[^n4][^n5] |
| Apache Gravitino | Apache License 2.0[^n6] | `/iceberg/` | Vended credentials for S3, GCS, OSS and ADLS; `remote-signing` is a configurable data access mode[^n7] |
| Project Nessie | Apache License 2.0[^n8] | `/iceberg` | Vended credentials and request signing; Iceberg REST support marked experimental[^nessie] |
| AWS Glue Data Catalog | Managed service | `/iceberg` on the regional Glue endpoint | S3 credentials vended for LoadTable; a subset of the REST operations[^glue] |

## Clients

Engines connect to a REST catalog through their Iceberg integration. [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) selects it with `iceberg.catalog.type=rest` and uses vended credentials when `iceberg.rest-catalog.vended-credentials-enabled` is set to true (the default is false).[^n9] [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB) attaches a REST catalog with `ATTACH ... (TYPE iceberg)`, and attaching a catalog is required for writes.[^n10] [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) uses the Iceberg `SparkCatalog` with the catalog type set to `rest`.[^glue]

# INT96 timestamp

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/INT96_timestamp

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">INT96; Impala timestamp</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data storage formats</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Physical type in [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet); written for timestamps by Impala, Hive and Spark</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">12 bytes: nanoseconds within the day (8 bytes) and a Julian day number (4 bytes)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) (read only)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Logical type](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Logical_type), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">parquet.thrift at parquet-format tags 2.4.0, 2.5.0, 2.12.0 and 2.14.0, the parquet-format 2.5.0 changelog, PARQUET-323 and PARQUET-1065, Apache Spark SQLConf.scala at v3.1.1, v3.5.0, v4.0.0 and v4.3.0, ParquetSchemaConverter.scala and DateTimeUtils.scala at v4.3.0, the Spark 3.5 to 4.0 SQL migration guide, SPARK-46440 and SPARK-46447, and the Apache Iceberg spec at apache-iceberg-1.12.0</Verified>

<Status level="deprecated" since="parquet-format 2.5.0">Use an `INT64` column with the Parquet `TIMESTAMP` [logical type](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Logical_type) instead. Apache Spark 4.3.0 still writes timestamps as INT96 by default.[^pq323]</Status>

An **INT96 timestamp** is a timestamp stored in the 12-byte `INT96` physical type of [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet): 8 bytes of nanoseconds within the day followed by 4 bytes of day number.[^thrift] The encoding was introduced for nanosecond timestamps in Impala, and [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) originally used the same timestamp type as Impala and Hive.[^sparkconv] INT96 carries no [logical type](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Logical_type) annotation, so a reader has to know the convention to treat it as a timestamp. The Parquet format has marked INT96 as deprecated since parquet-format 2.5.0, but the type is still common because Spark writes it by default.[^pq323][^conf]

## Status

**Parquet format.** PARQUET-323, "INT96 should be marked as deprecated", was fixed in parquet-format 2.5.0, together with PARQUET-1065, which deprecated type-defined sort ordering for INT96 statistics.[^pq323][^changes] In `parquet.thrift`, the `INT96` entry has no comment at 2.4.0, is commented "deprecated, only used by legacy implementations" from 2.5.0, and since 2.12.0 reads "deprecated, new Parquet writers should not write data in INT96".[^thrift240][^thrift250][^thrift2120] The type has not been removed: parquet-format 2.14.0 added an `INT96_TIMESTAMP_ORDER` column order, which tells readers that INT96 statistics are ordered chronologically, and the thrift file notes that INT96 is still used in many legacy systems.[^thrift]

**Apache Spark.** Spark has not deprecated writing INT96. In Spark 4.3.0, `spark.sql.parquet.outputTimestampType` still defaults to `INT96`, as it has since the setting was added in Spark 2.3.0.[^conf] A comment in Spark's Parquet schema converter says that `TIMESTAMP_MICROS` is recommended but INT96 stays the default to keep earlier behaviour.[^sparkconv]

## How it works

An INT96 value is 12 bytes. The thrift definition describes the legacy ordering rule: the last 4 bytes are the day as a little-endian 32-bit signed integer, and the first 8 bytes are nanoseconds as a little-endian 64-bit signed integer.[^thrift] Spark interprets the day as a Julian day number and converts the value to microseconds since the Unix epoch, dividing the nanoseconds by 1,000, so sub-microsecond precision is lost on read.[^dtu]

Because the type has no logical type, nothing in the file says whether a value is UTC-normalized or local time. Spark's `spark.sql.parquet.int96TimestampConversion` (default `false`) applies a time zone adjustment for INT96 data written by Impala, which the setting's documentation says uses a different offset than Hive and Spark.[^conf] Spark reads INT96 as a timestamp only while `spark.sql.parquet.int96AsTimestamp` is `true`, the default; otherwise it rejects the column.[^conf][^sparkconv]

## Calendar rebasing in Spark

Spark 3.0 moved from the hybrid Julian and Gregorian calendar to the Proleptic Gregorian calendar, which changes the meaning of very old dates and timestamps.[^mig30] Spark 3.1 added `spark.sql.legacy.parquet.int96RebaseModeInRead` and `InWrite`, defaulting to `EXCEPTION`, so that reading or writing INT96 timestamps before 1900-01-01 failed instead of silently shifting.[^conf311][^mig40]

Spark 4.0.0 changed the defaults of these rebase settings to `CORRECTED`, which reads and writes values as they are (SPARK-46440), and removed the `spark.sql.legacy` names in favour of `spark.sql.parquet.int96RebaseModeInRead` and `spark.sql.parquet.int96RebaseModeInWrite` (SPARK-46447).[^s46440][^s46447][^mig40] Both settings are internal in Spark 4.3.0 and default to `CORRECTED`.[^conf]

## INT96 compared with standard Parquet timestamps

|  | INT96 timestamp | INT64 with TIMESTAMP logical type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Status in Parquet | Deprecated since parquet-format 2.5.0[^pq323] | Current |
| Size | 12 bytes | 8 bytes |
| Precision | Nanoseconds in storage; Spark keeps microseconds[^dtu] | Unit stated in the annotation: `MILLIS`, `MICROS` or `NANOS`[^lt] |
| UTC or local time | Not recorded in the file | Recorded by `isAdjustedToUTC`[^lt] |
| Spark write setting | `spark.sql.parquet.outputTimestampType=INT96` (default)[^conf] | `TIMESTAMP_MICROS` or `TIMESTAMP_MILLIS`[^conf] |
| Apache Iceberg | Not used in the spec's Parquet type mapping; readable in imported data files[^icespec][^ice6962] | The spec's mapping for `timestamp` and `timestamptz`[^icespec] |

## Example

In Spark, setting the output type before writing produces standard `INT64` timestamps instead of INT96:[^conf]

```python
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.parquet.outputTimestampType", "TIMESTAMP_MICROS")

df = spark.sql("SELECT TIMESTAMP '2026-11-22 10:00:00' AS ts")
df.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("/tmp/ts_micros")
```

The setting changes only new files. Files already written with INT96 keep that encoding until they are rewritten.

# Job, stage and task

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Job,_stage_and_task

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Spark job, Spark stage, Spark task</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Action, job, `ShuffleMapStage`, `ResultStage`, task, stage attempt</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Directed acyclic graph (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph_(Spark)), [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Narrow and wide transformations](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Narrow_and_wide_transformations), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/cluster-overview.md, docs/web-ui.md, docs/configuration.md, docs/sql-performance-tuning.md, core DAGScheduler.scala), a PySpark 4.3.0 run with SparkStatusTracker, and the Trino 484 concepts page</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a **job** is the parallel computation that one action (such as `collect` or `save`) starts; Spark divides each job into **stages** at [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle) boundaries, and each stage into **tasks**, one per [partition](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), which run on [executors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor).[^cluster][^dag] These three terms are the units in which the Spark web UI, the driver logs and the scheduler describe work. Knowing how they map to code explains why one line of PySpark can show up as several jobs and hundreds of tasks.

## What are a job, a stage and a task?

| Term | Definition in Spark | Created when | Seen in the UI as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Job | A parallel computation of many tasks, spawned in response to an action[^cluster] | An action runs; the DAG scheduler receives it through `submitJob`[^dag] | A row in the Jobs tab |
| Stage | A set of tasks that compute the same function on different partitions of the same data; stages are separated at shuffle boundaries[^dag] | The DAG scheduler cuts the job's graph at each shuffle dependency[^dag] | A row in the Stages tab, and a box in the job's DAG visualization[^webui] |
| Task | A unit of work sent to one executor[^cluster], which processes one partition | A stage is submitted as a TaskSet with one task per partition to compute[^dag] | A row in the task table of the stage detail page[^webui] |

Spark has two kinds of stage. A **ShuffleMapStage** writes map output files for a shuffle, and a **ResultStage** is the final stage that runs the action.[^dag] A stage can be shared by several jobs if they reuse the same data.

## How does one action become jobs, stages and tasks?

The [driver](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Driver_(Apache_Spark)) builds the plan, and the action hands it to the DAG scheduler as a job. Operations with narrow dependencies, such as `map` and `filter`, are pipelined together into one set of tasks per stage; operations with shuffle dependencies need one stage to write map output files and another to read them after a barrier.[^dag] See [Narrow and wide transformations](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Narrow_and_wide_transformations).

The number of tasks in a stage is the number of partitions it computes. A stage that reads files has one task per input partition, and file partitions hold at most `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes` (default 128 MB) each; a stage after a shuffle has one task per shuffle partition, which for DataFrame and SQL queries is `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` (default 200) unless [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution) changes it.[^perf] An executor runs at most `spark.executor.cores` divided by `spark.task.cpus` tasks at once, so the tasks of a large stage queue for free slots.[^config]

## Example

This PySpark aggregation needs one shuffle, because rows with the same key must meet in one task:

```python
df = spark.range(1_000_000)
df.groupBy((df.id % 10).alias("m")).count().collect()
```

Run with `local[2]` on PySpark 4.3.0 and read back through `SparkContext.statusTracker()`, the same action produced these units:

| Setting | Jobs | Stages and tasks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=false` | 1 job | Stage 0: 2 tasks (read the range and write shuffle files); stage 1: 200 tasks (read the shuffle and finish the count) |
| `spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true` (default) | 2 jobs | Job 1: one stage of 2 tasks (the map side). Job 2: a reference to the same map stage, whose shuffle output already existed, and a result stage of 1 task, after AQE coalesced the 200 shuffle partitions into one |

The second row shows why job counts in the UI do not always match actions. AQE re-optimizes the plan during execution from runtime statistics,[^perf] and in this run it started the map side as its own job before planning the final stage. The DAG scheduler remembers which shuffle map stages have already produced output files and does not redo them;[^dag] the web UI lists such stages under "skipped".[^webui]

## Reading the Spark UI with these terms

The Spark web UI follows the same hierarchy:[^webui]

- The **Jobs** tab lists each job with its description, duration, a stage summary and a task progress bar. A job's detail page shows the DAG visualization and the job's stages grouped as active, pending, completed, skipped and failed.
- The **Stages** tab lists all stages. Each stage shows input and output bytes, **shuffle read** (bytes read from earlier stages) and **shuffle write** (bytes written for later stages).
- A **stage detail** page shows summary metrics over all tasks (duration, GC time, scheduler delay, peak execution memory, shuffle read fetch wait time, shuffle spill to memory and disk) and a table with one row per task.
- The **SQL / DataFrame** tab has a detail page per query that lists the jobs and stages associated with it and shows its parsed, analyzed and optimized logical plans and physical plan. The stage DAG groups nodes by operation scope, such as `WholeStageCodegen` and `Exchange`, and annotates code generation IDs, so a stage can be traced back to operators in the [physical plan](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Logical_plan_and_physical_plan).

## Failures and retries

A task that fails is retried by the task scheduler; `spark.task.maxFailures` (default 4) is the number of continuous failures of one particular task before Spark gives up on the job, so the default allows three retries.[^config] If a task fails because shuffle output from an earlier stage was lost, for example because an executor died, the DAG scheduler resubmits the earlier stage. Each run of a stage is called an attempt.[^dag]

## Spark terms compared with Trino

[Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) uses the words "stage" and "task" for related but different things.

|  | Apache Spark | Trino |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stage | A set of tasks that actually run on executors, between two shuffle boundaries[^dag] | A model of part of the distributed query plan used by the coordinator; stages themselves do not run on workers[^trino] |
| Task | One unit of work on one partition, sent to one executor[^cluster] | The implementation of a stage on a worker; tasks operate on splits[^trino] |
| Job | The work started by one action | No equivalent term; the unit is the query |

# Join strategy hints

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Join_strategy_hints

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Join hints (Spark SQL)</Field>
  <Field name="field">Query optimization</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">`BROADCAST` before Spark 3.0; `MERGE`, `SHUFFLE_HASH` and `SHUFFLE_REPLICATE_NL` in Apache Spark 3.0.0</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`BROADCAST`, `MERGE`, `SHUFFLE_HASH`, `SHUFFLE_REPLICATE_NL`</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution), [Data skew](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_skew), [Broadcast join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Broadcast_join)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-hints.md, docs/sql-performance-tuning.md, SparkStrategies.scala, adaptive/DemoteBroadcastHashJoin.scala, adaptive/ConvertSortMergeJoinToShuffledHashJoin.scala, adaptive/OptimizeSkewedJoin.scala, exchange/BroadcastExchangeExec.scala, SQLConf.scala, core unsafe/map/BytesToBytesMap.java) and SPARK-27225</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) SQL, **join strategy hints** are comments of the form `/*+ HINT(table) */`, or `DataFrame.hint()` calls, that ask the planner to use a specific physical join algorithm for a relation instead of the one it would pick from statistics.[^hints] Spark supports four: `BROADCAST`, `MERGE`, `SHUFFLE_HASH` and `SHUFFLE_REPLICATE_NL`. A hint is a suggestion, not a command: Spark ignores it when the hinted strategy does not support the join type.[^hints]

## Which join hints does Spark support?

Before Spark 3.0 only the `BROADCAST` hint existed. Spark 3.0.0 added `MERGE`, `SHUFFLE_HASH` and `SHUFFLE_REPLICATE_NL`, one for each of Spark's other join strategies.[^hints][^spark27225]

| Hint | Aliases | Physical join it asks for | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `BROADCAST` | `BROADCASTJOIN`, `MAPJOIN` | Broadcast hash join (with equi-join keys) or broadcast nested loop join (without) | The hinted side is broadcast even if it is larger than `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` (default 10 MB). If both sides are hinted, the smaller one by statistics is broadcast.[^hints][^perf] |
| `MERGE` | `SHUFFLE_MERGE`, `MERGEJOIN` | Shuffle sort-merge join | Needs sortable join keys.[^strategies] |
| `SHUFFLE_HASH` | none | Shuffle hash join | If both sides are hinted, the smaller side by statistics becomes the build side.[^hints] |
| `SHUFFLE_REPLICATE_NL` | none | Shuffle-and-replicate nested loop join (cartesian product) | Used only for inner-like joins.[^strategies] |

The `BROADCAST` hint is still bounded by hard limits: Spark fails a broadcast whose table is 8 GiB or larger (`spark.sql.maxBroadcastTableSize`, added in 4.1.0) or that has too many rows. The row limit depends on the broadcast mode: for a hash join whose key is not a single `LongType` column it is `BytesToBytesMap.MAX_CAPACITY / 1.5`, that is 2<sup>29</sup> / 1.5 or 357,913,941 rows, and in other cases it is 512,000,000 rows.[^btbm][^bee][^sqlconf]

## How to write a join hint

In Spark SQL the hint goes in a comment right after `SELECT` and names the table or alias it applies to. In PySpark the same hint is set with `hint()` on the DataFrame that should get the strategy, or with `broadcast()` from `pyspark.sql.functions`.[^perf]

```sql
SELECT /*+ BROADCAST(d) */ f.order_id, d.region
FROM sales f JOIN dim_store d ON f.store_id = d.store_id;

SELECT /*+ SHUFFLE_HASH(c) */ * FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.cust_id = c.cust_id;
```

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

orders.join(broadcast(stores), "store_id")
orders.join(customers.hint("merge"), "cust_id")
```

## Which hint wins when several are given?

When the two sides of a join carry different strategy hints, Spark prefers `BROADCAST` over `MERGE` over `SHUFFLE_HASH` over `SHUFFLE_REPLICATE_NL`, and logs a warning that the overridden hint will not take effect.[^hints]

Spark's join selection looks at hints before it looks at sizes. For an equi-join, it tries the hinted strategies in the order above; only if there is no hint, or no hint applies, does it fall back to its default order: broadcast hash join if a side is under the broadcast threshold, then shuffle hash join, then sort-merge join, then cartesian product, then broadcast nested loop join.[^strategies] A `MERGE` or `SHUFFLE_HASH` hint on a join without equi-join keys cannot be honored, and Spark reports it as unsupported.[^strategies]

## How do join hints interact with Adaptive Query Execution?

[Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution) (AQE), on by default since Spark 3.2.0, re-plans joins at runtime from the sizes of completed shuffle stages. Three AQE rules change joins, and each treats hints differently.[^perf]

- **Sort-merge join to broadcast join.** AQE turns a sort-merge join into a broadcast hash join when a side's runtime size is under `spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` (which defaults to `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`).[^perf] AQE also has a rule that marks a side with many empty partitions as "do not broadcast", but the rule leaves a side alone if the user already gave it a strategy hint.[^demote]
- **Sort-merge join to shuffled hash join.** AQE can switch a sort-merge join to a shuffled hash join when every partition is under `spark.sql.adaptive.maxShuffledHashJoinLocalMapThreshold` (default 0, so off). It skips joins that carry a `MERGE` hint.[^perf][^smj2shj]
- **Skew join splitting.** AQE splits skewed partitions of sort-merge and shuffled hash joins, whichever strategy chose them, so a `MERGE` or `SHUFFLE_HASH` hint does not turn off skew handling.[^skew] See [data skew](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_skew).

Hints and AQE work from different information. A hint records a choice the user knows in advance; AQE uses the measured size of each shuffle stage. With AQE on, a table that is small only after filtering can be broadcast without a hint, because AQE sees its runtime size; this is less efficient than planning the broadcast up front, but avoids the sort on both sides.[^perf]

## Join hints compared with partitioning hints

Spark SQL has a second family of hints that does not pick a join algorithm. **Partitioning hints** (`COALESCE`, `REPARTITION`, `REPARTITION_BY_RANGE`, `REBALANCE` and `REBALANCE_BY_SIZE`) set how a query's output is partitioned, for example to control the number of files written to a [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) or [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) table. `REBALANCE` and `REBALANCE_BY_SIZE` only work with AQE on.[^hints]

In [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), the closest equivalent is the `join_distribution_type` session property, which chooses between partitioned and broadcast joins for the whole query rather than per table.[^trinocbo]

# Kubernetes Operator for Apache Spark

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Kubernetes_Operator_for_Apache_Spark

<Infobox type="software" name="Apache Spark Kubernetes Operator">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) subproject)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">0.1.0 (May 2025)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">1.1.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-11-12</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Java</Field>
  <Field name="type">Kubernetes operator for Spark applications and clusters</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[Operator documentation](https://github.com/apache/spark-kubernetes-operator/tree/1.1.0/docs)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark-kubernetes-operator](https://github.com/apache/spark-kubernetes-operator)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark on Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_Kubernetes), [spark-submit](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark-submit), [Spark standalone cluster manager](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_standalone_cluster_manager)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the 1.1.0 tag of apache/spark-kubernetes-operator (README, docs/architecture.md, docs/spark_custom_resources.md, docs/operations.md, docs/migration_guide.md, SparkAppSubmissionWorker.java), its GitHub releases, SPARK-45923, docs/running-on-kubernetes.md at Spark v4.3.0, the kubeflow/spark-operator README and v2.6.0 release, and the Kubeflow announcement of April 2024</Verified>

The **Kubernetes Operator for Apache Spark** is software that runs Spark workloads on Kubernetes through the operator pattern: users describe a Spark application or cluster as a Kubernetes custom resource, and a controller creates and watches the driver, executor and other pods until the workload ends. The name covers two projects. The **Apache Spark Kubernetes Operator** is an official subproject of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) with the custom resources `SparkApplication` and `SparkCluster`.[^readme][^k8sdoc] The older **Kubeflow Spark Operator**, which began as Google Cloud Platform's Spark on Kubernetes Operator, moved to the Kubeflow community in 2024.[^kfblog]

## What does the Apache Spark Kubernetes Operator do?

The Apache Spark Kubernetes Operator acts as a control plane for the deployment lifecycle of Spark applications and clusters. It is installed with Helm, usually in its own namespace, and watches Spark custom resources in one or more workload namespaces.[^arch] It is built with the Java Operator SDK and talks to the Kubernetes API server with the fabric8 client.[^arch]

For a `SparkApplication`, the operator launches the driver, observes it and the executors it spawns, records their status until the application ends, and then releases the resources the application owned.[^arch] It builds the driver with Spark's own Kubernetes driver builder in-process, instead of starting a separate spark-submit process.[^worker] The Spark documentation describes the operator and spark-submit as complementary, because both use the same native Kubernetes scheduler backend; see [Spark on Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_Kubernetes).[^k8sdoc]

For a `SparkCluster`, the operator deploys a [Spark standalone](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_standalone_cluster_manager) master and workers as StatefulSets exposed through Kubernetes services, and garbage-collects them when the resource is deleted.[^crd]

## What does a SparkApplication look like?

A `SparkApplication` in API group `spark.apache.org/v1` names the entry point (`mainClass` and `jars` for JVM applications, `pyFiles` for Python), the Spark configuration in `sparkConf`, and the Spark version in `runtimeVersions`.[^crd] This example, adapted from the operator's Python example, runs the PySpark Pi program:[^n1]

```yaml
apiVersion: spark.apache.org/v1
kind: SparkApplication
metadata:
  name: pi-python
spec:
  pyFiles: "local:///opt/spark/examples/src/main/python/pi.py"
  sparkConf:
    spark.kubernetes.authenticate.driver.serviceAccountName: "spark"
    spark.kubernetes.container.image: "apache/spark:4.3.0-python3"
  runtimeVersions:
    sparkVersion: "4.3.0"
```

`kubectl get sparkapp` lists applications with their current state. Pod details that Spark configuration cannot set go in `spec.driverSpec.podTemplateSpec` and `spec.executorSpec.podTemplateSpec`, which take precedence over `spark.kubernetes.[driver|executor].podTemplateFile`.[^readme][^crd]

## What is the SparkApplication lifecycle?

The operator moves each `SparkApplication` through a state machine. A typical successful run goes `Submitted`, `DriverRequested`, `DriverStarted`, `DriverReady`, `RunningHealthy`, `Succeeded` and finally `ResourceReleased`.[^arch] While running, an application can also be in `RunningWithBelowThresholdExecutors` or `RunningWithPartialCapacity` when fewer executors are available than requested.[^arch]

The failure states are `SchedulingFailure`, `DriverStartTimedOut`, `DriverReadyTimedOut`, `ExecutorsStartTimedOut`, `DriverEvicted` and `Failed`. From a failure the application moves to `ScheduledToRestart` if a retry is configured, or to `ResourceReleased`; a retain policy can hold it in `TerminatedWithoutReleaseResources` first.[^arch] The operator treats `DriverStartTimedOut`, `ExecutorsStartTimedOut` and `SchedulingFailure` as likely infrastructure failures on a best-effort basis, and `restartConfig.restartPolicy` accepts `Never`, `Always`, `OnFailure` and `OnInfrastructureFailure`.[^crd]

Since 1.1.0, both custom resources have `spec.suspend` and a `Suspended` state, and the operator can queue workloads through Kueue when `spark.kubernetes.operator.kueue.enabled` is set.[^migration][^arch]

## Which versions does it support?

The 1.1.0 release, published on 12 November 2026, supports Kubernetes 1.35 to 1.37 and Apache Spark 4.0 to 4.3, is built with Spark 4.3.0, and deprecates the `v1beta1` custom resource definitions.[^r110] The migration guide says `spark.apache.org/v1beta1` is scheduled for removal in 2.0.0 and that `spark.apache.org/v1` should be used.[^migration] The operations guide lists Java 21 or newer and Spark 4.0 or above as requirements.[^n2]

## History

The Apache Spark Kubernetes Operator was proposed in SPARK-45923, opened in November 2023, and the ticket was resolved with the operator's 0.1.0 release.[^n3] Release v0.1.0 was published on GitHub on 8 May 2025 and 1.0.0 on 26 July 2026.[^n4]

The Kubeflow Spark Operator began at Google Cloud. In April 2024 the Kubeflow project announced that Google's Spark Operator had moved to Kubeflow, under the repository `kubeflow/spark-operator`, to be governed by an open community.[^kfblog]

## Apache Spark Kubernetes Operator vs Kubeflow Spark Operator

|  | Apache Spark Kubernetes Operator | Kubeflow Spark Operator |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Home | Apache Spark subproject[^readme] | Kubeflow community; formerly Google Cloud Platform's Spark on Kubernetes Operator[^kfblog] |
| API group | `spark.apache.org/v1` (`v1beta1` deprecated)[^migration] | `sparkoperator.k8s.io` (`v1beta2`, `v1alpha1`)[^kfcrd] |
| Custom resources | `SparkApplication`, `SparkCluster`[^crd] | `SparkApplication`, `ScheduledSparkApplication`, `SparkConnect`[^kfcrd] |
| How the driver is created | In-process with Spark's Kubernetes driver builder, no spark-submit process[^worker] | Runs spark-submit on behalf of the user; v2.6.0 adds a REST-based submitter as an option[^kfreadme][^kf260] |
| Spark versions | 4.0 to 4.3 (1.1.0)[^r110] | 2.3 and up[^kfreadme] |
| Scheduled (cron) runs | No dedicated resource; the examples use a Kubernetes `CronJob`[^n5] | `ScheduledSparkApplication` with cron schedules[^kfreadme] |
| Standalone clusters | Yes, `SparkCluster`[^crd] | No standalone cluster resource[^kfcrd] |
| Pod customization | Pod template specs in the resource[^crd] | A mutating admission webhook, for example for volumes and affinity[^kfreadme] |
| Queueing | Kueue integration since 1.1.0[^r110] | Kueue integration (referenced by the Apache operator documentation)[^crd] |
| Latest release (checked 2026-11-23) | 1.1.0, 12 November 2026[^r110] | v2.6.0, 11 November 2026[^kf260] |
| License | Apache License 2.0 | Apache License 2.0 |

## Is either operator deprecated?

Neither operator is deprecated. The Apache Spark Kubernetes Operator 1.1.0 deprecates only its `v1beta1` API version.[^migration] The Kubeflow Spark Operator v2.6.0 deprecates the client deploy mode (`spec.mode: client`) for `SparkApplication`, which still works but returns a warning.[^kf260]

# Lateral column alias

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Lateral_column_alias

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">LCA, reusable column alias, lateral alias reference</Field>
  <Field name="field">SQL name resolution</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Alias defined earlier in the same SELECT list; resolution after table columns</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (since 3.4.0), Databricks SQL, [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB), Snowflake</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Window functions](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Window_functions)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/sql-ref-name-resolution.md, SQLConf.scala, error-conditions.json), the Spark 3.4.0 and 3.5.0 release notes, the Databricks name resolution reference, DuckDB 2.0 friendly SQL page, Snowflake SELECT reference, BigQuery query syntax reference and PostgreSQL 19 SELECT reference</Verified>

A **lateral column alias** is a column alias defined in a `SELECT` list that later expressions in the same `SELECT` list can refer to, as in `SELECT price * qty AS total, total * 0.2 AS tax`; [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) supports it since version 3.4.0.[^r340][^nameres] It saves repeating an expression or wrapping the query in a subquery. Several engines, among them BigQuery and PostgreSQL, do not allow it,[^bq][^pg] so the same query can work in one engine and fail in another.

## How does Spark resolve a lateral column alias?

Spark SQL treats lateral column aliasing as one step of its name resolution order. Inside a `SELECT` list, Spark first tries to match an identifier to a column of the tables in the `FROM` clause; only if that fails does it match the leading identifier to a preceding alias in the same `SELECT` list.[^nameres] A real column with the same name therefore wins over an alias. Spark's documentation shows that `SELECT c1 AS a, a + c1 FROM VALUES(2, 3) AS T(c1, a)` returns `2, 5`, because `a` resolves to the table column (3), not to the alias.[^nameres]

If an identifier matches more than one preceding alias, Spark raises `AMBIGUOUS_LATERAL_COLUMN_ALIAS`.[^nameres][^errors] Further parts of a dotted name after the alias are resolved as struct fields or map keys.[^nameres]

The behaviour is controlled by `spark.sql.lateralColumnAlias.enableImplicitResolution`, an internal configuration added in 3.4.0 whose default is `true`.[^sqlconf]

## History in Spark

Spark 3.4.0 added lateral column alias references (SPARK-27561).[^r340] Spark 3.5.0 extended them to aggregate queries (SPARK-41631) and to queries with window functions (SPARK-42217).[^r350] Databricks documents the same rule for Databricks SQL and Databricks Runtime 12.2 LTS and above.[^dbx]

## What are the limits in Spark?

Spark 4.3 rejects some placements of a lateral alias with an `UNSUPPORTED_FEATURE` error. The error conditions name these cases:[^errors]
- inside the arguments of an aggregate function (`LATERAL_COLUMN_ALIAS_IN_AGGREGATE_FUNC`);
- inside a window expression (`LATERAL_COLUMN_ALIAS_IN_WINDOW`);
- inside a generator expression such as `explode` (`LATERAL_COLUMN_ALIAS_IN_GENERATOR`);
- through `GROUP BY` alias or `GROUP BY ALL` (`LATERAL_COLUMN_ALIAS_IN_GROUP_BY`);
- in an aggregate query that has both window expressions and a `HAVING` clause (`LATERAL_COLUMN_ALIAS_IN_AGGREGATE_WITH_WINDOW_AND_HAVING`).

A lateral alias may refer to the result of an aggregate, as in the second example below; it may not be fed into one.

## Example

Spark SQL, using an alias in a later expression of the same `SELECT` list:

```sql
SELECT name,
       salary * 12        AS annual,
       annual * 0.1       AS bonus
FROM employees;

-- An alias of an aggregate result, reused in the same SELECT list
SELECT dept,
       SUM(salary)        AS total,
       total / COUNT(*)   AS avg_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept;
```

In engines without lateral aliases, the first query has to repeat `salary * 12` or compute `annual` in a subquery.

## Which engines allow lateral column aliases?

| Engine | Alias reusable in the same SELECT list? | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Apache Spark (3.4.0 and later) | Yes[^r340] | Table columns take precedence over aliases; not allowed inside aggregate, window or generator arguments[^nameres][^errors] |
| Databricks SQL and Databricks Runtime | Yes, Databricks Runtime 12.2 LTS and above[^dbx] | Same rule as Spark: local column references take precedence[^dbx] |
| DuckDB 2.0 | Yes[^duck] | Also allows aliases in `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`, but not in a join's `ON` clause[^duck] |
| Snowflake | Yes[^snow] | Aliases can be used in other column expressions and in `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and joins; the documentation advises against aliases that share a name with a referenced column[^snow] |
| BigQuery (GoogleSQL) | No[^bq] | `SELECT` list aliases are visible only to `GROUP BY`, `ORDER BY` and `HAVING`[^bq] |
| PostgreSQL 19 | No; output names are documented only for `ORDER BY` and `GROUP BY`[^pg] | The documentation says an output column name cannot be used in `WHERE` or `HAVING`; the expression must be written out[^pg] |

Because precedence rules differ, a query that relies on a lateral alias whose name also matches a table column can return different results across engines. Choosing alias names that do not collide with column names avoids this.[^nameres][^snow]
