# Native execution engine (Spark)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Native_execution_engine_(Spark)

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Native engine, native accelerator, vectorized native execution</Field>
  <Field name="field">Query execution performance</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Plan conversion from Spark physical plans, vectorized columnar operators in C++ or Rust, off-heap memory, columnar shuffle, fallback to JVM operators</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Gluten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Gluten) (with [Velox](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Velox) or ClickHouse), [Apache DataFusion Comet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_DataFusion_Comet), Photon (Databricks, proprietary)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Project Tungsten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Tungsten), [Whole-stage code generation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Whole-stage_code_generation), [GPU acceleration in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GPU_acceleration_in_Spark)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Apache Spark 4.3.0 release (2026-10-30) and the v4.3.0 source tag (SQLConf, WholeStageCodegenExec), the Apache Gluten README and configuration guide (release 1.7.0), the Apache DataFusion Comet README, operator guide and Comet versus Gluten comparison (release 1.2.0), the Databricks Photon documentation, the Crossref record of the SIGMOD 2022 Photon paper, and the NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark README</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a **native execution engine** is a component that runs the physical operators of a Spark SQL or DataFrame query as vectorized, columnar code compiled to machine code (usually C++ or Rust) instead of as Java bytecode generated by Spark's whole-stage code generation in the Java virtual machine (JVM). Spark still parses, optimizes and schedules the query; the native engine replaces only the execution of the operators it supports and hands the rest back to Spark. Open source examples are [Apache Gluten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Gluten) and [Apache DataFusion Comet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_DataFusion_Comet); Databricks Photon is a proprietary example.[^glreadme][^cmreadme]

## What is a native execution engine?

Apache Spark's own engine runs in the JVM. Since Spark 2.0.0, whole-stage code generation, part of [Project Tungsten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Tungsten), compiles chains of operators into one generated Java function per stage; it is on by default through `spark.sql.codegen.wholeStage` in Spark 4.3.0.[^sqlconf][^wscg]

A native execution engine for Spark takes the physical plan that Spark has already chosen, converts the supported part of it into a plan for a native library, and runs that part outside the JVM on columnar batches. Apache Gluten converts the plan to Substrait and passes it through the Java Native Interface (JNI) to [Velox](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Velox) or ClickHouse.[^glreadme] Apache DataFusion Comet serializes it in its own Protocol Buffers format and runs it with Apache DataFusion, written in Rust.[^cmp]

## How does a native engine plug into Apache Spark?

Open source native engines attach to Apache Spark through its public extension points. Both Gluten and Comet are enabled with the `spark.plugins` setting, turn on Spark off-heap memory (`spark.memory.offHeap.enabled`, which is false by default), and replace `spark.shuffle.manager` with a columnar shuffle manager so that data stays columnar between stages.[^glreadme][^cmreadme][^sparkconf] Application code, SQL and DataFrame queries do not change.

## What runs natively and what falls back?

A native execution engine for Spark runs only the operators and expressions it supports. Everything else falls back to Spark's JVM operators, and the engine inserts conversions between its columnar format and Spark's row format at each boundary. Gluten calls these ColumnarToRow and RowToColumnar transitions.[^glreadme] Comet falls back at the level of a query stage: if a stage contains an unsupported operator, the stage runs in Spark.[^cmops] Photon also falls back to the Spark runtime for operations it does not support.[^photondocs] Because each transition has a cost, the share of a plan that runs natively matters as much as the speed of the native operators.

## What about Photon?

Photon is the vectorized query engine built by Databricks. Databricks describes Photon as a proprietary part of the Databricks Runtime that is not part of open source Apache Spark and is not distributed with it.[^photonoss] Databricks described it in the paper "Photon: A Fast Query Engine for Lakehouse Systems", published in the proceedings of the ACM SIGMOD 2022 conference (June 2022).[^paper] The Databricks documentation states that Photon replaces the JVM-based Spark SQL execution engine with a native C++ runtime for supported operations, keeps Spark's Catalyst optimizer for planning, and is compatible with Apache Spark APIs.[^photondocs]

## Native engines compared

|  | Apache Spark (JVM, Tungsten codegen) | Apache Gluten (Velox backend) | Apache Gluten (ClickHouse backend) | Apache DataFusion Comet | Photon |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Language of the execution code | Scala and Java; generated Java code in the JVM[^wscg] | C++ ([Velox](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Velox)), with a Scala/Java plugin layer[^glreadme][^velox] | C++ (ClickHouse built as the library `libch.so`)[^glch] | Rust (Apache DataFusion), with a Scala/Java plugin layer[^cmp] | C++[^photondocs] |
| License / open source | Apache License 2.0[^sparklic] | Apache License 2.0 (Gluten); Velox is also Apache License 2.0[^velox] | Apache License 2.0 (Gluten) | Apache License 2.0[^cmreadme] | Proprietary; not open source[^photonoss] |
| Foundation status | ASF top-level project[^sparkhome] | ASF top-level project since 2026-02-18[^incubator] | Same project as Gluten (Velox backend) | Sub-project of Apache DataFusion; a proposal to become top-level project "Apache Comet" is pending[^cmtlp] | None (Databricks product) |
| How it is enabled | Default; `spark.sql.codegen.wholeStage=true`[^sqlconf] | `spark.plugins=org.apache.gluten.GlutenPlugin`, off-heap memory, `ColumnarShuffleManager`[^glreadme] | Same plugin plus `spark.gluten.sql.columnar.libpath` pointing at `libch.so`[^glch] | `spark.plugins=org.apache.spark.CometPlugin`, off-heap memory, `CometShuffleManager`[^cmreadme] | Databricks compute setting; default on SQL warehouses[^photondocs] |
| Fallback behaviour | Not applicable; operators that do not support code generation run without it | Per operator, to vanilla Spark, with ColumnarToRow and RowToColumnar transitions[^glreadme] | Same mechanism as the Velox backend[^glreadme] | Per query stage, to Spark[^cmops] | To the Spark runtime for unsupported operations[^photondocs] |
| Primary source | [Spark 4.3.0 documentation](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/) | [gluten.apache.org](https://gluten.apache.org) | [Gluten ClickHouse backend guide](https://github.com/apache/gluten/blob/main/docs/backends/clickhouse/get-started/ClickHouse.md) | [datafusion.apache.org/comet](https://datafusion.apache.org/comet) | [Databricks documentation](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/photon); SIGMOD 2022 paper[^paper] |

## What a native execution engine is not

- **Not Project Tungsten.** [Project Tungsten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Tungsten) made Spark's JVM execution faster with binary rows, managed memory and generated Java code; it does not leave the JVM. Native engines replace those JVM operators.[^wscg]
- **Not GPU acceleration.** GPU plugins, such as the NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark (formerly the RAPIDS Accelerator for Apache Spark), also replace Spark operators, but run them on GPUs through the cuDF libraries.[^cudf] See [GPU acceleration in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GPU_acceleration_in_Spark).
- **Not a separate query engine.** A native execution engine for Spark has no SQL parser or scheduler of its own in this setup; Spark plans and distributes the work.[^glreadme]

# Open lakehouse

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Open data lakehouse</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data engineering, data management</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">2020 (term "lakehouse"); formalized in a 2021 paper</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Object storage, [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Open table formats](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog), query engines</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi), [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog), [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Agentic lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Agentic_lakehouse), [Medallion architecture](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Medallion_architecture)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the CIDR 2021 lakehouse paper, the Databricks January 2020 lakehouse post, the Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake specifications, the Unity Catalog OSS and Apache Polaris documentation</Verified>

An **open lakehouse** is a data platform architecture in which tables are stored as open file formats on low-cost object storage, managed by an open [table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), registered in an open [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog), and processed by any compatible engine. It combines the cheap, directly accessible storage of a data lake with the transactions, versioning and performance features of a data warehouse. The word "open" means that no layer depends on a single vendor: data written by one engine can be read by another without copying or conversion.

## Definition

The lakehouse paper presented at the Conference on Innovative Data Systems Research (CIDR) in January 2021 defines a lakehouse as a data management system built on low-cost, directly accessible storage that also provides analytical database features such as ACID transactions, data versioning, auditing, indexing, caching and query optimization.[^cidr] The same paper characterizes lakehouses by open direct-access data formats such as Apache Parquet and ORC, first-class support for machine learning and data science, and state-of-the-art performance.[^cidr]

An open lakehouse applies that definition with an added constraint: the formats, the table specification, the catalog interface and the engines are open source or openly specified. The openlakehouse.io guides describe this as an architecture assembled from open table formats, open catalogs, open compute engines and open machine learning tools, on storage the organization controls.[^olio-osde]

## History

Databricks described the lakehouse as a new, open architecture that combines elements of data lakes and data warehouses in a blog post published on 30 January 2020.[^dbx2020] The CIDR 2021 paper by Michael Armbrust, Ali Ghodsi, Reynold Xin and Matei Zaharia set out the argument in academic form.[^cidr]

The CIDR paper frames the lakehouse as a third generation of analytics platforms. The first generation loaded operational data into on-premises data warehouses that coupled compute and storage. The second generation put raw data into data lakes, which are low-cost storage systems with a file API holding open formats such as Parquet and ORC, and copied a subset of that data into a warehouse for business intelligence.[^cidr] The lakehouse removes the second copy by adding warehouse features directly on top of the lake.

The enabling technology, according to the paper, is a metadata layer over the files in the lake. The paper names [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) (begun at Databricks in 2016), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) (started at Netflix) and [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) (started at Uber) as systems of this kind.[^cidr] These metadata layers are now usually called open table formats.

## Architecture

An open lakehouse is usually described as a stack of independent layers. Each layer talks to the next through a published specification, so any one layer can be replaced.

| Layer | Role | Open source examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Object storage | Holds data files and metadata files | Any S3-compatible store, HDFS |
| File format | Stores rows in columnar files | [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet)[^parquet] |
| Table format | Groups files into tables with snapshots and atomic commits | [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) |
| Catalog | Names tables, stores the pointer to current metadata, enforces access | [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog), [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), any [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) |
| Engines | Read and write tables for SQL, batch, streaming and machine learning | [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB) |
| Pipelines and orchestration | Define and schedule transformations | [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines), [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Apache Airflow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Airflow) |

The table format is the layer that turns a directory of files into a table. In Apache Iceberg, every change writes a new metadata file and replaces the old one with an atomic swap, which gives readers serializable isolation without locks.[^icespec] In Delta Lake, writers add a new entry to a transaction log stored next to the data, and readers use the log to select the files that make up one consistent snapshot.[^deltaproto]

The catalog is the layer that makes tables discoverable and governable. The CIDR paper notes that a metadata layer can check whether a client may access a table before giving it credentials to read the underlying files.[^cidr] Unity Catalog OSS implements this as credential vending: the catalog issues short-lived storage credentials scoped to one table or volume.[^ucwhat]

## What makes a lakehouse open

A lakehouse is open when each interface between layers is public and implemented by more than one project. In practice this covers four interfaces: the data file format (for example Parquet), the table format specification (for example the Iceberg table spec or the Delta transaction log protocol), the catalog API (for example the [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) specification), and the engine connectors that read them.

The Iceberg REST catalog specification is a common example of an open interface. The Iceberg project created it so that a new language or engine can work with any catalog through one client implementation.[^icerest] Apache Polaris implements this API and lists Apache Spark, Apache Flink, Trino and other engines as clients.[^polaris]

Openness across table formats is partial. Delta Lake's Universal Format (UniForm) generates Iceberg metadata for a Delta table so that Iceberg clients can read it from the same data files.[^uniform] Apache XTable, an incubating Apache project, translates metadata between Hudi, Delta Lake and Iceberg.[^xtable]

## Comparison with data warehouses and data lakes

| Property | Data warehouse | Data lake | Open lakehouse |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Storage | Managed by the warehouse | Files on low-cost storage | Files on low-cost storage |
| Data format | Internal to the system | Open file formats | Open file formats plus an open table format |
| ACID transactions | Yes | No | Yes, through the table format |
| Access by other engines | Through the warehouse only | Direct file access | Direct access through the table format and catalog |

The comparison follows the generations described in the CIDR 2021 paper.[^cidr]

## Limitations

The CIDR 2021 paper noted that Delta Lake, Iceberg and Hudi supported transactions on only one table at a time, and that storing a transaction log in an object store limits the commit rate because of object store latency.[^cidr] The Iceberg REST catalog specification lists multi-table commits among the features the REST protocol enables.[^icerest]

Catalog-based access control applies only to requests that go through the catalog. The Unity Catalog OSS documentation warns that anyone with direct storage credentials can bypass catalog checks, so the storage itself must also be locked down.[^ucwhat]

## Use with AI agents

<Hatnote>Main article: [Agentic lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Agentic_lakehouse)</Hatnote>

An [agentic lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Agentic_lakehouse) is an open lakehouse designed so that AI agents can find, query and change data under platform-enforced controls. It adds agent tools, often served over the [Model Context Protocol](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Model_Context_Protocol), declarative pipelines that the platform validates before they run, and policies on every tool call.[^olio-agentic]

- [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog)
- [Medallion architecture](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Medallion_architecture)
- [Agentic lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Agentic_lakehouse)
- [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog)

# Open table format

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Lakehouse table format, metadata layer</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data management</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Data files, table metadata, snapshots, atomic commits</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Iceberg table spec, the Delta transaction log protocol (PROTOCOL.md on the master branch), the Apache Hudi table types and timeline documentation, the Delta UniForm and Apache XTable documentation</Verified>

An **open table format** is a publicly specified way of organizing data files and metadata on file or object storage so that a collection of files behaves as a single database table, with atomic commits, consistent snapshots and schema management. The format is a specification, not an engine: any engine that implements it can read and write the same table. Open table formats are the layer that turns a data lake into an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse). The best-known open table formats are [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) and [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi).

## Purpose

Plain files in a data lake have no notion of a transaction. Readers cannot tell a half-written batch from a complete one, and there is no record of which files belong to which version of a table. The CIDR 2021 lakehouse paper calls the solution a metadata layer: a record of which objects are part of a table version, updated transactionally, on top of open file formats such as [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) and ORC.[^cidr]

According to the same paper, metadata layers add transactions, zero-copy cloning and time travel to past table versions, and are a natural place to enforce data quality rules and access control.[^cidr]

## History

The CIDR 2021 paper traces the current open table formats to three origins. Databricks began developing Delta Lake in 2016, storing the list of a table's objects as a transaction log in the data lake itself. Apache Iceberg started at Netflix with a similar design. Apache Hudi started at Uber with a focus on streaming ingestion into data lakes.[^cidr]

Today Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi are projects of the Apache Software Foundation, and Delta Lake is a Linux Foundation project.[^iceberg-home][^hudi-overview][^deltaio]

## How it works

All three formats share a pattern. Data lives in immutable files, usually Parquet. A separate set of metadata files records which data files make up each version of the table. A writer prepares new files first, then commits by atomically publishing new metadata. Readers always see a complete version.

- **Apache Iceberg** keeps table state in metadata files. Each change creates a new metadata file and replaces the old one with an atomic swap, usually by updating a pointer held in a [catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog). A snapshot lists its data files through manifest files, which are reused across snapshots.[^icespec]
- **Delta Lake** keeps a transaction log in a `_delta_log` directory next to the data. Each commit is a newline-delimited JSON file named by version number, and periodic checkpoints summarize the log in Parquet. Writers first write data files optimistically, then commit by adding a new log entry.[^deltaproto]
- **Apache Hudi** records every change to the table (writes, table services, schema changes) as an action on a timeline. Each action has a requested instant, which acts as its transaction identifier, and a completed instant.[^hudi-timeline]

## Comparison

The table compares features as described in each project's own specification or documentation.

| Feature | [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) | [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) | [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Origin (per CIDR 2021 paper)[^cidr] | Netflix | Databricks (2016) | Uber |
| Governance | Apache Software Foundation | Linux Foundation | Apache Software Foundation |
| Metadata structure | Table metadata files, manifest lists and manifests[^icespec] | Transaction log of JSON commits with Parquet checkpoints[^deltaproto] | Timeline of actions at instants[^hudi-timeline] |
| Commit mechanism | Atomic swap of the table metadata pointer[^icespec] | New entry appended to the log; optimistic writes[^deltaproto] | Action moves from requested to completed on the timeline[^hudi-timeline] |
| Row-level deletes | Delete files; deletion vectors from format version 3[^icespec] | Optional deletion vectors[^deltaproto] | Copy-on-write rewrites base files; merge-on-read writes log files merged at query time[^hudi-types] |
| Reading past versions | Snapshots of the table at points in time[^icespec] | Snapshots by table version[^deltaproto] | Time travel queries at timeline instants[^hudi-types] |
| Incremental reads | Engines can read only the data appended between two snapshots, for example with the Spark `start-snapshot-id` and `end-snapshot-id` read options[^n1] | Readers can tail the log to find added data[^deltaproto] | Incremental and change data capture queries[^hudi-types] |
| Schema and partition evolution | Full schema evolution and partition spec evolution[^icespec] | Column mapping supports renaming and dropping columns without rewriting data[^deltaproto] | Supports schema evolution on write and through SQL DDL[^n2] |

## Format versions

Open table formats evolve through versioned specifications so that older readers do not misread newer tables.

Apache Iceberg numbers its format versions. Version 1 defines analytic tables over immutable Parquet, Avro and ORC files. Version 2 adds row-level deletes. Version 3 adds new data types (including variant, geometry and geography), column default values, row lineage, binary deletion vectors and table encryption keys. As of November 2026, the specification describes version 4 as under active development and not formally adopted.[^icespec]

Delta Lake versions its protocol with a reader version and a writer version. Reader version 3 and writer version 7 add named table features, which let a table declare the individual capabilities a client must support.[^deltaproto]

## Interoperability between formats

Because Iceberg, Delta Lake and Hudi all store Parquet data files under their own metadata, tools can expose one copy of the data in more than one format.

Delta Lake's Universal Format (UniForm) generates Iceberg metadata, and in preview Hudi metadata, for a Delta table, so that Iceberg and Hudi clients can read it.[^uniform]

Apache XTable, an incubating Apache project formerly named OneTable, reads a table's existing metadata and writes metadata for one or more of the other formats, in any direction among Hudi, Delta Lake and Iceberg.[^xtable]

## Relationship to catalogs

<Hatnote>Main article: [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog)</Hatnote>

A table format defines how one table is stored. A catalog maps table names to the current metadata of each table and coordinates commits. In Iceberg, the catalog stores the pointer to each table's current metadata file and performs the atomic update of that pointer.[^polaris-docs] Delta Lake's protocol also defines catalog-managed tables, in which the catalog is the source of truth for whether a commit succeeded.[^deltaproto]

- [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet)

# Output mode

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Output_mode

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Streaming output mode</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Append, update, complete; result table; [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (`outputMode` on `writeStream`)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), [Windowing (stream processing)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Windowing_(stream_processing)), [foreachBatch](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/ForeachBatch), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming programming guide (output modes, joins, unsupported operations, session windows) and Real-time Mode guide, the Delta Lake table streaming documentation and the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 Spark Structured Streaming page</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), the **output mode** of a streaming query says which rows of the query's result table are written to the sink after each trigger: only new rows (**append**), only rows that changed (**update**) or the whole result (**complete**). The mode is set with `outputMode(...)` on `writeStream`, and each kind of query supports only some modes.[^ss-out] The output mode also decides how a [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) affects state and when windowed results appear.

## What are the three output modes?

- **Append** is the default. Only rows added to the result table since the last trigger are written, and a row is written once. It is allowed only for queries whose result rows never change afterwards, such as `select`, `where`, `map`, `flatMap`, `filter` and joins.[^ss-out]
- **Update** writes only the rows of the result table that changed since the last trigger. It has been available since Spark 2.1.1.[^ss-out]
- **Complete** writes the whole result table after every trigger. It is supported for aggregation queries.[^ss-out]

The result table is a model, not a stored table: Spark keeps only the state it needs to produce the next output, and the sink decides how written rows are applied.

## Which queries allow which output modes?

The table follows the compatibility matrix in the Spark 4.3.0 guide.[^ss-out]

| Query type | Append | Update | Complete | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Aggregation on event time with a watermark | Yes | Yes | Yes | Append emits each window once, after the watermark passes it, and drops its state. Update also drops old state. Complete keeps all state. |
| Other aggregations | No | Yes | Yes | Without a watermark, aggregates can change at any time, so append is not allowed and old state is never dropped. |
| `mapGroupsWithState` | No | Yes | No | Aggregations are not allowed in the same query. |
| `flatMapGroupsWithState` | In append operation mode | In update operation mode | No | Aggregations are allowed after it only in append operation mode. |
| Joins | Yes | No | No | See [Stream-stream join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream-stream_join). |
| Other queries | Yes | Yes | No | Complete would mean keeping all unaggregated data. |

Further restrictions apply to some operators. Streaming [session window](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Session_window) aggregations do not support update mode.[^ss-types] Sorting a streaming DataFrame is supported only after an aggregation and in complete mode, and chaining several stateful operators is not supported in update or complete mode.[^ss-unsup] Real-time Mode, added in Spark 4.1.0, requires update mode; a query with any other mode fails to start.[^rtm]

## How does the output mode interact with watermarks?

For a windowed count with a 10-minute watermark, the three modes give different output streams for the same input:[^ss-out][^ss-late]
- In append mode, the window 12:00 to 12:10 is written once, with its final count, after the watermark passes 12:10. Its output is therefore delayed by the watermark threshold.
- In update mode, the window's running count is written after every trigger in which it changes, until the watermark passes it.
- In complete mode, every window ever seen is written after every trigger, and no state is dropped.

For the watermark to clean aggregation state, the output mode must be append or update, the aggregation must group by the event-time column or a window on it, and `withWatermark` must be called on that column before the aggregation.[^ss-late]

## Which output modes do table formats support as sinks?

The [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) streaming sink supports append mode, which adds new records to the table, and complete mode, which replaces the table with each batch's result.[^delta] To apply update-mode output to a Delta table as row-level upserts, the Delta documentation uses [foreachBatch](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/ForeachBatch) with `MERGE`, and describes update mode as much more efficient than complete mode for streaming aggregates.[^delta-merge]

The [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) Spark sink also supports append mode (append each micro-batch's rows) and complete mode (replace the table contents every micro-batch).[^iceberg]

## Example

```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

counts = (spark.readStream.table("main.web.page_views")
    .withWatermark("ts", "10 minutes")
    .groupBy(F.window("ts", "5 minutes"), "page")
    .count())

# Final counts only, one row per window, appended to a Delta table
(counts.writeStream
    .outputMode("append")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/checkpoints/page_counts")
    .toTable("main.web.page_counts"))
```

# Pandas API on Spark

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Pandas_API_on_Spark

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">pandas-on-Spark, `pyspark.pandas`; formerly Koalas</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data processing, Python DataFrames</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 3.2.0 (2021)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`pyspark.pandas` DataFrame, Series and Index; default index; options (`compute.*`); conversion to and from Spark DataFrames</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (PySpark) 3.2.0 and later; Koalas for Spark 3.1 and earlier</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [pyspark-client](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Pyspark-client)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">python/pyspark/pandas/config.py and python/pyspark/pandas/__init__.py at tag v4.3.0, the pandas-on-Spark options, best practices and FAQ pages under python/docs/source/tutorial/pandas_on_spark at v4.3.0 (and the options page at v3.2.0, v3.3.0, v3.5.0, v4.0.0 and v4.1.0), the Koalas migration guide at v4.3.0, the Spark 3.2.0, 3.5.0 and 4.0.0 release notes, SPARK-34849, SPARK-42497 and SPARK-52026, the databricks/koalas repository and README, and the koalas and pyspark packages on PyPI</Verified>

**Pandas API on Spark** (the `pyspark.pandas` module, also called pandas-on-Spark) is the part of PySpark in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) that implements the pandas DataFrame, Series and Index API on top of Spark, so code written for pandas can run distributed on a Spark cluster.[^r320] It was added in Spark 3.2.0 through SPARK-34849, which brought the Koalas project into PySpark.[^spip] The API looks like pandas, but results depend on Spark's distributed execution, which changes how the index, row order and some operations behave.[^options]

## What is pandas API on Spark?

Pandas API on Spark is imported as `import pyspark.pandas as ps`. A pandas-on-Spark DataFrame is backed by a Spark DataFrame and runs through the Spark SQL engine, so Spark configuration, the web UI and deployment modes apply to it unchanged.[^bp] The Spark 3.2.0 release notes describe it as letting pandas users scale out their applications on Spark with a one-line code change.[^r320]

The pandas-on-Spark FAQ recommends the pandas API for users who already know pandas and want to work with large data, and the PySpark DataFrame API for users learning Spark from the start.[^faq] In Spark 4.3.0, the pandas-on-Spark extra of the `pyspark` package requires pandas 2.2.0 or later and PyArrow 18.0.0 or later.[^n1]

## How is pandas API on Spark used?

A pandas-on-Spark DataFrame can be created directly, converted from a Spark DataFrame with `DataFrame.pandas_api()`, and converted back with `to_spark()`. Converting to a plain pandas DataFrame with `to_pandas()` collects all data to the client, so it suits only small results.[^pyspark-conv]

```python
import pyspark.pandas as ps

sdf = spark.createDataFrame(
    [(1, "a", 10.0), (2, "b", 20.0), (3, "a", 30.0)],
    ["order_id", "category", "amount"],
)

# Use a real column as the index instead of generating a default index
psdf = sdf.pandas_api(index_col="order_id")
psdf["amount_with_tax"] = psdf["amount"] * 1.2

print(psdf.groupby("category")["amount"].sum().sort_index())

result = psdf.to_spark(index_col="order_id")  # back to a Spark DataFrame
```

Pandas API on Spark also works over [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect): Spark 3.5.0 added pandas API support to the Python Spark Connect client (SPARK-42497).[^r350] The pure-Python [pyspark-client](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Pyspark-client) package includes `pyspark.pandas`.[^n2]

## How does pandas API on Spark differ from pandas?

### Default index

A pandas DataFrame always has an index. When pandas API on Spark creates a DataFrame from a Spark DataFrame without an index column, it attaches a **default index**, whose type is set by `compute.default_index_type`.[^options] The three types are:[^options]
- `sequence`: a sequence increasing by one, computed with a Window function without a partition specification, which moves all data to one partition; the documentation says to avoid it for large data.
- `distributed-sequence` (the default): a globally sequential index computed in a distributed way with a group-by and group-map approach.
- `distributed`: `monotonically_increasing_id` values, fully distributed but not consecutive and not deterministic.

The default was `sequence` in Spark 3.2.0 and has been `distributed-sequence` since Spark 3.3.0.[^opt320][^n3] The best practices guide warns that `distributed-sequence` does not keep the same row-to-index mapping across operations such as `apply()`, `groupby()` or `transform()`, which can attach results to the wrong rows. It recommends setting an explicit index column, persisting the DataFrame, or using `sequence`.[^bp]

### Row order

Pandas API on Spark does not guarantee row order. With `compute.ordered_head` at its default of `False`, `head()` can return rows from any partitions; setting it to `True` makes `head()` follow natural order at extra cost.[^options][^config]

### Operations that are slow or behave differently

- **Single-partition operations.** Some APIs, such as `DataFrame.rank`, use a Window without a partition specification and move all data to one machine; the guide suggests `GroupBy.rank` instead.[^bp]
- **Operations on different DataFrames.** Combining two DataFrames or Series needs an internal join. `compute.ops_on_diff_frames` defaulted to `False` through Spark 3.5 and defaults to `True` from Spark 4.0.0.[^n4][^opt400][^config]
- **Column names.** Names with leading and trailing double underscores are reserved, duplicate column names are not allowed, and case-sensitive column names are disallowed unless `spark.sql.caseSensitive` is enabled.[^bp]
- **Shortcut limits.** `compute.shortcut_limit` and `compute.max_rows` (both 1000 by default) control when small inputs are computed by collecting them and using pandas.[^options]
- **Streaming.** Pandas API on Spark does not officially support [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming); the FAQ suggests using it inside `foreachBatch`.[^faq]

### ANSI mode

Spark 4.0.0 enables ANSI SQL mode by default. In Spark 4.0.0, pandas API on Spark raises `PANDAS_API_ON_SPARK_FAIL_ON_ANSI_MODE` when ANSI mode is on, unless `compute.fail_on_ansi_mode` is set to `False` (SPARK-52026).[^jira52026][^opt400] Spark 4.1.0 added the option `compute.ansi_mode_support`, which defaults to `True`; the fail-on-ANSI check raises only when that option is `False`.[^n5][^config]

## Is pandas API on Spark deprecated?

No. As of Spark 4.3.0, `pyspark.pandas` ships in PySpark, and its module code and documentation contain no deprecation notice.[^config][^options] Individual methods have been removed: the Spark 4.0.0 release notes list the removal of deprecated APIs from pandas API on Spark (SPARK-45550), and the migration guide lists `DataFrame.koalas` and the PySpark `DataFrame.to_koalas` and `to_pandas_on_spark` aliases as removed in Spark 4.0, replaced by `pandas_on_spark` and `pandas_api`.[^r400][^k2p]

## History

Pandas API on Spark began as **Koalas**, a separate open source project in the `databricks/koalas` GitHub repository, created on 3 January 2019 and licensed under the Apache License 2.0.[^koalas-repo] Koalas 0.1.0 was published on PyPI on 23 April 2019, and its last release, 1.8.2, on 19 October 2021.[^koalas-pypi]

The SPIP SPARK-34849, "Support pandas API layer on PySpark", was filed on 24 March 2021 to port Koalas into PySpark, and the work shipped in Spark 3.2.0 as the `pyspark.pandas` module.[^spip][^r320] The Koalas README now marks the project as deprecated: it supports Spark 3.1 and earlier, the repository is in maintenance mode, and users of Spark 3.2 and later are told to use PySpark directly. The repository was not archived on the date checked.[^koalas-repo]

Migration from Koalas mostly means changing `import databricks.koalas as ks` to `import pyspark.pandas as ps`. The Spark migration guide lists the renamed and removed Koalas-specific names, such as `databricks.koalas.__version__`, replaced by `pyspark.__version__`.[^k2p] The usage-logger environment variable `KOALAS_USAGE_LOGGER` is still read for compatibility, after `PYSPARK_PANDAS_USAGE_LOGGER`.[^n6]

# Pandas UDF

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Pandas_UDF

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Vectorized UDF, `pandas_udf`</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 2.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`pandas_udf` decorator, Python type hints, Arrow record batches, Python worker</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (PySpark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[User-defined function (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/User-defined_function_(Spark)), [Arrow-optimized Python UDF](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Arrow-optimized_Python_UDF), [Apache Arrow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Arrow), [DataFrame](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DataFrame)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (python/pyspark/sql/pandas/functions.py, the "Apache Arrow in PySpark" tutorial, examples/src/main/python/sql/arrow.py, SQLConf.scala, the PySpark migration guide), the Spark 2.3.0 and 4.2.0 release notes and the 2017 Databricks blog post that introduced the feature</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a **pandas UDF** (also called a **vectorized UDF**) is a Python [user-defined function](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/User-defined_function_(Spark)) that Spark runs on batches of rows: Spark sends each batch to a Python worker as [Apache Arrow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Arrow) data, the function receives and returns pandas `Series` or `DataFrame` objects, and the results are sent back to the JVM.[^arrow] Pandas UDFs are defined with `pyspark.sql.functions.pandas_udf`, need no extra configuration, and are called like any other PySpark column function.[^arrow] They were added in Spark 2.3.0 to cut the serialization and per-row call overhead of row-at-a-time Python UDFs.[^api][^blog]

## How does a pandas UDF work?

Spark splits the input columns of a pandas UDF into Arrow record batches, calls the Python function once per batch with the batch as pandas objects, and concatenates the results.[^arrow] The maximum number of rows in one batch is `spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch`, which defaults to 10,000; the PySpark guide advises lowering it when a table has many columns, to avoid out-of-memory errors in the JVM.[^arrow][^sqlconf]

The pandas UDF was announced by Databricks engineers in 2017 for the Spark 2.3 release. Their post explained that row-at-a-time Python UDFs suffer from high serialization and invocation overhead, and reported a benchmark in which pandas UDFs were 3 to over 100 times faster than row-at-a-time UDFs.[^blog] The Spark 2.3.0 release notes list "fast data serialization and vectorized execution" for PySpark (SPARK-22216).[^n1]

## Which pandas UDF types exist?

Since Spark 3.0, the Python type hints of the function decide the kind of pandas UDF. The older `functionType` argument with `PandasUDFType` is still accepted, but PySpark 4.3.0 emits a `UserWarning` saying that it "will be deprecated in the future releases" (SPARK-28264).[^arrow][^api]

| Type | Type hints | Output length | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Series to Series | `pd.Series, ... -> pd.Series` | Same as input | Column transformations |
| Iterator of Series to Iterator of Series | `Iterator[pd.Series] -> Iterator[pd.Series]` | Same as input, in total | Expensive set-up (for example loading a model) done once per partition |
| Iterator of multiple Series to Iterator of Series | `Iterator[Tuple[pd.Series, ...]] -> Iterator[pd.Series]` | Same as input, in total | As above, with several input columns |
| Series to Scalar | `pd.Series, ... -> Any` (a scalar) | One value per group or window | Aggregations in `groupBy().agg()` and window functions |

Source for the table: the PySpark 4.3.0 Arrow guide.[^arrow] A `pandas.DataFrame` hint replaces `pandas.Series` when an input or output column is a `StructType`.[^arrow]

Series-to-Scalar pandas UDFs do not support partial aggregation: all data for a group or window is loaded into memory.[^arrow] Spark 4.2.0 added an iterator form for grouped aggregation.[^api]

## What are pandas function APIs?

Pandas function APIs apply a Python function to a whole PySpark [DataFrame](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DataFrame) instead of to a column. They use the same Arrow transfer as pandas UDFs.[^arrow]

- `DataFrame.mapInPandas` maps an iterator of `pandas.DataFrame` to another iterator, and the output can have any length.
- `DataFrame.groupBy().applyInPandas()` applies a function to each group as one `pandas.DataFrame` (the split-apply-combine pattern). It replaces the grouped map pandas UDF of Spark 2.x.
- `DataFrame.groupBy().cogroup().applyInPandas()` applies a function to two DataFrames that share a key.

For grouped and cogrouped maps, all data for a group is loaded into memory before the function runs, and `maxRecordsPerBatch` is not applied, so skewed groups can cause out-of-memory errors.[^arrow]

## Example

The following PySpark example works on Spark 4.3.0 with pandas and PyArrow installed. It defines a Series-to-Series UDF and a Series-to-Scalar UDF.

```python
import pandas as pd
from pyspark.sql.functions import pandas_udf

@pandas_udf("long")
def multiply(a: pd.Series, b: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    return a * b

@pandas_udf("double")
def mean_udf(v: pd.Series) -> float:
    return v.mean()

df = spark.createDataFrame([(1, 1.0), (1, 2.0), (2, 3.0)], ["id", "v"])
df.select(multiply("id", "id")).show()
df.groupBy("id").agg(mean_udf("v")).show()
```

## What are the requirements and type rules?

In PySpark 4.3.0 the minimum supported versions are pandas 2.2.0 and PyArrow 18.0.0.[^arrow] All Spark SQL data types are supported by Arrow-based conversion except an `ArrayType` of `TimestampType`.[^arrow]

Timestamps passed to a pandas UDF are converted to nanosecond precision and localized to the session time zone (`spark.sql.session.timeZone`); timestamps returned are converted to UTC microseconds.[^arrow]

Since Spark 4.2, a nullable integer column whose batch contains nulls arrives as a pandas nullable integer extension type (`Int8` to `Int64`) instead of `float64`.[^upgrade] Since Spark 4.1, `spark.sql.execution.pandas.convertToArrowArraySafely` is on by default, so unsafe conversions in returned data, such as integer overflow, raise errors.[^upgrade]

## Pandas UDF vs Arrow UDF and Arrow-optimized Python UDF

An [Arrow-optimized Python UDF](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Arrow-optimized_Python_UDF) also uses Arrow for transfer, but the function still runs once per row on Python objects.[^arrow] An Arrow UDF (`arrow_udf`, Spark 4.1.0 and later) is vectorized like a pandas UDF, but the function receives `pyarrow.Array` objects instead of pandas objects and avoids the pandas conversion.[^n2] Pandas UDFs have supported [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) since Spark 3.4.0.[^api] See [User-defined function (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/User-defined_function_(Spark)) for a comparison of all UDF types.

# Parameterized queries (Spark SQL)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Parameterized_queries_(Spark_SQL)

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Parameter markers, parameterized SQL, bind parameters</Field>
  <Field name="field">Query languages, application security</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 3.4.0 (named parameters); 3.5.0 (positional parameters)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Named markers (`:name`), unnamed markers (`?`), `args` of `SparkSession.sql()`, `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE ... USING`, `IDENTIFIER` clause</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark SQL](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_SQL), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [SQL injection](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SQL_injection)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/sql-ref-parameter-markers.md, docs/sql-ref-syntax-aux-exec-imm.md, docs/sql-ref-identifier-clause.md, python/pyspark/sql/session.py, python/pyspark/sql/sql_formatter.py, SQLConf.scala, ParameterHandler.scala, SparkSqlParser.scala, error-conditions.json) and the Spark 3.4.0, 3.5.0, 4.0.0 and 4.1.0 release notes</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) SQL, a **parameterized query** is a SQL statement that contains typed placeholders, called parameter markers, whose values are supplied separately by the calling API instead of being written into the SQL text.[^markers] Spark supports named markers (`:name`) and unnamed, positional markers (`?`). Because the values never become part of the statement text, the Spark documentation states that parameter markers protect code from SQL injection attacks.[^markers]

## What are parameter markers in Spark SQL?

A Spark SQL parameter marker stands for a value that the caller binds when the statement runs. The Spark documentation describes two kinds:[^markers]

- **Named parameter markers** are written as a colon followed by an unqualified identifier, for example `:min_amount`. The caller passes name-value pairs. The same name can appear several times in one statement, and the caller may pass names that the statement does not use. The colon keeps parameter names apart from column names and SQL variables.
- **Unnamed parameter markers** are written as `?`. The caller passes an ordered list, and each `?` consumes the next value. Extra values are allowed.

A statement cannot mix named and unnamed markers.[^markers] Spark raises the error `INVALID_QUERY_MIXED_QUERY_PARAMETERS` (SQLSTATE 42613) when it does, and `UNBOUND_SQL_PARAMETER` (SQLSTATE 42P02) when a marker has no value.[^errors]

## How do parameterized queries prevent SQL injection?

A Spark SQL parameter marker always receives a value as a typed literal, never as SQL text written by the caller, so the value cannot change the structure of the statement. The Spark documentation gives this separation of values from SQL text as the reason that parameter markers protect against SQL injection.[^markers] A string such as `' OR 1=1 --` passed as a parameter is treated as a string value, not as SQL.

In Spark 4.3 the binding happens in one of two ways. By default, a pre-parser finds the markers and replaces each one with the SQL form of a resolved `Literal` expression, which quotes and escapes string values; the parameter handler rejects any value that is not a resolved literal. With the legacy setting described below, the markers are kept in the parsed plan and substitution is deferred to the analysis phase.[^handler][^parser]

Parameter markers replace literal values only. Table names, column names and other identifiers cannot be passed as plain markers. For those, Spark SQL provides the `IDENTIFIER` clause, which turns a constant string, which can be built from string literals and parameter markers, into an object name. The Spark documentation states that the clause exists to allow templating of identifiers without opening up the risk of SQL injection, and that the string must be a valid, possibly qualified, identifier.[^identifier]

## How are parameters passed from PySpark?

In PySpark, `SparkSession.sql(sqlQuery, args=None, **kwargs)` takes the parameters in its `args` argument: a dictionary for named markers or a list for positional markers.[^session] Each value is a Python object that Spark converts to a SQL literal, or a `Column` made with a literal or with a collection constructor such as `array()`, `map()` or `struct()`.[^session] The method docstring marks parameterized SQL and Spark Connect support as added in 3.4.0 and positional parameters as added in 3.5.0.[^session] Scala and Java use the `args` parameter of `SparkSession.sql()` with a `Map` or an array.[^markers]

The following PySpark example runs on Spark 4.3, in classic mode or through [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect). The first query uses named markers, the second positional markers, and the third an `IDENTIFIER` clause for the view name:

```python
spark.range(10).createOrReplaceTempView("numbers")

# Named markers: a dictionary
spark.sql(
    "SELECT id FROM numbers WHERE id > :lo AND id < :hi",
    args={"lo": 3, "hi": 7},
).show()

# Positional markers: a list, consumed in order
spark.sql("SELECT id FROM numbers WHERE id BETWEEN ? AND ?", args=[2, 4]).show()

# A table name passed safely through IDENTIFIER
spark.sql("SELECT count(*) AS n FROM IDENTIFIER(:tbl)", args={"tbl": "numbers"}).show()
```

## How are parameters passed in pure SQL?

Spark SQL binds parameters without a host language through `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE`, which runs a SQL statement given as a string. Its `USING` clause supplies constant expressions that bind to the markers, by position for unnamed markers and by name or alias for named markers. An optional `INTO` clause stores the result of a single-row query in SQL variables.[^execimm]

```sql
DECLARE lo = 3;
EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'SELECT id FROM range(10) WHERE id > :lo AND id < :hi'
  USING lo AS lo, 7 AS hi;
```

## Where can parameter markers appear?

The Spark 4.3 documentation states that parameter markers can be used wherever literal values are allowed in SQL syntax.[^markers] Spark 4.1.0 extended this with SPARK-53573, which allows parameter markers everywhere through a pre-parser.[^r410] The internal configuration `spark.sql.legacy.parameterSubstitution.constantsOnly` (default `false`, added in 4.1.0) restores the older behavior, in which markers are allowed only where constant literals are expected in queries and data manipulation statements.[^sqlconf] The `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` reference shows markers used inside a type definition, `DECIMAL(:p, :s)`, and in a column alias through `IDENTIFIER(:col)`.[^execimm]

## Parameter markers vs Python string formatting

PySpark's `SparkSession.sql()` also accepts keyword arguments (`**kwargs`) that it substitutes into the SQL text with the Python standard string formatter, using `{name}` placeholders. The docstring marks this as added in 3.3.0 and describes it as experimental and unstable.[^session] The two mechanisms differ:

|  | Parameter markers (`args`) | Formatter placeholders (`**kwargs`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Syntax in SQL | `:name` or `?`[^markers] | `{name}`[^session] |
| When the value is applied | Bound as a typed literal by Spark, separately from the SQL text the caller writes[^markers][^handler] | Rendered into the SQL text before parsing[^session] |
| Handling of values | Python values converted to SQL literals; `Column` literals and collection constructors accepted[^session] | A `DataFrame` becomes a temporary view name, a `Column` must be a plain column reference, a Python string becomes an escaped string literal, and other values are inserted as formatted by Python[^formatter] |
| Available in | PySpark, Scala, Java, and SQL through `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE`[^markers] | PySpark only |

Both can be used in one call; the PySpark docstring includes an example that references a DataFrame with `{df}` and binds a value with `:minB`.[^session] For values that come from users, the parameter markers are the mechanism that the Spark documentation describes as injection-safe.[^markers]

## History

- **Spark 3.4.0** added parameterized SQL (SPARK-41271, SPARK-42702) and PySpark support for it (SPARK-41666).[^r340]
- **Spark 3.5.0** added positional parameters in Scala and Java (SPARK-44066) and in Python (SPARK-44140), and the `IDENTIFIER` clause (SPARK-43205).[^r350]
- **Spark 4.0.0** added `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` (SPARK-46246), and its release notes list support for map and array parameters in parameterized `sql()` (SPARK-45137, SPARK-45235).[^r400]
- **Spark 4.1.0** allowed parameter markers everywhere through a pre-parser (SPARK-53573).[^r410]

# Partition

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="field">Data engineering</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Spark partitions, table partitions (Hive-style, Iceberg, Delta Lake), Kafka topic partitions</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Kafka](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Kafka)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Predicate pushdown](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown), [Small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs and PySpark source), a run on a Spark 4.3.1-SNAPSHOT build, the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 spec and partitioning docs, the Delta Lake protocol at v4.4.1 and the clustering docs, and the Apache Kafka 4.4 introduction</Verified>

A **partition** is a subset of a dataset that a system stores or processes as one unit. In a lakehouse the word has several distinct meanings, depending on whether it refers to how an engine splits work, how a table lays out files, or how a message log splits a topic. An [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) partition is a slice of data processed by one task. A table partition in Hive, [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) or [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) is a group of files that share partition values. An [Apache Kafka](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Kafka) partition is an ordered log inside a topic. These meanings interact (a Spark job reads table partitions into Spark partitions, and a Kafka source maps topic partitions to Spark partitions), but they are not the same thing.

## Spark in-memory partition

<Hatnote>Main article: [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Hatnote>

In Spark, a partition is a piece of an RDD or DataFrame, and Spark runs one task for each partition.[^rddguide] The number of partitions therefore sets how much parallel work a stage can do on the cluster's [executors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor). When Spark reads files, it packs at most `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes` (default 128 MB) into one partition; after a join or aggregation, it uses `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` (default 200) partitions, which adaptive query execution can coalesce at runtime.[^perf]

Two DataFrame methods change the number of partitions. `repartition` hash-partitions the data and always causes a [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle).[^repartition][^rddguide] `coalesce` only reduces the number of partitions and creates a narrow dependency without a shuffle: going from 1,000 partitions to 100, each new partition claims 10 old ones.[^coalesce]

```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

df = spark.range(0, 1_000_000)
wide = df.repartition(8, "id")   # shuffle into 8 hash partitions
narrow = wide.coalesce(2)        # merge into 2 partitions, no new shuffle

narrow.select(F.spark_partition_id()).distinct().count()   # 2
```

A Spark partition exists only while a job runs. It is not stored, and it is unrelated to the directory layout of the table being read, except that file and partition layout influence how Spark splits its input.

## Hive-style table partitioning

Hive-style partitioning stores a table's files in directories named after partition column values, such as `gender=male/country=US/`. The partition values are encoded in the path of each directory. Spark's built-in file sources discover this layout automatically and add the partition columns to the schema.[^parquet]

Queries skip directories only when they filter on the partition column itself. In Hive, a table partitioned by `event_date` has an explicit `event_date` column, and a query without an `event_date` filter scans every file, even when it filters on the timestamp that the date was derived from.[^icebergpart] Very fine partitioning also produces many small files; see [small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem).

## Apache Iceberg hidden partitioning and partition evolution

<Hatnote>Main article: [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)</Hatnote>

Iceberg uses **hidden partitioning**. A partition spec derives partition values from table columns through transforms such as `identity`, `bucket[N]`, `truncate[W]`, `year`, `month`, `day` and `hour`. Because the table records the transform, Iceberg turns a filter on the source column into a partition filter, and users do not have to add partition predicates to their queries.[^ispec][^icebergpart] Partition values are stored in manifests for each data file, not taken from directory names.[^ispec]

Iceberg also supports **partition evolution**: a table's partitioning can change by adding, removing, renaming or reordering partition fields. Each change creates a new partition spec, and files written under an older spec keep it; at scan time, Iceberg converts filters using the spec each manifest was written with.[^ispec]

## Delta Lake partitioning and liquid clustering

<Hatnote>Main article: [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)</Hatnote>

A [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) table can have partition columns, recorded in the table metadata. The transaction log stores each file's partition values, and readers must take the values from the log. The reference implementation writes files into Hive-style `column=value` directories, but the protocol says this layout only follows convention and is not required.[^dproto]

**Liquid clustering** is Delta Lake's alternative to partitioning and `ZORDER`. A table declares clustering columns with `CLUSTER BY`, `OPTIMIZE` clusters the data incrementally, and the clustering columns can be changed later with `ALTER TABLE` without rewriting existing data. Clustering cannot be combined with partitioning or `ZORDER` on the same table. It is available from Delta Lake 3.1.0, and the preview flag was removed in 3.2.[^dcluster] The protocol requires writers of clustered tables to record per-file statistics for the clustering columns, which readers use for data skipping.[^dproto]

## Apache Kafka topic partitions

A Kafka topic is split into partitions spread over brokers. Events with the same key go to the same partition, consumers read each partition in the order its events were written, and replication works per partition.[^kafka] Ordering is guaranteed within a partition, not across a topic.

When [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) reads from Kafka, Spark by default maps each Kafka topic partition to one Spark partition. The `minPartitions` option asks Spark to split large Kafka partitions into more Spark partitions.[^sskafka]

## Which partition am I looking at?

| Meaning | Where it lives | Lifetime | Who decides it | Changed by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Spark partition | Memory and local disk of executors | One job or stage | Spark (file split size, shuffle partitions, AQE) or the user | `repartition`, `coalesce`, SQL hints[^perf] |
| Hive-style table partition | Directory names in storage (`col=value/`) | Permanent, part of the table | Table author (partition columns) | Writing the data into a new directory layout |
| Iceberg partition | Partition tuples in manifests, derived by transforms | Permanent, per partition spec | Table author (partition spec) | Partition evolution; old files keep their spec[^ispec] |
| Delta Lake partition or cluster | Partition values or statistics in the transaction log | Permanent | Table author (`PARTITIONED BY` or `CLUSTER BY`) | Clustering columns via `ALTER TABLE`[^dcluster] |
| Kafka topic partition | Brokers | Lifetime of the topic | Topic configuration; the event key decides which partition an event goes to[^kafka] | Kafka topic administration |

# Partition pruning

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition_pruning

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Partition elimination, partition filtering</Field>
  <Field name="field">Query optimization</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Partition columns or transforms, partition filters, catalog or table metadata, runtime filters</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Partition](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), [Dynamic partition pruning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dynamic_partition_pruning), [Predicate pushdown](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown), [Column pruning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Column_pruning), [Bucketing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Bucketing)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (SQLConf.scala, FileSourceStrategy.scala, DataSourceScanExec.scala, FileScan.scala, PartitionPruning.scala, SupportsRuntimeFiltering.java, SupportsRuntimeV2Filtering.java), Spark JIRA SPARK-11150 and SPARK-35779, the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 spec and Spark source, and the Delta Lake protocol at v4.4.1</Verified>

**Partition pruning** is a query optimization in which an engine uses the filters of a query to skip whole partitions of a table, so that the files in partitions that cannot match are never listed or read. In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) it comes in two forms: **static partition pruning**, where the filter on a partition column is known when the query is planned, and **[dynamic partition pruning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dynamic_partition_pruning)**, where the filter values are only known at run time, usually from the other side of a join. Table formats such as [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) and [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) do the pruning from their metadata instead of from directory names.

## What does partition pruning skip?

Partition pruning works at the coarsest level of data skipping. It removes whole [table partitions](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition) before any file is opened, while [predicate pushdown](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown) into the file format skips row groups and pages inside the files that remain. For built-in file sources, Spark sorts the filters of a scan into partition filters, which prune directories; bucket filters, which prune bucket files; data filters, which are pushed to the file reader; and filters that must be evaluated again after the scan.[^fss]

## Static partition pruning

Static partition pruning applies when a query filters a partition column with a value known at planning time:

```sql
-- sales is partitioned by sale_date
SELECT store_id, SUM(amount)
FROM sales
WHERE sale_date >= DATE'2026-11-01'
GROUP BY store_id;
```

For a Hive-style table, each partition is a directory such as `sale_date=2026-11-01/`, and Spark lists only the directories whose values satisfy the filter. For tables stored in a Hive metastore, `spark.sql.hive.metastorePartitionPruning` (default true, since 1.5.0) pushes partition predicates into the metastore, so that Spark fetches only the matching partition metadata.[^sqlconf]

Spark uses a filter for partition pruning when it is deterministic and refers only to partition columns; an expression over a partition column, such as `year(sale_date) = 2026`, still qualifies.[^fss] A filter on a different column does not, even when it is related: `WHERE sale_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2026-11-01 00:00:00'` on a table partitioned by a separate `sale_date` column prunes nothing, because Spark does not know how the two columns relate. Iceberg's hidden partitioning addresses this case (see below).

## Dynamic partition pruning

<Hatnote>Main article: [Dynamic partition pruning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dynamic_partition_pruning)</Hatnote>

Dynamic partition pruning (DPP) prunes partitions using values that Spark learns while the query runs. In a join of a partitioned fact table with a filtered dimension table, Spark uses the join keys that survive the dimension filter as a partition filter on the fact table. DPP was added in Spark 3.0.0 (SPARK-11150) and is on by default through `spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.enabled`.[^sqlconf][^n1]

Data Source V2 connectors take part in runtime pruning through `SupportsRuntimeFiltering` (since Spark 3.2.0) and `SupportsRuntimeV2Filtering` (since 3.4.0), which let a scan drop planned input partitions using predicates Spark infers during execution.[^rtf][^n2]

## Static vs dynamic partition pruning

|  | Static partition pruning | Dynamic partition pruning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When the filter is known | At planning time, from a literal or constant expression | At run time, from the result of another part of the query |
| Typical query | `WHERE sale_date = '2026-11-01'` | `JOIN dim_date d ON f.sale_date = d.date WHERE d.is_holiday` |
| Shown in Spark plans as | A plain predicate in `PartitionFilters` | `dynamicpruningexpression(...)` in `PartitionFilters`, fed by a subquery or a reused broadcast |
| Setting | Always on for partition columns | `spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.enabled` (default true)[^sqlconf] |

## What to look for in a Spark plan

`EXPLAIN FORMATTED` prints the metadata of each scan. For a built-in file source, the scan node lists `PartitionFilters`, `PushedFilters`, `DataFilters` and `ReadSchema`.[^scanexec][^n3]
- **Static pruning worked** if the partition predicate appears in `PartitionFilters`, for example `PartitionFilters: [isnotnull(sale_date#12), (sale_date#12 >= 2026-11-01)]`.
- **Static pruning did not happen** if `PartitionFilters` is empty and the predicate shows up only in `DataFilters` or in a `Filter` above the scan. Common causes are a filter on a column that is not a partition column, a non-deterministic filter, or a table that Spark does not see as partitioned.
- **Dynamic pruning was planned** if `PartitionFilters` contains `dynamicpruningexpression(...)`. Spark represents a planned dynamic filter with the `DynamicPruningExpression` marker.[^n4]

After the query runs, the scan node in the Spark UI's SQL tab shows the metrics `number of files read` and, for partitioned tables, `number of partitions read`, which measure pruning directly.[^scanexec][^n5]

## Partition pruning in table formats

**[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)** prunes from metadata rather than directory names. Each data file records the partition values it belongs to, and partitions are derived from source columns by transforms such as `day`, `bucket[N]` or `truncate[W]`.[^icebergspec] A filter on the source column, such as `WHERE sale_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2026-11-01 00:00:00'` on a table partitioned by `day(sale_ts)`, therefore prunes partitions without the query naming a partition column; this is called hidden partitioning. Iceberg's Spark batch scan also implements `SupportsRuntimeV2Filtering`, so it takes part in dynamic partition pruning.[^n6]

**[Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)** records the partition values of each data file in the `partitionValues` field of its `add` action in the transaction log, so a reader prunes partitions by filtering the log instead of listing directories.[^deltaprotocol] The same `add` actions can carry per-file column statistics, which Delta uses to skip files inside a partition.[^deltaprotocol]
