# Predicate pushdown

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Filter pushdown, data skipping (at the file level)</Field>
  <Field name="field">Query optimization</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Data source API, file format statistics (Parquet row groups, page indexes, bloom filters), table format metadata, catalog</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Partition](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), [Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (connector read interfaces, PushDownUtils.scala, FileSourceStrategy.scala, SQLConf.scala, docs), EXPLAIN runs on a Spark 4.3.1-SNAPSHOT build, the parquet-format 2.12.0 Thrift definition and parquet.apache.org docs, the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 spec and REST catalog OpenAPI definition, and the Delta Lake protocol at v4.4.1</Verified>

**Predicate pushdown** is a query optimization in which an engine sends the filter conditions of a query (the predicates in a `WHERE` clause) down to the layer that reads the data, so that rows, files or whole partitions that cannot match are never read. In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse) the predicate can travel through several layers: from the engine to the data source connector, from the connector to the file format, from the table format's metadata, and sometimes to the [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog). Each layer skips data in a different way, and a predicate may be used at one layer and not at another.

## Engine to data source

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a connector built on the Data Source V2 API opts in to pushdown by implementing mix-in interfaces on its `ScanBuilder`. `SupportsPushDownFilters` (since Spark 3.0.0) receives filters as `org.apache.spark.sql.sources.Filter` objects.[^spdf] `SupportsPushDownV2Filters` (since 3.3.0) receives V2 `Predicate` objects and is the preferred interface.[^spdv2] Sibling interfaces push down column pruning, limits, aggregates, top-N and joins.[^readpkg]

The source returns the predicates it cannot fully apply, and Spark evaluates those after the scan. A predicate can also be **partially** pushed: the Spark interface uses the Parquet row-group filter as its example of a filter that the source uses to skip data but that Spark must still evaluate on the rows that come back.[^spdf] Pushdown therefore reduces the data read; it does not always remove the `Filter` operator from the plan.

Spark can also push filters that it learns only at runtime. With `SupportsRuntimeV2Filtering` (since 3.4.0), a scan can drop planned input partitions using predicates that Spark infers during execution, for example from the other side of a join.[^runtime] Dynamic partition pruning, on by default (`spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.enabled`), uses a join key to generate a predicate on a partition column.[^sqlconf]

For its built-in file sources, Spark sorts filters into four groups: filters on partition columns, which prune directories; filters on bucket columns, which can prune files; filters on data columns, which are pushed into the file reader; and filters that must be evaluated again after the scan.[^fss]

## Engine to file format

<Hatnote>Main article: [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet)</Hatnote>

[Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) files carry statistics that a reader can compare with a predicate before decoding data:

- **Column chunk statistics.** The file metadata holds optional statistics for each column chunk in each row group, including minimum and maximum values and a null count.[^thrift] A reader skips a row group when, for example, its maximum is below the lower bound of a range filter.
- **Page index.** The optional column index stores lower and upper bounds for each data page, and the offset index locates pages by row number, so a reader can skip pages inside a row group.[^pageindex]
- **Bloom filters.** Minimum and maximum values cannot rule out a value that falls inside the range. A split block bloom filter answers whether a value might be present; it can return false positives but never false negatives, which makes it useful for equality filters on high-cardinality columns.[^bloom]

In Spark, Parquet filter pushdown is controlled by `spark.sql.parquet.filterPushdown` (default true); ORC has the equivalent `spark.sql.orc.filterPushdown`.[^sparkparquet][^sqlconf]

## Table format metadata

Table formats keep statistics for each data file in their metadata, so an engine can skip whole files before opening any of them.

In [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), scan planning first skips manifests whose partition summaries show no match. For the remaining manifests, Iceberg converts the query's predicates into partition predicates using the partition spec each manifest was written with, and then filters data files by the column lower and upper bounds and counts stored in the manifests.[^ispec] Because partition values come from transforms, a filter on a timestamp column can prune files of a table partitioned by `day(ts)`.[^ispec]

In [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), `add` actions in the transaction log can carry per-file statistics (record count, per-column minimum and maximum values and null counts), which the protocol describes as usable for eliminating files based on query predicates.[^dproto] Delta Lake collects these statistics automatically on write for columns up to the position set by `delta.dataSkippingNumIndexedCols`.[^dskip]

## Catalog

Some catalogs accept predicates too. Spark pushes some partition predicates to the Hive metastore so that it lists only matching partitions (`spark.sql.hive.metastorePartitionPruning`, default true).[^sqlconf] The [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) specification defines a server-side scan planning endpoint (`planTableScan`) whose request includes a filter predicate, so the catalog service can plan which files a client reads.[^rest]

## When pushdown does not happen

A predicate is pushed only if the engine can translate it into a form the source understands. Common reasons it stays in the engine:

- **Casts on the column.** Comparing a string column with a number makes Spark cast the column (`cast(code as bigint) = 7`), which has no translation to a source filter. Only `IsNotNull(code)` is pushed in the example below.
- **Functions and UDFs.** A predicate such as `upper(code) = 'A'` or a user-defined function cannot be compared with stored minimum and maximum values, so it is evaluated after the scan.
- **Non-deterministic expressions.** Spark does not push down non-deterministic filters, such as one that uses `rand()`, because a source might evaluate them a different number of times than Spark does.[^pdu][^fss]
- **Missing statistics.** File skipping needs statistics on the filtered column; Delta Lake, for example, collects none for columns past `delta.dataSkippingNumIndexedCols`.[^dskip]

## How to check

In Spark, `EXPLAIN` shows what was pushed. For a file scan, `PartitionFilters` lists predicates used to prune directories, `PushedFilters` lists filters handed to the file reader, and `DataFilters` lists data-column predicates before translation. The following output, from a Spark 4.3.1-SNAPSHOT build, shows a partition column filter, a pushed range filter, and a cast that blocks pushdown (paths shortened):

```
EXPLAIN SELECT order_id FROM orders
WHERE order_date = DATE'2026-11-01' AND amount > 100;

FileScan parquet spark_catalog.default.orders[order_id#20L,amount#21,order_date#23]
  DataFilters: [isnotnull(amount#21), (amount#21 > 100.0)],
  PartitionFilters: [isnotnull(order_date#23), (order_date#23 = 2026-11-01)],
  PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(amount), GreaterThan(amount,100.0)]

EXPLAIN SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE code = 7;   -- code is a STRING

Filter (isnotnull(code#22) AND (cast(code#22 as bigint) = 7))
+- FileScan parquet ... PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(code)]
```

A filter listed in `PushedFilters` can still appear in a `Filter` operator above the scan, because Parquet skips data by row group and page, not by row. The plan shows what was pushed, not how much data was skipped; the SQL tab of the Spark web UI shows run-time metrics for the scan, such as `number of output rows` and `scan time`.[^spdf][^webui]

# Project Nessie

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Nessie

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">Project Nessie contributors; started at Dremio</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">Announced October 2020</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">0.110.1</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-11-21</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Java</Field>
  <Field name="type">Transactional data catalog with Git-like versioning</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[projectnessie.org](https://projectnessie.org/)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/projectnessie/nessie](https://github.com/projectnessie/nessie)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog), [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), [Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the projectnessie/nessie GitHub releases (latest nessie-0.110.1) and CHANGELOG.md, the Nessie README, transactions guide, Iceberg REST guide and configuration reference, the August 2024 Nessie blog post on Apache Polaris, the October 2020 Dremio announcement, CatalogUtil.java at apache-iceberg-1.12.0 and the Trino 484 metastore documentation</Verified>

<Status level="active">Nessie is still released (0.110.1 on 21 November 2026) and no Nessie release or announcement deprecates it. In 2024 the Nessie team announced an intent to contribute Nessie's versioning features to [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris); that plan has not retired Nessie.[^releases]</Status>

**Project Nessie** is an open source transactional [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog) for data lakes that versions table metadata with Git-like commits, branches and tags.[^readme] A change to several tables can be made on a branch and published with one merge, so readers see all of the changes or none of them.[^tx] Nessie works with [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) tables and is reached through its own API or through the [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) API.[^readme][^rest]

## How it works

Nessie keeps a commit log of catalog changes, not of data files. Each commit records the operations it made, a timestamp and the user, and a single commit can change many tables at once.[^tx] For an Iceberg table, the catalog entry points to the table's current metadata; the data and metadata files stay in object storage.

- **Branches** are named, movable pointers to commits. Work done on a branch is invisible on `main` until it is merged.[^tx]
- **Tags** are named references to a fixed commit, used to pin a consistent state of many tables.[^guides]
- **Merges** publish a series of commits from one branch to another as one consistent view, which is how Nessie gives cross-table visibility to engines that have no multi-table transactions of their own.[^tx]

The transactions guide describes three optimistic isolation levels (read committed, repeated read and serializable), with conflicts detected per table; pessimistic locking is not available.[^tx] Nessie stores its commit log in a pluggable version store; the configuration reference covers JDBC, RocksDB, Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB, Bigtable and in-memory stores.[^config]

## How engines connect

Engines reach Nessie in two ways.

|  | Nessie catalog client | Iceberg REST API |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Endpoint | Nessie's own REST API | `/iceberg` on the Nessie server (port 19120 in the default Docker image)[^rest][^readme] |
| Client side | Iceberg's `NessieCatalog` (catalog type `nessie`); Trino's `nessie` Iceberg catalog type[^icebergcat][^n1] | Any Iceberg REST client |
| Choosing a branch | A client property naming the reference | The branch or tag name in the URI, with a mandatory `\|` before the warehouse name, for example `/iceberg/experiments\|sales`[^rest] |
| Maturity | The original integration | Added in Nessie 0.90.2 (June 2024) as beta;[^changelog] the current guide calls it experimental[^rest] |

With the Iceberg REST API, Nessie also manages table locations and vends storage credentials; the guide requires at least one object store and one warehouse to be configured, and notes that some storage integrations are still experimental.[^rest]

## Status

Nessie is an active project. Its latest release is 0.110.1, published on 21 November 2026, and the 0.x version numbers continue; no release marks the project or its server as deprecated.[^releases] Individual parts have been deprecated inside the project, for example the older JDBC, Cassandra and MongoDB version store types in favor of their `JDBC2`, `CASSANDRA2` and `MONGODB2` replacements.[^changelog]

On 2 August 2024, after Snowflake open-sourced the Polaris catalog, the Nessie project wrote that the intent is to contribute Nessie's capabilities, such as catalog-level versioning, Git-like semantics and multi-table transactions, to [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris).[^polaris] The post did not announce an end date for Nessie, and Nessie releases have continued since.[^polaris][^releases]

## History

Dremio announced Project Nessie on 1 October 2020; the announcement by Jacques Nadeau said a small team at Dremio had spent more than a year building it.[^n2] In October 2024 Dremio announced a commercial catalog built on Nessie.[^n3]

# Project Tungsten

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Tungsten

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Tungsten, Tungsten execution engine</Field>
  <Field name="field">Query execution performance</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Spark 1.4.0 (first pieces); phase 1 completed in Spark 1.5.0</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Explicit (on-heap or off-heap) memory management, `UnsafeRow` binary row format, cache-aware sorting and hashing, code generation including whole-stage code generation</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Catalyst optimizer](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Catalyst_optimizer), [Whole-stage code generation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Whole-stage_code_generation), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Native execution engine (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Native_execution_engine_(Spark))</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">SPARK-7075, SPARK-7081, SPARK-9697, SPARK-10708 and SPARK-12795, the Spark 1.4.0, 1.5.0 and 2.0.0 release notes, the v1.5.0, v1.6.0, v2.0.0 and v4.3.0 tags of apache/spark (SQLConf, SetCommand, SparkEnv, ShuffleManager, MemoryManager, TaskMemoryManager, UnsafeRow, WholeStageCodegenExec, docs/configuration.md) and EXPLAIN output from a Spark 4.3 build</Verified>

<Status level="active">Project Tungsten is not deprecated in any Spark release. It was a performance initiative, not a feature with an on/off switch; its code is the default execution path in Spark 4.3.0. Only its old configuration flag, `spark.sql.tungsten.enabled`, was deprecated (Spark 1.6.0) and later dropped.[^mm430]</Status>

**Project Tungsten** is the name of an [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) engineering initiative, started in 2015, to make Spark's execution more efficient in CPU and memory by managing memory explicitly, storing rows in a compact binary format, using CPU caches better and generating code at run time.[^jira7075] Tungsten is not a separate engine or a module that can be installed or turned off: its results (for example the `UnsafeRow` format, Tungsten-managed memory pages and whole-stage code generation) are part of how Spark SQL and DataFrame queries run in every current release. The name survives mostly in source code, configuration aliases and older documentation.

## What the name referred to

The umbrella ticket SPARK-7075, "Project Tungsten (Spark 1.5 Phase 1)", states the premise: most Spark workloads observed by its authors were bottlenecked by CPU and memory rather than by I/O or network. It names three areas of work:[^jira7075][^blog2015]

- **Memory management and binary processing.** Keep data in a binary format instead of as Java objects, to reduce garbage collection overhead and memory use; account for memory in bytes; and let operators that know the data types work directly on the binary data without serialization.
- **Cache-aware computation.** Algorithms and data structures, such as sorting and hashing, laid out to make better use of CPU caches.
- **Code generation.** Generate code at run time for expression evaluation and serialization, to use modern compilers and CPUs better.

The work arrived over several releases. The Spark 1.4.0 release notes list SPARK-7081, a faster sort-based shuffle path, as "Initial performance improvements in project Tungsten".[^r140][^n1] Phase 1 (SPARK-7075) has fix version 1.5.0, and the 1.5.0 release notes say that optimized execution with manually managed memory (Tungsten) was now on by default, together with code generation for expression evaluation.[^jira7075][^r150] A phase 2 umbrella followed (SPARK-9697).[^n2] Whole-stage code generation (SPARK-12795) shipped in Spark 2.0.0, and a 2016 Databricks post by Spark developers presented it as the core of a "second generation Tungsten engine".[^jira12795][^blog2016] The Spark 2.0.0 release notes describe whole-stage code generation without using the Tungsten name.[^n3]

## What remains in Spark 4

Project Tungsten has no deprecation or removal in any Spark release. Its pieces are ordinary parts of the engine:

- **Tungsten memory.** Spark's memory manager still allocates "Tungsten" memory pages for sorting, hashing and shuffle, on the JVM heap by default or off-heap through `sun.misc.Unsafe` when `spark.memory.offHeap.enabled` is true (default false, available since 1.6.0).[^mm430][^tmm430][^conf430] See [Spark memory management](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_memory_management).
- **The `UnsafeRow` format.** Spark SQL's internal row format is backed by raw memory instead of Java objects: a null-tracking bit set, one 8-byte word per field, and a variable-length region for strings and other variable-length values.[^unsaferow]
- **Whole-stage code generation.** Enabled by default through the internal setting `spark.sql.codegen.wholeStage` (default true, since 2.0.0). In `EXPLAIN` output, an operator compiled into a generated stage is prefixed with `*(n)`, where n is the code generation stage ID.[^sqlconf430][^wscg430] See [Whole-stage code generation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Whole-stage_code_generation).
- **The `tungsten-sort` shuffle alias.** Spark 1.5.0 mapped `spark.shuffle.manager=tungsten-sort` to a separate `UnsafeShuffleManager`. SPARK-10708 merged it into the sort shuffle manager in 1.6.0, and since then `tungsten-sort` is an alias for `SortShuffleManager`, as it still is in 4.3.0.[^env150][^n4][^sm430]

### The `spark.sql.tungsten.enabled` flag

The one Tungsten item that was deprecated is a configuration flag. In Spark 1.5.0, `spark.sql.tungsten.enabled` (default true) switched the Tungsten execution backend and code generation on or off.[^r150][^n5] Spark 1.6.0 removed the option to turn off the unsafe (Tungsten) and code generation paths (SPARK-11644)[^n6] and moved the flag to a list of deprecated keys: setting it logged a warning that the property "is deprecated and will be ignored. Tungsten will continue to be used."[^n7] By Spark 2.0.0 the `SET` command no longer has any special handling for it.[^n8] There has been no way to turn Tungsten off as a whole since 1.6.0.

## Example

This PySpark query runs a filter and an aggregation. After the query has run, `explain()` shows the final adaptive plan, where the `*(1)` prefix marks the three operators that were compiled together into one generated function.

```python
df = spark.range(1000).filter("id % 2 = 0").selectExpr("sum(id)")
df.collect()
df.explain()
```

Part of the output from a Spark 4.3 build:

```
   ResultQueryStage 0
   +- *(1) HashAggregate(keys=[], functions=[sum(id#0L)])
      +- *(1) Filter ((id#0L % 2) = 0)
         +- *(1) Range (0, 1000, step=1, splits=1)
```

## What Tungsten is not

- **Not the optimizer.** The [Catalyst optimizer](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Catalyst_optimizer) decides what plan to run; Tungsten work concerns how the chosen physical operators use memory and CPU. The MLlib guide, for example, lists "Tungsten and Catalyst optimizations" as benefits of DataFrames.[^n9]
- **Not a native engine.** Tungsten code runs in the JVM and generates Java code. Native execution engines for Spark, such as Apache Gluten (with Velox) and Apache DataFusion Comet, replace JVM operators with native code; Photon is a proprietary Databricks engine. See [Native execution engine (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Native_execution_engine_(Spark)).
- **Not available to RDD code.** The binary row format and generated code apply to DataFrame, Dataset and SQL operators, which know the data types. Programs that use the [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD) API with arbitrary JVM objects do not get these benefits.[^jira7075]

# Push-based shuffle

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Push-based_shuffle

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Push-based shuffle merge, `spark.shuffle.push`</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 3.2.0 (SPARK-30602)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Block pushing from map tasks, merger locations on external shuffle services, merged shuffle partitions, merge finalization</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) on YARN with the [external shuffle service](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/External_shuffle_service)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [External shuffle service](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/External_shuffle_service), [Dynamic allocation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dynamic_allocation)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/configuration.md, push-based shuffle section and spark.shuffle.push.\* settings) and SPARK-30602</Verified>

**Push-based shuffle** is an [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle) mode in which map tasks push their shuffle blocks to remote [external shuffle services](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/External_shuffle_service), which merge the blocks for each shuffle partition, so that reduce tasks can read a few large merged files instead of many small blocks. It was added in Spark 3.2.0 through the SPIP in SPARK-30602.[^spark30602] It is off by default and, in Spark 4.3.0, supported only for Spark on YARN with the external shuffle service.[^config] The Spark 4.3.0 documentation describes it without a deprecated or experimental label.

## What problem does push-based shuffle solve?

In a regular Spark shuffle, every reduce task fetches one block from every map task's output. The number of blocks therefore grows with the number of map tasks times the number of reduce tasks, and each block can be small. The SPIP describes large Spark-on-YARN deployments where the external shuffle service stores shuffle files on hard disks, and where these many small, random reads make the shuffle a scaling bottleneck and a source of inefficiency.[^spark30602]

## What does push-based shuffle change?

- **Map side.** After a map task writes its shuffle output as usual, Spark pushes the blocks, on a best-effort basis, to a set of external shuffle services chosen as **merger locations** for the shuffle.[^config]
- **Merge.** Each merger appends the pushed blocks for a partition into one merged shuffle file. After all map tasks are done, the driver waits `spark.shuffle.push.finalize.timeout` (default 10s) and then asks the mergers to finalize the merge.[^config]
- **Reduce side.** Reduce tasks read a combination of merged shuffle partitions and original shuffle blocks. Blocks that were not pushed or not merged are still fetched the normal way, which is why the push can be best effort.[^config]

The result, according to the Spark docs, is that small random disk reads by the external shuffle services become large sequential reads, and that reduce tasks may also get better data locality, which reduces network I/O.[^config] The docs describe the goal as improving both the reliability and the performance of the shuffle.[^config]

## Which cluster managers support push-based shuffle?

| Cluster manager | Push-based shuffle |
| --- | --- |
| YARN, with the external shuffle service | Supported[^config] |
| Standalone | Not supported[^config] |
| Kubernetes | Not supported; Spark on Kubernetes has no external shuffle service[^config][^jobsched] |

The Spark docs state that push-based shuffle helps long-running jobs and queries with large disk I/O during shuffle, and is currently not well suited to jobs that run quickly on a small amount of shuffle data.[^config]

## How to enable push-based shuffle

Push-based shuffle needs a setting on both sides. On the server side, the external shuffle service in each NodeManager must use the merging implementation; on the client side, the application turns pushing on.[^config]

```
# External shuffle service (server side), for example in the YARN shuffle service configuration
spark.shuffle.push.server.mergedShuffleFileManagerImpl  org.apache.spark.network.shuffle.RemoteBlockPushResolver

# Application (client side)
spark.shuffle.service.enabled   true
spark.shuffle.push.enabled      true
```

The server-side default, `NoOpMergedShuffleFileManager`, disables push-based shuffle.[^config]

## Main settings

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spark.shuffle.push.enabled` | false | Turn on pushing on the client side |
| `spark.shuffle.push.finalize.timeout` | 10s | Time the driver waits after all map tasks finish before finalizing the merge |
| `spark.shuffle.push.maxBlockSizeToPush` | 1m | Larger blocks are not pushed and are fetched the normal way |
| `spark.shuffle.push.maxBlockBatchSize` | 3m | Maximum size of a batch of blocks in one push request |
| `spark.shuffle.push.minShuffleSizeToWait` | 500m | Below this total shuffle size, the driver finalizes at once without waiting |
| `spark.shuffle.push.minCompletedPushRatio` | 1.0 | Fraction of map partitions that must finish pushing before finalization starts |
| `spark.shuffle.push.mergersMinStaticThreshold` | 5 | Minimum number of merger locations needed to use push-based shuffle for a stage |
| `spark.shuffle.push.mergersMinThresholdRatio` | 0.05 | Minimum merger locations as a ratio of the reduce stage's partitions; the larger of the two minimums applies |

<small>Source: Spark 4.3.0 configuration reference.[^config]</small>

If a stage cannot get enough merger locations, it does not use push-based shuffle. For example, a reduce stage with 100 partitions needs at least 5 merger locations with the default ratio.[^config]

# pyspark-client

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Pyspark-client

<Infobox type="software" name="pyspark-client">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) project)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">4.0.0 (2025-05-23)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Python</Field>
  <Field name="type">Pure-Python [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) client library</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[pypi.org/project/pyspark-client](https://pypi.org/project/pyspark-client/)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark (python/packaging/client)](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/v4.3.0/python/packaging/client)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Pandas API on Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Pandas_API_on_Spark)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the pyspark-client, pyspark and pyspark-connect release histories and metadata on PyPI (latest 4.3.0, uploaded 2026-10-30), python/packaging/client/setup.py and python/packaging/classic/setup.py at tags v4.0.0 and v4.3.0, python/docs/source/getting_started/install.rst at v4.0.0 and v4.3.0, docs/spark-connect-overview.md at v4.3.0, the Spark 4.0.0 release notes and SPARK-47540</Verified>

**pyspark-client** is the pure-Python [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) client for [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), published on PyPI, which lets a Python program use the PySpark DataFrame, SQL and streaming APIs against a remote Spark Connect server without a Java runtime or Spark JAR files on the client machine.[^install430] The package was first released with Spark 4.0.0, and its version numbers follow Spark releases.[^pypi] It is installed with `pip install pyspark-client` and supports only remote connections through `spark.remote` with an `sc://` connection URI.[^install430]

## What is pyspark-client?

pyspark-client is a separate distribution of the PySpark source tree that contains only Python code. The Spark installation guide describes it as a pure Python library that does not depend on non-Python components such as JARs or a Java Runtime Environment (JRE).[^install430] The PyPI package name is `pyspark-client`; the import name stays `pyspark`, so code written for Spark Connect runs unchanged.[^setup430]

The Spark 4.0.0 release notes list "a new lightweight Python client (pyspark-client) at just 1.5 MB" among the Spark Connect changes of that release.[^r400] On PyPI, the 4.3.0 source distribution of pyspark-client is 1,745,601 bytes, while the 4.3.0 source distribution of the full `pyspark` package, which bundles the Spark JARs, is 455,910,862 bytes.[^pypi][^pypi-pyspark]

## How is pyspark-client installed and used?

pyspark-client 4.3.0 requires Python 3.11 or later and installs pandas (2.2.0 or later), PyArrow (18.0.0 or later), grpcio and grpcio-status (1.76.0 or later), googleapis-common-protos, zstandard, NumPy and PyYAML as dependencies.[^setup430] The 4.0.0 release required Python 3.9 or later.[^setup400]

The Spark Connect documentation recommends pinning the client to the Spark release in use, for example `pip install pyspark-client==4.3`, and then creating a session with `SparkSession.builder.remote()`.[^overview] The server side is a Spark Connect server, which by default listens on port 15002; see [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect).[^overview]

```python
# pip install pyspark-client==4.3.0
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

spark = SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://localhost:15002").getOrCreate()

df = spark.range(10).withColumn("even", F.col("id") % 2 == 0)
df.groupBy("even").count().show()
```

## What is missing compared with PySpark?

pyspark-client leaves out the parts of PySpark that need a local JVM. Compared with the classic `pyspark` package at v4.3.0, its package list omits `pyspark.core` (the module that holds `SparkContext`, `RDD` and broadcast variables), `pyspark.sql.classic` (the Py4J-based DataFrame implementation), and the bundled `jars`, `bin` and `sbin` directories.[^setup430][^classic430] It also does not depend on Py4J, which the full package requires.[^setup430][^pypi-pyspark]

Because pyspark-client speaks only the Spark Connect protocol, the general Spark Connect limits apply to it. The Spark documentation lists them: the client cannot reach the driver JVM, so private fields such as `df._jdf` do not exist; RDDs are not supported; and the client has no access to `SparkContext` or to the static Spark configuration.[^overview] The [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD) API is therefore unavailable, and code that calls `spark.sparkContext` must be rewritten with DataFrame APIs.

pyspark-client cannot start Spark by itself. The installation guide says it supports only `spark.remote` with connection URIs; it has no local mode, and the user must run a Spark Connect server separately.[^install430] The SPIP that proposed the pure-Python package also excluded full compatibility with classic PySpark (such as the RDD API), launching the server and local mode from its scope.[^spip]

Most of the PySpark API is still present. The package includes `pyspark.sql` with its Spark Connect implementation, Structured Streaming, `pyspark.ml`, the [Pandas API on Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Pandas_API_on_Spark) (`pyspark.pandas`) and the `pyspark.pipelines` module of [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines).[^setup430] The Spark API reference labels each API that "Supports Spark Connect".[^overview]

## How does pyspark-client differ from pyspark and pyspark-connect?

Spark publishes three Python packages from the same source tree:[^install430][^setup430][^classic430]

| PyPI package | Contents | Bundles Spark JARs | Connection modes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pyspark-client` | Python code only; no JARs, no Py4J | No | `spark.remote` with an `sc://` URI only |
| `pyspark` | Full PySpark with the Spark JARs and Py4J; Spark Connect available through the `connect` extra | Yes | Classic (Py4J) and Spark Connect |
| `pyspark-connect` | A small package that depends on the same version of `pyspark` and makes Spark Connect the default | Yes, through its `pyspark` dependency | `spark.master` with a local Connect server, or `spark.remote` |

The `pyspark-connect` 4.3.0 package on PyPI depends on `pyspark==4.3.0`, so it brings in the full JVM-backed distribution; pyspark-client does not.[^pypi-connect]

## History

The pure-Python package was proposed in SPARK-47540, "SPIP: Pure Python Package (Spark Connect)", filed on 25 March 2024 with fix version 4.0.0.[^spip] The SPIP text used the name `pyspark-connect`; in the released code the pure-Python package is named `pyspark-client`, and `pyspark-connect` became the package that makes Connect the default for full PySpark.[^spip][^setup400] The Spark 4.0.0 release notes list SPARK-47540 and the 1.5 MB client.[^r400]

pyspark-client 4.0.0 was uploaded to PyPI on 23 May 2025, the release date of Spark 4.0.0. Later releases track Spark: 4.1.0 (16 December 2025), 4.2.0 (14 July 2026) and 4.3.0 (30 October 2026), with maintenance releases for older lines, such as 4.2.1, 4.1.4 and 4.0.5 on 27 October 2026.[^pypi]

[^pypi-connect]: [pyspark-connect 4.3.0](https://pypi.org/project/pyspark-connect/4.3.0/). *Python Package Index*. Retrieved 2026-11-23.

# Python data source API (Spark)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Python_data_source_API_(Spark)

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Python Data Source API, PySpark data source, `pyspark.sql.datasource`</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data integration, distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 4.0.0 (SPIP SPARK-44076)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`DataSource`, `DataSourceReader`, `DataSourceWriter`, `DataSourceStreamReader`, `SimpleDataSourceStreamReader`, `DataSourceStreamWriter`, `InputPartition`</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (PySpark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Predicate pushdown](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown), [Apache Arrow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Arrow), [Python UDTF](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Python_UDTF)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (the PySpark Python Data Source tutorial, python/pyspark/sql/datasource.py, SQLConf.scala, the PySpark migration guide) and the Spark 4.0.0, 4.1.0 and 4.2.0 release notes</Verified>

The **Python data source API** of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) is a set of PySpark base classes, in the module `pyspark.sql.datasource`, for writing a custom data source or sink entirely in Python and using it with `spark.read`, `df.write`, `spark.readStream` and `writeStream`.[^tut] The API was introduced in Spark 4.0.0 under the improvement proposal SPARK-44076.[^tut][^r400]

## How does a Python data source work?

A Python data source is a subclass of `DataSource`. It gives a short `name()` used in `format(...)`, an optional default `schema()`, and one factory method per capability.[^tut]

|  | Source (read) | Sink (write) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Batch | `reader()` returns a `DataSourceReader` | `writer()` returns a `DataSourceWriter` |
| Streaming | `streamReader()` returns a `DataSourceStreamReader`, or `simpleStreamReader()` returns a `SimpleDataSourceStreamReader` | `streamWriter()` returns a `DataSourceStreamWriter` |

Source for the table: the PySpark 4.3.0 Python Data Source tutorial.[^tut]

A batch reader can implement `partitions()` to return a list of `InputPartition` objects; if it returns N partitions, Spark plans N tasks that run `read(partition)` in parallel, and by default there is a single partition.[^api] `read` yields tuples or `Row` objects, or PyArrow `RecordBatch` objects.[^tut] The tutorial says that yielding Arrow record batches avoids row-by-row processing and can improve performance by up to an order of magnitude on large datasets.[^tut]

The data source, reader and writer classes and their methods must be picklable, because Spark ships them to executors. Libraries used inside a method must be imported inside that method.[^tut]

## Example: a batch reader

The following PySpark example works on Spark 4.3.0. It defines a source named `simple` that returns two rows.

```python
from pyspark.sql.datasource import DataSource, DataSourceReader
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType

class SimpleDataSource(DataSource):
    @classmethod
    def name(cls):
        return "simple"

    def schema(self):
        return "name string, age int"

    def reader(self, schema: StructType):
        return SimpleReader()

class SimpleReader(DataSourceReader):
    def read(self, partition):
        yield ("Alice", 20)
        yield ("Bob", 30)

spark.dataSource.register(SimpleDataSource)
spark.read.format("simple").load().show()
```

Options passed with `.option(...)` reach the source as `self.options`, a dictionary whose values are all strings. A caller can override the default schema with `.schema(...)`.[^tut]

## How do writers commit data?

A `DataSourceWriter` implements `write(rows)`, which runs in each task and returns a `WriterCommitMessage`. After all tasks succeed, Spark calls `commit(messages)` on the driver with the messages from every task; if any task fails, it calls `abort(messages)`.[^tut] Batch writes support the `append` and `overwrite` modes.[^tut] Spark 4.0.0 also added `DataSourceArrowWriter`, which receives PyArrow record batches instead of rows (SPARK-50471).[^api][^r400]

## How do streaming readers work?

A Python data source can act as a [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) source. A `DataSourceStreamReader` tracks progress with offsets, which are dictionaries:[^tut]
- `initialOffset()` returns the starting offset.
- `latestOffset()` returns the offset that the next micro-batch reads up to.
- `partitions(start, end)` splits the range between two offsets into `InputPartition` objects.
- `read(partition)` yields the rows of one partition on an executor.
- `commit(end)` is called after the query has processed data up to `end`, and can release resources.

`SimpleDataSourceStreamReader` is a lighter interface for low-throughput sources that do not need partitioning: `read(start)` returns both the rows and the next offset, and `readBetweenOffsets(start, end)` must return the same rows deterministically when Spark replays a batch after a restart or failure.[^tut] Since Spark 4.2, a simple reader that returns rows without advancing the offset fails with `SIMPLE_STREAM_READER_OFFSET_DID_NOT_ADVANCE`.[^upgrade]

Spark 4.2.0 added admission control and `Trigger.AvailableNow` support to Python streaming readers (SPARK-55304). A reader implements `getDefaultReadLimit()`, for example returning `ReadMaxRows(20)`, and its `latestOffset(start, limit)` must honour the `ReadLimit` that Spark passes in.[^tut][^r420]

A `DataSourceStreamWriter` has `write`, `commit(messages, batchId)` and `abort(messages, batchId)`, so a sink can commit each micro-batch as a unit.[^tut] An Arrow-based variant, `DataSourceStreamArrowWriter`, was added in Spark 4.1.0.[^api]

## Does the Python data source API support filter pushdown?

Spark 4.1.0 added a filter pushdown API (SPARK-51271).[^r410] A `DataSourceReader` can override `pushFilters(filters)`, which Spark calls once during planning with filter objects such as `EqualTo`, `GreaterThan`, `In`, `IsNull` and `StringStartsWith`; the method returns the filters that Spark must still evaluate after the scan. The API documentation recommends it only for sources that filter natively, such as databases.[^api] In Spark 4.3.0 the pushdown is controlled by the internal configuration `spark.sql.python.filterPushdown.enabled`, which defaults to `false` because it runs the Python worker one more time during planning.[^sqlconf] See [Predicate pushdown](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown).

## How is a Python data source registered?

`spark.dataSource.register(MyDataSource)` registers a source for the current session (SPARK-45600).[^tut][^r400] Registering a second source with the same name overwrites the first. Built-in and Scala or Java sources take precedence over a Python source with the same name.[^tut]

A package can register a source automatically by exporting it as `DefaultSource` in a top-level module whose name starts with `pyspark_`; the tutorial cites the `pyspark_huggingface` package as an example.[^tut] Spark 4.0.0 also added Python data sources for [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) clients (SPARK-47367), creating tables with a Python data source in SQL (SPARK-45597), and Python metrics (SPARK-46424).[^r400]

Since Spark 4.2, a source whose returned Arrow data has column types that do not match its declared schema fails with `DATA_SOURCE_RETURN_SCHEMA_MISMATCH`.[^upgrade]

# Python UDTF

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Python_UDTF

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Python user-defined table function, `@udtf`</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 3.5.0 (SPARK-43797)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Handler class with `eval`; optional `__init__`, `analyze`, `terminate`, `cleanup`; output schema; table arguments</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (PySpark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[User-defined function (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/User-defined_function_(Spark)), [Arrow-optimized Python UDF](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Arrow-optimized_Python_UDF), [Python data source API (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Python_data_source_API_(Spark))</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (the PySpark UDTF tutorial, python/pyspark/sql/functions/builtin.py, python/pyspark/sql/udtf.py, python/pyspark/sql/connect/udtf.py, examples/src/main/python/sql/udtf.py, SQLConf.scala, the PySpark migration guide) and the Spark 3.5.0 and 4.1.0 release notes</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a **Python UDTF** (**Python user-defined table function**) is a Python class, registered with PySpark, whose `eval` method can return zero or more rows for each call, so that the function produces a whole table instead of a single value.[^tut] A UDTF is called in the `FROM` clause of a SQL query or directly from Python, and its arguments can be scalar expressions or one input table.[^tut] Python UDTFs were introduced in Spark 3.5.0.[^r350]

## What is a Python UDTF used for?

The PySpark user guide recommends a Python UDTF when a function must generate several rows and columns and benefit from Python libraries.[^guide] It lists these use cases:[^guide]
- Exploding nested data such as arrays or structs into multiple rows.
- Splitting strings into several rows or columns.
- Generating rows from input ranges, such as sequences of numbers, timestamps or dates.
- Computations that need Python libraries, such as statistical functions or machine learning inference, where a SQL table function would not be enough.

A scalar [UDF](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/User-defined_function_(Spark)) returns exactly one value per input row; a UDTF can return any number of rows, each with several columns.[^guide]

## How do you write a Python UDTF?

A Python UDTF is a class with a required `eval` method that yields output rows as tuples, lists or `pyspark.sql.Row` objects. Optional methods are `__init__` (called once per UDTF instance on the executor), `terminate` (called after all input rows of a partition have been processed, and able to yield more rows), `cleanup` (always called at the end, even after an error) and a static `analyze` method.[^tut]

The output schema is a `StructType` or a DDL string, given in the `returnType` of the `@udtf` decorator or returned by `analyze`.[^tut] A one-column row must be yielded with a trailing comma, for example `yield x,`.[^tut]

The following PySpark example runs on Spark 4.3.0. It defines a UDTF, calls it from Python, registers it and calls it from SQL, including with a `LATERAL` join.

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import lit, udtf

@udtf(returnType="word: string")
class WordSplitter:
    def eval(self, text: str):
        for word in text.split(" "):
            yield (word.strip(),)

WordSplitter(lit("hello world")).show()

spark.udtf.register("split_words", WordSplitter)
spark.sql("SELECT * FROM split_words('hello world')").show()
spark.sql(
    "SELECT * FROM VALUES ('Hello World'), ('Apache Spark') t(text), "
    "LATERAL split_words(text)"
).show()
```

The example follows the UDTF examples shipped with Spark 4.3.0.[^ex]

## How do table arguments work?

A Python UDTF can take one input table as an argument, alongside scalar arguments. In SQL the table is passed with the `TABLE` keyword, either as `TABLE(t)` or as a subquery such as `TABLE(SELECT a, b FROM t)`. Each input row reaches `eval` as a `Row`.[^tut]

The call can ask Spark to partition the input table: `PARTITION BY` guarantees that all rows with the same values of the partitioning expressions are consumed by one instance of the UDTF class, and `WITH SINGLE PARTITION` sends all rows to one instance. An `ORDER BY` clause sets the row order within each partition.[^tut] For example: `SELECT * FROM my_udtf(TABLE(events) PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts)`.

The `analyze` method can request the same partitioning, ordering and column selection itself, through the `partitionBy`, `withSinglePartition`, `orderBy` and `select` fields of `AnalyzeResult`, so that callers can write just `TABLE(t)`.[^tut] `analyze` also lets a UDTF compute its output schema from its arguments at query planning time, instead of declaring a fixed `returnType`.[^tut]

An `eval` method can raise `SkipRestOfInputTableException` to skip the remaining rows of the current partition and go straight to `terminate`; any other exception aborts the UDTF and fails the query.[^tut]

## Is a Python UDTF Arrow-optimized?

Since Spark 4.2, Python UDTFs use [Apache Arrow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Arrow) for data transfer by default: `spark.sql.execution.pythonUDTF.arrow.enabled` defaults to `true`, and setting it to `false` restores the earlier behaviour.[^upgrade][^sqlconf] The `useArrow` argument of `@udtf` overrides the configuration for one UDTF.[^builtin] The tutorial says Arrow helps most when each input row produces a large result table.[^tut] Arrow optimization for UDTFs was first added in Spark 3.5.0 (SPARK-43964).[^r350]

An Arrow-optimized UDTF still runs `eval` on Python objects. Spark 4.1.0 added a separate decorator, `arrow_udtf` (SPARK-52979), whose `eval` receives PyArrow `RecordBatch` or `Array` objects and yields PyArrow tables or record batches, for vectorized processing without row-by-row overhead.[^builtin][^n1]

## Limitations

- A UDTF cannot create or reference the Spark session; trying to do so causes a serialization error.[^tut]
- A UDTF call accepts at most one table argument.[^tut]
- `terminate` may hold a whole partition in memory if the UDTF buffers rows until the end, and the tutorial warns about memory use in that pattern.[^tut]

PySpark 4.3.0 also ships a Python UDTF implementation for [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) clients (`pyspark.sql.connect.udtf`).[^n2]

# RDD

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Resilient distributed dataset</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Partitions, lineage of transformations, lazy transformations and actions, storage levels for persistence</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[DataFrame](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DataFrame), [Dataset (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dataset_(Spark)), [Partition](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [GraphX](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphX), [Spark Streaming (DStreams)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Streaming_(DStreams))</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/rdd-programming-guide.md, docs/quick-start.md, docs/spark-connect-overview.md, core/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/rdd/RDD.scala, python/pyspark/core/rdd.py, python/pyspark/sql/connect/dataframe.py), the Spark 4.0.0 to 4.3.0 release notes and the NSDI 2012 RDD paper</Verified>

<Status level="active">The RDD API is not deprecated in any Spark release up to 4.3.0; only some individual methods are. It is not supported by [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect).[^connect]</Status>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a **resilient distributed dataset** (**RDD**) is an immutable collection of elements split into partitions across the nodes of a cluster, which can be processed in parallel and is rebuilt from its lineage when a partition is lost.[^guide] The RDD was Spark's main programming interface before Spark 2.0; since then the Spark documentation recommends the [Dataset](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dataset_(Spark)) and [DataFrame](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DataFrame) APIs, which run through the Catalyst optimizer, while stating that the RDD interface is still supported.[^quick] RDDs still underlie older libraries such as [GraphX](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphX) and [Spark Streaming (DStreams)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Streaming_(DStreams)), but they are not available to [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) clients.[^connect]

## Status

The RDD API is not deprecated. The `RDD` class at the v4.3.0 tag of Spark carries no deprecation annotation, and the Spark 4.0.0 to 4.3.0 release notes list no deprecation of the RDD API.[^rddscala][^r400] Only single methods are deprecated; for example, PySpark's `mapPartitionsWithSplit` is deprecated in favor of `mapPartitionsWithIndex`.[^pyrdd]

The practical limit is Spark Connect. The Spark Connect documentation lists `SparkContext` and RDD as unsupported for both Python and Scala clients.[^connect] In the PySpark Connect client, `DataFrame.rdd` raises a not-implemented error.[^n1] Code that uses RDDs therefore needs a classic Spark application, which is the default: `spark.api.mode` defaults to `classic` in Spark 4.3.0.[^n2]

## How it works

An RDD is created from a file in a Hadoop-supported file system, from a collection in the driver program, or by transforming another RDD.[^guide] The design was described in the 2012 paper *Resilient Distributed Datasets: A Fault-Tolerant Abstraction for In-Memory Cluster Computing* by Matei Zaharia and others at the University of California, Berkeley.[^paper]

RDDs support two kinds of operations. **Transformations**, such as `map` and `filter`, return a new RDD. **Actions**, such as `reduce` and `collect`, return a value to the driver. Transformations are lazy: Spark records them and computes nothing until an action needs a result.[^guide] Each RDD is divided into [partitions](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), and the executors process one partition per task.

Fault tolerance comes from **lineage**, the record of the transformations that built an RDD. If a partition is lost, Spark recomputes it from that record instead of restoring a replica.[^guide][^paper] An RDD can be kept for reuse with `persist()` or `cache()`; `cache()` uses the default storage level `MEMORY_ONLY`, and other storage levels keep the data serialized, on disk or replicated.[^guide]

## RDD compared with DataFrame and Dataset

|  | RDD | DataFrame | Dataset |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Element type | Any JVM or Python object, opaque to Spark | Rows with a schema of named, typed columns | Typed JVM objects with an encoder (Scala and Java only) |
| Optimization | None by Spark SQL; the user's functions run as written | Spark SQL uses the schema to optimize the query | Spark SQL uses the schema to optimize the query |
| Languages | Scala, Java, Python | Scala, Java, Python, R | Scala, Java |
| Spark Connect | Not supported | Supported | Supported in the Scala client |

The Spark quick start recommends the Dataset over the RDD because it is strongly typed like an RDD but has better performance.[^quick] The Spark SQL guide describes the Dataset, added in Spark 1.6, as combining the benefits of RDDs (strong typing and lambda functions) with Spark SQL's optimized execution engine, and a DataFrame as a Dataset organized into named columns. Python and R have no Dataset API but use DataFrames.[^n3][^connect]

## Where RDDs still appear

- **Older libraries.** [GraphX](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GraphX) represents graphs as RDDs, and a DStream in [Spark Streaming (DStreams)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Streaming_(DStreams)) is a sequence of RDDs.[^n4] The RDD-based machine learning package, [spark.mllib (RDD-based API)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark.mllib_(RDD-based_API)), is in maintenance mode.
- **Low-level control.** The RDD API gives direct control over partitioning and over functions applied to each element, which some programs use for work that does not fit a tabular schema.
- **Execution internals.** DataFrame and SQL queries also end up as RDDs: in Spark 4.3.0, executing a physical plan node (`SparkPlan.execute()`) returns an RDD of internal rows.[^n5]

## Example

A word count with the RDD API in PySpark, in classic mode:

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[*]").getOrCreate()
sc = spark.sparkContext

lines = sc.parallelize(["a b", "b c", "c"])
counts = (lines.flatMap(lambda line: line.split())
               .map(lambda word: (word, 1))
               .reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b))

print(sorted(counts.collect()))  # [('a', 1), ('b', 2), ('c', 2)]
```

The same result with the DataFrame API also runs through Spark Connect:

```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

df = spark.createDataFrame([("a b",), ("b c",), ("c",)], ["line"])
df.select(F.explode(F.split("line", " ")).alias("word")).groupBy("word").count().show()
```

# Real-time mode (Structured Streaming)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Real-time_mode_(Structured_Streaming)

<Infobox type="concept" name="Real-time mode">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Real-time Mode (RTM), real-time trigger</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 4.1.0 (2025)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Real-time trigger, long-running tasks, pipelined shuffle, checkpoint interval, update output mode</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) 4.1.0 and later</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Trigger (Structured Streaming)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trigger_(Structured_Streaming)), [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [transformWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState), [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">docs/streaming/real-time-mode.md and Trigger.java at tag v4.3.0, Trigger.java at v4.1.0 and v4.2.0, python/pyspark/sql/streaming/readwriter.py at v4.1.0 and v4.3.0, SQLConf.scala at v4.3.0, the Spark 4.1.0, 4.2.0 and 4.3.0 release notes, and SPARK-53736, SPARK-53737, SPARK-54660 and SPARK-57281</Verified>

<Status level="active" since="Apache Spark 4.1.0">The `Trigger.RealTime` methods carried the `@Experimental` annotation in Spark 4.1.0; SPARK-57281, listed in the Spark 4.3.0 release notes, removed it, and the Spark 4.3.0 documentation does not label Real-time mode experimental.[^jira57281]</Status>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), **real-time mode** (Real-time Mode, RTM) is a streaming execution mode that runs long-lived tasks which process and emit each record as it arrives, instead of running a new short job for every micro-batch, to reach millisecond-scale end-to-end latency with the same DataFrame APIs and exactly-once processing guarantees.[^rtm] It was introduced in Spark 4.1.0 for stateless Scala queries and is enabled with a real-time [trigger](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trigger_(Structured_Streaming)) on the streaming write.[^r410] Spark 4.3.0 added a first set of stateful operations: deduplication, streaming aggregation and the Scala and Java [transformWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState) API.[^r430]

## What is real-time mode?

Real-time mode is an alternative to the default micro-batch engine of Structured Streaming. The Spark 4.3.0 documentation describes it as aimed at operational workloads that must react to data as soon as it arrives, and gives fraud detection, real-time alerting and live personalization as examples.[^rtm] The query code is the same as for a micro-batch query; only the trigger changes.[^rtm]

Real-time mode is not the same as continuous processing, the older low-latency mode started with `Trigger.Continuous`. The documentation calls continuous processing experimental and legacy, notes that it supports only map-like operations with at-least-once guarantees, and recommends real-time mode for new low-latency workloads.[^rtm]

## How does real-time mode work?

In micro-batch execution, the driver plans each batch and launches a fresh set of short tasks, and that fixed per-batch overhead sets a latency floor of about 100 milliseconds. Real-time mode instead launches one long-running task per input partition for the duration of a long batch, so records flow from source through transformations to sink without waiting for a batch boundary. The documentation puts the resulting latency at roughly the time to process and ship one record, often a few milliseconds.[^rtm]

In real-time mode the trigger duration is mainly a **checkpoint interval**, not a latency target. With the default duration of 5 minutes, results can still be emitted within milliseconds; the duration controls how often the query commits progress and starts the next batch. Batch-scoped work, such as advancing the [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) and firing processing-time timers on idle partitions, can wait for the boundary.[^rtm] A shorter duration gives finer-grained recovery but adds more commit gaps, which can raise tail latency.[^rtm]

Stateful operators need records grouped by key, which normally requires a [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle) whose producer stage finishes before the consumer stage starts. Because a real-time task never finishes its batch, Spark 4.3.0 runs these shuffles as a **pipelined shuffle**: producer and consumer stages are scheduled at the same time, and shuffle data is streamed over the network record by record rather than written to files. This is enabled automatically.[^rtm] The Spark 4.3.0 release notes describe stateful real-time queries as reaching end-to-end latency on the order of 100 milliseconds.[^r430]

## How is real-time mode enabled?

Real-time mode is enabled by setting a real-time trigger. In Scala and Java the trigger is `Trigger.RealTime()`, with forms that take a duration string, milliseconds, a value and `TimeUnit`, or a Scala `Duration`; with no argument the duration is 5 minutes.[^trig430] In PySpark the trigger is the `realTime` keyword of `DataStreamWriter.trigger()`, and a duration string is required.[^rtm] The PySpark keyword was added in Spark 4.2.0 (SPARK-54660); it is not in the 4.1.0 PySpark API.[^r420][^n1] The [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) Python client also accepts `realTime` at v4.3.0.[^n2]

The following PySpark query (Spark 4.2.0 or later) reads a Kafka topic, drops duplicate keys and writes to another Kafka topic in real-time mode. Deduplication needs Spark 4.3.0.[^rtm]

```python
query = (
    spark.readStream.format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "host1:9092")
    .option("subscribe", "input-topic")
    .load()
    .selectExpr("CAST(key AS STRING) AS key", "CAST(value AS STRING) AS value")
    .dropDuplicates(["key"])
    .writeStream.format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "host1:9092")
    .option("topic", "output-topic")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/tmp/checkpoints/rtm-dedup")
    .outputMode("update")
    .trigger(realTime="5 minutes")
    .start()
)
```

## What are the requirements and limits?

A real-time query is checked when it starts. The Spark 4.3.0 documentation lists these requirements:[^rtm]
- The output mode must be `update`; other modes fail with `STREAMING_REAL_TIME_MODE.OUTPUT_MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED`.
- A `checkpointLocation` is required.
- The trigger duration must be at least `spark.sql.streaming.realTimeMode.minBatchDuration`, which defaults to 5000 milliseconds; month-based intervals are not accepted.
- Stateful queries do not support asynchronous progress tracking.

Operators and sinks are checked against an allowlist before the query starts, controlled by `spark.sql.streaming.realTimeMode.allowlistCheck` (default `true`). Both settings were added in Spark 4.1.0.[^sqlconf]

For stateful real-time queries, Spark 4.3.0 applies soft defaults at query start: the RocksDB [state store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/State_store) provider, state store checkpoint format version 2, and RocksDB changelog checkpointing. Format version 1 is rejected unless `spark.sql.streaming.realTimeMode.dangerouslyAllowCheckpointV1.enabled` is set to `true`, which the documentation describes as unsafe for stateful queries.[^rtm]

### Which sources, sinks and operations are supported?

| Area | Supported in Spark 4.3.0 | Not supported |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sources | Kafka | Other sources, including the built-in `rate` source |
| Sinks | Kafka, `foreach` (`ForeachWriter`), console, memory | `foreachBatch` and other sinks |
| Stateless operations (since 4.1.0) | Projections, filters, UDFs, `explode`, unions of distinct sources, stream-static joins with a broadcast static side | Unions that read the same source twice |
| Stateful operations (since 4.3.0) | `dropDuplicates`, streaming aggregation including windowed aggregation, Scala and Java `transformWithState`, `withWatermark` | Stream-stream joins, `flatMapGroupsWithState`, session windows, `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark`, PySpark `transformWithState` and `transformWithStateInPandas`, range partitioning |

All rows are from the Spark 4.3.0 Real-time Mode documentation.[^rtm]

## What delivery guarantees does real-time mode give?

Real-time mode gives the same exactly-once processing guarantee as the micro-batch engine: each input record affects engine-managed state once, across failures and restarts. End-to-end delivery depends on the sink. Offsets are committed at the end of each batch, after records have reached the sink, so a failure can cause records to be written again; the built-in Kafka sink is at-least-once, and Spark does not yet ship an exactly-once sink for real-time mode.[^rtm] See [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics).

## History

Real-time mode was developed under the umbrella issue SPARK-53736, "Real-time Mode in Structured Streaming (Scala stateless support)", created on 27 September 2025, with fix version 4.1.0; SPARK-53737 added the trigger.[^jira53736][^n3] The Spark 4.1.0 release notes call it the first official support for Structured Streaming queries in real-time mode.[^r410]

| Spark release | Real-time mode change |
| --- | --- |
| 4.1.0 | Real-time trigger and stateless Scala and Java queries; `Trigger.RealTime` marked `@Experimental`[^r410][^n4] |
| 4.2.0 | PySpark `realTime` trigger keyword (SPARK-54660)[^r420] |
| 4.3.0 | Stateful queries on pipelined shuffles (SPARK-58508, SPARK-58635, SPARK-57228); async progress tracking (SPARK-58131); `@Experimental` removed (SPARK-57281)[^r430][^jira57281] |

# Remote shuffle service

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Remote_shuffle_service

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">RSS, disaggregated shuffle</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Shuffle manager plug-in in the engine, a coordinator or master, shuffle servers or workers, local disk or remote storage</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Celeborn](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Celeborn), [Apache Uniffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Uniffle)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [External shuffle service](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/External_shuffle_service), [Push-based shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Push-based_shuffle), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/job-scheduling.md, core config package.scala, shuffle/api), Apache Celeborn 0.7.0 (README.md, docs/deploy.md, docs/deploy_on_k8s.md), Apache Uniffle 0.10.0 (README.md, pom.xml), the Celeborn and Uniffle download pages and the Apache Incubator status pages</Verified>

A **remote shuffle service** (RSS) is a cluster of long-running servers that receives, stores and serves the intermediate [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle) data of distributed jobs, so that the data no longer lives on the local disks of the compute processes that wrote it.[^celebornreadme][^uniffereadme] In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a remote shuffle service plugs in as a custom shuffle manager: map tasks push their output to shuffle servers over the network, and reduce tasks read it back from those servers.[^coreconf] Two open source implementations at the Apache Software Foundation are [Apache Celeborn](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Celeborn) and [Apache Uniffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Uniffle).[^celebornincubator][^uniffleincubator]

## What problem does a remote shuffle service solve?

By default, a Spark executor writes shuffle files to its own local disk and serves them to the next stage; the [external shuffle service](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/External_shuffle_service) moves the serving to a long-running process on the same node, but the files still sit on that node.[^jobsched] When executors are removed, as happens with dynamic allocation or on [Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Kubernetes), the shuffle files must be kept somewhere else or the stages that produced them must run again.

Spark's documentation lists four ways to let dynamic allocation remove executors without losing shuffle files: the external shuffle service, shuffle tracking, shuffle block migration during decommissioning, or a custom `ShuffleDataIO` (set with `spark.shuffle.sort.io.plugin.class`) whose driver components support reliable storage.[^jobsched] A remote shuffle service is the fourth kind: shuffle data lives on separate servers, so compute nodes can be added and removed freely. Spark on Kubernetes does not support the built-in external shuffle service.[^jobsched]

Separating shuffle storage from compute is what both Apache projects name as their goal. Celeborn describes its features as disaggregated computing and storage, push-based shuffle write with merged shuffle read, and high availability.[^celebornreadme] Uniffle describes itself as changing shuffle from a "local file pull-like style" to a "remote block push-like style", with disaggregated storage and high elasticity.[^uniffereadme]

## How does a remote shuffle service plug into Apache Spark?

Spark loads its shuffle implementation from `spark.shuffle.manager` (default `sort`, since Spark 1.1.0), so a remote shuffle service ships a jar with its own `ShuffleManager` class and asks users to point this setting at it.[^coreconf] Since Spark 3.0.0 there is also a narrower shuffle storage API, `org.apache.spark.shuffle.api.ShuffleDataIO`, selected by `spark.shuffle.sort.io.plugin.class` (default `LocalDiskShuffleDataIO`).[^coreconf][^n1]

Both Celeborn and Uniffle use the two hooks together. The shuffle manager does the data transfer, and the `ShuffleDataIO` class tells Spark (3.5 and later) that shuffle data is stored reliably, so dynamic allocation can release executors without the external shuffle service:

```properties
# Apache Celeborn 0.7.0 client settings for Spark
spark.shuffle.manager                 org.apache.spark.shuffle.celeborn.SparkShuffleManager
spark.serializer                      org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer
spark.celeborn.master.endpoints       clb-1:9097,clb-2:9097,clb-3:9097
spark.shuffle.service.enabled         false
spark.shuffle.sort.io.plugin.class    org.apache.spark.shuffle.celeborn.CelebornShuffleDataIO
```

The settings above come from the Celeborn deployment guide.[^celebornreadme] Uniffle's equivalents are `spark.shuffle.manager=org.apache.spark.shuffle.RssShuffleManager`, `spark.rss.coordinator.quorum` for the coordinator addresses, and `spark.shuffle.sort.io.plugin.class=org.apache.spark.shuffle.RssShuffleDataIo` on Spark 3.5 or later; for older Spark versions Uniffle ships patches to Spark in its `patch/spark` folder.[^uniffereadme] Both projects require a serializer that supports relocation of serialized objects, such as Kryo.[^celebornreadme][^uniffereadme]

## Remote shuffle service implementations compared

The first column is Spark's built-in shuffle, shown for reference.

|  | Apache Spark built-in shuffle (with external shuffle service) | Apache Celeborn | Apache Uniffle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Where shuffle data lives | Local disks of the nodes that ran the map tasks[^jobsched] | Celeborn workers, which merge data per reducer and flush to disk; HDFS is a supported storage type[^celebornreadme] | Shuffle servers, which buffer data in memory and write to local disk, remote storage such as HDFS, or both[^uniffereadme] |
| Components | Executors, plus one external shuffle service per node[^jobsched] | Master (resource management, state replicated with Raft), Worker, and a LifecycleManager that runs in the Spark driver[^celebornreadme] | Coordinator cluster, shuffle server cluster, optional remote storage[^uniffereadme] |
| Write and read model | Map tasks write sorted files locally; reducers fetch blocks from many nodes[^jobsched] | Mappers push data to workers; reducers read merged partition files[^celebornreadme] | Tasks push blocks to shuffle servers; readers read from shuffle servers, remote storage or both[^uniffereadme] |
| Engines (latest release) | Spark only | Spark 3.0 to 4.2, Flink 1.18 to 2.3, Hadoop MapReduce 3; Tez client marked experimental[^celebornreadme] | Spark 2.3 to 3.5, Hadoop MapReduce, Apache Tez[^uniffereadme] |
| Kubernetes | External shuffle service not supported on Kubernetes[^jobsched] | Helm chart for deployment on Kubernetes[^celeborndeployk8s] | Kubernetes operator in `deploy/kubernetes`[^unifflek8s] |
| Origin | Part of Apache Spark | Started at Alibaba in 2020 as "RemoteShuffleService", open sourced in 2021[^celebornproposal] | Started at Tencent in 2020 as "Firestorm", open sourced in 2021[^uniffleproposal] |
| ASF top-level project since | (Spark is a top-level project) | 2024-03-21[^celebornincubator] | 2025-02-19[^uniffleincubator] |
| Latest release (checked 2026-11-23) | Spark 4.3.0[^n2] | 0.7.0, 2026-08-16[^celeborndl] | 0.10.0, 2025-09-25[^uniffledl] |

## Remote shuffle service vs external shuffle service vs push-based shuffle

The three terms are often confused. The **[external shuffle service](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/External_shuffle_service)** is part of Spark; it serves shuffle files that executors wrote to the node's local disk, and is off by default (`spark.shuffle.service.enabled`).[^jobsched] **[Push-based shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Push-based_shuffle)**, added in Spark 3.2.0, has map tasks push blocks to external shuffle services that merge them per partition; it works only on YARN.[^sparkconfdoc] A **remote shuffle service** is a separate cluster, outside Spark, that stores the shuffle data on its own servers.

## When is a remote shuffle service worth running?

A remote shuffle service is one more distributed system to deploy, size and monitor. Its configuration guidance shows the tradeoffs: Celeborn recommends server-side replication (`spark.celeborn.client.push.replicate.enabled=true`) unless there is only one worker or HDFS storage is used, and recommends turning off Spark's AQE local shuffle reader (`spark.sql.adaptive.localShuffleReader.enabled=false`).[^celebornreadme] Teams usually consider one when dynamic allocation on Kubernetes keeps losing shuffle data, or when shuffles are large enough to strain the local disks of compute nodes.
