# RocksDB state store

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RocksDB_state_store

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">`RocksDBStateStoreProvider`</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 3.2</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">One RocksDB instance per operator partition, local disk, uploaded SST files and `.zip` version files, optional changelog checkpointing, optional bounded memory</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark); a separate provider on Databricks</Field>
  <Field name="related">[State store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/State_store), [Streaming checkpoint](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_checkpoint), [transformWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming programming guide (RocksDB state store implementation, memory management, changelog checkpointing), `SQLConf.scala`, `RocksDB.scala`, `RocksDBFileManager.scala` and `pom.xml` at tag v4.3.0 of apache/spark, SPARK-43421, and the Databricks RocksDB state store page</Verified>

The **RocksDB state store** is a [state store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/State_store) implementation for [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) that keeps the state of stateful operators in RocksDB, an embedded key-value database, in native memory and on the executor's local disk, and uploads its files to the [streaming checkpoint](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_checkpoint) for fault tolerance. It was added in Spark 3.2 for queries with large state, such as millions of keys, where the default HDFS-backed state store causes long JVM garbage collection pauses.[^ss-rocks] It is the only built-in provider that supports [transformWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState).

## How is the RocksDB state store enabled?

The provider is chosen with `spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass`. In Apache Spark, set it to `org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider` before a query first starts; the provider cannot be changed between restarts from the same checkpoint.[^ss-rocks][^sqlconf]

```python
spark.conf.set(
    "spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass",
    "org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider",
)
spark.conf.set(
    "spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.rocksdb.changelogCheckpointing.enabled", "true"
)
```

On Databricks, RocksDB is the default state store provider in Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS and above. Older runtimes enable it with the provider class `com.databricks.sql.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider`.[^db]

Spark 4.3.0 is built against version 9.8.4 of the `rocksdbjni` library.[^pom] `spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.rocksdb.formatVersion` (default 5) is stored in the checkpoint when a query starts and used for its whole lifetime.[^sqlconf]

## How does it checkpoint state?

By default the RocksDB state store uses **incremental snapshot checkpointing**. At each commit it uploads the RocksDB manifest files and the SST data files that are new since the previous version.[^ss-cl] In the checkpoint, SST and log files get unique names in shared directories, and each version is described by a `''version''.zip` file with the metadata that maps local file names to the uploaded files. Unlike the HDFS-backed store, which has to replay earlier `.delta` files, each `.zip` is a complete description of one version.[^rocksfm]

### What is changelog checkpointing?

With **changelog checkpointing**, each commit uploads only the changes made to the state since the last checkpoint, in a `.changelog` file, instead of a snapshot. Snapshots are still written periodically in the background, to bound recovery time and allow old changelogs to be removed. The Spark guide states that this avoids the cost of capturing and uploading snapshots and reduces streaming query latency.[^ss-cl][^rocksfm]

Changelog checkpointing was added in Spark 3.5.0 (SPARK-43421).[^jira] In Apache Spark it is off by default and is turned on with `spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.rocksdb.changelogCheckpointing.enabled=true`. It is compatible in both directions with snapshot checkpointing: an existing query can switch to changelog checkpointing, or back, on restart without discarding its state.[^ss-cl] Snapshots are created after `spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.minDeltasForSnapshot` (default 10) changelog versions.[^rocksdbsrc][^sqlconf]

On Databricks, changelog checkpointing is available in Databricks Runtime 13.3 LTS and above and enabled by default in 17.3 LTS and above; Databricks recommends it for all stateful Structured Streaming queries.[^db]

## How is RocksDB memory controlled?

RocksDB allocates memory for memtables (write buffers), the block cache and filter and index blocks. Left unbounded, the instances on one executor can together use enough memory to cause out-of-memory errors.[^ss-mem]

Setting `spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.rocksdb.boundedMemoryUsage=true` caps the total memory of all RocksDB instances on a node at `maxMemoryUsageMB` (default 500), through RocksDB's write buffer manager. The cap is a soft limit: usage can briefly exceed it. Per-instance limits are set with `writeBufferSizeMB` and `maxWriteBufferNumber`, which by default use RocksDB's own defaults.[^ss-mem]

## Configuration

All keys start with `spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.rocksdb.`. Defaults are those of Spark 4.3.0.[^ss-rocks]

| Key suffix | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `changelogCheckpointing.enabled` | `false` | Upload changelogs instead of snapshots at commit |
| `compactOnCommit` | `false` | Run a range compaction at each commit |
| `blockSizeKB` | 4 | Approximate user data per block in a block-based SST table |
| `blockCacheSizeMB` | 8 | Block cache capacity |
| `lockAcquireTimeoutMs` | 60000 | Wait for the instance lock when loading |
| `maxOpenFiles` | -1 | Open file limit; -1 keeps all files open |
| `resetStatsOnLoad` | `true` | Reset RocksDB statistics on load |
| `trackTotalNumberOfRows` | `true` | Track total rows in state; costs an extra lookup per write |
| `writeBufferSizeMB` | -1 | Maximum memtable size; -1 uses the RocksDB default |
| `maxWriteBufferNumber` | -1 | Maximum number of memtables; -1 uses the RocksDB default |
| `boundedMemoryUsage` | `false` | Bound total RocksDB memory per node |
| `maxMemoryUsageMB` | 500 | Total memory limit per node when bounded |
| `writeBufferCacheRatio` | 0.5 | Share of the bound used for write buffers |
| `highPriorityPoolRatio` | 0.1 | Share of the bound used for high-priority blocks |
| `allowFAllocate` | `true` | Let RocksDB pre-allocate disk space with fallocate |
| `compression` | `lz4` | RocksDB compression type |

Turning off `trackTotalNumberOfRows` can improve write performance; the reported number of rows in state is then 0. It can be changed when the query restarts.[^ss-rocks]

## Comparison with Flink's RocksDB backend

[Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) also has an embedded RocksDB state backend, `EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend`. It stores state as serialized bytes, always takes asynchronous snapshots, and is the only Flink backend that offers incremental checkpoints.[^flink-sb] Flink's default is the heap-based `HashMapStateBackend`, as Spark's default is the heap-based HDFS-backed state store.[^flink-sb]

# Runtime filter

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Runtime_filter

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Bloom filter join, dynamic filtering (Trino), runtime filtering (Impala), semi-join reduction</Field>
  <Field name="field">Query optimization</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Creation side (small, filtered join input), application side (large join input), filter structure (bloom filter, value set or min/max range)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (since 3.3.0), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink), Apache Impala</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Dynamic partition pruning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dynamic_partition_pruning), [Bloom filter (data files)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Bloom_filter_(data_files)), [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Sort-merge join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Sort-merge_join), [Predicate pushdown](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (InjectRuntimeFilter.scala, BloomFilterMightContain.scala, FileSourceStrategy.scala, SQLConf.scala), Spark JIRA SPARK-32268 and SPARK-38841, the Trino 484 dynamic filtering page, the Apache Flink 2.3 table configuration page and the Apache Impala runtime filtering page</Verified>

A **runtime filter** is a filter that a query engine builds while a join is running from the join keys of the smaller, filtered input and applies to the larger input before the join, so that rows which cannot find a match are dropped early.[^rule] In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a runtime filter is a bloom filter built from one side of a shuffle join and applied to the other side to reduce the data that goes into the [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle); Spark added it in 3.3.0 and has enabled it by default since 3.4.0. Other engines have the same idea under other names, such as dynamic filtering in [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino).[^trino]

## How does a runtime filter work?

A runtime filter has two sides. The **creation side** is the join input with a selective predicate, for example a dimension table filtered to a few rows; the engine reads its join keys and builds a compact filter from them. The **application side** is the large input; the engine applies the filter to it, ideally at the scan, so that rows whose keys are not in the filter never reach the join.

The filter structure varies. A bloom filter answers "might this key be present?" in a fixed amount of memory; it can return false positives but never false negatives, so it never drops a row that would match.[^parquetbloom] Other engines also use exact value sets or minimum and maximum ranges.

## How does the runtime filter work in Apache Spark?

Spark's optimizer rule `InjectRuntimeFilter` inserts a runtime filter on one side of a join if it can build one from the other side. The source describes the filter as logically an `IN` subquery on the join keys, currently always implemented as a bloom filter.[^rule] The feature came from SPARK-32268, "Bloom Filter Join", fixed in 3.3.0, and SPARK-38841 enabled it by default in 3.4.0.[^n1][^n2]

At Spark 4.3.0, the rule adds a bloom filter on a join key only when:[^rule][^sqlconf]
- the join is a shuffle join, or a broadcast join with a shuffle below the side to be filtered;
- the join keys are simple, cheap expressions;
- there is no [dynamic partition pruning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dynamic_partition_pruning) filter on the same key already;
- the creation side has a selective predicate, or is a fully materialized, repeatable cached input with evidence that pruning helps;
- the creation side is small enough: its estimated size must be under `spark.sql.optimizer.runtime.bloomFilter.creationSideThreshold` (default 10MB), or, for a fully materialized, repeatable input with accurate statistics, under `spark.sql.optimizer.runtime.bloomFilter.materializedCreationSideThreshold` (default 100MB, since 4.3.0), which replaces the general threshold for such inputs;
- the application side's scan size is over `spark.sql.optimizer.runtime.bloomFilter.applicationSideScanSizeThreshold` (default 10GB);
- the query has fewer than `spark.sql.optimizer.runtimeFilter.number.threshold` (default 10) runtime filters already, a limit that protects the driver from running out of memory.

| Setting | Default | Since |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spark.sql.optimizer.runtime.bloomFilter.enabled` | true | 3.3.0 |
| `spark.sql.optimizer.runtime.bloomFilter.creationSideThreshold` | 10MB | 3.3.0 |
| `spark.sql.optimizer.runtime.bloomFilter.materializedCreationSideThreshold` | 100MB | 4.3.0 |
| `spark.sql.optimizer.runtime.bloomFilter.applicationSideScanSizeThreshold` | 10GB | 3.3.0 |
| `spark.sql.optimizer.runtime.bloomFilter.expectedNumItems` | 1000000 | 3.3.0 |
| `spark.sql.optimizer.runtime.bloomFilter.numBits` | 8388608 | 3.3.0 |
| `spark.sql.optimizer.runtimeFilter.number.threshold` | 10 | 3.3.0 |

All values are from `SQLConf.scala` at Spark 4.3.0.[^sqlconf]

In a Spark plan, an injected runtime filter appears as a `might_contain(...)` predicate in a `Filter` on the application side, which refers to a scalar subquery that builds the bloom filter.[^rule][^n3] Spark does not push the bloom filter into file scans as a data filter; it is evaluated on the rows after the scan.[^n4]

## Runtime filters in other engines

|  | Apache Spark | Trino | Apache Flink | Apache Impala |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Name | Runtime filter (bloom filter join)[^rule] | Dynamic filtering[^trino] | Runtime filter[^flink] | Runtime filtering[^impala] |
| On by default? | Yes, since 3.4.0[^sqlconf] | Yes[^trino] | No (`table.optimizer.runtime-filter.enabled` is false)[^flink] | Yes; `RUNTIME_FILTER_MODE` defaults to `GLOBAL` in Impala 2.6 and higher[^impala] |
| Filter structure | Bloom filter | Distinct value sets; falls back to per-column minimum and maximum when the build side exceeds size thresholds[^trino] | Not described on the configuration page | Bloom filter for HDFS-based tables; minimum and maximum filter for Kudu tables[^impala] |
| Applies to | Shuffle joins (and broadcast joins with a shuffle below them)[^rule] | Inner and right joins with `=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` or `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`, and semi-joins with `IN`[^trino] | Batch jobs only[^flink] | Joins; available since Impala 2.5[^impala] |
| Size limits | Creation side under 10MB (100MB for fully materialized inputs with accurate statistics), application side over 10GB by default[^sqlconf] | Build-side thresholds before falling back to min and max[^trino] | Build side under 150 mb, probe side over 10 gb, filter ratio over 0.5 by default[^flink] | Controlled by query options[^impala] |

## Runtime filter vs dynamic partition pruning

<Hatnote>Main article: [Dynamic partition pruning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dynamic_partition_pruning)</Hatnote>

Both techniques move information across a join at run time. [Dynamic partition pruning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Dynamic_partition_pruning) needs a partition column as the join key, and it skips whole partitions before they are read. A runtime filter works on any equi-join key, and it removes rows after the scan and before the shuffle. Spark checks for an existing DPP filter on a key before it injects a bloom filter on the same key.[^rule]

## Runtime filters vs bloom filters in data files

<Hatnote>Main article: [Bloom filter (data files)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Bloom_filter_(data_files))</Hatnote>

A runtime filter is built for one query and thrown away. A bloom filter in a data file, such as an [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) column bloom filter, is written once with the file and lets readers skip row groups for equality filters with a literal value.[^parquetbloom]

# Ryan Blue

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Ryan_Blue

<Infobox type="person">
  <Field name="known_for">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)</Field>
  <Field name="role">Software engineer</Field>
  <Field name="affiliations">[Databricks](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Databricks), [Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation)</Field>
  <Field name="projects">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Databricks and PR Newswire acquisition announcements, the Databricks Data + AI Summit speaker page and the ASF project leadership list</Verified>

**Ryan Blue** is a software engineer known as one of the original creators of [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), an [open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) for large analytic datasets. He developed Iceberg at [Netflix](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Netflix) with Daniel Weeks, co-founded the data management company [Tabular](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Tabular) around the format, and joined [Databricks](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Databricks) when it acquired Tabular in 2024.[^prnewswire][^dbxblog]

## Career and work

Blue worked at Cloudera before joining Netflix, where he was part of the big data platform team.[^dais] At Netflix, Blue and Daniel Weeks developed Apache Iceberg and later donated the project to the [Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation).[^dbxblog]

In 2021, Blue co-founded Tabular with Daniel Weeks and Jason Reid.[^techcrunch] Tabular built a data management platform around Iceberg, and Blue served as its chief executive officer.[^prnewswire]

On 4 June 2024, Databricks announced that it had agreed to acquire Tabular.[^prnewswire] Databricks stated that the acquisition completed on 7 June 2024.[^dbxblog] After the acquisition, Blue is listed as a Member of Technical Staff at Databricks.[^dais]

## Contributions to the open lakehouse

Apache Iceberg is the contribution for which Blue is most widely recognized. Iceberg was created at Netflix to address correctness, performance and scalability problems with the earlier [Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive) table layout, and was donated to the Apache Software Foundation as an open-source project.[^prnewswire][^dbxblog] Iceberg lets multiple query engines read and write the same tables on object storage with transactional guarantees, a pattern central to the [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse).

Blue chairs the Apache Iceberg Project Management Committee (PMC).[^prnewswire] The Apache Software Foundation lists him as Vice President, Apache Iceberg, the officer role that corresponds to the PMC chair of a top-level project.[^asf]

The 2024 Databricks acquisition was described as bringing together the original creators of Apache Iceberg and the creators of [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), with a stated goal of improving interoperability between the two open table formats.[^prnewswire][^dbxblog]

## Selected works

- Apache Iceberg, the open table format Blue co-created at Netflix and contributed to the Apache Software Foundation.[^prnewswire][^dbxblog]
- Conference presentations on Apache Iceberg and open table formats, including sessions at the Databricks Data + AI Summit.[^dais]

# Salting

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Salting

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Key salting, salted join</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Random salt column on the skewed side, replicated (exploded) other side, join on key plus salt</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">Applies to any shuffle-based engine; usually written by hand in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Data skew](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_skew), [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution), [Join strategy hints](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Join_strategy_hints)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/sql-performance-tuning.md, adaptive/OptimizeSkewedJoin.scala, python/pyspark/sql/functions, docs/rdd-programming-guide.md), SPARK-29544 and the Databricks skew and spill guide</Verified>

**Salting** is a manual technique for [data skew](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_skew) in which a random number, the salt, is added to a hot join or grouping key so that the rows for that key are spread over several tasks instead of one. In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) before 3.0 the engine had no automatic skew join handling, so salting was done by hand; since Spark 3.0, [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution) (AQE) splits most skewed joins automatically, and salting is kept for the cases AQE does not cover.[^perf][^spark29544]

## How salting works

A [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle) sends all rows with the same key to the same partition. If one key holds most of the rows, one task does most of the work.[^shuffle] The Databricks guide to skew describes the remedy as appending a random bucket suffix to the skewed keys, and, for an aggregation, grouping and aggregating in two stages.[^dbxskew] For a join, salting changes the shuffle key from `key` to `(key, salt)`, where `salt` is an integer from 0 to N - 1:

1. On the large, skewed side, add a column with a random salt for each row.
1. On the other side, replicate each row N times, once per salt value (for example with `explode` over a sequence, which returns one row per array element).[^pyfuncs]
1. Join on both the original key and the salt.

Each hot key is now split across N shuffle partitions. Because each salted row carries exactly one salt value and the other side has a copy for every value, each salted row still meets every matching row from the other side exactly once. The cost is that the other side grows N times, so N is kept as small as the skew allows.

The result is unchanged only when no row of the replicated side has to appear on its own. That holds for an inner join, a left outer join that preserves the salted side, and a left semi or left anti join with the salted side on the left. It does not hold when the join must keep unmatched rows of the replicated side, as a right outer join that preserves the replicated side or a full outer join does: an unmatched replicated row then appears once per salt value, N times instead of once.

## Example in PySpark

```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

N = 8  # number of salt values

orders_salted = orders.withColumn("salt", (F.rand() * N).cast("int"))

customers_salted = customers.withColumn(
    "salt", F.explode(F.sequence(F.lit(0), F.lit(N - 1)))
)

joined = orders_salted.join(customers_salted, ["customer_id", "salt"]).drop("salt")
```

`rand()`, `sequence()` and `explode()` are built-in functions of `pyspark.sql.functions`.[^pyfuncs] A variant salts only the known hot keys and leaves other keys unsalted, which keeps the replicated side small.

### Salting a full outer join

A full outer join can be rebuilt from parts that salt correctly: a salted left outer join that keeps every row of the skewed side, plus the rows of the other side that have no match, found with an unsalted left anti join against the distinct keys of the skewed side.

```python
matched_or_left = orders_salted.join(customers_salted, ["customer_id", "salt"], "left").drop("salt")

order_keys = orders.select("customer_id").distinct()
right_only = customers.join(order_keys, "customer_id", "left_anti")

full = matched_or_left.unionByName(right_only, allowMissingColumns=True)
```

### Salting an aggregation

For a skewed `GROUP BY`, salting runs the aggregation in two steps: first group by `(key, salt)`, then group the partial results by `key`.[^dbxskew] This works for aggregates that can be combined, such as `sum`, `count`, `min` and `max`; an average is computed from a salted sum and a salted count.

## When does AQE make salting unnecessary?

AQE skew join handling, added in Spark 3.0.0 and on by default whenever AQE is on (the default since Spark 3.2.0), detects a skewed shuffle partition at runtime and splits it into smaller tasks, replicating the matching partition of the other side. That is the same idea as salting, done by the engine and only for the partitions that need it.[^perf][^spark29544] A partition counts as skewed when it is over 5 times the median size and over 256 MB, by default.[^perf]

For an inner join, a left or right outer join on the side that can be split, or a semi or anti join, AQE usually makes salting unnecessary.[^rule] Salting is still used when:

- **The join type cannot be split.** In Spark 4.3.0, AQE splits the left side only for inner, cross, left semi, left anti and left outer joins, and the right side only for inner, cross and right outer joins. A full outer join, or a left outer join whose right side is skewed, is not split.[^rule]
- **The skew is in an aggregation or window.** The AQE skew rule targets sort-merge and shuffled hash joins, not aggregations.[^rule]
- **AQE is off** (`spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=false`) or skew join handling is off (`spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=false`).[^perf]
- **The skew is below the thresholds** but still slows the stage. Lowering `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes` or `skewedPartitionFactor` is often simpler than salting in that case.[^perf]

## Salting compared with other skew remedies

| Remedy | Who does it | Cost | Join types |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AQE skew join (Spark) | The engine, at runtime | Replicates only the matching partition of the other side | Splittable sides only (see above)[^rule] |
| [Broadcast join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Broadcast_join) | The planner, or a `BROADCAST` hint | The small side is copied to every executor[^perf] | Most join types; which side can be broadcast depends on the join type |
| Salting | The user, in the query | Replicates the whole other side N times | Inner joins; left outer, left semi and left anti joins with the salted side on the left; full outer joins only when rebuilt as above; also aggregations |

# Scala 2.12 and 2.13 in Spark

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Scala_2.12_and_2.13_in_Spark

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Scala binary version; Scala cross-build</Field>
  <Field name="field">Build and dependency management</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Scala 2.12 builds in Spark 2.4.0; Scala 2.13 builds in Spark 3.2.0</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Scala binary version, artifact suffix (`_2.12`, `_2.13`), Maven profiles</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">pom.xml at the v2.4.0, v3.0.0, v3.2.0, v3.5.0, v4.0.0 and v4.3.0 tags of apache/spark, docs/index.md and docs/building-spark.md at v3.5.0 and v4.3.0, the Spark 3.2.0, 3.5.0 and 4.0.0 release notes, SPARK-14220, SPARK-26132, SPARK-25075, SPARK-34218, SPARK-43836 and SPARK-45314, gradle.properties at apache-iceberg-1.12.0, and the Scala binary compatibility documentation</Verified>

<Status level="removed">Removed in Apache Spark 4.0.0. Use Scala 2.13 instead. This status is for Scala 2.12 support. Spark 3.5.0 announced the removal, and from Spark 4.0.0 Scala 2.13 is the only Scala version Spark is built for.[^s45314]</Status>

**Scala 2.12 and 2.13 in Spark** refers to the two Scala versions that [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) was built for during the Spark 3 series, and to the requirement that Scala and Java applications, libraries and connectors use the same Scala version as the Spark build they run on.[^index43] Spark 3.2.0 to 3.5.x published artifacts for both Scala 2.12 and 2.13, with 2.12 as the default build. Spark 4.0.0 removed Scala 2.12, so every Spark 4 release is built only for Scala 2.13.[^s45314] The version shows up in artifact names such as `spark-sql_2.13`, and it has to match for every jar that contains Scala code, including connectors and table format runtimes.

## Status

Scala 2.12 support was removed in Spark 4.0.0 by SPARK-45314, "Drop Scala 2.12 and make Scala 2.13 by default".[^s45314][^r400] The Spark 3.5.0 release notes had announced it in an "Upcoming Removal" section, which said that support for Scala 2.12 would be removed in the next major release and that the minimum Scala version would be 2.13.[^r350] An earlier proposal to make 2.13 the default already in Spark 3.5 (SPARK-43836) was closed as Won't Do.[^s43836]

At the v4.3.0 tag, the root `pom.xml` sets Scala 2.13.18 with binary version 2.13 and defines only a `scala-2.13` profile; there is no Scala 2.12 or Scala 3 build.[^pom430] The Spark 4.3.0 documentation says that Spark runs on Scala 2.13 and that applications using the Scala API must use the Scala version Spark was compiled for, which since Spark 4.0.0 is 2.13.[^index43]

## History

| Spark release | Default Scala build | Other Scala build | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2.4.0 | 2.11 | 2.12 | Scala 2.12 build added (SPARK-14220)[^s14220][^pom240] |
| 3.0.0 | 2.12 | None published (2.13 artifacts came in 3.2.0) | Scala 2.11 removed (SPARK-26132)[^s26132] |
| 3.2.0 | 2.12 | 2.13 | Scala 2.13 build and published artifacts (SPARK-25075, SPARK-34218)[^s25075][^r320] |
| 3.5.0 | 2.12 | 2.13 | Removal of 2.12 announced for the next major release[^r350] |
| 4.0.0 | 2.13 | None | Scala 2.12 removed (SPARK-45314)[^s45314] |
| 4.3.0 | 2.13 | None | No change; Scala 2.13.18[^pom430] |

In the Spark 3 series the 2.13 build was an alternative, not the default. The Spark 3.5.0 build documentation lists Scala 2.12 and 2.13 as supported and explains that switching requires `./dev/change-scala-version.sh 2.13` and the `scala-2.13` Maven or sbt profile.[^build350][^pom350]

## Why the Scala version matters

Scala's binary compatibility guarantee covers releases within one series, such as 2.13.x, and not across series, so code compiled for Scala 2.12 is not guaranteed to run with the Scala 2.13 library.[^scalabc] For that reason Scala libraries are published once per Scala binary version, with the version appended to the artifact name, and Spark follows the same convention: `spark-core_2.12` and `spark-core_2.13` are separate artifacts.[^pom350] The Spark 3.5.0 documentation gives the rule directly: when using Scala 2.13, use Spark compiled for 2.13 and compile applications for 2.13 as well.[^index350]

The rule reaches beyond user code. Connector and table format jars that contain Scala code are built per Scala version too. For example, the [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) documentation lists Spark runtime jars such as `iceberg-spark-runtime-3.5_2.12` and `iceberg-spark-runtime-3.5_2.13`, where the first number is the Spark version and the suffix is the Scala version; at apache-iceberg-1.12.0 the build knows Scala 2.12 and 2.13 and Spark 3.5, 4.0, 4.1 and 4.2.[^icegradle] Adding a `_2.12` connector to a Spark 4 cluster is a mismatch, because no Spark 4 build uses Scala 2.12.

Python users of PySpark and clients of [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) do not compile against Spark's Scala classes, so the Scala version is mostly invisible to them. It still matters when they add JVM packages to the server or session, for example with `--packages`, because those jars load into the Scala 2.13 JVM.

## Example

A Maven dependency for Spark SQL 4.3.0 names the Scala binary version in the artifact ID:[^pom430]

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.apache.spark</groupId>
  <artifactId>spark-sql_2.13</artifactId>
  <version>4.3.0</version>
  <scope>provided</scope>
</dependency>
```

The equivalent sbt line is `"org.apache.spark" %% "spark-sql" % "4.3.0" % "provided"` with `scalaVersion` set to a 2.13 release; the `%%` operator appends the project's Scala binary version to the artifact name.[^sbt]

# Session window

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Session_window

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Gap-based window, sessionization</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Spark 3.2.0 (`session_window`)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Grouping key, event-time column, gap duration (static or per record), [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) (`session_window`), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) (session window assigners, `SESSION` TVF), Kafka Streams (`SessionWindows`)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Windowing (stream processing)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Windowing_(stream_processing)), [Stateful stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stateful_stream_processing), [transformWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming programming guide and Real-time Mode guide, `python/pyspark/sql/functions/builtin.py` and `SQLConf.scala` at tag v4.3.0 of apache/spark, SPARK-10816, the Apache Flink 2.3 DataStream "Windows" and SQL "Windowing TVF" pages, and the Kafka Streams 4.4 DSL developer guide</Verified>

In [stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing), a **session window** is a window whose length is set by the data: it opens with a record for a key, extends each time another record for that key arrives within a **gap duration**, and closes when no record arrives for the length of the gap. Session windows group bursts of activity, such as one user's clicks during a visit, without fixing the window size in advance. In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), session windows are built with the `session_window` function, added in Spark 3.2.0.[^builtin][^jira]

## How is a session window different from a tumbling or sliding window?

Tumbling and sliding windows have a fixed size and fixed boundaries, so the engine can compute a record's window from its timestamp alone. A session window has neither: its start is the first record of the session and its end moves later with every new record. Spark's guide describes it as having a dynamic size that depends on the inputs.[^ss-types] See [Windowing (stream processing)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Windowing_(stream_processing)) for the other window types.

Because a later record can join two earlier sessions into one, engines implement session windows by merging. [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink)'s documentation states that its session window operator creates a new window for every record and merges windows that are closer to each other than the gap.[^flink-win]

## How does session_window work in Spark?

`session_window(timeColumn, gapDuration)` returns a struct column named `session_window` with `start` and `end` fields. The end of a session is the timestamp of its latest record plus the gap, so it grows as records join the session.[^builtin]

The gap can be a static string such as `"5 minutes"` or a column expression evaluated per row, for example a different gap per user type. With a dynamic gap, a session's range is the union of the ranges of its events (each event's time plus its own gap), and rows whose gap evaluates to zero or a negative value are filtered out of the aggregation.[^ss-types][^builtin]

A streaming session window query has these restrictions in Spark 4.3.0:[^ss-types]
- Update [output mode](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Output_mode) is not supported; use append (sessions are emitted when the [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) passes their end) or complete.
- The grouping key must contain at least one column besides `session_window`. A global session window, with `session_window` as the only key, is allowed only in batch queries.

By default Spark does not pre-aggregate sessions before the shuffle, because doing so needs an extra local sort. Setting `spark.sql.streaming.sessionWindow.merge.sessions.in.local.partition` (default `false`, since 3.2.0) to `true` sorts and merges sessions within each partition first, which helps when many rows of a batch belong to the same session.[^ss-types][^sqlconf]

Session-window aggregation is not supported in Real-time Mode as of Spark 4.3.0.[^rtm] Sessions with custom rules, such as closing a session on a logout event, need arbitrary stateful processing with [transformWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState).

### Example

This PySpark query counts page views per user session, where a session ends after 30 minutes without activity, and uses a shorter gap for one class of users:

```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

views = spark.readStream.table("main.web.page_views")   # columns: ts, user_id, user_type

gap = F.when(F.col("user_type") == "bot", "1 minute").otherwise("30 minutes")

sessions = (views
    .withWatermark("ts", "1 hour")
    .groupBy(F.session_window("ts", gap), "user_id")
    .agg(F.count("*").alias("views")))

(sessions.writeStream
    .outputMode("append")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/checkpoints/sessions")
    .toTable("main.web.user_sessions"))
```

In Spark SQL the same grouping is `GROUP BY session_window(ts, '30 minutes'), user_id`.

## Spark session_window compared with Flink

|  | Spark `session_window` | Flink DataStream session assigners | Flink SQL `SESSION` TVF |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gap | Static string or per-row column expression[^builtin] | Static gap, or a `SessionWindowTimeGapExtractor` for dynamic gaps[^flink-win] | Static gap only[^flink-tvf] |
| Key | At least one grouping column besides the window in streaming[^ss-types] | Keyed (`keyBy`) or non-keyed streams[^flink-win] | Optional `PARTITION BY` key columns[^flink-tvf] |
| Time | Event time; processing time by windowing on `current_timestamp`[^builtin] | Event-time and processing-time variants[^flink-win] | Event or processing time attribute[^flink-tvf] |

The two engines differ in batch support and in late data. Spark runs `session_window` in batch queries too, including a global session window, while Flink's `SESSION` TVF is not supported in batch mode.[^ss-types][^flink-tvf] In Spark, a record that arrives after the watermark has passed its session's end is not added to the session; Flink's DataStream session windows drop such records by default, and `allowedLateness` keeps windows open longer.[^ss-types][^flink-win]

Kafka Streams also has session windows: sessions are periods of activity separated by an inactivity gap, and the process is called sessionization.[^kstreams]

# Shuffle

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Exchange (Trino; the `Exchange` operator in Spark plans)</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Map side (shuffle write), shuffle files, reduce side (shuffle fetch), stage boundary</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Partition](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), [Small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/rdd-programming-guide.md, docs/sql-performance-tuning.md, docs/configuration.md, docs/job-scheduling.md, core DAGScheduler.scala), an EXPLAIN run on a Spark 4.3.1-SNAPSHOT build, the Trino 484 docs and the Apache Flink 2.3 docs</Verified>

A **shuffle** is the step in a distributed query engine that redistributes data across the cluster so that it is grouped differently across [partitions](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), for example so that all rows with the same key end up in the same task.[^rddguide] The term is most used in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), where a shuffle copies data between [executors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor) and machines and is one of the most costly operations in a job. Other engines do the same work under other names: [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) calls it an exchange, and [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) distinguishes pipelined shuffles for streaming jobs from blocking shuffles for batch jobs.

## Why a shuffle happens

A Spark task works on one partition at a time. Operations such as `groupBy`, `reduceByKey` or a join need all the values for a key in one place, but those values are usually spread over many partitions and machines. Spark must read from all partitions and bring the values for each key together; this all-to-all step is the shuffle.[^rddguide]

Operations whose output partition depends on many input partitions are often called **wide** transformations, and they cause a shuffle. Operations such as `map` and `filter` have **narrow** dependencies: each output partition depends on one input partition, so Spark can run them together in the same task.[^dag] The Spark documentation lists repartition operations, most `ByKey` operations and joins as operations that can cause a shuffle.[^rddguide] A broadcast join avoids a shuffle by sending the small side to every executor; Spark plans one automatically when a table is smaller than `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` (default 10 MB).[^perf]

## Stages and shuffle files

Spark builds stages by cutting the job's graph at shuffle boundaries. One stage writes a set of map output files; the next stage reads those files after all of them are written.[^dag] The writing side is called the map side and the reading side the reduce side, names taken from MapReduce rather than from Spark's own `map` and `reduce` functions.[^rddguide]

On the map side, each task keeps its output in memory until it no longer fits, then sorts it by target partition and writes it to a single file. Reduce tasks then read the sorted blocks that belong to them.[^rddguide] The files go to the directories in `spark.local.dir` (default `/tmp`) and are compressed by default (`spark.shuffle.compress`).[^config] Spark keeps shuffle files until the data that uses them is garbage collected, so that lost work can be recomputed without writing them again; long-running applications can therefore use a lot of disk.[^rddguide]

In a DataFrame or SQL plan, a shuffle shows up as an `Exchange` operator. The plan below, from `EXPLAIN` on a `GROUP BY` with adaptive query execution turned off, aggregates each partition first (`partial_sum`), shuffles by the grouping key into 200 partitions, and then finishes the aggregation:

```
*(2) HashAggregate(keys=[code#14], functions=[sum(amount#13)])
+- Exchange hashpartitioning(code#14, 200), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS, [plan_id=35]
   +- *(1) HashAggregate(keys=[code#14], functions=[partial_sum(amount#13)])
      +- *(1) Project [amount#13, code#14]
         +- *(1) ColumnarToRow
            +- FileScan parquet [amount#13,code#14,order_date#15] ...
```

The 200 comes from `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions`, whose default is 200.[^perf]

## Spill

Shuffle operations build in-memory structures to organize records before or after the transfer. When these do not fit in the [executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor)'s execution memory, Spark spills them to disk, which adds disk I/O and garbage collection.[^rddguide] Spilled data is compressed by default (`spark.shuffle.spill.compress`).[^config] Spill is a different thing from shuffle files: shuffle files are the normal output of the map side, while spill files are temporary overflow inside one task.

## Adaptive query execution

Adaptive query execution (AQE) re-plans a query while it runs, using statistics from completed shuffle stages. It is on by default since Spark 3.2.0.[^perf]

- **Coalescing partitions.** After a shuffle, AQE merges small contiguous shuffle partitions so that a query does not run many tiny tasks. The target size is `spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes` (default 64 MB), but by default (`spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.parallelismFirst` is true) Spark favors parallelism and only enforces a minimum partition size of 1 MB.[^perf]
- **Skew join handling.** A shuffle partition is treated as skewed when it is larger than 5 times the median partition size and larger than 256 MB (`spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor` and `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes`). AQE splits such partitions in sort-merge joins into smaller tasks, replicating the other side where needed.[^perf]
- **Join conversion.** When runtime statistics show that one side of a sort-merge join is small, AQE can switch to a broadcast hash join and read the shuffle files locally.[^perf]

A storage partition join avoids the shuffle altogether when both sides of a join come from a V2 data source, such as [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), that reports a compatible partitioning; the plan then has no `Exchange` before the join.[^perf]

## External shuffle service and push-based shuffle

By default, an executor serves its own shuffle files to other executors. The **external shuffle service** is a long-running process on each node that serves shuffle files instead, so they stay available after the executor that wrote them is removed. It is enabled with `spark.shuffle.service.enabled` (default false) and matters most for dynamic allocation.[^jobsched][^config] Spark on Kubernetes does not support it; there, shuffle tracking or decommissioning keeps shuffle data available instead.[^jobsched]

**Push-based shuffle**, added in Spark 3.2.0, has map tasks push their blocks to external shuffle services, which merge them per shuffle partition. Reduce tasks then read a mix of merged partitions and original blocks, which turns many small random disk reads into large sequential reads. It is off by default (`spark.shuffle.push.enabled`) and is supported only on YARN with the external shuffle service.[^config]

## Comparison: how engines exchange data between stages

|  | Apache Spark | Trino | Apache Flink |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Name | Shuffle (`Exchange` in plans) | Exchange[^trino] | Shuffle (pipelined or blocking network exchange)[^flinkshuffle] |
| How data moves | Map tasks write sorted files to local disk; the next stage fetches them after the map stage is done[^dag] | Tasks write into output buffers; tasks of the next stage read them through an exchange client[^trino] | Streaming: pipelined exchange between running tasks. Batch: blocking shuffle (data is persisted and read after it is fully produced) or experimental hybrid shuffle[^flinkshuffle] |
| Failure handling | Lost shuffle output makes Spark rerun the stages that produced it[^dag] | By default a node failure fails the query; with `retry-policy=TASK`, intermediate data is spooled through an exchange manager to storage such as S3 or HDFS[^trinofte] | Batch blocking shuffle keeps persisted results that consumers read later; hybrid shuffle can store data on remote storage[^flinkshuffle] |

# Shuffle hash join

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle_hash_join

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Shuffled hash join, SHJ, `ShuffledHashJoin`</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed query processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Shuffle exchange, build side, stream side, per-partition hash table</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Sort-merge join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Sort-merge_join), [Broadcast join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Broadcast_join), [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution), [Cost-based optimizer (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Cost-based_optimizer_(Spark))</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (SparkStrategies.scala, joins.scala, ShuffledHashJoinExec.scala, SQLConf.scala, sql-performance-tuning.md and sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-hints.md)</Verified>

A **shuffle hash join** is a distributed equality-join strategy that repartitions both inputs by the join keys, then builds a hash table from one input partition inside each join task.[^shjexec] In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), the physical operator is named `ShuffledHashJoin`. Shuffle hash join avoids sorting both inputs, but it uses more task memory than a [sort-merge join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Sort-merge_join) because every task constructs a hash table from its build-side partition.[^strategies]

## How does a shuffle hash join work?

A Spark shuffle hash join has three steps:[^shjexec]

1. **Shuffle both inputs.** Spark uses compatible hash partitioning so equal join keys from both sides reach the same partition number.
1. **Build a local hash table.** In every join task, Spark reads the selected **build-side** partition and creates a `HashedRelation` keyed by the join columns.
1. **Probe the table.** The task streams rows from the other partition, called the **stream side**, and looks each key up in the local hash table.

Unlike a [broadcast join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Broadcast_join), shuffle hash join does not collect the complete build side at the [driver](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Driver_(Apache_Spark)) or send a full copy to every executor. Each task receives only its build partition. Unlike sort-merge join, shuffle hash join does not require the two shuffled partitions to be sorted before they are joined.

## What does ShuffledHashJoin mean in EXPLAIN?

A representative plan forced with a `SHUFFLE_HASH` hint has this shape:

```
*(3) ShuffledHashJoin [customer_id#1L], [customer_id#8L], Inner, BuildRight
:- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id#1L, 200), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS
:  +- Scan parquet orders
+- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id#8L, 200), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS
   +- Scan parquet customers
```

The two `Exchange hashpartitioning` nodes show that both sides shuffle. `BuildRight` means each task builds its hash table from the right input partition and streams the left input partition through it. The absence of `Sort` operators is the main visual difference from a `SortMergeJoin` plan.

## When does Spark pick shuffle hash join automatically?

Without a hint, Spark 4.3.0 considers shuffle hash join after broadcast hash join. The non-adaptive planner chooses it only when all of these conditions hold:[^joins][^strategies]

- `spark.sql.join.preferSortMergeJoin` is `false`; it defaults to `true`.[^sqlconf]
- One input is estimated small enough to build a local hash map. Spark tests its total estimated bytes against the automatic broadcast threshold multiplied by the number of shuffle partitions.
- That input is estimated to be much smaller than the other. Spark multiplies the candidate build-side size by `spark.sql.shuffledHashJoinFactor` and requires the result to be no larger than the other side.
- The equality-key data types support Spark's binary hash equality, and the join type permits the selected build side.

Because the default prefers sort-merge join, a static plan commonly uses `SortMergeJoin` for two non-broadcast inputs even when one is smaller. This preference reflects the planner's source comment that sort-merge join consumes less memory, while shuffled hash join can improve performance when one input is much smaller.[^sqlconf]

## How does AQE choose shuffle hash join?

[Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution) can replace a planned sort-merge join after shuffle statistics reveal that every build-side partition is small enough for a local hash table. The threshold is `spark.sql.adaptive.maxShuffledHashJoinLocalMapThreshold`, which defaults to 0 bytes. For this preference to apply, the threshold must be at least `spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes`, and every relevant partition must be no larger than the threshold.[^perf]

Spark 4.3.0 also has `spark.sql.adaptive.convertSortMergeJoinToShuffledHashJoin.enabled`, on by default, as the master switch for this conversion.[^sqlconf] The zero-byte local-map threshold means that setting a useful positive threshold is still necessary before ordinary nonempty partitions qualify through this AQE rule.

## How can a query request shuffle hash join?

The `SHUFFLE_HASH` hint requests the strategy and identifies the preferred build relation:[^hints]

```sql
SELECT /*+ SHUFFLE_HASH(customers) */
       orders.order_id, customers.region
FROM orders
JOIN customers
  ON orders.customer_id = customers.customer_id;
```

If both relations carry `SHUFFLE_HASH` hints, Spark chooses the build side from the join type and relation statistics. A hint is not a guarantee: Spark cannot use the strategy when the join has no equality keys or the requested build side is invalid for that join type.[^hints][^strategies]

## What are the tradeoffs?

|  | Shuffle hash join | Sort-merge join | Broadcast hash join |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Network work | Shuffles both inputs | Shuffles both inputs | Broadcasts one complete input; normally leaves the streamed input in place |
| CPU work after shuffle | Builds and probes a hash table; no key sort | Sorts both inputs and merges ordered streams | Probes a hash table already distributed to each executor |
| Memory scope | One build partition per concurrent task | Primarily sort and match buffers, which can spill | The complete built relation on the driver and a copy available to executors |
| Best fit | Build partitions are reliably much smaller than stream partitions and fit in task memory | Both sides are large or build-side memory is uncertain | One complete side is small enough to broadcast |

Shuffle hash join can outperform sort-merge join by avoiding sorts, especially when the build side is much smaller. It can also fail or slow sharply when a build partition is larger than estimated: constructing `HashedRelation` is memory-intensive, and skew can concentrate many build rows in one task.[^strategies][^shjexec] Increasing task concurrency can multiply this pressure because several tasks may build hash tables in the same executor at once.

AQE can reduce the risk when runtime partition sizes are available, but AQE cannot make a single oversized or highly skewed build partition cheap merely by changing the operator. Splitting skewed partitions, filtering earlier, improving statistics, or using sort-merge join may be safer when build-side memory is uncertain.

# Small files problem

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Small file problem; file fragmentation</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data storage, table maintenance</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Target file size, compaction, write-time file sizing, clustering</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Copy-on-write and merge-on-read](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Copy-on-write_and_merge-on-read), [Deletion vector](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Deletion_vector), [Partition](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 documentation (configuration, maintenance, Spark procedures, Spark writes, Spark Structured Streaming), the Delta Lake optimizations documentation, the Apache Hudi file sizing, clustering and configuration documentation (version 1.2.1), and Apache Spark 4.3.0 (SQLConf.scala and the 4.3.0 documentation)</Verified>

The **small files problem** is the slowdown and extra cost that occur when a table's data is spread across many files that are much smaller than the size the storage and query engines work best with. Every file adds metadata to track, a request to open it, and planning and scheduling work, so a table with many small files is slower to query and maintain than the same data in fewer, larger files.[^hudi-size][^ice-proc] In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), small files come mostly from frequent small writes, and every major [open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) provides compaction and write-time sizing to control them.

## Causes

**Streaming and micro-batch writes.** Each batch commits its own files. The Iceberg documentation notes that the amount of data written by a streaming process is typically small, which makes the table metadata track many small files.[^ice-stream] Hudi's clustering documentation describes the same tension: ingestion prefers small files for parallelism and freshness, while queries degrade with many small files.[^hudi-cluster]

**Many partitions per write task.** A file cannot span a table partition, and in Spark a file cannot be larger than the task that writes it. When one Spark task writes to several Iceberg partitions, each partition gets its own, smaller file.[^ice-writes] High-cardinality [partitioning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition) multiplies the number of files per commit.

**Compression and columnar encoding.** The size on disk is much smaller than the in-memory size of the task's rows, because the data is compressed and columnar. The Iceberg documentation gives the example that a 100 MB Spark task produces a file much smaller than 100 MB.[^ice-writes]

**Row-level changes.** Merge-on-read writes add small delete files. Iceberg's maintenance guide recommends compacting small position delete files because of the metadata and file-open overhead they add.[^ice-maint]

## Costs

- **Metadata.** Iceberg tracks every data file in manifests, so more files means more metadata, and small files cause an unnecessary amount of it.[^ice-proc]
- **File open and request cost.** Hudi's documentation points out that object stores such as S3 rate-limit requests per prefix, and that each file needs at least one request regardless of size, plus fixed costs to open and close it.[^hudi-size] Spark models this fixed cost with `spark.sql.files.openCostInBytes` (default 4 MB) when packing files into read partitions.[^sparkconf]
- **Planning and scheduling.** More files mean more tasks, which adds scheduling overhead and memory pressure to Spark, Flink or Hive jobs.[^hudi-size]
- **Storage efficiency.** Many small files can compress less well and need more index and statistics metadata.[^hudi-size]

## Remedies by project

### Apache Iceberg

Iceberg writers roll over to a new file when it reaches `write.target-file-size-bytes`, default 536870912 bytes (512 MB); delete files have a separate target, `write.delete.target-file-size-bytes`, default 64 MB.[^ice-conf] Because a Spark task may be too small to reach the target, the Iceberg documentation advises controlling what data each task receives with `write.distribution-mode` or an explicit repartition.[^ice-writes]

For existing files, the `rewrite_data_files` procedure compacts small files into larger ones, using bin-packing by default or a sort. Its options include `target-file-size-bytes` (defaulting to the table's target), `min-file-size-bytes` (75% of the target), `max-file-size-bytes` (180% of the target) and `min-input-files` (5).[^ice-proc] The `rewrite_manifests` procedure addresses the matching problem in metadata, since fast appends in streaming workloads can leave many small manifest files.[^ice-stream]

```sql
-- Apache Iceberg (Spark SQL): compact one day's files toward 512 MB
CALL catalog.system.rewrite_data_files(
  table   => 'db.events',
  where   => 'event_date = "2026-11-21"',
  options => map('target-file-size-bytes', '536870912')
);
```

### Delta Lake

Delta Lake's `OPTIMIZE` command (from 1.2.0) coalesces small files into larger ones by bin-packing and can be limited to a partition predicate with `WHERE`.[^delta-opt]

Auto compaction (from 3.1.0) runs synchronously after a successful write and compacts small files in the affected partitions. It is enabled with the table property `delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact` or the session setting `spark.databricks.delta.autoCompact.enabled`, uses a 128 MB target by default, and is tuned with `spark.databricks.delta.autoCompact.maxFileSize` and `spark.databricks.delta.autoCompact.minNumFiles`.[^delta-opt]

Optimized writes (from 3.1.0) shuffle data before writing so that each partition receives fewer, larger files, at the cost of extra write latency. The feature is off by default and is enabled with the table property `delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite`, the setting `spark.databricks.delta.optimizeWrite.enabled`, or the writer option `optimizeWrite`; `spark.databricks.delta.optimizeWrite.binSize` (default 512 MiB) sets the target in-memory size of each output file.[^delta-opt]

### Apache Hudi

Hudi sizes files during writes. On insert and upsert, it adds records to existing files smaller than `hoodie.parquet.small.file.limit` (default 104857600 bytes, 100 MB) until they approach `hoodie.parquet.max.file.size` (default 125829120 bytes, 120 MB). The `bulk_insert` operation does not size files this way.[^hudi-size] For merge-on-read tables, `hoodie.merge.small.file.group.candidates.limit` (default 1) limits how many small file groups an upsert may expand, to limit rewriting.[^hudi-size]

After writes, Hudi's clustering table service stitches small files into larger ones and can sort data for locality. It runs inline after each write when `hoodie.clustering.inline` is true, or asynchronously with `hoodie.clustering.async.enabled`; both default to false.[^hudi-cluster][^hudi-conf] Files under `hoodie.clustering.plan.strategy.small.file.limit` (default 314572800 bytes) are candidates.[^hudi-conf]

### Apache Spark

Spark settings shape how many files a write produces, independent of the table format.

- `spark.sql.files.maxRecordsPerFile` caps the rows in one output file; the default 0 means no limit.[^sparkconf]
- The `COALESCE`, `REPARTITION`, `REBALANCE` and `REBALANCE_BY_SIZE` SQL hints, and the matching `coalesce` and `repartition` Dataset methods, control the number of output files. `REBALANCE` asks adaptive query execution (AQE) for output partitions of reasonable size, to avoid files that are too small or too big, and is ignored when AQE is disabled.[^spark-hints]
- With AQE (`spark.sql.adaptive.enabled`, default true), `spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled` (default true) merges small shuffle partitions toward `spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes`.[^spark-tuning][^sparkconf] The Iceberg documentation notes that this advisory size measures shuffle data, not the compressed columnar file, so it must be set larger than the desired file size.[^ice-writes]
- On the read side, `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes` (default 128 MB) and `spark.sql.files.openCostInBytes` control how many small files are packed into one read partition.[^sparkconf]

# Sort-merge join

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Sort-merge_join

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Shuffle sort-merge join, SMJ, `SortMergeJoin`</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed query processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Shuffle exchange, hash partitioning, per-partition sort, merge scan</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Broadcast join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Broadcast_join), [Shuffle hash join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle_hash_join), [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution), [Logical plan and physical plan](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Logical_plan_and_physical_plan)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (SparkStrategies.scala, SortMergeJoinExec.scala, joins.scala, SQLConf.scala, sql-performance-tuning.md and sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-hints.md)</Verified>

A **sort-merge join** is a distributed equality-join strategy that repartitions both inputs by the join keys, sorts each resulting partition by those keys, and merges the two ordered streams.[^smjexec] In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), `SortMergeJoin` is the usual physical operator for an equality join between two large inputs when neither side can be broadcast: Spark prefers it over a [shuffle hash join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle_hash_join) by default, and its memory use does not depend on building an entire input partition as a hash table.[^strategies][^sqlconf]

## How does a sort-merge join work?

A Spark sort-merge join has three distributed steps:[^smjexec]

1. **Shuffle both sides.** Spark applies compatible hash partitioning to the two inputs so rows with equal join keys arrive in partitions with the same partition number.
1. **Sort each partition.** Each side is ordered by its join keys. The `SortMergeJoinExec` operator declares ascending key order as a requirement for both children.
1. **Merge matching keys.** A task reads one partition from each side, advances through the two ordered streams, and emits rows when the keys compare equal. Spark may buffer rows that share a key and can spill that buffer when necessary.

The two exchanges are stage boundaries. The exchange writers create shuffle files, and later tasks fetch, sort and join the matching partitions. This makes sort-merge join suitable for inputs that are too large to copy to every executor, but it also means network I/O, disk I/O and sorting work on both sides.

## What does SortMergeJoin mean in EXPLAIN?

A representative physical plan has this shape:

```
*(5) SortMergeJoin [customer_id#1L], [customer_id#8L], Inner
:- *(2) Sort [customer_id#1L ASC NULLS FIRST], false, 0
:  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id#1L, 200), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS
:     +- Scan parquet sales
+- *(4) Sort [customer_id#8L ASC NULLS FIRST], false, 0
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id#8L, 200), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS
      +- Scan parquet customers
```

`SortMergeJoin` names the algorithm and lists the left and right join keys. The two `Exchange hashpartitioning` nodes show that both inputs shuffle. The `Sort` nodes satisfy the ordering required by the join. The partition count shown by a real plan comes from the chosen exchange partitioning and can be changed by [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution) after runtime statistics become available.[^perf]

If an input already has compatible partitioning or ordering, Spark can reuse those properties rather than inserting every operator shown above. `EXPLAIN FORMATTED` is useful for tracing each `Exchange` and `Sort` to its input.[^n1]

## When does Spark choose sort-merge join?

For an equality join without hints, Spark 4.3.0 tries a broadcast hash join first. It next considers a shuffled hash join only when one side meets the size tests and `spark.sql.join.preferSortMergeJoin` is false. Spark then chooses sort-merge join when the join keys have a sortable data type.[^strategies] The internal setting `spark.sql.join.preferSortMergeJoin` defaults to `true`.[^sqlconf]

The `MERGE` hint asks Spark to use sort-merge join. Its aliases are `SHUFFLE_MERGE` and `MERGEJOIN`:[^hints]

```sql
SELECT /*+ MERGE(large_orders, large_customers) */
       large_orders.order_id, large_customers.region
FROM large_orders
JOIN large_customers
  ON large_orders.customer_id = large_customers.customer_id;
```

A hint is a request rather than a guarantee. Spark ignores an inapplicable merge hint, including when there are no equality keys or the key type cannot supply the binary ordering required by the strategy.[^hints][^strategies]

## How does sort-merge join compare with other joins?

|  | Sort-merge join | Shuffle hash join | Broadcast hash join |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Data movement | Shuffles both inputs by the join keys | Shuffles both inputs by the join keys | Broadcasts the build side; normally does not shuffle the streamed side |
| Local work | Sorts both partitions, then merges ordered streams | Builds a hash table from one shuffled partition and probes it with the other | Builds one relation at the driver, broadcasts it, and probes it in each task |
| Main memory risk | Groups of equal keys may need buffering; the implementation can spill its match buffer[^smjexec] | The build partition must fit well enough to construct a local hash table | The complete build side must be collected and broadcast |
| Typical use in Spark | Two large inputs with sortable equality keys | One side is much smaller per partition, or the strategy is selected by hint or AQE | One complete input is small enough to broadcast |

Sort-merge join can be slower when the shuffle and sort dominate the query, especially if the inputs were not already partitioned compatibly. Skew can leave one reducer with far more rows than the others. AQE can split skewed sort-merge partitions, coalesce small shuffle partitions, or convert an eligible sort-merge join to a broadcast or shuffled hash join after it observes actual shuffle sizes.[^perf]

## What cannot sort-merge join do?

Spark's sort-merge implementation requires equality keys with sortable data types.[^strategies] A condition such as `left.ts > right.ts` by itself is not a sort-merge equality join; Spark must use another physical strategy. A sort-merge join also cannot remove the cost of a required shuffle merely because the SQL uses a `MERGE` hint.

# Spark 3 to Spark 4 migration

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_3_to_Spark_4_migration

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Upgrading from Spark 3.5 to 4.0</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">ANSI SQL mode by default, Java 17 and Scala 2.13 only, Python 3.9 minimum, removed Mesos support, deprecated SparkR</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) 4.0.0 (released 2025-05-23)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [SparkR](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkR), [Apache Mesos support in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Mesos_support_in_Spark), [Scala 2.12 and 2.13 in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Scala_2.12_and_2.13_in_Spark)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v3.5.0, v4.0.0, v4.1.0, v4.2.0 and v4.3.0 tags of apache/spark (docs/index.md, docs/sql-migration-guide.md, docs/core-migration-guide.md, python/docs/source/migration_guide/pyspark_upgrade.rst, SQLConf.scala), the Spark 4.0.0 release notes, the Spark news page and the Spark versioning policy</Verified>

**Spark 3 to Spark 4 migration** is the work of moving [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) applications from the 3.x line (in practice 3.5) to Spark 4.0 or later, the first major release since 3.0. Spark 4.0.0 was released on 23 May 2025.[^news] The changes most likely to break an upgrade are platform minimums (Java 17, Scala 2.13 only, Python 3.9) and the switch of Spark SQL to ANSI mode by default, which turns many silent nulls and overflows into runtime errors.[^r400] Spark 4.0 also removed Apache Mesos support and deprecated SparkR. This page summarizes those changes from the official migration guides; it does not replace them.

## Platform requirements

|  | Spark 3.5 | Spark 4.0 | Spark 4.3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Java | 8, 11, 17 | 17, 21 | 17, 21, 25 |
| Scala | 2.12, 2.13 | 2.13 | 2.13 |
| Python | 3.8+ | 3.9+ | 3.11+ |
| R (SparkR) | 3.5+ | 3.5+ (deprecated) | 4.0+ (deprecated) |

Sources: the "Spark runs on" line of `docs/index.md` at each tag.[^idx350][^idx400][^idx430] Spark 4.1 raised the Python minimum to 3.10, and Spark 4.2 added Java 25.[^n1][^n2]

- **Java.** SPARK-45315 dropped JDK 8 and 11 and made JDK 17 the default.[^r400] Hive metastore clients older than Hive 2.0.0 are no longer supported, because they need JDK 8.[^sqlmig]
- **Scala.** SPARK-45314 dropped Scala 2.12 and made 2.13 the default. Applications and libraries compiled for Scala 2.12 must be rebuilt for 2.13.[^r400][^idx400] See [Scala 2.12 and 2.13 in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Scala_2.12_and_2.13_in_Spark).
- **Python.** SPARK-47993 dropped Python 3.8. PySpark 4.0 also raised the minimum versions of pandas to 2.0.0, NumPy to 1.21 and PyArrow to 11.0.0.[^pymig]

## ANSI SQL mode by default

SPARK-44444 made Spark SQL use ANSI mode by default.[^r400] In Spark 4.0, `spark.sql.ansi.enabled` defaults to true unless the environment variable `SPARK_ANSI_SQL_MODE` is set to `false`.[^conf] In ANSI mode Spark throws an error at runtime, instead of returning null, when the inputs to a SQL operator or function are invalid; examples are integer overflow and invalid casts from string to a number.[^conf][^n3]

```sql
-- Spark 3.5 default: returns NULL.  Spark 4.0 default: fails with a CAST_INVALID_INPUT error.
SELECT CAST('abc' AS INT);

-- Works in both: try_cast returns NULL for invalid input.
SELECT try_cast('abc' AS INT);

-- Restore the Spark 3 behaviour for a session.
SET spark.sql.ansi.enabled = false;
```

Pipelines that relied on silent nulls should move to the `try_*` functions or fix the data, rather than turning ANSI mode off everywhere. The pandas API on Spark is a special case: in Spark 4.0.0 it fails with a `PANDAS_API_ON_SPARK_FAIL_ON_ANSI_MODE` error when ANSI mode is on, unless the pandas-on-Spark option `compute.fail_on_ansi_mode` is set to `False` (SPARK-52026).[^n4]

## Other SQL behaviour changes

The Spark 3.5 to 4.0 section of the SQL migration guide lists many changes. Among those most likely to matter in a lakehouse:[^sqlmig]

| Change in Spark 4.0 | Setting to restore the old behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `CREATE TABLE` without `USING` or `STORED AS` uses `spark.sql.sources.default` (Parquet by default) instead of Hive. | `spark.sql.legacy.createHiveTableByDefault=true` |
| The default ORC compression codec changed from `snappy` to `zstd`. | `spark.sql.orc.compression.codec=snappy` |
| `spark.sql.maxSinglePartitionBytes` defaults to `128m` instead of `Long.MaxValue`. | Set it to `9223372036854775807` |
| The `spark.sql.legacy.*` datetime rebase configs for Parquet and Avro were removed. | Use the same names without `legacy.`, for example `spark.sql.parquet.int96RebaseModeInWrite` |
| `spark.sql.legacy.timeParserPolicy` defaults to `CORRECTED` instead of `EXCEPTION`. | Set it back to `EXCEPTION` |
| Views tolerate column type changes in the underlying query and compensate with casts. | `spark.sql.legacy.viewSchemaCompensation=false` |
| JDBC type mappings changed for PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server and DB2 (for example timestamps and small integer types). | Per-database `spark.sql.legacy.*` flags listed in the guide |

## Core and cluster changes

From the core migration guide for 3.5 to 4.0:[^coremig]
- Support for Apache Mesos as a resource manager was removed (SPARK-44442).[^r400] See [Apache Mesos support in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Mesos_support_in_Spark).
- Internal servlet API references moved from `javax` to `jakarta`, which affects custom UI and servlet code.
- Event logs are rolled and compressed by default (`spark.eventLog.rolling.enabled`, `spark.eventLog.compress`).
- Speculative execution is less aggressive: `spark.speculation.multiplier=3` and `spark.speculation.quantile=0.9`.
- On Kubernetes, executor pods are allocated in batches of 10, and persistent volume claims use `ReadWriteOncePod`.
- The default Ivy user directory is `~/.ivy2.5.2`.

## Removed and deprecated APIs

| Item | Status in Spark 4.0 | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Apache Mesos resource manager | Removed | SPARK-44442[^r400] |
| Scala 2.12 builds | Removed | SPARK-45314[^r400] |
| Java 8 and 11 | No longer supported | SPARK-45315[^r400] |
| [SparkR](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkR) | Deprecated, still shipped (the `R` directory is present at the v4.3.0 tag) | SPARK-49347[^r400][^idx430] |
| Hive metastore versions before 2.0.0 | Removed | SPARK-45328[^r400] |
| Deprecated pandas API on Spark methods (for example `DataFrame.append`, `iteritems`, `to_koalas`) | Removed | PySpark migration guide[^pymig] |
| `pyspark.ml.connect` | Deprecated in favour of `pyspark.ml` on Spark Connect | SPARK-50828[^r400] |

## Spark Connect in Spark 4

Spark 4.0 is the first major release in which [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) is close to the classic API. The release notes list Scala client parity with the Dataset and DataFrame API, `pyspark.ml` support on Connect, a lightweight `pyspark-client` Python package, an extra release tarball with Connect enabled by default, and the `spark.api.mode` setting to switch an application between classic and Connect.[^r400] A migration is therefore a natural point to check whether code uses APIs that Connect does not have, such as RDDs and `SparkContext`.

## Timing

Spark 3.5 has an extended long-term support period that ends in November 2027, during which only security fixes are released.[^policy] Non-LTS release branches are generally maintained with bug fix releases for six months, and the policy names Spark 4.5.0 as the planned LTS release of the 4.x line.[^policy] Later 4.x releases have their own migration sections (4.0 to 4.1, 4.1 to 4.2, 4.2 to 4.3) in the same guide.[^n5]
