# Spark configuration precedence

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_configuration_precedence

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Spark property precedence</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`spark-defaults.conf`, `--properties-file`, `--conf`, `SparkConf`, session configuration, SQL `SET`</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[spark-submit](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark-submit), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/configuration.md, docs/submitting-applications.md, docs/sql-migration-guide.md, docs/spark-connect-overview.md, SQLConf.scala, StaticSQLConf.scala, classic/RuntimeConfig.scala, python/pyspark/sql/session.py and conf.py) and SPARK-48392</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), **configuration precedence** is the order in which Spark merges property values from the defaults file, the `spark-submit` command line and application code, and the rule that decides which of those values can still change after the application has started.[^config] Values set on a `SparkConf` in code win over `--conf` flags, which win over `spark-defaults.conf`.[^config] Once the application runs, only runtime SQL configurations can be changed per session, with `spark.conf.set` or the SQL `SET` command.[^config]

## What is the order of precedence for Spark properties?

Spark reads properties from several places when an application starts and merges them. The Spark 4.3.0 configuration guide gives this order, highest first:[^config]

| Rank | Source | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (highest) | Properties set directly on a `SparkConf` or the `SparkSession` builder in application code | `SparkSession.builder.config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "64")` |
| 2 | Flags passed to `spark-submit`, `spark-shell` or `pyspark`: `--conf`/`-c`, dedicated flags such as `--master` or `--executor-memory`, and a file given with `--properties-file` | `--conf spark.eventLog.enabled=true` |
| 3 (lowest) | `conf/spark-defaults.conf` under `SPARK_HOME` or `SPARK_CONF_DIR` | `spark.executor.memory 4g` |

Any property that none of these sources sets keeps its built-in default. The Environment tab of the Spark UI lists only values that were set explicitly through `spark-defaults.conf`, `SparkConf` or the command line.[^config]

When a configuration key has been renamed in a newer Spark version, Spark still accepts the old name, but any value under the new name takes precedence over the old one.[^config]

## How do spark-defaults.conf and --properties-file interact?

By default `spark-submit` reads `conf/spark-defaults.conf`, a file with one whitespace-separated key and value per line.[^config] Setting `SPARK_CONF_DIR` makes Spark read `spark-defaults.conf`, `spark-env.sh` and `log4j2.properties` from another directory instead of `SPARK_HOME/conf`.[^config]

When a file is passed with `--properties-file`, Spark no longer loads `spark-defaults.conf` unless the `--load-spark-defaults` flag is also given. With both, values in the `--properties-file` file take precedence over those in `spark-defaults.conf`.[^submit][^ssargs] The `--load-spark-defaults` flag was added in Spark 4.0.0 by SPARK-48392.[^n1] Within rank 2, `SparkSubmitArguments` at the v4.3.0 tag gives `--conf` values priority over the `--properties-file` file, and that file priority over `spark-defaults.conf`; a dedicated flag such as `--master` wins over the same property passed as `--conf spark.master`.[^ssargs]

To see which source supplied a value, the Spark documentation recommends running `spark-submit` with `--verbose`.[^submit]

## Which properties must be set before the application starts?

Spark's configuration guide divides properties into two kinds. Deploy-related properties, such as `spark.driver.memory` and `spark.executor.instances`, may have no effect when set in code at runtime, so the guide recommends setting them in a configuration file or on the `spark-submit` command line. Runtime-control properties, such as `spark.task.maxFailures`, can be set either way.[^config]

The driver's JVM settings are the most common case. In client deploy mode, `spark.driver.memory` (default `1g`) and `spark.driver.extraJavaOptions` must not be set through `SparkConf` in the application, because the driver JVM has already started when that code runs. They must be given with `--driver-memory`, `--driver-java-options` or the defaults file instead.[^config]

## What can change at runtime?

Spark SQL configurations come in two kinds:[^config]

- **Runtime SQL configurations** are per session and mutable. They take initial values from the defaults file, `--conf` or the `SparkConf` used to build the session, and can then be read and changed with `spark.conf.get`/`spark.conf.set`, the SQL `SET` command, and reset with `RESET`. `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` (default 200) is an example.[^config][^sqlconf]
- **Static SQL configurations** are shared by all sessions and fixed once the first session starts. They can be read with `spark.conf.get` or `SET key`, but not set or unset. `spark.sql.extensions` and `spark.sql.warehouse.dir` are static.[^config][^n2]

In Spark 4.3.0, `spark.conf.set` on a static SQL key fails with the error condition `CANNOT_MODIFY_STATIC_CONFIG`, and on a Spark core key (one registered as a `SparkConf` entry, such as `spark.executor.memory`) it fails with `CANNOT_MODIFY_CONFIG`.[^rtconf] The SQL `SET` command has rejected Spark core keys since Spark 3.0; before 3.0 it accepted them silently with no effect. The internal flag `spark.sql.legacy.setCommandRejectsSparkCoreConfs` controls this check: it defaults to `true`, and setting it to `false` restores the old behavior.[^migration][^sqlconf]

PySpark has a method that answers the question directly: `spark.conf.isModifiable(key)`, added in PySpark 2.4.0, returns whether a key can be changed in the current session.[^n3]

## Example

The following PySpark code runs against Spark 4.3.0 in classic mode. It reads one runtime and one static SQL configuration, changes the runtime one in two equivalent ways, and checks which keys can be changed.

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = (SparkSession.builder
         .appName("conf-demo")
         .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "64")   # rank 1: code
         .getOrCreate())

print(spark.conf.get("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions"))   # '64'

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "32")    # runtime SQL conf: allowed
spark.sql("SET spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=16")        # same effect in SQL

print(spark.conf.isModifiable("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions"))  # True
print(spark.conf.isModifiable("spark.sql.extensions"))          # False (static)
```

The same changes in Spark SQL:

```sql
SET spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=16;   -- change for this session
SET spark.sql.shuffle.partitions;      -- show the current value
RESET spark.sql.shuffle.partitions;    -- back to the value the session started with
```

The `SET` command sets, shows or lists SQL configuration properties; `SET -v` also prints each property's meaning.[^n4]

## How do sessions share configuration?

In PySpark, `SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()` returns the existing global default session if there is one, and applies the options given to the builder to that existing session.[^session] `spark.newSession()` returns a session with its own SQL configuration, temporary views and UDFs, sharing the `SparkContext` and the table cache.[^session] Runtime SQL configurations are therefore per session, while Spark core properties belong to the whole application.

## How does Spark Connect change this?

A [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) client gets a session on a remote Spark server and has no access to the static Spark configuration or the `SparkContext`; it cannot change settings that affect every client of that server.[^connect] In practice a Spark Connect client can set runtime SQL configurations for its own session, and cluster-level properties are set where the server is started.

# Spark Connect

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) project)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">Spark 3.4.0 (2023)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">Spark 4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala, Python</Field>
  <Field name="type">Client-server protocol for Apache Spark</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[Spark Connect overview](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/spark-connect-overview.html)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark (sql/connect)](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/v4.3.0/sql/connect)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Spark 4.3.0 Spark Connect documentation and source at tag v4.3.0, Spark release notes 3.4.0, 3.5.0 and 4.0.0, and PyPI</Verified>

**Spark Connect** is a client-server interface for [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) in which a thin client library sends DataFrame operations to a remote Spark server as unresolved logical plans and receives the results over the network.[^overview] Spark Connect separates the application process from the Spark driver, so an application can run in an IDE, a notebook or a service without sharing a process or dependencies with the cluster. It was introduced in Spark 3.4.[^overview]

## How it works

The Spark Connect client translates DataFrame operations into unresolved logical query plans, encodes them with Protocol Buffers and sends them to the server with gRPC.[^overview]

The Spark Connect endpoint on the server translates the received plans into Spark's logical plan operators, much as Spark parses a SQL query, and then runs them through the normal Spark optimizer and execution engine. Results return to the client over gRPC as Apache Arrow-encoded row batches.[^overview]

By default, a Spark Connect server listens on port 15002. The port is set by the static configuration `spark.connect.grpc.binding.port`, which has existed since Spark 3.4.0.[^overview][^n1] Clients address the server with a connection string that starts with `sc://`, for example `sc://localhost:15002`, given either in code or in the `SPARK_REMOTE` environment variable.[^overview]

## Differences from classic Spark

Spark Connect changes what an application can reach, because the client runs outside the driver process:[^overview]

- The client cannot access the driver JVM. In PySpark, the client does not use Py4J, so private fields such as `df._jdf` are not available.
- The protocol describes work as logical plans, so it does not support every Spark execution API. Most importantly, RDDs are not supported.
- Each client gets its own session. The client cannot change cluster-wide settings, and it has no access to the static Spark configuration or to the `SparkContext`.

The Spark documentation names stability, upgradability and debuggability as operational reasons for this split: an application that uses too much memory affects only its own process, the server can be upgraded independently of client applications, and applications can be debugged in a local IDE.[^overview]

## Using Spark Connect

A server is started from a Spark distribution with the `sbin/start-connect-server.sh` script. A PySpark application then connects by passing a remote address when it builds the session:[^overview]

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://localhost:15002").getOrCreate()
spark.range(10).filter("id % 2 = 0").show()
```

The shells accept the same address with `--remote`, for example `./bin/pyspark --remote "sc://localhost"`.[^overview] Scala applications use the `spark-connect-client-jvm` artifact and the same `remote` builder method. Scala code that contains user-defined functions must upload its class files and JAR dependencies to the server, for example with `SparkSession#addArtifact`.[^overview]

For Python, the `pyspark-client` package on PyPI contains only the Spark Connect client, without the JVM parts of PySpark.[^overview] Its latest version on 22 November 2026 is 4.3.0.[^n2]

Since Spark 4.0, the `spark.api.mode` configuration (values `classic` or `connect`, default `classic`) lets an existing classic application run through Spark Connect without code changes, by starting a local Spark Connect server for it.[^n3][^n4]

## Clients

| Client | Where it lives | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Python (PySpark) | apache/spark | First released in Spark 3.4.0[^r340] |
| Scala | apache/spark | First released in Spark 3.5.0[^r350] |
| Go | [apache/spark-connect-go](https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-go) | Announced with Spark 3.5.0[^r350] |
| Swift | [apache/spark-connect-swift](https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-swift) | Announced with Spark 4.0.0[^r400] |
| Rust | [apache/spark-connect-rust](https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-rust) | [^n5] |

## History

Spark Connect was proposed in the Spark Project Improvement Proposal (SPIP) tracked as SPARK-39375, filed in June 2022.[^n6] Spark 3.4.0 shipped the Python client.[^r340] Spark 3.5.0 added the Scala client, Structured Streaming support in Python and Scala, and pandas API on Spark support for the Python client.[^r350] Spark 4.0.0 added the `pyspark-client` package, an extra release tarball with Spark Connect enabled by default, the `spark.api.mode` setting and machine learning on Spark Connect.[^r400] Spark 4.3.0 added REST endpoints for inspecting sessions and operations, operation IDs for request attribution, and a more complete JDBC driver.[^n7]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Spark Connect lets light clients such as notebooks, services and AI agents run queries on a shared Spark cluster that holds the catalog and table format configuration. [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines) depends on it: in Spark 4.3 the `spark-pipelines` launcher requires `spark.api.mode` to be `connect` and rejects any other value.[^n8]

# Spark Connect client

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect_client

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Thin client, Spark Connect client library</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing, client-server protocols</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 3.4.0 (Python client)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Protocol Buffers plan builder, gRPC channel, Apache Arrow result decoder, `sc://` connection string</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">PySpark (`pyspark-client`), Scala (`spark-connect-client-jvm`), JDBC driver, Go, Swift, Rust</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [Spark Connect server](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect_server), [Spark Connect plugin](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect_plugin), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Spark 4.3.0 Spark Connect overview and sql/connect/docs/client-connection-string.md at tag v4.3.0; the GitHub repositories, READMEs, tags and releases of apache/spark-connect-go, apache/spark-connect-swift, apache/spark-connect-rust, GoEddie/spark-connect-dotnet and yaooqinn/spark.js; PyPI, crates.io, Maven Central and the Apache Spark download directory</Verified>

A **Spark Connect client** is a library that lets an application use [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) remotely through the [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) protocol: it builds unresolved logical plans as Protocol Buffers messages, sends them to a Spark Connect server over gRPC, and decodes the results, which come back as Apache Arrow record batches.[^overview] A Spark Connect client runs in its own process, separate from the Spark driver, and does not reach into the driver JVM; the PySpark client does not use Py4J.[^overview] The `pyspark-client` package leaves Py4J out and depends only on Python libraries such as `pyarrow` and `grpcio`, so it needs no local Spark JVM.[^clientsetup] Because the protocol is language-agnostic, a client can be written in any language with gRPC and Arrow support, and the Scala client (`spark-connect-client-jvm`) and the JDBC driver are themselves JVM libraries.[^overview][^mvnjdbc] The Apache Spark project ships Python and Scala clients and a JDBC driver, and maintains separate Go, Swift and Rust clients; other clients are community projects.

## What does a Spark Connect client do?

A Spark Connect client has three jobs. It turns DataFrame or SQL calls into a protobuf plan, manages a gRPC channel and session with the server, and turns Arrow batches into native values. The Spark documentation describes the protocol as language-agnostic, and the server runs every plan through the normal Spark optimizer and execution engine, so a query from a Go client and the same query from PySpark run the same way on the server.[^overview]

All official clients address the server with the same connection string format, `sc://host:port/;param=value`. The Spark Connect developer guidelines ask new clients to follow this format so that the user experience is the same in every language. The parameters include `token`, `use_ssl`, `user_id`, `user_agent`, `session_id` and gRPC keepalive settings, and the default port is 15002.[^connstr][^readme]

## Which Spark Connect clients exist?

The following table lists the clients maintained under the Apache Spark project, followed by two community clients. "Latest release" is the newest version found on 23 November 2026, and "stated status" quotes or paraphrases each project's own description.

| Client | Repository and package | Language | Latest release | Stated status | Notable gaps |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PySpark client | [apache/spark](https://github.com/apache/spark); PyPI `pyspark-client` | Python | 4.3.0 (30 October 2026)[^pypi] | Part of each Spark release; supports most PySpark APIs since Spark 3.4[^overview] | No `SparkContext` or RDD API[^overview] |
| Scala client | apache/spark; Maven `spark-connect-client-jvm_2.13` | Scala | 4.3.0[^mvnjvm] | Part of each Spark release; supports most Scala APIs since Spark 3.5[^overview] | No `SparkContext` or RDD API; UDF classes and JARs must be uploaded as artifacts[^overview] |
| JDBC driver | apache/spark; Maven `spark-connect-client-jdbc_2.13` | Java (JDBC) | 4.3.0[^mvnjdbc] | Added in Spark 4.1.0 (SPARK-53484); Spark 4.3.0 describes it as "more complete"[^r410][^r430] | SQL only; ARRAY, MAP and STRUCT support arrived in 4.3.0 (SPARK-57380)[^r430] |
| Go client | [apache/spark-connect-go](https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-go) | Go | v0.1.0 (GitHub release, 17 June 2025)[^gorel] | "Highly experimental and should not be used in any production setting"; the Spark PMC reserves the right to withdraw it[^goreadme] | The `spark/sql` package has session, DataFrame, reader, writer, grouping, NA and statistics APIs, but no streaming or UDF API; last commit on `master` in August 2025[^gocommits][^gotree] |
| Swift client | [apache/spark-connect-swift](https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-swift) | Swift | 0.8.0 (13 November 2026)[^swiftrel] | "Still experimental" (0.8.0 release notes); source releases published in the Apache Spark download directory[^swiftrel][^dist] | UDFs only by registering existing Java UDF classes on the server, not in Swift; README lists Spark 4.3.0 as the requirement[^swiftudf][^swiftreadme] |
| Rust client | [apache/spark-connect-rust](https://github.com/apache/spark-connect-rust); crate `apache-spark-connect`, PyPI `pyspark-client-rust` | Rust, with a Python wrapper | 4.3.0 (git tag and packages, 16 November 2026)[^crate][^rustpypi] | README claims full public-API parity with PySpark 4.3.0 for the Python wrapper; targets Spark 4.3.0 and later[^rustreadme][^rustcompat] | Native Rust API excludes APIs that need Python itself, such as pandas; UDFs are Rust functions compiled to WebAssembly[^rustdocs] |
| .NET client (community) | [GoEddie/spark-connect-dotnet](https://github.com/GoEddie/spark-connect-dotnet) | C# and other .NET languages | v4.0.0-build.41 (3 October 2026)[^dotnet] | Not an Apache project (MIT license)[^dotnet] | README says keeping up with new Spark versions is hard and advises users to be prepared to make their own gRPC calls for functions the library lacks[^dotnet] |
| JavaScript client (community) | [yaooqinn/spark.js](https://github.com/yaooqinn/spark.js); npm `@yaooqinn/spark.js` | TypeScript | v0.1.0 (git tag, January 2026)[^sparkjs] | "Experimental"; APIs may change without notice[^sparkjs] | Requires Spark 4.0 or later[^sparkjs] |

The Apache Spark download directory lists source releases of the Swift client but none of the Go or Rust clients.[^dist] The Rust client replaced an earlier community project, sjrusso8/spark-connect-rs, whose repository is now read-only and points to apache/spark-connect-rust.[^n1] The Rust repository also contains an unpublished, experimental Rust server frontend intended for local, trusted experiments.[^rustreadme]

## How is a client connected to a server?

In PySpark, the `pyspark-client` package contains only the Spark Connect client, and `SparkSession.builder.remote()` takes the connection string.[^overview] The following example connects over TLS with a bearer token; according to the connection string reference, setting `token` also enables TLS.[^connstr]

```python
# pip install pyspark-client==4.3.0
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = (
    SparkSession.builder
    .remote("sc://spark.example.com:443/;use_ssl=true;token=MY_TOKEN;user_agent=etl_app")
    .getOrCreate()
)
print(spark.version)
spark.sql("SELECT 1 AS ok").show()
```

The same string can be set in the `SPARK_REMOTE` environment variable. The Swift README states that its client also reads `SPARK_REMOTE`, and the Rust and JavaScript clients take an `sc://` address in their builders.[^overview][^swiftreadme][^rustreadme][^sparkjs]

## Spark Connect client vs classic Spark application

A Spark Connect client differs from a classic PySpark or Scala application because it runs outside the driver:[^overview]

|  | Spark Connect client | Classic Spark application |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Process | Separate from the driver; talks to it over gRPC | Runs inside the driver process (Py4J bridge for PySpark) |
| `SparkContext` and RDDs | Not available | Available |
| Cluster-wide and static configuration | Not accessible; session settings only | Accessible |
| Dependencies | Client library only; server upgraded independently | Shares the driver's process and dependencies |

# Spark Connect plugin

</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (sql/connect/server plugin interfaces, SparkConnectPluginRegistry.scala, SparkConnectPlanner.scala, config/Connect.scala, ConnectProtoUtils.scala, the Spark Connect protobuf files, SparkConnectPluginRegistrySuite.scala), the Spark 4.3.0 Application Development with Spark Connect and configuration pages, SPARK-47062, SPARK-51343, and the Delta Lake Delta Connect documentation</Verified>

A **Spark Connect plugin** is a server-side class that extends [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) with new relations, expressions or commands: the client packs a custom Protocol Buffers message into an extension field of the Spark Connect protocol, and the plugin on the server turns that message into a Spark logical plan, a Catalyst expression, or an action.[^appdev] Plugins let a library such as [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) expose features that classic PySpark reached through the driver JVM to clients that only speak the Spark Connect protocol. The Spark documentation calls a plugin together with its protocol messages and client package a *Spark Server Library* and says these extension points were offered with Spark 3.4.[^appdev]

## How does a Spark Connect plugin work?

The Spark Connect protocol reserves a field of type `google.protobuf.Any` in its three main message types: `Relation.extension` (field 998), `Expression.extension` (field 999) and `Command.extension` (field 999).[^relproto][^exprproto][^cmdproto] An `Any` holds any serialized protobuf message together with its type URL, so an extension author defines its own message and the core protocol does not change.[^appdev]

A Spark Server Library has four parts, according to the Spark documentation: the protocol extension (the custom protobuf messages), the Spark Connect plugin, the application logic it calls, and a client package that builds the messages for PySpark or Scala users.[^appdev]

When the Spark Connect planner meets an extension field, it passes the serialized `Any` to every registered plugin of the matching kind, in order, and uses the first one that handles it. A plugin signals "not mine" by returning an empty `Optional` (relations and expressions) or `false` (commands). If no plugin handles the message, the request fails with an error that names the type URL.[^planner]

## Which plugin interfaces does Spark provide?

In Spark 4.3.0 the plugin interfaces are Java interfaces in the package `org.apache.spark.sql.connect.plugin`, each registered with a static configuration key:[^iface][^connectconf][^config]

| Interface | Method | Returns | Configuration key | Since |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `RelationPlugin` | `transform(byte[] relation, SparkConnectPlanner planner)` | `Optional<LogicalPlan>` | `spark.connect.extensions.relation.classes` | 3.4.0 |
| `ExpressionPlugin` | `transform(byte[] relation, SparkConnectPlanner planner)` | `Optional<Expression>` | `spark.connect.extensions.expression.classes` | 3.4.0 |
| `CommandPlugin` | `process(byte[] command, SparkConnectPlanner planner)` | `boolean` | `spark.connect.extensions.command.classes` | 3.4.0 |
| `GetStatusPlugin` | `processRequestExtensions`, `processOperationExtensions` | `Optional<List<Any>>` | `spark.connect.extensions.getStatus.classes` | 4.1.0 |
| `MLBackendPlugin` (experimental) | `transform(String mlName)` | `Optional<String>` | `spark.connect.ml.backend.classes` | 4.0.0 |

Each key takes a comma-separated list of class names. Plugin classes must be trivially constructable and should not rely on internal state; the registry creates them by reflection the first time a plugin is needed.[^iface][^registry] The JAR with the plugin goes on the server's classpath, for example with `spark.jars`.[^appdev]

## Why do plugins receive bytes instead of protobuf objects?

Spark shades its copy of the protobuf library inside the Spark Connect server, so a plugin compiled against `com.google.protobuf` cannot share protobuf classes with the server. A 2025 bug report, SPARK-51343, describes the resulting mismatch for the older Scala `RelationPlugin` trait, whose bytecode referred to `org.sparkproject.connect.protobuf.Any`.[^jira51343] SPARK-47062, "Make Spark Connect Plugins Java Compatible", was fixed in Spark 4.0.0.[^jira47062] In the 4.3.0 source, the planner calls each plugin with `extension.toByteArray`, the bytes of the whole `Any` message.[^planner]

A plugin therefore parses the bytes with its own protobuf library. To turn nested Spark Connect messages (for example a child expression or input relation inside the custom message) back into Spark's own classes, Spark provides `org.apache.spark.sql.connect.ConnectProtoUtils`, whose documentation states that it exists for plugins because of the shading of `com.google.protobuf`.[^protoutils] The code samples on the Application Development page still show the older signature that takes a `protobuf.Any` and returns a Scala `Option`.[^appdev]

## Example

The following expression plugin follows the pattern of the plugin tests in Spark 4.3.0.[^suite] A custom message `MyUpper` (fields `spark.connect.Expression child = 1;`) is generated in the package `com.example.proto`, and the plugin turns it into Spark's `Upper` expression:

```scala
package com.example

import java.util.Optional

import com.google.protobuf
import org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.expressions.{Expression, Upper}
import org.apache.spark.sql.connect.ConnectProtoUtils
import org.apache.spark.sql.connect.planner.SparkConnectPlanner
import org.apache.spark.sql.connect.plugin.ExpressionPlugin

class MyUpperPlugin extends ExpressionPlugin {
  override def transform(
      relation: Array[Byte],
      planner: SparkConnectPlanner): Optional[Expression] = {
    val any = protobuf.Any.parseFrom(relation)
    if (!any.is(classOf[com.example.proto.MyUpper])) {
      return Optional.empty()
    }
    val msg = any.unpack(classOf[com.example.proto.MyUpper])
    // Re-parse the nested Spark Connect message into Spark's own (shaded) classes.
    val child = ConnectProtoUtils.parseExpressionWithRecursionLimit(
      msg.getChild.toByteArray, recursionLimit = 1024)
    Optional.of(Upper(planner.transformExpression(child)))
  }
}
```

The server is then started with the JAR and the class name, for example `--jars my-upper.jar --conf spark.connect.extensions.expression.classes=com.example.MyUpperPlugin`. On the client side, the Spark documentation shows a PySpark wrapper that subclasses the Spark Connect `Expression` class, packs the custom message into `proto.Expression().extension` in `to_plan()`, and wraps it in a `Column`.[^appdev] The Scala client offers the developer APIs `SparkSession.newDataFrame(f: proto.Relation.Builder => Unit)` and `SparkSession.execute(command: proto.Command)`, both since 4.0.0, for sending custom relations and commands.[^scalasession]

## Spark Connect plugin vs other Spark extension points

The Spark documentation says Spark Connect extension points differ from existing ones such as `SparkSessionExtensions` and `SparkPlugin`, because they expose functionality to a client.[^appdev]

|  | Spark Connect plugin | `SparkSessionExtensions` | `SparkPlugin` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Map a new protocol message to a plan, expression or command | Inject rules, parsers and functions into a Spark session | Run driver and executor components inside a Spark application |
| Visible to remote clients | Yes; clients send the custom message | Only through SQL or plans the client can already build | No |
| Registered with | `spark.connect.extensions.*.classes`[^config] | `spark.sql.extensions`[^n1] | `spark.plugins`[^n2] |

The Spark Connect server is itself loaded as a `SparkPlugin`, `org.apache.spark.sql.connect.SparkConnectPlugin`.[^sparkplugin]

## Use in an open lakehouse

[Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) uses Spark Connect plugins for Delta Connect, available from Delta Lake 4.0.0 and described in its documentation as a preview. The documented server command sets `spark.connect.extensions.relation.classes` to `org.apache.spark.sql.connect.delta.DeltaRelationPlugin` and `spark.connect.extensions.command.classes` to `org.apache.spark.sql.connect.delta.DeltaCommandPlugin`, alongside the usual Delta session extension and catalog. The Python `DeltaTable` API then works with a remote Spark Connect session.[^deltaconnect]

# Spark Connect server

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect_server

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Spark Connect endpoint, Spark Connect service</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing, client-server protocols</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 3.4.0</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">gRPC service in the Spark driver, session manager, execution manager, interceptors, `sbin/start-connect-server.sh`</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (`org.apache.spark.sql.connect.service.SparkConnectServer`)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [Spark Connect client](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect_client), [Spark Connect plugin](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect_plugin), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (sbin/start-connect-server.sh, sql/connect/server config/Connect.scala, SparkConnectService.scala, SparkConnectSessionManager.scala, PreSharedKeyAuthenticationInterceptor.scala, SparkConnectPlugin.scala, sql/connect/docs/client-connection-string.md, python/pyspark/sql/connect/client/core.py), the Spark 4.3.0 configuration, monitoring and Spark Connect overview pages, and the Apache Spark 4.3.0 download directory</Verified>

The **Spark Connect server** is the server side of [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark): a gRPC service that runs inside a Spark driver, accepts unresolved logical plans from remote clients, runs them in per-client Spark sessions and streams the results back as Apache Arrow batches.[^overview] Spark implements the server as a driver plugin, so any Spark application can host it, and ships a launcher script that starts a standalone server. By default it listens on port 15002 without TLS, and Spark's only built-in authentication is an optional pre-shared bearer token.[^connectconf][^service]

## How is a Spark Connect server deployed?

The usual way to start a Spark Connect server is `sbin/start-connect-server.sh` from a Spark distribution.[^overview] The script runs the class `org.apache.spark.sql.connect.service.SparkConnectServer` through `spark-submit` as a daemon named "Spark Connect server", and it accepts the normal `spark-submit` options such as `--master` and `--conf`. With `--wait` as the first argument it runs in the foreground instead of as a daemon. `sbin/stop-connect-server.sh` stops it.[^startsh][^stopsh]

Because the server is a Spark driver, it runs on any cluster manager that the driver supports, and its queries run on ordinary [executors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor). Inside the driver, the server is started by the driver plugin `org.apache.spark.sql.connect.SparkConnectPlugin`. Spark's source describes this design as a way to decouple the build of Spark Connect from Spark core: the server is enabled by putting its JAR on the classpath and loading the plugin through `spark.plugins`.[^plugin] PySpark uses the same plugin when `SparkSession.builder.remote("local[*]")` starts a local server for the current process.[^pysession]

The Spark 4.3.0 release is published both as the usual `spark-4.3.0-bin-hadoop3.tgz` and as `spark-4.3.0-bin-hadoop3-connect.tgz`, the variant with Spark Connect enabled by default that Spark 4.0.0 introduced.[^dl][^r400]

## Which configuration keys does the server use?

The main Spark Connect server settings are static configurations, set when the driver starts:[^config][^connectconf]

| Key | Default | Meaning | Since |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `spark.connect.grpc.binding.address` | (none) | Address to bind | 4.0.0 |
| `spark.connect.grpc.binding.port` | 15002 | Port to bind | 3.4.0 |
| `spark.connect.grpc.port.maxRetries` | 0 | Port retry attempts; 0 fails fast on a port conflict | 4.0.0 |
| `spark.connect.grpc.interceptor.classes` | (none) | Comma-separated `io.grpc.ServerInterceptor` classes | 3.4.0 |
| `spark.connect.grpc.maxInboundMessageSize` | 134217728 | Largest accepted gRPC request, in bytes | 3.4.0 |
| `spark.connect.grpc.keepAlive.enabled` | true | Server keepalive pings to detect dead client connections | 4.3.0 |
| `spark.connect.grpc.keepAlive.time` / `.timeout` | 60s / 20s | Idle time before a ping, and wait for its acknowledgement | 4.3.0 |
| `spark.connect.extensions.relation.classes`, `.expression.classes`, `.command.classes` | (none) | [Spark Connect plugin](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect_plugin) classes | 3.4.0 |
| `spark.sql.connect.ui.retainedSessions` / `retainedStatements` | 200 / 200 | Sessions and statements kept in the Spark Connect UI | 3.5.0 |

## How are client sessions isolated?

The Spark Connect server keeps one server-side Spark session for each pair of user ID and session ID sent by the client. A new pair gets a new session created with `SparkSession.newSession()` on the server's base session; the session ID must be a UUID, and an ID that was already closed cannot be reused.[^sessmgr] Clients set these values with the `user_id` and `session_id` parameters of the connection string; by default the session ID is a random UUID, and reusing one lets several clients, even in different languages, share a session.[^connstr]

Session isolation in the Spark Connect server covers session state, not the whole application. The Spark documentation states that temporary views, runtime SQL configurations and session artifacts are per session, while state backed by the shared `SparkContext`, such as the persistent catalog, global temporary views and cached datasets, is shared by all sessions.[^overview] The server starts its base session with artifact session isolation enabled, so JARs and files uploaded by one client are kept apart from other sessions.[^server] All sessions run on the same driver and executors.

## What timeouts apply to sessions and operations?

The Spark Connect server removes idle sessions and abandoned operations with internal settings:[^connectconf]
- `spark.connect.session.manager.defaultSessionTimeout` (default 60 minutes, since 4.0.0) removes a session that has received no RPC for that long; `-1` keeps sessions forever.[^connectconf]
- `spark.connect.execute.manager.detachedTimeout` (default 5 minutes, since 3.5.0) removes an execution that no RPC is attached to.[^connectconf]
- Reattachable execution (`spark.connect.execute.reattachable.enabled`, default true, since 3.5.0) lets a client reconnect to a running query; the server ends one response stream after `spark.connect.execute.reattachable.senderMaxStreamDuration` (default 2 minutes) or `spark.connect.execute.reattachable.senderMaxStreamSize` (default 1g), and the client reattaches.[^connectconf]

These keys are marked internal in the source, so they do not appear in the configuration page and may change without notice.[^connectconf] Spark 4.3.0 added REST endpoints under `/applications/[app-id]/connect/` that list and describe sessions and operations.[^monitoring][^r430]

## How are Spark Connect clients authenticated?

The Spark Connect overview states that Spark Connect has no built-in authentication and is designed to work with authenticating proxies in front of its gRPC HTTP/2 interface.[^overview] In the 4.3.0 source, the server has three layers to consider:

| Mechanism | Shipped with Spark? | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-shared token (`spark.connect.authenticate.token` or the `SPARK_CONNECT_AUTHENTICATE_TOKEN` environment variable) | Yes; internal setting added in 4.0.0 | Rejects any call whose `Authorization` header is not `Bearer` plus the token, with gRPC status `UNAUTHENTICATED`. One shared secret; no users or roles.[^connectconf][^psk] |
| Custom interceptors (`spark.connect.grpc.interceptor.classes`) | Hook only; the user supplies the classes | Runs `io.grpc.ServerInterceptor` code on every call, for example to validate a JWT or map a caller to a user. When the token check is on, it runs first, so interceptors see only authenticated calls.[^config][^service] |
| TLS and identity-aware proxy | No; external | The server's gRPC builder sets no TLS context, so encryption and single sign-on are added by a proxy or gateway in front of it.[^service][^overview] |

On the client side, the `token` parameter of the connection string sends a standard gRPC bearer token, and the connection string reference states that setting it enables TLS.[^connstr] The PySpark client makes one exception: for `localhost` without `use_ssl=true`, it sends the token over gRPC local channel credentials instead of TLS.[^core] When PySpark starts a local server itself, it generates a random token unless one is set.[^pysession] For a remote server, a token therefore needs a TLS-terminating proxy in front of the plaintext gRPC port.

## Example

The following commands start a server on a local master that requires a token and binds only to the loopback interface, then connect with PySpark:

```bash
export SPARK_CONNECT_AUTHENTICATE_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
$SPARK_HOME/sbin/start-connect-server.sh --master "local[*]" \
  --conf spark.connect.grpc.binding.address=127.0.0.1 \
  --conf spark.connect.grpc.binding.port=15002
```

```python
import os
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

token = os.environ["SPARK_CONNECT_AUTHENTICATE_TOKEN"]
spark = SparkSession.builder.remote(f"sc://localhost:15002/;token={token}").getOrCreate()
spark.range(5).show()
```

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Spark 4.3.0 Declarative Pipelines programming guide, the pyspark.pipelines and SparkPipelines sources at tag v4.3.0, SPARK-51727, and the Spark 4.1.0, 4.2.0 and 4.3.0 release notes</Verified>

**Spark Declarative Pipelines** (**SDP**) is a framework in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) for building batch and streaming data pipelines by declaring the datasets a pipeline should produce and the queries that fill them, while Spark handles execution order, parallelism, checkpoints and retries.[^r410] SDP was added in Spark 4.1.0.[^r410] Pipelines are written in Python or SQL and run with the `spark-pipelines` command line tool.[^guide]

## Key concepts

A **flow** reads data from a source, applies processing logic and writes the result into a target dataset. Flows support both streaming and batch semantics. A statement such as `CREATE STREAMING TABLE target_table AS SELECT * FROM STREAM source_table` creates both the table and a flow that writes new source data into it.[^guide]

A **dataset** is a queryable object produced by one or more flows. SDP has three kinds of dataset:[^guide]

| Dataset | Written by | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Streaming table | One or more streaming flows | A table that processes only new data as it arrives (incremental processing). |
| Materialized view | Exactly one batch flow | A view whose result is precomputed and stored as a table. |
| Temporary view | Its defining query | A view scoped to one run of the pipeline, used to share intermediate logic between flows; it cannot be read outside the pipeline. |

A **pipeline** is the unit of development and execution. When a pipeline runs, SDP analyzes the dependencies between its datasets and flows and decides the order of execution and which parts run in parallel.[^guide]

A **sink** lets a pipeline write to a destination outside its own tables, such as Apache Kafka, using any target that a [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) query can write to.[^guide]

## Pipeline spec file

A **pipeline project** is a set of `.py` and `.sql` source files plus a YAML spec file, conventionally named `spark-pipeline.yml` or `spark-pipeline.yaml`. The spec requires `name`, `libraries` (paths to the source files) and `storage` (a directory for streaming checkpoints). It may also set a default `catalog`, a default `database` (alias `schema`) and a `configuration` map of Spark properties.[^guide] An example for Spark 4.3:

```yaml
name: my_pipeline
libraries:
  - glob:
      include: transformations/**
storage: file:///absolute/path/to/storage/dir
catalog: my_catalog
database: my_db
configuration:
  spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: "1000"
```

## Defining datasets

The Python API lives in the `pyspark.pipelines` module, conventionally imported as `dp`. In Spark 4.3 it exports `materialized_view`, `table`, `temporary_view`, `append_flow`, `create_streaming_table`, `create_auto_cdc_flow` and `create_sink`.[^n1] A function decorated with `@dp.materialized_view` that returns a batch DataFrame defines a materialized view; one decorated with `@dp.table` that returns a streaming DataFrame defines a streaming table. The dataset takes the function's name unless a `name` argument is given.[^guide]

Since Spark 4.2, SDP injects the `spark` session into each pipeline file, so the file does not need to create one. In Spark 4.1 each file had to assign `spark = SparkSession.active()` itself.[^guide]

```python
from pyspark import pipelines as dp
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame

@dp.table
def raw_orders() -> DataFrame:
    return spark.readStream.table("orders_source")

@dp.materialized_view
def orders_by_state() -> DataFrame:
    return spark.table("raw_orders").groupBy("state").count()
```

The same datasets can be declared in SQL with `CREATE STREAMING TABLE ... AS SELECT ... FROM STREAM ...`, `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` and `CREATE TEMPORARY VIEW`. Several flows can append to one streaming table with `@dp.append_flow` in Python or `CREATE FLOW` in SQL.[^guide]

## The spark-pipelines CLI

The `spark-pipelines` CLI is built on `spark-submit` and accepts all of its arguments except `--class`, so it works with every cluster manager that `spark-submit` supports.[^guide] It has three commands:[^guide]

- `spark-pipelines init --name my_pipeline` creates a new project directory with a spec file and example definitions.
- `spark-pipelines run` runs the pipeline and monitors it until it completes. Options include `--spec` (path to the spec file), `--refresh` (update listed datasets), `--full-refresh` (clear and recompute listed datasets, including their checkpoints) and `--full-refresh-all`. Without these options, the run is an incremental update.
- `spark-pipelines dry-run` builds and checks the pipeline without reading or writing any data.

In Spark 4.3, the launcher always runs the pipeline in Spark Connect mode: it sets `spark.api.mode=connect` and fails if a user passes any other value.[^n2] A run can target a remote [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) server with `--remote sc://host:15002`.[^guide]

### Dry runs

A dry run catches many errors that would otherwise appear only during a real run: syntax errors in Python or SQL code, analysis errors such as a reference to a table or column that does not exist, and graph validation errors such as cyclic dependencies between datasets.[^guide] Because it reads and writes no data, a dry run can check a pipeline before it uses compute on real data.

## Change data capture

Spark 4.2.0 added **Auto CDC** to SDP, which applies a stream of insert, update and delete events to a target streaming table as Slowly Changing Dimension (SCD) Type 1 upserts.[^n3] Spark 4.3.0 added SCD Type 2, which keeps the history of how each record changed.[^r430] An Auto CDC flow needs key columns and a sequencing expression, and its target must be a streaming table backed by a format that supports row-level operations (MERGE); Spark's built-in file formats, including Parquet, do not qualify.[^guide]

## History

SDP was proposed in the Spark Project Improvement Proposal tracked as SPARK-51727, opened in April 2025 and resolved with fix version 4.1.0.[^n4] On 11 June 2025, Databricks announced that it would contribute its declarative ETL framework to Apache Spark as Spark Declarative Pipelines.[^n5] A Databricks blog post from the next day traces that framework to Databricks' DLT product.[^n6] Databricks documentation states that its Lakeflow pipelines product is built on SDP.[^n7]

## Use in an open lakehouse

SDP writes its datasets through Spark's catalogs, so the spec's `catalog` and `database` fields can point at a catalog such as an [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) or [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog). A pipeline of streaming tables feeding materialized views maps onto the bronze, silver and gold layers of a [medallion architecture](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Medallion_architecture). An orchestrator such as [Apache Airflow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Airflow) can run `spark-pipelines` as one task in a larger workflow.

# Spark error classes

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_error_classes

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Error conditions, error states, SQLSTATE codes</Field>
  <Field name="field">SQL query engines</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Error condition name, sub-condition, SQLSTATE (class and sub-class), message template with parameters</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark SQL ANSI mode](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_SQL_ANSI_mode), [Spark SQL scripting](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_SQL_scripting), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (common/utils/src/main/resources/error/, SparkThrowable.java, python/pyspark/errors/exceptions/base.py, docs/sql-error-conditions.md, SQLConf.scala), SPARK-46810 and the Spark 4.0.0 release notes</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), **error classes** (now documented as **error conditions**) are the structured identifiers that Spark attaches to user-facing errors: a stable name such as `DIVIDE_BY_ZERO`, an optional sub-condition, a five-character SQLSTATE code and a message template with named parameters.[^readme] They let programs and people identify an error without parsing its message text, which can change between releases. The Spark documentation lists them on the "Error Conditions" page, ordered by SQLSTATE.[^docs]

## Error class or error condition?

Spark uses the terms of the SQL standard, in which an "error class" is only the first two characters of a SQLSTATE. Spark's contributor guide defines a hierarchy of three levels: the error state (SQLSTATE), the error condition, and the error sub-condition. The SQLSTATE in turn has two parts, a class (for example `42`) and a sub-class (for example `K01`).[^readme]

Spark historically called a name like `DATATYPE_MISSING_SIZE` an "error class" as well, which clashed with the standard meaning. SPARK-46810, "Clarify error class terminology", fixed in Spark 4.0.0, settled on "error condition" for these names in user-facing documentation.[^jira46810] The guide notes that the code still calls the field `errorClass` in many places, so the same string is an "error condition" in the docs and an "error class" in the code.[^readme]

The public APIs followed the rename. In Spark 4.3.0 the Java and Scala interface `SparkThrowable` exposes `getCondition()` and marks `getErrorClass()` as deprecated.[^throwable] In PySpark, SPARK-50915 added `PySparkException.getCondition()` and deprecated `getErrorClass()` as of 4.0.0.[^r400][^pybase]

## How are Spark errors structured?

Spark defines its errors in three JSON files in the source tree: `error-conditions.json` (the conditions, their messages and SQLSTATEs), `error-states.json` (the SQLSTATE values) and `error-classes.json` (the two-character SQLSTATE classes).[^readme] An error condition is unique, stays the same across releases, and has a message template whose parameters are written in angle brackets, such as `<relationName>`.[^readme]

Some conditions have sub-conditions that add detail. For example `UNRESOLVED_COLUMN` (SQLSTATE `42703`) has the sub-conditions `WITH_SUGGESTION` and `WITHOUT_SUGGESTION`, and the full name is written `UNRESOLVED_COLUMN.WITH_SUGGESTION`.[^errjson]

Errors that have not yet been given a proper name use a legacy condition with the prefix `_LEGACY_ERROR_TEMP_` and a number. The contributor guide asks that no new uncategorized errors be added and that existing ones be converted.[^readme]

## What is a SQLSTATE in Spark?

A SQLSTATE is a five-character code that identifies an error category across SQL engines; the first two characters are the class and the last three the sub-class.[^readme] Spark's `error-states.json` records, for each state, its description, whether it comes from the SQL standard and which other systems use it. For example `22003` ("numeric value out of range") comes from SQL/Foundation, while `42P01` ("undefined table") originates in PostgreSQL.[^states] Spark 4.0.0 made a SQLSTATE mandatory for error conditions (SPARK-45581) and exposed it in error messages (SPARK-45595).[^r400]

| Error condition | SQLSTATE | Typical cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DIVIDE_BY_ZERO` | `22012` | Division by zero in [ANSI mode](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_SQL_ANSI_mode) |
| `ARITHMETIC_OVERFLOW` | `22003` | Numeric overflow in ANSI mode |
| `CAST_INVALID_INPUT` | `22018` | A string that cannot be cast to the target type |
| `TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND` | `42P01` | A table or view name that does not resolve |
| `UNRESOLVED_COLUMN` | `42703` | A column, variable or parameter name that does not resolve |

Source: `error-conditions.json` at v4.3.0.[^errjson]

## How to search Spark error conditions

The "Error Conditions" page of the Spark documentation is generated from `error-conditions.json` and lists every condition with its SQLSTATE and message, sorted by SQLSTATE and then by name.[^docs][^n1] Searching that page, or the JSON file at the matching release tag, for the condition name shown in brackets at the start of an error message (for example `[CAST_INVALID_INPUT]`) gives the message template and SQLSTATE for that release.

Programs can read the same fields from the exception. Every Spark exception that implements `SparkThrowable` provides `getCondition()`, `getSqlState()` and `getMessageParameters()`.[^throwable] PySpark exceptions provide methods of the same names.[^pybase]

```python
from pyspark.errors import PySparkException

try:
    spark.sql("SELECT 1 / 0").collect()   # ANSI mode is on by default in Spark 4
except PySparkException as e:
    print(e.getCondition())          # DIVIDE_BY_ZERO
    print(e.getSqlState())           # 22012
    print(e.getMessageParameters())  # e.g. {'config': '"spark.sql.ansi.enabled"'}
```

Branching on `getCondition()` or on the SQLSTATE class is more robust than matching message text. The contributor guide shows a check of the form `getSqlState.startsWith("42")` to catch all syntax and analysis errors.[^readme] In [Spark SQL scripting](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_SQL_scripting), condition handlers can name an error condition such as `DIVIDE_BY_ZERO` or a SQLSTATE directly.[^scripting]

## How are error messages formatted?

`spark.sql.error.messageFormat` sets how the Thrift Server and the SQL command-line interface print errors. The default, `PRETTY`, prints the error condition, message and query context and shows stack traces only for internal errors (SQLSTATE `XX***`); `DEBUG` always adds stack traces; `MINIMAL` and `STANDARD` produce JSON, with `STANDARD` adding a `message` field.[^sqlconf]

# Spark event log

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_event_log

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Event log, eventLog</Field>
  <Field name="field">Monitoring and debugging</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">EventLoggingListener, JSON lines (one listener event per line), compression codec, rolling files, compaction</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark History Server](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_History_Server), [Spark UI](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_UI), [Spark listener](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_listener)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (EventLoggingListener.scala, EventLogFileWriters.scala, config/package.scala, config/History.scala, docs/configuration.md, docs/monitoring.md, docs/core-migration-guide.md) and Spark JIRA SPARK-28594 and SPARK-45771</Verified>

The **Spark event log** is a file, or a directory of files, in which an [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) application records the listener events that its driver posts for jobs, stages, tasks, executors and SQL query executions, so that the application's [Spark UI](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_UI) can be rebuilt after it ends. Not every event is written: some are recorded only when a setting turns them on, events can opt out of logging, and `spark.eventLog.excludedPatterns` suppresses named events.[^ell] The [Spark History Server](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_History_Server) reads event logs to show finished applications. Event logging is off by default and is turned on with `spark.eventLog.enabled`.[^coreconf]

## What does the event log record?

The event log is written by `EventLoggingListener`, a [Spark listener](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_listener) that the driver registers when event logging is on. Each event that it logs is serialized to JSON and written as one line; the first line records the Spark version.[^ell] The events include application start and end, job start and end, stage submission and completion, task start and end with task metrics, executors added and removed, environment updates, and SQL execution start and end with the query plans. These are the kinds of events that also build the live Spark UI.

Some events are left out by default. `EventLoggingListener` writes block updates and stage executor metrics only when their settings are on, writes events from other modules only if the event's `logEvent` flag is true, and the log writer drops any line that starts with a pattern listed in `spark.eventLog.excludedPatterns`:[^ell][^writers][^coreconf][^confdoc]
- `spark.eventLog.logBlockUpdates.enabled` (default false) logs every block update. The documentation warns that this increases the size of the event log considerably.
- `spark.eventLog.logStageExecutorMetrics` (default false) writes per-stage peaks of executor metrics.

## Where is the event log written?

```properties
spark.eventLog.enabled  true
spark.eventLog.dir      hdfs://namenode/shared/spark-logs
```

`spark.eventLog.dir` defaults to `/tmp/spark-events`, a path on the driver's local file system, so on a cluster it is set to a shared location such as HDFS or object storage that the [Spark History Server](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_History_Server) also reads.[^coreconf][^ell][^monitoring]

A single-file event log is named after the application ID and carries an `.inprogress` suffix until the application ends. A rolling event log is a directory named `eventlog_v2_<appId>` that holds numbered `events_<index>_<appId>` files and an `appstatus_<appId>` file, which also has the `.inprogress` suffix while the application runs.[^writers]

## What changed in Spark 4.0?

Two event log defaults changed in Spark 4.0. The Spark migration guide says that since 4.0, Spark rolls event logs to archive them incrementally, and that it compresses event logs; setting `spark.eventLog.rolling.enabled` or `spark.eventLog.compress` to false restores the earlier behaviour.[^migration] The rolling default came from SPARK-45771.[^n1] Since Spark 3.2, the event log codec defaults to `zstd` and no longer falls back to `spark.io.compression.codec`.[^migration]

| Setting | Default in 4.3.0 | Since |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spark.eventLog.enabled` | false | 1.0.0 |
| `spark.eventLog.dir` | `/tmp/spark-events` | 1.0.0 |
| `spark.eventLog.compress` | true | 1.0.0 |
| `spark.eventLog.compression.codec` | zstd | 3.0.0 |
| `spark.eventLog.rolling.enabled` | true | 3.0.0 |
| `spark.eventLog.rolling.maxFileSize` | 128m | 3.0.0 |
| `spark.eventLog.excludedPatterns` | (none) | 4.1.0 |

All values are from the Spark 4.3.0 source.[^coreconf]

## Why do event logs get so large?

An event log grows with the number of tasks, because every task end event carries the task's metrics. Applications with many small tasks, long-running [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) queries that run a job for every micro-batch, and queries with very large plans produce the largest logs. A large single-file log is slow for the History Server to replay, because the whole file must be read to build the UI.[^monitoring]

Ways to keep event logs manageable:
- **Rolling.** With `spark.eventLog.rolling.enabled` (on by default since 4.0), Spark starts a new file when the current one reaches `spark.eventLog.rolling.maxFileSize` (default 128m). Rolling was added for running streaming applications in Spark 3.0.0 (SPARK-28594).[^coreconf][^n2]
- **Compaction.** Rolling alone does not reduce the total size. Setting `spark.history.fs.eventLog.rolling.maxFilesToRetain` on the History Server compacts older rolled files and drops events for finished jobs, terminated executors and finished SQL executions. The documentation describes compaction as lossy.[^monitoring][^history]
- **Excluding events.** `spark.eventLog.excludedPatterns` (since 4.1.0) takes a comma-separated list of event names that are not written.[^confdoc]
- **Leaving verbose events off**, such as block updates.[^confdoc]
- **Retention.** The History Server cleaner (`spark.history.fs.cleaner.enabled`, default false) deletes old logs.[^history]

## Reading an event log without the History Server

Because each line is a JSON object whose `Event` field names the event class (for example `SparkListenerStageCompleted`),[^jsonprotocol] a compressed log can be decompressed and read with ordinary JSON tools. Spark itself can read one as a JSON data source, which is a quick way to find the slowest stages of a finished run:

```python
events = spark.read.json("/tmp/spark-events/app-20261123120000-0000")
(events.filter("Event = 'SparkListenerStageCompleted'")
       .selectExpr("`Stage Info`.`Stage ID` AS stage",
                   "`Stage Info`.`Completion Time` - `Stage Info`.`Submission Time` AS ms")
       .orderBy("ms", ascending=False)
       .show(5))
```

The JSON format comes from Spark's `JsonProtocol`, an internal class whose source states that any version of Spark should be able to read event logs written by any other version, and that JSON fields are never deleted, only added as optional fields.[^jsonprotocol] For tools, the REST API of the History Server or the live UI, at `/api/v1`, is the documented interface to the same data and has its own versioning policy.[^monitoring]

# Spark History Server

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_History_Server

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">History server, port 18080</Field>
  <Field name="field">Monitoring and debugging</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Event log directory, FsHistoryProvider, local KV store, cleaner, REST API at /api/v1</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark UI](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_UI), [Spark event log](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_event_log), [Spark listener](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_listener)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/monitoring.md, config/History.scala, config/package.scala, EventLoggingListener.scala, docs/core-migration-guide.md)</Verified>

The **Spark History Server** is a long-running [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) service that reads the [event logs](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_event_log) of applications and rebuilds their [Spark UI](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_UI), so that jobs, stages, SQL queries and executors can be inspected after an application has finished. It is started with `./sbin/start-history-server.sh` and serves a web interface at `http://<server-url>:18080` by default, listing completed and incomplete applications.[^monitoring] The live Spark UI on port 4040 disappears when the driver exits; the History Server is how finished applications are debugged.

## How does the Spark History Server work?

The History Server and the applications share a directory. Each application writes its event log there, and the server reads it:[^monitoring]

```properties
# On the applications
spark.eventLog.enabled   true
spark.eventLog.dir       hdfs://namenode/shared/spark-logs

# On the History Server
spark.history.fs.logDirectory  hdfs://namenode/shared/spark-logs
```

Event logging is off by default (`spark.eventLog.enabled`, default false), and both `spark.eventLog.dir` and `spark.history.fs.logDirectory` default to `/tmp/spark-events`.[^coreconf][^history][^ell] `spark.history.fs.logDirectory` accepts a comma-separated list of directories, so one server can watch several locations.[^history]

The default provider, `org.apache.spark.deploy.history.FsHistoryProvider` (`spark.history.provider`), scans the directory every `spark.history.fs.update.interval` (default 10s) for new or changed logs.[^history] When a user opens an application, the server replays its event log through the same status listeners that build the live UI, and caches the result. `spark.history.retainedApplications` (default 50) sets how many applications' UI data stay in the cache; others are loaded from disk again when opened.[^history]

## Reading finished applications

The History Server shows the same tabs as the live [Spark UI](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_UI): Jobs, Stages, Storage, Environment, Executors and SQL. The same data is available from the REST API, at `http://<server-url>:18080/api/v1`, which is useful for scripts that compare runs.[^monitoring]

The Spark documentation lists several behaviours that surprise new users:[^monitoring]
- An application with several attempts shows its failed attempts, as well as the ongoing or final successful attempt.
- Incomplete (running) applications are refreshed only at each update interval. The documentation recommends viewing a running application in its own live UI.
- An application that exits without registering as complete, for example after a crash, stays listed as incomplete. Stopping the session explicitly (`spark.stop()`) marks it complete.

## Retention: how long are event logs kept?

The History Server does not delete event logs unless its cleaner is turned on. The cleaner settings at Spark 4.3.0 are:[^history][^monitoring]

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spark.history.fs.cleaner.enabled` | false | Turns on periodic deletion of event logs. |
| `spark.history.fs.cleaner.interval` | 1d | How often the cleaner runs. |
| `spark.history.fs.cleaner.maxAge` | 7d | Logs older than this are deleted. |
| `spark.history.fs.cleaner.maxNum` | Int.MaxValue | If there are more logs than this, the oldest completed attempts are deleted. |

A log is deleted if either condition holds. When several log directories are configured, one cleaner cycle covers all of them.[^monitoring]

For long-running applications, the History Server can also compact rolled event logs. Setting `spark.history.fs.eventLog.rolling.maxFilesToRetain` (default: all files kept) makes the server rewrite older rolled files into one compact file, dropping events for finished jobs, terminated executors and finished SQL executions. The documentation calls compaction lossy, notes that it may not run if little space would be saved, and asks users to use it with caution.[^monitoring] See [Spark event log](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_event_log) for rolling.

## Running a History Server at scale

Replaying a large event log takes time and memory. Several settings help:[^history][^monitoring]
- `spark.history.store.path` (no default) stores application data on local disk instead of in memory, and reuses it after a restart. `spark.history.store.maxDiskUsage` (default 10g) caps that disk.
- `spark.history.store.hybridStore.enabled` (default false, since 3.1.0) first parses logs into memory and then moves the result to disk, limited by `spark.history.store.hybridStore.maxMemoryUsage` (default 2g).
- `spark.history.fs.numReplayThreads` sets how many threads replay logs; its default is a quarter of the available cores.
- `SPARK_DAEMON_MEMORY` sets the server's memory (default 1g).

Access control uses `spark.history.ui.acls.enable` and the admin ACL settings, and Kerberos is supported with `spark.history.kerberos.enabled`.[^history]

# Spark Kubernetes pod template

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Kubernetes_pod_template

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Pod template file, driver pod template, executor pod template</Field>
  <Field name="field">Cluster resource management</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 3.0.0</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`spark.kubernetes.driver.podTemplateFile`, `spark.kubernetes.executor.podTemplateFile`, `podTemplateContainerName`</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark on Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_Kubernetes), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Spark Kubernetes shuffle storage](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Kubernetes_shuffle_storage), [Executor decommissioning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor_decommissioning)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/running-on-kubernetes.md and resource-managers/kubernetes/core/.../deploy/k8s/Config.scala), SPARK-24434 and the Kubernetes sidecar containers page</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a **Kubernetes pod template** is a YAML or JSON pod specification that Spark uses as the starting point when it builds the driver pod or the executor pods of an application on Kubernetes.[^k8s] A pod template sets pod fields that have no Spark configuration property, such as tolerations, security contexts, priority classes and extra containers. Spark still overwrites a fixed list of fields, so the template is a base that Spark completes rather than a final pod definition.[^k8s] The feature is part of [Spark on Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_Kubernetes) and is also used by the [Kubernetes Operator for Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Kubernetes_Operator_for_Apache_Spark), which runs applications on the same scheduler backend.[^k8s]

## Which configuration keys control a pod template?

Four Spark properties control pod templates. All four were added in Apache Spark 3.0.0 and have no default value.[^k8s][^config][^jira24434]

| Property | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `spark.kubernetes.driver.podTemplateFile` | File with the template for the driver pod |
| `spark.kubernetes.executor.podTemplateFile` | File with the template for every executor pod |
| `spark.kubernetes.driver.podTemplateContainerName` | Name of the container in the driver template that becomes the Spark driver container |
| `spark.kubernetes.executor.podTemplateContainerName` | Name of the container in the executor template that becomes the Spark executor container |

The template files must be readable by the `spark-submit` process, and the Spark documentation shows them read from object storage, for example `s3a://bucket/executor.yml`. In cluster mode Spark mounts the executor template into the driver pod as a volume, because the driver creates the executor pods.[^k8s]

Spark does not validate a template after parsing it. Validation is left to the Kubernetes API server, so an invalid field shows up as a rejected pod creation rather than a Spark error.[^k8s]

## How does Spark choose the Spark container in a template?

A pod template can list several containers. Spark uses the container named by `spark.kubernetes.driver.podTemplateContainerName` or `spark.kubernetes.executor.podTemplateContainerName` as the basis for the driver or executor container. If the property is unset, or names a container that does not exist, Spark takes the first container in the list.[^k8s]

Spark changes only the driver or executor container. Every other container in the template is passed to Kubernetes unchanged.[^k8s] If the template does not name the Spark container, Spark calls it `spark-kubernetes-driver` or `spark-kubernetes-executor`.[^k8s]

## Which pod template fields does Spark override?

The Spark documentation lists the fields that Spark always sets or adds to, whatever the template says.[^k8s]

| Level | Field | What Spark does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pod metadata | `name` | Sets the driver pod name from `spark.kubernetes.driver.pod.name`; executor pod names are not taken from the template |
| Pod metadata | `namespace` | Replaced by `spark.kubernetes.namespace` for driver and executors |
| Pod metadata | `labels`, `annotations` | Keeps the template's entries and adds those from `spark.kubernetes.{driver,executor}.label.*` and `.annotation.*` |
| Pod spec | `restartPolicy` | Always `Never` |
| Pod spec | `nodeSelector` | Adds selectors from `spark.kubernetes.node.selector.*` |
| Pod spec | `imagePullSecrets` | Adds secrets from `spark.kubernetes.container.image.pullSecrets` |
| Pod spec | `serviceAccount`, `serviceAccountName` | Driver only, and only when `spark.kubernetes.authenticate.driver.serviceAccountName` is set and no driver credentials are mounted |
| Pod spec | `volumes` | Adds volumes from `spark.kubernetes.{driver,executor}.volumes.*` plus the volumes that carry the Spark configuration and template files |
| Spark container | `image`, `imagePullPolicy` | Set from `spark.kubernetes.{driver,executor}.container.image` and `spark.kubernetes.container.image.pullPolicy` |
| Spark container | `resources` | CPU from `spark.{driver,executor}.cores` and `spark.kubernetes.{driver,executor}.limit.cores`; memory request and limit from memory plus memory overhead |
| Spark container | `env`, `volumeMounts` | Adds environment variables and mounts from the Spark configuration |

Fields not in this list, such as `tolerations`, `affinity`, `priorityClassName`, `securityContext` and `initContainers`, are taken from the template as written.[^k8s] The documentation uses `priorityClassName` in a template as its example of priority scheduling.[^k8s]

Resources in a template apply only to the default resource profile. With stage-level scheduling, custom ResourceProfiles do not inherit resources from the template file, so they must declare every resource they need.[^k8s]

## What is a pod template commonly used for?

**Scheduling.** Node selectors can be set without a template: `spark.kubernetes.node.selector.[labelKey]` (since Spark 2.3.0) applies to driver and executors, and the driver-only and executor-only variants were added in Spark 3.3.0.[^k8s] Tolerations and affinity rules have no Spark property and are set through the template.[^config][^k8s]

**Volumes.** Spark properties can mount `hostPath`, `emptyDir`, `nfs` and `persistentVolumeClaim` volumes.[^k8s] Other volume types, such as a ConfigMap or projected volume, are declared in the template. Volumes for shuffle and spill data are described in [Spark Kubernetes shuffle storage](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Kubernetes_shuffle_storage).

**Sidecars.** A template can add containers next to the Spark container, for example a log shipper. Kubernetes treats an init container with `restartPolicy: Always` as a native sidecar; it is stable since Kubernetes 1.33, and the kubelet waits until the main container has stopped before it terminates the sidecar.[^sidecar] Spark 4.3.0 documents Kubernetes 1.34 or later as a prerequisite.[^k8s]

**Security contexts.** The Spark images built from the project Dockerfiles run as UID 185. The documentation names the pod template as the way to add a security context with `runAsUser` that overrides the image's user.[^k8s] Apache Spark 4.3.0 added `spark.kubernetes.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation` (default false) and driver and executor variants, which set the `allowPrivilegeEscalation` field of the Spark containers.[^config]

## Example

An executor pod template that pins executors to a tainted node pool, runs them as a non-root user and adds a native sidecar. The `image` value is replaced by Spark.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    pool: spark
  tolerations:
  - key: dedicated
    operator: Equal
    value: spark
    effect: NoSchedule
  securityContext:
    runAsUser: 185
    runAsNonRoot: true
  initContainers:
  - name: log-shipper
    image: example.org/log-shipper:1.0
    restartPolicy: Always
  containers:
  - name: spark-executor
    image: will-be-overwritten
```

```
spark.kubernetes.executor.podTemplateFile           s3a://bucket/executor.yml
spark.kubernetes.executor.podTemplateContainerName  spark-executor
```
