# Spark Kubernetes shuffle storage

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Kubernetes_shuffle_storage

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Spark local storage on Kubernetes, spark-local-dir volumes</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`emptyDir` scratch volumes, `spark-local-dir-*` volumes, on-demand persistent volume claims, `KubernetesLocalDiskShuffleDataIO`</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Spark on Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_Kubernetes), [Executor decommissioning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor_decommissioning), [Spark Kubernetes pod template](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Kubernetes_pod_template)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/running-on-kubernetes.md, docs/job-scheduling.md, docs/configuration.md, docs/core-migration-guide.md, deploy/k8s/Config.scala, KubernetesLocalDiskShuffleDataIO.scala) and SPARK-25262, SPARK-28042, SPARK-32971, SPARK-35182, SPARK-35416, SPARK-35593</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), **shuffle storage on Kubernetes** is the set of pod volumes where executors write [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle) files and spill data; by default these are Kubernetes `emptyDir` volumes that last only as long as the executor pod.[^k8s] Spark on Kubernetes has no external shuffle service, so shuffle files written by an [executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor) are normally lost when its pod goes away.[^jobsched] Spark offers RAM-backed volumes, host disks, persistent volume claims (PVCs) that the driver reuses, and a shuffle plugin that recovers files from reused PVCs.[^k8s]

## Where does Spark write shuffle and spill data on Kubernetes by default?

When no volume is configured as local storage, Spark on Kubernetes mounts one `emptyDir` volume for each directory in `spark.local.dir` or the `SPARK_LOCAL_DIRS` environment variable. If neither is set, Spark creates and configures a default directory.[^k8s]

An `emptyDir` volume uses the ephemeral storage of the node and does not outlive the pod. Shuffle files on it disappear when the executor pod is deleted.[^k8s]

## How does spark.kubernetes.local.dirs.tmpfs work?

`spark.kubernetes.local.dirs.tmpfs` (default false, added in Spark 3.0.0) sets the medium of the scratch `emptyDir` volumes to `Memory`, so they are tmpfs, RAM-backed volumes.[^config][^n1] The documentation suggests it for nodes without local disks, where many executors writing to network-mounted storage can be slow.[^k8s]

With tmpfs, data in the local directories counts against the pod's memory. The Spark documentation suggests raising `spark.{driver,executor}.memoryOverheadFactor` to leave room for it.[^k8s]

## How do spark-local-dir volumes work?

Any volume mounted through the Spark volume properties whose name starts with `spark-local-dir-` is used as local storage for shuffle and spill instead of the default `emptyDir`.[^k8s] Volume properties have the form `spark.kubernetes.executor.volumes.[VolumeType].[VolumeName].mount.path`, and the supported types are `hostPath`, `emptyDir`, `nfs` and `persistentVolumeClaim`.[^k8s]

A `hostPath` volume puts local directories on a directory of the node itself; support for mapping `spark.local.dir` to `hostPath` volumes arrived in Spark 3.0.0.[^n2] The Spark documentation warns that `hostPath` volumes have known security weaknesses and advises cluster administrators to restrict them with the Pod Security Admission controller.[^k8s]

## How do on-demand persistent volume claims work for shuffle?

Setting a volume's `claimName` option to `OnDemand` makes Spark create one PVC per executor, with the size and storage class from the `sizeLimit` and `storageClass` options.[^k8s] Dynamic PVC creation and deletion for executors was added in Spark 3.1.0.[^n3] The Spark documentation recommends a PVC named `spark-local-dir-*` for jobs with large shuffles and sorts.[^k8s]

```
spark.kubernetes.executor.volumes.persistentVolumeClaim.spark-local-dir-1.options.claimName     OnDemand
spark.kubernetes.executor.volumes.persistentVolumeClaim.spark-local-dir-1.options.storageClass  gp
spark.kubernetes.executor.volumes.persistentVolumeClaim.spark-local-dir-1.options.sizeLimit     500Gi
spark.kubernetes.executor.volumes.persistentVolumeClaim.spark-local-dir-1.mount.path            /data
spark.kubernetes.executor.volumes.persistentVolumeClaim.spark-local-dir-1.mount.readOnly        false
```

Since Spark 4.2.0, the `ExecutorPVCResizePlugin` plugin can grow the storage request of an executor's `spark-local-dir-*` PVCs while the executor runs. It is controlled by `spark.kubernetes.executor.pvc.resizeInterval` (default 5 minutes), `resizeThreshold` (default 0.5) and `resizeFactor` (default 1.0), and requires a storage class that allows volume expansion.[^k8s][^config]

## Which configuration keys control PVC reuse?

Three driver properties let on-demand PVCs outlive the executor that first used them.[^config][^k8s]

| Property | Added in | Default in 4.3.0 | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `spark.kubernetes.driver.ownPersistentVolumeClaim` | 3.2.0 | true | The driver pod, not the executor pod, owns on-demand PVCs |
| `spark.kubernetes.driver.reusePersistentVolumeClaim` | 3.2.0 | true | The driver gives PVCs of deleted executors to new executors; requires driver ownership |
| `spark.kubernetes.driver.waitToReusePersistentVolumeClaim` | 3.4.0 | false | The driver holds back new executors while it already owns as many PVCs as the job may have; requires both settings above |

The first two properties defaulted to false when they were introduced. Since Spark 3.4, the driver owns PVCs and tries to reuse those not attached to live executors; setting both properties to false restores the earlier behaviour.[^migration] A pod in `Terminating` state has not yet released its PVCs, so the total number of PVCs can exceed the number of running executors.[^config]

## What is KubernetesLocalDiskShuffleDataIO?

`org.apache.spark.shuffle.KubernetesLocalDiskShuffleDataIO` is a built-in shuffle storage plugin that recovers shuffle data from reused PVCs, so a new executor that mounts a reused PVC tries to recover the shuffle data that dead executors left in its local directories.[^k8s][^execcomp] It was added in Spark 3.2.0 under SPARK-35593 and requires `spark.kubernetes.driver.reusePersistentVolumeClaim=true`.[^plugin][^n4]

The documented setup mounts the PVC at a path such as `/data/spark-x/executor-x` and sets `spark.shuffle.sort.io.plugin.class` to the plugin class. The documentation also suggests enabling `spark.kubernetes.driver.waitToReusePersistentVolumeClaim`.[^k8s]

## How does shuffle storage relate to dynamic allocation and decommissioning?

Dynamic allocation needs shuffle files to survive executor removal. On other cluster managers the external shuffle service can do this, but Spark on Kubernetes does not support it, so setting `spark.shuffle.service.enabled` to true is not an option there.[^jobsched] The remaining options are shuffle tracking (`spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled`), shuffle block migration through [executor decommissioning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor_decommissioning), or a shuffle plugin whose driver components support reliable storage.[^jobsched][^configdoc]

Decommissioning and PVC reuse address different failures. Decommissioning copies shuffle blocks from an executor that is being shut down to other executors, or to `spark.storage.decommission.fallbackStorage.path`, before the pod ends.[^configdoc] PVC reuse with `KubernetesLocalDiskShuffleDataIO` recovers files after a pod is already gone, as long as its PVC survives.[^k8s]

[^plugin]: [KubernetesLocalDiskShuffleDataIO.scala (v4.3.0)](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/v4.3.0/resource-managers/kubernetes/core/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/shuffle/KubernetesLocalDiskShuffleDataIO.scala). *Apache Software Foundation*. Retrieved 2026-11-23.
[^n4]: [SPARK-35593: Support shuffle data recovery on the reused PVCs](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-35593). *Apache Software Foundation JIRA*. Retrieved 2026-11-23.

# Spark listener

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_listener

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">SparkListener, QueryExecutionListener, StreamingQueryListener</Field>
  <Field name="field">Monitoring and extension APIs</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Listener bus with asynchronous event queues, SparkListener callbacks, SQL and streaming listener interfaces, registration by configuration or code</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark event log](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_event_log), [Spark UI](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_UI), [Spark History Server](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_History_Server), [Spark plugin](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_plugin), [MLflow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MLflow), [OpenLineage](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/OpenLineage)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (SparkListener.scala, LiveListenerBus.scala, AsyncEventQueue.scala, SparkContext.scala, QueryExecutionListener.scala, StreamingQueryListener.scala, python/pyspark/sql/streaming/listener.py, config/package.scala, StaticSQLConf.scala), the OpenLineage 1.55.0 Spark integration docs and MLflow v3.18.0 source</Verified>

A **Spark listener** is a class that [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) calls back when something happens inside an application, such as a job starting, a task ending, an executor being added or a SQL query finishing.[^listener] The core interface is `org.apache.spark.scheduler.SparkListener`; the SQL module adds `QueryExecutionListener` for completed queries, and [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) adds `StreamingQueryListener` for query progress. Listeners are how Spark builds its own [Spark UI](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_UI) and [Spark event log](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_event_log), and how external tools such as [OpenLineage](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/OpenLineage) and [MLflow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MLflow) observe Spark applications.

## How do Spark listeners work?

The driver posts every scheduler event to a **listener bus**, which delivers events to listeners on background threads, so that a slow listener does not block the scheduler. In Spark 4.3.0 the bus has separate queues: `shared` for user listeners, `appStatus` for the listener that feeds the Spark UI, `executorManagement` for dynamic allocation, and `eventLog` for the event log writer.[^bus]

Each queue has a fixed capacity, `spark.scheduler.listenerbus.eventqueue.capacity` (default 10000, since 2.3.0), which can be overridden for one queue with `spark.scheduler.listenerbus.eventqueue.<queueName>.capacity`.[^coreconf] When a queue is full, Spark drops events and logs an error saying that a listener is probably too slow to keep up.[^queue] Dropped events in the `appStatus` queue show up as missing or stuck jobs and stages in the UI, so listener code should return quickly.

## SparkListener

`SparkListener` is an abstract class with an empty method for each event, so a subclass overrides only what it needs. The methods include `onApplicationStart`, `onApplicationEnd`, `onJobStart`, `onJobEnd`, `onStageSubmitted`, `onStageCompleted`, `onTaskStart`, `onTaskEnd`, `onExecutorAdded`, `onExecutorRemoved`, `onEnvironmentUpdate` and `onOtherEvent`, which receives events from other modules such as SQL execution start and end.[^listener] The event classes are marked `@DeveloperApi`, and the underlying trait is documented as an internal interface that might change between releases; the source recommends extending `SparkListener` or `SparkFirehoseListener` instead of implementing it directly.[^listener]

A listener is registered in one of two ways:
- In configuration, with `spark.extraListeners` (since 1.3.0), a list of class names that Spark adds to the `SparkContext` when it starts. This catches events from the very start of the application.[^coreconf]
- In code, with `SparkContext.addSparkListener` and `removeSparkListener`.[^n1]

```scala
import org.apache.spark.scheduler.{SparkListener, SparkListenerStageCompleted}

class SlowStageListener extends SparkListener {
  override def onStageCompleted(e: SparkListenerStageCompleted): Unit = {
    val info = e.stageInfo
    for (start <- info.submissionTime; end <- info.completionTime if end - start > 60000) {
      println(s"Stage ${info.stageId} (${info.name}) took ${(end - start) / 1000}s")
    }
  }
}
// spark-submit --conf spark.extraListeners=com.example.SlowStageListener ...
```

## QueryExecutionListener

`org.apache.spark.sql.util.QueryExecutionListener` is called once per completed DataFrame or SQL action, with `onSuccess(funcName, qe, durationNs)` or `onFailure(funcName, qe, exception)`. The `QueryExecution` argument gives access to the logical and physical plans of the query.[^qel] The interface documentation notes that implementations must be thread-safe, because they can be called from several threads.

A query execution listener is registered per session with `spark.listenerManager.register(...)`, or for every new session with the static setting `spark.sql.queryExecutionListeners` (since 2.3.0).[^qel][^static] Internally, Spark delivers these callbacks from SQL execution end events on the listener bus.[^qel]

## StreamingQueryListener

`StreamingQueryListener` (since 2.0.0) receives `onQueryStarted`, `onQueryProgress` after each micro-batch, `onQueryIdle` (since 3.5.0) and `onQueryTerminated` for [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) queries.[^sql] It is registered with `spark.streams.addListener(...)` or the static setting `spark.sql.streaming.streamingQueryListeners` (since 2.4.0).[^static] PySpark has its own `StreamingQueryListener` class since 3.4.0, so a streaming listener can be written in Python:[^n2]

```python
from pyspark.sql.streaming import StreamingQueryListener

class ProgressLogger(StreamingQueryListener):
    def onQueryStarted(self, event):
        print(f"started {event.id}")
    def onQueryProgress(self, event):
        p = event.progress
        print(f"batch {p.batchId}: {p.numInputRows} rows")
    def onQueryIdle(self, event):
        pass
    def onQueryTerminated(self, event):
        print(f"terminated {event.id}")

spark.streams.addListener(ProgressLogger())
```

## What is built on Spark listeners?

- **The [Spark UI](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_UI) and [Spark History Server](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_History_Server).** Spark's status listener, on the `appStatus` queue, builds the data behind the UI, and the History Server replays event logs through the same kind of listener.[^bus][^n3]
- **The [Spark event log](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_event_log)**, written by `EventLoggingListener` on the `eventLog` queue.[^bus][^n4]
- **[MLflow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MLflow) autologging for Spark.** MLflow's `SparkDataSourceListener` extends `SparkListener` to detect data source reads, so that autologging can record which tables and paths a model was trained on.[^n5]
- **[OpenLineage](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/OpenLineage) lineage collection.** The OpenLineage Spark integration is a `SparkListener`, `io.openlineage.spark.agent.OpenLineageSparkListener`, enabled with `spark.extraListeners`; it reads the events that the SparkContext emits and extracts metadata about jobs and datasets from the RDD and DataFrame dependency graphs.[^n6]

## Spark listener vs Spark plugin

A listener only observes events on the driver. A [Spark plugin](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_plugin) runs code inside the driver and every executor, can register metrics, and can send messages from executors to the driver. Monitoring tools that need executor-side data use a plugin; tools that only need scheduler events use a listener.[^n7]

# Spark memory management

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_memory_management

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Unified memory model, unified memory manager</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 1.6.0 (unified memory manager)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Reserved memory, user memory, unified region (execution and storage), memory overhead, off-heap memory</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Executor memory overhead](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor_memory_overhead), [Spill (memory)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spill_(memory)), [Caching and persistence](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Caching_and_persistence), [Garbage collection in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Garbage_collection_in_Spark), [Project Tungsten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Tungsten)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/tuning.md, docs/configuration.md, core/memory/UnifiedMemoryManager.scala) and SPARK-10000</Verified>

**Spark memory management** is the way [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) divides the memory of each [executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor) between running tasks, cached data, user code and the JVM itself. Since Spark 1.6.0, a **unified memory manager** lets execution memory (for shuffles, joins, sorts and aggregations) and storage memory (for cached data) share one region and borrow from each other.[^spark10000][^tuning] Memory outside the JVM heap is requested separately as [executor memory overhead](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor_memory_overhead).

## How is executor memory divided?

An executor's JVM heap is set by `spark.executor.memory` (default `1g`).[^config] Spark splits the heap into three parts:

| Part | Size | What it holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reserved memory | 300 MiB, fixed | Kept back by Spark; the heap must be at least 1.5 times this (450 MiB) or the executor does not start[^umm] |
| User memory | (heap − 300 MiB) × (1 − `spark.memory.fraction`), 40% by default | User data structures, Spark internal metadata, and a margin for unusually large records[^tuning] |
| Unified region (M) | (heap − 300 MiB) × `spark.memory.fraction` (default 0.6) | Execution memory and storage memory, shared[^tuning] |

For an 8 GiB heap with the defaults, the unified region is (8192 − 300) × 0.6 ≈ 4,735 MiB and user memory is about 3,157 MiB. This follows the formula in `UnifiedMemoryManager`, which subtracts the 300 MiB reserve from the heap size the JVM reports (`Runtime.getRuntime.maxMemory`) and multiplies the rest by `spark.memory.fraction`; the JVM may report slightly less than `spark.executor.memory`, so the real figures can be a little lower.[^umm][^tuning]

## Execution memory and storage memory

**Execution memory** is used for computation in shuffles, joins, sorts and aggregations. **Storage memory** is used for caching and for propagating internal data across the cluster.[^tuning]

The two share the unified region M. When no execution memory is in use, storage can take all of M, and the other way round. Execution can evict cached blocks to get memory back, but only until storage falls to a protected share R, set by `spark.memory.storageFraction` (default 0.5 of M). Storage cannot evict execution memory.[^tuning] Applications that do not cache can therefore use the whole region for execution, and applications that cache keep at least R for their blocks.[^tuning]

When execution memory runs out, tasks [spill](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spill_(memory)) to disk instead of failing. When storage memory runs out, cached blocks are dropped in least-recently-used order, or written to disk if their storage level allows it.[^rddguide] The Spark docs recommend leaving both fractions at their defaults for most workloads.[^tuning]

## Off-heap memory

With `spark.memory.offHeap.enabled` (default false) set to true, Spark can use off-heap memory for certain operations, in an amount set by `spark.memory.offHeap.size` (default 0, must be positive when enabled). This memory is outside the JVM heap and does not change heap usage, so the heap should be shrunk if the total must fit a fixed limit.[^config] The `OFF_HEAP` storage level, marked experimental in the Spark docs, caches data in this memory.[^rddguide] Spark's task memory manager allocates the memory pages for sorting, hashing and shuffle either on the heap or, with this setting, off-heap; see [Project Tungsten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Tungsten).[^tmm]

## Memory outside the heap

On YARN and Kubernetes, the container for an executor is the sum of `spark.executor.memory`, `spark.executor.memoryOverhead`, `spark.memory.offHeap.size` and `spark.executor.pyspark.memory`.[^config] Overhead covers JVM overheads, interned strings and other native memory, and by default is 10% of executor memory with a minimum of 384 MiB. Python worker memory is part of the overhead unless `spark.executor.pyspark.memory` is set.[^config] See [Executor memory overhead](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor_memory_overhead).

## Example

```
spark.executor.memory              8g
spark.executor.cores               4
spark.memory.fraction              0.6
spark.memory.storageFraction       0.5
spark.memory.offHeap.enabled       true
spark.memory.offHeap.size          2g
```

With this configuration on YARN or Kubernetes, each executor container is sized at 8 GiB of heap plus about 819 MiB of overhead (10% of 8 GiB) plus 2 GiB of off-heap memory. The four tasks that run at once on the executor share one pool of execution memory.[^config]

# Spark on Kubernetes

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_Kubernetes

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Spark K8s, Kubernetes scheduler backend for Spark</Field>
  <Field name="field">Cluster management for distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Spark 2.3.0 (experimental); generally available in Spark 3.1.1</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Driver pod, executor pods, container image, service account, pod templates, volumes</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Kubernetes Operator for Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Kubernetes_Operator_for_Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[spark-submit](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark-submit), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Spark on YARN](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_YARN), [Spark standalone cluster manager](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_standalone_cluster_manager)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/running-on-kubernetes.md, docs/configuration.md, docs/job-scheduling.md), the Spark 2.3.0 and 3.1.1 release notes, SPARK-18278, SPARK-33005 and the Apache Spark Kubernetes Operator 1.1.0 release</Verified>

**Spark on Kubernetes** is the mode of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) in which Kubernetes is the cluster manager: the Spark driver and each [executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor) run as Kubernetes pods, and Spark asks the Kubernetes API server for executor pods directly through its native Kubernetes scheduler backend.[^k8s] Applications are submitted with [spark-submit](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark-submit) using a `k8s://` master URL, or declaratively through the [Kubernetes Operator for Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Kubernetes_Operator_for_Apache_Spark), a separate Apache Spark subproject that uses the same scheduler backend.[^k8s] Spark 4.3.0 documents Kubernetes 1.34 or newer as a prerequisite.[^k8s]

## How does Spark run on Kubernetes?

When an application is submitted in cluster mode, Spark creates the driver inside a Kubernetes pod. The driver then creates executor pods, connects to them and runs the application code. When the application finishes, the executor pods terminate and are cleaned up, while the driver pod stays in the "completed" state, keeping its logs, until it is garbage collected or deleted; a completed driver pod uses no compute or memory resources.[^k8s]

Kubernetes, not Spark, schedules the driver and executor pods onto nodes. Spark talks to the Kubernetes API through the fabric8 Kubernetes client, and node selectors can restrict pods to a subset of nodes.[^k8s] Spark launches executor pods in rounds; `spark.kubernetes.allocation.batch.size` (default 20) is the number of pods launched in each round.[^k8s]

The driver needs permission to manage its executors. The service account used by the driver pod must be allowed to create pods, services and configmaps, and it is set with `spark.kubernetes.authenticate.driver.serviceAccountName` (default `default`).[^k8s]

## How do you submit a PySpark application to Kubernetes?

The master URL has the form `k8s://<api_server_host>:<port>`; the port is required even when it is 443, and the scheme defaults to HTTPS.[^k8s] The application name is used to name the Kubernetes resources, so it must contain only lowercase alphanumeric characters, `-` and `.`.[^k8s] The image comes from `spark.kubernetes.container.image`; Spark ships Dockerfiles and `bin/docker-image-tool.sh` to build images (including a PySpark image), and the Apache Spark images on Docker Hub (`apache/spark`) can be used directly.[^k8s]

```bash
./bin/spark-submit \
  --master k8s://https://k8s-apiserver.example.com:6443 \
  --deploy-mode cluster \
  --name daily-orders \
  --conf spark.kubernetes.namespace=spark-jobs \
  --conf spark.kubernetes.authenticate.driver.serviceAccountName=spark \
  --conf spark.kubernetes.container.image=apache/spark:4.3.0-python3 \
  --conf spark.executor.instances=4 \
  local:///opt/app/daily_orders.py
```

The `local://` scheme points to a file already inside the image. Dependencies on the submitting machine (`file://` or a plain path) are uploaded to a Hadoop-compatible file system set by `spark.kubernetes.file.upload.path`, for example an S3 bucket, and downloaded by the driver pod.[^k8s] The namespace defaults to `default` when `spark.kubernetes.namespace` is not set.[^k8s]

In cluster mode, `spark-submit --status` and `spark-submit --kill` take a submission ID of the form `namespace:driver-pod-name`, and both accept glob patterns.[^k8s]

## What is the difference between cluster mode and client mode on Kubernetes?

In cluster mode the driver runs in a pod that Spark creates. Client mode, supported since Spark 2.4.0, lets the driver run in an existing pod or on a host outside the cluster.[^k8s] In client mode the executors must be able to reach the driver at a routable host name and port (`spark.driver.host`, `spark.driver.port`); for a driver in a pod, the documentation suggests a headless service.[^k8s]

In client mode inside a pod, setting `spark.kubernetes.driver.pod.name` to the driver pod's name makes Spark add an OwnerReference to each executor pod, so Kubernetes deletes the executors when the driver pod is deleted. Without it, executor pods can remain in the cluster if Spark's own deletion request fails.[^k8s]

## What are pod templates?

A pod template is a Kubernetes pod specification file that Spark uses as the starting point for the driver or executor pod, for settings that Spark configuration properties do not cover (for example security contexts or sidecar containers). The files are set with `spark.kubernetes.driver.podTemplateFile` and `spark.kubernetes.executor.podTemplateFile`.[^k8s]

Spark does not validate pod templates and leaves validation to the API server. Spark always overwrites some fields, such as the namespace and the driver's service account, so a template only gives Spark a non-empty pod to start from. When a template defines several containers, `spark.kubernetes.driver.podTemplateContainerName` and `spark.kubernetes.executor.podTemplateContainerName` choose the Spark container; otherwise the first container is used.[^k8s]

## How are volumes and local storage configured?

Spark on Kubernetes can mount four volume types into driver and executor pods: `hostPath`, `emptyDir`, `nfs` and `persistentVolumeClaim`. Volumes are declared with properties of the form `spark.kubernetes.[driver|executor].volumes.[VolumeType].[VolumeName].mount.path`, plus type-specific `options.*` properties.[^k8s] The documentation warns that `hostPath` volumes have known security risks and recommends the Pod Security Admission controller to limit them.[^k8s]

For executors, a claim name of `OnDemand` creates a persistent volume claim per executor, with `storageClass` and `sizeLimit` options. Since Spark 3.4 the driver can own these claims and reuse them for new executors (`spark.kubernetes.driver.ownPersistentVolumeClaim`, `spark.kubernetes.driver.reusePersistentVolumeClaim`, `spark.kubernetes.driver.waitToReusePersistentVolumeClaim`).[^k8s]

Volumes whose names start with `spark-local-dir-` are used as Spark local storage for shuffle and spill data. Without one, Spark uses an `emptyDir` volume, which does not outlive the pod; `spark.kubernetes.local.dirs.tmpfs=true` makes these volumes RAM-backed, which counts toward the pod's memory.[^k8s]

```properties
spark.kubernetes.executor.volumes.persistentVolumeClaim.spark-local-dir-1.options.claimName=OnDemand
spark.kubernetes.executor.volumes.persistentVolumeClaim.spark-local-dir-1.options.storageClass=gp
spark.kubernetes.executor.volumes.persistentVolumeClaim.spark-local-dir-1.options.sizeLimit=500Gi
spark.kubernetes.executor.volumes.persistentVolumeClaim.spark-local-dir-1.mount.path=/data
spark.kubernetes.executor.volumes.persistentVolumeClaim.spark-local-dir-1.mount.readOnly=false
```

## How does memory and dynamic allocation differ on Kubernetes?

Each executor pod requests its heap plus overhead memory. `spark.executor.memoryOverheadFactor` defaults to 0.10, except for Kubernetes non-JVM jobs (such as PySpark), where it defaults to 0.40 because non-JVM tasks need more memory outside the heap.[^config] CPU requests and limits for pods can be set separately with `spark.kubernetes.executor.request.cores` and `spark.kubernetes.executor.limit.cores`.[^k8s]

Dynamic allocation works on Kubernetes, but Spark on Kubernetes does not support the external shuffle service, so `spark.shuffle.service.enabled=true` cannot be used to keep shuffle files.[^jobsched] Shuffle tracking, decommissioning with shuffle block migration, or a shuffle storage plugin are used instead; see [Executor: dynamic allocation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor#dynamic-allocation). Spark 4.3.0 also ships a `KubernetesLocalDiskShuffleDataIO` plugin that recovers shuffle data from reused persistent volume claims.[^k8s]

## How does it relate to the Kubernetes Operator for Apache Spark?

<Hatnote>Main article: [Kubernetes Operator for Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Kubernetes_Operator_for_Apache_Spark)</Hatnote>

The Apache Spark Kubernetes Operator is a separate Apache Spark project that manages Spark workloads declaratively through custom resources: `SparkApplication` for applications and `SparkCluster` for [standalone](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_standalone_cluster_manager) clusters. The Spark documentation calls the two approaches complementary, because the operator runs applications on the same native Kubernetes scheduler backend that spark-submit uses.[^k8s] Its latest release is 1.1.0, published on 12 November 2026.[^n1]

## History

Spark 2.3.0 added the Kubernetes scheduler backend for native submission to Kubernetes (SPARK-18278) and marked it experimental.[^n2] Spark 3.1.1 declared Kubernetes support generally available (SPARK-33005).[^n3][^n4] Spark on Kubernetes is not deprecated in Spark 4.3.0.

## Spark on Kubernetes compared with other cluster managers

|  | Spark on Kubernetes | [Spark on YARN](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_YARN) | [Spark standalone](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_standalone_cluster_manager) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Driver and executors run in | Kubernetes pods[^k8s] | YARN containers[^yarn] | Processes on standalone workers[^standalone] |
| Master URL | `k8s://HOST:PORT` | `yarn` | `spark://HOST:PORT`[^submit] |
| External shuffle service | Not supported | Supported | Supported[^jobsched] |

# Spark on YARN

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_YARN

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Running Spark on Hadoop YARN</Field>
  <Field name="field">Cluster resource management</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">YARN ResourceManager, NodeManagers, containers, the Spark application master, queues</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) with Apache Hadoop YARN</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark standalone cluster manager](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_standalone_cluster_manager), [Spark on Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_Kubernetes), [spark-submit](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark-submit), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/running-on-yarn.md, docs/submitting-applications.md, docs/configuration.md, docs/job-scheduling.md, docs/cluster-overview.md, docs/core-migration-guide.md) and the Spark 0.6.0 release notes</Verified>

**Spark on YARN** is the deployment of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) applications on Apache Hadoop YARN (Yet Another Resource Negotiator), where the YARN ResourceManager grants containers on cluster nodes and Spark runs its application master, its driver (in cluster mode) and its [executors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor) inside those containers.[^yarn] It lets Spark share a Hadoop cluster with other YARN workloads under the same queues and Kerberos security.[^yarn] YARN is one of the three cluster managers supported in Spark 4.3.0, with the [standalone manager](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_standalone_cluster_manager) and [Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_Kubernetes).[^overview]

## Is Spark on YARN deprecated?

No. YARN support is not deprecated in Spark 4.3.0; the cluster mode overview lists Hadoop YARN as a supported cluster manager.[^overview] Individual YARN settings have been deprecated: since Spark 3.5, `spark.yarn.max.executor.failures` and `spark.yarn.executor.failuresValidityInterval` are replaced by `spark.executor.maxNumFailures` and `spark.executor.failuresValidityInterval`.[^coremig]

## History

Spark 0.6.0 added experimental support for running on YARN, then in a separate branch; the Spark documentation dates YARN support to that release.[^n1][^yarn]

## How does Spark run on YARN?

Every Spark application on YARN has an **application master** (AM), a process managed by YARN that requests executor containers from the ResourceManager; in cluster mode the driver also runs inside it. In YARN terminology, both executors and the AM run inside **containers**.[^yarn]

Spark does not take the ResourceManager address from `--master`. The master URL is simply `yarn`, and Spark reads the cluster location from the Hadoop configuration directory given by `HADOOP_CONF_DIR` or `YARN_CONF_DIR`; that configuration is also shipped to every container.[^yarn]

## What is the difference between client and cluster mode on YARN?

|  | Cluster mode | Client mode |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where the driver runs | Inside the YARN application master container | In the client process that ran `spark-submit` |
| Role of the AM | Runs the driver and requests executors | Only requests executors |
| Can the client exit? | Yes, after the application starts | No, the driver lives in it |
| AM sizing | `spark.driver.memory`, `spark.driver.cores` | `spark.yarn.am.memory` (default `512m`), `spark.yarn.am.cores` (default 1) |
| Local directories of the driver | YARN's `yarn.nodemanager.local-dirs` | `spark.local.dir` |

Source: Running Spark on YARN (Spark 4.3.0).[^yarn]

The Spark documentation runs interactive shells such as `spark-shell` in client mode, where the console stays attached to the driver. In cluster mode, local files that the driver needs must be shipped with `--jars`, `--files` or `--archives`, because the driver runs on another machine.[^yarn]

```bash
export HADOOP_CONF_DIR=/etc/hadoop/conf
./bin/spark-submit \
  --master yarn \
  --deploy-mode cluster \
  --queue analytics \
  --driver-memory 4g \
  --executor-memory 8g \
  --executor-cores 4 \
  --num-executors 20 \
  etl_job.py
```

## How do queues work?

YARN schedules applications into queues defined by the cluster's YARN scheduler configuration. A Spark application chooses its queue with `--queue` or `spark.yarn.queue`, which defaults to `default`.[^yarn] Whether YARN honors the number of cores requested when placing containers depends on which YARN scheduler is in use and how it is configured.[^yarn] `spark.yarn.tags` attaches YARN application tags that can be used to filter applications.[^yarn]

## How is container memory sized?

Each executor container on YARN holds the executor heap (`spark.executor.memory`) plus non-heap overhead (`spark.executor.memoryOverhead`), which defaults to the executor memory times `spark.executor.memoryOverheadFactor` with a minimum of `spark.executor.minMemoryOverhead`. The overhead covers JVM overheads, interned strings and other native memory, and includes PySpark worker memory unless `spark.executor.pyspark.memory` is set.[^config] In client mode the AM has its own overhead, `spark.yarn.am.memoryOverhead`, which defaults to 10% of the AM memory with a minimum of 384 MiB.[^yarn] The [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor) article covers the memory layout inside the heap.

On YARN, `spark.executor.cores` defaults to 1 and `spark.executor.instances` (`--num-executors`) to 2.[^config][^yarn]

## What still matters when running Spark on YARN?

- **Java version.** Spark 4.0.0 and later need at least Java 17, and Hadoop supports Java 17 from 3.5.0. On a YARN cluster with an older Hadoop, the Spark documentation says to configure a separate JDK for Spark by setting `JAVA_HOME` for the AM (`spark.yarn.appMasterEnv.JAVA_HOME`) and executors (`spark.executorEnv.JAVA_HOME`).[^yarn]
- **Spark JARs.** Unless `spark.yarn.archive` or `spark.yarn.jars` points to a prepared copy, Spark zips every JAR under `$SPARK_HOME/jars` and uploads it to the distributed cache for each application.[^yarn]
- **Hadoop classpath.** A Spark distribution built with Hadoop does not add YARN's classpath to the application by default (since Spark 3.1), to avoid dependency conflicts; `spark.yarn.populateHadoopClasspath=true` changes this.[^yarn][^coremig]
- **Dynamic allocation and shuffle files.** To remove executors without losing their shuffle files, Spark needs an external shuffle service, shuffle tracking, shuffle block migration on decommission, or a reliable shuffle storage plugin.[^jobsched] On YARN the external shuffle service runs inside each NodeManager as the auxiliary service `spark_shuffle`, implemented by `org.apache.spark.network.yarn.YarnShuffleService` from the `spark-<version>-yarn-shuffle.jar`.[^yarn]
- **Kerberos.** On YARN, Spark obtains delegation tokens for the default Hadoop file system and for the service that hosts the application's staging directory; an application can log in to the Kerberos KDC with `--principal` and `--keytab`.[^yarn][^ssargs]
- **Logs.** With YARN log aggregation (`yarn.log-aggregation-enable`), container logs are copied to HDFS after the application ends and can be read with `yarn logs -applicationId <app ID>`.[^yarn]
- **Retries.** `spark.yarn.maxAppAttempts` sets how many times YARN attempts the application, and must not exceed YARN's own `yarn.resourcemanager.am.max-attempts`.[^yarn]

# Spark plugin

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_plugin

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">SparkPlugin, driver plugin, executor plugin</Field>
  <Field name="field">Extension APIs</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">SparkPlugin, DriverPlugin, ExecutorPlugin, PluginContext (metrics, configuration, driver RPC), spark.plugins</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (since 3.0.0)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark listener](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_listener), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Native execution engine (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Native_execution_engine_(Spark)), [Apache Gluten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Gluten), [DataFusion Comet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DataFusion_Comet)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (SparkPlugin.java, DriverPlugin.java, ExecutorPlugin.java, PluginContext.java, config/package.scala, docs/monitoring.md), Spark JIRA SPARK-29397, the Apache Gluten v1.7.0 README, the Apache DataFusion Comet 1.2.0 README and source, and the spark-rapids v26.10.0 configuration docs</Verified>

A **Spark plugin** is a class implementing `org.apache.spark.api.plugin.SparkPlugin` that [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) loads into an application at startup, running one component inside the driver and one inside every [executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor). Plugins can initialize resources before tasks run, publish custom metrics through Spark's metrics system, react to task start and end on executors, and send messages from executors to the driver. The API was added in Spark 3.0.0 and is marked as a developer API.[^sparkplugin][^n1]

## How do you load a Spark plugin?

Plugins are loaded by listing their class names in `spark.plugins` (since 3.0.0). A second setting, `spark.plugins.defaultList`, is prepended to it, so that a platform can put its plugins in the default configuration file and users can still add more on the command line without overwriting them. Duplicate plugins are ignored.[^coreconf][^monitoring]

```bash
spark-submit \
  --jars my-plugin.jar \
  --conf spark.plugins=com.example.MyPlugin \
  app.py
```

The plugin jar must be on the classpath of both the driver and the executors, because Spark creates one instance in each.

## What are the parts of the plugin API?

A `SparkPlugin` returns two optional components. The driver component has a single instance per application, inside the driver; the executor component has one instance in each executor that Spark starts.[^sparkplugin]

**DriverPlugin** (since 3.0.0) has these methods:[^driver]
- `init(SparkContext, PluginContext)` runs early in driver startup, before the task scheduler is initialized, and blocks startup until it returns. The map it returns is passed to every executor plugin's `init`.
- `registerMetrics(appId, PluginContext)` runs later, once the application ID is known. Metrics added to the context's registry by then are published as a metrics source named after the plugin.
- `receive(Object)` handles messages sent from executor plugins.
- `shutdown()` runs when the driver stops.

**ExecutorPlugin** (since 3.0.0) has these methods:[^executor]
- `init(PluginContext, Map<String, String> extraConf)` runs during executor startup and blocks it. Executor metrics must be registered here; metrics registered later may not show up.
- `onTaskStart()`, `onTaskSucceeded()` and `onTaskFailed(TaskFailedReason)` (all since 3.1.0) run on the task's own thread. The documentation warns against expensive work here, such as calls to remote services, because they run for every task.
- `shutdown()` runs during executor shutdown and blocks it.

**PluginContext** gives both sides a Dropwizard `MetricRegistry`, the `SparkConf`, the executor ID, the host name and the resources assigned to the process. On executors, `send(Object)` sends a message to the driver plugin without waiting, and `ask(Object)` waits for a reply, up to `spark.rpc.askTimeout`.[^context]

## Example: counting failed tasks per executor

```scala
package com.example

import java.util.{Collections, Map => JMap}
import com.codahale.metrics.Counter
import org.apache.spark.TaskFailedReason
import org.apache.spark.api.plugin._

class TaskFailurePlugin extends SparkPlugin {
  override def driverPlugin(): DriverPlugin = null   // no driver-side component

  override def executorPlugin(): ExecutorPlugin = new ExecutorPlugin {
    private var failures: Counter = _

    override def init(ctx: PluginContext, extraConf: JMap[String, String]): Unit = {
      failures = ctx.metricRegistry().counter("failedTasks")
    }

    override def onTaskFailed(reason: TaskFailedReason): Unit = failures.inc()
  }
}
```

Loaded with `--conf spark.plugins=com.example.TaskFailurePlugin`, the counter appears in each executor's metrics under the `plugin.<Plugin Class Name>` namespace, alongside Spark's own executor metrics.[^monitoring]

## What is built on the Spark plugin API?

The plugin API is the entry point for several projects that replace or extend Spark's execution:
- **[Apache Gluten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Gluten)** offloads compute-intensive SQL processing to native engines such as Velox and ClickHouse while reusing Spark's control flow. It translates Spark physical plans into Substrait plans and is enabled with `spark.plugins=org.apache.gluten.GlutenPlugin`.[^n2] Gluten graduated from the Apache Incubator on 2026-02-18.[^n3]
- **[DataFusion Comet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DataFusion_Comet)** (Apache DataFusion Comet), which describes itself as an accelerator for Apache Spark that runs on commodity hardware, is enabled with `spark.plugins=org.apache.spark.CometPlugin`. Its `CometPlugin` class implements both a driver and an executor plugin.[^n4][^n5]
- **RAPIDS Accelerator for Apache Spark**, from NVIDIA, runs SQL operations on GPUs and is enabled with `spark.plugins=com.nvidia.spark.SQLPlugin`.[^n6]

## Spark plugin vs Spark listener

|  | Spark plugin | [Spark listener](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_listener) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Runs on | Driver and every executor[^sparkplugin] | Driver only, on the listener bus[^n7] |
| Timing | Synchronous; `init` blocks startup[^driver][^executor] | Asynchronous; events can be dropped if a queue is full |
| Can publish metrics | Yes, through the metrics system[^context] | No built-in metrics registry |
| Configured with | `spark.plugins`[^coreconf] | `spark.extraListeners`[^coreconf] |
| Typical use | Native or GPU execution engines, executor-side instrumentation | Lineage, auditing, job monitoring |

# Spark resource profiles

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_resource_profiles

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Stage-level scheduling, ResourceProfile, accelerator-aware scheduling</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 3.1 (stage-level scheduling); Apache Spark 3.0 (GPU and custom resource scheduling)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`ResourceProfile`, `ResourceProfileBuilder`, `ExecutorResourceRequests`, `TaskResourceRequests`, `RDD.withResources`</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [GPU acceleration in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GPU_acceleration_in_Spark), [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/configuration.md, docs/running-on-yarn.md, docs/running-on-kubernetes.md, docs/spark-standalone.md, python/pyspark/resource/, python/pyspark/core/rdd.py, python/pyspark/sql/dataframe.py), Apache JIRA SPARK-24615, SPARK-27495, SPARK-29150, SPARK-39853, SPARK-45495 and SPARK-46812, and the Spark 3.0.0, 3.1.1 and 4.0.0 release notes</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a **resource profile** (`ResourceProfile`) is a set of executor and task resource requirements, such as cores, memory and GPUs, that Spark applies to one stage of a job instead of to the whole application.[^conf] The feature is called **stage-level scheduling** and was added in Spark 3.1.[^r311] It builds on the accelerator-aware scheduling of Spark 3.0, which lets an application request GPUs and other custom resources for its [executors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor) and tasks.[^r300]

## What problem do resource profiles solve?

Without resource profiles, a Spark application asks for one kind of executor at startup and keeps it for every stage. The Spark documentation gives the case of an ETL stage that needs only CPUs followed by a machine learning stage that needs GPUs: with stage-level scheduling, the application can request GPU executors only when the ML stage runs, instead of holding idle GPUs during the ETL stage.[^conf]

## How does GPU scheduling work in Apache Spark?

Spark 3.0 added accelerator-aware scheduling under the SPARK-24615 proposal, part of Project Hydrogen.[^r300][^jira24615] A resource is identified by a name such as `gpu`, and Spark schedules its individual addresses (for example GPU indexes) to tasks. The cluster manager must support and be configured for the resource; the feature is not available in local mode.[^conf]

The Spark GPU settings, all added in Spark 3.0.0, are:[^conf]
- `spark.executor.resource.gpu.amount` (default 0): GPUs per executor.
- `spark.executor.resource.gpu.discoveryScript` (no default): a script the executor runs at startup; it prints a JSON object with the resource name and an array of addresses. It is required on YARN and Kubernetes.
- `spark.executor.resource.gpu.vendor` (no default): Kubernetes only; the device plugin vendor and domain, for example `nvidia.com` or `amd.com`.
- `spark.task.resource.gpu.amount` (default 1): GPUs per task. Fractional values up to 0.5 let several tasks share one GPU; 0.25 means four tasks per GPU.
- `spark.driver.resource.gpu.amount` and `spark.driver.resource.gpu.discoveryScript`: the same for the driver.

The Spark source tree ships a sample GPU discovery script, `examples/src/main/scripts/getGpusResources.sh`.[^script] Inside a task, `TaskContext.get().resources()` returns the addresses Spark assigned; Spark does not use the GPU itself, so the user code or the ML library must use those addresses.[^conf]

## How is a resource profile built?

A resource profile is built from two request objects. `ExecutorResourceRequests` sets executor cores, memory, memory overhead, PySpark memory, off-heap memory and custom resources; `TaskResourceRequests` sets the CPUs and custom resources each task needs. `ResourceProfileBuilder.require()` adds both, and `build` returns the `ResourceProfile`.[^pyreq][^pyprof] The same classes exist in Scala and Java in the `org.apache.spark.resource` package.[^conf]

`RDD.withResources(profile)` attaches a profile to an RDD, and the stage that computes that RDD uses it. The RDD API for stage-level scheduling was tracked as SPARK-29150 and released in Spark 3.1; the PySpark `withResources`, `ResourceProfile` and `ResourceProfileBuilder` APIs are marked "new in version 3.1.0" and "evolving".[^jira29150][^pyrdd][^pyprof]

## Example in PySpark

The example asks for executors with 4 cores, 8 GiB of memory and one GPU for one stage, and lets four tasks share each GPU. It assumes dynamic allocation and a GPU discovery script on the executor image.

```python
from pyspark.resource import (
    ExecutorResourceRequests,
    TaskResourceRequests,
    ResourceProfileBuilder,
)

ereqs = (ExecutorResourceRequests()
         .cores(4)
         .memory("8g")
         .resource("gpu", 1, "/opt/spark/examples/src/main/scripts/getGpusResources.sh"))
treqs = TaskResourceRequests().cpus(1).resource("gpu", 0.25)
gpu_profile = ResourceProfileBuilder().require(ereqs).require(treqs).build

rdd = spark.sparkContext.parallelize(range(1000), 8)
result = rdd.withResources(gpu_profile).mapPartitions(lambda it: [sum(it)]).collect()
```

In PySpark, `build` is a property, not a method.[^pyprof]

## Which cluster managers support stage-level scheduling?

In Spark 4.3, stage-level scheduling works on YARN, Kubernetes and Spark standalone.[^conf] Spark 3.1 shipped it with Kubernetes support listed as a separate item (SPARK-33288) under the SPARK-27495 umbrella.[^r311][^jira27495]

| Cluster manager | With dynamic allocation | Without dynamic allocation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| YARN | New executors per profile; each profile id becomes a YARN container priority[^yarn] | Task requirements only, on the startup executors[^yarn] |
| Kubernetes | New executors per profile; requires `spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled`[^k8s] | Task requirements only (SPARK-45495, Spark 3.5.1 and 4.0.0)[^k8s][^jira45495] |
| Standalone | New executors per profile; only executor memory, cores and custom resources take effect[^standalone] | Task requirements only (SPARK-39853, Spark 3.4.0)[^standalone][^jira39853] |

## Why does stage-level scheduling need dynamic allocation?

A profile that changes executor resources needs new executors, and Spark gets them through dynamic allocation. With dynamic allocation on, Spark acquires new executors for each profile, and a task runs only on an executor created with exactly its profile; unused executors time out under the normal dynamic allocation rules. With dynamic allocation off, tasks with different task requirements share the executors of the default profile (`DEFAULT_RESOURCE_PROFILE`).[^conf]

On Kubernetes, shuffle tracking keeps executors that hold shuffle data, so executors from an earlier profile may not time out. The Spark documentation warns that this can use more cluster resources and, if the cluster runs out, the application can hang; `spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.timeout` limits this at the cost of possible recomputation.[^k8s]

## What happens when two profiles meet in one stage?

By default Spark allows one profile per stage and throws an exception if RDDs with different profiles are combined into the same stage. Setting `spark.scheduler.resource.profileMergeConflicts` (default false, since 3.1.0) to true makes Spark merge them into a new profile that takes the maximum of each resource.[^conf]

## Can DataFrames use resource profiles?

The Spark 4.3 configuration guide still describes stage-level scheduling as available "only for the RDD API in Scala, Java, and Python".[^conf] One exception exists in PySpark: since Spark 4.0.0, `DataFrame.mapInPandas` and `DataFrame.mapInArrow` take an optional `profile` argument with a `ResourceProfile` (SPARK-46812).[^pydf][^jira46812][^r400] Other DataFrame and Spark SQL operators run with the application's default profile.

## What a resource profile is not

A Spark resource profile is not a Kubernetes pod resource request or a YARN container size, although Spark translates it into one. On YARN, Spark converts `gpu` and `fpga` to the built-in types `yarn.io/gpu` and `yarn.io/fpga`.[^yarn] On Kubernetes, resources from a pod template apply only to the default profile and are not copied into custom profiles.[^k8s] A resource profile also does not make Spark SQL operators run on a GPU; that is the role of plugins such as the RAPIDS Accelerator, described in [GPU acceleration in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GPU_acceleration_in_Spark).

# Spark SQL ANSI mode

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_SQL_ANSI_mode

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">ANSI SQL mode, ANSI dialect</Field>
  <Field name="field">SQL query engines</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`spark.sql.ansi.enabled`, `spark.sql.storeAssignmentPolicy`, runtime errors on overflow and invalid casts, `try_*` functions</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark error classes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_error_classes), [Spark 3 to Spark 4 migration](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_3_to_Spark_4_migration), [Spark SQL scripting](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_SQL_scripting)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/sql-ref-ansi-compliance.md, docs/sql-migration-guide.md, SQLConf.scala, error-conditions.json) and the Spark 4.0.0, 4.1.0 and 4.3.0 release notes</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), **ANSI mode** is the Spark SQL dialect, controlled by `spark.sql.ansi.enabled`, in which invalid operations such as integer overflow, division by zero and malformed casts raise runtime errors instead of returning null or a wrapped value, and type coercion follows rules aligned with the ANSI SQL standard.[^ansi] ANSI mode has been the default since Spark 4.0.[^migration] With ANSI mode off, Spark SQL uses a Hive-compatible dialect that returns null for many invalid operations.[^ansi] The change matters most when moving workloads from Spark 3 to Spark 4.

## What is ANSI mode in Spark SQL?

Spark SQL has two settings that bring it closer to the SQL standard. `spark.sql.ansi.enabled` switches the dialect: with it on, Spark throws runtime exceptions on invalid operations and uses type coercion rules based on a data type precedence list. `spark.sql.storeAssignmentPolicy` separately controls implicit casts when rows are inserted into a table. Both settings exist since Spark 3.0.0; in Spark 4.3.0 their defaults are `true` and `ANSI`.[^ansi]

The Spark documentation notes that some ANSI-mode behaviours do not come from the ANSI SQL standard itself but follow its style.[^ansi] ANSI mode is therefore a Spark dialect, not a certification of full standard compliance.

## Is ANSI mode on by default in Spark 4?

Yes. SPARK-44444, listed in the Spark 4.0.0 release notes, made ANSI mode the default.[^r400] The migration guide says that since Spark 4.0 `spark.sql.ansi.enabled` is on by default, and that the previous behaviour returns when either the configuration or the environment variable `SPARK_ANSI_SQL_MODE` is set to `false`.[^migration] In the v4.3.0 source the default is computed as true unless `SPARK_ANSI_SQL_MODE` equals `false`.[^sqlconf] The [Spark 3 to Spark 4 migration](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_3_to_Spark_4_migration) page covers the upgrade work around this change.

Spark 4.1.0 added two related changes: views now always persist the ANSI setting in force when they were created (SPARK-53348), and ANSI mode became the default for the pandas API on Spark (SPARK-53295).[^r410] Spark 4.3.0 made `ceil` and `floor` throw overflow errors in ANSI mode (SPARK-58052).[^r430]

## What does ANSI mode change?

### Arithmetic overflow

With ANSI mode on, Spark throws an arithmetic exception when a numeric or interval operation overflows. With it off, decimal overflow produces null and other numeric types wrap around as they do in Java or Scala, so `2147483647 + 1` returns `-2147483648`.[^ansi] In ANSI mode the same query fails with the error condition `ARITHMETIC_OVERFLOW`, whose SQLSTATE is `22003`; division by zero fails with `DIVIDE_BY_ZERO` (SQLSTATE `22012`).[^errjson]

### Casts

In ANSI mode an explicit `CAST` that cannot succeed raises an error: a string that does not parse as the target type, or a numeric value out of the target type's range. ANSI mode also forbids some conversions that the non-ANSI dialect allows: numeric to and from binary, date to and from boolean, timestamp to and from boolean, and date to numeric.[^ansi] `CAST('a' AS INT)` fails with `CAST_INVALID_INPUT` (SQLSTATE `22018`) and `CAST(2147483648L AS INT)` with `CAST_OVERFLOW` (SQLSTATE `22003`); with ANSI mode off both return a value (null and `-2147483648`).[^ansi][^errjson]

### Table inserts

Under the default `ANSI` store assignment policy, inserting a value of an incompatible type, such as a string into an `INT` column, fails at analysis time, and inserting an out-of-range number fails with `CAST_OVERFLOW_IN_TABLE_INSERT`. The `LEGACY` policy allows any valid cast, as Spark 2.x did, and the `STRICT` policy forbids any cast that could lose precision.[^ansi]

### Functions and operators

Several functions behave differently under ANSI mode. `element_at`, `elt` and the `array[index]` operator throw on an invalid index; `to_date`, `to_timestamp`, `unix_timestamp` and `make_date` throw when input cannot be parsed or the result is invalid.[^ansi]

### Keywords

ANSI mode does not by itself reserve SQL keywords. Spark uses the ANSI keyword parser, which forbids reserved keywords as identifiers, only when both `spark.sql.ansi.enabled` and `spark.sql.ansi.enforceReservedKeywords` are true, and the second defaults to false.[^ansi]

## Summary of ANSI and non-ANSI behaviour

| Expression | ANSI mode on (Spark 4 default) | ANSI mode off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `2147483647 + 1` | Error `ARITHMETIC_OVERFLOW` | `-2147483648` |
| `1 / 0` | Error `DIVIDE_BY_ZERO` | `NULL`[^n1] |
| `CAST('a' AS INT)` | Error `CAST_INVALID_INPUT` | `NULL` |
| `CAST(2147483648L AS INT)` | Error `CAST_OVERFLOW` | `-2147483648` |
| `CAST(DATE'2020-01-01' AS INT)` | Analysis error | `NULL` |

Sources: Spark ANSI compliance documentation and error condition list.[^ansi][^errjson]

## How to tolerate bad data in ANSI mode

Spark provides `try_*` variants that return `NULL` instead of raising an error. They include `try_cast`, `try_add`, `try_subtract`, `try_multiply`, `try_divide`, `try_mod`, `try_sum`, `try_avg`, `try_element_at`, `try_to_timestamp`, `try_to_date` and `try_parse_url`.[^ansi] Using these functions on the columns that may hold bad values keeps the rest of a query strict, which is narrower than turning ANSI mode off for a whole session.

```sql
-- Spark 4.3 default: spark.sql.ansi.enabled = true
SELECT CAST('a' AS INT);             -- fails with CAST_INVALID_INPUT
SELECT try_cast('a' AS INT);         -- NULL
SELECT try_add(2147483647, 1);       -- NULL
SELECT try_divide(10, 0);            -- NULL

-- Restore the Spark 3 behaviour for one session only
SET spark.sql.ansi.enabled = false;
SELECT CAST('a' AS INT);             -- NULL
```

# Spark SQL scripting

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_SQL_scripting

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">SQL Scripting, procedural SQL in Spark</Field>
  <Field name="field">SQL query engines</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Compound statement (`BEGIN ... END`), local variables, `IF`, `CASE`, `WHILE`, `REPEAT`, `LOOP`, `FOR`, `LEAVE`, `ITERATE`, condition handlers, cursors</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark error classes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_error_classes), [Spark SQL ANSI mode](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_SQL_ANSI_mode), [SQL pipe syntax](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SQL_pipe_syntax)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/sql-ref-scripting.md, docs/control-flow/\*.md, SqlBaseParser.g4, AstBuilder.scala, SQLConf.scala, classic SparkSession.scala), SPARK-48338, SPARK-54499 and the Spark 4.1.0 and 4.2.0 release notes</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), **SQL scripting** is the procedural extension of Spark SQL that runs a block of statements written between `BEGIN` and `END`, with local variables, loops, conditional logic and error handlers, as a single request. The Spark documentation describes the syntax as based on the SQL/PSM standard.[^doc] SQL scripting lets ETL and analysis logic that used to need Python or Scala driver code stay entirely in SQL; the umbrella ticket also names it as a step toward stored procedures and data warehouse migrations.[^jira48338]

## Is SQL scripting enabled by default?

Yes, since Spark 4.1.0. The Spark 4.1.0 release notes state that SQL Scripting is generally available (GA) and enabled by default (SPARK-54499).[^r410][^jira54499] The switch is `spark.sql.scripting.enabled`, a configuration added in Spark 4.0.0 whose default in Spark 4.3.0 is `true`. Its description in the 4.3.0 source still calls the feature "under development", a wording older than the GA decision.[^sqlconf]

Two parts of SQL scripting stay behind internal flags in Spark 4.3.0, both off by default. `CONTINUE` handlers need `spark.sql.scripting.continueHandlerEnabled` (added in 4.1.0), and cursors (`DECLARE CURSOR`, `OPEN`, `FETCH`, `CLOSE`) need `spark.sql.scripting.cursorEnabled` (added in 4.2.0). Without them the parser rejects these statements.[^sqlconf][^astbuilder] The release notes list `CONTINUE HANDLER` support under 4.1.0 (SPARK-53621) and cursor support under 4.2.0 (SPARK-54759).[^r410][^r420]

## What does Spark SQL scripting support?

Every SQL script is a compound statement: `BEGIN`, an optional declaration section, a body of statements separated by semicolons, and `END`.[^doc] The declaration section can declare local variables (with an optional `DEFAULT`), named conditions, cursors and condition handlers.[^compound]

The body of a Spark SQL script can contain:[^doc]
- control flow: `IF`, `CASE`, `WHILE`, `REPEAT`, `LOOP`, `FOR` loops over query results, and `LEAVE` and `ITERATE` to exit or continue a labelled loop;
- DDL such as `CREATE`, `ALTER` and `DROP`, and DML such as `INSERT`;
- queries, whose result sets are returned to the caller;
- `SET` for local and session variables, and `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE`;
- nested compound statements, each with its own scope for variables, cursors, conditions and handlers.

Compound statements are not atomic. The only supported mode is `NOT ATOMIC`: when a statement fails, earlier statements in the block are not rolled back.[^compound]

## How does error handling work in SQL scripts?

A condition handler catches errors raised inside its compound statement. A handler can name a Spark error condition such as `DIVIDE_BY_ZERO`, a user-declared condition, one or more SQLSTATE values, `SQLEXCEPTION` (any SQLSTATE except the `XX` and `02` classes) or `NOT FOUND` (the `02` class).[^doc] When several handlers apply, Spark uses the one in the innermost compound statement and, among those, the most specific: a named condition beats a SQLSTATE, which beats a generic handler.[^doc] The error names and SQLSTATEs are the ones described in [Spark error classes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_error_classes).

An `EXIT` handler runs its action and then leaves the compound statement that declared it. A `CONTINUE` handler runs its action and resumes with the statement after the one that failed.[^doc] A user-declared condition without an explicit SQLSTATE gets `45000`.[^compound]

## Example

The following script, adapted from the Spark compound statement reference, catches a division by zero with an `EXIT` handler. It runs with the Spark 4.3.0 defaults, because `EXIT` handlers do not need an extra flag.[^compound]

```sql
BEGIN
  DECLARE a INT DEFAULT 1;
  DECLARE b INT DEFAULT 5;
  DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR DIVIDE_BY_ZERO
    div0: BEGIN
      VALUES (15);
    END div0;
  SET a = 10;
  SET a = b / 0;      -- raises DIVIDE_BY_ZERO under ANSI mode
  VALUES (a);         -- not reached
END;
-- returns 15
```

A `FOR` loop iterates over the rows of a query:[^for]

```sql
BEGIN
  DECLARE total INT DEFAULT 0;
  sumOdd: FOR r AS SELECT num FROM range(1, 20) AS t(num) DO
    IF r.num > 10 THEN
      LEAVE sumOdd;
    ELSEIF r.num % 2 = 0 THEN
      ITERATE sumOdd;
    END IF;
    SET total = total + r.num;
  END FOR sumOdd;
  VALUES (total);     -- 25
END;
```

The Spark documentation notes that such loops can often be replaced by a single relational query, which is usually more efficient; here `SELECT sum(num) FROM range(1, 10) AS t(num) WHERE num % 2 = 1`.[^for]

## How to run a SQL script from PySpark or Scala

A script is passed as one string to `spark.sql()`; the parser returns a compound body instead of a single query, and the returned DataFrame holds the result set of the last query the script ran.[^e2e] Named parameter markers can be passed in, but positional parameters are rejected for SQL scripts, and a script cannot be run through `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE`.[^session] The documentation describes two ways to pass data in and out of a script: session variables and parameter markers.[^doc]

```python
df = spark.sql("""
BEGIN
  DECLARE n INT DEFAULT 0;
  SET n = :iterations;
  WHILE n > 0 DO
    SET n = n - 1;
  END WHILE;
  VALUES (n);
END
""", args={"iterations": 3})
df.show()   # one row: 0
```

[^for]: [FOR Statement (Spark 4.3.0)](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/control-flow/for-stmt.html). *Apache Software Foundation*. Retrieved 2026-11-23.

# Spark standalone cluster manager

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_standalone_cluster_manager

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) project)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">Spark 0.6.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">Spark 4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala</Field>
  <Field name="type">Cluster manager bundled with Apache Spark</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[Spark Standalone Mode](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/spark-standalone.html)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark (core/.../deploy)](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/v4.3.0/core/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/deploy)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark on YARN](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_YARN), [Spark on Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_Kubernetes), [spark-submit](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark-submit)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/spark-standalone.md, docs/cluster-overview.md, docs/submitting-applications.md, docs/core-migration-guide.md, docs/job-scheduling.md) and the Spark 0.6.0 release notes</Verified>

The **Spark standalone cluster manager** is the cluster manager that ships with [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark): a master process and one worker process per node, started with scripts in Spark's `sbin` directory, that allocate executors to Spark applications without an external resource manager such as YARN or Kubernetes.[^standalone][^overview] It needs only a Spark distribution on each node, and it offers high availability through standby masters coordinated by Apache ZooKeeper.[^standalone] The standalone cluster manager is one of the three cluster managers that Spark 4.3.0 supports, with [Hadoop YARN](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_YARN) and [Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_Kubernetes).[^overview]

## Is the standalone cluster manager deprecated?

No. The standalone cluster manager is not deprecated in Spark 4.3.0. The Spark 4.3.0 cluster mode overview lists it as a supported cluster manager, and recent releases still change it: Spark 4.1 turned on the master's REST API by default, and Spark 4.3 changed which environment variables are forwarded to a driver submitted in cluster mode.[^overview][^coremig] Only individual settings have been deprecated, such as `SPARK_WORKER_INSTANCES`; the migration guide recommends one worker per node with several executors instead.[^coremig]

## History

Spark 0.6.0 added the standalone deploy mode, so that a cluster could be launched with only Java and Spark installed on each machine. At that time Spark otherwise ran on Apache Mesos.[^n1] Mesos support was later removed from Spark; see [Apache Mesos support in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Mesos_support_in_Spark).

## How does a standalone cluster work?

A standalone cluster has one active **master** and any number of **workers**. The master tracks the workers and their free cores and memory, and launches executors on them for each application. Its web UI is on port 8080 by default, and it accepts applications at a `spark://HOST:PORT` URL, port 7077 by default. Each worker has its own web UI on port 8081.[^standalone]

The cluster is started either by hand (`sbin/start-master.sh`, then `sbin/start-worker.sh spark://HOST:7077` on each node) or with launch scripts that read a `conf/workers` file of host names and reach each host over SSH. `sbin/start-all.sh` starts the master and all workers; `sbin/start-connect-server.sh` starts a [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) server on the local machine.[^standalone] The daemons can also all run on one machine for testing.[^standalone]

Executor placement depends on `spark.executor.cores`. When it is set, the master can start several executors of one application on the same worker if the worker has enough cores and memory. When it is not set, each executor takes all available cores on its worker, so one application gets at most one executor per worker in each scheduling round.[^standalone] `--total-executor-cores` caps the total cores an application takes.[^standalone]

## How are applications submitted?

Applications are submitted with [spark-submit](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark-submit) and `--master spark://HOST:7077`. In `client` mode the driver runs in the submitting process; in `cluster` mode the master launches the driver on one of the workers and the client exits once submission is done.[^standalone] The Spark 4.3.0 documentation states that standalone cluster mode is not supported for Python applications, so PySpark jobs on a standalone cluster run in client mode.[^submit]

```bash
# Start a one-node cluster and run a PySpark job on it (client mode)
./sbin/start-master.sh
./sbin/start-worker.sh spark://$(hostname):7077
./bin/spark-submit \
  --master spark://$(hostname):7077 \
  --total-executor-cores 4 \
  --executor-memory 2g \
  examples/src/main/python/pi.py 100
```

In cluster mode, `--supervise` makes the master restart the driver if it exits with a non-zero code.[^standalone] The master also has a REST API for submitting, querying and killing drivers on `spark.master.rest.port` (default 6066). Since Spark 4.1 the master starts this REST API by default; `spark.master.rest.enabled=false` restores the earlier behavior.[^standalone][^coremig]

## How does high availability work?

By default the standalone master is a single point of failure for scheduling: `spark.deploy.recoveryMode` is `NONE`.[^standalone] Spark 4.3.0 offers these recovery modes:[^standalone]

| `spark.deploy.recoveryMode` | How it works | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ZOOKEEPER` | Several masters connect to the same ZooKeeper ensemble (`spark.deploy.zookeeper.url`, `spark.deploy.zookeeper.dir`). One is elected leader; if it dies, a standby is elected and recovers the state. | Production high availability |
| `FILESYSTEM` | The master writes application and worker registrations to `spark.deploy.recoveryDirectory` and recovers them when it restarts. | Single-node recovery after a restart |
| `ROCKSDB` | Like `FILESYSTEM`, but the state is kept in RocksDB. | Single-node recovery |
| `CUSTOM` | A class given in `spark.deploy.recoveryMode.factory` provides the persistence. | Custom stores |

With ZooKeeper, failover from the time the leader goes down takes between one and two minutes according to the Spark documentation, and it affects only the scheduling of new applications; applications already running continue.[^standalone] Applications and workers list every master in the URL, for example `spark://host1:7077,host2:7077`, so that they can find the current leader at registration.[^submit] If several masters run without a correct ZooKeeper configuration, each one considers itself the leader and they schedule independently.[^standalone]

## When is the standalone cluster manager used today?

The Spark documentation describes the standalone manager as a simple cluster manager included with Spark that makes it easy to set up a cluster.[^overview] It fits cases where Spark is the only workload on a set of machines and no YARN or Kubernetes cluster is available, single-machine test clusters, and hosting a [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) server started with the bundled launch scripts.[^standalone] The standalone manager supports dynamic allocation, and workers started with `spark.shuffle.service.enabled=true` run the external shuffle service. Because an executor takes all of a worker's cores when `spark.executor.cores` is not set, the Spark documentation recommends setting it explicitly when dynamic allocation is on.[^jobsched]

Security is off by default. The Spark documentation warns that a standalone cluster open to an untrusted network must have authentication configured, and notes that the standalone manager lacks the fine-grained access control of other resource managers.[^standalone]

## Standalone compared with YARN and Kubernetes

|  | Spark standalone | [Spark on YARN](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_YARN) | [Spark on Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_Kubernetes) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Master URL | `spark://HOST:7077` | `yarn` (address from the Hadoop configuration) | `k8s://HOST:PORT` |
| Resource manager | Spark master and workers | YARN ResourceManager and NodeManagers | Kubernetes API server; driver and executors run in pods |
| Default `spark.executor.cores` | All available cores on the worker | 1 | 1 |

Sources: the Spark 4.3.0 standalone, YARN, Kubernetes and submission guides.[^standalone][^k8s][^yarn][^submit][^ssargs][^config]
