# Spark Streaming (DStreams)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Streaming_(DStreams)

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Spark Streaming, DStream API, discretized streams</Field>
  <Field name="field">Stream processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 0.7.0 (alpha)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`StreamingContext`, DStream, receivers, batch interval, checkpointing</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (`streaming` module)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (streaming module source, PySpark StreamingContext, streaming programming guide), the Spark 0.7.0 and 3.4.0 release notes and SPARK-42075</Verified>

<Status level="deprecated" since="Apache Spark 3.4.0">Use [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) instead. Still included in Spark 4.3.0; the documentation calls it a legacy project that receives no further updates.[^jira][^r340]</Status>

**Spark Streaming**, also called the **DStream API**, is the original stream processing library of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), in which a live data stream is divided into small batches and represented as a **discretized stream** (DStream): a continuous series of RDDs, each holding the data received in one time interval.[^guide] The API has been deprecated since Spark 3.4.0. Spark's documentation calls it the previous generation of Spark's streaming engine and directs all new streaming applications to [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming).[^guide][^jira]

## Status

The DStream API was deprecated in Apache Spark 3.4.0 under SPARK-42075, "Deprecate DStream API", and the 3.4.0 release notes list the deprecation.[^jira][^r340] At the v4.3.0 tag the deprecation is still in place:

- The Scala `StreamingContext` and the Java `JavaStreamingContext` carry `@deprecated("DStream is deprecated. Migrate to Structured Streaming.", "Spark 3.4.0")`.[^scala]
- The PySpark `StreamingContext` constructor issues a `FutureWarning`: "DStream is deprecated as of Spark 3.4.0. Migrate to Structured Streaming." Its docstring adds that there are no longer updates to DStream and that it is a legacy project.[^py]
- The Spark 4.3.0 programming guide opens with a note that Spark Streaming "is the previous generation of Spark's streaming engine", that "there are no longer updates to Spark Streaming and it's a legacy project", and that users should use Structured Streaming.[^guide]

The API has not been removed. The `streaming` module and its programming guide are still part of Spark 4.3.0, and the guide still documents the Kafka and Kinesis integrations.[^guide] No Spark release up to 4.3.0 announces a removal date.

## Programming model

A Spark Streaming application creates a `StreamingContext` with a **batch interval**, such as one second. **Input DStreams** receive data from a source; every input DStream except file streams is associated with a **receiver**, which receives the data and stores it in Spark's memory for processing. Basic sources include sockets and file systems, and advanced sources such as Kafka and Kinesis come from separate artifacts (`spark-streaming-kafka-0-10` and `spark-streaming-kinesis-asl`).[^guide]

Each operation on a DStream becomes an operation on the RDDs underneath it. The API offers RDD-style transformations (`map`, `flatMap`, `reduceByKey`), window operations such as `reduceByKeyAndWindow`, stateful `updateStateByKey`, `transform` for arbitrary RDD-to-RDD functions, and output operations such as `foreachRDD`. Stateful transformations, such as `updateStateByKey` or `reduceByKeyAndWindow` with an inverse function, require a checkpoint directory.[^guide] The window length and sliding interval of a window operation must be multiples of the batch interval.[^guide]

The following PySpark example, adapted from the programming guide, counts words in one-second batches from a socket. On Spark 4.3 it runs but prints the deprecation warning.[^guide][^py]

```python
from pyspark import SparkContext
from pyspark.streaming import StreamingContext

sc = SparkContext("local[2]", "NetworkWordCount")
ssc = StreamingContext(sc, 1)  # 1-second batches; emits a FutureWarning

lines = ssc.socketTextStream("localhost", 9999)
counts = (lines.flatMap(lambda line: line.split(" "))
               .map(lambda word: (word, 1))
               .reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b))
counts.pprint()

ssc.start()
ssc.awaitTermination()
```

DStreams are built on RDDs and the `SparkContext`, which the Spark Connect documentation lists as unsupported, so DStream applications cannot run through a [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) client.[^connect]

## History

Spark Streaming first appeared as an alpha in Spark 0.7.0, which described it as an extension adding near-real-time processing, with transformations such as `map`, `filter`, `reduce` and sliding windows.[^n1] Structured Streaming, built on the Spark SQL engine, arrived as an experimental API in Spark 2.0.0.[^n2] The Spark 4.3 documentation recommends it for all new streaming applications and pipelines.[^guide]

## Migration to Structured Streaming

<Hatnote>Main article: [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming)</Hatnote>

There is no automatic converter. Migration means rewriting the job against the DataFrame API. The table maps DStream concepts to their usual Structured Streaming counterparts in Spark 4.3.[^guide][^ssapis]

| DStream API | Structured Streaming |
| --- | --- |
| `StreamingContext` with a batch interval | `SparkSession`; `spark.readStream` to read, `writeStream` with a processing-time trigger to set the micro-batch interval |
| DStream (series of RDDs) | Streaming DataFrame or Dataset (an unbounded table) |
| RDD transformations (`map`, `reduceByKey`) | DataFrame operations (`select`, `groupBy`, `agg`) or SQL |
| `window`, `reduceByKeyAndWindow` (multiples of the batch interval) | `groupBy(window(...))` on an event-time column, with a [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) for late data |
| `updateStateByKey`, `mapWithState` (Scala and Java)[^n3] | Built-in stateful aggregations, or `transformWithState` (Spark 4.0 and later) for arbitrary state[^tws] |
| `foreachRDD` | `foreachBatch` or a built-in sink |
| `ssc.checkpoint(dir)` | `checkpointLocation` option on each query |
| `spark-streaming-kafka-0-10` | Kafka source and sink in `spark-sql-kafka-0-10`[^n4] |

The word count above becomes the following query, taken from the Structured Streaming quick example.[^ssstart] One semantic difference matters: the DStream version prints counts for each batch, while this query keeps a running count over all data received, because the result table is cumulative and is written in complete mode.

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import explode, split

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("StructuredNetworkWordCount").getOrCreate()

lines = (spark.readStream.format("socket")
         .option("host", "localhost").option("port", 9999).load())
words = lines.select(explode(split(lines.value, " ")).alias("word"))
counts = words.groupBy("word").count()

query = counts.writeStream.outputMode("complete").format("console").start()
query.awaitTermination()
```

Unlike DStreams, Structured Streaming queries run on the optimized Spark SQL engine and provide end-to-end [exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics) through checkpointing and write-ahead logs.[^ssindex] Most of the Structured Streaming API, including `DataStreamReader`, `DataStreamWriter` and `StreamingQuery`, is supported in [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect).[^connect]

# Spark Thrift Server

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Thrift_Server

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) project)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">Spark 1.1.0 (as the Spark SQL JDBC/ODBC server)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">Spark 4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala, Java</Field>
  <Field name="type">JDBC/ODBC server for Spark SQL (HiveServer2 protocol)</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[Distributed SQL Engine](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/sql-distributed-sql-engine.html)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark (sql/hive-thriftserver)](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/v4.3.0/sql/hive-thriftserver)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive), [Hive Metastore](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_Metastore)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/sql-distributed-sql-engine.md, docs/sql-migration-guide.md, sbin/start-thriftserver.sh, SQLConf.scala, sql/connect/client/jdbc), the Spark 1.1.0, 4.1.0 and 4.3.0 release notes, SPARK-53484 and the Databricks Connect and Databricks JDBC Driver documentation</Verified>

The **Spark Thrift Server** is the JDBC/ODBC server of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) SQL: a long-running Spark application that implements the HiveServer2 Thrift protocol, so that BI tools, SQL clients and the `beeline` shell can run SQL on Spark over standard JDBC or ODBC connections without writing Spark code.[^dse] Each client connection gets its own session on a shared Spark application.[^sqlmig] Since Spark 4.1, [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) also offers a JDBC driver, which gives JDBC clients a second way to reach Spark.[^r410]

## Is the Spark Thrift Server deprecated?

No. The Spark Thrift Server is not deprecated in Spark 4.3.0. It is documented in the Spark 4.3.0 SQL guide, and the Spark 4.3.0 release notes include changes to it, such as making its JDBC metadata operations aware of DataSource V2 catalogs (SPARK-57518, opt-in with `spark.sql.thriftServer.catalogMetadata.enabled`) and disallowing JVM system properties in its sessions (SPARK-57441).[^dse][^r430]

## History

Spark 1.1.0 introduced a JDBC/ODBC server for Spark SQL that let many applications connect to Spark SQL and share cached tables.[^n1] Spark 1.6 made the server multi-session by default.[^sqlmig]

## How does the Spark Thrift Server work?

The Spark Thrift Server corresponds to HiveServer2 in [Apache Hive](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hive), and clients connect to it with Hive JDBC URLs of the form `jdbc:hive2://host:port`.[^dse] The server is a Spark application: `sbin/start-thriftserver.sh` submits the class `org.apache.spark.sql.hive.thriftserver.HiveThriftServer2` with the application name "Thrift JDBC/ODBC Server", and it accepts every [spark-submit](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark-submit) option plus `--hiveconf` for Hive properties.[^dse][^n2] Queries therefore run on the server's own executors, on whatever cluster manager it was started on.

By default the server listens on `localhost:10000`. The port and host can be changed with the environment variables `HIVE_SERVER2_THRIFT_PORT` and `HIVE_SERVER2_THRIFT_BIND_HOST` or the properties `hive.server2.thrift.port` and `hive.server2.thrift.bind.host`.[^dse] Hive configuration comes from `hive-site.xml`, `core-site.xml` and `hdfs-site.xml` in Spark's `conf/` directory.[^dse]

```bash
# Start the server on YARN, then connect with beeline
./sbin/start-thriftserver.sh \
  --master yarn \
  --conf spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=64 \
  --hiveconf hive.server2.thrift.port=10000

./bin/beeline -u jdbc:hive2://localhost:10000
```

```sql
-- Inside beeline: plain Spark SQL
SHOW TABLES;
SET spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=200;   -- affects this session only
SELECT count(*) FROM sales WHERE region = 'EMEA';
```

The server can also carry Thrift RPC over HTTP. Setting `hive.server2.transport.mode=http` enables it, by default on port 10001 (`hive.server2.thrift.http.port`) at endpoint `cliservice` (`hive.server2.http.endpoint`); clients add `transportMode=http;httpPath=cliservice` to the JDBC URL.[^dse] `sbin/stop-thriftserver.sh` stops the server.[^dse]

## How do sessions work?

Since Spark 1.6 the Spark Thrift Server runs in multi-session mode: each JDBC/ODBC connection has its own copy of the SQL configuration and its own temporary function registry, while cached tables are shared by all connections. Setting `spark.sql.hive.thriftServer.singleSession=true` restores the older single-session mode.[^sqlmig] Because all sessions share one Spark application, they share its executors and its Spark core configuration; a `SET` in one session changes only runtime SQL configurations for that session (see [Spark configuration precedence](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_configuration_precedence)).

Several behaviors changed in recent releases:[^sqlmig]
- Since Spark 3.5, cancelling a running statement interrupts its tasks; `spark.sql.thriftServer.interruptOnCancel=false` restores the old behavior.
- Since Spark 4.1, `GetColumns` returns a 1-based `ORDINAL_POSITION` instead of the previous 0-based value.
- Since Spark 4.3, sessions cannot set JVM system properties through the `set:system:` configuration overlay, for example in a JDBC connection string; `spark.sql.legacy.hive.thriftServer.allowSettingSystemProperties=true` restores the old behavior.

## Spark Thrift Server vs Spark Connect

[Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) is a gRPC protocol through which a thin client sends unresolved DataFrame plans to a Spark server.[^connect] Spark 4.1.0 added a JDBC driver for Spark Connect (SPARK-53484), and Spark 4.3.0 extended it, for example with support for `ARRAY`, `MAP` and `STRUCT` results (SPARK-57380).[^r410][^r430][^n3] The driver accepts URLs that start with `jdbc:sc://`.[^n4]

|  | Spark Connect | Spark Thrift Server |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Protocol | gRPC with Protocol Buffers; results as Apache Arrow batches | HiveServer2 Thrift (binary or HTTP) |
| Clients | PySpark, Scala and other Spark Connect clients (DataFrame API and SQL); JDBC driver since Spark 4.1.0 | Any HiveServer2-compatible JDBC/ODBC client, such as `beeline` |
| JDBC URL | `jdbc:sc://host:port` | `jdbc:hive2://host:port` |
| Default port | 15002 | 10000 (binary), 10001 (HTTP) |
| Start script | `sbin/start-connect-server.sh` | `sbin/start-thriftserver.sh` |
| Session isolation | One session per client; no access to static configuration or the `SparkContext` | One session per connection with its own SQL configuration and temporary functions; shared cache |

Sources: the Spark 4.3.0 Spark Connect and distributed SQL engine guides, the standalone guide, the SQL migration guide and the Spark Connect JDBC driver source.[^connect][^dse][^sqlmig][^n5]

The two servers address different clients: the Thrift Server serves tools built for HiveServer2, while Spark Connect also serves DataFrame programs written against the Spark client libraries. On Databricks, Databricks Connect is an extension of Spark Connect for Databricks Runtime 13.3 LTS and above.[^n6] For SQL tools, Databricks publishes the Databricks JDBC Driver under the Apache 2.0 license; it can run queries either through the Statement Execution API or over Thrift.[^n7]

Outside the Spark project, Apache Kyuubi describes itself as a multi-tenant Thrift JDBC/ODBC server and a distributed, multi-tenant gateway that provides serverless SQL on lakehouses.[^n8]

# Spark UI

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_UI

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Spark web UI, application UI, port 4040</Field>
  <Field name="field">Monitoring and debugging</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Jobs, Stages, Storage, Environment, Executors and SQL tabs; Structured Streaming tab; REST API at /api/v1</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark History Server](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_History_Server), [Spark event log](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_event_log), [Spark listener](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_listener), [Job, stage and task](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Job,_stage_and_task), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/web-ui.md, docs/monitoring.md, docs/configuration.md, config/UI.scala, config/Status.scala)</Verified>

The **Spark UI** is the web interface that the driver of an [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) application serves while the application runs, by default at `http://<driver-host>:4040`, to show the application's jobs, stages, tasks, cached data, configuration, executors and SQL queries. It runs when `spark.ui.enabled` is true, which is the default.[^uiconf][^webui] The UI exists only while the application runs; for finished applications, the [Spark History Server](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_History_Server) rebuilds the same pages from the [Spark event log](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_event_log).

## How do you open the Spark UI?

The UI is on by default (`spark.ui.enabled`, default true) and listens on `spark.ui.port` (default 4040).[^uiconf] When the port is taken, for example by another application on the same host, Spark tries 4041, 4042 and so on, and logs the chosen port at startup.[^webui] The same data is available as JSON from the REST API at `http://localhost:4040/api/v1` for a running application.[^monitoring]

## Jobs tab

The Jobs tab lists every job of the application with its status, duration and progress, and shows an event timeline of executors being added and removed alongside the jobs.[^webui] A job is the work that one action, such as `count()` or `write`, triggers (see [Job, stage and task](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Job,_stage_and_task)).

The job detail page shows the job's stages grouped by status, a DAG visualization, and per-stage **Input** (bytes read from storage), **Output** (bytes written), **Shuffle read** and **Shuffle write**. It also links to the SQL query that created the job.[^webui]

**What to look for:** a job that is much slower than its neighbours, failed jobs, and long gaps in the timeline where no executors were available.

## Stages tab

The Stages tab lists all stages by status: active, pending, completed, skipped and failed. Only failed stages show a failure reason, and an active stage can be cancelled with its **(kill)** link, which `spark.ui.killEnabled` (default true) allows.[^webui][^uiconf]

The stage detail page is where most performance problems show up. It gives summary statistics (minimum, percentiles, maximum) over all tasks for these metrics:[^webui]
- **Duration** and **GC time**. A maximum far above the median means data skew or a straggler.
- **Scheduler delay** and **task deserialization time**, which are large when tasks are tiny or closures are big.
- **Shuffle Read Size / Records**, **Shuffle Read Fetch Wait Time** and **Shuffle Remote Reads**, which show how much the stage depends on the network.
- **Shuffle spill (memory)** and **Shuffle spill (disk)**. Any spill means execution memory ran out for this stage (see [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle)).
- **Peak execution memory** used by shuffles, aggregations and joins.

The page also aggregates the metrics by executor, lists named accumulators, and has a task table with links to each task's executor logs.[^webui]

## Storage tab

The Storage tab lists the RDDs and DataFrames that the application has persisted, with their storage level, size in memory and on disk, and number of cached partitions. The detail page shows which executors hold each partition.[^webui]

**What to look for:** a cached DataFrame with fewer cached partitions than total partitions, which means part of it was evicted or never computed.

## Environment tab

The Environment tab shows the configuration the application is actually running with, in sub-tabs: **Runtime Information** (JVM and Scala versions), **Spark Properties**, **Resource Profiles**, **Hadoop Properties**, **System Properties**, **Metrics Properties** and **Classpath Entries**. Properties set as `spark.hadoop.*` appear under Spark Properties, not Hadoop Properties.[^webui]

**What to look for:** whether a setting passed at submit time was applied, and which jar versions are on the classpath when there is a class conflict.

## Executors tab

The Executors tab lists every executor, including the driver, with its memory, disk, cores, storage memory used for cached data, task counts, shuffle totals and GC time. Each row has **Thread Dump**, **Heap Histogram** and **Flame Graph** links that open live data for that executor, and **stderr** and **stdout** links to its logs.[^webui]

**What to look for:** executors with high GC time, a few executors that ran most of the tasks, and executors that were lost (see [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor)).

## SQL tab

The SQL tab, sometimes called the SQL / DataFrame tab, lists every SQL query and every DataFrame action that triggered execution, not only queries written as SQL strings.[^webui] Each query has a graph of its physical operators with their metrics, and a detail page with the parsed, analyzed and optimized logical plans and the physical plan.

The operator metrics are the most direct view of what a query did. Examples include `number of output rows` on filters and joins, `data size` on exchanges, `shuffle bytes written` on a shuffle exchange, `spill size` on sorts and hash aggregates, and the file and partition counts on scans.[^webui]

**What to look for:** an unexpected `Exchange`, a scan that read many more files or partitions than the filter should allow (see [Partition pruning](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition_pruning)), and a join whose output row count is far larger than its inputs.

## Other tabs

- **Structured Streaming** appears when micro-batch streaming queries run. It shows input rate, process rate, batch duration, operation durations, watermark gap and state store metrics for each query.[^webui]
- **Streaming (DStreams)** appears for applications that use the legacy [DStream API](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Streaming_(DStreams)).[^webui]
- **JDBC/ODBC Server** appears when Spark runs as a distributed SQL engine through the Thrift server.[^webui]

## How much history does the Spark UI keep?

The live UI keeps a bounded amount of history in driver memory. By default it remembers 1000 jobs (`spark.ui.retainedJobs`), 1000 stages (`spark.ui.retainedStages`), 100000 tasks per stage (`spark.ui.retainedTasks`) and 1000 finished SQL executions (`spark.sql.ui.retainedExecutions`).[^statusconf][^n1] Older entries are garbage collected, so a long-running application loses its early history from the live UI.

To see an application after it ends, set `spark.eventLog.enabled` to true before starting it, and read the logs with the [Spark History Server](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_History_Server).[^monitoring]

- [Spark listener](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_listener)
- [Job, stage and task](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Job,_stage_and_task)
- [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor)

# spark-submit

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark-submit

<Infobox type="software" name="spark-submit">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) project)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">Spark 1.0.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">Spark 4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Shell script, Scala</Field>
  <Field name="type">Application launcher for Apache Spark</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[Submitting Applications](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/submitting-applications.html)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark (core/.../deploy/SparkSubmit.scala)](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/v4.3.0/core/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/deploy/SparkSubmit.scala)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark configuration precedence](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_configuration_precedence), [Spark on YARN](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_YARN), [Spark on Kubernetes](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_on_Kubernetes), [Spark standalone cluster manager](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_standalone_cluster_manager)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/submitting-applications.md, docs/configuration.md, docs/spark-standalone.md, docs/running-on-yarn.md, SparkSubmitArguments.scala and JavaUtils.java), SPARK-48392 and the Spark 1.0.0 release notes</Verified>

**spark-submit** is the command-line script in the `bin` directory of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) that launches a packaged Spark application (a JAR, a Python file or an R file) on a local machine or on any supported cluster manager through one interface.[^submit] It sets up the classpath with Spark and its dependencies, chooses where the driver runs, ships the application's files to the cluster and passes configuration to the application.[^submit] The `spark-shell`, `pyspark` and `spark-sql` shells and the [Spark Thrift Server](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Thrift_Server) start script accept the same options.[^submit][^thrift]

`spark-submit` was introduced in Spark 1.0.0, whose release notes describe it as a new tool for submitting an application to any Spark cluster, including local, [Mesos](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Mesos_support_in_Spark) and YARN clusters, through a common process.[^r100]

## How is spark-submit used?

The general form is `spark-submit [options] <app jar | python file | R file> [app arguments]`.[^ssargs] For a Python application, the `.py` file takes the place of the JAR, and extra `.py`, `.zip` or `.egg` files go on the Python path with `--py-files`.[^submit]

```bash
# A PySpark job on YARN, driver inside the cluster
./bin/spark-submit \
  --master yarn \
  --deploy-mode cluster \
  --name nightly-etl \
  --executor-memory 4g \
  --num-executors 10 \
  --py-files libs.zip \
  --conf spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=400 \
  etl_job.py --date 2026-11-23
```

Everything after the application file is passed to the application as its own arguments, so Spark options must come before it.[^submit]

## What are the main arguments?

The following options are listed by `spark-submit --help` in Spark 4.3.0.[^ssargs]

| Option | Meaning | Default or scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--master` | Master URL: `local[*]`, `spark://host:port`, `yarn` or `k8s://https://host:port` | `local[*]` |
| `--deploy-mode` | Run the driver in the submitting process (`client`) or on a cluster node (`cluster`) | `client` |
| `--class` | Main class of a Java or Scala application | Java/Scala only |
| `--name` | Application name |  |
| `--conf`, `-c` | Any Spark property as `key=value`; repeat the flag for each property |  |
| `--properties-file`, `--load-spark-defaults` | Load properties from a file; also load `spark-defaults.conf` | see [Spark configuration precedence](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_configuration_precedence) |
| `--jars`, `--packages`, `--repositories`, `--exclude-packages` | JARs, or Maven coordinates resolved with transitive dependencies, for the driver and executor classpaths |  |
| `--py-files`, `--files`, `--archives` | Python dependencies; files and archives placed in each executor's working directory |  |
| `--driver-memory`, `--executor-memory` | Driver and executor memory | 1024 MiB and 1 GiB |
| `--executor-cores` | Cores per executor | 1 on YARN and Kubernetes; all cores of the worker in standalone mode |
| `--num-executors` | Executors for static allocation | 2; YARN and Kubernetes only |
| `--total-executor-cores` | Total cores for the application | Standalone only |
| `--queue` | YARN queue | `default`; YARN only |
| `--supervise` | Restart the driver if it exits with a non-zero code | Standalone cluster mode only |
| `--kill`, `--status` | Kill or query a submitted driver by submission ID | Standalone or Kubernetes cluster mode |
| `--remote` | [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) server URL such as `sc://host:port`; cannot be combined with `--master` or `--deploy-mode` | Spark Connect only |
| `--verbose` | Print debug output, including where each configuration value came from |  |

The default driver memory comes from the constant `DEFAULT_DRIVER_MEM_MB`, 1024 in Spark 4.3.0.[^n1]

## What is the difference between client and cluster deploy mode?

In **client** mode, the driver runs inside the `spark-submit` process, and the application's input and output are attached to the console. The Spark documentation recommends it when submitting from a gateway machine close to the workers, and for interactive shells.[^submit] In **cluster** mode, the driver is launched on a node inside the cluster; the documentation recommends it when submitting from a machine far from the workers, such as a laptop, to reduce network latency between driver and executors.[^submit] On YARN, cluster mode runs the driver inside the YARN application master, and the client can exit after submission.[^yarn]

The Spark 4.3.0 documentation states that the standalone cluster manager does not support cluster mode for Python applications.[^submit]

## How are dependencies shipped?

The application JAR and any JARs given with `--jars` are transferred to the cluster and put on the driver and executor classpaths. `--jars` takes a comma-separated list and does not expand directories.[^submit] Spark uses the URL scheme to decide how to distribute a file: `file:` paths are served by the driver's file server, `hdfs:`, `http:`, `https:` and `ftp:` are downloaded from the URI, and `local:` means the file already exists at that path on every node.[^submit]

`--packages` takes Maven coordinates in the form `groupId:artifactId:version` and resolves their transitive dependencies from the local Maven repository, Maven Central and any repositories given with `--repositories`.[^ssargs] For example, a [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) or [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) runtime can be added this way at launch time instead of being bundled into the application JAR.

## What are common mistakes?

- **Options after the application file.** Arguments after the JAR or `.py` file go to the application, not to Spark.[^submit]
- **Setting driver memory in code in client mode.** In client mode, `spark.driver.memory` set on a `SparkConf` inside the application has no effect, because the driver JVM is already running; use `--driver-memory` or the defaults file.[^config]
- **Several properties in one `--conf`.** Each property needs its own `--conf` flag, and a value containing spaces must be quoted as `"key=value"`.[^submit]
- **Local paths in cluster mode.** The application JAR URL must be visible from inside the cluster, for example an `hdfs://` path or a `file://` path present on every node.[^submit]
- **Bundling Spark into the application JAR.** When building an assembly JAR, Spark and Hadoop should be `provided` dependencies, because the cluster supplies them at runtime.[^submit]
- **`--properties-file` dropping the defaults.** Since Spark 4.0.0 the `--load-spark-defaults` flag is needed to keep `spark-defaults.conf` when a properties file is given.[^submit][^n2]
- **Unused JAR copies on standalone workers.** Files and JARs are copied to each executor's working directory; YARN cleans them up automatically, while standalone workers need `spark.worker.cleanup.appDataTtl`.[^submit]

## Is spark-submit still needed with Spark Connect?

A [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) client does not need `spark-submit`: it connects to a running Spark Connect server with a connection string such as `sc://localhost:15002`.[^connect] `spark-submit` still launches classic applications and the servers themselves; `sbin/start-connect-server.sh` starts a Spark Connect server.[^standalone] `spark-submit` also has a `--remote` option for running an application as a Spark Connect client.[^ssargs] On Kubernetes, the [Kubernetes Operator for Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Kubernetes_Operator_for_Apache_Spark) submits applications from a `SparkApplication` resource instead of a manual `spark-submit` call.

# spark.mllib (RDD-based API)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark.mllib_(RDD-based_API)

<Infobox type="software" name="spark.mllib (RDD-based API)">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) project)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">Spark 0.8.0 (as MLlib)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">Spark 4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala, with Python and Java APIs</Field>
  <Field name="type">Machine learning API (RDD-based)</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[MLlib: RDD-based API guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/mllib-guide.html)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark (mllib/.../mllib)](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/v4.3.0/mllib/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/mllib)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[MLlib](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MLlib), [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/ml-guide.md, docs/mllib-guide.md, docs/ml-migration-guide.md, docs/mllib-pmml-model-export.md, python/pyspark/mllib/), the v2.0.0 to v2.4.0 tags of docs/ml-guide.md, the Spark 2.0.0 and 4.0.0 release notes and SPARK-30934</Verified>

<Status level="maintenance" since="Apache Spark 2.0.0">Use the DataFrame-based `spark.ml` API of [MLlib](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MLlib) instead. Only bug fixes are accepted. The package as a whole is not deprecated in any release up to 4.3.0 and is still included.[^guide][^r200]</Status>

**spark.mllib** is the original, [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD)-based API of [MLlib](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MLlib), the machine learning library of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), found in the `org.apache.spark.mllib` package in Scala and Java and `pyspark.mllib` in Python.[^rddguide] Since Spark 2.0 it has been in maintenance mode: it receives bug fixes but no new features, and the DataFrame-based `spark.ml` package is the primary machine learning API.[^guide][^r200] The MLlib guide states that neither API is deprecated; spark.mllib is still part of Spark 4.3.0, but it cannot be used from a [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) client.[^guide][^connect]

## Status

**Is spark.mllib deprecated?** No, as a package it is in maintenance mode, not deprecated.

- **Maintenance mode since 2.0.** The Spark 2.0.0 release notes say the DataFrame-based API became the primary API and the RDD-based API entered maintenance mode.[^r200] The MLlib guide at v4.3.0 says that MLlib still supports the RDD-based API with bug fixes and will not add new features to it.[^guide] The Python package docstring says the same for `pyspark.mllib`.[^pyinit]
- **Planned removal that did not happen.** The MLlib guide in Spark 2.0.0 through 2.4.0 said the RDD-based API was "expected to be removed in Spark 3.0".[^guide240] The guide update for the 3.0 release removed that sentence, and the package was not removed. The package's Scala documentation at v4.3.0 still says the package "will be deprecated" once the DataFrame-based API reaches feature parity, while the MLlib guide says that parity was reached in the Spark 2.x releases; no release has deprecated it.[^n1][^guide][^jira30934]
- **Individual APIs deprecated and removed.** Some classes and methods in the package were deprecated and later removed. Spark 3.0 removed, among others, the Scala classes `LogisticRegressionWithSGD`, `LinearRegressionWithSGD`, `LassoWithSGD` and `RidgeRegressionWithSGD` (deprecated in 2.0), and the `runs` parameter of `KMeans.train` (deprecated in 2.1).[^migration] For the SGD classes, removal meant the public API: at v4.3.0 the Scala classes remain with constructors private to the `mllib` package, used by the PySpark wrappers.[^n2] Those PySpark wrappers are still public in 4.3.0, marked deprecated since 2.0.0, and emit a `FutureWarning`.[^n3]
- **No Spark Connect.** The Spark Connect documentation lists RDD and `SparkContext` as unsupported, so spark.mllib code needs a classic Spark application.[^connect] The DataFrame-based `pyspark.ml` API works on Spark Connect from Spark 4.0.0.[^n4]

## What the package contains

The RDD-based guide at v4.3.0 covers data types (local vectors and matrices, `LabeledPoint`, distributed matrices), basic statistics, linear models, naive Bayes, decision trees and tree ensembles, isotonic regression, alternating least squares, clustering (including streaming k-means), dimensionality reduction (SVD and PCA), feature extraction, frequent pattern mining (FP-growth, association rules, PrefixSpan), evaluation metrics, PMML model export and low-level optimization (SGD and L-BFGS).[^rddguide] Export to the Predictive Model Markup Language (PMML) is documented for spark.mllib models.[^n5]

## spark.mllib compared with spark.ml

|  | spark.mllib | spark.ml |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input | [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD) of `LabeledPoint` or vectors | [DataFrame](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DataFrame) with a vector column |
| Training call | Static `train` methods on algorithm objects | `Estimator.fit`, usually inside a `Pipeline` |
| Vector type | `org.apache.spark.mllib.linalg.Vector` | `org.apache.spark.ml.linalg.Vector` |
| New features | None (maintenance mode) | Yes |
| Spark Connect | Not supported | Supported from Spark 4.0.0 (Python) |

The two vector types are separate since Spark 2.0; the RDD-based API still depends on `spark.mllib.linalg`. To move data between them, the migration guide points to `asML` on an mllib vector or matrix, `Vectors.fromML` and `Matrices.fromML`, and the column converters in `MLUtils`.[^migration]

## Migrating to spark.ml

The Spark 3.0 entries in the migration guide name replacements for the removed classes: for example, `org.apache.spark.ml.classification.LogisticRegression` (or `LogisticRegressionWithLBFGS`) instead of `LogisticRegressionWithSGD`, and `org.apache.spark.ml.regression.LinearRegression` with `elasticNetParam` set to 1.0 instead of `LassoWithSGD`. The guide notes that default regularization differs: `regParam` was 0.01 for `LassoWithSGD` and `RidgeRegressionWithSGD`, but is 0.0 for `LinearRegression`.[^migration]

## Example

The same logistic regression in both APIs, in a classic PySpark session where `spark` is the `SparkSession`:

```python
# spark.mllib (RDD-based): classic mode only
from pyspark.mllib.classification import LogisticRegressionWithLBFGS
from pyspark.mllib.regression import LabeledPoint

rdd = spark.sparkContext.parallelize([
    LabeledPoint(0.0, [1.1, 0.1]), LabeledPoint(1.0, [2.0, 1.0]),
    LabeledPoint(0.0, [1.3, -0.5]), LabeledPoint(1.0, [2.2, 1.5])])
old_model = LogisticRegressionWithLBFGS.train(rdd, iterations=10)

# spark.ml (DataFrame-based): also runs on Spark Connect from 4.0.0
from pyspark.ml.classification import LogisticRegression
from pyspark.ml.linalg import Vectors

df = spark.createDataFrame([
    (0.0, Vectors.dense(1.1, 0.1)), (1.0, Vectors.dense(2.0, 1.0)),
    (0.0, Vectors.dense(1.3, -0.5)), (1.0, Vectors.dense(2.2, 1.5))],
    ["label", "features"])
new_model = LogisticRegression(maxIter=10).fit(df)
```

# SparkContext

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkContext

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">`sc` (the variable name in shells)</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Connection to the cluster manager, executors, DAG and task schedulers, RDD API, broadcast variables, accumulators, job groups and tags</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (Spark Classic only)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[SparkSession](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkSession), [Driver (Apache Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Driver_(Apache_Spark)), [RDD](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (core SparkContext.scala, the Spark 2.0.0 release notes, docs/cluster-overview.md, docs/spark-connect-overview.md, docs/app-dev-spark-connect.md, python/pyspark/sql/connect/session.py, python/pyspark/sql/session.py, sql/api SparkSession.scala)</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a **SparkContext** is the object in the [driver](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Driver_(Apache_Spark)) that represents the connection to a Spark cluster; it acquires [executors](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), schedules work on them and is used to create [RDDs](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RDD), accumulators and broadcast variables.[^sc] The source code still calls it the "main entry point for Spark functionality", but since Spark 2.0.0 DataFrame and SQL code starts from a [SparkSession](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkSession), which creates or reuses a SparkContext underneath.[^sc][^r200] In Spark 4 the SparkContext still runs every classic application, but [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) clients cannot use it.

## What does SparkContext still do in Spark 4?

SparkContext remains the core of a Spark Classic application in Spark 4.3.0. The cluster overview describes Spark applications as independent sets of processes coordinated by the SparkContext in the driver program: it connects to the cluster manager (standalone, YARN or Kubernetes), acquires executors, sends them the application code and then sends them tasks.[^cluster] DataFrame and SQL queries are planned by the [SparkSession](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkSession) and then run as jobs submitted through this SparkContext.

Only one SparkContext may be active per JVM. Creating a second one while the first is running fails with "Only one SparkContext should be running in this JVM (see SPARK-2243)"; the first must be stopped with `stop()` before a new one is made.[^sc] A side effect of this design is isolation: each application has its own executors, so two applications cannot share in-memory data except through external storage.[^cluster]

The public API of SparkContext in Spark 4.3.0 still covers these areas:[^sc]

| Area | Examples of SparkContext methods |
| --- | --- |
| Creating RDDs | `parallelize`, `textFile`, `runJob` |
| Shared variables | `broadcast`, `longAccumulator` |
| Shipping dependencies | `addFile`, `addJar` |
| Grouping and cancelling jobs | `setJobGroup`, `cancelJobGroup`, `setLocalProperty` |
| Inspecting the application | `applicationId`, `uiWebUrl`, `statusTracker`, `defaultParallelism`, `setLogLevel` |
| Fault tolerance for long lineages | `setCheckpointDir` |

In PySpark Classic, `spark.sparkContext` returns the SparkContext behind a session. Code that uses only DataFrames and SQL seldom needs it; code that uses the RDD API, accumulators or `sc.setJobGroup` does.

## Why do Spark Connect clients not have a SparkContext?

A Spark Connect client does not run in the same process as the Spark driver. It builds logical plans and sends them to a Spark Connect server, which runs the driver and its SparkContext. The Spark Connect overview lists two consequences: the protocol, which is built on logical plans, does not support all of Spark's execution APIs, "most importantly RDDs"; and the client, which gets a session rather than the whole application, has no access to the static Spark configuration or the SparkContext.[^connect]

The reason is that one server's SparkContext serves many client sessions. The overview explains that a Connect client gets a session-based interface and has no access to properties that change the environment for all connected clients, the SparkContext above all.[^connect] In PySpark 4.3.0, reading `spark.sparkContext` on a Connect session raises `JVM_ATTRIBUTE_NOT_SUPPORTED`, and the Scala API marks `SparkSession.sparkContext` as `@ClassicOnly`.[^connsession][^scalasession]

## What replaces SparkContext calls in Spark Connect?

The Spark Connect application guide says that RDDs can no longer be used directly from Spark Connect clients, and that alternatives for missing RDD functionality are provided in the higher-level APIs.[^appdev] For common SparkContext calls, the [SparkSession](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkSession) has methods that work over Spark Connect:

| SparkContext usage | Session-level alternative |
| --- | --- |
| `sc.parallelize(data)` | `spark.createDataFrame(data)` or `spark.range(n)`, which build a DataFrame instead of an RDD[^pysession] |
| `sc.addFile`, `sc.addPyFile` | `spark.addArtifacts(...)`[^pysession] |
| `sc.setJobGroup`, `sc.cancelJobGroup` | `spark.addTag(tag)`, then `spark.interruptTag(tag)` or `spark.interruptAll()`[^pysession] |

The session-level methods in this table work in both Connect and Classic sessions since Spark 4.0.0, so code that uses them runs in either mode.[^pysession]

# SparkR

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkR

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) project)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">Spark 1.4.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">Spark 4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">R, Scala</Field>
  <Field name="type">R language frontend for Apache Spark</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[SparkR (R on Spark)](https://spark.apache.org/docs/4.3.0/sparkr.html)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark (R/)](https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/v4.3.0/R)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [MLlib](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MLlib)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.0.0 to v4.3.0 tags of apache/spark (docs/sparkr.md, docs/sparkr-migration-guide.md, R/pkg/DESCRIPTION, R/pkg/R/zzz.R), the Spark 1.4.0, 4.0.0, 4.1.0, 4.2.0 and 4.3.0 release notes, SPARK-49347 and the August 2024 dev-list discussion and vote</Verified>

<Status level="deprecated" since="Apache Spark 4.0.0">Use the separately maintained sparklyr package instead. SparkR is still included in Spark 4.3.0 and has not been removed.[^jira49347]</Status>

**SparkR** is the R package that ships with [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) and lets R programs use Spark: it provides a distributed data frame, the `SparkDataFrame`, with selection, filtering and aggregation, and access to Spark's machine learning library.[^guide] SparkR is deprecated as of Spark 4.0.0 and will be removed in a future version, but it is still part of every release up to Spark 4.3.0.[^guide][^jira49347] The Spark project points R users to sparklyr, a separate R package for Spark.[^zzz]

## Status

SparkR was deprecated in Spark 4.0.0 under SPARK-49347, after a vote on the Spark dev mailing list.[^jira49347][^r400] The deprecation shows up in three places in Spark 4.x:

- **Programming guide.** The SparkR guide opens with the sentence that SparkR is deprecated from Spark 4.0.0 and will be removed in a future version.[^guide]
- **Migration guide.** The SparkR migration guide says, under "Upgrading from SparkR 3.5 to 4.0", that SparkR is deprecated and will be removed in a future version.[^n1]
- **Startup message.** When the package is attached, SparkR prints a warning that it is deprecated and recommends sparklyr. Setting the environment variable `SPARKR_SUPPRESS_DEPRECATION_WARNING` to any non-empty value hides the message.[^zzz]

SparkR has not been removed. The `R/pkg` directory is present at the v4.1.0, v4.2.0 and v4.3.0 tags, with the package version matching each Spark release.[^desc] The Spark 4.1.0 release notes do not mention SparkR. The 4.2.0 release notes list maintenance work on it, such as Java 25 support and dropping support for R 3.x, and none of the 4.x release notes announce a removal.[^n2][^r420][^n3]

## Why it was deprecated

The proposal came from Shivaram Venkataraman, who created the original SparkR package as research at UC Berkeley. In an August 2024 thread on the Spark dev mailing list he argued that sparklyr is more idiomatic R than SparkR's Scala-like API, that contributions to SparkR had slowed, that sparklyr's newer Spark Connect based architecture removed the need to align its version with Spark's, and that sparklyr is maintained on CRAN while SparkR could not stay there under Spark's release process.[^discuss] The vote to deprecate SparkR followed on 21 August 2024, and the deprecation was merged for Spark 4.0.0.[^n4][^jira49347]

## History

Spark 1.4.0 was the first release to package SparkR, described in the release notes as an R binding built on Spark's then-new DataFrame API.[^n5] The SparkR package in Spark 4.3.0 requires R 4.0 or later and Java 17 or later.[^desc]

## How it works

SparkR starts or connects to a Spark application through `sparkR.session()`, which creates a `SparkSession`. From RStudio or another R environment, SparkR uses `SPARK_HOME` to find a Spark installation and can download one if none is found.[^guide] R code talks to the Spark driver JVM through a backend in Spark core (`org.apache.spark.api.r.RBackend`).[^n6] The guide also documents running R functions on the data with `dapply` and `gapply`, Apache Arrow for faster transfer between the JVM and R, and MLlib model training.[^guide]

The following R example runs with the Spark 4.3 distribution. It starts a session, converts the built-in `faithful` data frame to a `SparkDataFrame` and filters it.

```r
library(SparkR)
sparkR.session(appName = "faithful-example")

df <- createDataFrame(faithful)
head(filter(df, df$waiting < 50))

sparkR.session.stop()
```

## Comparison with sparklyr

|  | SparkR | sparklyr |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Maintained by | The Apache Spark project, inside the Spark repository[^desc] | A separate open source project (github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr)[^sparklyr] |
| Status | Deprecated since Spark 4.0.0[^jira49347] | Recommended by the SparkR startup message[^zzz] |
| Installation | Ships with the Spark distribution; not maintained on CRAN[^discuss] | `install.packages("sparklyr")` from CRAN[^sparklyr] |
| API style | Its own functions over `SparkDataFrame` (`filter`, `select`, `agg`)[^guide] | Described in the deprecation proposal as more idiomatic R[^discuss] |
| Spark Connect | Not a Spark Connect client; connects through the R backend in the driver | `spark_connect(method = "spark_connect")`[^sparklyr] |

# SparkSession

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkSession

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Spark session, `spark` (the variable name in shells and notebooks)</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 2.0.0</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Builder (`master`, `remote`, `appName`, `config`, `getOrCreate`), runtime configuration (`spark.conf`), catalog, DataFrame readers, SQL</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) (Spark Classic and [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect))</Field>
  <Field name="related">[SparkContext](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkContext), [Driver (Apache Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Driver_(Apache_Spark)), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect), [Lazy evaluation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Lazy_evaluation)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Spark 2.0.0 release notes, the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (python/pyspark/sql/session.py, python/pyspark/sql/connect/session.py, python/pyspark/shell.py, sql/api SparkSession.scala, docs/configuration.md, docs/spark-connect-overview.md, docs/spark-connect-gotchas.md) and a PySpark 4.3.0 run</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a **SparkSession** is the entry point for programming with the DataFrame and Dataset API: it reads data, runs SQL, holds session configuration and temporary views, and gives access to the catalog.[^pysession] SparkSession was added in Spark 2.0.0 to replace `SQLContext` and `HiveContext`, which were kept for backward compatibility.[^r200] In Spark 4 the same SparkSession API exists in two forms: a classic session that runs inside the [driver](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Driver_(Apache_Spark)) next to a [SparkContext](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkContext), and a [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) session that is a thin client sending plans to a remote server.

## How is a SparkSession created?

Code creates or reuses a SparkSession through its builder. In PySpark the main builder methods are:

- `master(url)`: the cluster manager URL for a classic session, for example `local[*]`.
- `remote(url)`: the Spark Connect server URL, for example `sc://localhost:15002`; this makes the session a Connect session.
- `appName(name)`: the application name shown in the web UI.
- `config(key, value)`: any Spark setting; values are passed to both the `SparkConf` and the session's own configuration.
- `enableHiveSupport()`: connect to a [Hive Metastore](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Hive_Metastore) for persistent tables (not implemented for Connect sessions).
- `getOrCreate()`: return the existing global default session, applying the builder's options to it, or create a new one.[^pysession][^connsession]

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = (
    SparkSession.builder
    .master("local[*]")
    .appName("orders-report")
    .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "64")
    .getOrCreate()
)
spark.sql("SELECT 1 AS x").show()
```

Interactive tools usually create the session in advance. The PySpark shell creates it at startup and prints "SparkSession available as 'spark'."; in such environments the API documentation says to use the builder to get the existing session.[^pyshell][^scalasession]

Settings fall into two kinds. Runtime SQL settings such as `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` can be changed at any time with `spark.conf.set`. Settings that shape the driver or executors, such as `spark.driver.memory` or `spark.executor.cores`, take effect only when the application starts; in client mode, driver memory must even be passed on the `spark-submit` command line.[^config]

## How does SparkSession relate to SparkContext?

A classic SparkSession wraps a [SparkContext](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SparkContext). The SparkContext is the connection to the cluster and owns the executors, the schedulers and the RDD API; only one SparkContext may be active per JVM.[^sc] Several SparkSessions can share that one SparkContext: `newSession()` returns a session with its own SQL configuration, temporary views and UDFs, but the same SparkContext and table cache.[^pysession] Spark Connect sessions gained `newSession()` in PySpark 4.3.0; the new Connect session starts empty against the same server.[^connsession]

In classic mode, `spark.sparkContext` returns the underlying SparkContext. In the Spark 4.3.0 Scala API, the `sparkContext` member is marked `@ClassicOnly`, and in a PySpark Connect session, reading `spark.sparkContext` raises the error `JVM_ATTRIBUTE_NOT_SUPPORTED`.[^scalasession][^connsession]

## Spark Connect sessions vs classic sessions

A [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) SparkSession offers the same DataFrame and SQL API, but the client and the Spark driver are separate processes. The client builds unresolved logical plans and sends them over gRPC to a Spark Connect server, which analyzes and runs them.[^connect]

|  | Classic SparkSession | Spark Connect SparkSession |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where it runs | In the driver JVM (PySpark talks to it through Py4J) | In the client process; the driver runs on the Connect server[^connect] |
| How it is created | `SparkSession.builder.master(...)` | `SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://host:port")`, or the `SPARK_REMOTE` environment variable[^pysession] |
| Access to `SparkContext` and RDDs | Yes | No; SparkContext and the RDD API are not supported[^connect] |
| When a query is analyzed | Eagerly, when each transformation is defined | Lazily, when the plan is needed: schema access, `explain`, persisting or an action[^gotchas] |
| Static Spark configuration | Set by the application | Not accessible to the client[^connect] |
| Client package for Python | `pyspark` | `pyspark`, or the lighter `pyspark-client`[^connect] |

Spark 4.0.0 added the `spark.api.mode` setting (default `classic`). Set to `connect`, it makes a Spark Classic application start a local Spark Connect server and use a Connect session automatically.[^config]

Spark Connect introduced session-scoped methods that cover tasks once done through the SparkContext: `addArtifacts` adds local files, Python files or archives to the session, and `addTag` with `interruptTag` or `interruptAll` cancels running operations. They were added in PySpark 3.5.0 for Connect and work in Spark Classic since 4.0.0.[^pysession]

# Speculative execution

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Speculative_execution

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Speculation, speculative tasks, `spark.speculation`</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Straggler detection, duplicate task attempts, first attempt wins, output commit coordination</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Data skew](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_skew), [Accumulator](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Accumulator), [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/configuration.md, docs/rdd-programming-guide.md, docs/streaming/apis-on-dataframes-and-datasets.md, docs/sql-performance-tuning.md, core scheduler/TaskSetManager.scala, core scheduler/OutputCommitCoordinator.scala, sql adaptive/OptimizeSkewedJoin.scala) and the Delta Lake protocol at tag v4.4.1</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), **speculative execution** is a scheduler feature that launches a second copy of a task that is running much slower than the other tasks in its stage, on another [executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor), and uses whichever copy finishes first. It targets stragglers caused by a slow machine or disk, and is off by default (`spark.speculation=false`).[^config] Because the same task can run twice, any side effect that is not idempotent can happen twice.

## How does speculation decide which tasks to copy?

Spark checks for slow tasks every `spark.speculation.interval`. Speculation for a stage starts only after a fraction `spark.speculation.quantile` of its tasks has finished; then a running task is a candidate if it is `spark.speculation.multiplier` times slower than the median of the finished tasks and has run at least `spark.speculation.minTaskRuntime`.[^config]

| Setting | Default | Since | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `spark.speculation` | false | 0.6.0 | Turn speculation on |
| `spark.speculation.interval` | 100ms | 0.6.0 | How often to look for slow tasks |
| `spark.speculation.multiplier` | 3 | 0.6.0 | How many times slower than the median a task must be |
| `spark.speculation.quantile` | 0.9 | 0.6.0 | Fraction of tasks that must be done before speculating in a stage |
| `spark.speculation.minTaskRuntime` | 100ms | 3.2.0 | Minimum run time before a task can be speculated |
| `spark.speculation.task.duration.threshold` | none | 3.0.0 | Speculate stages with few tasks once a task runs longer than this |
| `spark.speculation.efficiency.enabled` | true | 3.4.0 | Speculate only tasks that are inefficient by data processing rate or duration |

<small>Source: Spark 4.3.0 configuration reference.[^config]</small>

The duration threshold helps stages that have no more tasks than one executor has slots, where the median rule has too few finished tasks to work with.[^config] With `spark.speculation.efficiency.enabled`, a task is speculated only if its data processing rate is below the stage average times a multiplier, or if its duration exceeds the threshold times `spark.speculation.efficiency.longRunTaskFactor`.[^config]

## What happens when a speculative copy finishes?

When one attempt of a task succeeds, the scheduler kills the other running attempts of the same task, with the reason "another attempt succeeded".[^tsm] The killed attempt may have already done part of its work.

For file output written through Spark's commit protocol, the **output commit coordinator** on the driver decides which attempt may commit each partition, with a "first committer wins" policy. This keeps two attempts from both committing their output files.[^occ] Table formats add their own commit on top. In [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), a table snapshot consists of the `add` actions in committed log entries, so a data file written by an attempt whose transaction never committed is not part of the table.[^delta]

## Side effects with non-idempotent writes

Code that writes to an external system directly from tasks is outside the commit coordinator. With speculation on, two attempts of the same task can run that code at the same time, and the killed attempt may have written some or all of its data before it was stopped.[^tsm] Examples are:

- `foreach` or `foreachPartition` code that inserts rows into a database, posts to an HTTP API or sends messages to a queue;
- UDFs with side effects, such as writing a log record per row;
- [Accumulator](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Accumulator) updates inside transformations, which the Spark docs say may be applied more than once when tasks are re-executed.[^rddguide]

The same duplication can happen without speculation, from task retries, so code that writes externally should be idempotent anyway: use upserts or `MERGE` keyed on a stable ID, or write to a staging location and commit once from the driver. In [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), `foreachBatch` gives only at-least-once write guarantees by default, and the docs suggest using the batch ID passed to the function to deduplicate output.[^ss] See [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics).

## When to use speculation

Speculation helps when tasks are slow because of the machine they run on, for example a node with a failing disk or a noisy neighbour. It does not help with [data skew](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_skew), because a copy of a skewed task has the same amount of data and is just as slow. For skewed joins, Spark's [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution) can split large partitions instead.[^perf] In Spark 4.3.0 this applies to sort-merge and shuffled hash joins, and only to a side the join type allows to split: the left side of inner, cross, left semi, left anti and left outer joins, and the right side of inner, cross and right outer joins. It also applies to the streamed side of a broadcast hash join when `spark.sql.adaptive.localShuffleReader.enabled` is false. It does not split skewed aggregations, windows or full outer joins; for those, see [salting](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Salting).[^skewrule] Each speculative copy also uses a task slot that another task could have used.

```
spark.speculation                          true
spark.speculation.multiplier               3
spark.speculation.quantile                 0.9
spark.speculation.minTaskRuntime           30s
```

# Spill (memory)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spill_(memory)

<Infobox type="concept" name="Spill">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Spill to disk, memory spill</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Execution memory, spill files on local disk, spill metrics</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark memory management](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_memory_management), [Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Data skew](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_skew), [Executor](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Executor)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/web-ui.md, docs/monitoring.md, docs/tuning.md, docs/configuration.md, docs/rdd-programming-guide.md), the Trino 484 docs (Spill to disk, Spilling properties) and the Apache Flink 2.3 docs (TaskManager memory, memory tuning, configuration)</Verified>

**Spill** is the act of a query engine writing intermediate data from memory to local disk while an operation runs, because the data for a sort, aggregation, join or shuffle does not fit in the memory the operation is allowed to use. In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a task spills when its share of execution memory is full; the task keeps running, reads the spilled data back later, and finishes slower instead of failing.[^rddguide][^tuning] [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) and [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) spill too, under different rules.

## What is spill in Apache Spark?

Spark divides each executor's unified memory region into execution memory, used for shuffles, joins, sorts and aggregations, and storage memory, used for cached data.[^tuning] Shuffle operations build in-memory structures to organize records; when these do not fit, Spark spills them to disk, which adds disk I/O and garbage collection.[^rddguide] Spill files go to the scratch directories in `spark.local.dir` (default `/tmp`), and data spilled during shuffles is compressed by default (`spark.shuffle.spill.compress`).[^config]

Spill is not the same as shuffle files. Shuffle files are the normal output of the map side of a [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), written by every shuffle; spill files are temporary overflow inside one task. A shuffle with no spill still writes shuffle files.[^rddguide]

## Spill metrics in the Spark UI

The Spark UI reports spill in two places.

- **Stage page.** The task summary and the per-executor table show **Shuffle spill (memory)**, the size of the spilled data in its deserialized form in memory, and **Shuffle spill (disk)**, the size of its serialized form on disk.[^webui] The memory figure is usually the larger of the two, because the serialized and compressed form on disk is smaller.
- **SQL tab.** Operators such as `Sort` and `HashAggregate` show a `spill size` metric (bytes spilled to disk by that operator) next to `peak memory`.[^webui]

The same numbers are in the task metrics of the REST API and event log as `memoryBytesSpilled` and `diskBytesSpilled`.[^monitoring]

## What causes spill?

- **Too few shuffle partitions.** Each task gets a larger slice of data. `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` defaults to 200; with [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution) on, Spark starts from that number and coalesces small partitions.[^perf]
- **[Data skew](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_skew).** One task gets most of the data, so only that task spills.
- **Little execution memory per task.** All running tasks on an executor share its execution memory, so more cores per executor means less memory per task. The region size is set by `spark.executor.memory` and `spark.memory.fraction` (default 0.6).[^tuning][^config]
- **Large cached datasets.** Cached blocks occupy storage memory. Execution can evict them, but only down to `spark.memory.storageFraction` (default 0.5) of the region.[^tuning]

Common fixes follow from the causes: more shuffle partitions, fixing skew, more memory per executor or fewer cores per executor, and caching less. A small amount of spill is normal; it matters when spill dominates a stage's run time.

## Spill compared across engines

|  | Apache Spark | Trino | Apache Flink |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Default behaviour | Always on; tasks spill execution data when memory runs out[^rddguide] | Off (`spill-enabled` defaults to false); without it, queries over the memory limits are killed[^trinospillprops][^trinospill] | For batch jobs, Flink spills to disk when managed memory is not enough[^flinktuning] |
| Memory that spills | Execution memory in the executor's unified region (heap, or off-heap if enabled)[^tuning] | Revocable memory, which does not count toward query limits and which the memory manager can take back[^trinospill] | Managed memory, native (off-heap) memory used for sorting, hash tables and cached intermediate results; by default 0.4 of total Flink memory (`taskmanager.memory.managed.fraction`)[^flinkmem][^flinkconfig] |
| Where spill goes | `spark.local.dir`[^config] | `spiller-spill-path`, which must be set when spilling is on; a comma-separated list spreads spill over several disks[^trinospillprops] | `io.tmp.dirs` (default: the JVM temporary directory), which also holds RocksDB files and cached jars[^flinkconfig] |
| Operations that spill | Shuffle, sort, aggregation and join structures[^rddguide][^webui] | Joins, aggregations, `ORDER BY` and window functions[^trinospill] | Batch algorithms such as external sorts and hash joins[^flinkconfig] |
| Status | Core part of execution | The Trino docs call spill to disk legacy functionality and point to fault-tolerant execution with the task retry policy instead[^trinospill] | Core part of batch execution |

In Trino, spill is enabled per cluster and is limited by `max-spill-per-node` (all queries on a node) and `query-max-spill-per-node` (one query on a node), both 100GB by default.[^trinospillprops] The Trino docs warn that a query forced to spill may run orders of magnitude longer than one that runs in memory, and that spill does not guarantee that every memory-intensive query will succeed.[^trinospill]

# SQL pipe syntax

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/SQL_pipe_syntax

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Pipe syntax, operator pipe syntax, `|>` syntax</Field>
  <Field name="field">SQL query languages</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`FROM` or `TABLE` source, pipe operator `|>`, operators `SELECT`, `EXTEND`, `SET`, `DROP`, `AS`, `WHERE`, `AGGREGATE`, `JOIN`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), GoogleSQL (BigQuery), ZetaSQL</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark SQL scripting](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_SQL_scripting), [Spark SQL ANSI mode](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_SQL_ANSI_mode)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/sql-pipe-syntax.md, SqlBaseParser.g4, SQLConf.scala), SPARK-49555, the Spark 4.0.0 and 4.2.0 release notes, the PVLDB 17(12) paper by Shute et al. and the BigQuery pipe syntax reference</Verified>

**SQL pipe syntax** is an extension of SQL in which a query is written as a sequence of operators joined by the pipe symbol `|>`, each operator taking the table produced by the previous one, so that the query reads top to bottom in the order of its logical transformations. [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) SQL supports pipe syntax since Spark 4.0.0 (SPARK-49555).[^r400][^doc] Pipe syntax keeps standard SQL working unchanged: a query can use standard clauses, pipe operators, or both.[^doc]

## Where does SQL pipe syntax come from?

Pipe syntax was described by Jeff Shute and other Google engineers in the paper "SQL Has Problems. We Can Fix Them: Pipe Syntax In SQL", published in the Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment, volume 17, issue 12 (2024). The paper presents it as an addition to GoogleSQL, Google's SQL dialect, that fixes the rigid clause order of standard SQL without replacing the language.[^paper] BigQuery documents pipe syntax as an extension to GoogleSQL, and Google announced that it would be available to all BigQuery users by default from 4 February 2025.[^bq][^bqblog] The Spark ticket SPARK-49555 links to the paper and to the open source ZetaSQL implementation.[^jira]

## How does pipe syntax work in Spark SQL?

A pipe query in Spark SQL usually starts with `FROM table_name`, which Spark accepts as a standalone query equivalent to `TABLE table_name`. Any number of pipe operators can follow, in any order, each starting with `|>` and one or more SQL keywords.[^doc] Pipe operators can also be appended to the end of any ordinary Spark SQL query.[^doc]

Spark's documentation states several invariants. Each operator works the same way on its input regardless of how that input was computed. For a valid chain of N operators, the first M operators (M ≤ N) also form a valid query, which lets a user run a prefix of a query while debugging. Subqueries, views and DDL or DML statements can contain queries in either syntax.[^doc]

Pipe syntax is controlled by `spark.sql.operatorPipeSyntaxEnabled`, added in Spark 4.0.0 and `true` by default in Spark 4.3.0.[^sqlconf] Since Spark 4.2.0 a single `|` can also be used as the pipe token (SPARK-51518). This is governed by `spark.sql.parser.singleCharacterPipeOperator.enabled`, true by default; the parser tells a pipe apart from bitwise OR by checking whether a pipe operator keyword follows.[^r420][^sqlconf][^grammar]

## Which pipe operators does Spark SQL support?

| Operator | What it does | Closest standard Spark SQL |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SELECT` | Evaluates expressions over each input row | Outermost `SELECT` of a subquery |
| `EXTEND` | Appends computed columns | `SELECT *, expr AS col` |
| `SET` | Replaces the values of existing columns | `SELECT * REPLACE (expr AS col)` |
| `DROP` | Removes columns | `SELECT * EXCEPT (col)` |
| `AS` | Gives the input a new table alias | Table alias |
| `WHERE` | Filters rows; can appear anywhere, so no separate `HAVING` or `QUALIFY` is needed | `WHERE`, `HAVING`, `QUALIFY` |
| `AGGREGATE` | Aggregates, with or without `GROUP BY` | `SELECT ... GROUP BY` |
| `JOIN` | Joins the input (left side) with a table argument (right side) | `JOIN` |
| `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT` | Sorts and limits rows | `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT` |
| `UNION`, `INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT` | Set operations with another table | Same set operations |
| `TABLESAMPLE`, `PIVOT`, `UNPIVOT` | Sampling and reshaping | Same clauses |

Source: Spark 4.3.0 pipe syntax documentation.[^doc]

`AGGREGATE` differs most from standard SQL. Its output holds the grouping columns first and then the aggregate columns, so the grouping expressions are not repeated in a `SELECT` list. `GROUP BY` ordinals refer to the columns of the input table, not to a select list.[^doc] In Spark 4.3.0 a pipe `SELECT` also accepts aggregate functions and an optional `GROUP BY`, as in `TABLE t |> SELECT a, SUM(b) AS s GROUP BY a`: the grammar allows a `GROUP BY` clause after the select list, the analyzer permits aggregate functions in `SELECT` but rejects them in `EXTEND`, `SET` and other pipe operators, and the Spark test suite runs such queries.[^grammar][^pipeops][^pipetests] The Spark 4.2.0 release notes list this change as SPARK-54292.[^r420] The 4.3.0 pipe syntax documentation still says that aggregate functions are not supported in a pipe `SELECT` and should go in `AGGREGATE`.[^doc]

## Example

The Spark documentation rewrites query 13 of the TPC-H benchmark, which in standard SQL needs a subquery for its two levels of aggregation, as a straight sequence of operators:[^doc]

```sql
-- Standard SQL
SELECT c_count, COUNT(*) AS custdist
FROM (
  SELECT c_custkey, COUNT(o_orderkey) c_count
  FROM customer
  LEFT OUTER JOIN orders ON c_custkey = o_custkey
    AND o_comment NOT LIKE '%unusual%packages%'
  GROUP BY c_custkey
) AS c_orders
GROUP BY c_count
ORDER BY custdist DESC, c_count DESC;

-- The same query with pipe syntax
FROM customer
|> LEFT OUTER JOIN orders ON c_custkey = o_custkey
   AND o_comment NOT LIKE '%unusual%packages%'
|> AGGREGATE COUNT(o_orderkey) c_count
   GROUP BY c_custkey
|> AGGREGATE COUNT(*) AS custdist
   GROUP BY c_count
|> ORDER BY custdist DESC, c_count DESC;
```

A smaller example builds columns step by step and filters on an aggregate without `HAVING`:

```sql
VALUES ('a', 10), ('a', 5), ('b', 3) AS t(k, v)
|> EXTEND v * 2 AS v2
|> AGGREGATE SUM(v2) AS total GROUP BY k
|> WHERE total > 10
|> ORDER BY total DESC;
-- one row: k = 'a', total = 30
```

## Is pipe syntax more readable?

The paper's authors argue that standard SQL's fixed clause order forces subqueries and "inside-out" data flow, and that operators applied in sequence are easier to read, write and extend.[^paper] In Spark SQL, pipe syntax also lets a computed column be used by the next operator without a lateral column alias or a subquery.[^doc] Pipe syntax is optional: any query can be written in standard Spark SQL, in pipe syntax or in a mix of the two, so it can be adopted one query at a time.[^doc]
