# State store

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/State_store

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">State store provider</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Versioned key-value store per operator and partition, state store provider class, checkpointed files, maintenance task</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming): `HDFSBackedStateStoreProvider` (default) and `RocksDBStateStoreProvider`</Field>
  <Field name="related">[RocksDB state store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RocksDB_state_store), [Streaming checkpoint](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_checkpoint), [Stateful stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stateful_stream_processing), [Watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming programming guide (State Store section) and miscellaneous notes, `SQLConf.scala`, `HDFSBackedStateStoreProvider.scala` and `RocksDBFileManager.scala` at tag v4.3.0 of apache/spark, the state data source guide, SPARK-45511, the Databricks RocksDB state store page, and the Apache Flink 2.3 "State Backends" page</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), a **state store** is the versioned key-value store in which stateful operators keep the data they carry from one micro-batch to the next, such as running aggregates, deduplication keys, buffered join rows and user state. Each stateful operator has one state store per shuffle partition, running on an executor, and every batch produces a new version that is saved to the [streaming checkpoint](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_checkpoint) so the state survives failures.[^ss-store] Spark ships two implementations, the HDFS-backed state store and the [RocksDB state store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RocksDB_state_store), and the choice between them mostly decides how much state a query can hold without memory problems.

## Which operators use the state store?

Streaming aggregations, streaming deduplication with `dropDuplicates`, stream-stream joins and the arbitrary stateful operators (`mapGroupsWithState`, `flatMapGroupsWithState` and [transformWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState)) all keep state in the state store.[^ss-store] Stateless operations, including [stream-static joins](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream-static_join), do not.[^ss-join] See [Stateful stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stateful_stream_processing).

## How does the state store work?

A state store is a versioned key-value store with reads and writes. Updates are applied in sets, transactionally, and each set increments the store's version; a retried task can therefore re-run its updates against the correct earlier version.[^ss-store] The version of a store matches the batch id of the query.

The state store provider is set with `spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass`. Its default is `org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.HDFSBackedStateStoreProvider`, and it cannot be changed between restarts from the same checkpoint location.[^sqlconf][^misc] Users can also write their own provider by extending the `StateStoreProvider` interface.[^ss-store]

State is partitioned by hashing the grouping key, which is why `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` cannot change for a query that already has a checkpoint.[^misc]

Spark tries to run each state store on the same executor in every batch, using the preferred-location feature of RDDs, because loading a store on a new executor means reading its checkpointed files. The preference is not a guarantee; raising `spark.locality.wait` makes it more likely to hold. A background maintenance task, run every `spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.maintenanceInterval` (default 60 seconds), runs background maintenance in every loaded provider and unloads providers that are no longer active on an executor.[^ss-store][^sqlconf]

## HDFS-backed vs RocksDB state store

The **HDFS-backed state store** keeps all of its data in an in-memory map in the executor JVM and saves it to files in an HDFS-compatible file system.[^ss-store] Each batch writes a `''version''.delta` file with that batch's changes, and Spark consolidates deltas into a `''version''.snapshot` file after `spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.minDeltasForSnapshot` (default 10) delta files.[^hdfs][^sqlconf]

The **RocksDB state store**, added in Spark 3.2, keeps state in RocksDB in native memory and on local disk instead of the JVM heap, and uploads its files to the checkpoint location. The Spark guide recommends it for queries with millions of keys in state, where the HDFS-backed store causes long JVM garbage collection pauses and uneven micro-batch times.[^ss-store] It is the only provider that supports [transformWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState). See [RocksDB state store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RocksDB_state_store).

|  | HDFS-backed state store | RocksDB state store |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Provider class | `HDFSBackedStateStoreProvider` (default in Apache Spark)[^sqlconf] | `RocksDBStateStoreProvider`[^ss-store] |
| Where live state is held | In-memory map on the executor JVM heap[^ss-store] | RocksDB, in native memory and on local disk[^ss-store] |
| Checkpoint files | `.delta` per batch, `.snapshot` after consolidation[^hdfs] | A `''version''.zip` per version plus shared SST files; optionally changelog files[^rocksfm] |
| State size limit in practice | Executor heap; large state causes GC pauses[^ss-store] | Local disk and the configured memory bound[^ss-store] |
| transformWithState | Not supported | Supported |

On Databricks, RocksDB is the default state store provider in Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS and above.[^db-rocks]

## How big does state get?

State size is driven by the number of distinct keys each operator keeps and how long it keeps them. A [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) bounds it for windowed aggregations, deduplication and stream-stream joins; without one, aggregation and deduplication state grows for as long as new keys arrive.[^ss-dedup] Each operator reports state metrics in the query progress, including the number of rows in state (`numTotalStateRows`), updated and removed rows.[^ss-store]

The **state data source** reads the state of a checkpoint as a batch DataFrame, which helps to inspect state size and contents. It is experimental and, as of Spark 4.0, read-only.[^ss-store][^jira45511]

```python
spark.conf.set(
    "spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass",
    "org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider",
)  # set before the query first starts; fixed for its checkpoint

state = spark.read.format("statestore").load("/checkpoints/page_counts")
state.groupBy("partition_id").count().show()
```

## Comparison with Flink state backends

[Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) calls the same component a **state backend**. Without other configuration it uses the `HashMapStateBackend`, which holds state as objects on the Java heap, much like Spark's HDFS-backed store. The `EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend` keeps state as serialized bytes in RocksDB and is the only Flink backend that offers incremental checkpoints; the `ForStStateBackend` is experimental.[^flink-sb]

# Stateful stream processing

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stateful_stream_processing

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Stateful streaming</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Keyed state, timers, time-to-live (TTL), [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), fault-tolerant state storage</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) (built-in stateful operators, [transformWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState)), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) (keyed state, `KeyedProcessFunction`), Kafka Streams</Field>
  <Field name="related">[State store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/State_store), [RocksDB state store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RocksDB_state_store), [Streaming checkpoint](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_checkpoint), [mapGroupsWithState and flatMapGroupsWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MapGroupsWithState_and_flatMapGroupsWithState)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming programming guide (arbitrary stateful operations, unsupported operations) and transformWithState guide, `SQLConf.scala` at tag v4.3.0 of apache/spark, SPARK-40925, the Databricks "What is stateful streaming?" page, and the Apache Flink 2.3 "Working with State", "Process Function", "State Backends" and "State Schema Evolution" pages</Verified>

**Stateful stream processing** is stream processing in which the result for a record depends on information kept from earlier records, such as a running count, the last value seen for a key, or rows waiting for a join partner. The engine stores this **state**, usually partitioned by key, saves it to durable storage so it survives failures, and removes it when it is no longer needed. In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), state is held in a [state store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/State_store) and used by built-in operators (aggregations, deduplication, stream-stream joins) and by the [transformWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState) operator for custom logic.[^ss-store][^tws]

## What is the difference between stateless and stateful streaming?

A stateless query handles each record on its own: filters, projections, parsing, and joins with a static table. The only thing a stateless Structured Streaming query tracks is which input has been processed. A stateful query updates intermediate state in every batch.[^db-stateful] State makes results possible that depend on history, but it costs memory and storage, adds checkpointing time, and fixes parts of the query for the life of its checkpoint.

## What are state, timers and TTL?

**State** is data kept per key between records. In Spark's built-in operators, the engine decides what to keep: partial aggregates per group and window, the keys already seen for deduplication, or buffered rows for a join.[^ss-store]

A **timer** is a callback that the application registers for a future time, so that it can act when nothing arrives, for example to close a session or raise an alert after silence. An event-time timer fires when the [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) passes its time; a processing-time timer fires when the wall clock does.[^flink-pf]

**Time-to-live (TTL)** makes state expire a set time after it was written, so that state for keys that go quiet does not stay forever. Both Spark and Flink measure state TTL in processing time.[^tws][^flink-state]

## How does Structured Streaming handle state?

Most stateful Spark queries use built-in operators, and Spark manages their state. Streaming aggregations, `dropDuplicates` and stream-stream joins keep state per key in the state store and use the watermark to drop state that can no longer change; see [Watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), [Streaming deduplication](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_deduplication) and [Stream-stream join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream-stream_join).[^ss-store]

For logic that does not fit them, Spark has arbitrary stateful operators. `mapGroupsWithState` and `flatMapGroupsWithState` date from Spark 2.2 and are now called legacy; since Spark 4.0, the guide encourages `transformWithState` instead.[^ss-arb] In transformWithState, a stateful processor class declares named state variables of three types, **ValueState**, **ListState** and **MapState**, registers timers, sets optional TTL per variable and can be seeded with an initial state DataFrame. It is available in Scala, Java and Python.[^tws]

transformWithState timers can be listed, added and removed; a key can have several; and timers are checkpointed, so they can fire after a restart. TTL works only with `TimeMode.ProcessingTime`.[^tws] The operator requires the [RocksDB state store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/RocksDB_state_store).

Since Spark 3.4.0, a query can chain several stateful operators, for example an aggregation followed by a stream-stream join, in append mode. Late records are then filtered against the watermark of the previous micro-batch; `spark.sql.streaming.statefulOperator.allowMultiple=false` restores the earlier behavior with a single stateful operator.[^jira40925][^sqlconf] Chaining stateful operators is not supported in update or complete [output mode](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Output_mode).[^ss-unsup]

## How does Flink handle state?

[Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink)'s **keyed state** is scoped to the key of the current record and is available only on a `KeyedStream`, created with `keyBy`. The state primitives are `ValueState`, `ListState`, `ReducingState`, `AggregatingState` and `MapState`, each created from a state descriptor.[^flink-state]

Flink timers are registered through the `TimerService` of a `KeyedProcessFunction`. When a timer fires, `onTimer` runs with state scoped to the key that set the timer.[^flink-pf]

Flink TTL is configured with a `StateTtlConfig` on any keyed state type, with per-entry TTL for list elements and map entries. The update type (by default `OnCreateAndWrite`) decides when the TTL is refreshed, and the visibility setting decides whether expired values that have not been cleaned up yet can still be read. Only processing-time TTL is supported.[^flink-state] Flink keeps state in a state backend: the heap-based `HashMapStateBackend` by default, or the `EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend`.[^flink-sb]

## transformWithState vs Flink keyed state

|  | Spark `transformWithState` | Flink keyed state with `KeyedProcessFunction` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Programming model | A `StatefulProcessor` class with `init`, `handleInputRows`, `handleExpiredTimer`, `handleInitialState` and `close`[^tws] | A `KeyedProcessFunction` with `processElement` and `onTimer`[^flink-pf] |
| Input per call | All rows of a key in the micro-batch (one row in Real-time Mode)[^tws] | One record[^flink-pf] |
| State types | ValueState, ListState, MapState[^tws] | ValueState, ListState, ReducingState, AggregatingState, MapState[^flink-state] |
| Timers | Processing-time and event-time, several per key, checkpointed[^tws] | Processing-time and event-time through the `TimerService`[^flink-pf] |
| TTL | Per state variable, processing time only[^tws] | Per state descriptor with `StateTtlConfig`, processing time only, per entry for collections[^flink-state] |
| Storage | RocksDB state store, required[^tws] | Heap (`HashMapStateBackend`, default) or RocksDB[^flink-sb] |
| State schema changes | State variables can be added or removed; value fields can evolve with Avro encoding[^tws] | Migrated automatically when a job is restored from a savepoint with changed state types, for serializers that support it[^flink-se] |

## What does state cost?

State has to be stored, checkpointed and restored. Databricks advises setting the number of shuffle partitions to one to two times the number of cluster cores for stateful queries, and notes that the partition count is fixed when the checkpoint is created.[^db-stateful] In open source Spark, `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` and the state store provider cannot change between restarts from the same checkpoint.[^misc] See [Streaming checkpoint](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_checkpoint) for what else is fixed.

# Stream processing

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Streaming, unbounded data processing</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data engineering, distributed systems</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Unbounded input, event time, windows, state, [Watermarks](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), triggers, checkpoints</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink), Kafka Streams ([Apache Kafka](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Kafka))</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics), [Streaming lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_lakehouse), [Spark Streaming (DStreams)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Streaming_(DStreams))</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming guides, the Apache Flink 2.3 documentation, the Apache Kafka 4.4 Streams documentation and the Dataflow Model paper (VLDB 2015)</Verified>

**Stream processing** is the continuous computation of results over data that has no defined end, in which an engine processes records as they arrive and keeps its output up to date instead of waiting for a complete dataset. The input is called an **unbounded** dataset or stream; data with a fixed start and end is **bounded**.[^flink-arch] In the open lakehouse, the term covers engines such as [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) and Kafka Streams, which read from message buses and write to tables, topics or other systems.

## Unbounded data, not a kind of engine

The Dataflow Model paper (Akidau et al., Google, published in the Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment in 2015) prefers the terms "unbounded" and "bounded" to "streaming" and "batch", because the latter imply a particular execution engine. The paper notes that unbounded data has long been processed by repeated batch runs, and that well-designed streaming systems can also process bounded data; it reserves "streaming" and "batch" for describing runtime engines.[^dataflow]

The Apache Flink documentation draws the same line: batch processing is processing of a bounded stream, where the engine may read the whole input before producing results (for example, to sort it), while an unbounded stream must be processed continuously as data arrives.[^flink-learn]

## Core ideas

### Event time and processing time

Every record has at least two times. **Event time** is when the event occurred on the device or system that produced it. **Processing time** is the clock time of the machine that handles the record.[^flink-time] Kafka Streams adds a third, **ingestion time**: when a Kafka broker stored the record in a topic partition.[^kstreams]

The Dataflow paper points out that event time for an event never changes, while the skew between event time and processing time varies constantly because of network delays, scheduling and processing time.[^dataflow] Records therefore arrive out of order, and a result grouped by event time is never certain to be complete. A [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) is the engine's estimate of how far event time has progressed, and it lets the engine decide when a result is final.

### Windows

Aggregations over an unbounded stream need finite groups, called **windows**. Three types are common across engines:[^dataflow][^ss-apis][^flink-time]

| Window | Definition | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tumbling (fixed) | Fixed size, non-overlapping, contiguous intervals; each record belongs to one window | Counts per 5-minute interval |
| Sliding | Fixed size with a slide shorter than the size, so windows overlap and a record can belong to several | 10-minute windows starting every 5 minutes |
| Session | Variable size; a window grows while records keep arriving within a gap duration, and closes after a gap with no input | One window per user visit, closed after 30 idle minutes |

In PySpark the three types map to two functions: `window()` for tumbling and sliding windows and `session_window()` for session windows.[^ss-apis]

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import window, session_window

events.groupBy(window("ts", "5 minutes"))                 # tumbling
events.groupBy(window("ts", "10 minutes", "5 minutes"))   # sliding
events.groupBy("user", session_window("ts", "30 minutes")) # session
```

### State

Aggregations, joins and deduplication must remember earlier records, so the engine keeps **state** between inputs. Structured Streaming keeps it in a state store, with an optional RocksDB-based provider.[^ss-apis] Flink keeps task state in memory and moves large state to on-disk structures.[^flink-arch] State grows without bound unless something says when old entries can be dropped; in event-time queries that signal is the watermark.[^ss-apis]

### Triggers, latency and throughput

A **trigger** decides when an engine computes and emits results. Engines that group records into small batches gain throughput and simpler fault tolerance, but each batch adds scheduling overhead that sets a floor on latency. Engines that keep long-lived tasks and handle each record as it arrives reach lower latency.[^ss-rtm]

## Execution models

<Hatnote>Main article: [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming)</Hatnote>

Two execution models are common:

- **Micro-batch**: the engine runs the query as a series of small batch jobs. This is the default in [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), with end-to-end latencies as low as about 100 milliseconds and exactly-once guarantees.[^ss-index]
- **Continuous or record-at-a-time**: long-running operators process each record as it arrives. Kafka Streams describes its processing as one record at a time, with millisecond latency.[^kstreams] Flink processes unbounded streams continuously and keeps state local to each task for low latency.[^flink-arch]

Spark offers three modes on the same DataFrame API. The Spark 4.3 documentation compares them as follows:[^ss-rtm]

| Spark mode | Typical latency | Processing guarantee | Supported queries |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Micro-batch (default) | About 100 ms | Exactly-once | All streaming operations |
| Real-time Mode (Spark 4.1.0 and later) | Millisecond scale | Exactly-once | Stateless queries; since Spark 4.3.0 also deduplication, aggregation and JVM `transformWithState` |
| Continuous Processing (experimental) | About 1 ms | At-least-once | Map-like operations only; the documentation calls it legacy and points to Real-time Mode |

In Real-time Mode, the trigger duration (default 5 minutes) is mainly a checkpoint interval, not a latency target; records are processed and emitted as they arrive.[^ss-rtm]

## Comparison with batch processing

|  | Batch processing | Stream processing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input | Bounded; all data present at start | Unbounded; data keeps arriving |
| Completeness | Known when the job starts | Estimated, usually with a watermark |
| Output | Produced once, at the end | Produced incrementally and updated |
| Failure recovery | Rerun the job | Restart from a checkpoint and replay the source |

The boundary is not strict. Structured Streaming's available-now trigger processes all data present at start and then stops, which runs a streaming query as an incremental batch job.[^ss-apis] In a [streaming lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_lakehouse), the same table is written by a stream and read by batch queries.

- [Streaming lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_lakehouse)
- [Spark Streaming (DStreams)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Streaming_(DStreams))
- [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines)

# Stream-static join

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream-static_join

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Stream-table join, stream enrichment join</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">A streaming DataFrame, a static (batch) DataFrame or table, join keys; no streaming state</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark); related forms in [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) SQL (temporal and lookup joins)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Stream-stream join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream-stream_join), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Broadcast join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Broadcast_join), [Stateful stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stateful_stream_processing)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming programming guide (join operations, support matrix) and Real-time Mode guide, the Databricks "Work with joins" page, and the Apache Flink 2.3 SQL "Joins" page</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), a **stream-static join** joins a streaming DataFrame with a static DataFrame, for example a stream of orders with a table of customers. Each micro-batch of the stream is joined with the static side, and the join keeps no streaming state, so it needs no [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark). Structured Streaming has supported stream-static joins, inner and some outer types, since Spark 2.0.[^ss-ss] It is the usual way to enrich events with reference or dimension data held in a lakehouse table.

## How does a stream-static join work?

The static side is an ordinary batch DataFrame read with `spark.read`, and the streaming side comes from `spark.readStream`. The join is written like a batch join:[^ss-ss]

```python
customers = spark.read.table("main.crm.customers")          # static side
orders = spark.readStream.table("main.sales.orders")       # streaming side

enriched = orders.join(customers, "customer_id", "left_outer")

(enriched.writeStream
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/checkpoints/orders_enriched")
    .toTable("main.sales.orders_enriched"))
```

Because only the streaming side changes, each batch's new rows are joined with the static data and the result is final; nothing is buffered for later matches. The Spark guide states that stream-static joins are not stateful and need no state management.[^ss-ss] This is the main difference from a [stream-stream join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream-stream_join), which buffers both inputs.

## Which join types are supported?

The support matrix in Spark 4.3.0 allows only the join types in which the streaming side's rows can be completed from the static side alone:[^ss-matrix]

| Left input | Right input | Inner | Left outer | Right outer | Full outer | Left semi |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stream | Static | Yes | Yes | No | No | Yes |
| Static | Stream | Yes | No | Yes | No | No |

The unsupported types would need to emit a static row once it is clear that no streaming row will ever match it, which cannot be known for an unbounded stream without state.

## How is the static side refreshed?

The Databricks documentation, for a static side stored in [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), states that each micro-batch joins the latest valid version of the static Delta table with the records of that micro-batch. The static table should therefore change slowly. If it changes between runs, reprocessing the same streaming data can give different results, so the output is not deterministic while the static side is changing.[^db-join]

Rows already written are not revised when the static side changes later. An order joined with a customer's old address keeps the old address in the output, because the join keeps no state with which to revisit it.[^ss-ss] Pipelines that need updates on both sides use a [stream-stream join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream-stream_join) or a materialized view instead; Databricks recommends a materialized view for incremental results of an inner join.[^db-join]

## Stream-static joins in Real-time Mode

Real-time Mode, added in Spark 4.1.0, supports stream-static joins only when the static side is broadcast with the `broadcast(...)` hint, because the join must not add a shuffle.[^rtm]

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

enriched = orders.join(broadcast(customers), "customer_id")
```

In micro-batch mode the hint is optional and follows the usual [join strategy](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Join_strategy_hints) rules.

## Stream-static join vs stream-stream join

|  | Stream-static join | Stream-stream join |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inputs | One streaming, one batch DataFrame[^ss-ss] | Two streaming DataFrames[^ss-sts] |
| State | None[^ss-ss] | Both inputs buffered in the state store[^ss-sts] |
| Watermark | Not needed[^db-join] | Needed to bound state; required for outer and semi joins[^ss-sts] |
| Since | Spark 2.0[^ss-ss] | Spark 2.3[^ss-sts] |
| Real-time Mode (Spark 4.3.0) | Supported with a broadcast static side[^rtm] | Not supported[^rtm] |

## Comparison with Flink

[Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) SQL has two related joins. A **temporal join** joins against a versioned table, so that each row can be matched with the version valid at its event time. A **lookup join** enriches a table with data queried from an external system; one side needs a processing-time attribute and the other must be backed by a lookup source connector.[^flink-join] A Spark stream-static join against a Delta table is closest to a processing-time lookup: each batch sees the table as it is when the batch runs.[^db-join]

- [Broadcast join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Broadcast_join)
- [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)
- [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming)

# Stream-stream join

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream-stream_join

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Streaming join, interval join (Flink)</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 2.3</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Two streaming inputs, join keys, [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) on each input, event-time range or window condition, buffered state</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) (interval join, regular join), Kafka Streams (`JoinWindows`)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Stream-static join](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream-static_join), [Watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), [State store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/State_store), [Stateful stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stateful_stream_processing)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming programming guide (join operations, support matrix, recovery semantics) and Real-time Mode guide, the Apache Flink 2.3 DataStream "Joining" and SQL "Joins" pages, and the Kafka Streams 4.4 DSL developer guide</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), a **stream-stream join** joins two streaming DataFrames, so that each new row from one stream is matched with rows that have arrived, or will arrive, on the other. Because a match can come later, Spark buffers past rows of both inputs as state; [watermarks](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) on both inputs and a time condition in the join let Spark drop buffered rows that can no longer match, so that state does not grow without limit. Spark added stream-stream joins in Spark 2.3.[^ss-join] The result of the join is the same as a batch join over the same data.[^ss-joinops]

## Why does a stream-stream join need state?

At any moment, both sides of a stream-stream join are incomplete. A row received now on one input can match a row that the other input has not received yet. Spark therefore keeps past input from both streams in the [state store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/State_store), matches every new row against it, and handles late and out-of-order data the same way as for aggregations.[^ss-join]

Without limits, all past input must be kept, because any new row could match any old one.[^ss-inner] In a long-running query, that state grows until the query fails or slows down.

## How do watermarks and time constraints bound state?

To let Spark clear old rows, a join needs two things:[^ss-inner]
1. a watermark on both inputs, saying how late each input's data can be; and
1. an event-time constraint between the inputs, so that Spark can tell when an old row of one input can no longer match the other. The constraint is either a time range, such as `leftTime BETWEEN rightTime AND rightTime + INTERVAL 1 HOUR`, or a join on event-time windows, such as `leftTimeWindow = rightTimeWindow`.

With both, the rows kept for each side are roughly those within the other side's watermark delay plus the width of the time range. The guarantee follows the watermark rule: with a 2-hour watermark, no row less than 2 hours late is dropped, but a row later than that may or may not be processed.[^ss-join]

### Example

The Spark guide's example joins ad impressions with ad clicks. Impressions can be up to 2 hours late, clicks up to 3 hours late, and a click counts if it happens within 1 hour after its impression.[^ss-inner]

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import expr

impressions = spark.readStream.table("main.ads.impressions")   # impressionAdId, impressionTime
clicks = spark.readStream.table("main.ads.clicks")             # clickAdId, clickTime

joined = (impressions.withWatermark("impressionTime", "2 hours")
    .join(
        clicks.withWatermark("clickTime", "3 hours"),
        expr("""
            clickAdId = impressionAdId AND
            clickTime >= impressionTime AND
            clickTime <= impressionTime + interval 1 hour
        """),
        "leftOuter",
    ))
```

## Which join types are supported?

Inner joins are supported on any columns and conditions; watermarks and time constraints are optional, but without them state is unbounded. Outer and semi joins require them, because Spark must know when a row will never match in order to emit the outer row with nulls, or to evict an unmatched left row.[^ss-join] The support matrix in Spark 4.3.0:[^ss-matrix]

| Join type | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Inner | Supported; watermarks on both sides and a time constraint are optional and enable state cleanup |
| Left outer | Watermark on the right side and a time constraint required; left watermark optional, for full cleanup |
| Right outer | Watermark on the left side and a time constraint required; right watermark optional |
| Full outer | Watermark on one side and a time constraint required; the other watermark optional |
| Left semi | Watermark on the right side and a time constraint required; left watermark optional |

Other rules apply. Joins can be chained (`df1.join(df2, ...).join(df3, ...)`), and a query with a stream-stream join must use append [output mode](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Output_mode). `mapGroupsWithState` and `flatMapGroupsWithState` cannot be used before or after a join, but in append mode aggregations, deduplication and other joins can.[^ss-matrix] Changing the join type, the equi-join columns or the input schema is not allowed between restarts from the same [streaming checkpoint](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_checkpoint).[^ss-changes] Stream-stream joins are not supported in Real-time Mode as of Spark 4.3.0.[^rtm]

## Why are outer join results delayed?

An outer row with nulls is emitted only after Spark is sure no match will arrive, so its delay depends on the watermark delay and the time range. In the micro-batch engine, the watermark advances at the end of a batch and the next batch uses it to clean state and emit outer rows. Since a batch runs only when there is new data, outer output can be held back if either input stops receiving data for a while.[^ss-outer]

## Stream-stream joins in other engines

[Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink)'s DataStream API has an **interval join**: elements of stream B with the same key match an element of stream A when `a.timestamp + lowerBound <= b.timestamp <= a.timestamp + upperBound`. It supports only inner joins.[^flink-dsjoin]

Flink SQL distinguishes **regular joins**, which keep both inputs in state forever unless a state TTL is configured (which can affect correctness), from **interval joins**, which need at least one equi-join predicate and a condition that bounds time on both sides.[^flink-sqljoin] A Spark join with a time-range condition and watermarks corresponds to an interval join; a Spark inner join without them corresponds to a regular join without TTL.

Kafka Streams uses `JoinWindows`, a sliding window over record timestamps, for windowed stream-stream joins.[^kstreams]

|  | Spark stream-stream join | Flink DataStream interval join | Flink SQL interval join | Flink SQL regular join |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Time bound | Optional for inner, required for outer and semi[^ss-join] | Required (lower and upper bound)[^flink-dsjoin] | Required on both sides[^flink-sqljoin] | None[^flink-sqljoin] |
| Can state grow without limit? | Yes, for an inner join without watermarks and a time constraint[^ss-inner] | No; the time bounds are part of the join[^flink-dsjoin] | No; the time condition is required[^flink-sqljoin] | Yes, unless a state TTL is configured[^flink-sqljoin] |

## See also

# Streaming checkpoint

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_checkpoint

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Checkpoint location, `checkpointLocation`</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Offset log (`offsets/`), commit log (`commits/`), state (`state/`), query metadata (`metadata`)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Checkpointing (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Checkpointing_(Spark)), [State store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/State_store), [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics), [Flink checkpoint and savepoint](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Flink_checkpoint_and_savepoint)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming programming guide (recovering from failures, recovery semantics after changes) and miscellaneous notes, and `StreamingCheckpointConstants.scala`, `StreamingQueryCheckpointMetadata.scala`, `StreamMetadata.scala`, `CommitLog.scala`, `OffsetSeq.scala` and `SQLConf.scala` at tag v4.3.0 of apache/spark, the Delta Lake table streaming documentation and the Apache Flink 2.3 "Checkpoints vs. Savepoints" page</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), a **streaming checkpoint** is the directory, set with the `checkpointLocation` option, where a streaming query records which input offsets each micro-batch covered, which batches finished, and the state of its stateful operators, so that after a failure or a restart the query continues exactly where it stopped.[^ss-ckpt] A checkpoint belongs to one query. Some changes to the query can be made between restarts from the same checkpoint and others cannot. Lineage checkpoints of RDDs and DataFrames are a different feature; see [Checkpointing (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Checkpointing_(Spark)).

## What is inside a streaming checkpoint?

At tag v4.3.0, Spark names four entries under the checkpoint root: `offsets`, `commits`, `state` and `metadata`.[^consts]

| Entry | Contents | Written |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `offsets/` | The offset log: one file per batch with the offsets of every source for that batch, plus a set of session configurations that must stay fixed for the query[^offsetseq] | Before the batch is processed[^commitlog] |
| `commits/` | The commit log: one file per batch that marks the batch as complete[^commitlog] | After the batch succeeds, before the next batch starts[^commitlog] |
| `state/` | Versioned files of the [state store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/State_store), per stateful operator and partition | At the end of each batch of a stateful query |
| `metadata` | The query's unique id, which stays the same across restarts[^streammeta] | When the query first starts |

The order of writes is what makes recovery work. For each batch, Spark writes the batch's offsets to the offset log, processes the batch, and then writes the batch to the commit log.[^commitlog] On restart, a batch that has an offset entry but no commit entry is run again with exactly the same offsets. Combined with a replayable source and an idempotent or transactional sink, this gives the end-to-end guarantee described in [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics).

Spark keeps a bounded history. `spark.sql.streaming.minBatchesToRetain` (default 100, since 2.1.1) is the minimum number of batches that stay recoverable; state, offset and commit log files older than that are eligible for cleanup.[^sqlconf]

The checkpoint location must be a path in an HDFS-compatible, fault-tolerant file system, such as HDFS or an object store.[^ss-ckpt] `spark.sql.streaming.checkpointLocation` sets a default parent directory for queries that do not set the option.[^sqlconf]

## What is safe to change between restarts?

The Spark guide lists which query changes are allowed when restarting from the same checkpoint. "Allowed" means the query starts, but whether the result is well defined depends on the change; "not allowed" means the restart is likely to fail with unpredictable errors.[^ss-changes]

| Change | Verdict | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Number or type of input sources | Not allowed | Adding a second Kafka source |
| Source rate limits | Allowed | Adding `maxOffsetsPerTrigger` |
| Subscribed topics or input files | Generally not allowed | `subscribe` from `topic` to `newTopic` |
| Sink type | Some combinations | File sink to Kafka sink is allowed; Kafka sink to file sink is not |
| File sink output directory | Not allowed | Changing `path` |
| Kafka sink topic | Allowed | Changing `topic` |
| Filters and projections | Allowed; a different output schema only if the sink accepts it | Adding a `where` |
| Stateful operators (aggregation keys or aggregates, deduplication columns, stream-stream join type or keys, user state schema) | Not allowed | Adding a grouping column |

Some configurations are also fixed for the life of a checkpoint. The Spark notes name `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` (state is hash-partitioned by key, so the number of state partitions cannot change), `spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass` and `spark.sql.streaming.multipleWatermarkPolicy`; to change them, start a new query with a new checkpoint.[^misc] Spark stores the values of these and other state-related configurations in the offset log and reuses them on restart, whatever the session sets.[^offsetseq]

[transformWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState) is an exception for user state: state variables can be added and removed between runs, and with `spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.encodingFormat` set to `avro`, fields of a state variable's value can be added, removed, widened or reordered.[^tws]

## What happens if the checkpoint is deleted?

Without its checkpoint, a query starts as a new query: sources start from their configured starting position, state is empty, and batch ids start again from 0. Sinks that deduplicate by batch id must be told. The [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) documentation warns that a query restarted with a new checkpoint must use a different `txnAppId` in [foreachBatch](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/ForeachBatch) writes; otherwise its writes are ignored as duplicates.[^delta]

Delta Lake's `VACUUM` skips directories whose names begin with an underscore, so a checkpoint can be kept next to the table it writes, for example in `<table>/_checkpoints`.[^delta]

## Example

```python
(spark.readStream.format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker:9092")
    .option("subscribe", "orders")
    .option("maxOffsetsPerTrigger", 100000)   # safe to change between restarts
    .load()
    .writeStream
    .option("checkpointLocation", "s3a://lake/checkpoints/orders_bronze")
    .toTable("main.sales.orders_bronze"))
```

## Comparison with Flink checkpoints

[Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) also uses the word checkpoint. A Flink checkpoint is a recovery mechanism for unexpected job failures; Flink creates, owns and releases it without user action, and deletes it when the user terminates the job unless retention is configured. A Flink **savepoint** is created with the same mechanism but is owned by the user and designed for portability, for example for upgrades and redeployment; the Flink documentation compares the two to backups and recovery logs in a database.[^flink-cvs] See [Flink checkpoint and savepoint](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Flink_checkpoint_and_savepoint).

A Spark streaming checkpoint is closer to a retained Flink checkpoint: it is a directory the user names, it stays after the query stops, and a restarted or changed query reads it, within the limits listed above.[^ss-ckpt][^ss-changes]

# Streaming deduplication

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_deduplication

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Stream deduplication</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Unique identifier column(s), [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), deduplication state in the [state store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/State_store)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming): `dropDuplicates`, `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark` (Spark 3.5.0 and later); [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) insert-only `MERGE` in [foreachBatch](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/ForeachBatch)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics), [State store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/State_store), [Stateful stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stateful_stream_processing)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming programming guide (streaming deduplication, recovery semantics) and Real-time Mode guide, `python/pyspark/sql/dataframe.py` at tag v4.3.0 of apache/spark, SPARK-42931, and the Delta Lake merge documentation</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), **streaming deduplication** is removing repeated records from a stream by a unique identifier, so that each event is passed on once even if the source delivers it several times. Spark keeps the identifiers it has already seen as state; `dropDuplicates` does this with or without a [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), and `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark`, added in Spark 3.5.0, deduplicates within the watermark delay when duplicates carry different event times.[^ss-dedup][^jira] Duplicates are common in streaming because producers and connectors retry, and at-least-once delivery means a record may arrive more than once.

## How does dropDuplicates work on a stream?

On a batch DataFrame, `dropDuplicates` (available since Spark 1.4.0) simply drops duplicate rows. On a streaming DataFrame, it keeps the data it needs from all earlier triggers as state in order to drop duplicates in later ones.[^df] The Spark guide describes two ways to use it:[^ss-dedup]

- **Without a watermark**, there is no bound on when a duplicate may arrive, so the query keeps state for every record it has ever seen. State grows for the life of the query.
- **With a watermark**, if duplicates arrive no later than a known bound, the query sets a watermark on an event-time column and deduplicates on both the identifier and the event-time column. Spark then drops state for records older than the watermark, which bounds state.

Records older than the watermark are dropped, to avoid any chance of emitting a duplicate.[^df]

```python
events = spark.readStream.table("main.iot.raw_events")   # columns: event_id, event_time, ...

# Unbounded state: every event_id is remembered
dedup_all = events.dropDuplicates(["event_id"])

# Bounded state: event_id plus event_time, cleaned by the watermark
dedup_bounded = (events
    .withWatermark("event_time", "10 seconds")
    .dropDuplicates(["event_id", "event_time"]))
```

## What is dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark?

The bounded form of `dropDuplicates` works only if the event time is part of the identity of a record, so that true duplicates share it. Sometimes they do not, for example when a non-idempotent writer sets the event time at write time and a retried write gets a new one. `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark` handles this case: it deduplicates on the identifier alone, within the time range of the watermark.[^ss-dedup]

```python
dedup = (events
    .withWatermark("event_time", "10 hours")
    .dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"]))
```

The guarantee is that events are deduplicated as long as the distance between the earliest and the latest copy is smaller than the watermark delay, so the delay should be longer than the largest time difference expected between duplicates. A watermark is required, and the operator works only on streaming DataFrames. Data older than the watermark is dropped.[^df][^ss-dedup]

## dropDuplicates vs dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark

|  | `dropDuplicates` without watermark | `dropDuplicates` with watermark | `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Available since | Spark 1.4.0[^df] | Spark 1.4.0[^df] | Spark 3.5.0[^jira] |
| Key | Identifier columns[^ss-dedup] | Identifier and event-time columns[^ss-dedup] | Identifier columns only[^ss-dedup] |
| State | Unbounded[^ss-dedup] | Bounded by the watermark[^ss-dedup] | Bounded by the watermark[^ss-dedup] |
| Duplicates with different event times | Removed[^ss-dedup] | Not removed, because event time is part of the key | Removed if within the watermark delay[^df] |
| Batch DataFrames | Supported[^df] | Supported[^df] | Streaming only[^df] |
| Real-time Mode (Spark 4.3.0) | Supported[^rtm] | Supported[^rtm] | Not supported[^rtm] |

The deduplication columns are part of the query's state schema: changing their number or type is not allowed between restarts from the same [streaming checkpoint](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_checkpoint).[^ss-changes] The plain `distinct` operation is not supported on streaming DataFrames.[^ss-unsup]

## Deduplicating against a table

`dropDuplicates` only removes duplicates that the query itself sees within its state. To avoid inserting a record that is already in the target table, for example one written by an earlier query or a backfill, the [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) documentation uses an insert-only `MERGE` inside [foreachBatch](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/ForeachBatch), which inserts only rows whose key is not yet in the table.[^delta-merge]

```python
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

target = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "main.iot.events")

def insert_new(batch_df, batch_id):
    (target.alias("t")
        .merge(batch_df.dropDuplicates(["event_id"]).alias("s"),
               "t.event_id = s.event_id")
        .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
        .execute())

(dedup_bounded.writeStream
    .foreachBatch(insert_new)
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/checkpoints/iot_events")
    .start())
```

Deduplication in the stream and an insert-only merge into the table can be combined: the first bounds the work per batch, the second protects the table across queries and restarts.

# Streaming lakehouse

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Streaming_lakehouse

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Real-time lakehouse, streaming into the lakehouse</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data engineering, [stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Streaming writers, [Open table formats](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), incremental and change-data reads, table maintenance</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi), [Apache Paimon](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Paimon), [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink), [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), [Medallion architecture](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Medallion_architecture), [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics), [Small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 Spark and Flink documentation, the Delta Lake streaming, change data feed and optimization documentation, the Apache Hudi 1.2.1 documentation, the Apache Paimon 1.4 documentation and 2024 graduation announcement, the Apache Fluss 0.9 documentation and the Spark 4.3.0 Declarative Pipelines guide</Verified>

A **streaming lakehouse** is a data architecture in which streaming jobs write directly into tables in an [open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), so that the same tables serve both streaming readers, which consume new changes incrementally, and batch readers, which query a consistent snapshot. It applies the [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse) idea to continuously arriving data: instead of keeping a separate real-time store next to the lake, the table itself is the hand-off point between pipeline stages.

## Terminology

The term is used loosely and has no single defining paper or specification. Some projects use it as a name for their own design:

- [Apache Paimon](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Paimon), formerly Flink Table Store, describes itself as "a lake format for building Lakehouse Architecture for both streaming and batch operations".[^paimon-tlp][^paimon-docs] The Apache Software Foundation's announcement of Paimon's graduation to a top-level project, on 16 April 2024, calls it "a streaming data lake platform" and a format that enables real-time lakehouse architectures.[^paimon-tlp]
- Apache Fluss, a streaming storage project (incubating at its 0.9 release), uses "Streaming Lakehouse" as the name of the setup in which its tiering service moves table data into Paimon or Iceberg, with recent data held in Fluss and historical data in the lake table, and queries combining both.[^fluss]

[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) and [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) document the same pattern (streaming writes and incremental reads on one table) without using the name. This page uses "streaming lakehouse" for the general pattern, not for any one product.

## How it works

A streaming lakehouse has three moving parts.

### Streaming writes

A streaming engine writes each micro-batch or checkpoint interval as one atomic commit to the table. [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) can write to Iceberg tables in append or complete output mode, to Delta tables, and to Hudi tables.[^iceberg-ss][^delta-stream][^hudi-ss] The Iceberg Flink sink commits to the table after each successful Flink checkpoint and supports upserts on tables with a primary key or identifier fields.[^iceberg-flink] Because each commit is atomic, batch readers never see a half-written batch, and the sink can be part of an [exactly-once](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics) pipeline.[^delta-stream]

### Incremental and change-data reads

Downstream jobs read only what changed since their last position, which turns each table into a source for the next stage, as in a [medallion architecture](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Medallion_architecture). What a reader can see differs by format:

| Format | Incremental read | Updates and deletes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) | Spark streaming reads start from a timestamp (`stream-from-timestamp`); Flink streaming reads start from a snapshot and poll for new ones[^iceberg-ss][^iceberg-flinkq] | Spark streaming reads only append snapshots; overwrite and delete snapshots raise an error unless skipped with `streaming-skip-overwrite-snapshots` or `streaming-skip-delete-snapshots`[^iceberg-ss] |
| [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) | A streaming read processes the existing table and then new data[^delta-stream] | Plain streaming reads fail on non-append commits unless `skipChangeCommits` is set; the change data feed (`readChangeFeed`) returns row-level inserts, updates and deletes[^delta-stream][^delta-cdf] |
| [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) | Incremental queries return data written since an instant on the table's timeline[^hudi-types] | Incremental CDC queries return inserts, updates and deletes with before and after images[^hudi-types] |
| [Apache Paimon](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Paimon) | Streaming updates on an LSM-tree structure, typically written with Flink[^paimon-docs] | Changelog producers generate a complete changelog for merge engines[^paimon-docs] |

The Delta change data feed is enabled with the table property `delta.enableChangeDataFeed` and adds the columns `_change_type` (`insert`, `update_preimage`, `update_postimage` or `delete`), `_commit_version` and `_commit_timestamp`. Only changes made after it is enabled are recorded.[^delta-cdf]

### Declarative streaming tables

[Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines) (SDP) expresses the pattern declaratively. An SDP **streaming table** is a table filled by one or more streaming flows that process only new data, and it can read from any source that `spark.readStream` supports, including Kafka.[^sdp] In Spark 4.3, **Auto CDC** applies a stream of change events to a target streaming table by key and sequence value, handling out-of-order and duplicate events.[^sdp]

```sql
CREATE STREAMING TABLE orders
AS SELECT * FROM STREAM orders_source;
```

## Example

This PySpark sketch writes a Kafka topic into an Iceberg table once a minute, then reads the same table as a batch snapshot and as an incremental stream. It assumes the Iceberg Spark runtime and Kafka connector are on the classpath and that a catalog named `lake` is configured.

```python
orders = (
    spark.readStream.format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker:9092")
    .option("subscribe", "orders")
    .load()
    .selectExpr("CAST(key AS STRING) AS order_id",
                "CAST(value AS STRING) AS payload",
                "timestamp")
)

(orders.writeStream.format("iceberg")
    .outputMode("append")
    .trigger(processingTime="1 minute")          # one commit per minute
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/bronze_orders")
    .toTable("lake.bronze.orders"))

spark.table("lake.bronze.orders").count()        # batch reader: a snapshot
spark.readStream.format("iceberg").load("lake.bronze.orders")  # streaming reader
```

## Limits

### Latency is bounded by commit frequency

Readers see new data only after it is committed, so freshness is set by how often the writer commits, not by how fast the engine processes records. Iceberg recommends a trigger interval of at least 1 minute for streaming writes, because frequent commits create many data files, manifests and snapshots.[^iceberg-ss] With Flink, Iceberg commits follow checkpoints, so the checkpoint interval is also the commit interval.[^iceberg-flink] Systems such as Fluss address this by keeping the most recent data in a separate low-latency store and combining it with the lake table at query time.[^fluss]

### Small files and metadata growth

<Hatnote>See also: [Small files problem](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Small_files_problem)</Hatnote>

Each streaming commit usually writes small files. Iceberg's documentation states that streaming writes typically produce small amounts of data per commit, leading to many small files, and recommends compacting data files (`rewrite_data_files`), expiring old snapshots and rewriting manifests (`rewrite_manifests`) on tables written by streams.[^iceberg-ss] Delta Lake offers `OPTIMIZE` to coalesce small files, and since Delta 3.1.0, auto compaction and optimized writes.[^delta-opt] In Hudi, merge-on-read tables lower write latency for near real-time availability, at the cost of query performance until log files are compacted.[^hudi-types] See [Copy-on-write and merge-on-read](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Copy-on-write_and_merge-on-read).

### Updates downstream

Append-only incremental reads are the simplest case. When an upstream table receives updates or deletes, downstream streams need a change feed (Delta, Hudi, Paimon) or must skip those commits and lose the changes, as with Iceberg's and Delta's skip options.[^iceberg-ss][^delta-stream]

# Structured Streaming

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">[Apache Software Foundation](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Software_Foundation) ([Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) project)</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">Spark 2.0.0 (2016-07-26, experimental)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">Spark 4.3.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-30</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Scala, Java, Python</Field>
  <Field name="type">Stream processing engine</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[Programming guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/streaming/index.html)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/apache/spark](https://github.com/apache/spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming guides (overview, APIs, Real-time Mode, transformWithState) and the Spark 2.0.0, 2.2.0, 4.0.0, 4.1.0 and 4.3.0 release notes</Verified>

**Structured Streaming** is the stream processing engine of [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), built on the Spark SQL engine, in which a streaming computation is written with the same DataFrame and Dataset operations as a batch computation on static data.[^overview] Spark runs the query incrementally as new data arrives and keeps the result up to date. Through checkpointing and write-ahead logs, Structured Streaming provides end-to-end exactly-once guarantees with sources and sinks that support them.[^overview]

## Programming model

Structured Streaming treats a live data stream as a table that grows as new rows arrive. A streaming query is a query on that input table, and its output is a result table that Spark updates each time it processes new data.[^start]

The **output mode** says what part of the result table is written to the sink after each update:[^start]

- **Append**: only rows added since the last trigger. It applies to queries whose existing result rows never change.
- **Complete**: the entire result table.
- **Update**: only rows that changed since the last trigger (available since Spark 2.1.1). Without aggregations it behaves like append mode.

Streaming queries can aggregate over event-time windows, including tumbling, sliding and session windows. A **watermark** tells Spark how late data may arrive, so that it can finalize old windows and drop their state. Structured Streaming also supports stream-static joins, stream-stream joins and deduplication.[^apis]

The following PySpark example counts rows from the built-in `rate` test source in 30-second event-time windows and prints finished windows to the console. It runs on Spark 4.3.

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import window

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("rate-counts").getOrCreate()

events = spark.readStream.format("rate").option("rowsPerSecond", 10).load()

counts = (
    events.withWatermark("timestamp", "1 minute")
    .groupBy(window("timestamp", "30 seconds"))
    .count()
)

query = (
    counts.writeStream.outputMode("append")
    .format("console")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/tmp/rate-counts-checkpoint")
    .start()
)
query.awaitTermination()
```

## Sources, sinks and state

Built-in sources include files, Apache Kafka, a socket source for testing and rate sources that generate test data.[^apis] Built-in sinks include files, Kafka, `foreach`, `foreachBatch`, and console and memory sinks for debugging.[^apis] Connectors for [open table formats](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format) such as [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) and [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) let their tables serve as streaming sources and sinks.[^n1][^n2]

Stateful operators such as aggregations, joins and deduplication keep state between batches in a **state store**. Since Spark 3.2, Spark includes a RocksDB-based state store provider that keeps state in native memory and on local disk instead of the JVM heap.[^apis]

`transformWithState`, available since Spark 4.0, is the operator for arbitrary stateful processing. It replaces the older `mapGroupsWithState` and `flatMapGroupsWithState` APIs in Scala and `applyInPandasWithState` in Python, and adds features such as timers and time-to-live (TTL) eviction of state. It is available in Scala, Java and Python.[^tws]

## Execution modes and triggers

By default, Structured Streaming runs a query as a series of small batch jobs (**micro-batches**), with end-to-end latencies as low as about 100 milliseconds.[^overview] The **trigger** controls timing:[^apis]

| Trigger | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| Unspecified (default) | Starts the next micro-batch as soon as the previous one finishes. |
| Fixed interval (`processingTime`) | Starts micro-batches at a set interval; skips a batch when there is no new data. |
| Available-now (`availableNow`) | Processes all data available at start, possibly in several micro-batches, then stops. |
| One-time | Processes available data in one micro-batch, then stops. Deprecated in favour of available-now. |
| Continuous | Experimental low-latency mode, added in Spark 2.3, with at-least-once guarantees.[^overview] |
| Real-time | Real-time Mode, added in Spark 4.1.0 (see below). |

**Real-time Mode** runs long-lived tasks, one per input partition, that process records as they arrive instead of waiting for a batch boundary. The Spark documentation states that this lowers end-to-end latency from the micro-batch floor to roughly the time needed to process and send one record. The trigger's duration (default 5 minutes) then mainly sets how often the query checkpoints.[^rtm] Spark 4.1.0 supported stateless queries in this mode.[^r410] Spark 4.3.0 added streaming aggregation, `dropDuplicates` and the Scala and Java `transformWithState` operator, using a pipelined shuffle; stream-stream joins and `flatMapGroupsWithState` are not yet supported in this mode.[^rtm][^r430] In PySpark, the mode is enabled with `.trigger(realTime="5 minutes")`.[^rtm]

## History

Spark 2.0.0 shipped the first, experimental release of Structured Streaming as a higher-level streaming API on Spark SQL and the Catalyst optimizer.[^n3] Spark 2.2.0 removed the experimental label and declared the APIs generally available (SPARK-20844).[^n4] Spark 4.0.0 added the Arbitrary State API v2 (`transformWithState`) and a State Data Source for reading state when debugging.[^n5] Real-time Mode followed in 4.1.0 (SPARK-53736) and gained stateful queries in 4.3.0.[^r410][^r430]

The older Spark Streaming API, based on discretized streams (DStreams), is described in the Spark 4.3 documentation as the previous generation of Spark's streaming engine; it receives no further updates, and the documentation directs new work to Structured Streaming.[^n6]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Structured Streaming typically ingests events from a message bus into bronze tables and keeps downstream tables current. [Spark Declarative Pipelines](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Declarative_Pipelines) builds on it: SDP streaming tables are filled by Structured Streaming flows, and SDP can read from any source that `spark.readStream` supports.[^n7]

# Time travel (SQL)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Time_travel_(SQL)

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">AS OF query, temporal query, snapshot query</Field>
  <Field name="field">Table formats and SQL</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">VERSION AS OF, TIMESTAMP AS OF, table versions or snapshots, retention</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) with [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) and [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi); [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), Snowflake, BigQuery</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), [Data Source V2](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_Source_V2), [Catalog plugin API (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Catalog_plugin_API_(Spark))</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (SqlBaseParser.g4, SQLConf.scala, TableCatalog.java, TimeTravelSpec.scala, DataFrameReader.scala, docs/sql-migration-guide.md), the Spark 3.3.0, 3.4.0, 4.0.0 and 4.3.0 release notes, Delta Lake batch reads and writes docs, Apache Iceberg 1.12.0 Spark queries and configuration docs, Apache Hudi 1.2.1 SQL queries and quick start docs, Trino 484 Iceberg and Delta Lake connector docs, the Snowflake AT/BEFORE reference and the BigQuery query syntax and time travel docs</Verified>

**Time travel** in SQL is a query that reads a table as it was at an earlier version or point in time, written in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) SQL as `SELECT ... FROM t VERSION AS OF v` or `SELECT ... FROM t TIMESTAMP AS OF ts`.[^grammar] Spark parses the clause, and the table format resolves it: [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) maps the version to a commit in its transaction log, and [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) maps it to a snapshot ID, branch or tag. Time travel is used to reproduce reports and models, audit changes and recover from bad writes, and it works only while the old data and metadata are still retained.[^delta]

## What is the syntax in Apache Spark?

The Spark SQL grammar accepts four spellings after a table name: `VERSION AS OF` and `FOR SYSTEM_VERSION AS OF` take an integer or string literal; `TIMESTAMP AS OF` and `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF` take an expression.[^grammar] The timestamp expression must be deterministic and evaluable once at analysis time, and a query cannot carry both a version and a timestamp.[^ttspec]

Spark 3.3.0 added the `AS OF` syntax (SPARK-37219), and Spark 3.4.0 allowed a scalar subquery in the timestamp (SPARK-39306).[^r330][^r340] Spark 4.0.0 added time travel options to the `spark.read` API (SPARK-45575); the option names are `versionAsOf` and `timestampAsOf` by default, configurable with `spark.sql.timeTravelVersionKey` and `spark.sql.timeTravelTimestampKey`.[^r400][^sqlconf]

Spark 4.3.0 added an `@` suffix on table names (SPARK-57421, SPARK-58012): `name@v123` reads version 123, and `name@20240101000000000` (format `yyyyMMddHHmmssSSS`, in the session time zone) reads the table at that timestamp to millisecond precision. The suffix is controlled by `spark.sql.timeTravel.atSyntax.enabled`, default `true`.[^r430][^sqlconf] Also since 4.3, Spark rejects these time travel options on catalog-backed Data Source V2 writes with `UNSUPPORTED_FEATURE.TIME_TRAVEL`, because a write must target the current table state.[^migration]

## How does a connector implement time travel?

For catalog tables, Spark passes the parsed clause to the [catalog plugin](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Catalog_plugin_API_(Spark)). `TableCatalog` has `loadTable(ident, String version)` and `loadTable(ident, long timestamp)`, where the timestamp is in microseconds since the Unix epoch. Their default implementations throw a "no such table" error, so a catalog that does not override them does not support time travel.[^tablecatalog]

## Example

Spark SQL against a Delta Lake or Iceberg table named `sales.orders`:[^delta][^iceq][^sqlconf]

```sql
-- Delta Lake: commit version from DESCRIBE HISTORY
SELECT * FROM sales.orders VERSION AS OF 12;
SELECT * FROM sales.orders TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-11-01 00:00:00';

-- Iceberg: snapshot ID, branch or tag name
SELECT * FROM lake.sales.orders VERSION AS OF 10963874102873;
SELECT * FROM lake.sales.orders VERSION AS OF 'audit-branch';

-- Spark 4.3 @ suffix (for catalogs that implement time travel)
SELECT * FROM sales.orders@v12;
```

The same reads with the DataFrame API, where `spark.read.table` passes its options to the relation that Spark resolves:[^reader][^r400]

```python
df_v12 = spark.read.option("versionAsOf", 12).table("sales.orders")
df_nov = spark.read.option("timestampAsOf", "2026-11-01 00:00:00").table("sales.orders")
```

## How do table formats compare?

|  | Delta Lake | Apache Iceberg | Apache Hudi |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What a version is | A commit version in the transaction log, listed by `DESCRIBE HISTORY`[^delta] | A snapshot ID, or a branch or tag name[^iceq] | A commit time (instant)[^hudiqs] |
| Spark SQL syntax | `VERSION AS OF`, `TIMESTAMP AS OF`[^delta] | `VERSION AS OF`, `TIMESTAMP AS OF`, `FOR SYSTEM_VERSION AS OF`, `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF`[^iceq] | `TIMESTAMP AS OF`[^hudisql] |
| Timestamp forms | Any expression castable to a timestamp, such as `'2018-10-18'` or `current_timestamp() - interval 12 hours`; no subqueries[^delta] | Timestamp string, or Unix time in seconds in SQL[^iceq] | `yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS`, `yyyy-MM-dd` or `yyyyMMddHHmmssSSS`[^hudisql] |
| DataFrame options | `versionAsOf`, `timestampAsOf`[^delta] | `snapshot-id`, `as-of-timestamp` (milliseconds), `branch`, `tag`[^iceq] | `as.of.instant`[^hudiqs] |
| What limits how far back | `delta.logRetentionDuration` (default 30 days) and `VACUUM`, governed by `delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration` (default 7 days)[^delta] | Snapshot expiration; `history.expire.max-snapshot-age-ms` defaults to 5 days and `history.expire.min-snapshots-to-keep` to 1[^icecfg] | Not described on the cited Hudi pages |

Delta Lake documents that, by default, a table can be read up to 30 days back unless `VACUUM` has run or the retention properties were changed. Because version timestamps come from log file timestamps, time travel by timestamp can break if the table directory is copied to a new location, while time travel by version is unaffected.[^delta]

Iceberg branches and tags give names to snapshots. A query by snapshot ID or timestamp uses the schema of that snapshot, a query on a branch uses the table's current schema, and a query on a tag uses the schema of the tagged snapshot.[^iceq] Iceberg snapshots remain until they are expired, so expiration settings, not a fixed window, decide what can be read.[^icemaint]

## Time travel in other engines

| Engine | Syntax |
| --- | --- |
| [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino) 484 (Iceberg and Delta Lake connectors) | `FOR VERSION AS OF` and `FOR TIMESTAMP AS OF`; on Iceberg, the version can be a branch or tag name[^n1][^n2] |
| Snowflake | `AT` or `BEFORE` in the `FROM` clause, for example `AT (TIMESTAMP => ...)`[^n3] |
| BigQuery | `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF`; the time travel window is seven days by default and can be set between two and seven days[^n4][^n5] |
