# transformWithState

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/TransformWithState

<Infobox type="concept" name="transformWithState">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Arbitrary State API v2, TWS</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Stateful processor, state variables (value, list, map), timers, TTL, time mode, output mode, optional initial state</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) 4.0 and later (Scala, Java, Python)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[mapGroupsWithState and flatMapGroupsWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MapGroupsWithState_and_flatMapGroupsWithState), [Watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), [State store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/State_store)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.0.0, v4.1.0 and v4.3.0 tags of apache/spark (KeyValueGroupedDataset.scala, StatefulProcessor.scala, TransformWithStateExecBase.scala, python/pyspark/sql/pandas/group_ops.py, python/pyspark/sql/connect/group.py, docs/streaming/structured-streaming-transform-with-state.md), the Spark 4.0.0, 4.1.0, 4.2.0 and 4.3.0 release notes, and SPARK-46815, SPARK-50770, SPARK-50855, SPARK-50856, SPARK-51814 and SPARK-51827</Verified>

<Status level="active" since="Apache Spark 4.0.0">The current operator for arbitrary stateful processing in Structured Streaming. Its public interfaces (`StatefulProcessor`, `TimeMode`) carry the `@Evolving` annotation at v4.3.0, not `@Experimental`.[^jira46815]</Status>

In [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), **transformWithState** is the operator for arbitrary stateful processing: user code, written as a stateful processor class, receives the rows for each grouping key, keeps any number of typed state variables for that key across micro-batches, registers timers and emits zero or more output rows.[^guide] It was added in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) 4.0.0 as the "Arbitrary State API v2".[^r400] The Spark documentation calls it the next-generation replacement for [mapGroupsWithState and flatMapGroupsWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MapGroupsWithState_and_flatMapGroupsWithState) in Scala and Java and for `applyInPandasWithState` in Python; those older operators are still supported and are not deprecated.[^guide]

## What transformWithState is for

Built-in stateful operators such as streaming aggregation, deduplication and stream-stream joins cover common patterns, and Spark manages their state. Some logic does not fit them: sessionization with custom rules, downtime detection, fraud scoring over a user's history, or emitting an alert when nothing has arrived for a key. For these, Structured Streaming offers arbitrary stateful operators, where user code decides what to store, when to emit and when to forget.[^ssguide] transformWithState is the second generation of that API. The guide says that since Spark 4.0 users are encouraged to build complex stateful applications on it rather than on the older operators.[^ssguide]

## How it works

A query groups a streaming Dataset or DataFrame by key and passes a **stateful processor** to `transformWithState`. The processor is a class that extends `StatefulProcessor` and implements these methods:[^guide][^sp]
- `init`, called once to declare state variables through the processor's handle.
- `handleInputRows`, called with the key and an iterator of that key's new rows; it returns output rows.
- `handleExpiredTimer`, called once for each timer that has fired; by default it returns nothing.
- `handleInitialState`, available on `StatefulProcessorWithInitialState`, called once per key of an optional initial-state DataFrame before any input is processed.
- `close`, for cleanup.

### State variables

State is declared as named variables, not as a single object per key. There are three types: **ValueState** (one value), **ListState** (appends are cheap) and **MapState** (point lookups by a user key are cheap). A processor can declare several of each, and each has its own encoder.[^guide] Variables can be added between runs of the same query, and removed with `deleteIfExists` in `init`. With the Avro state encoding (`spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.encodingFormat` set to `avro`), the schema of a variable's value can evolve by adding, removing, reordering or widening fields.[^guide]

### Timers and TTL

The time mode is chosen per query: `TimeMode.None()`, `TimeMode.ProcessingTime()` or `TimeMode.EventTime()`.[^timemode] In processing-time or event-time mode, the processor can register, list and delete any number of timers per key; timers are checkpointed and can fire after a restart.[^guide] In event-time mode, timers fire as the [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) passes them.

Each state variable can have a time-to-live (TTL) through `TTLConfig`. Values are not returned after the TTL has passed and are eventually removed; every update resets the TTL. TTL works only with `TimeMode.ProcessingTime`.[^guide][^n1]

### State store requirement

transformWithState runs only on the RocksDB [state store](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/State_store). In a streaming query, the operator checks `spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass` and fails with the error `STORE_BACKEND_NOT_SUPPORTED_FOR_TWS` unless it is `RocksDBStateStoreProvider`.[^base] The default provider in Spark 4.3.0 is still the HDFS-backed state store, so the setting must be changed before the query first starts; the provider cannot be changed between restarts of a query.[^n2] The operator stores its several variables as column families in one RocksDB instance.[^r400]

### Debugging and testing

The state data source can read a transformWithState query's state one variable at a time (option `stateVarName`) and list registered timers (option `readRegisteredTimers`). `TwsTester`, in Scala and Python, runs a stateful processor without a streaming query for unit tests; it does not model TTL or automatic watermark advancement.[^guide]

## Language and Spark Connect support

| API | Language | Data passed to the processor | Added in | Spark Connect support |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `KeyValueGroupedDataset.transformWithState` | Scala, Java | Typed objects (encoders) | 4.0.0[^r400][^jira50770] | 4.1.0[^jira50855] |
| `GroupedData.transformWithStateInPandas` | Python | pandas DataFrames | 4.0.0[^groupops] | 4.1.0[^jira50856] |
| `GroupedData.transformWithState` | Python | `Row` objects | 4.1.0[^jira51814] | 4.1.0[^jira51827] |

In Spark 4.0.0 the [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect) Scala client declared `transformWithState` but threw `UnsupportedOperationException`, and the Python Connect client had no `transformWithStateInPandas`; both work over Connect from 4.1.0.[^n3][^r410] The guide suggests the pandas variant for most Python users and the Row variant for high key cardinality, where conversion to pandas costs more.[^guide]

From Spark 4.3.0 the Scala and Java API can run with the real-time trigger (SPARK-57228); the two Python APIs are not supported in Real-time Mode.[^guide][^n4] transformWithState also runs in batch queries (SPARK-46865 for Scala, SPARK-50428 for Python).[^r400]

## Comparison with mapGroupsWithState

<Hatnote>Main article: [mapGroupsWithState and flatMapGroupsWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MapGroupsWithState_and_flatMapGroupsWithState)</Hatnote>

|  | transformWithState | mapGroupsWithState / flatMapGroupsWithState |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Added in | Spark 4.0.0[^r400] | Spark 2.2.0[^r220] |
| User code | A class with `init`, `handleInputRows`, `handleExpiredTimer` and other methods[^sp] | One function of key, values and a `GroupState`[^gs] |
| State per key | Any number of named value, list and map variables[^guide] | One state object[^gs] |
| Timers | Many timers per key, listed and deleted by the processor[^guide] | One timeout per key[^gs] |
| Automatic expiry | TTL per state variable (processing time)[^guide] | None; the function removes state itself, usually on timeout |
| State schema evolution | Supported for values with Avro encoding[^guide] | Not offered |
| State store | RocksDB only[^base] | HDFS-backed (default) or RocksDB |
| Python API | `transformWithStateInPandas` (4.0.0), `transformWithState` (4.1.0)[^groupops] | `applyInPandasWithState` (3.4.0)[^groupops] |
| Deprecated? | No | No; see [mapGroupsWithState and flatMapGroupsWithState](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/MapGroupsWithState_and_flatMapGroupsWithState) |

## Example

A running count per word in Scala, for Spark 4.0 or later. `words` is a streaming `Dataset[String]` and `spark.implicits._` is imported.

```scala
import org.apache.spark.sql.Encoders
import org.apache.spark.sql.streaming._

class RunningCount extends StatefulProcessor[String, String, (String, Long)] {
  @transient private var count: ValueState[Long] = _

  override def init(outputMode: OutputMode, timeMode: TimeMode): Unit = {
    count = getHandle.getValueState[Long]("count", Encoders.scalaLong, TTLConfig.NONE)
  }

  override def handleInputRows(
      key: String,
      rows: Iterator[String],
      timerValues: TimerValues): Iterator[(String, Long)] = {
    val updated = (if (count.exists()) count.get() else 0L) + rows.size
    count.update(updated)
    Iterator((key, updated))
  }
}

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass",
  "org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider")

val counts = words
  .groupByKey(identity)
  .transformWithState(new RunningCount, TimeMode.None(), OutputMode.Update())
```

# Trigger (Structured Streaming)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trigger_(Structured_Streaming)

<Infobox type="concept" name="Trigger">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Streaming trigger, trigger policy</Field>
  <Field name="field">Stream processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Unspecified (default), processing time, once (deprecated), available now, continuous (experimental), real time</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), [Watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark), [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics), [Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v2.0.0, v2.2.0, v3.3.0, v3.4.0 and v4.0.0 to v4.3.0 tags of apache/spark (Trigger.java, Triggers.scala, python/pyspark/sql/streaming/readwriter.py, docs/streaming/apis-on-dataframes-and-datasets.md, docs/streaming/performance-tips.md, docs/streaming/real-time-mode.md), the Spark 3.4.0, 4.1.0, 4.2.0 and 4.3.0 release notes, SPARK-39805, SPARK-53737 and SPARK-57281</Verified>

In [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), a **trigger** is the setting on a streaming query that decides when the query processes data and which execution mode runs it: micro-batches as fast as possible, micro-batches on a fixed interval, all available data and then stop, or one of the low-latency modes.[^ssguide] The trigger is set with `DataStreamWriter.trigger()`, and a query can have only one.[^pyrw] Of the trigger types, **once** is deprecated since Spark 3.4.0 in favor of **available now**, and **continuous** is still experimental; the **real-time** trigger was added in Spark 4.1.0.[^triggerjava][^perf][^jira53737]

## Trigger types and status

| Trigger | Scala/Java | Python keyword | Added | Status in Spark 4.3.0 | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unspecified (default) | none | none | Spark 2.0.0[^pyrw] | Active | Starts each micro-batch as soon as the previous one finishes; the same as a processing-time trigger of 0 seconds[^ssguide][^pyrw] |
| Processing time | `Trigger.ProcessingTime(interval)` | `processingTime` | Spark 2.2.0 for `Trigger.ProcessingTime`[^triggerjava] | Active | Starts micro-batches at a fixed interval[^ssguide] |
| Once | `Trigger.Once()` | `once` | Spark 2.2.0[^triggerjava] | **Deprecated** since Spark 3.4.0[^triggerjava][^r340] | Processes all available data in a single micro-batch, then stops[^triggerjava] |
| Available now | `Trigger.AvailableNow()` | `availableNow` | Spark 3.3.0[^triggerjava] | Active; the replacement for once | Processes all available data in one or more micro-batches, then stops[^ssguide] |
| Continuous | `Trigger.Continuous(interval)` | `continuous` | Spark 2.3.0[^triggerjava] | **Experimental**[^perf] | Runs the continuous processing engine with the given checkpoint interval; at-least-once[^perf] |
| Real time | `Trigger.RealTime(duration)` | `realTime` (from Spark 4.2.0)[^r420] | Spark 4.1.0[^jira53737] | Active; see [Real-time trigger](#real-time-trigger) | Runs Real-time Mode with long-running batches; the duration is mainly a checkpoint interval[^rtm] |

## Processing-time and default triggers

With no trigger set, Structured Streaming runs in micro-batch mode and starts the next micro-batch as soon as the previous one completes.[^ssguide] A processing-time trigger adds a fixed interval. If a micro-batch finishes early, the engine waits for the interval to end; if it runs past the interval, the next micro-batch starts as soon as it completes, without waiting for the next boundary. If no new data has arrived, no micro-batch starts.[^ssguide]

Triggers have been part of Structured Streaming since Spark 2.0.0.[^pyrw] Spark 2.2.0 added the `Trigger.ProcessingTime` factory methods and deprecated the older `ProcessingTime` class in their favor.[^triggerjava][^n1]

## Once and available now

**Trigger.Once** runs one micro-batch over all available data and stops the query. The programming guide describes its use for clusters that start on a schedule, process what arrived since the last run and shut down.[^ssguide] Trigger.Once is deprecated as of Spark 3.4.0 (SPARK-39805): the Java API carries `@Deprecated(since = "3.4.0")` and points to `AvailableNow()`.[^triggerjava][^r340] It has not been removed; it is still in the Spark 4.3.0 API.[^triggerjava]

**Trigger.AvailableNow**, added in Spark 3.3.0, has the same goal but can split the work into several micro-batches according to source options such as `maxFilesPerTrigger`.[^triggerjava][^ssguide] The guide gives these reasons to prefer it over Once:[^ssguide]
- All data available when the query starts is processed before it stops, including batches left uncommitted by an earlier run.
- The [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) advances after each batch, and a final no-data batch runs if the last batch moved the watermark, which keeps state small for stateful operators.

If any source in the query does not support AvailableNow, Spark falls back to a single micro-batch, as with Once.[^ssguide]

## Continuous trigger

The continuous trigger runs **continuous processing**, an execution mode introduced in Spark 2.3 that the Spark 4.3.0 documentation still labels experimental. It aims at end-to-end latency near 1 millisecond with at-least-once guarantees, compared with about 100 milliseconds and exactly-once for the micro-batch engine.[^perf] The argument is a checkpoint interval, not a batch interval. Continuous processing supports only map-like operations (projections and selections), no aggregations, and a small set of sources and sinks such as Kafka and the rate source.[^perf] The Real-time Mode documentation describes continuous processing as legacy and recommends Real-time Mode for new low-latency workloads.[^rtm]

## Real-time trigger

The real-time trigger enables **Real-time Mode**, added in Spark 4.1.0 (SPARK-53737, part of the SPARK-53736 SPIP) with support for stateless Scala queries.[^jira53737][^n2] Spark 4.2.0 added the `realTime` keyword to PySpark (SPARK-54660).[^r420] Spark 4.3.0 added a first set of stateful queries: streaming deduplication, streaming aggregation and the JVM `transformWithState` operator.[^r430][^rtm]

Real-time Mode launches long-running tasks instead of one job per micro-batch, so records are processed and emitted as they arrive. The duration passed to the trigger (default 5 minutes) is mainly the checkpoint interval; it must be at least `spark.sql.streaming.realTimeMode.minBatchDuration`, which defaults to 5 seconds. A real-time query must use the `update` output mode. The Kafka source supports Real-time Mode, and supported sinks include Kafka, console and memory.[^rtm]

In Spark 4.1.0 the internal `RealTimeTrigger` class carried the `@Experimental` annotation; the public `Trigger.RealTime` methods did not.[^n3] SPARK-57281 removed the annotation. Its JIRA fix version is 4.3.0 and the Spark 4.3.0 release notes list it, although the change is also present at the v4.2.0 tag.[^n4][^r430]

## Example

The following PySpark code, valid for Spark 4.3, runs a streaming query from JSON files into Parquet with the available-now trigger: it processes every file present at start, in one or more micro-batches, and then stops. Replacing `availableNow=True` with `processingTime="1 minute"` keeps the query running and starts a micro-batch every minute.

```python
query = (spark.readStream.format("json").schema("id LONG, msg STRING")
         .option("maxFilesPerTrigger", 100)
         .load("/data/in")
         .writeStream.format("parquet")
         .option("path", "/data/out")
         .option("checkpointLocation", "/data/chk")
         .trigger(availableNow=True)
         .start())
query.awaitTermination()
```

The Scala equivalent of the real-time trigger, for a supported query with a Kafka source and sink, is `.outputMode("update").trigger(Trigger.RealTime("5 minutes"))`.[^rtm]

# Trino

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">Trino Software Foundation and contributors</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2019 (as PrestoSQL); renamed Trino in December 2020</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">484</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-15</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Java</Field>
  <Field name="type">Distributed SQL query engine</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[trino.io](https://trino.io)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/trinodb/trino](https://github.com/trinodb/trino)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi), [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Trino release notes (release 484) and the Trino 484 documentation</Verified>

**Trino** is an open source distributed SQL query engine for analytical queries over large datasets. It does not store data itself; it queries data where it lives, through connectors for data lakes, [open table formats](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), relational databases and other systems.[^usecases][^concepts] Trino was known as PrestoSQL until December 2020, and it is supported by the Trino Software Foundation.[^rename]

## History

Dain Sundstrom, David Phillips and Martin Traverso joined the Facebook data infrastructure team in 2012 and created Presto there, to run low-latency interactive queries against the company's large Hadoop data warehouse.[^rename]

According to the creators, it became clear in 2018 that Facebook management wanted tighter control over the project. In January 2019 they started the Presto Software Foundation as an independent entity to oversee the software and its community, and the project continued under the name PrestoSQL. In September 2019, Facebook established a separate Presto Foundation at the Linux Foundation.[^rename]

On 27 December 2020, the creators announced that PrestoSQL was being renamed Trino. The announcement gives the reason as Facebook's application for a trademark on the name "Presto" and its enforcement, after attempts to agree on terms with Facebook and the Linux Foundation failed.[^rename]

Trino releases are numbered with a single integer. Release 484, the latest at the time of writing, is dated 15 October 2026 in the release notes.[^release] Trino is licensed under the Apache License 2.0.[^rename]

## Architecture

A Trino cluster has one coordinator and zero or more workers. Users connect to the coordinator with their SQL client. The coordinator parses SQL statements, plans queries and manages the workers. Workers execute tasks and process data, fetching it from connectors and exchanging intermediate results with each other.[^concepts]

A query runs as a hierarchy of stages that the coordinator builds as a distributed plan. Each stage runs as a set of tasks on workers, and tasks process splits, which are sections of a larger dataset.[^concepts]

A connector adapts Trino to a data source, much like a database driver, by implementing Trino's service provider interface. A catalog is a set of configuration properties that uses a connector to reach one specific data source; the catalog name comes from the name of its properties file.[^concepts]

## What Trino is not

The Trino documentation states that Trino is not a general-purpose relational database and is not a replacement for databases such as MySQL, PostgreSQL or Oracle. It was not designed for online transaction processing (OLTP). It targets analytical workloads such as aggregating large datasets and producing reports.[^usecases]

## Lakehouse connectors

Trino's connector list includes connectors for [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Hudi](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Hudi) and Hive, as well as connectors for relational databases, Kafka and other systems.[^n1]

The Iceberg connector reads and writes data files in Avro, ORC and [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) format, with Parquet as the default. It supports `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `TRUNCATE` and `MERGE` statements; row-level deletes need tables that use version 2 of the Iceberg specification.[^iceberg]

The Iceberg connector supports table maintenance through `ALTER TABLE EXECUTE`, with procedures including `optimize`, `expire_snapshots` and `remove_orphan_files`. It exposes metadata tables such as `$snapshots`, `$history` and `$files`, and it supports time travel by snapshot ID, timestamp, branch or tag:[^iceberg]

```sql
SELECT *
FROM example.testdb.customer_orders
FOR VERSION AS OF 8954597067493422955;
```

## Catalog support

The Iceberg connector needs a metastore or catalog. The property `iceberg.catalog.type` accepts the values `hive_metastore`, `glue`, `jdbc`, `rest`, `nessie` and `snowflake`.[^metastores]

With the `rest` type, Trino connects to an [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) at the URI set in `iceberg.rest-catalog.uri`. The property `iceberg.rest-catalog.vended-credentials-enabled` controls whether Trino uses storage credentials supplied by the REST catalog; it defaults to false.[^metastores] Through this connector type Trino can use REST catalogs such as [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris), whose site lists Trino among compatible engines, and the open source [Unity Catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog), whose documentation gives a Trino configuration for its Iceberg REST endpoint.[^n2][^n3]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Trino is a distributed engine for interactive SQL over shared tables. A single Trino cluster can define many catalogs with different or identical connectors, and one SQL query can read from more than one of them, so tables from different systems can be queried together.[^concepts]

## See also

- [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg)
- [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog)
- [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB)
- [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)
- [Open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse)

# Unity Catalog

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Unity_Catalog

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">Unity Catalog community, hosted by the LF AI & Data Foundation</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2024-07-09 (v0.1.0)</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release">0.7.0</Field>
  <Field name="latest_release_date">2026-10-13</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">Java</Field>
  <Field name="type">[Data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog)</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[unitycatalog.io](https://unitycatalog.io)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog), [Apache Polaris](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Polaris)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Unity Catalog v0.7.0 GitHub release, unitycatalog.io documentation and the LF AI & Data announcement</Verified>

**Unity Catalog** is an open source [data catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Data_catalog) for tables, files, functions and machine learning models in an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse). It records which data and AI assets exist, where their data is stored and who can use them, and query engines reach it through open REST APIs.[^what] The project is hosted by the LF AI & Data Foundation, part of the Linux Foundation, as a sandbox project.[^readme] This article covers the open source project (sometimes called Unity Catalog OSS), not the managed service of the same name.

## History

Databricks developed Unity Catalog and introduced it in 2021 as part of its commercial platform.[^lfai] On 13 June 2024, Databricks announced that it was releasing Unity Catalog as open source, with the server under the Apache License 2.0 and the API defined by an OpenAPI specification.[^dbblog]

The LF AI & Data Foundation announced Unity Catalog as its newest sandbox project in June 2024, stating that Databricks had open sourced the project and donated it to the foundation.[^lfai] The first tagged release, v0.1.0, was published on GitHub on 9 July 2024.[^n1]

The open source documentation describes Databricks Unity Catalog as a managed service that shares the same API lineage and has a larger feature set. The project documentation covers only the open source server.[^what]

## Data model

Unity Catalog organizes assets in a three-level namespace. A catalog is the top level, a schema belongs to one catalog, and every table has a three-part name of the form `catalog.schema.table`.[^quickstart]

The assets that Unity Catalog governs are:[^what]
- **Tables**: [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) tables, tables in other formats registered as external tables, and [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) tables. For managed Delta tables, the catalog allocates storage and coordinates commits.
- **Views and metric views**: stored SQL or YAML definitions that an engine runs.
- **Volumes**: governed directories for non-tabular files.
- **Functions**: registered Python or SQL functions, which run in the caller's environment.
- **Registered models**: MLflow models and their versions.

## APIs

Unity Catalog exposes three REST interfaces. The Unity Catalog REST API manages catalogs, schemas, tables, volumes and other objects. The Delta API serves catalog-managed Delta tables. The Iceberg REST Catalog API serves Iceberg clients.[^what]

The Delta API was added in version 0.5.0. It lets Delta clients create, load, list, alter, rename and delete catalog-managed Delta tables, and it validates commits on the server before they land.[^n2]

Unity Catalog implements the [Iceberg REST catalog](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Iceberg_REST_catalog) specification at the path `/api/2.1/unity-catalog/iceberg`. Through this endpoint the server lists Iceberg tables, and lists Delta tables only when they carry UniForm Iceberg metadata.[^irc] Version 0.7.0 extended this endpoint so that any engine that supports the Iceberg REST protocol can create, write, read, rename and drop Iceberg tables in Unity Catalog.[^rel070] The project documentation shows [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB), PyIceberg and DataFusion as clients of this endpoint.[^irc]

## Access control and credential vending

When authentication and authorization are enabled, the Unity Catalog server validates tokens from an external identity provider, maps them to known users, and checks ownership and privileges such as `USE_CATALOG`, `SELECT` and `MODIFY` on each request.[^what]

Unity Catalog uses credential vending to give engines access to storage. The server holds the storage identity. After an authorization check, it returns a short-lived credential that is limited to one location and one kind of access, and the client then reads and writes data directly in object storage.[^vend]

The documentation describes per-cloud mechanisms: an AWS STS session policy for Amazon S3, a user-delegation SAS token for Azure Data Lake Storage, and a downscoped Google STS token for Google Cloud Storage. Credentials cannot be recalled once issued, so revoking a grant blocks only new credentials. Access is all-or-nothing per location, so row and column filtering must be enforced by the engine.[^vend]

## Use in an open lakehouse

In an [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), Unity Catalog acts as the shared catalog that several engines use for the same tables. Delta clients can use the Delta API, and Iceberg clients can use the Iceberg REST endpoint without a Unity Catalog connector.[^what][^rel070] The project documentation also includes guides for connecting Apache Spark and DuckDB.[^n3][^n4]

# User-defined function (Spark)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/User-defined_function_(Spark)

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">UDF, Spark UDF, PySpark UDF</Field>
  <Field name="field">Distributed data processing</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Python UDFs since Spark 1.3.0 (`pyspark.sql.functions.udf`)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Function body, return type, evaluation type (JVM, pickled Python, Arrow-optimized Python, pandas, Arrow)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Pandas UDF](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Pandas_UDF), [Arrow-optimized Python UDF](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Arrow-optimized_Python_UDF), [Python UDTF](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Python_UDTF), [Apache Arrow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Arrow), [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (python/pyspark/sql/functions/builtin.py, python/pyspark/sql/pandas/functions.py, SQLConf.scala, the PySpark Arrow, Arrow UDF and UDF user guides, the PySpark migration guide, docs/sql-ref-functions-udf-scalar.md, docs/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-create-sql-function.md), the Spark 2.3.0, 3.5.0, 4.1.0, 4.2.0 and 4.3.0 release notes, and two Databricks engineering blog posts</Verified>

In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), a **user-defined function** (**UDF**) is a function written by the user in Scala, Java, Python or SQL and registered with Spark so that it can be called on columns of a [DataFrame](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DataFrame) or in a Spark SQL query, like a built-in function.[^scalar] A scalar UDF acts on one row and returns one value.[^scalar] PySpark offers several kinds of Python UDF that differ in how data moves between the Java virtual machine (JVM) and the Python worker: pickled Python UDFs, [Arrow-optimized Python UDFs](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Arrow-optimized_Python_UDF), [pandas UDFs](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Pandas_UDF) and Arrow UDFs. The choice decides how much serialization overhead each call pays.[^guide]

## What kinds of UDF does Spark support?

The PySpark user guide for Spark 4.3.0 names three main categories of Python UDF: scalar Python UDFs, pandas UDFs and Arrow UDFs.[^guide]

- **Scalar Python UDFs** take and return Python objects one row at a time. The objects are serialized with pickle (through cloudpickle) or with [Apache Arrow](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Arrow).[^guide]
- **Pandas UDFs**, also called vectorized UDFs, take and return pandas `Series` or `DataFrame` objects and work on a batch of rows at a time; Arrow carries the data.[^guide]
- **Arrow UDFs** take and return `pyarrow.Array` objects (or iterators of them) directly, without converting to pandas.[^guide][^arrowudf]

JVM UDFs are written in Scala or Java with `udf(...)` and `spark.udf.register`, and the class `UserDefinedFunction` provides `asNonNullable`, `asNondeterministic` and `withName`.[^scalar] Spark SQL also has SQL UDFs, created with `CREATE FUNCTION ... RETURN`, whose body is a SQL expression or query and which can return a scalar or a table.[^sqlfn] Functions that return a table from Python are [Python user-defined table functions](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Python_UDTF).

## Spark UDF types compared

|  | JVM UDF (Scala/Java) | Pickled Python UDF | Arrow-optimized Python UDF | Pandas UDF | Arrow UDF |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| How it is defined | `udf(...)`, `spark.udf.register`[^scalar] | `@udf(..., useArrow=False)` or with `spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled=false`[^upgrade] | `@udf` (default since Spark 4.2) or `useArrow=True`[^upgrade] | `@pandas_udf` with pandas type hints[^arrowpandas] | `@arrow_udf`, or `@udf` with `pyarrow.Array` type hints[^arrowudf] |
| Where the code runs | Inside the executor JVM | Python worker process | Python worker process | Python worker process | Python worker process |
| Unit of work for the function | One row | One row[^guide] | One row; data moves in Arrow batches[^arrowpandas] | A batch, as pandas `Series` or `DataFrame`[^guide] | A batch, as `pyarrow.Array`[^arrowudf] |
| JVM to Python serialization | None | Pickle (cloudpickle)[^guide] | Arrow[^guide] | Arrow[^guide] | Arrow, with no pandas conversion[^arrowudf] |
| Available since | Spark 1.3.0 (`functions.udf` in Scala)[^scalafn] | Spark 1.3.0[^udfapi] | Spark 3.5.0 (SPARK-40307); default in 4.2.0[^r350][^r420] | Spark 2.3.0[^pandasapi] | Spark 4.1.0 (SPARK-52214)[^r410] |

## Which UDF type is fastest?

The performance tiers follow from how much work each call spends moving data between the JVM and Python. A JVM UDF runs in the executor JVM and needs no transfer to Python. Every Python UDF runs in a separate Python worker process, so its input and output must cross from the JVM to Python and back; PySpark uses Arrow to make that transfer efficient.[^arrowpandas]

Among Python UDFs, pickled UDFs pay the most serialization overhead. The PySpark user guide says they rely on cloudpickle and meet performance bottlenecks with large inputs and outputs.[^guide] When Databricks engineers introduced pandas UDFs for Spark 2.3 in 2017, they wrote that row-at-a-time Python UDFs "suffer from high serialization and invocation overhead", which led many pipelines to write UDFs in Java or Scala and call them from Python; their benchmark found pandas UDFs 3 to over 100 times faster than row-at-a-time UDFs.[^blog2017]

Arrow-optimized Python UDFs keep the row-at-a-time function but replace pickle with Arrow for the transfer. In a Databricks benchmark for Spark 3.5, an Arrow-optimized Python UDF ran about 1.6 times faster than a pickled UDF on one transformation, and about 1.9 times faster when UDFs were chained, on a 32 GB dataset.[^blog2023] These are measured results for one cluster and dataset, not general guarantees.

Pandas UDFs and Arrow UDFs are vectorized: the function receives a whole batch, so library code (pandas or PyArrow compute functions) can process many rows per call. Arrow UDFs keep the columnar layout end to end and avoid the extra copies of a pandas conversion.[^arrowudf] The batch size for Arrow transfers is `spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch`, default 10,000 rows.[^arrowpandas]

A Python UDF is opaque to the Spark optimizer. Spark 4.3.0 adds an experimental option, `spark.sql.experimental.optimizer.transpilePyUDFs` (default `false`), that tries to rewrite simple Python UDFs as Catalyst expressions; it requires ANSI mode and does not yet work with [Spark Connect](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Spark_Connect).[^sqlconf][^r430]

## How to write a UDF in PySpark

The following PySpark example defines the same string function three ways. It runs on Spark 4.3.0 with PyArrow installed.

```python
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc
from pyspark.sql.functions import udf, pandas_udf, arrow_udf

# Scalar Python UDF: one row per call (Arrow-optimized by default since Spark 4.2)
@udf(returnType="int")
def slen(s: str) -> int:
    return len(s)

# Pandas UDF: one pandas Series per batch
@pandas_udf("string")
def upper_pd(s: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    return s.str.upper()

# Arrow UDF: one pyarrow.Array per batch
@arrow_udf("string")
def upper_pa(s: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pc.ascii_upper(s)

df = spark.createDataFrame([("John Doe",)], ["name"])
df.select(slen("name"), upper_pd("name"), upper_pa("name")).show()
```

A Python UDF can be registered for SQL with `spark.udf.register("slen", slen)` and then called as `SELECT slen(name) FROM t`.[^udfapi]

## What changed in Spark 4.x?

- **Spark 4.0.0** added keyword arguments for Python UDFs.[^udfapi]
- **Spark 4.1.0** added Arrow UDFs (`arrow_udf`, SPARK-52214) and Arrow UDTFs (`arrow_udtf`, SPARK-52979). From 4.1.0, `udf` also creates a vectorized UDF when the type hints match a pandas UDF or Arrow UDF pattern and `useArrow` is not set.[^r410][^udfapi]
- **Spark 4.2.0** made regular Python UDFs Arrow-optimized by default: `spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled` now defaults to `true` (SPARK-54555). Setting it to `false` restores pickled UDFs.[^upgrade][^r420]

The pandas UDF API dates from Spark 2.3.0.[^pandasapi] Arrow-optimized Python UDFs were introduced in Spark 3.5.0.[^r350]

## Limitations

SQL boolean expressions do not short-circuit around a UDF: in `WHERE cond AND udf(x)` the UDF may be called on every row regardless of `cond`, so a UDF that can fail on some inputs must handle them itself.[^arrowudf]

# Variant type

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Variant_type

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">VARIANT, variant data type</Field>
  <Field name="field">Data types, semi-structured data</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 4.0.0 (2025); Parquet format 2.11.0; Iceberg format v3; Delta Lake 4.0.0</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`metadata` and `value` binaries, primitive / array / object values, shredding into `typed_value` columns</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet), [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg), [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Logical type](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Logical_type), [Open table format](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_table_format), [Predicate pushdown](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Predicate_pushdown)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark, the Spark 4.0.0, 4.1.0 and 4.3.0 release notes, apache/parquet-format tags 2.11.0 and 2.14.0, the Apache Iceberg table spec, Delta Lake PROTOCOL.md at v4.4.1 and the Delta and Iceberg release notes</Verified>

A **variant** (SQL type `VARIANT`) is a data type for semi-structured data such as JSON, in which each value carries its own structure in a compact binary encoding, so that rows in the same column can have different shapes and nested fields can be read by path without a fixed schema.[^enc] In the [open lakehouse](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Open_lakehouse), the same variant binary encoding is defined once in the [Apache Parquet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Parquet) project and referenced by [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), the [Apache Iceberg](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Iceberg) table spec and the [Delta Lake](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Delta_Lake) protocol.[^sparkreadme][^ice][^delta]

## Encoding

The Variant Binary Encoding specification defines a variant as one of three things: a **primitive** (a type and a value, such as an integer or a string), an **array** (an ordered list of variant values) or an **object** (an unordered set of string keys with variant values, without duplicate keys). Each variant is stored as two binary values:[^enc]

- **metadata**: a header and a dictionary of the field-name strings used in the value.
- **value**: the encoded data. Object keys are stored as indexes into the metadata dictionary.

The specification states that the encoding is designed for efficient access by path, even in very wide or deep structures, and that each nested value is contiguous and self-contained: an inner value, paired with the metadata of the whole variant, is itself a valid variant.[^enc] The allowed primitive types are a subset of Parquet's [logical types](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Logical_type).[^enc]

In a Parquet file, a variant column is a group annotated with the `VARIANT` logical type that contains a required binary field `metadata` and a binary field `value`. The `value` field is required for an unshredded variant and optional when parts of the value are shredded.[^lt]

```
optional group event (VARIANT(1)) {
  required binary metadata;
  required binary value;
}
```

## Shredding

**Shredding** stores selected paths of a variant as ordinary typed Parquet columns next to the binary value. Each `value` field may have a sibling field named `typed_value` that holds the value when it matches a given type, and readers must reconstruct the full variant from both. All field names stay in the shared metadata.[^shred]

The shredding specification gives the reason: data is often partly homogeneous, and shredded fields gain columnar encoding, column statistics for data skipping and partial projection. A query that extracts one field from a variant can read only that shredded column, and a filter on a shredded field can use its statistics to skip data.[^shred] Shredding is a storage choice. It does not change the logical value a reader returns.

## Origin of the specification

The variant encoding began in Apache Spark. In 2024 the Spark and Parquet communities agreed to move the Spark variant specification into the Parquet project, tracked as parquet-format issue 455.[^n1] `VariantEncoding.md`, `VariantShredding.md` and the `VARIANT` logical type are present in parquet-format from release 2.11.0, and are not in 2.10.0.[^lt]

At the v4.3.0 tag, Spark's own variant README says the spec "is being developed in the Apache Parquet project", that Spark implements a specific commit of the Parquet spec, and that Spark does not yet support variant values containing UUID, Time or nanosecond-precision timestamps.[^sparkreadme]

## Apache Spark

Spark 4.0.0 added the `VARIANT` data type (SPARK-45827), with `VariantVal` for PySpark, variant support in PySpark UDFs, UDTFs and UDAFs, and variant support in the Spark Connect Scala client.[^r400] Spark 4.1.0 describes VARIANT as generally available "with shredding for faster reads on semi-structured data". That release enabled the Parquet variant logical type and the shredding configurations by default (SPARK-54454), infers a shredding schema in the Parquet writer (SPARK-53659), reads the Parquet `VARIANT` logical type, and adds the colon operator for field access.[^r410] Spark 4.3.0 added functions that modify variant values (`variant_set`, `variant_insert`, `variant_delete`, `variant_array_append`, `variant_strip_nulls`), `JSON_TABLE`, and pushdown of `variant_get` filters to DataSource V2 sources.[^r430]

The main functions in Spark 4.3 are `parse_json` (parse a JSON string into a variant; `try_parse_json` returns null on invalid input), `variant_get` (extract a path and cast it to a type; `try_variant_get` returns null when the cast fails), `schema_of_variant`, `is_variant_null`, `to_variant_object` and the `variant_explode` generator.[^fn] The JSON, CSV and XML readers can also load each record into a single variant column with the `singleVariantColumn` option.[^n2]

The following Spark SQL query runs on Spark 4.3 and returns `42` and `b`:[^fn]

```sql
SELECT
  variant_get(v, '$.user.id', 'int')    AS user_id,
  variant_get(v, '$.tags[1]', 'string') AS second_tag
FROM (SELECT parse_json('{"user": {"id": 42}, "tags": ["a", "b"]}') AS v);
```

## Apache Iceberg

The Iceberg table spec adds `variant` in format version 3, along with nanosecond timestamps, geometry, geography and unknown types.[^ice] The spec classes variant as a semi-structured type, neither primitive nor nested, and states that "the variant type and binary encoding are defined in the Parquet project, with support currently available for V1". In Parquet files Iceberg uses the Parquet `VARIANT` encoding and shredding; in Avro and ORC a variant is a record or struct with `metadata` and `value` fields. The spec also defines lower and upper bounds for fields inside a variant, keyed by normalized JSON path, and defines no 32-bit hash for variant because equal values can have several representations.[^ice]

In the Java implementation, Iceberg 1.9.0 added the variant type to core with Parquet variant readers and writers, and Iceberg 1.10.0 added variant read support for Spark Iceberg tables.[^i190][^i1100]

## Delta Lake

The Delta Lake protocol defines variant as the `variantType` table feature, which requires reader version 3 and writer version 7. Variant data is written to Parquet as a struct of two binaries, `value` and `metadata`, following the Parquet Variant binary encoding. A variant column cannot be a partition or clustering column, because variant is not a comparable type.[^delta] A separate `variantShredding` feature, which depends on `variantType`, allows shredded variants, and with it Delta can keep min and max statistics for variant columns.[^delta]

Delta Lake 4.0.0 made the variant type generally available (it was a preview in the Delta 4.0.0 preview release) and added shredded variants as a preview.[^d400] In Delta Lake 4.3.0 the variant shredding RFC was accepted into the protocol, and Delta Spark began collecting variant statistics on write.[^d430]

## Support summary

| Project | Variant type | Shredding | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Apache Parquet (format) | Encoding spec and `VARIANT` logical type from 2.11.0[^lt] | `VariantShredding.md` from 2.11.0[^lt] | Home of the shared specification |
| Apache Spark | 4.0.0[^r400] | Writer infers shredding schema by default from 4.1.0[^r410] | Implements a pinned commit of the Parquet spec; no UUID, Time or nanosecond timestamp values as of 4.3.0[^sparkreadme] |
| Apache Iceberg (spec) | Format v3[^ice] | Uses Parquet shredding[^ice] | Variant v1 encoding |
| Apache Iceberg (Java) | 1.9.0 (core and Parquet)[^i190]; 1.10.0 (Spark read)[^i1100] | Shredding fixes and Flink shredded writes listed in 1.11.0 and 1.12.0[^i1110][^i1120] | Variant is a v3 type[^ice] |
| Delta Lake | 4.0.0, `variantType` feature[^d400] | Preview in 4.0.0[^d400]; RFC accepted in 4.3.0[^d430] | Reader v3 / writer v7[^delta] |

# Velox

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Velox

<Infobox type="software">
  <Field name="developer">Meta, with contributors from other companies</Field>
  <Field name="initial_release">2021 (GitHub repository created)</Field>
  <Field name="written_in">C++</Field>
  <Field name="type">Execution engine library</Field>
  <Field name="license">Apache License 2.0</Field>
  <Field name="website">[velox-lib.io](https://velox-lib.io)</Field>
  <Field name="repo">[github.com/facebookincubator/velox](https://github.com/facebookincubator/velox)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Apache Gluten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Gluten), [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), [Native execution engine (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Native_execution_engine_(Spark)), [Apache DataFusion Comet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_DataFusion_Comet)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the facebookincubator/velox README, LICENSE, repository metadata and tags, the VLDB 2022 Velox paper, Meta's "Introducing Velox" post, the apache/gluten README (main and v1.7.0) and Velox getting-started guide at v1.7.0, and the prestodb/presto presto-native-execution README</Verified>

**Velox** is an open source C++ library that provides the execution layer of a data processing engine: columnar vectors, vectorized expression evaluation, functions and relational operators, which other systems embed instead of writing their own.[^readme] Meta created Velox, and it is developed with IBM/Ahana, Intel, Voltron Data, Microsoft, ByteDance and other companies under the Apache License 2.0.[^readme] For [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), Velox is one of the two native backends of [Apache Gluten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Gluten), a plugin that offloads Spark SQL execution from the JVM to native code.[^gluten]

## What does Velox provide?

Velox takes a fully optimized query plan as input and runs it. It does not include a SQL parser, a DataFrame layer or a query optimizer, so it is meant for developers who build or speed up engines, not for end users.[^readme]

The Velox README lists these components:[^readme]
- **Type**: a type system with scalar, complex and nested types such as structs, maps and arrays.
- **Vector**: an Arrow-compatible columnar memory layout with flat, dictionary, constant and sequence (run-length) encodings, lazy materialization and out-of-order writes.
- **Expression evaluation**: a vectorized engine that evaluates expressions on vector-encoded data.
- **Functions**: vectorized scalar, aggregate and window functions that follow Presto and Spark semantics.
- **Operators**: scans, writes, projections, filters, grouping, ordering, shuffle and exchange, hash, merge and nested loop joins, unnest and others.
- **I/O**: a connector interface for data sources and sinks, with ORC/DWRF, Parquet and Nimble file formats and storage adapters for S3, HDFS, GCS, ABFS and local files.
- **Network serializers**: wire formats including PrestoPage and Spark's UnsafeRow.
- **Resource management**: memory arenas, buffer management, tasks, drivers, thread pools, spilling and caching.

The Velox source tree keeps Spark and Presto function sets in separate directories, `velox/functions/sparksql` and `velox/functions/prestosql`, so that each engine gets its own SQL dialect behavior.[^funcs] Developers can add their own types, functions, operators, file formats, storage adapters and serializers.[^readme]

## How is Velox used with Apache Spark?

Velox runs Spark SQL through Apache Gluten. Gluten converts Spark's physical plan into a Substrait plan, passes it over JNI to a native backend, which builds and runs native operators, and returns results to Spark as columnar batches. Operators that the backend does not support fall back to vanilla Spark, with columnar-to-row and row-to-columnar conversions between them.[^gluten] Gluten v1.7.0 supports two backends, ClickHouse and Velox, and Spark 3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 4.0 and 4.1.[^gluten]

A Spark application turns on the Gluten Velox backend with the Gluten plugin, off-heap memory and Gluten's columnar shuffle manager. The configuration below is taken from the Gluten v1.7.0 Velox guide; the off-heap size is an example value.[^glutenvelox]

```
spark.plugins            org.apache.gluten.GlutenPlugin
spark.memory.offHeap.enabled  true
spark.memory.offHeap.size     20g
spark.shuffle.manager    org.apache.spark.shuffle.sort.ColumnarShuffleManager
```

Gluten's main branch also documents an experimental GPU mode in which Velox plan nodes are replaced by operators built on NVIDIA cuDF; see [GPU acceleration in Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/GPU_acceleration_in_Spark).[^glutengpu] For other native engines for Spark, such as [Apache DataFusion Comet](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_DataFusion_Comet), see [Native execution engine (Spark)](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Native_execution_engine_(Spark)).

## Which other engines use Velox?

Prestissimo, the native worker of Presto in the `presto-native-execution` directory of the prestodb/presto repository, implements the Presto worker REST API in C++ on top of Velox.[^prestissimo] Meta's March 2023 post describes Prestissimo as replacing Presto Java workers with a Velox-based C++ process, and names Spark (through Gluten) and TorchArrow, a PyTorch data preprocessing library, as the other main integrations at the time.[^meta]

## What is the history of Velox?

The facebookincubator/velox repository on GitHub was created on 23 July 2021.[^repo] Meta engineers described the design in the paper "Velox: Meta's Unified Execution Engine", published in the Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment, volume 15 (2022).[^paper] Meta's 2023 post states that Velox was already being integrated with more than a dozen data systems at Meta, including Presto and Spark.[^meta]

Velox does not publish GitHub releases with version numbers; its repository uses date-based tags such as `v2026.10.23.00`.[^tags] Velox requires at least GCC 11 or Clang 15 to build.[^readme]

## How does Velox differ from a query engine?

Velox is a library, not a complete query engine. A system such as Spark or Presto keeps its own SQL parsing, optimization, scheduling and cluster management, and hands Velox the plan fragment to run on one machine.[^readme][^meta] Without a plugin such as Gluten, Spark runs plans on its own JVM execution layer, described in [Project Tungsten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Tungsten).

# Watermark

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Event-time watermark, low watermark</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Event-time column, maximum observed event time, allowed delay (lateness threshold)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) (`withWatermark`), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) (`WatermarkStrategy`), Kafka Streams (grace period)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing), [Exactly-once semantics](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Exactly-once_semantics)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-22">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming guides and `SQLConf.scala` at tag v4.3.0, the Apache Flink 2.3 documentation and the Dataflow Model paper (VLDB 2015)</Verified>

In [stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing), a **watermark** is a moving timestamp that tells the engine how far event time has progressed in a stream, so that it can treat earlier event times as complete, emit final results for them and discard the state it kept for them. Watermarks let an engine handle data that arrives out of order while still bounding the memory and storage that stateful operators use. [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) and [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) both use watermarks, with different APIs and defaults.

The word is also used for unrelated offset markers in message queues and connectors; this page covers only event-time watermarks in streaming engines.

## Why streaming engines need watermarks

Records carry an **event time** (when the event happened) and are handled at a **processing time** (when the engine sees them). The gap between the two changes all the time, so records arrive late and out of order.[^dataflow] An engine that counts events per 10-minute window cannot know when a window has received all its records.

Without a signal, the engine has two bad choices: keep every window open forever, so that state grows without limit, or close windows by processing time, so that late records are counted in the wrong window. The Spark guide states that to run a windowed query for days, the engine must know when an old aggregate can be dropped because no more late data will arrive for it.[^ss-apis]

The Dataflow paper, building on Google's MillWheel, describes a watermark as a lower bound on the event times that have been processed, and notes that for most real-world data the system cannot know this bound with certainty, so watermarks are usually heuristic.[^dataflow] A watermark is therefore a trade-off: a longer delay accepts more late data but holds state longer and emits final results later.

## Watermarks in Structured Streaming

Spark added watermarking in Spark 2.1. A query declares a watermark with `withWatermark(eventTimeColumn, delayThreshold)`. At the start of every trigger, the engine sets the watermark to the maximum event time seen so far minus the delay. For a window that ends at time *T*, the engine keeps state and accepts late records until the watermark passes *T*; after that, the window's state is cleared and later records for it are ignored.[^ss-apis]

The guarantee runs in one direction only. With a delay of 2 hours, the engine never drops a record that is less than 2 hours late, but a record more than 2 hours late is not guaranteed to be dropped; it may still be aggregated.[^ss-apis]

The output mode decides what the watermark does:[^ss-apis]

- In **update** mode, the engine writes changed window counts after every trigger until the window falls behind the watermark.
- In **append** mode, the engine writes each window once, with its final count, after the watermark passes the window's end. Sinks that cannot apply fine-grained updates, such as files, use this mode.
- In **complete** mode, all aggregate data must be kept, so the watermark cannot drop state.

For the watermark to clean aggregation state, the aggregation must group by the event-time column or a window on it, and `withWatermark` must be called on that same column before the aggregation. Watermarks also bound state for stream-stream joins and for deduplication with `dropDuplicates` or `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark`. On a batch DataFrame, `withWatermark` has no effect.[^ss-apis]

### Multiple watermarks

When a query unions or joins several streams, each with its own watermark, Spark tracks each one and combines them into a single global watermark. By default it takes the minimum, so the query moves at the pace of the slowest stream and no stream's data is dropped as too late. Since Spark 2.4, setting `spark.sql.streaming.multipleWatermarkPolicy` to `max` makes the global watermark follow the fastest stream instead, at the cost of dropping more data from slower streams.[^ss-apis] The setting cannot be changed between restarts of a query from the same checkpoint location.[^sqlconf]

In Real-time Mode, records are processed as they arrive, but watermark advancement still waits for the batch boundary, which in that mode is the checkpoint interval.[^ss-rtm]

### Example

This PySpark query counts rows from the built-in `rate` test source in 1-minute tumbling windows and accepts records up to 30 seconds late. In append mode, each window is printed once, after the watermark passes its end.

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import window

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("watermark-demo").getOrCreate()

events = spark.readStream.format("rate").option("rowsPerSecond", 5).load()

counts = (
    events.withWatermark("timestamp", "30 seconds")   # before the aggregation
    .groupBy(window("timestamp", "1 minute"))         # same column
    .count()
)

(counts.writeStream.outputMode("append")
    .format("console")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/tmp/watermark-demo")
    .start()
    .awaitTermination())
```

## Watermarks in Apache Flink

In Flink, a watermark is an element in the stream that carries a timestamp *t* and declares that event time has reached *t*, meaning no more records with timestamps at or before *t* are expected.[^flink-time] Each parallel source subtask usually generates its own watermarks, and an operator with several inputs uses the minimum of its inputs' event times as its current event time.[^flink-time]

Watermarks are defined with a `WatermarkStrategy`, which combines a `TimestampAssigner` (which reads the event time from each record) and a `WatermarkGenerator`. The built-in bounded out-of-orderness strategy is the closest equivalent of Spark's delay threshold:[^flink-wm]

```java
WatermarkStrategy
        .<Tuple2<Long, String>>forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(20))
        .withTimestampAssigner((event, timestamp) -> event.f0);
```

Because the combined watermark is a minimum, one idle input (for example, a Kafka partition that receives no data) holds back the watermark for the whole job. `withIdleness(...)` lets a source mark an input as idle so that the others can advance. Watermark alignment, enabled with `withWatermarkAlignment(...)`, stops fast sources or splits from moving too far ahead of the rest.[^flink-wm]

By default, Flink window operators drop records that arrive after the watermark has passed the end of their window; the allowed lateness is 0. `allowedLateness(...)` keeps windows open longer and may fire them again, and `sideOutputLateData(...)` sends dropped late records to a separate stream.[^flink-windows]

Kafka Streams uses a related idea without the name: a window's **grace period** controls how long the engine waits for out-of-order records, and later records are discarded for that window.[^kstreams]

## Comparison

|  | Spark Structured Streaming | Apache Flink |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How it is defined | `withWatermark(column, delay)` on a DataFrame[^ss-apis] | `WatermarkStrategy` on a source or stream[^flink-wm] |
| What it is | A value the engine computes: max event time seen minus delay[^ss-apis] | An element that flows through the stream[^flink-time] |
| When it advances | At the start of each trigger (micro-batch)[^ss-apis] | When the `WatermarkGenerator` emits one; periodic generators run at an interval set with `ExecutionConfig.setAutoWatermarkInterval(...)`[^flink-wm] |
| Several inputs | One global watermark; minimum by default, maximum with `spark.sql.streaming.multipleWatermarkPolicy=max`[^ss-apis] | Each operator takes the minimum of its inputs[^flink-time] |
| Idle inputs | Under the default policy, a stalled stream holds the global watermark back[^ss-apis] | `withIdleness` marks an input idle so it no longer holds the watermark back[^flink-wm] |
| Late records | Dropped once their window's state is cleared; records within the delay are always kept[^ss-apis] | Dropped by default (allowed lateness 0); can be kept with `allowedLateness` or captured with `sideOutputLateData`[^flink-windows] |

# Whole-stage code generation

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Whole-stage_code_generation

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">WholeStageCodegen, whole-stage codegen, WSCG</Field>
  <Field name="field">Query execution performance</Field>
  <Field name="introduced">Apache Spark 2.0.0 (SPARK-12795)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">`WholeStageCodegenExec`, `CollapseCodegenStages`, `InputAdapter`, codegen stage ID, Java source compiler (Janino by default)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Project Tungsten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Tungsten), [Catalyst optimizer](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Catalyst_optimizer), [Logical plan and physical plan](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Logical_plan_and_physical_plan), [Job, stage and task](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Job,_stage_and_task)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Spark 2.0.0 release notes, SPARK-12795, the 2016 Databricks engineering post on whole-stage code generation, the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (WholeStageCodegenExec.scala, SQLConf.scala, docs/sql-ref-syntax-qry-explain.md, docs/web-ui.md) and EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN CODEGEN output from a PySpark 4.3.0 run</Verified>

**Whole-stage code generation** is the technique by which [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) compiles a chain of physical operators, such as a scan, a filter, a projection and a partial aggregation, into a single generated Java function at run time.[^wscg][^sqlconf] It shipped in Spark 2.0.0, whose release notes credit it with 2 to 10 times speedups for common SQL and DataFrame operators, and it is part of the work known as [Project Tungsten](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Project_Tungsten).[^r200][^jira] It is on by default in Spark 4.3.0 and applies to DataFrame, Dataset and SQL queries.

## Why does Spark generate code?

Before whole-stage code generation, Spark ran each physical operator as an iterator that pulls rows from its child, the "Volcano" model used by many databases. Spark developers Sameer Agarwal, Davies Liu and Reynold Xin explained in a 2016 Databricks post that each such call is a virtual function dispatch and keeps the row in memory. Collapsing a fragment of the query into one function eliminates those calls and lets the JVM JIT compiler keep intermediate data in CPU registers, close to what hand-written code would do.[^blog2016]

Spark turns the generated Java source into bytecode at run time. Spark 4.3.0 added an internal setting, `spark.sql.codegen.compiler`, with the values `janino` (the Janino library, the default) and `jdk` (`javax.tools.JavaCompiler`); its documentation says Janino is several times faster and remains the better choice for most workloads.[^sqlconf]

## What do WholeStageCodegen nodes mean in a plan?

In a physical plan printed by `EXPLAIN` or `df.explain()`, an operator that is part of a generated function is prefixed with `*(n)`. The number *n* is the **codegen stage ID**: all operators with the same ID are fused into one generated function. IDs start at 1 in each query and are assigned in depth-first post-order, so not all neighbouring operators with a star share an ID.[^wscg] In `EXPLAIN FORMATTED` the same information appears as `*` in the outline and `[codegen id : n]` in each node's details.[^explain]

This sort-merge join plan from PySpark 4.3.0 (with [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution) and broadcast joins turned off; plan IDs removed) has five codegen stages:

```
*(5) Project [k#9L]
+- *(5) SortMergeJoin [k#9L], [k#11L], Inner
   :- *(2) Sort [k#9L ASC NULLS FIRST], false, 0
   :  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(k#9L, 200), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS
   :     +- *(1) Project [id#8L AS k#9L]
   :        +- *(1) Range (0, 1000000, step=1, splits=2)
   +- *(4) Sort [k#11L ASC NULLS FIRST], false, 0
      +- Exchange hashpartitioning(k#11L, 200), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS
         +- *(3) Project [id#10L AS k#11L]
            +- *(3) Range (0, 100, step=1, splits=2)
```

How to read it:

- **Operators without a star are not generated.** `Exchange` is a [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle) boundary and is never part of a generated function. The generated code of stage 1 ends where it writes rows to the shuffle.
- **An `InputAdapter` is hidden.** Where a generated stage reads from an operator that does not support code generation, Spark inserts an `InputAdapter`, which feeds rows from that operator into the generated code. In Spark 4.3.0 it is not printed in the tree.[^wscg]
- **Codegen stages are not Spark stages.** A [scheduler stage](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Job,_stage_and_task) is bounded by shuffles; one scheduler stage can contain several codegen stages. Above, codegen stages 2, 4 and 5 all run in the final scheduler stage, after both shuffles.
- **Before AQE runs, stars are missing.** With [Adaptive Query Execution](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Adaptive_Query_Execution) on (the default), the plan printed before execution starts with `AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false` and shows no `*(n)` prefixes; they appear in the final plan printed after an action.

The Spark web UI uses the same IDs. Stage DAGs group nodes under `WholeStageCodegen` boxes annotated with the codegen ID, which links a stage to the query in the SQL tab.[^webui]

## How do you see the generated code?

`EXPLAIN CODEGEN` (or `df.explain(mode="codegen")`) prints the physical plan and the generated Java source of each stage.[^explain] Each subtree comes with statistics on the compiled code:

```sql
EXPLAIN CODEGEN SELECT sum(id) FROM range(10) WHERE id > 2;
```

```
Found 2 WholeStageCodegen subtrees.
== Subtree 1 / 2 (maxMethodCodeSize:282; maxConstantPoolSize:217(0.33% used); numInnerClasses:0) ==
*(1) HashAggregate(keys=[], functions=[partial_sum(id#4360L)], ...
```

`maxMethodCodeSize` is the largest compiled method in bytes of bytecode. It matters because of the fallback rule for huge methods described below.

## When does whole-stage code generation fall back?

Spark falls back to the interpreted, operator-at-a-time path for part of a plan in these cases, all defined in the Spark 4.3.0 source:[^wscg][^sqlconf]

| Case | Effect | Setting (default) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The operator does not implement code generation, for example the Python UDF operator `BatchEvalPython` | The operator runs without a star; an `InputAdapter` connects it to generated neighbours | (none) |
| An expression in the operator only supports interpreted evaluation (`CodegenFallback`) | The whole operator is left out of code generation | (none) |
| The operator's input or output schema has more fields, counting nested fields, than the limit | The operator is left out of code generation | `spark.sql.codegen.maxFields` (100) |
| The generated Java code fails to compile | A warning "Whole-stage codegen disabled for plan (id=n)" is logged and the subtree runs interpreted | `spark.sql.codegen.fallback` (true) |
| A compiled method is larger than the limit in bytecode | An info message "Found too long generated codes and JIT optimization might not work" is logged and the subtree runs interpreted | `spark.sql.codegen.hugeMethodLimit` (65535) |
| Code generation is turned off | No whole-stage code generation at all | `spark.sql.codegen.wholeStage` (true) |

The 65535 default for `spark.sql.codegen.hugeMethodLimit` is the largest bytecode size of a valid Java method. On HotSpot, a method larger than 8 KB of bytecode is not JIT-compiled, so Spark also splits long generated functions into smaller ones (`spark.sql.codegen.methodSplitThreshold`).[^sqlconf] All settings in this table are internal configurations in Spark 4.3.0.[^sqlconf]

Two of these cases were seen in PySpark 4.3.0 runs. A Python UDF produced `BatchEvalPython` without a star between two generated stages:

```
*(2) Project [pythonUDF0#21L AS <lambda>(k)#20L]
+- BatchEvalPython [<lambda>(id#8L)#19L], [pythonUDF0#21L]
   +- *(1) Range (0, 1000000, step=1, splits=2)
```

A `select` of 101 computed columns left the `Project` unstarred, while the `Filter` and `Range` below it, which have one column, kept `*(1)`.

# Window functions

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Window_functions

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Analytic functions, OVER clause</Field>
  <Field name="field">SQL query processing</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Partitioning, ordering, window frame (ROWS or RANGE), ranking, offset and aggregate functions</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark), PostgreSQL, [Trino](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Trino), [DuckDB](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/DuckDB), Snowflake</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle), [Partition](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Partition), [Lateral column alias](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Lateral_column_alias)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the v4.3.0 tag of apache/spark (docs/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-window.md, docs/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-qualify.md, docs/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select.md, SqlBaseParser.g4, python/pyspark/sql/window.py, WindowExecBase.scala, sql-tests/inputs/window.sql), the Spark 4.2.0 release notes, PostgreSQL 19 documentation, Trino 484 documentation, DuckDB 2.0 documentation and Snowflake documentation</Verified>

A **window function** is a SQL function that computes a value for each row from a group of related rows, called the window, without collapsing those rows into one as `GROUP BY` does; in [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) it is written as a function followed by an `OVER` clause that names the partitioning, the ordering and an optional frame.[^sparkwin] Window functions are used for rankings, running totals, moving averages and comparisons with the previous or next row. SQL engines that support them differ in frame types, null handling and the filtering clause `QUALIFY`, which the comparison table below sets out.

## How does a window function work?

The `OVER` clause has three parts. `PARTITION BY` splits rows into independent groups; `ORDER BY` orders rows inside each group; and the frame clause picks which rows around the current row the function sees. In Spark SQL the frame is written `{ RANGE | ROWS } { frame_start | BETWEEN frame_start AND frame_end }`, with bounds `UNBOUNDED PRECEDING`, `offset PRECEDING`, `CURRENT ROW`, `offset FOLLOWING` or `UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`; an omitted `frame_end` means `CURRENT ROW`.[^sparkwin]

A `ROWS` frame counts physical rows. A `RANGE` frame uses value distance on the ordering column, so rows with equal ordering values (peers) are in or out of the frame together. Spark accepts numeric, date and interval offsets in `RANGE` frames, for example `RANGE BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND INTERVAL 23 DAYS 4 HOURS FOLLOWING`.[^wintests]

## What is the default frame?

In Spark, when a window has no ordering, the frame is the whole partition (`ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`). When ordering is defined, the default is a growing frame, `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`.[^pywin] This is why `last_value(x) OVER (ORDER BY t)` returns the current row's value (or that of its last peer) unless the frame is extended to `UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`.

## Which kinds of window functions are there?

Spark groups window functions into three kinds.[^sparkwin]
- **Ranking functions:** `ROW_NUMBER`, `RANK`, `DENSE_RANK`, `PERCENT_RANK`, `NTILE`.
- **Analytic (offset and value) functions:** `LAG`, `LEAD`, `NTH_VALUE`, `FIRST_VALUE`, `LAST_VALUE`, `CUME_DIST`.
- **Aggregate functions** used with `OVER`, such as `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX` and `COUNT`.

`LAG`, `LEAD`, `NTH_VALUE`, `FIRST_VALUE` and `LAST_VALUE` accept `IGNORE NULLS` in Spark; the default is `RESPECT NULLS`.[^sparkwin] `RANK` leaves gaps after ties and `DENSE_RANK` does not.[^sparkwin]

## How do you filter on a window function?

Spark SQL has a `QUALIFY` clause that filters rows after window functions are evaluated, either by referring to a window function's alias in the `SELECT` list or by writing the window function in the condition itself; it was added in Spark 4.2.0 (SPARK-31561).[^qualify][^r420] Without `QUALIFY`, the same result needs a subquery or common table expression with a `WHERE` on the computed column. A named window can be declared once with the `WINDOW` clause and reused.[^select]

## Example

PySpark, with a rank, the previous salary and a three-row moving average per department:[^pywin]

```python
from pyspark.sql import Window, functions as F

w = Window.partitionBy("dept").orderBy("salary")

df.select(
    "name", "dept", "salary",
    F.rank().over(w).alias("rank"),
    F.lag("salary").over(w).alias("prev_salary"),
    F.avg("salary").over(w.rowsBetween(-1, 1)).alias("moving_avg"),
).show()
```

Spark SQL, keeping the highest-paid employee of each department with `QUALIFY`:[^qualify]

```sql
SELECT name, dept, salary
FROM employees
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1;
```

## How do window functions run in Spark?

Spark's physical window operator requires its input to be clustered by the `PARTITION BY` columns and sorted by the partition and `ORDER BY` columns, so the planner usually adds a [shuffle](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Shuffle) and a sort before it. A window with no `PARTITION BY` requires all rows in one partition, and Spark logs a warning that this "can cause serious performance degradation".[^winexec]

## Engine differences

| Feature | Apache Spark 4.3 | PostgreSQL 19 | Trino 484 | DuckDB 2.0 | Snowflake |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Frame types | `ROWS`, `RANGE`[^sparkwin] | `ROWS`, `RANGE`, `GROUPS`[^pgexpr] | `ROWS`, `RANGE`, `GROUPS`[^trinomr] | `ROWS`, `RANGE`, `GROUPS`[^duck] | `ROWS`, `RANGE`[^snowwin] |
| Frame exclusion (`EXCLUDE`) | Not in the frame grammar[^grammar] | Yes[^pgexpr] | Yes[^trinoselect] | Yes[^duck] | Not documented[^snowwin] |
| Default frame with `ORDER BY` | `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`[^pywin] | Same[^pgexpr] | Same[^trinoselect] | Same[^duck] | Same for aggregates; `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING` for `FIRST_VALUE`, `LAST_VALUE`, `NTH_VALUE`[^snowwin] |
| `IGNORE NULLS` on offset and value functions | Yes[^sparkwin] | Yes[^pgfunc] | Yes[^trinowin] | Yes[^duck] | Yes (for example `LAG`)[^n1] |
| `QUALIFY` | Yes, since 4.2.0[^r420] | Not documented[^pgselect] | Not documented[^trinoselect] | Yes[^duck] | Yes[^n2] |
| Named `WINDOW` clause | Yes[^select] | Yes[^pgselect] | Yes[^trinowin] | Yes[^duck] | Not documented[^snowwin] |

"Not documented" means the cited documentation page for that engine does not describe the feature.
