# Windowing (stream processing)

Source: https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Windowing_(stream_processing)

<Infobox type="concept">
  <Field name="also_known_as">Time windows, windowed aggregation</Field>
  <Field name="field">[Stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing)</Field>
  <Field name="key_parts">Window type (tumbling, sliding or hopping, session), window size, slide, gap, time column, [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark)</Field>
  <Field name="implementations">[Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming) (`window`, `session_window`), [Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink) (window assigners, windowing TVFs), Kafka Streams (`TimeWindows`, `SlidingWindows`, `SessionWindows`)</Field>
  <Field name="related">[Session window](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Session_window), [Event time and processing time](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Event_time_and_processing_time), [Watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark)</Field>
</Infobox>

<Verified date="2026-11-23">the Spark 4.3.0 Structured Streaming programming guide and `python/pyspark/sql/functions/builtin.py` at tag v4.3.0 of apache/spark, the Apache Flink 2.3 DataStream "Windows" and SQL "Windowing TVF" pages, and the Kafka Streams 4.4 DSL developer guide</Verified>

In [stream processing](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Stream_processing), **windowing** is dividing an unbounded stream into finite groups of records, usually by time, so that aggregations such as counts and averages can be computed and emitted for each group. The three common window types are **tumbling** (fixed size, no overlap), **sliding** or **hopping** (fixed size, overlapping) and **session** windows (variable size, closed by a gap of inactivity). In [Apache Spark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Spark) [Structured Streaming](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Structured_Streaming), a window is a grouping key built with the `window` or `session_window` function over an [event-time](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Event_time_and_processing_time) column, and a [watermark](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Watermark) decides when a window is complete.[^ss-apis]

## What window types exist?

Structured Streaming supports three types of time windows: tumbling, sliding and session.[^ss-types]

- A **tumbling window** is one of a series of fixed-size, non-overlapping, contiguous time intervals. Each record belongs to exactly one window.[^ss-types]
- A **sliding window** also has a fixed size, but a new window starts every *slide* interval. When the slide is shorter than the size, windows overlap and one record belongs to several windows.[^ss-types]
- A **session window** has no fixed size. It starts with a record and grows while further records arrive within a gap duration; it closes when no record arrives within the gap. See [Session window](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Session_window).[^ss-types]

Spark's guide uses the example of counting words in 10-minute windows that slide every 5 minutes: a word received at 12:07 is counted in both the 12:00 to 12:10 window and the 12:05 to 12:15 window.[^ss-apis]

## How does windowing work in Structured Streaming?

The `window(timeColumn, windowDuration, slideDuration=None, startTime=None)` function, available since Spark 2.0.0, assigns each row to one or more windows. Without `slideDuration`, the windows are tumbling; the slide must be less than or equal to the window size.[^builtin]

Window starts are inclusive and ends are exclusive, so 12:05 falls in `[12:05, 12:10)` and not in `[12:00, 12:05)`. Windows are aligned to 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC; `startTime` shifts them, for example to hourly windows that start 15 minutes past the hour. Durations are fixed lengths of time, not calendar units, and windows measured in months are not supported. The result is a struct column named `window` with `start` and `end` fields.[^builtin]

Because a window is just a grouping key, a windowed aggregation is written as `groupBy(window(...), ...)`, and the same query runs on a batch DataFrame and on a stream.[^ss-apis] The `window_time` function, added in Spark 3.4.0, returns a timestamp for a window column, which lets one windowed aggregation feed another, for example 5-minute windows rolled up into 1-hour windows.[^builtin][^ss-apis]

On a stream, a windowed aggregation keeps state for every open window. A watermark on the same event-time column lets Spark drop the state of windows that the watermark has passed; in append [output mode](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Output_mode), each window is emitted once, after that point.[^ss-late]

### Example

```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

events = spark.readStream.table("main.web.page_views")   # columns: ts, page

tumbling = (events.withWatermark("ts", "10 minutes")
            .groupBy(F.window("ts", "5 minutes"), "page")
            .count())

sliding = (events.withWatermark("ts", "10 minutes")
           .groupBy(F.window("ts", "10 minutes", "5 minutes"), "page")
           .count())

sessions = (events.withWatermark("ts", "10 minutes")
            .groupBy(F.session_window("ts", "30 minutes"), "page")
            .count())
```

The same queries in Spark SQL use `window(ts, '5 minutes')` and `session_window(ts, '30 minutes')` in the `GROUP BY` clause.

## Windowing in other engines

[Apache Flink](https://openlakehouse.io/wiki/Apache_Flink)'s DataStream API defines windows with a **window assigner**. It ships assigners for tumbling, sliding, session and **global** windows; a global window puts all records of a key into one window and computes nothing unless a custom trigger is set. Tumbling and sliding assigners take an optional offset, similar to Spark's `startTime`.[^flink-win]

Flink SQL uses windowing table-valued functions (TVFs): `TUMBLE`, `HOP`, `CUMULATE` and `SESSION`. Each adds `window_start`, `window_end` and `window_time` columns, where `window_time` equals `window_end` minus 1 millisecond. The session TVF is supported only in streaming mode. Windowing TVFs replace the older grouped window functions.[^flink-tvf]

Kafka Streams names its window types differently. It has hopping, tumbling, sliding and session windows; hopping and tumbling windows are aligned to the epoch, with an inclusive lower bound and an exclusive upper bound. A Kafka Streams **sliding window** is not the same as a Spark sliding window: it is aligned to record timestamps, both bounds are inclusive, and it is used for joins (`JoinWindows`) and for `SlidingWindows` aggregations. The Kafka documentation notes that what other tools call sliding windows, Kafka Streams calls hopping windows.[^kstreams]

## Comparison

| Window type | Spark Structured Streaming | Apache Flink DataStream | Apache Flink SQL | Kafka Streams |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed, non-overlapping | `window(ts, size)`[^builtin] | `TumblingEventTimeWindows`, `TumblingProcessingTimeWindows`[^flink-win] | `TUMBLE`[^flink-tvf] | Tumbling time window[^kstreams] |
| Fixed, overlapping | `window(ts, size, slide)` (sliding)[^builtin] | Sliding window assigners[^flink-win] | `HOP`[^flink-tvf] | Hopping time window[^kstreams] |
| Gap-based | `session_window(ts, gap)`, static or per-row gap[^builtin] | Session window assigners, static gap or `SessionWindowTimeGapExtractor`[^flink-win] | `SESSION`, streaming only, static gap[^flink-tvf] | Session window[^kstreams] |
| Other types | None built in | Global windows with a custom trigger[^flink-win] | `CUMULATE`[^flink-tvf] | Sliding windows based on record time differences[^kstreams] |
| Window bounds | Start inclusive, end exclusive, aligned to the Unix epoch with an optional `startTime`[^builtin] | Aligned to the epoch, optional offset[^flink-win] | `window_start`, `window_end`, `window_time` columns[^flink-tvf] | Hopping and tumbling aligned to the epoch; sliding aligned to records[^kstreams] |

# Data Engineering Reference Architectures

URL: https://openlakehouse.io/reference-architectures

An open reference architecture is a documented, runnable blueprint for a data platform in which every layer is open source and every interface between layers is an open format or protocol: Parquet files in an open table format such as Delta Lake or Apache Iceberg, an open catalog API such as Unity Catalog or the Iceberg REST specification, and open engine protocols such as Spark Connect or Arrow Flight SQL. Because the interfaces are open, any box in the diagram can be swapped for another project that speaks the same interface, and the whole architecture can run on a laptop, a Kubernetes cluster or any cloud.

### What is a reference architecture in data engineering?

A reference architecture is a reusable blueprint that names the layers of a data platform (sources, ingestion, storage, table format, catalog, compute, orchestration, serving and governance), the component in each layer, and how data flows between them. Teams start from it instead of designing a platform from a blank page.

### What makes a reference architecture open?

Every component is open source and every interface between components is an open format or protocol, so any box can be replaced by another project that speaks the same interface without migrating the data.

### What is the best open source data engineering stack?

There is no single best stack; it depends on the workload. A common open baseline is Apache Spark for compute, Delta Lake or Apache Iceberg for tables, Unity Catalog OSS or an Iceberg REST catalog for governance, Apache Kafka for events, Apache Airflow for orchestration and MLflow for models. The architectures on this page show which combination fits batch, streaming, real-time, sharing and AI workloads.

### Is there a reference architecture for an agentic lakehouse?

Yes. The governed AI agents architecture is the production shape of an agentic lakehouse: agents write Spark Declarative Pipelines as pull requests, CI dry-runs them against the real catalog, each tenant reaches Spark through an identity-pinned Spark Connect endpoint, and a governed Iceberg REST catalog authorizes every request. The agentic lakehouse and agentic data engineering guides on this site explain the concepts.

### Can I run these reference architectures myself?

Yes. Every architecture links to at least one public repository with the versions it pins and the commands from its README, and most run on a laptop with Docker.

### How are these different from vendor reference architectures?

Vendor reference architectures keep the vendor's platform fixed in the middle and vary the industry around it. Here the middle is also open: you can swap the table format, catalog, engine or orchestrator, and each choice is backed by code you can run.

### Is there a machine-readable version?

Yes. /reference-architectures.json contains every architecture, component and industry lens, and each architecture page has a Markdown twin at the same path with a .md suffix.

# The agentic lakehouse: Omnigent and MLflow over sandboxed Spark Connect sessions, on Iceberg and Unity Catalog

> Agents get a sandbox, a Spark session and a catalog identity. The platform decides the rest.

The agentic lakehouse architecture gives each AI agent a governed path to data. Omnigent runs the agent and evaluates policies on every tool call, model request and file operation, at session, agent and server level; MLflow traces and evaluates every step and fronts model providers. Each agent session runs in a sandbox, locally or on Kubernetes, with provider credentials kept outside it. Inside, the agent gets a Spark client over Spark Connect: a local Spark with Project Feather's shuffle-free execution for fast work on a subset of data, or a remote session pinned to its identity. Through Spark it can run batch, streaming, Real-Time Mode and declarative pipelines against Apache Iceberg tables in Unity Catalog, which authorizes each request and vends storage credentials scoped to what the agent may touch.

## When to use it
- You want agents to build and operate pipelines, not only answer questions.
- You need one governance story for people, services and agents.
- You want agents to iterate fast on small data without touching production.

## When not to
- A single question-answering assistant over a few tables: the semantic layer architecture is lighter.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | Operational systems and event streams | The data agents work on |  |
| Event streaming | Apache Kafka | Events agents can build streaming pipelines over |  |
| Agent harness and policy | Omnigent | Runs agents; policies return ALLOW, DENY or ASK at session, agent and server level |  |
| Agent sandboxes | Omnigent sandbox hosts | A container or microVM per session; provider credentials never enter it |  |
| Agent sandboxes | Kubernetes | Cluster for sandboxes and Spark executors |  |
| Tools and skills | Model Context Protocol | Named lakehouse tools: read a table, dry-run a pipeline, run one SQL statement |  |
| Models and gateway | MLflow | AI Gateway in front of hosted providers |  |
| Tracing and evaluation | MLflow | Traces every agent step; evaluates results against trusted tables |  |
| Spark Connect sessions | Spark Connect | One client session per agent: local in the sandbox, or a remote endpoint pinned to its identity |  |
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Batch and SQL on the cluster after review |  |
| Declarative pipelines | Spark Declarative Pipelines | The agent's output; a dry run must pass before it runs |  |
| Structured Streaming | Apache Spark | Structured Streaming jobs agents can author |  |
| Real-Time Mode | Spark Real-Time Mode | Real-Time Mode for millisecond paths |  |
| Local mode (Project Feather) | Spark local mode (Project Feather) | Fast local Spark on a subset of data, same catalog | Spark 4.3 |
| Catalog and credentials | Unity Catalog OSS | Authorizes each request; vends credentials scoped to the agent's namespace |  |
| Open table format | Apache Iceberg | Snapshots make every agent write inspectable and reversible |  |
| Object storage | SeaweedFS | Object storage |  |
| Lineage | OpenLineage | Which tables each agent job read and wrote |  |
| Orchestration | Apache Airflow | Runs approved pipelines; agents trigger runs through it |  |
| Runtime, CI/CD and IaC | GitOps CI gate | Agent changes arrive as pull requests; CI dry-runs them before anything is applied |  |
| Identity and secrets | SPIFFE / SPIRE | A workload identity per agent and tenant |  |

## How data flows
1. **A session starts in a sandbox.** Omnigent starts the agent in a container or microVM, locally or on Kubernetes. The sandbox gets the agent's own identity; provider credentials stay outside.
2. **Policies wrap every call.** Each tool call, model request and file operation passes session, agent and server policies. Any DENY blocks it; any ASK waits for a person.
3. **The agent gets a Spark session.** Inside the sandbox it connects over Spark Connect to a local Spark with Project Feather enabled, working on a subset of the data registered in the same catalog.
4. **It writes declarative pipelines.** The agent writes Spark Declarative Pipelines into its own namespace and dry-runs them against the real catalog.
5. **Changes go through review.** Passing work becomes a pull request; CI dry-runs it again and a controller applies it after approval.
6. **Production runs under identity.** Approved pipelines run on the cluster in batch, streaming or Real-Time Mode, through an endpoint pinned to the agent's or tenant's identity; the catalog vends credentials only for its tables.
7. **Everything is traced.** MLflow records each agent step and evaluation; OpenLineage records every table read and written; Iceberg snapshots let you roll back.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass)

The local version: an SDP agent on Omnigent with a local model, MCP tools and ALLOW, DENY and ASK policies, writing into a sandbox namespace on Iceberg and Unity Catalog (chapters 3 and 13).

### [open-lakehouse/safe-spark-agents-paper](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/safe-spark-agents-paper)

The production version: PR-only agent output, CI dry runs, identity-pinned Spark Connect behind mTLS, Kubernetes executors and a governed Iceberg REST catalog with per-tenant credential vending.

### [lisancao/spark-demos](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos)

Demo 07 measures the local-mode overheads Project Feather targets; demo 16 shows Spark 4.3's shuffle-free single-task execution.

## Caveats
- Project Feather's shuffle-free single-task execution ships off by default in Spark 4.3 and applies to in-memory relations at or below 1,000 rows by default.
- Omnigent sandbox providers differ in network egress control; check the provider before relying on it for isolation.
- This architecture combines the masterclass and the paper; no single repo deploys all of it yet.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do you give an AI agent access to Spark safely?

Give each agent its own Spark Connect session: a local Spark in its sandbox for fast work on a subset of data, and a remote endpoint pinned to its identity for production runs. The catalog authorizes every request and vends storage credentials scoped to the agent's namespace.

### What do Omnigent and MLflow each do in an agentic lakehouse?

Omnigent runs the agent, keeps its session in a sandbox, and enforces policies on every tool call, model request and file operation. MLflow traces and evaluates what the agent did and can front model providers through its AI Gateway.

### What is Project Feather and why does it matter for agents?

Project Feather (SPARK-56978) cuts Spark's local-mode latency. Spark 4.3 adds shuffle-free single-task execution for small queries, which suits agents that issue many small queries while they iterate.

# Batch medallion with Spark Declarative Pipelines: Spark 4.3, Apache Iceberg and Unity Catalog with bronze, silver and gold

> Declare the tables, let Spark work out the order, keep every layer in an open format.

A batch medallion architecture organizes lakehouse tables into three layers: bronze holds raw records as they arrived, silver holds cleaned and conformed records, and gold holds aggregates shaped for a specific use. In this open reference architecture, Spark Declarative Pipelines (Spark 4.1 and later) defines each layer as a table or materialized view, Spark resolves the dependency graph and runs it, the tables are Apache Iceberg in Unity Catalog OSS 0.7 on S3-compatible storage, Apache Airflow schedules and backfills the runs, and DuckDB reads the gold tables through the catalog's Iceberg REST endpoint.

## When to use it
- Your sources arrive as files, extracts or database snapshots on a schedule.
- You want idempotent bronze loads and reproducible silver and gold tables.
- You want to change a transformation without hand-ordering every downstream job.

## When not to
- Sub-second latency: use the real-time streaming pattern.
- Teams that need a released Iceberg runtime for Spark 4.3 today: the course builds one from an open Iceberg pull request as a temporary step.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | Order-event generator and batch extracts | Daily and hourly files |  |
| Batch and file ingestion | Idempotent bronze loader | Appends each batch once, keyed so reruns do not duplicate |  |
| Change data capture | AUTO CDC (Spark Declarative Pipelines) | Applies change feeds as SCD type 1 or 2 |  |
| ML lifecycle | MLflow | Logs the gold snapshot id with each model run | 3.1.0 |
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Runs the pipeline over Spark Connect | 4.3.0 |
| Declarative pipelines | Spark Declarative Pipelines | Declares bronze to silver to gold and resolves order | pyspark[pipelines]==4.3.0 |
| Other engines | DuckDB | Reads gold through Iceberg REST | 1.5.6 |
| Catalog and credentials | Unity Catalog OSS | Writable Iceberg REST catalog | 0.7.0 |
| Open table format | Apache Iceberg | Bronze, silver and gold tables | runtime 4.3_2.13 built from apache/iceberg#18749 |
| Object storage | SeaweedFS | s3://lakehouse/warehouse | 4.51 |
| Orchestration | Apache Airflow | DAG with schedules and backfills | 3.3.2 |

## How data flows
1. **Land bronze once.** Each batch is appended to a bronze Iceberg table with a key that makes reruns idempotent.
2. **Declare silver and gold.** A Spark Declarative Pipelines spec declares silver as cleaned bronze and gold as aggregates over silver.
3. **Spark plans the graph.** spark-pipelines run resolves dependencies, creates or updates each table in Unity Catalog and records the run.
4. **Airflow schedules.** An Airflow DAG triggers the pipeline on a schedule and replays past intervals for backfills.
5. **Serve from the same tables.** DuckDB attaches the Unity Catalog Iceberg REST endpoint and queries gold without copying it.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass)

Chapters 6 to 11 build this pattern: Iceberg through Unity Catalog, idempotent bronze, the SDP medallion, Airflow backfills and DuckDB serving.

### [open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse)

An open reference architecture for the lakehouse that runs on Docker, deploys to AWS, and is designed so an AI agent can set it up and tear it down.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse
cd open-lakehouse

cp .env.example .env       # fill in POSTGRES_*, S3_* placeholders
./lakehouse setup          # validate env, install deps, download ~860MB of JARs
./lakehouse start all      # Spark 4.1 master + worker + Connect server + Kafka
./lakehouse start unity-catalog
./lakehouse start mlflow
./lakehouse status --json  # confirm healthy (incl. spark.connect_grpc_listening)
```

### [lisancao/spark-demos](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos)

Demo 16 includes an AUTO CDC flow that writes SCD type 2 into Iceberg on Spark 4.3.0.

## Caveats
- There is no released Iceberg Spark runtime for Spark 4.3 yet; the course's chapter 5.5 builds it from apache/iceberg#18749 as a temporary step.
- Unity Catalog 0.7 or later is required for Iceberg writes through its REST catalog.
- Older SeaweedFS releases have an S3A _temporary rename bug; the course pins 4.51.

## Industry use cases
- **Payments and fintech: Ledger reconciliation.** Match gateway, processor and bank files every day and surface the breaks.
- **Healthcare providers: FHIR bulk export to OMOP.** Land FHIR NDJSON in bronze and transform it into the OMOP common data model.
- **Manufacturing: Quality and scrap analytics.** Join MES quality checks with ERP orders every shift to find where scrap comes from.
- **Energy and utilities: Meter data at scale.** Process billions of interval reads a day through bronze, VEE silver and billing gold.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a medallion architecture?

A layout of lakehouse tables in three layers: bronze for raw data as it arrived, silver for cleaned and conformed data, and gold for aggregates built for a specific consumer.

### Do I need Databricks to use declarative pipelines?

No. Spark Declarative Pipelines is part of open source Apache Spark from 4.1, run with the spark-pipelines CLI against a Spark Connect server.

### Can DuckDB read tables that Spark writes?

Yes, when both go through the same catalog. In the masterclass, DuckDB attaches Unity Catalog's Iceberg REST endpoint and reads the gold Iceberg tables Spark wrote.

# Change data capture with SCD type 2: AUTO CDC in Spark Declarative Pipelines, from a Kafka change feed into Apache Iceberg

> Keep the current state and every past version of each row, without hand-written MERGE logic.

Change data capture (CDC) with slowly changing dimensions type 2 turns a feed of row-level changes from an operational system into a table that holds both the current state and the full history of each row. In open source Apache Spark 4.3, an AUTO CDC flow in Spark Declarative Pipelines reads the change feed, orders events by a sequence column, applies inserts, updates and deletes by key, and stores the result as SCD type 2: a change to a tracked column closes the old version and opens a new one, while changes to untracked columns update the current version in place. The target must support row-level operations, which Apache Iceberg provides.

## When to use it
- An operational database or service emits change events and you need its tables in the lakehouse.
- Auditors or analysts ask what a row looked like at a past point in time.
- You want to stop maintaining hand-written MERGE statements for every replicated table.

## When not to
- Targets without row-level operations: AUTO CDC needs a DSv2 table that supports them.
- Spark releases before 4.3 for this exact flow; the reference demo is verified on Spark 4.3.0.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | Operational database or service | Emits one event per insert, update or delete |  |
| Event streaming | Apache Kafka | The change feed topic (menu-changes in the demo) | apache/kafka 4.0.0 image |
| Change data capture | Debezium | Turns database transaction logs into change events |  |
| Change data capture | AUTO CDC (Spark Declarative Pipelines) | KEYS, SEQUENCE BY, APPLY AS DELETE WHEN, STORED AS SCD TYPE 2 |  |
| Declarative pipelines | Spark Declarative Pipelines | Runs the pipeline with spark-pipelines run | pyspark==4.3.0 |
| Catalog and credentials | Iceberg hadoop catalog | Declared in the pipeline spec |  |
| Open table format | Apache Iceberg | SCD type 2 target with row-level operations | Spark 4.3 runtime built from source |
| Object storage | Local filesystem | Iceberg warehouse directory in the demo |  |

## How data flows
1. **Changes are published.** Each insert, update or delete arrives on a Kafka topic as one JSON event with a key, a sequence number and an operation.
2. **Read the feed.** A Python table in the pipeline reads the topic with Structured Streaming and parses each event.
3. **Apply by key, in order.** The AUTO CDC flow groups events by key and orders them by the sequence column, so late or out-of-order events land correctly.
4. **Track history.** A change to a tracked column (price or station in the demo) closes the current version and opens a new one; a change to another column updates the current version in place; a delete closes the row's window.
5. **Query any point in time.** The Iceberg table holds every version with its validity window, so you can read the current state or the state at any past sequence.

## Run it

### [lisancao/spark-demos](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos)

Demo 16 (Spark 4.3 guide), scd2/ folder: a ghost-kitchen menu change feed on Kafka applied with AUTO CDC as SCD type 2 into Iceberg.

```bash
scd2/reset.sh       # Kafka up, an empty menu-changes topic, no table, no checkpoints
scd2/publish.sh scd2/incoming/batch-1.json && scd2/run.sh && scd2/history.sh
scd2/publish.sh scd2/incoming/batch-2.json && scd2/run.sh && scd2/history.sh
scd2/publish.sh scd2/incoming/batch-3.json && scd2/run.sh && scd2/history.sh
docker compose -f scd2/compose.yaml down -v   # when done
```

## Caveats
- Iceberg has not published a Spark 4.3 runtime (Maven Central stops at iceberg-spark-runtime-4.1); the demo builds iceberg-spark-runtime-4.3_2.13 from an Iceberg checkout with Spark 4.3 support.
- AUTO CDC needs a target that implements DSv2 row-level operations.
- The jars and spark.sql.extensions are static configs, so they are passed to spark-pipelines run, not set in the pipeline spec.
- Pipeline storage must be an absolute URI.

## Industry use cases
- **Banking: Core banking CDC into the lakehouse.** Keep a current and historical (SCD type 2) view of accounts without full nightly reloads.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is SCD type 2?

Slowly changing dimension type 2 keeps every version of a row: when a tracked attribute changes, the current version is closed and a new one is opened, so the table answers both what is true now and what was true at any earlier time.

### Can open source Spark do CDC without hand-written MERGE?

Yes. Spark Declarative Pipelines in Spark 4.3 has AUTO CDC flows: you declare the keys, the sequence column, the delete condition and STORED AS SCD TYPE 1 or 2, and Spark applies the change feed.

### How does AUTO CDC handle out-of-order events?

It orders events per key by the SEQUENCE BY column, so an event that arrives late is applied in sequence order rather than arrival order.

- [menu.sql (the AUTO CDC flow)](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos/blob/main/demos/16_spark_43_guide/scd2/transformations/menu.sql)

# Streaming medallion: Kafka, Spark Structured Streaming and Apache Iceberg in Unity Catalog

> Events in, governed tables out, seconds behind the source.

A streaming medallion architecture applies the bronze, silver and gold layout to event streams. Apache Kafka buffers events, an Apache Spark Structured Streaming query appends them to a bronze Apache Iceberg table with its checkpoint on object storage, and a Spark Declarative Pipeline derives silver and gold. Because the tables are open and registered in Unity Catalog OSS, batch jobs, other engines and AI agents read the same data the stream writes.

## When to use it
- Sources emit events continuously and consumers want tables, not topics.
- Latency of seconds to minutes is enough.
- You want one copy of history that streaming jobs, batch jobs and agents all read.

## When not to
- Request-path latency in milliseconds: see the real-time streaming architecture.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | Applications, devices and CDC | Emit events |  |
| Event streaming | Apache Kafka | Durable event buffer (the orders topic) | Confluent 7.5.0 images |
| Change data capture | Debezium | Turns database changes into Kafka events |  |
| Spark Connect sessions | Spark Connect | The streaming query runs over Spark Connect | 4.3.0 |
| Declarative pipelines | Spark Declarative Pipelines | Silver and gold derived from bronze | 4.3.0 |
| Structured Streaming | Apache Spark | Kafka to iceberg.bronze.orders_raw, checkpoint at s3a://lakehouse/_checkpoints | 4.3.0 |
| Catalog and credentials | Unity Catalog OSS | Iceberg REST catalog for every layer | 0.7.0 |
| Open table format | Apache Iceberg | Bronze, silver and gold tables |  |
| Object storage | SeaweedFS | Tables and streaming checkpoints | 4.51 |
| Orchestration | Apache Airflow | Runs the batch side and table maintenance | 3.3.2 |
| Table maintenance | Iceberg maintenance procedures | Compaction keeps small streaming files in check |  |

## How data flows
1. **Buffer events.** Producers write JSON events to a Kafka topic, including resends and late events.
2. **Append to bronze.** A Structured Streaming query reads Kafka and appends to a bronze Iceberg table; its checkpoint makes the write exactly-once.
3. **Clean and deduplicate.** Silver handles late and repeated events deterministically.
4. **Aggregate.** Gold computes the aggregates consumers read.
5. **Compact.** Streaming writes many small files; a scheduled rewrite_data_files keeps reads fast.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass)

Chapter 9 streams Kafka into iceberg.bronze.orders_raw over Spark Connect; chapter 8 builds silver and gold; chapter 10 adds maintenance.

### [open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse)

The same flow writing Delta Lake bronze into Unity Catalog 0.6.0.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse
cd open-lakehouse

cp .env.example .env       # fill in POSTGRES_*, S3_* placeholders
./lakehouse setup          # validate env, install deps, download ~860MB of JARs
./lakehouse start all      # Spark 4.1 master + worker + Connect server + Kafka
./lakehouse start unity-catalog
./lakehouse start mlflow
./lakehouse status --json  # confirm healthy (incl. spark.connect_grpc_listening)
```

## Caveats
- Match the Kafka connector to your Spark version exactly; a spark-sql-kafka build for one Spark minor version can fail with NoSuchMethodError on another.
- Kafka itself is not registered in the catalog; only the tables are.

## Industry use cases
- **Payments and fintech: Streaming payment history into tables.** Land every gateway event in a bronze table and keep silver current within seconds.
- **Manufacturing: Telemetry into tables.** Land MQTT and OPC UA readings in bronze and keep asset-level silver current.
- **Retail and e-commerce: Real-time inventory.** Keep stock positions current from POS and warehouse events so online orders do not oversell.
- **Retail and e-commerce: Clickstream to sessions.** Sessionize web and app events with watermarks and land them as tables for funnel analysis.
- **Telecommunications: CDR processing.** Process mediation files into rated usage tables every few minutes.
- **Cybersecurity: Security data lake.** Normalize every source to OCSF in silver and keep years of history cheaply.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do I stream Kafka into Apache Iceberg with open source tools?

Run an Apache Spark Structured Streaming query with the Kafka source and an Iceberg table as the sink, with its checkpoint on object storage, and register the table in an Iceberg REST catalog such as Unity Catalog OSS 0.7 so other engines can read it.

### Is the Kafka to Iceberg write exactly-once?

Yes for the table: Structured Streaming records Kafka offsets in its checkpoint and commits each micro-batch atomically, so a restarted query neither skips nor duplicates batches.

- [Structured Streaming + Kafka integration](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/streaming/structured-streaming-kafka-integration.html)

# Real-time streaming with Spark Real-Time Mode: Kafka in, Kafka out, milliseconds in between

> Continuous processing for fraud, recommendations and live boards, measured end to end.

Real-time streaming is the architecture for decisions that must happen while an event is still in flight: score a payment, update a recommendation, move a leaderboard. In open source Apache Spark, Real-Time Mode is a Structured Streaming trigger that processes records continuously instead of in micro-batches. The reference pipelines read from Kafka, transform or keep state with transformWithState, and write back to Kafka or a key-value store, with latency measured from producer timestamp to consumer.

## When to use it
- Your SLA is in tens or hundreds of milliseconds, not seconds.
- You are porting Apache Flink jobs and want to know which ones move to Spark.
- You already run Spark for batch and want one engine for both.

## When not to
- Writing large analytical tables: use the streaming medallion pattern and keep this path thin.
- Python UDFs in the hot path: Real-Time Mode does not support them.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | Payments, clicks, game events | Producers with event timestamps |  |
| Event streaming | Apache Kafka | Input topic, 16 partitions in the reference runs | Confluent 7.6.0 image |
| Real-Time Mode | Spark Real-Time Mode | Continuous processing trigger | Spark 4.1 to 4.3 |
| Real-Time Mode | Apache Spark | transformWithState for keyed state, on RocksDB | 4.3.0 |
| Real-Time Mode | Apache Flink | The engine being compared or migrated from |  |
| Open table format | Apache Iceberg | Optional history table written by a separate query |  |
| Apps and APIs | Kafka sink topic | Output and latency topics |  |
| Apps and APIs | Redis | Latest state for applications |  |
| Apps and APIs | Fraud engine, app UI, live board | Read results within milliseconds |  |

## How data flows
1. **Produce with timestamps.** A generator writes keyed events to Kafka with the send time embedded.
2. **Process continuously.** A Structured Streaming query with the real-time trigger processes each record as it arrives instead of waiting for a micro-batch.
3. **Keep state.** Stateful steps such as deduplication, windows or a custom transformWithState processor keep per-key state in RocksDB.
4. **Emit.** Results go to an output Kafka topic or a key-value store.
5. **Measure.** A consumer subtracts the embedded send time from arrival time and reports p50, p95 and p99.

## Run it

### [lisancao/spark-rtm-quickstart](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-rtm-quickstart)

Five Real-Time Mode pipelines on Spark 4.1 with Kafka and a latency consumer, compared against micro-batch.

```bash
# Start Kafka + Spark
docker compose up -d

# Create Kafka topics
docker exec kafka kafka-topics --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
    --create --topic rtm-input --partitions 16 --if-not-exists
docker exec kafka kafka-topics --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
    --create --topic rtm-output --partitions 16 --if-not-exists
docker exec kafka kafka-topics --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
    --create --topic rtm-latency --partitions 16 --if-not-exists

# Start the data generator (in a separate terminal)
python data_generator/producer.py --rate 1000 --keys 100

# Run a pipeline
docker exec spark spark-submit /opt/spark-data/pipelines/01_stateless_passthrough.py
```

### [lisancao/spark-demos](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos)

Demo 14 (bookshop recommender, Spark 4.3.0) and demo 10 (chained transformWithState lobby board) compare micro-batch with Real-Time Mode and commit the numbers in NOTES.md.

### [lisancao/flink-to-spark-rtm](https://github.com/lisancao/flink-to-spark-rtm)

Four streaming patterns (stateless, tumbling window, sliding window, keyed state) written for both Flink 1.20 and Spark 4.1 Real-Time Mode, with migration notes.

## Caveats
- Open source Spark 4.1 Real-Time Mode is stateless only; stateful queries need a later release (the stateful demos run on Spark 4.3).
- Python UDFs are not supported in Real-Time Mode.
- PySpark 4.1 has no trigger(realTime=...) argument; the quickstart uses a Py4J helper.
- transformWithState requires the RocksDB state store provider.
- Size task slots to source partitions plus shuffles times shuffle partitions, or the query stalls.

## Industry use cases
- **Banking: Real-time card fraud scoring.** Score each authorization against recent account behaviour before the switch times out.
- **Payments and fintech: Sub-second fraud features.** Maintain velocity counters per card and device and serve them while the payment is still in flight.
- **Payments and fintech: Migrating a Flink fraud job to Spark.** Port keyed state and windows to Spark and measure whether latency holds.
- **Healthcare providers: Real-time deterioration alerts.** Score streaming vitals against early-warning rules and push alerts to care teams.
- **Manufacturing: Predictive maintenance.** Compute rolling sensor features per asset and score failure risk continuously.
- **Energy and utilities: Outage detection from streaming telemetry.** Correlate last-gasp meter events and SCADA alarms within seconds.
- **Retail and e-commerce: In-session recommendations.** Update product recommendations while the shopper is still browsing.
- **Telecommunications: Service assurance.** Correlate alarms and KPI drops across cells within seconds.
- **Cybersecurity: Streaming detections.** Evaluate detection rules on normalized events within seconds of arrival.

## Frequently asked questions

### How fast is Spark Real-Time Mode?

In the spark-rtm-quickstart run committed in results/latency-results.md (stateless, 500 events per second, 16 cores), end-to-end p50 was 17 ms and p99 was 21 to 26 ms across six runs. In spark-demos demo 14 on Spark 4.3.0, a stateless enrichment step measured p50 0 ms and p99 1 ms in real-time mode against 115 ms and 204 ms in micro-batch.

### Can Spark replace Flink for low-latency streaming?

For many stateless and windowed jobs, yes; flink-to-spark-rtm writes the same four patterns for both engines. Keyed state with timers is where migrations need the most care, since Spark expresses it through transformWithState.

### Does Real-Time Mode support stateful queries?

Not in open source Spark 4.1. The stateful reference demos (transformWithState, dedup and windows) run on Spark 4.3.

# One catalog, many engines: Unity Catalog OSS with Spark, DuckDB, PyIceberg and Trino on Delta and Iceberg

> Write once, read from whatever engine fits the question.

A multi-engine catalog architecture puts an open catalog between the tables and every engine that uses them. Unity Catalog OSS stores table metadata in Postgres, exposes Delta tables through its own API and Iceberg tables through the Iceberg REST catalog specification, and vends short-lived storage credentials per table. Apache Spark, DuckDB, PyIceberg and Trino then read and write the same data without copies, and access is decided once, in the catalog.

## When to use it
- Different teams prefer different engines for the same data.
- You want to stop copying data into a warehouse per tool.
- You want storage credentials vended per table instead of shared keys.

## When not to
- Expecting identical feature support in every engine: write support differs by engine, format and catalog version.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | Pipelines and notebooks | Create and update tables |  |
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Delta notebooks on Spark 4.2.0; Iceberg notebooks on Spark 4.1.3 | 4.2.0 / 4.1.3 |
| Other engines | PyIceberg | JVM-free Iceberg reads and writes |  |
| Other engines | DuckDB | Attaches the Iceberg REST endpoint for SQL reads |  |
| Other engines | Trino | Distributed SQL over the same catalog |  |
| Catalog and credentials | Unity Catalog OSS | Delta API, Iceberg REST catalog and credential vending | 0.7.0 |
| Catalog and credentials | PostgreSQL | Catalog metadata | 16.3 |
| Open table format | Delta Lake | Catalog-managed Delta tables |  |
| Open table format | Apache Iceberg | Native Iceberg tables through Iceberg REST |  |
| Object storage | RustFS | S3-compatible storage with STS credentials | 1.0.0 |
| Dashboards and notebooks | marimo | Reactive notebooks on :2718 and :2719 |  |

## How data flows
1. **Create through the catalog.** A Spark session configured with the Unity Catalog connector creates a managed Delta table, or an Iceberg table through the Iceberg REST endpoint.
2. **Catalog records metadata.** Unity Catalog stores the table, its location and its format in Postgres.
3. **Credentials are vended.** When an engine loads a table, the catalog returns short-lived storage credentials scoped to that table's path.
4. **Another engine reads.** DuckDB or PyIceberg connects to the same Iceberg REST endpoint and reads the table directly from object storage.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/unitycatalog-playground](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/unitycatalog-playground)

Unity Catalog OSS on your machine with Spark, Delta and Iceberg in marimo notebooks, Postgres for metadata and RustFS for storage.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/open-lakehouse/unitycatalog-playground.git
cd unitycatalog-playground
just uc=local start
```

### [open-lakehouse/unitycatalog-rs](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/unitycatalog-rs)

A Rust implementation of the same catalog APIs, useful when you want a single binary or Helm chart.

```bash
pip install 'unitycatalog-rs[all]'   # the Python client, the uc CLI, the server and the web UI
uc dev                               # a server on http://localhost:8080, with the web UI
uc catalog list                      # upstream's bin/uc commands
```

### [open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass)

Chapter 11 has DuckDB read the Spark-written Iceberg tables through Unity Catalog 0.7's Iceberg REST endpoint.

## Caveats
- iceberg-spark-runtime exists only for Spark 4.0 and 4.1 at the time of writing, which is why the playground's Iceberg notebook runs Spark 4.1.3.
- The RustFS STS credential in the playground expires after 12 hours; refresh it with just uc=local rotate-creds.
- The playground needs at least 4 GB of Docker memory and is not for production.

## Industry use cases
- **Telecommunications: Network planning on many engines.** Run heavy jobs in Spark and interactive exploration in Trino against one catalog.
- **Cybersecurity: Threat hunting with any engine.** Hunt in DuckDB or Trino over the same tables that Spark writes.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is an Iceberg REST catalog?

An HTTP API defined by the Apache Iceberg project for creating, loading and committing Iceberg tables. Any engine that speaks it can use any catalog that implements it, including Unity Catalog OSS, Apache Polaris and Lakekeeper.

### Can Spark and DuckDB share the same tables?

Yes. Point both at the same catalog: Spark through the Unity Catalog connector or Iceberg REST, DuckDB through its Iceberg extension attached to the Iceberg REST endpoint.

### What is credential vending?

The catalog hands an engine short-lived storage credentials scoped to one table's location when the engine loads it, so engines never hold long-lived bucket keys.

- [unitycatalog-playground README](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/unitycatalog-playground#readme)
- [Iceberg REST catalog spec](https://iceberg.apache.org/rest-catalog-spec/)
- [Unity Catalog OSS](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog)

# Governed AI agents for data engineering: Spark Declarative Pipelines, Spark Connect, Kubernetes and a governed Iceberg REST catalog

> Agents write pipeline specs; the platform decides what they are allowed to touch.

Governed AI data engineering is an architecture in which AI agents author data pipelines but never hold direct power over data. The agent writes declarative Spark Declarative Pipelines specs as a pull request; CI dry-runs them against the real catalog; a controller applies approved changes. Each tenant reaches Spark only through one identity-pinned Spark Connect ingress behind mTLS, executors run as Kubernetes pods, and a governed Iceberg REST catalog authorizes every request and vends storage credentials scoped to that tenant. Each layer owns one job, so a mistake in one does not become a breach in another.

## When to use it
- You want AI agents to build or change pipelines without giving them production credentials.
- You need per-tenant isolation on shared Spark infrastructure.
- You want defects caught before any data is processed.

## When not to
- A single-user sandbox: the masterclass's local agent chapter is the lighter starting point.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | AI coding agent | Writes inert pipeline specs as a pull request |  |
| Agent harness and policy | Omnigent | Agent harness with tools and policies |  |
| Models and gateway | Ollama | Local model for the course's agent chapter |  |
| Spark Connect sessions | Spark Connect | The single identity-pinned ingress per tenant | 4.1.2 |
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Executors do the work | 4.1.2 |
| Declarative pipelines | Spark Declarative Pipelines | Declarative authoring: specs, not imperative jobs | Spark 4.1.2 |
| Catalog and credentials | Lakekeeper | Governed Iceberg REST catalog with per-principal authorization and credential vending | 0.13.1 |
| Open table format | Apache Iceberg | Tables under per-tenant prefixes | 1.11.0 |
| Object storage | Amazon S3 | Data under per-tenant prefixes with STS-scoped credentials |  |
| Access control and policy | Envoy | mTLS on :15009; routes each client certificate to its tenant | 1.31.5 |
| Access control and policy | OpenFGA | Authorization model behind the catalog | 1.14.0 |
| Runtime, CI/CD and IaC | GitOps CI gate | PR-only output, dry run against the real catalog, reconcile |  |
| Runtime, CI/CD and IaC | Kubernetes | Client-mode driver plus executor pods on EKS | EKS 1.31 |

## How data flows
1. **Agent proposes.** The agent writes Spark Declarative Pipelines specs and opens a pull request; it has no direct write path.
2. **CI dry-runs.** CI runs the pipeline in dry-run mode against the real catalog, catching structural defects before any data is processed.
3. **Identity-pinned ingress.** The tenant's client certificate reaches Envoy, which routes by its SPIFFE URI SAN to that tenant's Spark Connect server.
4. **Executors run.** Kubernetes schedules executor pods that do the work.
5. **Catalog authorizes.** Lakekeeper with OpenFGA authorizes each table operation and vends STS credentials scoped to the tenant's prefix.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/safe-spark-agents-paper](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/safe-spark-agents-paper)

Working paper, reproducible study and open reference architecture for safe, governed AI data engineering on Apache Spark.

```bash
cd study
python3 analysis/analyze.py results/results.powered.AB.n12.final.jsonl --tasks config/TASKS.lock.json --assume-backend local
```

### [open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass)

Chapter 3 runs an agent on Omnigent with a local Ollama model, MCP tools and ALLOW, DENY and ASK policies; chapter 13 has a coding agent operate the stack through AGENTS.md.

### [open-lakehouse/lakehouse-agent-kit](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/lakehouse-agent-kit)

Early-stage agent skills for the open lakehouse, driven by a connection profile instead of hardcoded hosts (lakehouse-core ships today).

## Caveats
- The isolation proof runs on one Spark Connect server per tenant; a shared-server design is described as frontier work in the paper.
- The five isolation links are proven one at a time, not as one composed request.
- Unity Catalog OSS 0.5.0, evaluated as an alternate catalog, could not do per-principal authorization on its Iceberg REST path.

## Industry use cases
- **Payments and fintech: Governed agent for merchant support.** Let an agent answer settlement questions with tools limited by policy.
- **Cybersecurity: Investigation agents.** Let an agent query logs and draft incident timelines under strict tool policy.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do you let AI agents build data pipelines safely?

Give them a declarative output and no direct path to data: the agent writes Spark Declarative Pipelines specs as a pull request, CI dry-runs them against the real catalog, and execution happens through an identity-pinned Spark Connect ingress with a catalog that authorizes every table operation.

### Do declarative pipelines catch more agent mistakes?

In the safe-spark-agents study (528 runs: 22 tasks, 12 seeds, 2 arms), the Spark Declarative Pipelines dry run caught 79 structural defects before any data was processed, against 0 for the imperative arm. SDP output was 49% fewer lines at about 2.3 times the tokens.

## Sources
- [safe-spark-agents-paper](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/safe-spark-agents-paper)
- [Paper site](https://open-lakehouse.github.io/safe-spark-agents-paper/)

# Open data sharing: Delta Sharing servers over Unity Catalog and open tables

> Share live tables with another organization without copying them or sending files.

Open data sharing is an architecture for giving another organization read access to live lakehouse tables through an open protocol instead of file exports. A Delta Sharing server authenticates the recipient, checks which shares and tables they may read, and returns short-lived URLs or credentials for the underlying files; the recipient reads them with any Delta Sharing client, including pandas, Spark and other engines. Data stays in the provider's storage and the recipient always sees the current version.

## When to use it
- Partners, customers or regulators need recurring access to the same tables.
- You want to stop running file-drop jobs.
- Recipients use different tools than you do.

## When not to
- Write access for recipients: the protocol is read-only.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | Provider pipelines | Maintain the tables to share |  |
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Provider-side writes |  |
| Catalog and credentials | Unity Catalog OSS | Source of shares and table locations |  |
| Open table format | Delta Lake | Shared tables |  |
| Object storage | Amazon S3 | Provider's bucket; data never moves |  |
| Data sharing | Delta Sharing | Open REST protocol for recipients | server 1.3.10 in open-lakehouse |
| Data sharing | distributary | Composable Rust sharing server with Postgres or SQLite stores |  |

## How data flows
1. **Define a share.** The provider groups tables into a share and grants it to a recipient.
2. **Issue a profile.** The recipient receives a profile file with the server endpoint and a bearer token.
3. **Recipient queries.** The client lists shares and tables and asks to read one, optionally with predicate hints.
4. **Server returns file URLs.** The server checks the grant and returns short-lived URLs for the current table files.
5. **Read directly.** The client reads Parquet files from the provider's storage; nothing is copied into the recipient's platform.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/distributary](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/distributary)

OpenSharing and Delta Sharing in Rust: protocol models, client, admin API and a composable sharing server.

```bash
cargo check --workspace --all-features
cargo nextest run --workspace --all-features
```

### [open-lakehouse/unitycatalog-rs](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/unitycatalog-rs)

A catalog that serves a Delta Sharing server alongside the Unity Catalog, Delta and Iceberg REST APIs.

```bash
pip install 'unitycatalog-rs[all]'   # the Python client, the uc CLI, the server and the web UI
uc dev                               # a server on http://localhost:8080, with the web UI
uc catalog list                      # upstream's bin/uc commands
```

### [open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse)

Ships an opt-in Delta Sharing server (1.3.10) on :8443 next to the rest of the stack.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse
cd open-lakehouse

cp .env.example .env       # fill in POSTGRES_*, S3_* placeholders
./lakehouse setup          # validate env, install deps, download ~860MB of JARs
./lakehouse start all      # Spark 4.1 master + worker + Connect server + Kafka
./lakehouse start unity-catalog
./lakehouse start mlflow
./lakehouse status --json  # confirm healthy (incl. spark.connect_grpc_listening)
```

## Caveats
- distributary's README gives developer commands only; its architecture document plans presigned-URL queries, change data feed and recipient tokens.

## Industry use cases
- **Healthcare providers: Research data sharing.** Share de-identified cohorts with a university partner as live tables.
- **Manufacturing: Supplier data exchange.** Share quality and demand tables with suppliers as live tables.
- **Energy and utilities: Regulator and partner sharing.** Share reliability metrics with regulators as live tables.
- **Retail and e-commerce: Supplier collaboration.** Share sell-through and stock tables with suppliers instead of sending reports.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is Delta Sharing?

An open REST protocol, governed with Delta Lake under the Linux Foundation, for sharing live tables across organizations. Recipients read the provider's files through short-lived URLs with any compatible client.

### Do recipients need the same platform as the provider?

No. Clients exist for pandas, Apache Spark and other tools, and the open-lakehouse repos include Rust implementations of the server and client.

## Sources
- [Delta Sharing protocol](https://github.com/delta-io/delta-sharing/blob/main/PROTOCOL.md)
- [distributary](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/distributary)

# The open lakehouse on a laptop: Spark 4.3, Apache Iceberg, Unity Catalog, Kafka, Airflow, MLflow and an agent, in Docker

> The whole stack, one service at a time, on the machine in front of you.

The open lakehouse on a laptop runs every layer of an open source data platform in Docker on one machine: SeaweedFS as S3-compatible storage, Apache Iceberg tables in Unity Catalog OSS 0.7 through its Iceberg REST endpoint, Apache Spark 4.3 behind a Spark Connect server, Spark Declarative Pipelines for the medallion, Kafka for events, Airflow 3 for scheduling and table maintenance, DuckDB reading the same tables, MLflow for models, and an AI agent on Omnigent with a local model, MCP tools and policies. It exists so a data engineer, a student or an AI agent can build, test and tear down a real lakehouse without a cloud account.

## When to use it
- You want to learn how the layers of an open lakehouse fit together by building them.
- You need a local integration environment with a real catalog and object store.
- You want an AI agent to have a full, disposable stack to work against.

## When not to
- Production: the course's Terraform chapter is illustrative and not applied.
- Teams that need a released Iceberg runtime for Spark 4.3 today: the course builds one from an open Iceberg pull request.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | Order-event generator | Batch and streaming order events, the course's one dataset |  |
| Batch and file ingestion | Idempotent bronze loader | Appends each batch once |  |
| Event streaming | Apache Kafka | Order events for the streaming chapter | Confluent 7.5.0 images |
| Agent harness and policy | Omnigent | Runs the SDP agent and evaluates ALLOW, DENY and ASK policies on every tool call | 0.22.0 |
| Tools and skills | Model Context Protocol | Named tools: read and write pipeline files, dry-run or run the pipeline, run one SQL statement; no shell |  |
| Models and gateway | Ollama | Local model sdp-qwen3, built from qwen3:14b with a 16K context window |  |
| ML lifecycle | MLflow | Tracks a model trained on gold and logs the gold snapshot id | 3.1.0 |
| Spark Connect sessions | Spark Connect | sc://spark-connect:15002 for every client, the agent included | 4.3.0 |
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Ingestion and queries over Spark Connect | 4.3.0 |
| Declarative pipelines | Spark Declarative Pipelines | Bronze to silver to gold; the agent's output, gated on a dry run | pyspark[pipelines]==4.3.0 |
| Structured Streaming | Apache Spark | Kafka to iceberg.bronze.orders_raw with a checkpoint on S3 | 4.3.0 |
| Other engines | DuckDB | Reads gold through the Iceberg REST endpoint | 1.5.6 |
| Catalog and credentials | Unity Catalog OSS | Writable Iceberg REST catalog; a sandbox namespace for the agent | 0.7.0 |
| Open table format | Apache Iceberg | Bronze, silver and gold tables; snapshots for time travel and rollback | runtime 4.3_2.13 built from apache/iceberg#18749 |
| Object storage | SeaweedFS | s3://lakehouse/warehouse | 4.51 |
| Orchestration | Apache Airflow | Schedules the medallion with backfills | 3.3.2 |
| Table maintenance | Iceberg maintenance procedures | A DAG that runs rewrite_data_files, rewrite_manifests and expire_snapshots |  |

## How data flows
1. **Storage and compute.** SeaweedFS serves the S3 API; Spark 4.3 runs behind a Spark Connect server that every client, including the agent, reaches at sc://.
2. **Tables and catalog.** Unity Catalog OSS 0.7 is the Iceberg REST catalog; tables are named iceberg.<namespace>.<table>, and the agent gets its own sandbox namespace.
3. **Bronze, silver, gold.** Batch loads and a Structured Streaming job land bronze; a Spark Declarative Pipeline derives silver and gold.
4. **Schedule and maintain.** Airflow runs the pipeline with backfills and a second DAG compacts files and expires snapshots.
5. **Serve and learn.** DuckDB reads gold through the same catalog, MLflow trains on it and records the snapshot id.
6. **Hand it to an agent.** An agent on Omnigent with a local model and MCP tools writes pipelines into its sandbox; policies require a passing dry run and ask before code pulls results onto one machine.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass)

The course that builds this stack chapter by chapter, from storage to agents. You write the Compose file yourself; there is no single command.

### [open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse)

The same layers prebuilt, writing Delta Lake into Unity Catalog 0.6.0 with Spark 4.1, started with one script.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse
cd open-lakehouse

cp .env.example .env       # fill in POSTGRES_*, S3_* placeholders
./lakehouse setup          # validate env, install deps, download ~860MB of JARs
./lakehouse start all      # Spark 4.1 master + worker + Connect server + Kafka
./lakehouse start unity-catalog
./lakehouse start mlflow
./lakehouse status --json  # confirm healthy (incl. spark.connect_grpc_listening)
```

## Caveats
- There is no released Iceberg Spark runtime for Spark 4.3; chapter 5.5 builds it from apache/iceberg#18749 as a temporary step.
- Unity Catalog 0.7 or later is required for Iceberg writes through its REST catalog.
- The course recommends 16 GB of RAM; the agent's model needs about 12 GB of memory.
- Older SeaweedFS releases have an S3A _temporary rename bug; the course pins 4.51.
- In open-lakehouse, writes are Delta only: Unity Catalog 0.6.0 serves Iceberg read-only.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I run a full open source lakehouse on a laptop?

Yes. The lakehouse masterclass builds Iceberg tables in Unity Catalog OSS 0.7 on SeaweedFS with Spark 4.3, Kafka, Airflow 3.3.2, DuckDB and MLflow in Docker, and adds an AI agent on Omnigent with a local Ollama model. The open-lakehouse repository offers a prebuilt Delta variant.

### Can an AI agent work on a local lakehouse safely?

Yes. In the masterclass the agent writes only to its own sandbox namespace, uses named MCP tools instead of a shell, and policies require a passing dry run before any pipeline runs.

### How do other engines read the tables?

Through Unity Catalog's Iceberg REST endpoint. DuckDB attaches it and reads the gold tables Spark wrote, without copies.

## Sources
- [lakehouse-masterclass](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass)
- [open-lakehouse docs/compatibility.md](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse/blob/main/docs/compatibility.md)

# Policy pushdown and open lineage: Cedar policies compiled to CEL, enforced in Spark and DataFusion, with OpenLineage

> Write access rules once, enforce them inside every engine, and record where every column came from.

Policy pushdown and open lineage is a governance architecture for multi-engine lakehouses. Access rules are authored once in the Cedar policy language, compiled to portable CEL expressions, and enforced inside each query engine's plan as row filters and column masks, so no engine depends on SQL views or per-engine rewrites. Alongside, every job emits OpenLineage events, which are stored as lakehouse tables and served through a lineage API, so auditors can trace a published number back to its sources.

## When to use it
- Several engines read the same sensitive tables.
- You need row filters and column masks that cannot be bypassed by choosing a different engine.
- Regulators or auditors ask where a value came from.

## When not to
- Production lineage storage today without evaluation: headwaters describes itself as experimental and recommends Marquez for production.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | Policy authors | Write Cedar policies and tag templates |  |
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Enforcement as Catalyst rules | 4.2 plugin |
| Other engines | Apache DataFusion | Enforcement as plan rewrites | 53.1 |
| Catalog and credentials | Unity Catalog OSS | Policy decision point resolving tags | 0.4.1 in the demo |
| Open table format | Apache Iceberg | Lineage event tables, written through Lakekeeper (Delta also supported) |  |
| Object storage | RustFS | Demo object store |  |
| Access control and policy | Cedar | Policy language; deny always wins | cedar-policy 4 |
| Access control and policy | policast | Compiles Cedar to CEL and injects enforcement into the physical plan |  |
| Access control and policy | breakwater | Row filters and column masks inside the DataFusion planner |  |
| Lineage | OpenLineage | Lineage events from every job, column level from Spark |  |
| Lineage | open-lineage-connect | Ingests events and writes them to Delta and Iceberg tables |  |
| Lineage | headwaters | Lineage read API and UI |  |

## How data flows
1. **Author once.** A policy author writes Cedar policies, including tag-based templates that apply to every column tagged, for example, as PHI.
2. **Compile.** policast compiles the policies to CEL expressions that any engine can evaluate.
3. **Enforce in the plan.** Spark applies them as Catalyst rules and DataFusion as plan rewrites, so filters and masks run inside the query, not in a view.
4. **Emit lineage.** A Spark 4 plugin emits OpenLineage events with column-level lineage for each job.
5. **Store lineage as tables.** An ingest service writes the events to Delta or Iceberg tables, which a lineage API and UI read.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/policast](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/policast)

Author governance once in Cedar, compile it to portable CEL, and push enforcement into Spark and DataFusion physical plans.

```bash
cp docker/.env.example .env
docker compose up -d sidecar
docker compose --profile demo run --rm datafusion-demo

# Same policies enforced on Spark (Catalyst rules, no sidecar):
docker compose --profile spark run --rm spark-demo   # or: just spark-demo
```

### [open-lakehouse/open-lineage-connect](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lineage-connect)

OpenLineage end to end: a Go ingest service, a Rust service that writes events to Delta and Iceberg tables, and a Spark 4 plugin for column-level lineage.

```bash
make docker-compose-up        # builds both images, starts both services + MinIO
curl -sf http://localhost:8090/health
curl -sf http://localhost:8091/health
make docker-compose-down      # tears it down and removes the Delta volume
```

### [open-lakehouse/breakwater](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/breakwater)

Cedar fine-grained access control for DataFusion, with OCI-distributed policy bundles and a policy decision point service.

### [open-lakehouse/headwaters](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/headwaters)

Experimental Rust OpenLineage service with a Marquez-inspired read API and UI.

## Caveats
- In policast, deny always wins and grants never bypass column masks.
- headwaters is experimental and not a drop-in Marquez replacement.
- The policast demo pins Unity Catalog 0.4.1 as its policy decision point.

## Industry use cases
- **Banking: Regulatory reporting from one copy.** Build liquidity and capital reports from conformed silver tables with lineage an auditor can follow.
- **Healthcare providers: Patient-level access policy.** Enforce row filters and column masks on PHI the same way in every engine that reads the tables.
- **Telecommunications: Subscriber data protection.** Mask subscriber identifiers for analysts and keep lineage for regulators.
- **Cybersecurity: Least-privilege access to logs.** Restrict sensitive log fields by role in every engine.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do you enforce the same access policy in Spark and other engines?

Compile one policy source into an engine-neutral form and inject it into each engine's query plan. policast compiles Cedar policies to CEL and enforces them as Catalyst rules in Spark and as plan rewrites in DataFusion.

### What is OpenLineage?

An open standard, hosted by the LF AI & Data Foundation, for lineage events that describe jobs, runs and the datasets they read and write. Spark, Airflow, Flink and dbt have integrations.

### Can lineage be stored in the lakehouse itself?

Yes. open-lineage-connect writes OpenLineage events to Delta tables, Iceberg tables through a REST catalog, or both.

## Sources
- [policast README](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/policast#readme)
- [open-lineage-connect README](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lineage-connect#readme)
- [OpenLineage](https://openlineage.io)

# Semantic layer with Spark metric views: Metrics declared in YAML, served over Spark Connect to BI, notebooks and agents

> Define revenue once. Every dashboard, notebook and agent gets the same number.

A semantic layer is the set of governed metric and dimension definitions that sit between tables and the tools that query them. In open source Apache Spark, a metric view declares measures and dimensions in YAML over a source table; consumers query it with the MEASURE() function and Spark expands the definition at query time. Served over Spark Connect or JDBC, the same definitions answer dashboards, notebooks and AI agents, so a metric cannot drift between tools.

## When to use it
- Different teams report different numbers for the same metric.
- You want AI agents to answer questions from governed definitions instead of writing raw SQL.

## When not to
- Spark versions before metric views shipped; the reference demo is verified on Spark 4.2.0.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | Gold tables | Facts and dimensions to measure |  |
| Spark Connect sessions | Spark Connect | Remote access for clients and agents |  |
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Expands MEASURE() at query time | 4.2.0 |
| Catalog and credentials | Hive Metastore | Registers the metric view in the demo |  |
| Open table format | Delta Lake | Source tables |  |
| Semantic layer | Spark metric views | YAML measures and dimensions |  |
| Dashboards and notebooks | Apache Superset | Dashboards over the metric view |  |

## How data flows
1. **Declare metrics.** Write measures and dimensions in YAML over a source table.
2. **Register.** Create the metric view in the catalog.
3. **Query with MEASURE().** Clients select dimensions and MEASURE(metric); Spark expands the definition and aggregates at the requested grain.
4. **Serve everyone.** Dashboards connect over JDBC or Spark Connect, and agents use the same views as tools.

## Run it

### [lisancao/spark-demos](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos)

Demo 01_metrics_views: eight metric view examples, a doctor script and a grammar probe, verified on Spark 4.2.0.

## Caveats
- The reference demo is verified on Spark 4.2.0 and awaits official Spark 4.3 images for re-verification.

## Industry use cases
- **Banking: Analyst questions in plain language.** Let relationship managers ask about balances and products through governed metric definitions.
- **Manufacturing: OEE dashboards with one definition.** Define availability, performance and quality once and query them from BI and agents.
- **Retail and e-commerce: One definition of margin.** Define revenue, margin and sell-through once for BI, notebooks and agents.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does open source Spark have a semantic layer?

Yes. Spark metric views declare measures and dimensions in YAML over a table, and queries use the MEASURE() function to evaluate them.

### Why give AI agents a semantic layer?

Because an agent querying metric views uses the governed definition of each metric instead of inventing its own SQL, so its answers match the dashboards.

## Sources
- [spark-demos 01_metrics_views](https://github.com/lisancao/spark-demos/tree/main/demos/01_metrics_views)

# ML and GenAI lifecycle on the lakehouse: MLflow tracking, registry and AI Gateway over open tables

> Every model run points at the exact table version it was trained on.

The ML lifecycle on an open lakehouse ties experiments, models and GenAI traces to versioned tables. Features are built by Spark from silver and gold tables in an open format; each MLflow run records parameters, metrics, artifacts and the table snapshot or version it trained on; the MLflow model registry promotes versions; and the MLflow AI Gateway fronts model providers for GenAI applications. Because tables support time travel, any run can be reproduced against the exact data it saw.

## When to use it
- You need to reproduce a model from months ago.
- You train on lakehouse tables and want lineage from data to model.
- You run GenAI applications and want tracing and evaluation in the same place.

## When not to
- Low-latency online feature serving by itself: pair it with the real-time streaming pattern and a key-value store.

## Components

| Capability | Component | Role | Version |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source systems | Gold feature tables | Training data |  |
| ML lifecycle | MLflow | Tracking, registry, tracing, evaluation and AI Gateway | 3.14.0 in open-lakehouse; 3.1.0 in the course |
| Batch and SQL | Apache Spark | Feature engineering and batch scoring |  |
| Catalog and credentials | Unity Catalog OSS | Tables, and in the course, the catalog the run reads through |  |
| Open table format | Apache Iceberg | Snapshot ids give reproducible training sets |  |
| Orchestration | Apache Airflow | Retraining schedules |  |
| Dashboards and notebooks | Jupyter | Experiments |  |

## How data flows
1. **Build features.** Spark reads gold tables and writes a feature table.
2. **Record the data version.** The training run logs the table's snapshot id or version to MLflow alongside parameters and metrics.
3. **Register.** A good run's model is registered and promoted in the MLflow model registry.
4. **Serve and trace.** Applications call models and providers through the MLflow AI Gateway; traces land back in MLflow for evaluation.

## Run it

### [open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse)

Runs MLflow 3.14.0 tracking (:5000) and AI Gateway (:5001) next to Spark, Delta and Unity Catalog.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/open-lakehouse/open-lakehouse
cd open-lakehouse

cp .env.example .env       # fill in POSTGRES_*, S3_* placeholders
./lakehouse setup          # validate env, install deps, download ~860MB of JARs
./lakehouse start all      # Spark 4.1 master + worker + Connect server + Kafka
./lakehouse start unity-catalog
./lakehouse start mlflow
./lakehouse status --json  # confirm healthy (incl. spark.connect_grpc_listening)
```

### [open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/lakehouse-masterclass)

Chapter 12 trains a model on gold and logs the gold Iceberg snapshot id to MLflow.

## Caveats
- MLflow 3.x matches --allowed-hosts exactly; the open-lakehouse stack sets localhost:5000 explicitly.

## Industry use cases
- **Banking: Credit risk model lifecycle.** Track, register and compare probability-of-default models trained on governed features.
- **Healthcare providers: Readmission risk models.** Track experiments and promote models with a registry that records the training data version.
- **Energy and utilities: Load forecasting.** Train and track forecast models on years of interval data plus weather.
- **Retail and e-commerce: Demand forecasting.** Train store-by-SKU forecasts and track which model version produced each order.
- **Telecommunications: Churn models.** Train and track churn models on usage, care and billing features.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do I make an ML model reproducible on a lakehouse?

Log the table snapshot id (Iceberg) or version (Delta Lake) used for training to the MLflow run; time travel then lets you read exactly that data again.

### Is MLflow open source?

Yes. MLflow is Apache-2.0 licensed and hosted by the Linux Foundation.

## Sources
- [MLflow docs](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/)
